Lore-wise: great game. Interface-wise: moderately annoying. All in all, decent gameplay.
Except for occasional characters with bad voice acting, the game really makes you feel like you're in Middle-Earth, with all the place and people names mentioned, sentence structures reminiscent of Tolkien, and good character design. The graphics can, at some places, be artificial-looking; but not to the extent of significantly affecting immersion.
There are two points that I think break immersion: One is how most parts of maps cannot be interacted with (i.e. you can't enter through doors you are not meant to, can't talk to people you are not meant to). So it's more or less a linear hack and slash game with RPG elements rather than an actual RPG with great freedom of interaction. The other is the odd shiny warp spots within dungeons that act as merchants you can buy from or sell to. There is no meaningful explanation of what they are, so they just stand out like a sore thumb.
The interface leaves a lot to be desired. The single player game is meant to be played with a 3 people party where you can switch between the characters. Yet, you can only switch characters at checkpoints, or if you exit to the main menu. This is problem when you want to equip one of your members the way you want. And it's even more annoying when you use the "give" feature in the inventory to give items/equipment to one of the party members; only to find that item lost forever the next time you switch to that party member. The "give" feature DOES NOT work in a user friendly fashion -most of the time, the party members trash what you gave them unless they auto-equip it- so DON'T USE it.
Another annoying bit is the buy/sell menus. You cannot access your own inventory when buying items, so it's not possible to compare items or to see how many of a certain item (say, a potion) you have when on the buy menu. It's also odd that a game with so much loot does not grant you the option to rotate your character in the equipment menu to see what changes visually with what equipment.

To save writing and rewriting, or extending 'update reviews' for this game, let me just summarise how it goes over time:  Stainless releases a new update.  Things fall apart.  Bugs everywhere.  4-20 weeks later.  Mostly fixed.  MtG is such an amazing game, the few rare bugs left are nothing to worry about.
And what can I say about it that is stable regardless: The gameplay is fantastic and it's endlessly replayable.
MtG is easily the best TCG around.  I've played scores and scores of TCGs and regularly play 5-6 particularly good ones, but MtG is in another league entirely.  And for Duels they carefully choose cards that make for a fun experience, with a nice balance between strategic and random factors, a bit like playing limited; but also give you tonnes of options for deckbuilding.  I currently have about 25 decks and none of them feel or play the same way - and I've seen plenty more both online and in the developer designed decks for AI play.
It's challenging to unlock more cards without paying... but that actually brings with it a key part of what makes MtG what it is: because you have different cards from your friends, there's more variety and surprise when you play each other.
Summary: If an update has just been released, wait a few weeks.  Otherwise - get it get it get it!

This War of Mine is a sometimes bleak, sometimes hopeful take on the survival genre of games: survive a war, as a civilian.  The interface is dead simple and clearly designed with portability to tablets in mind, but it is largely effective.  Your band of survivors often has serious qualms with violence and thievery, and learning how to avoid stealing from other groups of survivors while also avoiding starving to death can be a bit of a handful.

The game has come a long way from its initial release, with the option to actually select your survivor group and thus the scenario you're likely to be playing through.  Different characters have different strengths and weaknesses they bring to the group, and these advantages can make a huge difference.  Playing with a weak group with few or no obvious advantages brings its own challenge.

I play in English and notice occasional quirks in the characters stories, but nothing too jarring to affect my enjoyment of the game.  This one's a winner.

Okay; so it wouldn't give me the option to recommend and not recommend the game. I wanted to do both for various reasons; so let me break it down for everyone:
I would recommend because:
-- It's a great way to learn Magic and test out new playstyles for the newer sets.
-- It has a sleek interface and smooth gameplay, interesting stories in the Story Mode, and forces you to have to think of a gameplay strategy you may not normally use to defeat your opponent.
I would NOT recommend because:
-- The game does not include the actual Origins booster set; but rather a 80% Origins 20% older card mix because the creators are so scared everyone would stop buying physical cards if they included the actual set.
-- You can only buy boosters or gold for real money in the Store; and you get no discount for bulk-buying your boosters.(Though the boosters are 'smart' and designed to only give you cards you don't have to complete your collection).
-- After you complete your first campaign (Gideon); subsequent campaigns only offer basic gold-per-level rewards; no completion of campaign rewards which makes all the hours you may spend on it kind of a wasted effort.
For these reasons; I personally would not recommend because the cons outweigh the pros in my book.

The Stanley Parable is a type of game genre that's become more popular over recent memory known as a walking simulator. As the name would suggest, all you really do is walk around in a first-person point of view while occasionally interacting with the environment, making the gameplay itself very lacking. As such, these games take a large risk since they entirely rely on the story in order to engage the player, and if they find it to be lacking...well, the game as whole will suffer.
But the Stanley Parable's story is not only exceptional, but one of the most innovative and smart narratives I've seen in gaming.
The game is told via voiceovers from The Narrator, who explains that the protagonist Stanley is a man who works in an office building, and is tasked to monitor data coming on a computer screen and press buttons appropriately without question. But suddenly, one day the screen goes blank without warning. Unsure of what to do, Stanley begins to explore the building and finds it devoid of people. What happens next is a game that flips videogames entirely on their head.
The writing is entirely self-aware and knows that it's a game. So it decides to have as much fun with itself as possible, so no matter how absurd the scenarios appear to be or how many dead ends you run into, it all connects perfectly to the engaging and fascinating meta-narrative.
The game not only constantly breaks the fourth wall, but breaks it down entirely. Which is of course guided by the Narrator, who is fully-voiced and by far the best aspect of this game.
He's just filled with so much charm and wit that despite him being against what matters in videogames the most, choice...well, it's more or less a commentary about videogames's structural tropes, poking fun at them and highlighting how little choice players truly do have a majority of the time despite having the illusion of choice.
While he may seem friendly and amiable, his patronizing tone makes you feel like a child who must follow the orders of an adult. And so naturally, you would do what children are famous for: rebel.
Doing so will cause the narrator to lose his temper and become exceptionally more rude and malicious, saying that this's his story and that you will follow it the way he's envisioned it. And since this causes him to do everything in his power to stop you, even directly controlling the game itself, he suddenly becomes an antagonist.
The first choice that you're given is between two doors: the left door, which is the one he tells you to go through, and the right door, which he doesn't tell you to go through. So will you follow the Narrator's directions, and despite not having any choice or input, have the game works in your favor? Or disobey him and try and decide your own choices, but instead have the work against you?
You can even choose to follows his orders for a while, and then suddenly decide to rebel in order to trigger entirely different endings and events, each one more unpredictable than the next. What's crazy is that this game has has a total of SEVENTEEN endings (including two joke endings), so despite it being short, it has a ridiculous amount of replay value if you're curious to see all the possible outcomes.
While I won't spoil them, my personal favorite ending is when the game referenced other PC games.
The graphics are the basic, stock-Valve graphics engine used for games such as Half-Life 2, Team Fortress 2, Left 4 Dead 2 and Garry's Mod, and that's due to this game originally being a mod of Half-Life 2. Yet it's not the graphics themselves that are interesting and impressive, but just seeing the many creative nooks and crannies that reside in the office building.
The only flaw to the game is that the loading times when starting a new game from the main menu are a bit long, which is counterproductive since you need to constantly reset the game in order to try different routes and endings. While you can do this from the pause menu, you also have the ability to make make multiple saves, and the only way to load them is from the main menu.
Despite simplistic gameplay and graphics, and long loading times when starting up the game, The Stanley Parable is a game with an engaging story that explores how many videogame stories confine the player to its rules by having someone that does exactly that, has many different routes and endings depending on the player's actions, well-written dialogue that constantly breaks the fourth wall, and a charming and memorable narrator who is voiced exceptionally well.
While it may look simple on the surface, I recommend it to anyone, even those that dislike walking simulators, since I'd say that the narrative more than makes up for the lack of gameplay.
What's even more interesting is that before the term walking simulator was coined, this time of game genre was called 'interactive fiction.' Walking simulator definitely sounds a lot better.

Thought I'd leave a review for this game, but mainly to tell you guys how solid the PC Version is. I went from a 1080p/60hz monitor to a 1440p/144hz/G-Sync monitor, and the difference is huge. With that said, a lot of these Japanese games have notoriously been ported pretty lazily to the PC, with games like Tales of Zestiria being capped at 30fps, which is borderline unnacceptable, The Dynasty Warriors series is capped at 1080p/60fps, or Final Fantasy XIII and its performance issues even on higher end machines. Surprisingly enough, The Last Remnant blows pretty much every single JRPG that's been ported over to the PC out the water and here's why:
- The framerate is uncapped and not tied to the game's speed, so it's a brilliant game to try out on your high refresh rate monitor.
- It runs amazingly well, even though the cutscenes are compressed to♥♥♥♥♥♥and locked at 30fps (kind of a bummer, but not at all surprising).
- Native 1440p and 4K support, which is a must in my opinion, and I legit don't get why certain games can't go above 1080p, so that's a big plus.
- Tons of options, so even if you're playing at 720p/30fps the game is certain to look way better than the console versions.
- There's 5.1 and 7.1 Surround Sound support, and it controls "ok" on a mouse and keyboard, so you don't necessarily need a 360 pad to get the most out of this game, unlike a lot of JRPGs on Steam.
- There's no FOV Slider, and no AA options in-game, but both of these things can be tweaked in the config files and through your GPU's driver so that's not TOO terrible imo.
The game itself is pretty decent, but this "review" is just to show you guys how underrated its PC Version is. Definitely recommend it if you're into stuff like FF and the Tales series, but care more than your average Joe about PC centric features, like myself. Cheers.

Just to get it out of the way: XIII has beautiful graphics. The environment, cutscenes, character portraits etc. are mindblowingly gorgeous. If you end up playing XIII-2 and LR, the graphics are not nearly as great, but I'd return to XIII's Nautilus and Lake Bresha any day.
The music: good, but not spectacular (that I'd give to something like Bastion). I love Saber's Edge, Blinded by Light, and the arrangements of Hope's theme, but those are the only ones that I remember off the top of my head.
The battle system: takes quite a while to learn and master, especially if you're not a confident gamer, but very rewarding and fun once you get it right. Yeah I had a few cases of trying to get past a boss for like an hour. Yeah it was frustrating. But I think in the end I enjoyed it more than the systems of, say, VII where I just power grinded a bit and was able to breeze through the rest of the game without worrying about ever losing.
Misc: The pacing can use some help. I found all the open world sidequests and grinding on Pulse to be an enormous chore but a lot of people love those and claim that they're the only good things about the game so *shrug*. I disliked the two chapters on the Palamecia and the Fifteenth Ark but I guess you do get awarded with plot revelations at the ends of both? Oh, and they probably could have made the ending a bit easier to understand. With all that said though...
I won't comment much about the linearity because I think that's a case of you either like it or you don't, but as for the characters... well, okay, one can make the argument that XIII is "different" from the other FFs. That it doesn't have a clear antagonist and that the characters are not overtly inspiring. But that does not make it an objectively worse game. It makes it a more realist (genre) and human fantasy. The issues the cast faces in XIII are more existentially complex and difficult than those faced by say the casts of VII and X, and because of that they make less straight-up noble and/or badass choices, but I really appreciate seeing that in a beautifully rendered and carefully constructed game because that's... closer to real life. I appreciate the XIII cast a lot and they're my favorite cast by a mile by virtue of how much they managed to do and love despite everything that had happened to them. I'd argue, really, that I enjoyed XIII similarly to how I enjoyed The Last of Us or Nier Automata - it's a game that ultimately ponders on the human condition.

This game is an
blast ;) I've not really played the older Hitman games, but I felt home going into this epic game. For those unfamiliar with the gameplay, it's third-person stealth shooter with cover systems, disguises to fool your enemies, and silenced weapons to help you become a deadly assassin. It looks great, it plays great, and overall it's just a really awesome game that I would recommend to most people.
The story is really captivating and takes you on a journey through various locations whereby you have to find information on your targets in order to hunt them down and kill them. In most levels there are a variety of ways in which you can fulfill your contract. You can take a head-on approach, guns blazing, lead flying everywhere, OR, you can take the more appropriate approach and be a true assassin, hiding in the shadows, only killing necessary targets, and walking straight by unsuspecting enemies dressed in their uniform.
There's "point shooting" which acts as a slow-motion targeting system to take down multiple enemies with speed and silence, there's "instinct" which allows you to see where enemies and items of interest are in your close proximity, and of course there are your Silver Ballers. As you can probably tell, there is a lot of content within this game and a large host of options of which you can take to tackle your current objective. On top of this there are challenges within each level, such as only using your suit and no disguises, killing someone with explosives, or crushing them with a chandelier.
The visuals and sound are also superb, and so there's really nothing to complain about when it comes to Hitman: Absolution. Performance is great too as far as I could tell. Just get this game!
Enjoy! :)

EDIT: Added spoiler tags to the loose description of the bosses.
I'll try and keep it short and to the point. This is an excellent game. It's essential. It's fun. It's addictive and rewarding.
You have classes with genuine differences. All are fun. The weapons and violence are exceptional. Heads come off, chunks fly. Bullets whizz and lasers feel hot and clinical. It has recoil mechanics and stealth, alert and line of sight mechanics and varying levels of weapon penetration.
Destructible environment. If you see a heavy guard with a riot shield in the next room, they are invulnerable to regular weapon-fire from the front, you blow a hole in the wall behind him and blast him to chunks from the back with a critical sneak attack. You can melee. You can upgrade the melee skill, you can smash through walls like robocop and unleash hell.
There are excellent bosses with phases. I've put in 22 hours and I have seen 3 of the total 6(?).
It's procedural and has permadeath. You loot cash and energy from your foes. When you die you are disconnected from your puppet of flesh. You get out of the immersion chair and spend the cash on skills and weapons. When you are ready to go again, you go back to the chair, and awake another "body" from the rows and rows of stasis pods. So there is a lovely and macabre sense of cost, drive and a seemingly morally ambiguous protagonist. I'm responsible for about 79 now empty pods. I keep throwing bodies at The Overseer of the Neon Chrome building and it's security which he controls. Learning the really solid gameplay mechanics and getting stronger though the incremental upgrades in Damage, Health, Energy, Luck, Augment Slots etc etc.
I could talk all day just about the gameplay mechanics and how fun and gripping it is, but it looks great, has brilliant sound design and good music as well. A very polished and well tuned action rogueLITE that rewards skill and thought while staying absolutely action packed and fluid. There's no fat on this game. You start it, you get in the chair, you start with the death-dealing. There's no painful intro/splash screens, no long periods of downtime between deaths.
I love this game. If I had more than two thumbs to give it, I would. I would raise thumbs till none were left.

a person?" so it loses points for that as well. building an empire takes a lot of time, so its not for casual players. this is the kind of game that you need to get in to, and really it doesnt have much of a problem achieving that sort of immersion if you are playing the story (even if you arent familiar with the previous titles in the series, you can be drawn into the high stakes world of multi galaxy war easily). its easy for me to care what races win the war, and what races are exterminated in the process. but the fact remains that if you intend to play this game and enjoy it, you must also intend to spend 20-40 hours learning the game systems as well. for a lot of people, this will drop the score. for me, this increases it. the more complex the systems are, the more freedom we are generally given to play our way. and in this series, and this game in particular, playing our way is the key. the music seems deliberately strange (it always has in x games though). traveling around in space is also quite boring at times. if you want to know why, read the hitchhikers guide to the galaxy's entry on the size of space to understand why. the number of mods available on the workshop to enhance the game is gaining momentum as new fans are brought in to the series by this title, and often egosoft turns to the modding community when deciding what dlc or patches should be applied to their product so they not only listen to community input, occasionally they use it directly. but new players to the series need to remember one thing- you are playing a sim of sorts. this is not intended to be all action all the time. there are lags of hours and hours spend making the credits you need to continue, and it can be a little tedious. and frustrating when that ship you just spent the day making money to buy gets destroyed cause it had no excorts protecting it. but, this game is also easy as pie to cheat at so... taken out of its own context, i would rate it 6/10.

Neon Chrome is a cyberpunk, top-down shooter from the developer of Crimsonland, 10tons. In Neon Chrome you play as assets, used by a strange character (who you also play as, sort of) in order to try and take down the mysterious Overseer. The Overseer has full control over Neon Chrome’s human and robotic guards and he’s more than happy to use brutal force to stop anyone in his way. That includes you by the way. As you battle through thirty-one levels, taking place over six levels of the building, you’ll face increasingly difficult enemies and even a few mini-bosses and bosses. It won’t be easy but you’re not exactly in short supply of assets, you’ll get there eventually.
Full Disclosure: A review copy was provided by the developer.
Before every run you can move around a level of Neon Chrome which is halfway between an apartment and a human storage complex. I’m not sure how to label the character but they have a strange chair/headset device that they use to control the assets, the assets are who you mainly play as. In this stage of the game you can also buy upgrades (such as improved health or damage) as well as purchase weapons, abilities and cybernetic enhancements that your next asset will use when you use them. In this area you can also track your stats, such as how many assets you’ve used, as well as see what achievements you’ve unlocked and what rewards they have earned you.
The assets themselves vary a fair bit, the main variation coming from what class they are. There are a few different classes in the game, ranging from Assassin (my personal favourite) to Cyber Psycho, each with their own class-specific ability. The Assassin’s ability, for example, is that they become completely invisible when they are standing or moving around in shadows while the Cyber Psycho has +20% Hit Points and +2 Enhancement slots. Each class also has its own stats, i.e. health, energy (used for the asset’s other ability), speed, damage and critical hit chance. The classes are very different to each other and require slightly to drastically different strategies to be successful with them, adding a nice level of depth to the game.
The assets also have a weapon, a non-class-specific ability and a name (well duh). The weapon can be any of the weapons you have unlocked (more can be unlocked by finding special box-type things in the levels, which also applies to enhancements and the second kind of abilities.) You can also unlock the same weapon but with a different projectile, for example you can have a regular shotgun as well as an Ion Shotgun or a Plasma Shotgun. The second type of ability is effectively a secondary attack, this could be lock-on missiles or blast grenades, there are quite a few to unlock. These abilities require energy which is collected from loot boxes. Each ability can be used a certain number of times before you run out and need more energy, for example you can use your grenades three times. Enhancements can be equipped from a CyberHance Express station (found on most levels). You have a certain amount of slots for these enhancements (upgradeable) so if you run out of slots you’ll have to choose one to replace with the new enhancement. There’s a wide variety of enhancements available from the basic stuff that increases health or speed to enhancements that cause your bullets to split and cause 30% more damage.
As I said earlier, Neon Chrome consists of thirty-one levels across six floors. When you reach a new floor (the level after a boss fight) you can then start from that new floor and skip the levels leading up to that. It’s a great way to help you progress through the game though it does mean you miss out on all the loot from the previous floors when starting from that floor which is a problem seeing as there’s a spike in difficulty from one floor to the next. There is of course a difference in difficulty between the levels too but it’s more noticeable when you reach a new floor. For the most part, you just have to reach the green (or purple for a special level) elevator at the end of the level to go to the next one but some levels will have objectives for you to complete first, e.g. destroy five specific targets. The levels are also randomly generated (apart from the boss fight levels) so you’ll never see the same run twice.
An increase in difficulty doesn’t just mean more enemies though, it means harder enemies and new kinds of enemies. From what I’ve played, enemies don’t get phased out, they just get phased in meaning you’ll be introduced to new enemy types every few levels. You’ll also face off against ‘special’ enemies. These consist of normal enemies with some kind of buff/special ability, for example an enemy marked as SWIFT as a much higher movement speed than a regular enemy. Some levels have a mini-boss, again this is a variation of a regular enemy with a special ability and in this case better stats too and at the end of every floor you come across a full boss. The boss fights are incredibly challenging, it took me several attempts to get through the first one for example. Thankfully (if you’ve collected a lot of loot) you’ll be able to buy new upgrades which will help you next time you take on the boss. Furthermore, once you beat the Overseer you reach a new OS level which significantly increases the difficulty across all levels. As far as I’m aware there’s no limit on OS levels but it does take a lot longer to get through them anyway.
So, let’s talk about loot. There’s quite a lot of it. Most of what you’ll find are small boxes which, when opened, will net you a couple of hundred bucks and a little bit of energy, you generally find one or two in each room when playing. Then you’ve got slightly bigger boxes in which you’ll find more money and energy as well as (sometimes) health kits and even weapons. Then you’ve got healing stations, unlock boxes (the things I mentioned earlier which contain new abilities, weapons or enhancements), weapon crates and weapon upgrade machines (levels up your gun which improves its stats). Also, enemies drop loot in the form of money and energy, they drop about the same as a small box but special enemies drop more. While energy, weapons etc. only matter for the asset you collect them with, your money and unlocks are persistent.
Just a couple more things to mention. The sound track is absolutely fantastic, it really fits the game well but there didn’t seem to be many tracks so it would’ve been nice to see a few more. The controls are also really good, they felt very responsive and the default configuration works well (though it can be changed). While I’m talking about controls, it’s worth knowing that your asset’s speed has an impact on how quickly they turn, it’s not a case of the controls being unresponsive, this also applies to enemies which can be used to your advantage.
Neon Chrome is a thoroughly enjoyable top-down shooter with a lot of gameplay variation, unlockables and quite a bit of replay value. All of this wrapped up in an awesome cyberpunk setting. If you’re a fan of top-down shooters, I’d definitely recommend checking this one out.

If you're looking for gameplay to factor into your purchasing decision:
I've logged over 22 hours in the game (and finished it once). I get a lot of game keys from developers each week and usually never play any game this much, so do me a solid favor and buy the game, so we can all get an expansion or sequel ASAP ;)
What you get:
PROS:
- An extremely polished gameplay experience with neon 80ies like graphics set in a cyberpunk world and a fully voiced Overseer
- Gameplay that can easily hold its own with other titles in the top-down shooter genre
- Lots of customization options and weapons for your characters that keeps things fresh
- That "Just one more run" feeling. And also your run never feels wasted as you can always put credits into permanent atrribute upgrages.
- Firing the guns feels and sounds impactful so does all of the destruction in the environment.
- A lot of interesting level design in the purple elevators (bonus levels)
- You can play Co-op with friends
CONS:
- There might have been more diversity in the bosses, the spider is reused a few times with a different loadout.
- Many of the standard floors have the same objective - take out X number of targets to open the elevator.
- Having some kind of dodge or increased option for flexible movement in a character might feel more dynamic (just an idea)
- I felt like I needed a bit more story after sitting in the Overseer chair (but again, just personal preference).
All in all an awesome game & keep up the good work!

Lord of the Rings: War in the North is a fairly fun action RPG that is vaguely reminiscent of the fantasy classic coming-of-age novel "Wizard of the Winds," by Allan Cole. Also, of course, it's much like the classic Game of Thrones series of books which were written by George R.R. Martin. There is fairly well-done combat and a storyline that isn't too heavily visceral but also isn't too lightweight either. You play a member of a small group of older heroes, guys AND girls, who kill the marauding smaller & younger orc enemies by the dozens in your quest to defeat Agaundar. He is a minor lieutenant of the "devil" figure of the Lord of the Rings universe, Sauron. In a pivotal scene early on in the quest, you free a massive EAGLE who you & your team help to defeat the enemy army that is in control of a castle & kill the losers.
In any case, the game is good clean fun & there is no clear push for a hard "Rated M for Mature" ESRB rating here. It's basically an Elfquest graphic novel in video game form, so it is definitely playing in the "Rated T for Teen" sandbox, so to speak. In the late 90's there was a game called Everquest that was out that is essentially this game but with not as good graphics. Graphics-wise it does the job but would not be considered "beautiful" by 2016 standards. For nostalgia purposes, impressive graphics are not required so by that metric it passes & is sort of a fun "time-capsule" of that period of time in video game form.
I can personally attest to this game being fun to play with the help of some Leann Chin takeout Chinese dinner & a NOS energy drink, & it relieves the boredom of a Saturday with not too much going on that is scheduled ahead of time. Similarly to Diablo2&3, the clothing, or I guess i should say, the EQUIPMENT (since you are a sword-wielding adventurer, NOT an unemployed student living off student loans) is a big deal. You make changes to your stuff over a long period of time & get the better stuff along the way. The game, which was published in 2011, is similar to the 2017 game Vikings: Wolves of Midgard, but with orc enemies instead of trolls.
There is something new you can do in this game - choose to be FEMALE! In the character selection screen you can pick a female elf character & as you are running around middle-earth killing bad guys & hitting orcs with arrows, as you do in any fantasy adventure game, but as a girl. Definitely there is something special about going through various life scenarios but as a WOMAN instead of as a MAN

In this highly immersive game you not only test the limitations of what desperate civilians can do, but also test the morality of your own conscious.  Stranded on the battlefield and deserted by the very soldiers that your country had sworn to protect various scavengers come together to fight against rising raids and thugs that have taken over the city when nightfall comes.  Resources are scarce, happiness dwindling, there are no moral decisions on the battlefield, only survival.  The scavengers all have various skills, some are faster than others, some stronger, and others still are good at boosting the happiness of those around them even when blood is staining their hands.
The first game that has ever truthfully brought me to tears, I spent the first part of the game shifting through abandoned houses, taking what little I could find in hopes of just feeding the two friends I had left at the house to guard the small amount we could call our own.  Even from the beginning Pavle became my savior, his speed and his ability to talk others out of depression was what made him my most-played character, where he would sleep and talk to others during the day, and at night he was my main scavenger in hopes of quickly gathering what we needed without drawing any attention.  But once the majority was taken from abandoned houses that were quickly sapped dry of their resources, morality became nothing more than an afterthought.
Pavle had to start making impossible decisions to obtain food, where first he went into armed buildings and got what little he could without engaging others, but once food hadn't come back night after night and Bruno's wounds were only getting more severe from constant raids, Boris began to take the reign.  His strength was my ally, and our first kill was made against an armed man, and where I expected more to follow I was horrified by not armed guards coming to mow Boris down, but rather the dead man's friends, disregarding me as they ran past and wept at the sight of their dead friend (I get chills even as I imagine those horror-stricken voices), however Boris had already fled with the man's gun and other belongings.  So broken upon returning Pavle did what little he could to console the tough man, but it was futile, and Pavle was forced to take the lead once more to find bandages for Bruno's increasing wounds.
It took some adjusting, but gradually I was able to take Pavle into more armed places, having to do nothing more than flash his knife to scare away those that would of otherwise harmed him, and although his own depression quickly set in Pavle charged through it all, sifting through inhabited houses and leaving small amounts of food and a knife for those that remained in hopes of them finding some hope as well.  But soon raids began, and with Bruno incapacitated Boris guarded the shelter at night, armed with a shotgun and enough bullets to fell a few thugs.  But devastation struck when Pavle killed a young man who had shot him, my own desperation for all three to survive kicking in when I had seen the young man with a gun, and knew how useful it could be against stronger raids.  But then the young man's parents came down, tears streaming down their cheeks and their voices filled with horror as the old couple grappled uselessly to their son, as if they thought he would just get up and hug them.
That was what did it, Pavle was broken.  My main scavenger incapacitated by his own mind, where only Boris could console him, but once Boris became my main scavenger due to his strength and his depression seldom ever became broken, I left Pavle to the dangerous task of guarding the shelter, tending to Bruno's severe wounds.  Things only got worse, after things seemed to be getting better, Boris had brought guns, food, bandages and medicine, Pavle was still depressed however no longer broken, Bruno took it all.  He didn't make it far, in the end I know that now, but he took everything, food, shotguns, bandages, medicine, we were left where we were to begin with.  Boris was the second to leave, wounded and hungry I like to think he simply didn't want to have Pavle see another good man die, so he left the young man alone, and what became of depression quickly turned into a mind broken.  I survived with Pavle alone for a good 10 days, taking important things with me so that when the inevitable raid did come, they didn't get much, however I only brought back small things from his scavenging that was becoming more gruesome by the night.  He was broken, I wanted him to sleep it off after getting large amounts of food that could keep him to guard for a few more days at the least, but what it showed on the screen brought me to tears, after hours of making sure Pavle survived, that he helped some people just to take something off of his mind.
Day 27: Pavle hung himself.
What will you do, allow those around you to gradually crumble into their own minds and hands, or throw caution to the wind and fight against everything you have ever been taught about right and wrong?
TLDR;  I cannot recommend this game enough, I am usually very picky (unfortunately) when it comes to games, however I have always been able to appreciate hard work and great graphics or story line, but usually never enough to buy it.  This game just intrigued me to no end, and after playing it for my first time (and certainly not my last) I can truthfully say it is one of the best games I've ever played.  Mechanics is great, character design near flawless, it's a little difficult to begin with to figure out some of the controls and what everything does, but you learn quickly, you have to in order to survive.  It's not tedious, it's enthralling all the way through, not your usual hunt-and-gather mechanics but taken to the next level as something too real to not be labeled as horrifying.  Play at the risk of your own view of the world.

I've never been much of a fan of Final Fantasy games, but this entry has changed my mind - even if I'm quite a few years behind in having picked this up.
Many people complain of linearity in the game, and they'd certainly be right in saying that - the game's one long corridor with a large blob at a relatively late stage. However, unlike many others, I consider this linearity to be a stength. The linearity allowed the narritive to advance at a comfortable pace that maintained momentum. Sure, the game opens up for a while later on, but the lack of narrative advancement durig this period just made the game utterly drag - largely because the pacing had become just so familiar. Yeah, you're given cutscenes but the characters have fully developed by this point - they contribute very little to any facet of the story.
The story of Final Fantasy XIII does not draw its sterength from its narrative, but rather from its character development and interactions. Despite any marketing, Lightning is not the centre of this world - and I may even argue that she is perhaps the individual of least significance, being regularly overshadowed by playable and non-playable characters alike. She also remains consistently unlikable throughout, jumping back and forth in terms of development and going from being antagonistic, and sometimes just outright cruel, to suddenly becoming unbearably optimistic.
However, for all Lightning's faults everyone else makes up for it, with some going from being completely unbearable (looking at you, Hope) to decently tolerable, some balancing out much more as they warm to the others they're with, and Sazh just being and outright fantastically drawn-up character - being incredibly likable whilst sacrificing nothing in depth and obvious struggles.
Of course, all this talk of characters isn't to say that the rest of the story doesn't have any merits; there's a lot of depth and intrigue to be found in the narrative. I see a lot of complaints of confusion regarding the narrative although, personally, I feel that's exactly the point - the motives and relationships of the fal'Cie, Pulse and the Sanctum are not well understood by the populace of cocoon, and neither are they to the protagonists. You're supposed to feel lost and conflicted with them, and I think the writers have done a fantastic job of ensuring that you can only ever be sure of the motives of those close to you.
There is a massive glaring issue with this confusion, though - concepts are not introduce in any clear or organic way: if you don't read the datalogs the first few chapters, and possibly even beyond, will not make any sense whatsoever - and that goes well beyond the scope of mystery set out.
Speaking of narrative issues: the ending is absolutely atrocious. Whilst motives of the protagonists remain clear throughout the story, the last 15-30 minutes of the game just make an utter mess of this. Your suddenly doing things that you agreed not to for no clearly stated reason before an embarassing♥♥♥♥♥♥pull is made to tie the game up. It was an unfortunate end to something that was otherwise beautifull crafted.
And what of gameplay? Put it this way: if you pick up this game you're definitely picking it up for the story. The battle system is quite nice, conceptually, but seems to have been implemented in the most frustrating way - giving you the absolute minimum level of control.
For those of you, like myself, who had not yet had the pleasure of engaging with an ATB system I'll sum it up briefly:
Rather than the traditional system of limiting actions by a finite resource pool, actions are instead based upon the time taken to charge them. A bar, divided into a variable number of segments, will fill throughout all idle time in a battle (and sometimes during actions, depending on equipment). Actions may be set in advance and will be executed all at once when enough segments have been filled to carry out those actions (some of which may require the maximum number of segments filled). This leaves the battles being rather desynchronised, which really adds a level of dynamicism to fight. Or rather, it would if they didn't have such clear-cut best strategies. Unfortunately enemies tend to be quite predictable, and so particular teams tend to be very stand-out due to the paradigm deck system which limits your tactically possibilities quite severely. For example the majority of the (free team choice) game I was ble to retain Lightning, Sazh and Vanille since the sentinel class had fairly limited applications - especially with ratings being based on the speed of battle clearance - and Hope being far too squishy for the extra healing power to pay off. I could definitely feel the potential, but it just feels like it missed the mark. Still, the flashiness at least gives you something to look at. Shame that you ave no control over positioning in a system where positioning can be potentially important at times.
Earlier I mentioned equipment, and this is easily the most frustrating thing about this game. You're introduced to item levelling early on but given almost no detail on the process. Pumping all these items into your equipment feels useless, so after a while you wouldn't be amiss to just give up. In fact, I'd say with a little grinding it's perfectly feasible to finish the game without ever really touching the upgraes system. That's a problem - because the upgrades become seriously worthwhile. There's never any indicator as to what you gain from an upgrade, or how best or upgrade, or what you lose from it, or how the dismantling system works. Unless you're willing to look to the internet you're simply left with a giant, confusing mess that might pay off if you can actually bring yourself to stick with it. Sprint Shoes, the Enkindler,  Aurora Scarf, Energy Sash, Malboro Wand, Procyons - all incredibly useful items that can be a complete pain to come by if you're dead-set on playing the game the way it was intended. The equpment systems just reek of poorly-designed afterthoughts that could have added some much-needed depth.
Graphically, the game is really something nice to look at, even if it's showing its age quite a bit with some muddy textures, clumpy hair and predictable garments. It's saved by some simply gorgeous designs, both of the environments nad the entities within them. Sure, some of it's a bit over-the-top but there's a something strangely compelling about all those mad protrusions and blade-like wings.
It's also well worth mentioning that the soundtract is downright gorgeous - I could happily leave the title screen running for hours just for the sake of that theme. It's really quite something.
Overall, I can certainly say I love the game - and my opinon of the franchise has been turned completely on its head. It's such a shame, then, that the port quality should upset the experience so much. Framerates were all over the place - from 60 to 30 to 15 to 60 again. The options were incredibly limited - with your choices existing only in resolution and shadow maps - not particularly desirable when you can't guarantee any stability.
Another maor issue I had was the lack of any sound setting. There were none at all. I can only be thankful that my output device is variable, because the system volume wasn't going to cut it with how ridiculously quiet this could be at times.
Most of the time sound balancing wasn't much of an issue, since the developers did a good job there, at least, but I'm certainly glad I have a habit of playing with subtitles for those times that things just didn't quite match up.
Do I reccomend this game? Definitely.
Do I reccomend it to everybody ever? Not a chance.
Do I reccomend it on this platform? Certainly not if you can help it.

War in the North is an RPG based in the lord of the rings universe. It takes part during the events of the movies and tells the story of the battle for control and word of Sauron in the north.
The games campaign is singleplayer, co-op or up to 3 players and personally I enjoyed playing with one other. The campaign is closely connected to the movies and there are hints to the movie as well as the events of the hobbit and history of middle earth that you can find out by speaking with people.
The gameplay itself plays like a hack and slash RPG with an emphasis on combos. There are 3 different classes, Mage, Ranged Archer and Melee Tank so there’s a play style for everyone. The looting system is really enjoyable when you get new pieces of gear from enemy drops and chests, there are abilities and passives you unlock and upgrade when you level up. You also get stat increases that you can put into what you like (mana, health, strength & dexterity)
Graphics are pretty outdated at this point but it did release 6 years ago so it’s fine and passable to not notice anything bad.
There are a few bugs and missing features you should know about before playing however. The game uses open mic which you cannot switch off through the game, I had to look up how to do some kind of audio change through windows and my voice chat program to play with a friend and not get double audio...
The game was crashing for me on Windows 10 which I also managed to fix after a quick google search.
There are some basic RPG features that are just...missing as well. There’s no repair all gear/ equip gear button so you have to manually go through each one to fix.
There’s no loot all shortcut key when you loot a chest, you have to click in the button left each time to take all.
You can't compare stat differences between gear which is the biggest one for me. You can see if the gear will increase/ decrease stats but its shows no values nor takes into account set bonus.
You cannot bind any potions beyond health and mana (power) which means you have to access your inventory and right click use any other potions during battle. As a result I ended up not using crafted potions at all.
Putting aside the minor issues and missing features the game is a really fun RPG with a good story that you can play with others.

Although it could never have lived up to its predecessor, BS2 was still a high quality entry into the FPS/RPG-lite subgenre and another well thought-out adventure into Rapture.  The sequel provides welcome insights into the Big Daddies and other aspects of the underwater dystopia that were not fully addressed in the original, in addition to building on the story some years after the events of BS1.  Not unlike the original, I think that FPS's that are this deep and story-driven have a difficult time ending, since they do not necessarily need the Big Baddie-style end game confrontation, but the expectations of the genre nonetheless require it.  With that in mind, I felt that BS2 did a good job of setting the stage for the final confrontation and then closing things off at the end in a satisfying and emotionally gratifying fashion.

I just finished my first Final Fantasy game!
Just to get my biggest complaint out of the way: The real game(play) doesn't really start until chapter 11, which is more than 20 hours into the game. Up until that point the game is pretty linear and you can not rearrange your team freely. However, if you manage to get past the first 20 hours or so the game becomes much more interesting, and you actually have to consider what characters, paradigms (formations) and equipment to use for each fight. Some enemies will completely crush you if you do not come well prepared.
My only other complaint is that when playing with Japanese audio and English subtitles the subtitles are often completely off. My guess is that the English subtitles is just a transcript of the English audio, and not really a translation, which can get a bit annoying when the meanings are way too different.
Other than that, I have mostly positive things to say about the game.
The story is very confusing - but in a good way (once you get into it):
There are two worlds, Cocoon and Gran Pulse, both inhabited by godlike creatures called Fal'Cie as well as humans. Fal'Cie can grant humans special powers, turning them into L'Cie. L'Cie have to complete their mission ("Focus"). L'Cie are not told what their Focus is (...), however if they fail to complete it they are turned into a Cie'th (monster). L'Cie who complete their focus are only turned into a crystal ("yay"). Lightning and the rest of the main characters are all turned into L'Cie by the Pulse Fal'Cie, meaning that they are hunted by the Fal'Cie of their homeworld, Cocoon. Many other things happen, but in the end you have to defeat the bad Fal'Cies, complete your Focus, and save the world. Simple.
The battle system, as mentioned above, opens up when you reach chapter 11. Each character can be assigned any one of six different roles which can be used to form various paradigms, and you can freely jump from one paradigm to another as many times as you like during a fight. There are tons of weapons and accessories which come with buffs, resistances or other beneficial effects, which is of great importance when fighting tougher enemies. Then you have summons, which (with one exception)... felt pretty useless.
The game also looks
. The game is currently 8 years old, but it still looks amazing. Part of the reason why I chose Final Fantasy as my first Final Fantasy game was because I wanted a game that looks great even today, and not only do the cut-scenes look stunning, the fights were amazing as well, and the music sounded just as good as the rest of the game looked. I had heard that Final Fantasy games both look and sound great - and I was not disappointed.
I guess a third, and minor, complaint would be that some (most?) of the characters were pretty annoying. You will probably be able to tell right away who the most annoying characters are, however this didn't really bother me that much, and I still ended up enjoying the game.
All in all I'm happy that this was my first Final Fantasy game, and I will almost certainly try out the sequels (Final Fantasy 13-2 and Lightning Returns), as well as other games in the series.
Recommended!

I am writing this under the assumption you have played the original Bioshock... Also this is my opinion, and your own experiences maybe different from my own...
I feel Bioshock 2 is more of an expansion than a true sequel to the original game. However saying that, isn't necessarily a bad thing, as Bioshock 2 is a lot of fun and I would argue is more fun compared to the original.
However Bioshock 2's weapons are a bit of a let down. I much preferred the weapons from the orignal Bioshock comparred to number 2, with an exception. Namely I loved the spear gun, where I could pincer splicers heads to walls.
Story wise, I found that it wasn't as good as the first (maybe because it's more of the same), however I did feel it was better paced and the areas you went to, were just a lot more interesting.
There's also another nice twist to the game, that changes up the gameplay a bit, which can be found right near the end of this sequal (expansion), which I appreciated a lot.
I also wanted to give a compliement to the DLC Minerva's Den, which in a single player campaign with roughly 4+ hrs of gameplay.
Nowadays you see a lot of games advertising that they have an extra hour of exclusive content but when played, it turns out to be a rushed bit of content which doesn't really add anything to your experience.
Well I definately found that Minerva's Den did add a bunch of new and intriguing backstory to another part of rapture and I myself played a good 8 - 12 hours on it. I would also highly recommend playing it, if you finish the second game and didn't want to finish playing yet.
Also Minerva's Den, brings with it, a new plasmid, weapon, ammo types and playable character. (You don't play as the Big Daddy from 2, but another Alpha series).
Something I wanted to point out about the Steam version of this game and it's DLC which obviously runs through it, is that it frequently corrupted my save files, resulting in having to exit the game completely and delete the affected files from the Bioshock 2 save game folder, before I could continue. (The only way to reduce this problem, was to save frequently and create multiple save files).
Overall the second game is a must play for fans of the series and I would rate this....

First Review of 3.0 and DLC
3.0 and DLC are well done. These changes and improvements are EXACTLY the thing, Rebirth needed. Features like crafting, lockboxes, secret collections etc. made the THINK part complete for the first time- now, collecting items and exploring the inner part of a station makes much more sense- it's not longer unuseful and boring after a short time. Secret boxes you can find in the universe improved the long time playing- it is really hard to find everything for every collection, and made exploring the universe much more exiting.
I'm also exited about the little things you did to make the life of gamers easier- features like running and the clickable map where overdue. Rebirth becomes more and more the game we expected once.
The DLC shows, that Rebirth can also deal with missing local highways. Interesting fact is the pathfinding with navi-barks- an alternate way of pathfinding to give the player the opportunity to get safe through dangerous regions. Ah, of course, these dangerous nebulae- so, finally, genius ideas from 'X2-the threat' get their comeback...
The Teladi stations have their unique teladian design- even the 'teladian green' from Helge T. Kauz' novels. Nice little thing is the form of the new Teladi ships- it's like the top of an egg and reminds me of Nopileos beloved ship known from the novel Nopileos''- a 'eggy' design bound deep in teladi background story from Helges books. Great! And of course, it's also nostalgic (in a good way) to see known shipnames from the X game history coming back- like phoenix and falcon.
But of course, there are still hair-raising problems, especially in ship moving. for example the thing with local highways and bigger ships. Every time, you attack a capital, it tries to fly into a highway- ok, good way to prevent small ships from hiding in nishes, but also a big problem for attacking/boarding them (highway tube protects the ship)! It also happens often that such large ships just fly through highway streams following their path, because in normal flight, they ignore them! NPC Ships just fly through the intruder, but the playership hits it and pops out of the highway. It would make more sense, when larger ships avoid local highways and probably bounce back when they hit them (without getting damage).
The new boarding concept is ok- but it is not well balanced. I had to destroy nearly EVERY drone and surface element on a Titurel to succeed- so It takes hours for the ship to get the engines repaired and fly to a shipyard to get repaired or sold. Train the marines is a nice way because it's realistic and not as expensive as to buy them- but I think buying Elites and Veterans is still ok, the price is high enough to make training still a sinful option- and the need boarding smaller ships first can be a problem for someone who wants to board only criminal elements like reivers (not much size m and l ships there).
Balancing in general is still a huge problem. And it gets worser and worser. With all criminal factions using larger ships like Titurels (an XL, well armed, Freighter), there are too few protecting units left, even in Omicron Lyrae, intended as the safest of the Systems. After playing a while, many stations have already broken parts because large ships destroyed them without being stopped by any allied XL ship. No save areas left, even in OL. It should be possible to restrict them to only border or less save sectors to get regions, safer than others. In DeVries nearly every landing platform outside of 'glaring truth' is destroyed- I know, it's planned as dangerous place, and you wanted more action, but this destroys every NPC trade left in DV! An option would be that reivers just attack ships and not stations- or only larger Titurels attack stations. Or let more of the faction ships protect their property. But something must be done.
Exept for these Problems still remaining, 3.0 and DLC are big steps in the right direction. After all, Rebirth turns to everything we dream for- thank you for that!

If you're looking for elitist  3D space combat with twitchy impossible combat and hardcore navigation and think it's fun to die trying to dock your ship, don't waste your money.
If you want a fun game that's rewarding in small doses or good for an epic gaming weekend, this is it.  But warn your friends and family that they will be seeing less of you for a while....
It's a beautifully done space combat/trading/questing game.  You can be a trader, you can be a miner, you can be a pirate, you can be a quester, or most likely you'll find yourself doing a little bit of all of it.  Or a LOT of all of it.
I will suggest playing with a controller...I'm a longtime keyboard and mouse guy and I never use a controller for anything.  Thats a big part of why my Nintendo was gifted to my nephew and my xbox hasnt been plugged in for 2 years, but with this game the controller just feels right and works perfectly.
Pros:
*  It looks 3D, but it's mostly a 2D game, so it simplifies the navigation and combat
*  Its very open.  There is a story line to progress through , but you're free to ignore it, or progress at your own pace
*  You can fire it up, do a couple of quick quests, and feel like you accomplished something.
* And then a couple more, and then just one more, and then another one.....and 8 hours later you've played a quick game
* It autosaves every time you visit a station.  So if your next quest goes horribly wrong, and you die a fiery death, then reload and try again.
* If an objective is too hard, there are plenty of options to go make a little money, buy some better armor and weapons, and try it again.  Yet somehow it doesnt feel grindy, it's fun.
* After over 30 hours, I still have the music turned on.  I saw one review call it "Cowboy butt-rock" - I'm not sure if they meant that as a compliment or an insult, but it kind of fits.  Either way, I like it.
* The one time I had a problem, I posted a question on the support forum and got a response in 15 minutes
Cons
* If you're not a fan of the "Cowboy butt-rock", turn it off.  The game is still worth it.
* The game is so awesome it will inspire you to take time out to write a review, which takes time away from playing the awesome game.
* I can't think of any other cons to put here
* Really, why are you still reading?  Buy the game already

SUMMARY: A simple to play, but surprisingly deep space adventure sim with a lot of personality and style that gives you a solid "Space Western" adventure where you can carve your own path.
It took me awhile to get into Rebel Galaxy as, early on, the directions weren't that clear and the difficulty was erratic.  That's when I realized Rebel Galaxy, for all its great graphics and soundtrack, really is a throwback to the old "drop 'em in space and good luck" games of the past.  Once you realize you are on your own in just about every way, it all comes together.
In Rebel Galaxy you come to a distant set of stars to find out what happened to your Aunt Juno.  And from there you can do anything you want, from following her legacy, to trading, to piracy, to naming your ship "Cosmic Bannanahammer" and doing donuts in space.  It's pretty much up to you.
Basic gameplay involves piloting your ship to different locations and pursuing different tasks - trading goods, fighting enemies, raiding ships, mining asteroids.  From firing broadsides to talking to people everything can be done with a standard game controller, which makes it extremely easy to play.  Though controls can get complex, the layout and design makes it very easy to get into the game.
So let's break down the usual parts of these games:
PILOTING: Space is 2D here.  Sorry, 3D is just for display.  This may seem limiting, but it fits the easy-to-control method and keeps the game from getting insanely complex.  See, battles are done by . . .
NAVAL BATTLE TACTICS: This may take a bit of getting used to, but the game emphasizes a mix of broadside weapons, turrets, and specailized items.  Learning to juggle when to attack, maneuver, and fire takes a bit of work, but is rewarding to get right.  Also some of your weapons are AI controlled, making life much easier.  Speaking of ship components . . .
PLENTY OF SHIP OPTIONS: Equipment really matters in Rebel Galaxy and has tradeoffs.   Once you get your playstyle down you can buy and customize ships that fit you.  Little changes mean a lot, which is good because . . .
PLENTY OF MISSIONS: Sure they're often find, kill, or trade, but they're fun and more importantly they have impact with your standing of various groups.  Pirates, Militia, Citizens, and more will come to regard you differentlly depending on what you do.  This gives you quite a few ways to play the game.
LOTS OF LITTLE BITS: There's also a delightful amount of extras.  Trade advice and data that appears to help you trade.  Guilds to join. Bits of humor.  Random events that pop up to keep the game rich, from ambushes to data transponders.  The more you play the more you find.
A STORY THAT SEEMS INTERESTING: At first I wasn't sure about the story, but a few missions in it actually got my attention.  You don't have to play the story, but still.
A SENSE OF ATMOPSHERE: Finally the game really manages to create a great "Space Western" atmosphere, somewhere between Firefly, Cowboy Bebop, and its own thing.  This is helped by . . .
A COWBOY BUTTROCK SOUNDTRACK: Really, the soundtrack is the icing on the cake, a bunch of country-rock hard-edged western type songs that complete the experience.  The details in this game really make it.
Is the game perfect?  No.  Some of it's very standard game-play, if well-implemented.  The combat can be a bit twitchy and confusing.  Some of the data and info layouts could have been better done.
The thing is with Rebel Galaxy, most issues are really minor.  The game is fun, obviously made by people who love games, and has a clear, well-defined identity.  It delivers.
So if you like a good space adventure game, want one that's challenging but you can pick up with realtive ease, then buy the game, get on board the Cosmic Bannanahammer, and head on out to find Aunt Juno.

The game tries to put focus on trying to outmaneuver your oppponents, bait them in certain situations and eventually understanding them enough to know what they will most likely do in certain situations and thus enabling yourself to act accordingly. The game has it's ups and downs but cmon, what else is new in video games? Here is a list of pros and cons:
PROS:
-Balanced champion roster
-Nice visual effects
-Engaging gameplay
-Robust gameplay mechanics
-Short matches(5-10 minutes tops)
-Tons of cosmetics(a lot more to be added in the coming days for F2P launch)
-PC and Console support
-Odeum
-Low system requirements(runs smoothly on my potato i3 laptop)
-Seasonal events, tournaments, achievements(with in-game rewards), quest system, champion progression etc.
CONS:
-Ai is pretty bad and many champions are missing AI profiles(only a couple of champions keep rotating when you play vs AI)

The game still needs a lot of work to reach it's full potential but man is it good even now. Matches can be really close and there is never a boring match, especially if it's ranked. It feels exciting to play the game and cmon, once it goes F2P(in 3 days) there is nothing stopping you from trying it out. It's a super fun game but don't expect to go winning all the time at first. Also, to share this with the community, there isn't actually a need to use unofficial patches to get proper widescreen resolutions. RTCW runs on Tech3, the same engine that powered Quake III. Simplest method is to use the console:
r_customwidth 1920
r_customheight 1080
r_mode -1
vid_restart
Replace 1920 and 1080 with your native display resolution.

You get exactly what you see with this game; a platformer with an above average idea done with subpar, flash game level execution. There is a total woping nine 3-5 minute long levels, all of which have 3 difficulties in which to scrape your teeth on.
The gameplay is flat and mildly annoying, and the soundtrack is forgettable. Assets include lasers and red spike balls. You play as a cube with a dot that I assume is supposed to be its eye. The gimmick is that it grows while you play. This leads to some well executed panning out as you go through the levels, and can screw up runs on higher difficulties since you grow a bit faster, but other than that it's really just a gimmick.
This isn't helped by the fact that these increasingly difficult levels all have a finite number of lives for you to play, demanding that the player master each challenge in a single level. This can lead to frustration, especially on the higher difficuties where "challenge" is presented through more spike balls to kill you. The janky camera also has a way of panning out at the weirdest times,  and the level design doesn't follow any consistant pattern.
Once again, there are only 9 levels. in less than half an hour I blazed through them without much trouble, and even got through a few of the higher difficulties before I just stopped caring. It seems the real motivation here is the leaderboards since that takes front and center, but the game as a whole does little for want to keep you around.
A competant, yet depressingly mediocre game that does little to differentiate itself, Growing Pains suffers most from its lacking ambition and lacking controls. There are far worse games to pick up for 5 bucks, but unless you're really desperate for a platformer, this one you can pass on.
Smudged Cat has done some pretty phenomenal games, so it's kind of sad to find a game so lacking in that same passion. Hopefully whatever stupor they're in they'll bounce back from, but Growing Pains is an example of squandered and lazy development, and that just sucks.

Boy, am i glad i got this game on sale! I cannot say it is worth the asking price, but it is a very good game. Some points though.
There is no story. I was very confused when presented with a long list of map options and no "Campaign" button. Based on the trailers i thought there would be a story mode. So that was odd.
Favortie child. The game favors a certain kind of strrategy, which is swift and agressive. If you like to methodically plunder and settle, consolidating for safety between conquests, this game is not for you. Sure you can win your start system, which is the reqirement in the smaller maps. But past that goal the cautious, developmetal approach simply cannot win. There is an inflexible number of ships you can produce, and unless you hit your multiple opponents fast, they will simply have the same number of ships as you, most likely in a more optimal, calculated configuration.
Same ol same ol. Replay ability for this game is very high, don't get me wrong. But you really have to get outside your comfort zone to acheive a different experience. There are a wide range of factions, but finding a niche in this game makes all the maps seem the same as your're presented with the same planets, ships and tech over and over again.
War, what is it good for? As far as this game is concered, everything. Diplomacy is not only difficult to use, its totally optional. There is no way to win through cultural supremacy at all, and no way to barter out of a conflict. So don't come looking for a peacepipe.
Really though, this is a great game. Not worth 40.00 (as currently is) but certainly worth half. The combat can be impersonal or up close, your preference here. The ship designs are lovingly constructed and fluid. My awful computer has never lagged, and you really do get a sense of space combat as you agonize over whether your reinforcements will warp to you in time. 8/10

You know that moment when you put on your favorite pair of pants, only to find you’ve gotten too big to wear them anymore, leading you to sulk and binge on ice cream and bad television? Growing Pains is built on a similar idea, with an ample dose of claustrophobic entrapment thrown in for good measure.
You take control of a (originally) tiny, fuzz ball, tumbleweed, alien...thing, in a state of constant expansion. Evidently the labyrinth you’re within is only so big, creating a race to get through the passages before you become too large to fit. Toss in some spike traps, some collectibles, and a ticking clock for speedruns and you’ve got a fairly typical platformer with a neat idea to help it stand out.
But that’s all Growing Pains is; one new idea poorly fitted on a thinly designed framework that isn’t enough to keep it afloat in the midst of so many other similar games. With only 9 very short levels (you can blow through them all well under an hour), it feels like a proof of concept more than a finished product. Multiple difficulties add a small amount of replay value, but the added challenge rarely does anything but highlight how inadequate the controls are when any sort of precision is required. It’s as if the entire environment is made of ice, causing me to constantly slip out of control, usually into spikes or another source of instant death. It’s frustrating in the worst way, rarely feeling as failure is my own fault, and making it very hard not to throw down my controller in rage and quit.
I wouldn’t consider myself a stickly for graphics, but the art design in Growing Pains is so unbelievably terrible that it actively made my eyes hurt to play. There’s constantly a ton of stuff happening on screen, but it’s like the developers tried to throw on every photoshop filter they could to the backdrops and it came out looking like absolute rubbish. There’s no ascetic consistency, and when put together I find it actively offensive to look at.
The foremost mechanic of Growing Pains is one I find rather interesting and would love to see pan out in another game, but in its current state GP feels like something that came out of a game jam and not at all ready for the general public. It’s shallow and unpolished from every angle, with artwork that shouldn’t have ever made it out of the prototype stage, and controls in need of serious improvement. I like what the developers were going for, but they’re going to need to do a lot before Growing Pains becomes something people should pay anything to play.

After lamenting the fact that raiders pilfered all of their medical supplies the night before, she slept while Bruno stood watch and Pavle scavenged for supplies.  Pavle returned bearing herbal remedies for Katia to consume.  Believing herself to be on the mend, Katia went out on a foraging mission the next night.  She returned with a nasty cough, but felt fairly chipper after quaffing a mug of coffee.  However, a cold front moved in; dark clouds rumbled and spat down water, worsening Katia's illness.
By day 23, she was severely ill.  Not wanting to steal anything, Pavle searched for a trading partner in order to barter for the pills that would eliminate Katia's pallor.  No one had any to spare, though, so he returned empty handed.  Katia remained bedridden while the other denizens of the meager shelter shot worried whispers to each other.
As day 25 rolled around with no improvement in Katia's condition, Pavle resolved to obtain the medicine for her by any means necesary.  Tired, hungry, and sad, Pavle set out to steal from a warehouse  which was patrolled by heavily armed men.  Furtively dodging the patrols and rifling through drawers, Pavle raced against the approaching dawn to find his prize.  Finally, an hour from dawn, he unveiled a bottle of asprin to bring down his friend's fever.  He raced home.
Throwing open the door, Pavle joyously announced "I'm back, and I've got the meds!"
But it was too late.  Katia died in the night.  Pavle collapsed in the doorway and grieved for his friend the whole day through.
Glancing at my wall-mounted map of the world, my eyes danced between the Middle East, Ukraine, and Africa, and I considered joining Pavle in the splintered door frame.

Let me start by saying that I thought that the "survival" genre was on its way out of popularity before I started playing this game. That being said, This War of Mine is a brilliant minimalist survival experience that will have you playing through multiple times. The basic premise of the game is simply to survive the horrors of a war-torn city experiencing an armed rebellion.  To do this you must control a cast of characters and fortify a shelled out home to endure the coming days. The characters you get are pre set, but you unlock more combinations of characters as you progress through the game. Each character has basic needs; hunger, sleep, and their general health (ie: keeping their wounds treated and sick characters healthy). Some characters also have additional needs that make taking care of them slightly more difficult, such as an addiction to cigarettes. These needs and wants are what will influence your decision making as you progress through the game.
This War of Mine focuses on survival, but also allows players to choose the easy way out of a situation by sacraficing their humanity in order to live. What I mean by this is that you will encounter situations where you can easily obtain food or medical supplies, but you must steal or kill to obtain them. The option to scavenge and create your own supplies exists, but if someone is dying from a gunshot wound, then you may have no choice but to rob the doctor down the street who is doing all he can to treat civilians who are injured in the conflict. Performing such an act will have a negative influence on morale, and has a chance to break the character who performed the deed, rendering them useless for some time and possibly even pushing them to suicide.
The game is not flawless. One big problem that I had was that little to no game mechanics are explained. There is no legend to tell players what icons mean, and combat is a veritable trial by fire that will most likely claim the life of the first character that encounters it. Once you have become a veteran all this will mean nothing, but as a new player to the game it can be frustrating. That is certainly the biggest error I have detected, and it is not enough to stop me from labeling this as an excellent game.
What is being presented to us as gamers is more than just another "get wood, make fire, cook meat, live" survival game; it is The Sims meets Fallout. Control your party's emotions and physical and mental state of being. Juggle your characters needs, make or steal the weapons you need to survive, and ultimately do what you need to in order to live through the war.
9/10: highly reccomended.

Dead Rising 2 is a game that drops you in the middle of a zombie infested mall, with your ability to concoct the strangest weapon in existence as your only weapon. The greatest asset of this game is the ways in which you can take the environement, and destroy hordes of zombies with it. With some of the most enjoyable weapons in games, memorable and challenging boss battles, some of the best coop gameplay I've seen in years, time management mechanics that add replayability, great controls, some nice visuals for the time of its release, a lovable Capcom style campy story and cheesy dialogue that keeps you anticipating the next one-liner, Dead Rising 2 offers hours and multiple playthroughs of fun.
I'm also glad to say that the PC port is the superior version minus the lack of availability of the Case West DLC, and is actually one of the best PC ports I've played in a while. The PC controls are intuitive, the graphics are a step up from its console iterations, and the patches for the game's major issues on release (saving kicking coop partner and inability for coop partner to save progress are examples) is included.
The game has its problems however, which I think are necessary to point out for the sake of the reader and potential buyer. The first is the overabundance of quick-time-events. I honestly consider QTEs to be a bad mechanic 100% of the time, due to it stripping the gameplay to, "press x to watch what happens next" or, "press x to not die." Unfortunately this game makes you go through one everytime a zombie gets his hands on you. The button prompt changes everytime, so you can't just anticipate it and get it over with quickly, luckily the prompts are always one of the movement keys or waving the mouse around. The PC port's use of Game for Windows Live is probably the PC version's second greatest flaw. Games for Windows Live is horribly unoptimized, and is a chore to use in comparison to Steam. Another issue is one I previously mentioned, the fact that the Case West DLC has not been ported, and is not available on PC, so if playing Case West is a must for you, you might want to consider getting this game for PS3 or Xbox 360, although I'd argue it isn't worth the sacrifices made for the console versions. Two very minor complaints are Chuck's slow movement speed, because sometimes I find myself getting impatient with Chuck's inability to go faster than a jog, and how New Game+ doesn't up the difficulty any. I will say however, that New Game+ is fun in the way that you can try and complete all of the missions before their timers run out, due to you being much stronger.
Despite its issues, Dead Rising 2 rounds out to be a wonderful game, that I whole-heartedly recommend buying.
