I just finished my first Final Fantasy game!
Just to get my biggest complaint out of the way: The real game(play) doesn't really start until chapter 11, which is more than 20 hours into the game. Up until that point the game is pretty linear and you can not rearrange your team freely. However, if you manage to get past the first 20 hours or so the game becomes much more interesting, and you actually have to consider what characters, paradigms (formations) and equipment to use for each fight. Some enemies will completely crush you if you do not come well prepared.
My only other complaint is that when playing with Japanese audio and English subtitles the subtitles are often completely off. My guess is that the English subtitles is just a transcript of the English audio, and not really a translation, which can get a bit annoying when the meanings are way too different.
Other than that, I have mostly positive things to say about the game.
The story is very confusing - but in a good way (once you get into it):
There are two worlds, Cocoon and Gran Pulse, both inhabited by godlike creatures called Fal'Cie as well as humans. Fal'Cie can grant humans special powers, turning them into L'Cie. L'Cie have to complete their mission ("Focus"). L'Cie are not told what their Focus is (...), however if they fail to complete it they are turned into a Cie'th (monster). L'Cie who complete their focus are only turned into a crystal ("yay"). Lightning and the rest of the main characters are all turned into L'Cie by the Pulse Fal'Cie, meaning that they are hunted by the Fal'Cie of their homeworld, Cocoon. Many other things happen, but in the end you have to defeat the bad Fal'Cies, complete your Focus, and save the world. Simple.
The battle system, as mentioned above, opens up when you reach chapter 11. Each character can be assigned any one of six different roles which can be used to form various paradigms, and you can freely jump from one paradigm to another as many times as you like during a fight. There are tons of weapons and accessories which come with buffs, resistances or other beneficial effects, which is of great importance when fighting tougher enemies. Then you have summons, which (with one exception)... felt pretty useless.
The game also looks
. The game is currently 8 years old, but it still looks amazing. Part of the reason why I chose Final Fantasy as my first Final Fantasy game was because I wanted a game that looks great even today, and not only do the cut-scenes look stunning, the fights were amazing as well, and the music sounded just as good as the rest of the game looked. I had heard that Final Fantasy games both look and sound great - and I was not disappointed.
I guess a third, and minor, complaint would be that some (most?) of the characters were pretty annoying. You will probably be able to tell right away who the most annoying characters are, however this didn't really bother me that much, and I still ended up enjoying the game.
All in all I'm happy that this was my first Final Fantasy game, and I will almost certainly try out the sequels (Final Fantasy 13-2 and Lightning Returns), as well as other games in the series.
Recommended!

Final Fantasy is one of those franchises that has been part of gaming history and just that name alone sets a very high bar as to what can be expected from a game. Sadly, FFXIII doesnt live up to those expectations from the Final Fantasy fanbase.
As it can be expected from a Square Enix game, the graphics on this game are amazing for its time and the CGs look almost as good as any late 2010's game CG. The music is very well written and has some amazing tracks that can help set the tone of a couple of important sections on the game.
The level design on this FF can be considered one of the worst on the whole series of games, the linearity on most levels is just annoying and it doesnt help a lot the fact that exploration is pretty much a plain with not much to do besides farming and a couple late game bosses.
The story is another componen that I really enjoyed, not as deep as in other Final Fantasies, but still very entertaining and with it fair share of serious and/or mature themes behind all the action and dialog.
This game gets a lot of things right, the only problem is that is called Final Fantasy, as it suffers from the expectations from pretty much the whole FF fanbase and by having a lot of things changed, like the combat system, the free open world map and party member control, this game does a lot of Final Fantasy-ish things wrong, but as a stand alone game without its name and everything that it represents, it becomes a really good RPG.
Tl;dr: Bad FinalFantasy, great JRPG. 8.2/10

The gameplay is identical to the original Bioshock in every way (including the annoying Little Sister escort mission). If you enjoyed the original Bioshock, you'll enjoy this game even more thanks to textures and lighting which look like they actually came from 2016. Throughout the levels you can also find bonus director commentary tapes, which weren't in the original game. They're worth watching if you have any curiosity about Bioshock's early development history.
Now on to start the Bioshock 2 remaster!

I really wanted to finish the game's story before I wrote a review. And I'm not gonna lie this game at times were a slugfest. I will try to point out all things I consider good to know for any RPG or Final Fantasy lover.  Keep in mind that a lot of things are personal taste so even if I complain or compliment something you can of course have a different take on it
It will be lengthy so There will be a TLDR version at the bottom.
Let's start out with a few things that will be different from more traditional RPG/FF's. like pretty much all FF's you have a party of 3 max where the difference is that you only control a leader this time. The other two party members are AI controlled. This is in combination with a "role system" where you can say which party member is which role , (like healer, tank , mage , support , debuffer etc) so you can control their general moveset. Role switching can be done at a whim in battle and is mandatory to make it through fights. It is a very action oriented system. Another more "non FF thing" this game has is that you will see random encounters on the road instead of randomly spawning into one. This will allow you to pretty run from boss fight to boss fight advancing story content and only fight mobs you wish 75% of the time. the rest of the game is pretty RPG as you can get
As stated this game uses a leader system with role switching to control the flow of battle. While I know that fighting is a core concept of a FF game I had the most difficulties with this system. This was because of the fact that if the leader was downed you instantly fail the fight while the other two can be phoenix downed/raised back no problem. This can make it so that if an enemy mob just happen to have something that causes instant death and happen to cast it at your leader who fails his save. you just lose the fight instantly. Some fights can be lengthy and have that happen to you is just frustrating. The other part is the AI controlled party members which in certain situations just won't do what you want them to do.  for example you have a tank / healer /healer comp for a moment to recover from a heavy hit. while recovering a random party member dies because of.... reasons. you would want your other healer to raise him as soon as he can to have a double healer back. but the AI just keeps healer everything that is still up to 90% first before even considering to raise the 2ed person. and more quirky things like that. Now this will only really be a thing at certain bosses but it can be really frustrating. The role switching gave it a fun action element to fights in how to handle certain bosses. and with enough practise the AI can be useful enough. Another small element of combat is that positioning in fights is actually a thing but you have NO control over any of it (may be pro people can but casual playthrough won't know)
Which means that if a mob/boss has area attacks or attacks in a straight line or anything. if a character just happens to land behind that mob/boss that character won't be hit anymore by that stuff. significantly reducing their healing needs. and if all party members get into a triangle pattern the fight would be really easy. but the other side is also true where they can happen to land clumped up and get hit by everything. reducing DPS time and lengthening fights significantly.
Making certain fights really luck based like that felt annoying since you have no control over any of that.
Role switching was fun and interesting though AI and positioning out of your control van dictate fights. also the leader going down instantly loses you the fight can be ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t (like with death spells)
The game is divided in 6 different "classes" and for about 50% of the game they are set per character ( so only 2 can be healers at the start for example ) after that mark all characters will get all roles available. Leveling a role goes in a sort of grid where you earn XP from battles and you can spend that XP in a role to advance it. I liked this idea since especially in the later stages you can make the party you want with the roles you like and play the game. The only bad thing with this is that XP gains in this game make NO SENSE IN ANY WAY. An RPG player will say. the more I play and further I get in the story. the fights will get harder (random encounters as well) and my XP will slide with that to make sense... but here that is NOT the case. as an example. If I would fight a current mob for the story I would gain like... 2000 XP for a good 1 minute fight. however if I would go back to an area that was like.... 4 hours earlier and fight a group of 4 specific mobs I would gain 8000 XP for 20 second fight. it makes no sense what so ever. and when nodes can cost up to 20K XP at times. that only 2000 XP per fight for so much more time makes no sense what so ever and can make the game feel like such a drag when you actually WANT to grind some extra levels/roles.
the role system was fun and gave you the option to use characters in what ever role you wish. thought grinding for it makes NO SENSE with weird XP gains throughout the game.
This will be tricky since I don't want to give any story related information. The only thing I can say about this is that... the story was ok but confusing as ♥♥♥♥ at the start. and if the game would be like 40 hours long it takes about 10-15 hours for getting some momentum and things to get really intriguing. everything before that I was mostly "Wtf'ing" most of the time.
mostly WTF a whole lot and takes a good while to get going. but it was a nice story
As expected from a Final Fantasy title the graphics are smooth and stunning. not really anything to say about this besides that I like them.
I am struggling really hard to give a set verdict on this. combat and leveling could be a chore sometimes and there have been frustrating moments.. like dying to a boss because he death magiced my leader after a 25 minute fight... It happens. but on the other hand I loved the role system and action switching between them in fights to respond to fights. I have grinded for some extra levels but don't know if that was really needed to finish the game so grinding feels optional if you want it for sidequests.
as a side note for achievement hunters you do need to beat the game at least once to unlock the grid to max out a role.
In general... the game was sometimes confusing as hell or frustrating but I did enjoy it ( even after some rage moments) but I must also admit that I finished this game on pure willpower in the end. I hope this massive bulk of information gave enough insight to decide if this game is for you or not.

As a tech demo, it's pretty good. It showcases some impressive destructible environments and gorgeous visuals.
As a subversive art piece, it's a striking work of Grunge Noir. The world is bleached in high-contrast monochrome with things that really catch the protagonist's interest being colored (and those would typically be on fire). The tone is dark, somber, and horrifying with comic relief being rare.
As a game, however, it's mediocre. The AI has its hiccups (civilians sometimes run towards you when they should logically be running away), the sound effects for the guns are weak (I'd say the game would be improved by a fair margin if they were as good as Hotline Miami's), the execution animations and repetitive phrases wear most peoples' patience thin since they're done ad nauseum, the protagonist gets caught up in doorways and is unable to vault over things he should be able to (a railing blocking his way when he's standing in a sewer canal), and the game is often hampered by frame rate drops and spontaneous freezing. Finally, the appeal of the game is bound to wear off in a matter of days because there's little variety to be had in level structure (go here, kill people, go there, etc.)
In spite of these complaints: the game is not so hampered by its faults that it renders the game unenjoyable. It offers a challenging experience and some of the most satisfying kicks since Dark Messiah of Might and Magic (one patented Chuck Norris action kick turns almost any door into a gust of splinters). And, of course, it features impressive environment destruction.
It's a competently designed game that's bound to be a cult classic but also destined to age poorly.

I spent a lot of time grinding and restarting the game (see my playing hours) because I wanted an ultimate army. Despite the cons, if you are still interested in the game (not because it’s cheap), here are some VIT (very important tips) for you:
a) MUST first read up and research on the characters, the weapons, the skills, the spells etc in the Internet! Tons of information there! If not, you will regret and then you will decide to restart the game.
b) Recruit Zolean and Yuniver early (once available) and train their HEX spells to Cachexia! This will definitely help you to complete the game without pulling your hair or shouting the F words too much.
c) Get the Mystic Seal formation early! The formation actually sucks but it will help you get new spells and skills fast. Read it up in the Internet.
d) Your sparring opponent for grinding is none other than Bai Ze, the dragon from the Kosmofest quest. Read it up in the Internet.
e) Train Remedies and Herbs early as well! They will save you uncountable times, early in the game! By the way, death is normal in this game.
I have never written such a long review before but this game is really good (minus the grinding). It gave me a 120% satisfaction.

This is game is pretty amazing.
The original Bishock set high bar to cope with, but this game achieves set it even further. New enchanced game mechanics, a fresh new character and almost new environment sum up to a pretty awesome gameing experience.
The character models in particular have been improved greatly and do not look like a TV supper meal gone wrong. Now, you are able to wield a weapon and a plasmid at the same time. Minigames have been improved too as well as the research mechanic.
And the guns, holy crap. You would not stop making a mean grin when firing the gatling gun or the double barreled for the first time. And the combined gunplay is just hilarious. Electrolyting emenies constantly while shredding them apart with anti-personell rounds is pretty cool.
The Little Sister mechanic improved in a logical way too. You as a protector can 'collect' one Little Sister and let her gather for you, instead of just simply 'processing her'.
The only bad thing I can say is that the 'end boss' is pretty lame as there is none. Sure - Fontaine was pretty easy to deal with  the right loadout and lots of electrical gel but it set a real end. Instead you have to fend off waves of enemies. Pretty boring. But the end sequence pretty much makes up for it.
All in all, Bioshock 2 is a big improvement over the first game and a good ending of the true Rapture Saga. For now atleast.

Is it actually enjoyable though? Definitely not, unless you have a strong sadistic urge, you most likely won't enjoy this AT ALL. Be prepared to wait hours upon hours for stuff to actually happen, cope with a ridiculously unintuitive user interface that requires you to click options for 5 minutes to do the most simplistic things imaginable and other highly annoying things to that nature.
The previous games actually had sensibly structured menues and allowed you to configure hotkeys for every single important function you would ever need and then quite a few more. With this though? No Hotkeys whatsoever. Heck even within the dialogs it's ridiculously unintuitive. Press Enter to confirm stuff and/or make stuff actually happen? You'd better forget about that. Enter get's replaced by 4 in most of the dialogs, unless of course you hit one of the many exceptions to this rule when it's some random other number key or, in very rare circumstances, they actually stuck with the proven Enter key.
Hit Escape to go back? Not so much in this game.
The list actually goes on and on, but suffice to say that the UX is actually the worst one could possibly imagine for any game to have.
Which leads to actually having to answer the question about whether or not it's playable with "no" since the UX is so freaking terrible, there are no words for it.
Remote trading is pretty much gone, for like the first 10 hours or so there doesn't seem to be any way to remote trade or control anything. It continues to be this way until, by accident / pure luck, you spot the top part of the Trade dialog actually has an option to select one of several (not all) of your ships to do the trade.
After you did that, you'll have to wait for endless hours for it to actually do it. Since there is no SETA anymore you're actually forced to sit there and wait, or do other stuff in the real world (as you can't use your PC since it has to run X).
So yeah, I ended up going outside playing some Ingress sessions while the game was running waiting for your stupid ships to actually do something you are required to do and wait for.
You can pretty much forget about fighting too, your ship is way to weak under any circumstances and pretty much uncontrolable in any fashion required to be able to dogfight, which unfortunately is being pretty heavily focused in the storyline so far. So be prepared to die A LOT, until you're so frustrated by even just flying around that you either say screw this piece of $60+♥♥♥♥♥♥or go and make yourself invulnerable by means of cheating.
Long story short: DO NOT BUY THIS! Go buy any of the previous titles really, they're fine and you will have lots of fun with the previous titles. They have a logical and sensible UI, and even though it might seem  a lot at first it actually provides a good UX.
This one however has the most terrible UX & UI that has ever been created in the history of mankind and unfortunately that cannot ever be fixed.
If you absolutely want this to complete your collection of X titles then maybe get it when it's on sale for less than like $5 or something. Anything more than that is simply not worth it.

Outstanding space adventure game!
Ever since Freespace 2, there is a complete lack of decent space combat games. This new take on the matter does away with everything too daunting or complicated for more casual players, (target your target's target, I'm looking at you Freespace!) and adds the interesting poing of view of sandboxing it, and make it from the point of view of a civilian trying to make due.
You don't HAVE to do anything, you can just explore, mine, find a space station that is not hostile towards you and make commerce. In fact, I was expecting something quite like it from the Campaign Interface of Starcraft 2! Gosh, your starting ship already looks like with the eponymous battlecruiser Hyperion. Of course, carrying away the main quests will lead the story further, but you can spend hours upon hours doing errands and getting into trouble on your own.
It took a nice 3D engine to prove to you that in fact, you don`t need a 3D engine to make a fine space-faring game. The whole navigation and combat, despite you are interacting with 3D objects, is happening on an immense 2D plane, which is a whole solar system. And that's just the neighborhood. Speaking of that, no more disorienting spins, complicated escort missions (so far) or plain stupid tiny-ship-versus-behemoth situations that you can`t RUN away.
Am I still comparing to Freespace? Well, yes. Let me add Star Trek into the mix. Since there is an element of RPG into it, you have different, and sometimes warring factions. But because you are not bound by those lores and canon facts present in ST, you can take sides with any of them, just choose your missions wisely.
There is commerce? Yes. Mining? Yes. Online gameplay? I don`t think so, because you'd be chewed alive by any pirate-players, which I heard that's exactly what happens in Eve Online, unless I'm not out of the walled garden for beginners. I never played Eve, but that's as far as I heard, Eve Online is not meant for casual players, has complex economy simulations, and people actually invested tens of thousands of DOLLARS in building ships or whatever that game has to offer. Just bumping into these players would force you to play under their rule or face obliteration, which scares off casuals, like me.
Somebody mentioned Firefly, and the look and feel are surprisingly similar with this cable show. But not knowing the show won't make the game less enjoyable.
Well, in short, the game is a blast, no previous knowledge of other games required, no need for a gamepad or joystick, and apparently, which is not the norm, no microtransactions. Whatsoever. If you want the cool stuff, earn it.
For the icing on the cake, the gaming is surprisingly small, never even fazed my dated Intel i7 920 CPU, or hogged down my graphics card, and allows you to just tell the game where your music stash is, and mix it with the own game soundtrack. Flying around the galaxy listening to your favorite tunes: priceless.
Definitely, buy it. Worth. Every. Dime.

of Growing Pains. Below, I will summarise my thoughts in a written form.
In Growing Pains, you as a player control a fluffy ball of fur that tries to navigate from start to finish as quick as possible, meanwhile avoiding the traps that are in your way. The graphics are pschedelic but not too distracting. The same goes for the audio, which is okay but not really memorable. Both graphics and sound are functional, however not amazing. Luckily, the gameplay is on the stronger side. The fine balance between staying small for increased precision and growing larger for increased speed is brilliant, once the initial hurdles of getting to know the controls are overcome. I have played the game both with keyboard and controller and find both similarly good (and managed to reach some #1 spots with either), thus you can play with what inut device you prefer! The design of the nine levels (each with three difficulty settings) is good, however the levels are rather large, which might frustrate beginners when trying to get a good time. The big selling point of Growing Pains is the integrated online leaderboard, which allows friendly competition between friends and frienemies. There are some minor problems here and there, but nothing that would stop me from playing. The high jump mechanic feels odd and needs some getting used too. The same goes for the camera which sometimes reacts weirdly due to the zooming out, while your character grows. Nontheless, if you like games like Ten Second Ninja or the later stages of Super Meat Boy, you'll have to give Growing Pains a shot.

PLEASE READ MY REVIEW BEFORE ASSUMING THAT MY BIG BLUE THUMB IN THE CORNER IS INDICATIVE OF MY FINAL THOUGHTS ON THIS GAME; IT'S NOT.
Where to begin on this title... Growing Pains is a platformer, that much is easily discernible through its screenshots to anyone yet to play it. But platformers can come in all shapes and sizes; some are casual, some are Indie (whatever that means), some will put a gun in hand and throw dozens of zombies at you, and some still will bend time and space to tell you a most wondrous tale of little men jumping left and right. But then there are some whose sole purpose is to aggravate, irritate, exasperate, peeve and pester you until your are near pulling the hair from your head. Some of these, still, can be fun. Take Super Meat Boy, for example, a game whose sole purpose is to tease you with the sweet candy of a new character or collectible, only to stick you in a multi-spike-walled room of death that you can't possibly hope to best until...oh, 100 tries later, when you finally, FINALLY, succeed!
Growing Pains can make SMB's Dark World feel like playing New Super Mario Bros.
Unfortunately for the sort of people who enjoy that kind of thing, Growing Pains isn't harder for the right reasons.
But let's start with the good: Growing Pains, even with it's very, very simple "flash game" aesthetic, manages to look like, well, a good flash game. Psychadelic lava lamp backgrounds move along with a hip techno soundtrack to keep the mood bright and cheerful. The rest of the moving bits consist of admittedly cheap looking wiggling rainbow gifs and semi 3D spike balls that look like they were lifted straight out of Bubzy 3D.

There's no story to worry about here, other than the clever premise behind the game. See your character, (we'll call him Cousin "It"), grows in size. It does this involuntarily, but this process can be sped up with the push of a button. Doing so allows It to move and jump around the level faster than he could before, although his larger size makes him no less susceptible to spiky ball death, and if the player isn't careful, It may be struck down by something that a smaller version could have easily avoided.
The levels that you must guide Cousin It through are broken up into individual gauntlets, each with their own rainbow gifs to collect before the exit to the next gauntlet will open. Each gauntlet is filled with spikeballs, moving and not, waiting to burst our hero into pixely bits. Getting smacked down by a ball to the face won't set you back far, however, just to the entrance of the gauntlet that you currently reside in. Your rainbow gifs won't reset either, so the threat of death only brings a lower total time, unless you die enough to burn through your finite supply of lives.
For the every level, of which there are only 9, you will have three medal options: Bronze, Silver, and Gold, each defining a level of difficulty. Bronze, for the most part can be achieved with little fuss, until the last few, anyway. Gold, on the other hand, requires a true measure of patience, regardless of level. There are rainbow gifs in every direction, and brand new spiky death traps in addition to whatever filled the level in the pubescent Bronze medal stages. You'll be lucky if you can even succeed one of these levels, let alone get a good end time.
Here, now, finally, is the bad bit. These types of games live and die by their controls. Super Meat Boy arguably has the nearest thing to perfect 2D platformer controls; any death I suffered in that game, felt like it was due only to my own negligence, and not to poor mechanics or unfair circumstance. Growing Pains does not benefit from a similar condition. Your character simply becomes far too slippery and uncontrollable, and suffers from stop/go movement syndrome. There is no buildup from when you are standing still to when you begin to move, and vice versa. There is only one speed, and that speed grows as quickly as your size, and often quickly moves you out of control. The greatest travesty that this game commits is that your movements simply don't feel natural. It felt impossible to develop a clear rhythm, and in a game about speed and precision platforming, that simply won't do, and the already difficult levels can feel near impossible to succeed in.
Now, to explain why, after all the negative and backhanded things I've said about this game, I've still given this game a passing grade. While I feel that the control doesn't live up to the very necessary standards set by it's predecessors, it's not necessarily broken in any way, just flawed. And, truth be told, I find the cheap graphics and the unique take on growth to be charming, in its own mediocre way. While I personally could not create a solid rhythm with the controls, I would be remiss to just assume that no one else could. Not to mention the simple fact that this game has some of the most devilishly difficult level design that I've yet encountered. And for that, Growing Pains gets a decidedly hesitant "thumbs up" from me.

In this highly immersive game you not only test the limitations of what desperate civilians can do, but also test the morality of your own conscious.  Stranded on the battlefield and deserted by the very soldiers that your country had sworn to protect various scavengers come together to fight against rising raids and thugs that have taken over the city when nightfall comes.  Resources are scarce, happiness dwindling, there are no moral decisions on the battlefield, only survival.  The scavengers all have various skills, some are faster than others, some stronger, and others still are good at boosting the happiness of those around them even when blood is staining their hands.
The first game that has ever truthfully brought me to tears, I spent the first part of the game shifting through abandoned houses, taking what little I could find in hopes of just feeding the two friends I had left at the house to guard the small amount we could call our own.  Even from the beginning Pavle became my savior, his speed and his ability to talk others out of depression was what made him my most-played character, where he would sleep and talk to others during the day, and at night he was my main scavenger in hopes of quickly gathering what we needed without drawing any attention.  But once the majority was taken from abandoned houses that were quickly sapped dry of their resources, morality became nothing more than an afterthought.
Pavle had to start making impossible decisions to obtain food, where first he went into armed buildings and got what little he could without engaging others, but once food hadn't come back night after night and Bruno's wounds were only getting more severe from constant raids, Boris began to take the reign.  His strength was my ally, and our first kill was made against an armed man, and where I expected more to follow I was horrified by not armed guards coming to mow Boris down, but rather the dead man's friends, disregarding me as they ran past and wept at the sight of their dead friend (I get chills even as I imagine those horror-stricken voices), however Boris had already fled with the man's gun and other belongings.  So broken upon returning Pavle did what little he could to console the tough man, but it was futile, and Pavle was forced to take the lead once more to find bandages for Bruno's increasing wounds.
It took some adjusting, but gradually I was able to take Pavle into more armed places, having to do nothing more than flash his knife to scare away those that would of otherwise harmed him, and although his own depression quickly set in Pavle charged through it all, sifting through inhabited houses and leaving small amounts of food and a knife for those that remained in hopes of them finding some hope as well.  But soon raids began, and with Bruno incapacitated Boris guarded the shelter at night, armed with a shotgun and enough bullets to fell a few thugs.  But devastation struck when Pavle killed a young man who had shot him, my own desperation for all three to survive kicking in when I had seen the young man with a gun, and knew how useful it could be against stronger raids.  But then the young man's parents came down, tears streaming down their cheeks and their voices filled with horror as the old couple grappled uselessly to their son, as if they thought he would just get up and hug them.
That was what did it, Pavle was broken.  My main scavenger incapacitated by his own mind, where only Boris could console him, but once Boris became my main scavenger due to his strength and his depression seldom ever became broken, I left Pavle to the dangerous task of guarding the shelter, tending to Bruno's severe wounds.  Things only got worse, after things seemed to be getting better, Boris had brought guns, food, bandages and medicine, Pavle was still depressed however no longer broken, Bruno took it all.  He didn't make it far, in the end I know that now, but he took everything, food, shotguns, bandages, medicine, we were left where we were to begin with.  Boris was the second to leave, wounded and hungry I like to think he simply didn't want to have Pavle see another good man die, so he left the young man alone, and what became of depression quickly turned into a mind broken.  I survived with Pavle alone for a good 10 days, taking important things with me so that when the inevitable raid did come, they didn't get much, however I only brought back small things from his scavenging that was becoming more gruesome by the night.  He was broken, I wanted him to sleep it off after getting large amounts of food that could keep him to guard for a few more days at the least, but what it showed on the screen brought me to tears, after hours of making sure Pavle survived, that he helped some people just to take something off of his mind.
Day 27: Pavle hung himself.
What will you do, allow those around you to gradually crumble into their own minds and hands, or throw caution to the wind and fight against everything you have ever been taught about right and wrong?
TLDR;  I cannot recommend this game enough, I am usually very picky (unfortunately) when it comes to games, however I have always been able to appreciate hard work and great graphics or story line, but usually never enough to buy it.  This game just intrigued me to no end, and after playing it for my first time (and certainly not my last) I can truthfully say it is one of the best games I've ever played.  Mechanics is great, character design near flawless, it's a little difficult to begin with to figure out some of the controls and what everything does, but you learn quickly, you have to in order to survive.  It's not tedious, it's enthralling all the way through, not your usual hunt-and-gather mechanics but taken to the next level as something too real to not be labeled as horrifying.  Play at the risk of your own view of the world.

Quick Review:
I really liked this game for a few reasons, mainly because of the challenges presented to the player, but also the style of the game and the overall gameplay. However, there were aspects that I did not enjoy as a new player (not to CIV games, just this one). Overall, I would say that this game is worth getting, but only if it is on sale and near the price of CIV 5 Complete and your not sick of Civ 5.
Long Review:
Pros:
+Good Gameplay
+Like the story behind it, but that is more of just my opinion
+Long games can keep on the edge of your seat the whole time
+Still challenging, even to the vets.
+Lots of replay value
Cons:
-A little hard to pick up at first (for a guy who played Civ 4 and 5)
-Plays exactly like Civ 5
-A little over priced for what it is
-Overall, doesn't bring many new features that change overall gameplay
This evaluation should be taken knowing two things, 1, I did not play more than 30 minutes, 2, I was able to see that it was like Civ 5, so some of the points here are taken from that game as well.
Big Conclusion:
In the long run, I think this game would be a great purchase for any CIV player. While the game is lacking in "new" content (meaning game changing features) and plays exactly like Civ 5, that is not necesarily a bad thing. Bottomline: Get it if your new to the series, but consider getting Civ 5 Complete, because that seems to be around the same price, with more content and about the same type of gameplay.

Out of all kinds of survival simulators, this one stands out.
As the game tells you, war games are all about the armies. The soldiers. The countries fighting for glory. But what about the citizens?
In This War of Mine, you play as a generally helpess civilian alongside your other friends in an attempt to survive during a time of war, where the city you reside in is under siege.
Your survivors can be easily wounded by constant attacks by thugs and bandits on your shelter, finding a good meal is sparse, and each day is a struggle to survive.
Do you have the supplies to make a good meal, or will you eat raw food? Do you have enough items of value to trade in order to survive? Do your medical supplies allow for bringing your near-dying friend to health?
Should you uphold your morals in this time of crisis, or will you murder, steal, and sack just to live? Your decisions lie with you, and the effects they have on your characters will show.
Will you help some children's dying mother get to health, or are you too desperate to live and must preserve what you do have? Will you risk saving a girl from being rap3d by a soldier, or disregard the effort in fear of death? Will you threaten to murder an old couple, just to steal from their supplies?
Survival is a gift in this game, and the strategy, thought, and your own morals will be brought to the test in this game. Not many other games can boast of giving you the challenge of surviving down to the letter.
Would recommend to anyone looking for a challenging, intriguing game, rather than a hack-and-slash one.

I had trouble deciding if I should buy this or not, what made it difficult is the fact I am a fan of Civ and have been since the first game near 20 years ago. However I recalled I was never a fan of Alpha Centari, not sure why but couldn't get into.
Then the reviews from players can out, and it was sad to read them, some had good views but there were a number of bad, which had put me off again buying it, even when it was on sale. However this free weekend event came up so this was now the opportunity I was waiting for, and after spending some time playing it, I am glad I have not bought it.
There is no question that this game is simply a revamped Civ 5 map, there are too many similarities to consider this a unique game, so to pay the asking price for a mod seems a bit scandelous imo.
One of the things I loved about Civ is its feel of urgancy, the need to progress and expand etc, unfortunatly I don't feel it in this game at all. Yes you go through the same process of creating cities (now called outposts), modify/improve the terrain to harvest resources etc, and decide if you are going to win via peace or by war. But the feeling is different, almost like its lost its passion for progress.
I found most of my time fighting aliens who are just modified barbarians from Civ, although they are a lot more tougher here then in Civ, especially the Worms (yes they ripped off Dune) or the Krakens (yes they ripped off Clash of the Titans). I would say that I spent most of my time fighting aliens and developing tech and units specifically to fight/defend against them then play the primary game, of politics and faction development. In fact by the time I was in a comfortable position I was lagging behind. In so many ways I did actually like this, after all you are on an alien world, but it simply stole the focus for me far too much. In Civ you could have raging barbarians enabled and still focus on other things.
Definatly one of things that is clearly missing in this game is its diversity of nations and attention to detail that came with said nations. Of course in this game its corporations that have merged such as the Pacific alliance etc, but still I didn't feel it, I didn't feel the passion that you got from meeting Catherine or Elizabeth or any other of the nation leaders in Civ in comparrison to this game, no feeling and in the end I didn't care about anything.
Unfortunatly with Steam reviews you can't put a score out of 10, but I would personally give it 6/10 because inspite its major flaws there are some good features, and features I would like to see again in say the next Civ game. Features such as the way units are upgraded or become unique depending on the chosen afiliation such as purity or dominance, this I really liked. Also the use of satalites was interesting, and never really expanded upon in the Civ games, except that you research the tech and it may offer some new unit or clear the map, but in this game you can use satalite based weapons or resource gathering. Another thing I liked was the specific special bonus you could choose when you built something for the first time, for example one specific building could offer either a science boost or culture boost, the choice was yours, that I liked. Imagine building a barracks and the bonus option would be if new units recieved attack or defensive or even line of sight or movement bonuses, some great ideas there I think could be developed more.
So I am sorry to say but this game is not being bought anytime soon, but for all the negatives there were some positives and I suppose if any subsequent DLC added a bit more passion into the game that fans of Civ expect, there is potential to turn this game around, it would make the fact that this is purely a mod a bit easier to swollow.

Tiny and Big is a prime example of what makes a good indie game, with brilliantly realised mechanics wrapped up in a charming presentation. Though the game will take, at most, a few hours to be completed, you won't really mind once you realise just how much fun you can have slicing at the environment and playing around with the physics. The intentionally sketchy cel-shaded comic strip artstyle isn't bad on the eyes either, with practically every scene of the game suffused with vibrant colour that brings to mind a graphic novel. The soundtrack, drawn from a variety of bands both eclectic in nature and independant in mode, is notably unique, while still being catchy and fitting the game itself perfectly. There are a number of collectables and challenges for completionists to work with. In short, it's an unknown gem, a perfect example of what makes an indie game good.
Besides, how many games revolve around recovering a pair of supernatural underwear?

I came across this game for a dollar while I was looking for a decent action/adventure game. What I was found gave me mixed feelings. The game "Silver Knight," while looking like a school project thrown together in a week at first look, is actually a decent game. Its nice, simple use of pixelated graphics compliment it nicely with the environments. However, the gameplay can be rather dull. It boils down to you entering room after room, killing all inside before moving on. I've yet to find powerups or anything that could spice it up a bit. It feels slower than it should be, but that issue is easily fixable through the game's "dash" action. Something I actually haven't seen much use of in other RPGs. The battle is pretty hit and miss, but the rooms being so small limit your ability to actually do much first off without falling flat on your face and having to start over. Each enemy will aimlessly rush you with no sense of surprise or actual strategy, and bombs will be the lifeblood of your playthrough. The controls, to be blunt, are awkward and shoddy, the whole character stops moving when you swing your sword in a decently-lengthed animation, but in crowds this becomes a futile task that only dashing out or using a bomb will fix.
Overall?: 6/10 as a game, 7/10 for the price, even on sale.

This was my first game on steam and is, to date, the one I enjoyed the most.
It may not be a game for everyone: difficulty can get high at times and the random aspect of things sometimes manages to put you in a tight place, but it's so... majestic.
You face actual battlefield problems: your units don't follow your every whim, and you can't tell them what to do step by step, you can only order them in a general way (and actually know what actions they'll do before deciding). Same with equipment: every unit manages its own gear, and sometimes asks for material or advice. (Wiki can help if you want more control in this field).
Story is interesting, with quite the plot twist towards the ending, beware.
Art is still quite good despite its age (and was actually too heavy at the time).

This game, though not as atmopsheric as the first game is nonetheless a wonderful experience to behold. The combat system, if somewhat imbalanced the first round is more exciting here. You get a whole host of new weapons to wield and with the camera research system, it also awards you for being creative enough to combine multiple ways to destroy your enemies. The hacking system has also been revamped and greatly improved, no longer must you figure out how to twist and place tubes but instead try to hack system whilst dodging enemy fire makes for a exciting experience.
The choice system is also more nuanced and rather than ending with Very Good vs Very Bad, it takes into account how your actions with non-Little Sister characters would affect you (greatly missing from the first game).
The story expands the Rapture universe, if the first game is somewhat large-than-life when it comes to your characters, Bioshock 2 helps makes them more human. It also smartly avoids to try and emulate the first twist that was the first game and made the storyline simple, you're a Big Daddy and now you must rescue your Little Sister. Rather than just keeping it that simple, it also introduces Ryan's counterpart with Sofia Lamb, who is an antagonist who took the extreme version of Ryan's much hated Altruism to its logical point (and this works better here than Bioshock Infinite's extremism comparisons but I digress).
One of the few cons, however is that the creepy atmosphere of the first game is quite missing. Even though you're exploring the more downtrodden areas of Rapture, I find it more bright and more combat focused than the beginning. And the PC version had audio bugs and glitches that seriously undermines the more dramatic aspects of the game. Imagine you're playing an area where you're besieged by Splicers but the audio decides to fritz up and you fight in total silence. I would also like to comment on how this game crashes at odd moments - if you're the sort to forget to save once in a while, say goodbye to your progress and you will be forced to replay the level from the beginning.
The Multiplayer aspect is a hit and miss. It would have been fun but due to a lack of servers, you'd forced to either wait for some time for everyone to play (and even then it's rare for one to be able to play anything besides Civil War). Forget about a balance firefight as well, since this game loves to match the newbies with veterans and it's not uncommon to pitch a group pf low leveled players against more experienced ones and watch as a team gets slaughtered in the process. But to be able to see the areas you could only explore in Bioshock return here was amazing, even if you could only explore it solo.
I would still recommend this game to anyone who enjoyed Bioshock but wanted some improvements with certain game mechanics. All in all, this game is a worthy addition to the Bioshock series. 4/5

2K Games does it again with a beautiful story, fantastic gameplay, and wonderful internal environment. BioShock 2 has it all and pushes the greatness of the series to new heights.
Taking place after the original life has been brought back to the lost, but never forgotten city of Rapture. Professor Lamb has started working to bring young girls back down to the deep city and start cultivating Adam once again. Her idea of a utopia exists unlike Ryan’s which is based on uncontrolled capitalism Lambs is based on true altruism, the idea of the true utopia. You as one of the original Big Daddy’s have been brought back to life to save Eleanor, your Little Sister from a fate worse than death. Will you be able to make it in time?
There are nine levels: Adonis Luxury Resort, Atlantic Express, Ryan Amusements, Pauper’s Drop, Siren Alley, Dionysus Park, Fontaine Futuristics, Outer Persephone, and Inner Persephone. The levels in this campaign vary in length drastically, some of them being relatively short while others are overly massive. You have varying objectives in each area: find items, fight bosses, activate switches, find little sisters, etc. These keep the campaign interesting and each area has its own spin on how it wants you to play. The campaign is well laid out and each area has its own twists that make it unique.
The game plays differently than the original, as you are no longer a mere mortal but rather one of the machines you fought so hard to defeat. You wield all weapons single handedly allowing you to equip plasmids in your other hand. This way you can shoot a gun as well as light a foe on fire, personally I was so used to the first one I forgot half the time I could do this. When I finally realized I still found myself not using it as the menu interface to change between plasmids was not as dynamic. This games combat realistically was drastically improved; no longer did you need to keep pulling out the camera during battle to get the best shot, instead you just clicked and it recorded while you were in combat giving you a score for the battle. The remote hacking tool allows you to actually hack cameras, which you could do in the first one but was very tricky as they would almost always detect you before you started the hack. Plus the wrench was changed to a drill which had multiple attack types making it more dynamic. In BioShock I actually used the Wrench all game, so I decided to only use ranged weapons this time round. There are three key combat elements in this game: Weapons, Plasmids (like spells), and tonics (like buffs). The weapons, plasmids, and tonics really allow you to customize your play style. By choosing specific tonics in combination with weapon choose and plasmid choice you can decide if you want to be a melee master, a total hacker, or gunning madman. Plus each weapon, plasmid, and tonic has upgraded versions which make them even more effective and variable.
I wasn't sure about Minerva's Den, usually DLC campaigns are just extra levels and lose the elements that make a game great. Minerva's Den was the complete opposite, in fact this DLC story rivals that of the original. There are three levels: Minerva's Den, Operations, and The Thinker. The first two levels are exceptionally large and have many missions/puzzles invovled and the final level is a boss fight. This DLC adds an exceptional amount of depth including a new weapon (Ion Laser) a new Plamid (Gravity Well), two new tonics, and four new enemies. This is an amazing new campaign which offers a brilliant story and fantastic new elements to the BioShock series.
BioShock 2 is an amazing game; although, it doesn’t stand up to the story of the original it still provides an amazing play-through. The story itself is relatively well written, and in comparison to non-BioShock games is actually quite brilliant. The combat is fun and rather in-depth with each weapon having three ammo types including the melee tool gives a huge variety to your combat style. You can even customize your tonics and plasmids to enforce the type of gameplay you desire. BioShock really is the FPS for anyone looking for a great story, invigorating combat, epic boss battles, and cool puzzles. I would recommend this game at full price, but if you’re frugal like me and only buy games on sale then wait as anything below its normal price is a steal.
Pros:
+Fantastic story
+Beautiful game environment
+Loads of weapons, with different ammo types
+Many plasmids (spells) to choose from with upgraded levels
+Loads of tonics (passives) to equip which customize your gameplay experience
+Three difficulty settings, for all levels of gamers to enjoy.
+New dynamic to the BioShock series revealing the inner sanctum of the Big Daddy.
+Offers DLC to extend the experience.
Cons:
-The game allows you to set the difficulty in the menu. I started the game on “Hard” and somehow it dropped to “Medium” at some point. I didn’t notice until a hint popped up about 1/3 the way through when I thought to myself how easy the game was. I bumped it up again to “Hard” and kept a check on it for the rest of the campaign, but this change resulted in my not being able to get the “Against All Odds” achievement.
-The game would crash randomly for no reason, I did a verify integrity check but it said the game was fine. In turn I started saving every five minutes so I wouldn’t lose much if it crashed.
For the love of god..... DISABLE VOICE CHAT. How this feature isn't in the game, I don't know. Other than that, great game!

Story
Story revolves around a man who is sick and tired of humanity's existence. Wants to get his revenge on all of the human existence and starts a "genocide crusade" in suburban neighborhood. You get initial cut scene also cut scenes at the end of each level to learn what is happening in the story. Mostly just letting you where and what you will be doing next the story really does not really dig in the character mental state or of his past. The writing in the game is the really where the game fell short I liked the cheesy on liners but after a while got very repetitive.
Gameplay
Is a solid stick-shooter has very intense moments and the destructive environment really is top notch. Really pushes the player to pay attention, move and dodge. There are a variety of weapons to choose from but some ammo for the better weapons is scares so use wisely. There are some fantastic mission location in the game making every level a new experience and feel refreshed. Most of the missions are kill xx many civilians, shields (Police), and military with some survive xx amount of time. Also you have the option to do have few side missions to gain respawn tokens to help with the hard missions so you won’t have to start the mission over again. Controls are great for a stick shooter and respond as expected. There have been a few game bugs and had a few crashes but nothing too serious and hoping to be patched in the future. Game is around 4 to 6 hours depending if you explore the levels or just speed run threw them. Also have 3 different difficulty levels to keep thing interesting.
Visuals and Sound
The visuals are great Black/white but have color on blood, fire, Lights and explosions this really works in this game. The only issue is sometimes enemies get lost in dark spots and you have to highlight them by viewing your objectives. Voice acting is solid but suffers from some cheesy writing and one liners that get repetitive. The music is hit and miss for me some of the levels I feel there was more intense situations going on and the music did not match. Other times the music really felt like it added to the level and really felt like it belonged on that mission.

The Last Remnant is simply put, not my cup of tea. Though Graphically pretty, and with a soundtrack that is altogether pleasing to hear- it's bogged down by a number of it's other elements.
First and foremost is the story itself, which places you in the shoes of 'Rush', a none-too-bright seeming hot-blooded youth whose on a quest to save his sister, because she was kidnapped in the first 5 minutes of the game. Not only is the main character tedious to listen to, if only because he comes off as dense (and not really comically so), but the game's story tends towards being presented in drawn out cutscenes which tend to either obligate you to sit through the entire thing, or skip it and potentially miss some important plot points. Really, the moments where I got exposition or party quests where I could click X to advance when I had read something? I was blissfully happy.
So, the Storys a bust, but can the fighting system and rpg elements save it? ...Sadly, not for me. Last remnant has mechanics which make me -long- for when I was playing FF13 ..And I wasn't a large fan of that game either.
My specific issue is this :: First off, you are given squads to toss your various characters into, and you give orders to those squads as a whole- though, the way that they execute these orders is seemingly random at times. (And no, you can't set someone to predictively heal, even though you totally know a lightning bolt is coming your way). Healing can only be done as an order -after- you've taken damage.And that's -if- the option comes up, which can make combat frustrating, even when you placed healers in multiple of your squads.
Sure, you can direct your squad tot ry and use their magic or physical special attacks, but you can't actually control which individuals in the squad use them.
Which, I suppose is compounded by the fact that whilst the levelups/stat gains your characters get are semi random (Though partially associated with the actions you take), your overall battle level is not random, and as that increases ..it increases the overall difficulty of the game. meaning that if you stop to run sidequests, to try and farm for equipment material, or simply get lost - Well, you're quite liable to make the game more difficult for yourself, than if you had simply endeavoured to rush towards the end.
Mechanically, the idea of moving your squads around the battlefield was interesting, as was flanking- but at the end of the day, it generally seemed to almost always work more in the favor of the enemy than yourself , as you frequently end up in 2 squad vs 8 squad fights if you're not diligent at picking 1 on 1 fights. And, flanking is frequently moot against a number of the tougher enemies, since they -can't- be flanked (But can flank you).
Overall, had there been less left up to RNGesus, I would have continued to persist in attempting to slog through the game- but after 12 or so hours, my patience finally exhausted itself.

YS, Final Fantasy, Phantasy Star, Chrono-Trigger and dragon quest introduced us to RPG games.
They are games built on wide open world exploration, character interaction, story development and combat mechanics.
Final fantasy being one of the star RPG game Serie evolved greatly over the years.
From massive maze exploration, character class system, mini-game, card game, 2D, 3D and even racing everything has been tried and changed over the years from game to game. From 13 days before the game begin to the 13 chapter of game.
From Moral conflict to meaning of life and death.
From 3as1 final boss to complete focus in life.
This is probably the one and only final fantasy game that made me stop and think for deeper meaning that may or may not be there.
Fantastic Graphics, Wondrous music, well done Sound effect, semi realistic CG graphics, Typical Japanese game setting built up into one very solid RPG. I can even overlook the lack of side quests, mini-game and linear map design and automatic fast pace combat. (I want to control my teammate damn it...) Make a bit story choice here and there with consequence would be better.
9/10 for solid Japanese RPG and may this RPG Serie live long and prospers.

Hatred is dull.  Why is that you say?  Because, every aspect of this twin-stick shooter is dull, repetitive, frustratingly difficult at the later levels.  Oh and the game is 4 hours...  Giving how little this game offers, there's absoultely no reason to replay it once the credits starts rolling.  Hatred tries to go for dark/edgy story and it ends up being pointless and very comical.  In fact, the game tries to make the main character feel very important, but given how stereotypical his character is.  He ends up being so unlikable throughout this boring genocidal rampage.  His lines are so cringeworthy that I almost feel sick from hearing it.
The levels are extremly repetitive, as you go out shoot and kill many civiains in order to advance to the next area and do it again.  You do sometimes have different objectives that isn't invold in killing, but getting to one place and then you go kill more people...  That's pretty much what Hatred is.  The game suprisingly have fantastic controls and thats the only good part about this game.  The destruction is also nice, but not as impressive like in Battlefield: Bad Company 2!  The shooting itself is ok and the enemy AI is decent at best.  Not much to say a whole lot thou.
Oh right, Hatred also has the worst checkpoint system ever and it adds nothing but problems to the game.  Those checkpoints gives you continues as you do repetitive side task by doing exact same thing that you do throughout the whole game. (KILLING PEOPLE!!!)  Once you earned it, you better make sure you don't die that often, because this game gets ridiciously hard very late in the game.  If you die you will respawn back to the first checkpoint.  Sadly, the game does a very poor job on this, as you will mostly respawn back to the first place you earned it at or sometimes the respawns can get you killed or worse, getting stuck!  Make one fatal mistake and it will cost you a continue, lose all those continues and its game over and you'll have to start all over at the beginning of the god damn level.
Overall, its a poor game and a waste of value!  There's no multiplayer for that matter and a lack of bonus extras.  I don't know why this got so much attention, its a painfully average game with almost nothing new brought to the table.  Do yourself a favor: go spend your money on The Witcher III, than playing this game!

This is one of those very rare games that gets EVERYTHING right. It's an instant recommendation to anybody with even a passing interest in space combat/trading games. 10/10.
Gameplay: Starting out with a peice of junk spaceship/peashooter, you fight and trade across a number of solar systems, buying upgrades & better ships as you go. Combat is really good fun - like Sid Miers Pirates! on steroids. Configurable turrets, loads of cominations of weapons with different stats, shield arcs, subsystems damage, free for all and group battles. Basically everything. Trading is really fun too, with supply/demand, random events, and smuggling. You can get hidden weapons and ships by joining guilds. The controls also deserve a mention - perfect with an xbox pad.
Presentation: The game is gorgeous, both technically and in design. The devs have nailed the space cowboy/western trope. The ship and station design has a good rugged industrial feel to it, and the space environments are spectacular. Beautiful blue nebula, fading atmospheres extending up from the surface of planets, and searing white heat from stars have all been rendered perfectly. Charachter models in stations/via-comms are excellent too, which is nice considering they're not the main focus. The devs clearly know their way around the graphics API because all the shiny bells & whistles are implimented to good effect and in the right places.
Sound: This should be under "presentation", but it deserves it's own catagory because it's so good. SLIDE GUITAR. Good grief I love slide guitar. If there soundtrack were an album, it's one I'd actually buy, which is something I've never thought about a game before. It changes dynamically on the situation too, which is great. The music really cements the feel of the game and it's a big contribution to the success in nailing the space cowboy theme.
Content: I'm 20 hours in and I'd guess I'm around 1/3 of the way through the game. That's plenty of content for the price. The placement of stations and missions are procedurally generated too, so there will be some variation if you want to have more than one playthough. You'll get your moneys worth out of this game.
Technical: I run the game on max settings on 3 year old hardware, with no issues. The devs are actively pushing out patches and post on the forums. Good job.
Overall: 10/10. The devs nailed this one and they must be delighted. Buy it.

I feel my time spent with this game warrants that I write a review about it. Considering I managed to play it all the way back during beta even before early access I think my review should be acceptable in the least.
Battlerite is, simply put, an arena brawler. No farming no towers no cores nothing. Just teamfights. Dynamic, fast-paced and ultimately rather fun teamfights. The game tries to put focus on trying to outmaneuver your oppponents, bait them in certain situations and eventually understanding them enough to know what they will most likely do in certain situations and thus enabling yourself to act accordingly. It is a very, very skill based game.
The game has it's ups and downs but cmon, what else is new in video games? Here is a list of pros and cons:
PROS:
-Balanced champion roster
-Nice visual effects
-Engaging gameplay
-Robust gameplay mechanics
-Short matches(5-10 minutes tops)
-Tons of cosmetics(a lot more to be added in the coming days for F2P launch)
-PC and Console support
-Odeum
-Low system requirements(runs smoothly on my potato i3 laptop)
-Seasonal events, tournaments, achievements(with in-game rewards), quest system, champion progression etc.
CONS:
-Ai is pretty bad and many champions are missing AI profiles(only a couple of champions keep rotating when you play vs AI)
-Requires an excellent internet connection(avoid playing on WiFi or you will rage, a lot xd)
-New UI still needs ton of work(altho it's pretty good to use on consoles since it was made specifically with them in mind)
-Tends to become stale when there are no special events and no new champion releases for a while
-One mistake can lose you the round(not sure if a con tho or something else entirely xd)
-Ranked matchmaking can be pretty bad if you don't tick the "Strict Matchmaking" option(which prolongs the waiting time for quite a bit, might not be an issue after F2P launch since more ppl will play it)
The game still needs a lot of work to reach it's full potential but man is it good even now. Matches can be really close and there is never a boring match, especially if it's ranked. It feels exciting to play the game and cmon, once it goes F2P(in 3 days) there is nothing stopping you from trying it out. It's a super fun game but don't expect to go winning all the time at first. You will struggle. It's just how the game is. Very competitive. That's it from me.

Version 3.53 :
Egosoft has finally made X Rebirth a proper X3 sequel!  Although X3 Terran Conflict (TC) and Albion Prelude (AP) are arguably better games for many reasons, X Rebirth is finally in a state that is worth playing.  It's not perfect – there are still many graphical issues, performance bottlenecks, and annoying restrictions that keep the game from being great, but it is worth 15 or 20 dollars if you find it on sale for that price.
For fans of X3 and the series, it is worth coming back to and trying again.  I waited until 3.0 to get back into the game since its disappointing release.  It wasn't unexpected that release day would be problematic: There was plenty of evidence that this happened to prior games in the series and that Egosoft added many features post-release that should have been available on release day.  Still, despite how bad the game was when it came out, Egosoft has written the wrongs right.  I never had any doubt that they would get to 3.0.  But for those who are still bitter about the release: Their anger is justified, however, outdated.  X Rebirth has had a second rebirth.
Why does this game now deserve your time?  It is probably the easiest X game in the series to get started with.  Unlike the other X games, the story/tutorial does explain most of what you need to know in the game(although the campaign gets frustrating at times).  Egosoft recently posted videos explaining advanced features that I would have never been able to figure out on my own.  The missions are also more friendly, giving you the ability to make money early without drudging through 50 hours of poverty trading energy cells.  The combat isn't the best part; and I find that exploration is lacking a bit as well.  So if those two features drew you to this game, get X3TC or AP instead.  This game highlights station building with an emphasis on building an empire as well as trading and building a fleet.  Station building is the only feature I can definitively say I like more than X3.  It is my personal favorite part of the X series, and it may be the reason I end up playing X Rebirth more than the 1000 hours I put into X3.
If you are new to the X series, you may want to move on to X3 TC and AP if you're looking for more fun and more challenge after X Rebirth.  AP is also easier than TC, so that game may be a preferable next step.  I would recommend playing all these games with a joystick though.  I use a yoke myself, and I find that much more immersive.  You may also want to run the soundtrack for X Rebirth in the background -- it is absolutely awesome but half of the music doesn't seem to appear anywhere in the whole game.
In the end, this game isn't worth 40 dollars.  It probably isn't even worth 30 unless you've already paid 300 bucks for a ship in Star Citizen.  I'd say buy it if it's under 25 if you're a space genre fan or empire builder.  This is just my opinion of course; I preordered the collector's edition.  I have no regrets though.  It was worth it for me.
Note: The Teladi Outpost DLC is a small addition of content, probably worth 3 to 5 dollars.  It's nice to explore and build in a new region of space.
My opinion and final thoughts: This huge game was made by a small developer, which inevitably means it's very rough around the edges. It's my opinion that most people who gave this game negative reviews think that it had a development team as large as Skyrim with a massive budget. I read many times about how X Rebirth (the game) was compared against Star Citizen (the idea), and somehow Star Citizen won almost every time. I find that line of thinking to be completely irrational. And I'm hard-pressed to find a game on steam that received lower ratings than X Rebirth (27% in 2014), even amongst games that were abandoned by their developers. X Rebirth seems to be the game that appeared at the wrong place and the wrong time.
I nominated this game for the "Test of Time" award.

When X-Rebirth came out now a year ago, I did not write a review although I definetly wanted to, there where however enough negative reviews already and that was all I was going to contribute, I wanted to back off from the whole debacle to allow for the devs to fix the bugs, make improvements and deliver new content. I was a big fan of this company and played all the previous X titles, spending thousands of hours in total across all the X series.
My first experience with X-Rebirth the moment it became available to play just as so many others had experienced was terrible, below are some of the many problems at the time I found with the inital release.
1) The first few times it crashed at menu.
2) The next several times it crashed 10-30 minutes in the game and a few more crashes at menu in between.
3) The FPS was terrible getting 10-15 FPS when panning mostly.
4) I could not proceed with missions after the first few.
5) Once my freighter got stuck and would not collect the energy cells, causing me to have to restart.
6) I found it absolutely ridicoulous that some way into the missions I was the enemy of most sectors.
7) The menu system was cumbersome.
8) I was stuck in one ship
9) NPC's being terrible drawn and the annoying character Yisha, particularly saying shutup to the computer.
10) I could go on with many more.
So there have been quite a few updates and 2 expansions since then, I have kept the game updated and tried it out a few times to see its progress, If it becomes as good as the existing titles I will play it through. It has in my opinion not changed enough for me to want to play it through.
A lot of the bugs have been fixed, It no longer crashes at the menu nor while playing, the NPCs are still terrible in rendering, animation and dialogue, Yisha no longer says shutup everytime to the computer, it has been greatly limited. It's still there and really needs to be removed all together. The biggest thing however is that the menu has not changed in the slightest, it is still needlessly cumbersome.
Also you are still stuck in one ship, no matter what game option you want to play you are still in the Albion Pride and still with Yisha. In the other X titles, choosing a different game start ment you where in a different ship, this really needs to be introduced into the game.
The new expansion The Teladi Outpost does not deliver on all the improvements it claims just as the inital release did not deliver on what it claimed, X Rebirth is still a failure and worthy of its low rating amongst critics and customers both new and old alike.

Long story short, this is not a complete game.
For what civ 5 offers, the cost of this is waaaaaaay over priced and offers even LESS than what civ 5 offers. Yea, you can argue that civ 5 had add ons that improved it drastically and added even mroe diversity to what was already a decent game. The civs in this game are a great concept but there isn't enough diversity in them to make multible matches interesting. Resources in this game are really lacking and units barely have any diversity. The affinities are an interesting idea but the fact that they are required for most win conditions force you to reasearch multiple sciences which makes the complex looking science tree suffer from a similar issue to what civ 5's tree did (a false sense of complexity). The win conditions also seem similar and some win conditions are much easier to acomplish than others.
The pros of this game are it's ideas and what the creaters are attempting to accomplish. The fact that you are attempting to survive on on a alien world and the tiemline takes palce in a futuristic timeline is what makes things appealing. The nature of the aliens isn't as linear as the civ 5 barbarians and the environment is very well established.
Wait until the developers improve this game and/or until add on content.

So the Silver Knight, you are probably wondering whats it about. Well in this 16-bit Dungeon Crawling RPG, there is a devious Black Knight who travels the world to hunt down princesses and torture them. You as the "Silver Knight" are chosen to slay this wicked fiend for his trechery and at the same time reacquaint with your lover. He comes across the Black Knight and starts following him to wherever he is going. That's the pretty much general story of whats happening. After that you left in a room dying and you must begin your journey.
The game controls are quite simple with the usual WASD to move, Number 1 to Attack and Number 2 to Dash while dropping sweet bombs with E. With these weapons in your arsenal you are expected to traverse through these dungeons. In my first few attempts in this game I noticed had similar gameplay as Binding of Issac, with moving around dungeons and planting bombs on the ground wasn't a bad feeling. The hit mechanics majority of the time is perfect and dashing helps ya a lot although would be nice if there was some stamina bar (as you can constantly spam dash). Pretty much in this game you will be hack'n'slashing for quite some time with a diverse list of enemies including  the usual spiders, wretched fairies (no idea), some toxic waste slime monster, suicide bombing imps and occasionally a mixture of both fused in one (Slime spewing out fairies).
The Map design and graphics so far are quite morbid and desolate which compliments with the constant music that is playing on the background. Each map level is quite different from the other and as the game mentions monsters spawn differently everytime you replay the game. With this factor sometimes the game can get a bit hectic and quite challenging as you also have a limited health supply of 5 HP. That saying the game is great so far but as expected from any early access it is not complete.
There are some bugs in this game which can make this game frustrating and some a bit more entertaining in which I will take the time to point out. Some of the maps if ya spam your dash can actually make you go through the wall and into a different part of the game. However please be advised by doing this some maps can trap you in limbo thanks to invisible walls and you are pretty much screwed. Enemies sometimes cannot be hit and can double hit ya even before whacking it and sometimes they spawn invisibly and you won't know killed ya. At occasions when potions are dropped in-game your character might have to spam the dash button into and eventually it will pick it up. These bugs are expected in this early access so shouldn't detract you from playing.
Only thing I wish the developer could have done was perhaps add some more RPG elements say leveling to improve the protagonist as he can be puny against baby spiders and perhaps some more abilities.
Anyway this game ain't your walk in the park type, you will die quite a lot and from that you learn more about this game. I have played a good hour and I haven't encountered the bosses yet due my lack of skills. If you are thinking off trying this game out I highly recommend it as it is quite unique with a straightfoward story, near-perfect mechanics and great design however, if ya not a fan of bugs I'd wait it out to be more completed. To the developer kudos for the and I hope you this review to better improve your game.

First of all: yes, as of now (i.e. without DLCs) Beyond Earth is indeed not much more than Civ V with a stellar paint job. But that does not make it a game not worth recommending, in my opinion. It does set its own accents and brings a bit of a fresh breeze to the Civ franchise with the new unit upgrade paths and all the other affinity-specific gimmicks.
However, this game would have greatly benefited from more features distinguishing it from its predecessor... just like good ol' Alpha Centauri was very different from Civ 2 (and Call To Power, which was released around the same time) with its 3D terrains, well thought-through diplomacy and modular units.
Nonetheless, Beyond Earth still gets the Civ formula right ("...just one more turn and then I might do something useful instead...") and is enjoyable to play, although I can imagine that one might be prone to putting this game aside sooner than Civ V with all major DLC in its current state.
Still, I would rate Civ:BE with something like 7/10, which is admittedly not very good for a Civ game, but still something 4X fans shouldn't miss out on. Current recommendation: Get it while on sale or if you don't own Civ V. Otherwise, wait for the first DLC ;)
