I feel like my last review wasn't clear enough about what I disliked about the game, so I will edit it down to be more concise:
The game itself feels unfinished, like it was a weekend project being churned out to make a quick buck, in this case literally, since the game itself, upon this review, is about $1.79 to play.
So, what makes this game unfinished? Well, many of the sounds are missing, mainly around the player character. Considering the character is a knight, it's generally expected you'd have a "whoosh" whenever you swing, but in this case, there's no sound. When you take damage, there aren't any indicators, visibly nor audibly, which makes managing how many hits you've taken rather difficult to maintain. Minor complaint, but it serves as a disconnect to the gameplay, in my opinion. Also, for some reason, there isn't even a death animation, so when you die, it says "Game Over", but you can still move around and attack.
As for the layout, it's rather linear. A lot of the rooms appear to have other areas to explore, but in reality, it's just a small cell where you defeat enemies and move on, much like Binding of Isaac, without the variation.
Story-wise, well, there isn't much of one, to be honest. The main antagonist apparently kidnaps and tortures princesses, but in the illustrations, it shows him murdering, maiming, and dismembering them, FAR from what the story leads to believe. And apparently your role is to save your princess...as far as from what I can tell, she's probably already dead. Apart from the story, as this game is being catered to an English-literate community, more effort needs to be made into proofreading, since there are many mistakes that need correction in that regard.
Overall, the game is an interesting concept, despite the flaws. For now though, unless the developer adds more content and variety, asking for people to pay, even the current $1.79 as of the re-writing of this review, is not acceptable in the game's current state. Until more is added and the game is better completed, I cannot recommend the game.

You may have heard of this game a couple years ago when it came out on the XBox 360 (alright, more than a couple years.) It received mediocre reviews many because the game was a technical mess. Several years after that, it was released on PC, with additional content and most of the technical issues fixed. The result is a great JRPG that feels truly spectacular.
THE STORY
The story is easily the main reason to play this game. It never failed to entertain, and I ended up actually caring about what was happening to the onscreen characters. The world feels lived in, and every city is bustling with life. There are different races of beings, and lots of monsters to fight and quests to undertake. The Voice Acting is actually really good for it being a JRPG. All of the characters are voiced well, even if there are some lines that still sound a little weird.
THE GAMEPLAY
This is genrally where people have problems. The game doesn't explain a whole lot in terms of gameplay mechanics, so much like Dark Souls, I strongly suggest frequently consulting the wiki or online forums to fully understand how every system works and the different items that come into play during battles. Speaking of battles, fighting enemies is Fast, Fun, and Flashy. It's a turn based RPG, but has a battle system most similar to Xenoblade Chronicles. There's different kinds of attacks that you can do, summons you can call, and special moves that come into play. Units gain stats at the end of battles rather than levels. You also command the entire unit, rather than individual characters. The effects for battles look cool, and strategy must be used for the tougher battles. This is one of the few RPG's where grinding doesn't actually guarantee you'll have an easier time. You gain Battle Ranks (BR) after a certain amount of enemies or encounters have been defeated. However, enemies and bosses scale their levels with you, often times gaining more health or learning new moves after you reach a certain rank. There are frequent quicktime events during battle, often times to parry or improve unit cohesion, letting you move before the enemy. There is a setting you can turn on where MOST of these are automatically resolved, and they almost always succeed.
THE WORLD
All the characters and creatures are beautifully designed and animated. As mentioned before, the world feels lived in, with lots of NPC's to interact with. While it's not an open world, the map is expansive, split into segments of places you can go, which include a multitude of environments. There are components to collect, weapons you can upgrade, craft, or improve, and lots of rare items and weapons are hidden throughout each "level."
THE MUSIC
Definitely one of the highlights of the game. The music is awesome, and even after almost 80 hours of play, it never got old, and the rousing battle music never failed to inspire. There were certain taverns I would just stand in so I could listen to the music. It's always appropriate to the situation, changing to reflect how you're doing in battle.
THE BAD
While I enjoyed the vast majority of the game, there were still a few gripes. Technical issues still exist, though not nearly at the level they did before. There's some screen tearing during the first and last cutscenes of the game, and pop-in textures almost always occured when entering a new area or seeing a new story element, though the issues stop after a second or so. Much of the game's combat and crafting systems I had to look up on wiki's to understand, as the game doesn't do a great job of explaining them (if it explains them at all). The ending of the game I also wished would have been fleshed out more, as it can be a bit abrupt (but it's not a bad ending).
OVERALL
Overall, this was an excellent game marred by some minor technical issues and confusing gameplay, but bolstered by it's strong story, combat, and music. I recommend it if you are a fan of RPG's JRPG's or have a lot of time to spend on big games. I'd rate this game 8/10.

Consider the start of FF4; once the king orders you to go to Mist, you really only have two meaningful options: go to Mist, or diddle around and fight random encounters. Only one of them is going to progress the story. The situation is much the same in FF13 (though with a different definition of "random encounters"). In fact, consider most of FF4. Consider the first half of FF6. Consider everything before getting the Epoch in Chrono Trigger*. In all these cases, the situation is the same. All three of those games are exceptionally good, yet are all about as linear as FF13.

To get it out of the way, I start by saying I have been a fan of Final Fantasy since the original NES game.  It's a series I grew up on.  Games with a group of characters that I (mostly) enjoyed to journey with.  This is also my second purchase of this game, since I had it on my PS3 but had only got to Gran Pulse before my console died.
With that all out of the way...
This game continues a loss of direction for the franchise as a whole.  While you are a party trying to accomplish heroic deeds, you never feel like you are playing as a party.  You are controlling 1 character, while the rest of the group mills about to themselves.  It means the game lacks the "plucky group of adventurers" part of FF I enjoyed.  It's also super obvious they focus the game around Lightning, which doesn't help the storytelling at all.  She suffers little growth throughout the game other than accepting Snow at the end (spoilers), and that has more to do with him impressing upon her that he's not just a headstrong idiot.
Which leads me in to the likeability of the character.  They range from annoying to insufferable.  By the end of the game, the only character who I didn't actively dislike was Sazh, and even then they make him annoyingly bumbling at times.  Your mileage may vary, but I really didn't bond with this group.  Since the introduction of set characters, there is always at least one companion in each game that will be met with derision.  This game is unique because it's not just some characters, but all of the characters.
I generally don't play games for story; I have yet to play a game with a story that engaged me (I play for characters).  However, even with objective eyes this game is a little lacking in narative.  It has good snippets, mostly the flashbacks to events before the game, but the game itself lacks interesting evolution with ever worsening dialogue as the game progresses.  A good story should stir emotion and make your brain work...  This game will do neither.
Combat is flawed.  9/10 times you just select auto combat because it's faster than manual input and it's reasonably smart.  Sometimes, though, it will do stupid things, like use ruin as a commando instead of attack when attack is clearly doing significantly more damage to that target.  There is also noticeable delay in action activation after you fill your action queue which is aggrevating in a game with time sensitive combat.  Overall, it's frustrating and not actually fun.
Presentation-wise, it's fairly pretty.  While it has aged a bit since launch (mostly textures, specifically Lightning's skin) it's still nice to look at.  I do find the overall aesthetic pleasing, but character's are a little too noodle-y for me.  I also don't like the hanging sideburns on the Chocobo redesigns.  These are mostly nit picks, but I can't really complain too much about how it looks.
Specific comments about the port:  It's pretty bad.  While I didn't have crashing problems and my controller worked decently, there are huge performance drops.  You can mitigate it some with mucking with graphics options in your graphics driver's utility software or by using a 3rd party mod.  Still, no matter what you do, you will still have noticeable frame drops, and occasionally ♥♥♥♥♥ge like controls while the system is chugging around the problem.
I really can't recommend this game.  It's a disappointment for me, from start to finish.  It's not even a flawed gem, as the PC version is sometimes frustratingly unplayable because of slowdowns.  Add in repulsive characters, awful combat and ho-hum story to the technical shortcomings and you have a pretty game with nothing of value in it.

This game is for masochists. It probably has the most RNG out of any RPG I have ever played. Win? Lose? It is almost entirely up to the game to decide who wins or lose almost every battle.
That being said. I still love it. Although the game's RNG is so prevalent, there are also a ton of ways to slightly tip the scales in your favor (and boy do I mean very slightly). You choose the characters in each squad, the formation of the squads, the currently usable abilities of every character, making sure you have enough recovery items, manipulating characters into equiping stronger equipment, selecting how many "enemies" to pull into a single fight from the exploration view, ...
Yeah... this game is complex. Possibly the most complex RPG I have ever played, and that is saying something.
Another MAJOR topic before people get this game is the grinding and backtracking. You will be grinding, backtracking, and micromanaging a TON. But I always find it satisfying for some reason. You don't simply "level up." Instead your stats for each character are gradually granted at the end of each battle. Thus you have various stat ups on your characters pretty much every single battle. So you always get the sense that you are improving, even if it doesn't amount to most traditional leveling systems when you do the math.
Skipable Cutscenes!!!! Yay. Most RPG's do not contain skipable cutscenes (at least the RPG's I have played), and there are multiple bosses I had to fight ~10+ times. If I had to watch all the cutscenes again, it would have 100% been a dealbreaker. But so far I believe every cutscene is skipable.
Anywhere saving!!!! Yay. You can save your game pretty much anywhere in the game. No need to run back to a save circle. I often made save files after simply reorganizing my army in hopes that my new strategy would work better. There are lots of save slots (I think like 50 or something) so save away.
Also be prepared to google the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of this game. The game does absolutely nothing to teach you how equipment, items and customization work. There is no in-game beastary to find what enemy drops the item you need. There a lots of levels that require you to unlock successive areas via quests.
I really like how quests are handled in this game. You just do the quest on the spot. No saving up a giant list of things to do. No forgetting what part of a quest yo are on or who you need to talk to. Every quest is self contained.
Other topics:
Story? It's okay, but nothing amazing.
Voice acting? really hit or miss.
Sound/Music? surprisingly good. I love the world map theme especially.
Graphics? Really good. Tons of enemies and allies with great animations all around. However, the cutscenes are not up to pair with other Square Enix titles. But this game isn't really focused on the cutscenes.
Meh.... hopefully that is enough infor for you to judge if you want to give the game a try. If you are an RPG enthusiast this game is a must play due to how unique it is, and how incredibly complex the game is. I have currently played it for like 80 hours and I am still learning new things constantly.

I need only do it for a moment."
Then I got the citizens who went out for a stroll that evening and decided that they'd be buggered before they let some mass murdering lunatic ruin their night walk. However, there are some who are proactive and will grab firearms from their homes or one discarded by a long dead police officer and use it to defend themselves. Police have a tendency to to get close when it's not needed thus putting themselves needlessly in harms way but, a group of them can spell ruin for you if not handled cautiously. The controls could use some fine tuning and perhaps a lock-on function as I have to waste a small portion of ammo to get my aiming on target. Making the onscreen crosshair white so it blends with all the other black and white wasn't the best idea. There is stuttering here and there especially when near several police prowlers. Loading is tad too long and the switching between weapons should be shorten as it feels almost delayed.
There are also executions in the game which you are forced to perform on victims in anguish since by doing these you recover health. It won't take too long before you start to see a repeated execution animation and some are just you shooting them in the head. So this feature of the game can get a bit banal after a while. Not all executions are punctuated by an animation to save time you will just shoot them without cutting away. Still the animations will wear thin and start negatively impacting the flow of gameplay. The executions should've been optional like in God of War and used medkits, chicken, or a pork chop you pick from the ground as health items.
As a whole, it's a solid enough isometric shooter with a fresh enough premise to engage you with. If you enter in not expecting some outlandish gorefest, developer agenda, or Spec Ops: The Line styled narrative then you'll walk away with a decent experience that you can enjoy until something more substantial comes out.

I am going to make this as simple as possible:
PROS
* Awesome soundtrack!
* It's like Firefly, with aliens...
* Lots of ships, lots of gear!
* There is a story, but it's not required to enjoy the game!
* Combat is fast and furious.
* Lots of potential for future content.
* Random galaxy with each new character.
CONS
* It's space, but it's not a 3D experience... wut?
* No multiplayer... here's a suggestion: Rebel Galaxy: Empires (MMO)
* Travel is very time consuming which means a long grind for good gear.
* While the soundtrack is awesome, the limited number of tracks becomes repetitive.
* Ship customization/personalization is unavailable (paintjobs)
* Combat can be a bit chaotic at times. I find, by the time I get to precise targeting, the battle is over.
* No crew or ship boarding. No hijacking of other ships.
* It feels empty at times... I have a HUGE ship. Where are my crew? Better crew, better performance?
All in all, I am 8 hours into the game and JUST traveled to the second system. It's very easy to get lost in just existing in the galaxy without ever chasing the storyline. RG has incredible potential to be one of those games that I just play when I have nothing else to do. I can jump on, do a few missions, and jump off. I can play one character as a law abiding merchant that helps others and keeps their nose clean, and then start another character to join up with pirates and be a menace to the galaxy. There are many missed opportunities (3D galaxy, multiplayer, crews, explorable stations, actual character creation, etc) but there is a lot of room for them to expand on the game in the future. As it stands currently, it is a game I will use as a time filler when I just want to kick back, relax, and enjoy a stress-free gaming experience.
This is a great game, a little techincal difficulties, but it can be even greater when you play with your friends. So overall this would be a great game if you had friends, and you can play around!

After playing both games, I can honestly say that Bioshock had a better story compared to its sequel, which may be due to the original developer’s (Irrational Games) decision to not take part in making Bioshock 2, its sequel.
Nothing as prominent as:
Not to say that 2K Marin did a bad job.
They did, however, depict the symbiotic relationship between Big Daddy and Little Sister very well.
Particularly during Adam extraction, you must protect your Little Sister as she extracts Adam from dead splicers, which inevitably draws in Splicers to attack you for the Adam. Once you aquire all Adam from all the Little Sisters, you are forced into a fight with a Big Sister, an enemy more powerful than the Big Daddy.
Throughout the game, you will act, feel and immerse yourself as the Big Daddy until it becomes natural instinct.
9/10
In the first Bioshock the combat controls did not flow well, being unable to Shoot & Use Plasmids at the same time meant that you’d have to switch back and forth between Plasmid and Gun.
Now in Bioshock 2, they have made it possible to use Both Hands.
Hacking Turrets/Safes etc. are also simplified and improved. You no longer have to play these mini-games with pipes and instead land a needle on specific areas of the meter to hack. They’ve also included Remote-Hack darts that you can use to hack objects at far ranges, making you less reliant on freezing machines and hacking from close range.
Unfortunately, hacking now takes place in real time, meaning hacks don’t pause the game.
7/10
The Scares/Thrills from the first game’s atmosphere are not the same in this sequel. It feels diluted and unfresh, a possible product of having experienced Rapture before in the first game. I guess they decided to take away the Horror/Thriller element and replace it with a better gameplay experience.
Still, expect to see a small number of jump scares.
10/10

Battlerite is, simply put, an arena brawler. No farming no towers no cores nothing. Just teamfights. Dynamic, fast-paced and ultimately rather fun teamfights. The game tries to put focus on trying to outmaneuver your oppponents, bait them in certain situations and eventually understanding them enough to know what they will most likely do in certain situations and thus enabling yourself to act accordingly. It is a very, very skill based game.
The game has it's ups and downs but cmon, what else is new in video games? Here is a list of pros and cons:
PROS:
-Balanced champion roster
-Nice visual effects
-Engaging gameplay
-Robust gameplay mechanics
-Short matches(5-10 minutes tops)
-Tons of cosmetics(a lot more to be added in the coming days for F2P launch)
-PC and Console support
-Odeum
-Low system requirements(runs smoothly on my potato i3 laptop)
-Seasonal events, tournaments, achievements(with in-game rewards), quest system, champion progression etc.
CONS:
-Ai is pretty bad and many champions are missing AI profiles(only a couple of champions keep rotating when you play vs AI)
-Requires an excellent internet connection(avoid playing on WiFi or you will rage, a lot xd)
-New UI still needs ton of work(altho it's pretty good to use on consoles since it was made specifically with them in mind)
-Tends to become stale when there are no special events and no new champion releases for a while
-One mistake can lose you the round(not sure if a con tho or something else entirely xd)
-Ranked matchmaking can be pretty bad if you don't tick the "Strict Matchmaking" option(which prolongs the waiting time for quite a bit, might not be an issue after F2P launch since more ppl will play it)
The game still needs a lot of work to reach it's full potential but man is it good even now. Matches can be really close and there is never a boring match, especially if it's ranked. It feels exciting to play the game and cmon, once it goes F2P(in 3 days) there is nothing stopping you from trying it out. It's a super fun game but don't expect to go winning all the time at first. You will struggle. It's just how the game is. Very competitive. That's it from me.

After reading the reviews posted by users within two weeks of Civ:BE's release, I decided to hold off on buying the game until some DLCs and patches came out (or maybe even an expansion). I was mostly concerned by opinions stating that this game is just a rehashed version of Civ5, with very little discernible new content.
Now, after actually playing one full game of Civ:BE, I can disagree with those reviewers, up to a point. As similar as BE is to Civ5, major changes have been made to nearly every aspect of gameplay. On one hand, I didn't have to learn to play the game, since it was so similar to Civ5 (getting used to the UI took a little while, though), and on the other hand, the reworked culture system, technology web, the orbital layer, and the victory conditions themselves definitely made me think beyond the confines that Civ5 had set. I think I appreciated the tech web the most - your research decisions matter A LOT in this game, and it is NOT true that there is only one "best" tech path, no matter what the skeptics will have you believe.
I should also add that, when all is said and done, the game is FUN. I expect that it could be even more fun in multiplayer than in single player mode.
However I must admit that there is a reason for the mixed reviews the game has been getting, and I believe price (at this time: 49.99€ base price not including any discount) is a factor here. Some new features introduced into the Civilization franchise with Beyond Earth, i.e. quests and victory conditions involving the completion of "storyline" quests, are not entirely original when contrasted with other turn-based strategy titles - you can find them in earlier games, like Endless Legend, to name one off the top of my head. Moreover, carrying over the same "leader" text from Civ5 was not a smooth move - nothing angers gamers more than even the slightest hint that a game is made using a "cookie cutter" (particularly those who have paid full price), even if the game is essentially different.
My final problem with Civ:BE is the AI, case in point: first playthrough, difficulty level Gemini, I made huge mistakes choosing research in mid-game, was slow to expand, had next to no military for a long while, CRUSHED THE COMPS UTTERLY AND COMPLETELY IN SPITE OF IT ALL. Unfortunately, this was also a problem in Civ5 (a game I love dearly for its hotseat mode).
To those who have read this far, here's my final recommendation: the game is fun and interesting but not worth 49.99€. I recommend it as a game, not as a purchase at base price (at this time). Sorry Firaxis, sorry 2K, and sorry Sid, I like your work, but you're going to have to put in more effort to claim a product is worth that much.
P.S. At this point in time (January 18th in my time zone), if you haven't yet played Civ III or Civ IV, get the Classics Bundle. Compare the raw brutality of the AI in Civ III/IV (at above average difficulty level) to the apparently confused machinations of the Civ V/BE AI.

Normally I don't bother with RPG maker games. The ones I've played were mediocre at best. And then I got THIS game. It's a tad short, but I have to admit I have enjoyed it a great deal. It's a tad grindy, but that said it is an RPG, so that kind of thing is to be expected. Still, the atmosphere, the NPCs, the randomized dungeons and overall mystery of the game lead to a pretty solid RPG in my opinion. The game revolves around discovering various monsters, gathering money and gear, and then training the monsters you purchase. It's not like pokemon or other games where you capture them, rather, you have to run into a monster and then it goes up for sale for you to buy. Rares are actually just that, rare. Some of them are particularly tricky to get ahold of. I'd say that my only real complaint is that to some degree the game relies upon RNG for progression, so you can run into a brick wall that seemingly no amount of effort can get you past, EG: at one point you have to collect orbs that rarely drop off the boss monster of dungeons, and you have to get 5 of them. It took me almost 5 hours just to get the last two orbs because the bosses just weren't dropping them.
Beyond that, I had a great deal of fun on the game. For the sale price I picked the game up for, which was $0.59? It has to be the best 59 cents I've ever spent so far. haha.

I will give away as little as I can about this game, a common theme among other reviews for it. Look, just trust me on this; The Stanley Parableis one of the most unforgettable games ever made.
Without giving too much away: it is very much a comedy game, but it has several layers of depth to its narrative that make it very much reflective of games as a whole. Your choices will actually matter and change the outcome. The world will shift constantly in certain intervals, making each playthrough of the game a varied and different experience. The game has more cleverly hidden easter eggs than there are stars in the sky, making you feel like you will never see everything no matter how long you play. Even the achievements reflect this absurdist comical nature of the game.
I realize that this review may be strangely uninformative or confusing, but it is probably the best way to convey how this game feels without spoiling it too much. Perhaps I should start again: This is the story of a man named Stanley...
Final Rating: 10 / 10
Verdict: As it is, the Stanley Parable is an almost perfect game in its own genre, and in its own right a fantastic narrative experience.

3. Controller. This game doesn't recognize any controller besides the 360 controller. so, if you have a dualshock or any other type, it won't read it.
If you can put up with those things up there, you'll get to enjoy a pretty enjoyable game.
Update: Problems 1 and 2 are gone. After the steamworks update, the game doesn't require data and tweaks to run anymore and Steamworks is smooth as silk compared to GFWL old bloated overlay.
Complete recommendation, get this or Off the Record when you get the chance.

General plotline was ok. The execution was horrible. Really, it feels like reading a script rather than watching a story unfold. Background context was only ever so subtly insinuated, character growth remains a mystery. At the start of the game, Rush was this crybaby fresh outa the nest, and at the end game he's the classic wisdom-endowed hero and I have absolutely no idea how that happened.
You're also going to miss some of the major selling points of the main story if you skipped some optional quests, which are VERY easy to miss. I wouldn't recommend playing this game without a wiki guide if you don't want to cry after playing 20 hours and find out that you've missed an important sidequest. Tips for first-timers: unlock every city that you can before going to the aqueducts in nagapur (in fact, do it when you go to Elysion for the first time). And talk to NPCs at the bars.
Battle mechanics are completely shrouded in mystery until you've played about 10 hours or so, and even then a large part is still a mystery.
Buy this only if you're a diehard fan of storylines, otherwise, skip it. There are better square enix games.

Dead Rising 2 is a sequel to a zombie slaying game - Dead Rising. Dead Rising 2 is set a bit after Dead Rising, but has nothing to do with the original game. Dead Rising 2 has been developed by Blue Castle Games, and published by Capcom! It's funny how Capcom has so many well known zombie games...
Dead Rising 2 is an open world zombie survival game. In Dead Rising 2 you have couple of missions (one main mission and a lot of side missions) which you do not need to follow at all! You see, Dead Rising 2 is a game in which you can do almost anything. Grab a motorbike, put a chainsaw on it and run over zombies. Or grab a motorbike, put machine gun on it and kill more zombies! Or just run around with nothing but a blade in your hands, chopping down everything in your path. The ways you can kill this zombies are almost limitless!
What makes this game far better than the first one is co-op option! You can call a friend to play this game with you and destroy the zombies with you! It's very fun indeed! Imagine two motorbikes with chainsaws, just driving down the street, ending every single zombie's life that is currently present.  This game also gives you and ability to craft a weapon out of two other weapons. For example, with a broom and a machete you make something like a spear. With knife and boxing gloves you make razor claws. With nails and a baseball bat... Very deadly baseball bat! You get the point - it's extremely fun!
So, as I said, you can chose to do the mission or you could just chose to ignore it and have loads of fun in the game. The game has six different endings, which all happen with a reason. For example, if you do whole main mission and then chose option A on some point (i don't plan to give out any spoilers!) You'll get first and best ending. If you do main mission and chose option B, you'll get almost same thing as A case. Everything else is more or less failure.
The game also futures a four person co-op in which all you can do is drive around a small area on a motorcycle and kill tones and tones and tones of zombies. I can't tell you much about that because I never managed to get into a game. There are just not enough players that play it..
Graphically speaking the game looks very very sweet. There's just enough blood, the zombies are quite detailed and everything seems in place. They could have added more different looking zombies though. Audio is very awesome and never gets too boring to listen to! It keeps changing as you enter stores, menu and so on and on. Only positive thoughts about Audio of this game!
Pros:
- Great co op fun.
- A lot of different clothing and weapons.
- Audio never gets boring.
- A lot of vehicles.
- You can keep on playing even if you decide not to do missions.
Cons:
- Main mission forces you to wait a long time before continuing the story..
- Only two people co op.
- No players so the 4 person co-op is impossible without friends.
- The game uses Games for Windows Live so it might become unplayable next year since GFWL is going down..
Overall grade: 8.5 / 10

The game itself is of course amazing. The original Bioshock is legendary, and this nice coat of paint does exactly what a remaster is intended to do (make the graphics somewhat modern and cleanup gameplay). Maybe I just got lucky and my system is "simpatico" with the game, but if you have never played Bioshock or looking to head back to rapture, or just want to play a true masterpiece of gaming, this is it!

Because of this I cannot recommend new players buy this version of the game, even if it is pretty fun. Maybe get this if it's on sale for like 90% off or something like that, I guess.

Long version: This game holds both elements of genius and failure. It had so much potential. Lets start with the positives. X Rebirths most alluring factor is it's universe; it's Bladerunner environment is a real sight to behold and i loved every minute of flying around this busy and alive space. Watching the capital ships dock and unload their cargo via drones was amazing and watching each and every ship go about it's task was cool. I loved zipping about and popping out of the highways and the sheer scale of the galaxy is immense. Watching your capital ships being built at the shipyards is a joy. There is no question that this game is beautiful but this is where the good things end.
Now lets come to the bad points. The trade system even after 25 patches (or however many) is simply broken. There isn't a single element to the trading system that i can name any positives to without stretching to lying about it. Why they thought anyone would want to fly around in circles reactivating trade offers every few hours (instead of using the simple but effective Advanced Satellite option from X3) is beyond me and even though they introduced trade agents later on why on Earth would i want to run around each and every station talking to every single person looking for one?
The other awful feature is your miners. You cannot activate their mining remotely at least i haven't found a way of doing so. You can tell them to fly to a zone where there is ore - you can tell them to sell the ore once they are fully loaded but you cannot tell them to ore remotely without the player being in the same sector. What? Why? Was this basic feature left out purposely or simply forgotten? If i have 40 miners going about their tasks, i would have to go to every single one of them each time to have them start mining (and then go around in circles after reactivating trade offers for them to sell to). Terrible.
From what i could see the stations were an utter waste of time docking to unless you wanted to find crew members for your ships or watch poorly animated character models stand about insulting you. There are only a few weapon types, shield types, missile types and only ONE...yes ONE installable software device for the Skunk. Where did all of the software from X3 go? (I'm holding my hands up in frustration). Where did everything go?
The campaign story was dull and not exactly entertaining. The voice acting was bordering on college hired actors sitting around eating coco pops while reading from a script and i ended up eventually going on to play free play just to avoid it.
Look, this game has a lot of gripes, some small which are worthless discussing some very gaping as mentioned above. The point is X Rebirth is a game that is missing being given a blank cheque. It's beautiful, truly - i cannot stress that enough. But some of the design choices are unbelievable. If X Rebirth had all of the features, options, wares, fleet commands and brilliance of X3 Terren Conflict and the beauty and busyness of X Rebirth this game would be unforgettable; at the moment it's just completely missable.
Until we all risk playing the Teladi DLC X3 Albion Prelude is your best bet.

This War of Mine is a survival-themed strategy game made by 11 bit studios. This game was inspired by the 1992-96 Seige of Sarajevo during the Bosnian War (the longest city siege in modern history), and the story-line is centered around the civilian experience of war (the poor living conditions and wartime atrocities) rather than front-line combat. It was released in November 2014.
You control a number of civilians trying to survive in a makeshift shelter in a war-torn city. Each civilian has a specific skill, i.e. a good cook, skilled scavenger, and these characteristics need to be taken advantage of in order to survive.
During the day your civilians cannot leave the makeshift shelter due to hostile snipers, so it is during this time that you can get your civilians to rest, build new items for the shelter, make weapons, and also ensure that their basic needs: health, hunger, rest, etc., are catered for.
Night time is one of the most important times of the game - this is when your civilians can go to scavenge for supplies such as food, water, weapons, wood, medicine, etc. This part of the game is particularly stressful as you genuinely feel the pressure of needing to return to the shelter with a good haul of items which is never as easy as you'd like it to be. Scavenging missions are particularly dangerous as the military or other survivors can attack you on sight, other times they could ask you for things to trade you don't have with you, other survivors may also be trying to scavenge in the same location and they may hear you digging through rubble to get the best items, all of which leads to a tense night for your scavenger, and also for you as the player.
You are able to build a radio in the shelter which does help towards planning what to scavenge for trade, or what the surrounding areas are currently like in terms of shelters getting raided, or the likelihood of getting attacked while on scavenging missions, etc.
Your civilians can meet other NPC survivors throughout the game which enables trade for items. The items that you will need the most, however, are often the most expensive, and you will need to really think about the impact it will make giving away half of your items in storage just to get one bandage for a poorly civilian of your own.
Choices are very tough in this game, and I found myself feeling as desperate and anxious as my in-game civilians were feeling towards the end - particularly after my first civilian died during a scavenging mission after getting into a fight. Your decisions are genuinely a matter of life-and-death, and are very much conscious based: save your own civilians, or run the risk of other civilians dying just so you can save yourselves. The decisions you make also affect the mood of the civilians that you control, and once morale within the shelter is low it makes life even more difficult.
The game is 'won', or more completed/finished by managing to keep one or more civilians alive until a ceasefire is called. Even though I managed to finish my very first game, it didn't really feel much of a win, or an achievement considering I'd lost all but one of my civilians, and my last surviving civilian wasn't going to be able to hold on much longer. The ceasefire is called at random, and mine was called on day 42 - it took me around 7hrs of gameplay to get to this point.
The soundtrack (by Piotr Musial) and 2D charcoal artwork of this game are perfectly matched to the style and genre as they completely capture the bleak, tense and somber atmosphere/situation. The character animation is beautiful, and should you be lucky enough to be able to get a guitar made for your shelter, the music created by the civilians playing the instrument sent chills down my spine.
This game has tons of replay ability as it is random each time you play. You can start with different survivors, different seasons, different locations to scavenge from at night, and a random ceasefire date each play though - all of which will make for a different experience each time.
I am still thinking about my first play-through: could I have done things differently, could I have had more civilians alive at the ceasefire? It's not often that a game continues to make me think about it once a few days have passed by after completing it; it's also not often that a game would draw me back for multiple play-throughs. I really adored everything about this game from start to finish.
For anyone that likes The Sims style games, but fancies something tougher, more RPG like, this will definitely be one for you to try though it is no easy ride - it is difficult, brutal and harrowing, but equally fantastic.
This War of Mine is available DRM free from 11 bit studios' website, or on Steam. Current full-price cost is £14.99.

Honestly, it seems beyond earth struggles to really figure out what it is.  There are plenty of design decisions that on their own make perfect sense. An extremely limited roster of unit types can work very well if there's customization that adds depth to that (for example Endless Legend does a good job of a very limited roster working well).  Here it just seems empty without more diversity or customization, and there are several unit roles that seem to go completely unfilled (melee naval, air bomber etc).
The mechanics are largely the same as Civ V, though they decided to reverse their decision with happiness they made in Civ V.  In Civ IV each of your cities had to balance their happiness and health to be productive, it was a highly effective, though I guess moderately complicated system. Civ V decided that was too complicated, completely eliminated health, and removed city-specific happiness in favor of a civilization wide set.  Here they decided instead that getting rid of happiness in favor of health would be a better idea to limit expansion.  Unfortunately some of the unintended consequences are that all non-strategic resources are now nothing more than tile bonuses, trading with AI civs is all in all a bad idea, and it sure doesn't seem like they told the AI what they messed around with.
If this were a Civ V mod, it'd be a pretty decent conversion mod with a lot of polish needed.  As it is it struggles to really show why it isn't just an expansion or mod for Civ V, but instead a full-price game on its own.
TLDR: reasonably fun, buy it if you just can't get enough of Civ V's mechanics but absolutely hate being able to remember the names of the other faction leaders.

Fun game and slick design.  I got it because I've long enjoyed games that allow me to create  my own party of monsters like this dating back to the old Game Boy title Final Fantasy Legend (yeah the one where you eat monster meat) - and more recent fare like the casual Line Rangers, and ER has that in spades within the first 5 minutes of play. I have enjoyed the play experience so far, it's exactly what I wanted - exceeded my expectations in fact - and my daughter is getting into it as well.
I haven't really noticed any kind of overarching epic storyline but actually that's a welcome relief. I have too many unfinshed RPGs with epic quests.  Instead there are a bunch of fun little NPCs, some quests that seem more like achievements (some you can also pick up from random NPCs) and generated dungeons that are actually fun and interesting to search around.  Of course the collector in me wants go "get em all" (yeah I never really got into Pokemon but I guess this game might appeal to fans of those games as well). The monsters are also your choice to fight or not -- not like some of those cheap JRPGs that lead you down a seemingly endless corridor of frustrating random monster attacks to add to their "40 hours of gameplay".  No, in this title -- so far at least -- it's just me and my crazy party of misfit monsters like the creepy eye monster with approriate names like "peeker" that can be changed if you like.  Fun stuff, worth the sale price for sure.  Will the fun last when I'm 10 hours in?  Will see but so far I'm hopeful.  Everything is within easy reach and it's quick to get to the action - meaningful action. At least I'm not slogging across a continent of nothing with endless random battles with pre-made cliche character archetypes.
Controls I'm using are simple cursor keys and space.  The battle system is exactly what you'd expect from a classic JRPG like the one I mentioned above - nothing fancy or deep. For full screen, just type ALT+ENTER.  And ESC for the menus. Pretty simple stuff - again, nice for a change.
Summary: If you are looking for a casual, inexpensive top down JRPG with simple controls and interesting replay elements as well as collecting monsters in a party of your own making, this game is for you.
Pros:
-Nice sounds, gameplay, and the screens keep the action coming. Little "dead space" - the town is jam-packed with points of interest.  Exploration and searching is rewarded.
-The items on-screen are not always just useless furniture or obstacles - some can be used if you move up to them an hit space, and they are not always immediately obvious. In cheaper titles using similar engines I notice almost nothing is useable - so it's a nice step up even in "random" dungeons, which speaks to good design.
-Random generated dungeons for replay value. I've found these generally really work well and the corny names remind me of my early days of BASIC programming. Note that not all dungeons will neccessarily have the items you require to bypass all obstacles. Sometimes you may need an extra item already in your inventory.
-Fun voice acting in battle that differs by the main character you select in the beginning.  Will I tire of the Werewolf's corny battle cries?  Perhaps but so far they are amusing.
Music is decent enough that I can keep it on when playing and seems professional and appropriate for where it is used, but not very memorable.
-A manly middle-aged main character you can choose to play. Or not. Play the other guy or the cool witch if you like. Decent selection between the 3 main characters. Would have some impact on the type of companion you choose from what I can tell of the skills.
-Just when I thought I had seen all the little tricks each randomly generated dungeon had to offer, I run into a block-slide puzzle that's new.
Cons:
-No earth-shattering story about how you need to defeat the great bad Wizard Frobozzle from taking over the world.  OK, maybe that's not a con.
-Only 2 party members fight at the same time and the rest "tag" in.  Not a terrible arrangement and your opponents are limited to the same rule, but I would have preferred 4 party members in the same fight.  That said it forces you to be choosy and the skills an individual monster owns become more important.
-Seems like an indie effort (but a good one) and the tiny postage-stamp sized screen at start up that requires the arcane use of "ALT-ENTER" to resize it to useable full-screen levels is a bit crude.  That said the option to go full-screen is available in the options/settings menu once you're in the game
-Seems to be some framerate loss with Options set to "full effects" when you are in combat. I expect this is a limitation of the engine, but I can live with it
-Voice acting recordings sound a bit flat and like they were not done on high grade recording equipment. The voices themselves are fine and amusing, however.

This is a fun game though I feel the interface can be annoying. I will get out the cons out of the way before I can say what I enjoyed, which I feel if you liked the trailer, then you'll like the game.
Cons:
1) Story is very light, I feel the DLC Monsterville Handbook does a better job immersing the player than just doing quests.
2) The interface is a pain. I don't think I can switch monsters outside of battle, and it takes a turn to switch. I also cannot set up my party with 2 monsters fighting at once; if the main character uses switch, then the monster switches for someone else.
3) Loading the game takes you to the beginning of the 1 town in the game.
4) Poison sucks; when it hits enemies, it only took 1% of a boss. In other words, I'm doing 300 damage to a boss, and the poison does 17, and it takes a couple turns to work. If it was 17 per second maybe, it would be fine.
5) You have to finish the 2nd dungeon before saving. However, once you are done with that, you can save as you please.
Here are the pros of the game, which is why I'm recommending it though it's a tough sell:
Pros:
1) This game is funny. From the voice acting (The witch ironically says, "Ding Dong, you're dead," when she wins), to the flavor text, I can enjoy myself. I think it's a game for those who enjoy NPC's in an rpg, more than character development or dramatic stories. For example, The wolf's description says it uses puppy eyes to stall its victims.
2) The Monsterville Handbook DLC feels like a beautiful tour, although it's a PDF manual. The trailer and screenshots were very honest. I liked the story about the werewolf most, and the interview with Peter Pretzel felt like an immersive tabloid.
3) I like the entry monsters. The wolf can do a lot of damage, though the skorpion I chose is like a tank. It can take some damage, and slow down enemies with charge.
4) The way you choose between the grizzler, skorpion, and attacknid (I believe the attacknid was the 3rd one, but these are puns as you can see), with the ones you didn't choose ganging up on you out of a jealous rage is hilarious.
5) I like the looting celebrations to feel like an accomplishment every time I finish a dungeon.
Overall, I feel the game is fun though needs some patience. An update will definitely make it an easy sell, though I feel the handbook is definitely worth the purchase, with the game's potential as the add-on.

This game is in alpha, and you can definitley feel it when you start playing. Everything is very unpolished and needs work. That being said however, I had alot of fun playing this, and I think it has a lot of potential. Hopefully the develepors are reading this because I have alot of feedback.
My thoughts:
-It felt kinda like overwatch, which isn't bad but please don't make it too much like overwatch. I liked it because it felt genuinley new and fresh, don't turn it into something we already have.
-The third person camera needs some serious work.
-The funnest part IMO was how fast and vertical the combat was. The ruins map I played on was infinitley funner than the underground mining town because the ruins were totally built for teleporting and mana sprinting all over it, finding vantage points and flanking routes to get an advantage on my enemies was really fun, but the mining town was the exact opposite. It was a large mostly flat area with some houses that had a few balconies. You could improve it by allowing us too walk on the rooftops, populating it with more houses, and adding an abundance of scaffolds in other areas to climb around.
-The ultimate being charged from the start seemed a little ridiculous. but having it charge over time is too overwatch-ish. Perhaps you could have pick ups that generate around the maps over time, or reward players for completing objectives and preforming well. if not, you could have the ultimate just take time to charge.
-Teleporting and mana jumping was so much fun, but it felt a little limited. One thing i hated was i couldn't ever tell EXACTLY where i was going to teleport, so i thought you could make it where when you hold the cast key, it shows a little sillouette where you're going to teleport, and when you release, you go there.
-why is control jump? make it crouch.
-I understand that teleporting shouldn't be spammable, especially in combat, but I also often found myself waiting at a ledge that was just a little to far to mana sprint across while my teleport recharged. perhaps you could make it so that mana sprinting, jumping across gaps, and other things like that slightly reduce the timer? idk just a suggestion.
-Another idea, which could solve the OP ultimate problem, is too have instead of every spell set on its own charge, have a mana pool (you know, like the name?) that you draw from too cast spells. It recharges over time, so you won't find yourself empty very often so long as your smart. Your first spell could cost nothing and be your most basic spell for any situation (cantrip) and your ultimate could cost EVERYTHING so you could use it right off the bat but you'd be crippled immediatley as a consequence. Perhaps mana could recharge slowly, but there would be pickups around the map that speed up the process temporarily.
-Add descriptions for the movement spells and whatnot.
Haven't played much, but definitley will continue to. With some love and effort from the devs and the players, this game could become legendary. Until then, i'll be playing it as it's updated and leaving more feedback.

TLDR: The game is fun, but it's unlikely it will hold you long enough for you to finish it because of the amount of grinding and RNG later in the game.
I've played the game for 70 odd hours, so obviously i think it has something going for it.
I've tried playing it twice, and both times I've run into the same issue - I get to a fight where the games just seems unfair.
In this game, you control a group of squads, not individual characters. Each squad acts as one unit. They all have a single health bar and mana pool. You can say "using healing abilities" or "sword techniques" or "debuff magic" etc, and the game will decide who in each squad uses each ability based on that.
The best and worst part of the game is these abilities. They, and I mean each person individually, have a small chance to increase the power of the ability. For example, after a fight an ability may go from Cure to Cura/Cure 1 for a single person. There are ways to increase the likelihood, but for the most part its random.
This means after mosts fights you might get a few people to increase some skills. However, because you have so many people and you cant choose who does what each turn, these small increases mean fairly little. In later boss battles, your team can be wiped out before you have the chance to get enough mana to really fight.
For the part that I got stuck on both times I played it i went online looking for advice. For the most part, the advice was "hope you get lucky and your team executes blackout/whiteout" (RNG AOE abilities that have RNG on top of the RNG already in place.
This game is good. The abilities and stuff in the game are all really cool. The RNG and lack of transparency with how you can level up abilities and actually win some of the fights is awful, and grinding isnt fun enough to keep you interested.

This entry of the Final Fantasy series is famous for controversy it have brought to the fanbase. But Final Fantasy XIII is still
playing. The story is engaging and the world is beautiful and well-written. The combat system is fresh and has a lot of common with traditional FF gameplay despite being real-time with mostly automated action sequences (don't worry, you'll be very busy controlling them nontheless). The graphics and visual design is jaw-dropping even by today's standards. And most important - this game still makes you dive into magical Final Fantasy atmosphere that we all know and love it for. This game does a lot of things differently but it stays true to it's roots.

Don't expect this to be a Hitman game, because it isn't. It is nothing like Blood Money, or any of the previous Hitman games for that matter. But except for the misleading name, this game does its own thing and it does it well. It is a good action game, that can be played either stealthily or full-rambo (Not sure about higher difficulties though). The audio cues that occur when you set up traps, or do other hitman-like things, are a nice touch. Get this if you like sneaking around with cover mechanics, don't expect a lot of "blending in with the crowd". It also reduces your points for being seen while trespassing, even if you leave the area and don't alert anyone. This discourages experimentation, unlike in Blood Money where you would just walk around and if someone tells you to go away you would do so and nothing would happen. The disguise system is also not in favor of hiding in plain sight, which strengthens the idea of sneaking and hiding instead. These things don't necessarily make this a bad game, but they make it a different game from what you would expect out of a Hitman game (Just letting you know). There are some missions that resemble Blood Money a bit better. While the level design is not nearly as good, missions like The King of Chinatown give you a target to execute and leave you in an open area to do whatever you want with that objective, without worrying about sneaking and hiding for the most part.
I'll give this a 8/10. Now before you go and rant to me about how Blood Money was way better and this game is horrible:
Blood Money was better at being a HITMAN game. This game is better at being a planned-stealth game. Other than the misleading name that the game was given, there is no problem with that. It does a great job at being what it is, apart from a few disagreements I have with this game's score system.
Conclusion: 8/10 had a lot of fun with this game, don't get it if you don't like stealth* and sneaking.
* I don't mean stealth as in just not being noticed, I mean it as in evading enemies in a hostile area where you must not be seen at all.

This game is different from Hitman Blood Money and previous Hitman games as it is more linear and has a more heavy story than Hitman Blood Money. The graphics are really nice and adds to the overall feeling of the game, combined with the new technique of rendering lots of people, some maps lets you hide in the crowd.
Sadly, the replayability of the game is low for the main story. I played through the story only once on second hardest difficulty and then replayed some maps on easy just to play around with the AI and test different outcomes. Difficulty scales for every map, so on harder difficulty you won't be able to use the new quickshoot feature and there's almost the double amount of enemies to stop you.
The stealth in the game is easier than in previous games as you can now take cover behind chest high walls and hide inside boxes. To compensate for this, lots of maps are difficult on higher difficulty but compared to Hitman BM, it is easy. The costume game play is also a little better as not all disguises gives a 100% foolproof disguise while some do. It gets outright ridiculous on the court house mission where you can actually disguise yourself as the judge.
All in all, I don't see this as a Hitman game that carries the pride of the last games in the series, but rather an appetizer and a sidetrack story for the upcoming Hitman game. The story in the game is a 8 hours long constant raining Chicago with targets spread out without any backstory or explanation. In previous games, you were always given information for why you are killing people and information about their "pedophile" network which would justify their brutal deaths. In Hitman Abs. you just go along side a linear story as a shooting gallery and occasionally some targets pop up for you with name and picture. After the Chinatown mission, there's little to no explanation for why you kill any person up until you get to Texas.
Remember to play this game on a higher difficulty than you feel comfortable with. If this game is too easy, the game will just loose its gameplay value. I recommend second most difficult settings and the last difficulty for the replay.

This is a game that I have 100%d, playing it entirely co-op with my brother. Simple review:
Pros:
- Entertaining co-op gameplay: be rewarded for working together
- Game is cheap
Cons:
- Not enough inventory space, especially playing as the elf mage
- There are a lot of bugs and issues. Just some we encountered:
- One player being forced back to the beginning of the level on reload
- Voice chat is always on (have to mute mic)
- Gold does not display past 999,999
- It crashes after 10 minutes on windows 10 if you don't disable TapTip process
- If you started the game as the elf or human and then play the dwarf, it doesn't show the secrets in the wall/mines that he can smash
- As the non-host I managed to go past one of the areas which usually prevents you from passing until all players are there - effectively forcing us to restart the level
- If you have enough cooldown reduction on the mage, you can cast the armour buff on yourself before the first buff finishes. This refreshes the duration but also stacks the armour, you can stack infinite armour this way.
Neutral:
- Story lasts about 15 hours, with 2 new game + options (I finished them both)
- Difficulty is reasonable
- Voice acting is bearable
- UI is ok, controls feel decent
Despite all of this I will recommend the game because despite its flaws I had an enjoyable time playing through it with my brother. I can only recommend it because I bought it on a sale for the price of a coffee - it is not worth more than that.

I just finished this game for the first time less than 10 minutes ago... it's got to be one of my favourite shooters ever!
I remember the really old Wolfenstein 3D (not the original mind, that one was way back in '84. Look it up!) on PC and Xbox 360 Arcade. For the time, it must have been mindblowing but when I played it, it was laughably bad. Yet the new Wolfensteins have felt like they've drifted too far into Call of Duty territory, as well as other common trappings of modern games with unneccessary challenges popping up all the time, 'cinematic' moments and upgrade trees.
RtCW finds that sweet spot between the dated old school mid 90s shooter and the dull modern one. It's very challenging, yet adrenaline pumping and adaptive to different playstyles, like stealth. Stealth is based on alarms being sounded or not... as long as alarms aren't rung, you can go in guns blazing and win the mission.
The story is just bonkers, but it's so enjoyable because of that. You've got crazy Nazi scientists summoning the dead in order to create the ultimate army of deadly super soldiers. Throw in stereotypical British and German accents and an overly sexualised group of female ninjas, and you've got a premise which would have to carry a massive badge stating boldly 'I AM TAKING THE♥♥♥♥♥♥ to get past the overly-sensitive online communities of today.
I love how there is a sprint button. I could barely tell the difference between normal running and sprinting!
The secrets are great. It's not based upon trial and error so much to find them, like in the 1992 3D version. The level design is impeccable. The environments and enemy design still look stylish and unique even after 15 years of graphics evolution. That there is the power of great artistic design, something lost in the processor hungry AAA shooters of today.
It has its fair share of 'cheaply' difficult moments, though actually not as many as I was expecting. I could do without doors to open areas full of snipers closing without me telling them to (especially frustrating near the end). Only one boss battle out the three I actually found fun (the second one...beat him with literally 1 HP remaining!). Some of the Panzer troopers were just too difficult to take down without kiting like it was going out of fashion, and cover was often too far to get to, so a battle of attrition was often out of the question.
Oh and grenades. Only ever useful against the undead. Totally useless against nearly everything else.
But these are just a few nitpicks and, to be honest, can be applied to mostly any shooter of the period, even Half-Life (actually, ESPECIALLY Half-Life!). Overall, RtCW is a great blast from the past, with only a couple of the cheap difficulty tricks old PC shooters were infamous for, some of the best FPS level design ever, a crazy story and very fast paced gameplay.

Bioshock 2 Review
(Story)
If you go through the worst, can you still do what's best?  Set years after the events of the first Bioshock, Bioshock 2 takes place once again in Rapture.  This time though, you play as the Big Daddy, "Delta", attempting to rescue his kidnapped little sister.  Old and new faces help or hinder you and this time around, what you choose to do with them affects the ending to the game.  The emphasis or theme of this entry in the series is psychology and philosophy rather than lack of choice.  You do not need to have played Bioshock to play Bioshock 2, however you will have Bioshock's twist spoiled for you if you do.
(Gameplay)
Bioshock 2 is a close-quarters, first person shooter.  What makes it different from its predecessor is that its mechanics have been vastly improved and expanded.  For example, you can now wield a gun in your right hand and a plasmid in your left instead of switching between the two in one hand.  Visual weapon modifications and plasmid upgrades return with a few new wepaons and plasmids as well.  As a Big Daddy, you gain Adam through escorting Little Sisters (once you kill their protector), ferrying them around to corpses to gather Adam.  Once the Little Sister starts to gather, you have to defend her from a wave of enemies.  Once she completes a few gathers, you will have the option to save or harvest the Little Sister with the respective consequences from the first game.  Be warned, the defense segments can get very intense so make sure to stock up on everything you think you will need.  You repeat the escort/defend process a few times per level then advance to the next.  Levels are very open with plenty of secrets strewn about to those who pay attention for clues.  Hacking gets a downgrade to pushing a button at the right time but I didn't miss the old way of doing it.  The research mechanic also returns, but this time you film enemies as you fight them, rather than take their picture, to gain combat advantages.  As for the multiplayer, I did not invest much time because it just felt too strange for me.
(Design)
Compared to the first game, Bioshock 2 appears more stylized to me, almost like a cartoon.  A really, really dark cartoon.  You do not revisit any of the locations from the first game, but the new ones are just as detailed and cool to look at as in Bioshock.  There are even some really neat underwater segments.  The overlapping sound issue still exists for me like in the first game.  However, I found the sound design here to be an improvement.  The game does not feel as scary as the first, mostly because you play as a man in a bulky suit of armor, but it has its moments.
(Final Comments)
This game has my vote for the best in the Bioshock series.  It improves on Bioshock and adds its own flavor too without ceasing to lose its fun.  Once you get the swing of things, the game does feel a bit repetitive.  However, the interesting chracters and new locales make it worht your while.  Come for the excellent lore, stay for the gameplay.

I've been wanting Civ : Beyond Earth since it was released, and actually almost got it when it was on sale during Christmas but couldn't due to having to buy gifts for others, and just a general lack of funds. Because of this, as a fan of the Civ games and an owner of Civ IV GOTY Edition and Civ V, I jumped at the opportunity to play it on the free weekend. Logging in a straight 13 hours in one sitting, I can honestly say that I have enjoyed it more than I did Civ V and Civ IV, and I plan on buying it.
There are a LOT of reviews saying that this is "Civ V Reskin" and that isn't true. I've played around 250 hours of Civ V, and this is a good bit different from Civ V.
That being said, Civ : Beyond Earth adds a lot of new features that were either absent or very miniscule in the previous games. Some of these features include:
-Covert ops
-Branches determining what stlye of civilization you will run
-Unit upgrades, determined by your civilization's style
-More resources, different trading methods, different UI
-New diverse and sometimes kinda scary "Alien" units to replace the "Barbarians" of the previous games
Everything is just reworked and really great.
However, I did run into a few cons
-When I launched the game, the introduction cinematic played, and then the screen displaying the title and the 3 ships was shown. This display was stuck, and I was a bit confused at first, but upon alt-tabbing out and then back in, I was brought to the main menu. Nothing really of botherance, just a little confusing.
-The game, while it did add a LOT of new features, did not really change the overall style of a Civ game, but that's expected, because it's a ♥♥♥♥ing Civ game. It's not gonna all of a sudden be innovative. It's gonna add these small details, small features, and move on.
Overall: If you're into the Sci-Fi, space exploration, or robotic scene, this is a good Civ game for you.
However, if you like Civ V more than you like your mother/children/girlfriend, stick to Civ V.

This here is one of the 'lost' JRPG's in my opinion. It's a great game from the makers of Final Fantasy, yes that's right they make RPGs Other than FF. The interesting thing in this is two fold, first it's on the Unreal Engine, not a in house engine. Second it's M rated for blood. Now the blood is pretty old school, especially by todays standards. We aren't talking dismemberment gore here, just people get hit and blood splashes out of a non-existant wound. The graphics aren't horrible, they were good when it was new. The interesting mechanic here is the combat, it's turn based but more strategic than just waiting for your turn. The gameplay is actually quite a lot of fun, and in typically JRPG fashion the story is convoluted and extremely long, with lots of little hidden things to find around towns, cities and caves. Overall, if you're a JRPG fan, I recommend giving this a shot if it's at a price you like. HOWEVER, there is one IMPORTANT catch, this game uses one of those awful 'keep up' leveling systems from what I've been told, the higher you level up your characters the stronger the game becomes, your true 'power' comes from the skills you obtain and they can be obtained in many cases at any time. Like most games as complex as this one, you're better offer doing a lot of research before you even start to know exactly what you should do and how to go about it, NOT pursuing certain things right away and trying to power level your character ever will really really hurt you. The old enjoyable act of running around leveling to gain an edge is ruined with this design. Now if you don't enjoy old school RPGs and like a game that keeps pace with your level, this should be your thing. If you like old school RPGs though where you level up and eventually feel like a super Hero, this might be a struggle. You NEED to follow a guide that explains everything, because becoming powerful is about keeping your level low while doing everything to enhance your skills. You also have to recruit nearly an army, since in this combat is between squads of characters and not one on one.

Grimoire: Manastorm is a Mage FPS game that is mostly Multiplayer oriented.
Since is released in Oct 2017 (year in which I am writing this review), it is fairy new on the market.
Being made in Unreal Engine and having really good music and based on the screenshots from the Steam page, it might sound like a good game but is really not. Let me explain why.
Game is splitted into two parts: PvE - Survival, which have two sets of difficulty (Normal and Hard) and Multiplayer mode, where in order to play you must select a server (official or unofficial).
PvE - Survival is fairy simple: You are the only man alive and you must defend an objective, Church door for Normal Mode and an Yggdrasil in Hard Mode. The difference between Normal and Hard Mode, is the type of enviroment and ammount of enemies. While in Normal Mode, where you are basically in a town, you can use your surroundings to dodge some attacks, even tho, I have noticed that buildings doesn`t always provide cover against the Skeleton Mages.
I also saw that there is no such thing as difficulty curve. At Wave 1, you might start with easy type of enemies (Armless Skeletons, Child Warror Skeletons, Adult Warrior Skeleton and Mage Skeletons) at Second Wave things get complicated really quick. You get to find the above enemies in large numbers plus Earth Trolls and Ice Trolls  combined.
I have died a couple of times at Wave 2, while I was trying to keep myself alive rather than the objective itself.
Hard Mode consist of defending the legendary Yggdrasil (The Tree of the World). Here things gets really complicated, since the enviroment is alot darker and is open, with no covers. From what I`ve noticed the numbers of enemies are increased but there is only one type of troll who spawn, that being the Shadow Troll.
Combat is really simple, you have an 100 HP health, two types of mages unlocked by default, Fire and Ice, rest of the mages being unlocked by playing Multiplayer. Ammount of damage taken by different types of enemies are somewhat fixed and doesn`t change. Neither your damage.
You have 6 basic skills, which are found on Right and Left Mouse Button, Q, E, R, F.
4 of them are for damage and 2 of them are for protection (Shield and Teleportation).
Other classes and skills are only unlocked in 2 ways: Multiplayer Warrioror Wallet Warrior.
And since, I reached the final part of my review, let`s have a very short insight about Multiplayer.
Multiplayer is DEAD. Literally dead. On both Official and Unofficial servers. Sure,you could join a server, but you will be the only player playing it and matches takes 10 minutes each. Doubtfuly that anyone who is sane, will play 10 minutes ALONE capturing the adversaries points, while having no opponents.
*Game is visually stunning and has nice music.
* Crappy animations for skills.
* Crappy sounds FX.
* Game has both Single Player and Multiplayer Modes.
Singleplayer content is extremely unbalanced and unpolished.
Multiplayer Mode is basically DEAD since nobody wants to play this game, for some reason.
* Game is still being updated regulary.
* They even have a Discord server where developers and players can talk and chat about game.
Not worth picking up, in this current state.

I've played and beaten this game on xbox multiple times and have gotten mostly through the PC version. This game is seriously flawed. The only reason that I'm recommending it is because it's fairly cheap and does have its upsides, but I'd still wait until it's on sale.
Pros:
-Interesting and numerous sidequests.
-Interesting concept
-Great battle music
-Lots of arts
-Some cool animation
Cons:
-Battle system is extremely random, if you play the same fight twice you can get absolutely destroyed the first time and completely slaugher them the second time doing pretty much the same thing.
- Punishes you for leveling up (strangley enough the surest way to beat this game is to avoid fighting as much as possible)
-Punishes you for trying several weapons (you will wind up downgrading your nimble/mighty arts unless you stick with those types of weapons.)
- Characters and story are pretty generic and boring.
- 99% of important stats and exp happen off screen.
- The game does not teach you how the battle system works, you need to look it up and study it.
- Morale system doesn't work well, if your winning by a landslide this just makes it easier, if your getting beaten down this just makes it worse, and some enemies will constanly lower morale gauge regardless of how you are doing.
- Area attacks and some status ailments are horribly broken. Area attacks basically do normal damage times however many units you have in a union and may even hit other unions. This will often oneshot you and they use them VERY often. Some status ailments in this game are easy to deal with (silence, burn) while others are pretty much a death sentence (poison, curse).
All in all this game isn't amazing and somtimes it feels like the bad outweighs the good but you might like it so it may be worth dropping a few bucks on. Still wait for a sale though. Also if you do get this game make sure you turn on autosave, it's not the default setting and you really need it.

My few gripes of this game are the low player count, minimalistic setting configs, bland singleplayer, and the outdated graphics. The outdated graphics doesn't bother me too much and a low player count is to be expected of a game that just came out. The sounds config should have a little more options to change other than just Master Volume. Singleplayer is pretty boring as all you do is defend a building and survive, which in of itself isn't a bad concept, but the gamemode is pretty boring to play as there is no upgrades. So overall this game is has come pretty great combat and movement and that itself is pretty good for a free to play game.

Kinda late, kinda bored now that I finished the game (35 hours or so-not sure if steam keeps the correct track since I did it mostly offline), so here are my thoughts about it!
I could start by saying that it took me a while to get used to the fighting style, which has a very fast pace (you can also set it to a slow mode but... come on, fast thinking its the hardest challenge in this game), I could also say that the clusterf***ck of a story it has prevented me from playing it as soon as I bought the game (which I regret tremedously).
Here you get involved in a journey which will drive you from Fal'cies to L'cieth, from Cocoon to Pulse, and from Pulse to Ragnarok! I wont spoil the story for you, it's rich but it creates a whole another level for the word "cliché", but somehow it manages to keep the player trapped into the game, due to great graphycs, fast paced turn by turn combat action. That and the fact that after 1 hour of gameplay you just wanna get rid of all those god damn fal'cies.
ORRRR...the things we do for a Chocobo!
What's a FF game without them?....it could not even be called a spin-off.
Near the end of the game, on chapter 11 (out of 13), we get into Pulse, a wide open area full of powerfull enemies, secrets and side quests that will help you get your characters stronger...its optional, but if you are into RPGs, you know the deal, this is the only reasonable farming place, and thankfully it's a pleasant zone to spend some time and getting your Chocobo, and get access to many hidden areas that are only reachable while riding those filthy-ugly-but-cute-horse-wannabe-bird! (I am registering that under TM!) (No, Im not!).
Its a long game, with plenty of challenges so, here are the pros and cons:
PROS:
-Geniune battle system, wierd at 1st, but excellent to make fast paced fights.
-A LOT OF CUSTOMIZATION, you can make your party so versatile that there is more than 1 way of beating a hard boss!
-Remember GFs? Here those are called Eidollons, and not only you can ride them, but you can controll them on the fights, choosing which skill the have to cast.
-If you play on the normal mode (if you chose Easy, I will haunt you!), CONGRATULATIONS, not only you are brave, but you are heading towards really hard challenges.
-A DOOM timer on the final boss fight was just hilarious (I had never seen a DPS-race on a Final Fantasy boss encounter!)
CONS:
-Linear: The 1st RPG I play where the path is linear. You can get used to it or you can just hate it, ask for a refund and move on. I get used to it but was dissapointed at the beginning.
-Upgrade system trolls new players, after you spend all your gill to upgrade your weapon for  the 1st time, you come to realize that the the levels and items used are wasted since the new version it´s a lvl 1 weapon with very lame stats, that eventually will get stronger after you farm your♥♥♥♥♥off and upgrade it again (Im looking at you LionHeart).
-You can choose to do the sidequests before or after you actually beat the game, If you did the former, your player power will be tremendous, I was able to beat the Final Boss on my 1st try without even reading a guide because I had a maxed Crystarium, Weapons and Items...so dont grind too hard to make it Epic!
Final Words:
A game that filled up my expectations, felt weird the first time because it's very different from the previous FF's I had played (all but 12 and 14), and has a fun story, cliché's aside (dont wanna ever hear Snow say "Hero" again). Totally worth  the time you gotta invest to finish it!
