The online multiplayer is dead. No one play that game anymore. And the ranked match *requires* 4 players to start, so if you wanna play online multiplayer, you will need a gaming session of 4 players.

I'm a avid fan of dinosaurs, have been since preschool honestly. So perhaps my review is a bit bias?? Mayhaps? Welp, I'm not instantly in love with every dino related thing that comes out. There is a lot that can go wrong. so some pros and cons.
Pros:
1) The dinosaurs have skills and powers that fit with what it is. The animation of these is terrific. I'v been charged at when I was a human and punted around. It feels smooth and not wonky and awkward so when your a raptor pouncing on someone there isn't this a awkward glitchy *waiting for animation to line up* thing that you might get from other games. Which makes it feel more epic and fluid. Also, they don't needlessly have guns attached like in other titles since well lets face it they are pretty badass without them.
2) Yeh I like dinosaurs, and I like playing as the dinosaurs but I legitmentally enjoyed playing both sides. I was concerned that I'd be upset at playing the humans because I'd be waiting to switch sides. Not the case at all. It was really thrilling to be running around, hiding and hunting and really fun to try to kill these beasts. The balence is really great and far too often games like this would tip the scale to make the humans stronger to stand a chance but no everything feels accurate.
3) This is sort of a mix of TF2/CSGO/Jurassic Park, I found out about this when I was playing CSGO and had an idea of, 'wouldn't it be great if like the entire Terrorist Side was replaced by Raptors?' And to my delight someone says 'that exists'! If you want to, join or host a server with your friends. Play as all raptors if you wanted.
4) NOMNOMNOM! Pouncing, teamwork and straight up clever girl moments. I <3 it.
Cons:
1) I'v only played about an hour so far but had trouble figureing out some of the controls. My poor little Pteranodon floundered around like a wounded bird for a little while, honestly I expected it to glide. It was still fun, but yeh spend a little bit of time to play with the controls before you judge it. I have a feeling some people just didn't bother to learn before they reviewed. They aren't difficult honestly, just don't expect any tutorials. Also, I'v seen people do things that I can't figure out how to do. Not sure if it is controls related or dlcs.
2) uuuuh... Maybe more dinos? This isn't a con really, there are only 5 but I think a lot can be done and who knows maybe it can but I haven't explored that far. But yeh like host a server and change up what type of dinos are allowed of a like pick 5 from a list of 20. Or even limit it to 1 type. Who knows, maybe future updates but either way awesome the way it is.
3) Would be nice if you could earn skins or gear from in game. Like earn points per kill or even a drop system like csgo. I'm not a huge fan of buying dlc's for that, but I don't feel it is pay to win or anything so I'm putting it as a minor offence.
4) Would love the option to first person as the dinos. 3rd person is nice and all for the epic jumps and animation but still would like to toggle between the two options. Heck they could even use it to nerf a trex by giving it motion based vision.
I'v glanced at some other reviews and not sure why people would not recommend this. So take those with a grain of salt. It's pretty clear about what it is on the tin, so if you aren't into that then well move on.

Rating : 7/10
Overview: Active Turn Based RPG
The Good:
+  The overall presentation and graphics is fantastic.
+ Variety of environments
+ When you finally can command your own team, the combat system is fun, fast and challenging. Changing between roles constantly to survive, making sure you have the right equipment and party members all lead to an engaging battle system.
+ The UI is very well done, everything is laid out in clear concise manner, switching party members, equipment, roles are very easy
+ Enemy design
+ Great music and sound
+ Impressive CGI cutscenes
The Average:
+/- Level Design is VERY linear for most of the game. Most levels are literally a straight line with the occasionally branching path that leads to a treasure chest. The game does open up more in the later sections of the game.
+/- Leveling up your party, like level design, is also very linear. You are not given much choice in how to develop your character.
The Bad:
- no volume control, lack of graphical options and any serious graphical settings etc, and an inconsistent framerate.
- The game takes way too long to really get going. Some people saying that this game has a 10-hour tutorial is not that far off. It feels like the first half of the game is just busy work.
- A story that starts off interesting but turns into a convoluted mess filled with stereotypical JRPG characters and terrible dialogue, in other words like every other modern Final Fantasy Game
Conclusion:
Though I enjoyed my time with this game, it just doesn’t hold up that well. The post game content (after you beat the final boss) is much better, giving you harder enemies to fight and more interesting areas to explore. Overall though this game feels like a giant step back from Final Fantasy 12.

This game has been on my wishlist since it first came out in October of last year. I'm not a direhard fan of the Civ games, having played Civ IV and Civ V, but I was looking to pick this up, because Civ in space sounded pretty cool. I didn't buy this game right away, because 1) I felt like it was overpriced for what essentially looked liked a Civ V clone, I perhaps would spend $30 on it, but no way was I going to sink $50 into it, and 2) This is Steam, and a new game from a very renowned developer as Firaxis was very likely to go on sale during the winter sale. So the game was released and I waited until Christmas to check it out. I went onto the store page, and noticed that this game got 'mixed' reviews. What? A game with the Sid Meier's Civilization name not getting at least above average reviews? I was skeptical about the reviews, but ultimately decided to hold onto my money. And then, to put the final nail in the coffin, the free weekend rolled around. I could finally try this game out for myself before deciding if I wanted to buy it. I no longer regret my decision to hold onto my money. This game is unfortunately a reskinned Civ V, with pretty much every good feature of it dumbed down. AI personalities are boring, the tech tree was interesting, but confusing and eventually just became a game of "research the technologies that will get you affinity points". There was hardly any intro or help when starting the game, aside from choosing your previous Civ exposure. My first, and only, game essentially became a game of finding research to gain affinity, minimal interaction with the AI nations, and waiting out to victory.
TL:DR; reskinned, dumbed down Civ V in space. Only buy if you really, really enjoy Civ V and are willing to overlook the many flaws, then maybe for you it will be enjoyable. I personally, however, am glad to remove this game from my wishlist.

I've tried some other high rated survival games like Don't Starve and just found them tedious.  So, I wasn't sure about this one before I bought it.  I did anyway, and it turned out to be a really awesome game.  Despite some relatively simple gameplay that seems like it should be repetitive, the fact that you're almost always in the brink of disaster (starvation, sickness, having to take risks) makes you always want to just play one more day to see if it's going to turn out alright.  This also makes it very satisfying when you find a valuable item or enough food for the whole house.  And materials are always just scarce enough for you to have to really choose between your short term needs and your long term goals.
I've played quite a few hours before finally surviving to the end of the war.  I'm not sure how much depends on dumb luck or strategy or what is pre-scripted.  It SEEMS to be a rather random game regarding what items you find, however I could only know that with multiple playthroughs and remembering what items I found where.  Based on comments I've seen from other players, I fear there might be some pre-determined item locations (for example) which could be learned and used, unforunately.  I always find it
The different characters you can end up with are neat, though I'm not sure they change your approach in any integral way.  Still, you can easily identify and use the strong points of most of your survivors.
After having beaten it once, I'm pretty confident I'll go back to it, though between my successful playthrough and my failed oens, I think I've pretty much seen all the possible locations and events.  I'll be looking forward to some updates or DLC to increase the replayability.
A very satisfying game.  I recommend it.  Any additional content to be released at a later date can only make it better!

This is a tough recommendation, but I had to ultimately say "Yes".
Unfortunately, the late game (around 9-10 hours in at a reasonable pace) is nothing like what the early game presents you. Even in some of the best gear, a single Uruk-Hai deals, and tanks, an incredible amount of damage, and you're often swarmed by 4-5 around this time, among a host of other enemies. Many attack hitboxes are absurdly inaccurate, and oftentimes you'll find yourself getting struck by an attack that very obviously swung WILDLY away from your character. The combat AI is also rather dense: allies don't seem to be able to learn basic tactics like what abilities are useful against which enemies (for example, Andriel will often drop a Sanctuary when you are on low health, but as soon as even a single Uruk-Hai comes close, she will use its knockback burst, which Uruk-Hai are immune to), and when knocked down will crawl TOWARD YOU even if you're being swarmed by enemies, many of whom have essentially a stunlock that'll keep you from even getting a chance to revive them; and enemies will often attack once then stand still as you wail on them for a few seconds.
The writing and voice acting are also notably.... well, bad. In terms of the voice acting, there are a few that stand out as being particularly good (Urgost, Gandalf, Radaghast, Beleram, Gwaihir, and Bilbo), most of them are lacking in a certain professional quality. The most egregious example of this is the human ranger player character, Eradan. His voice actor is monotone for the entire game, to the point where I started questioning if he was voiced by an advanced text-to-speech program. Much of the dialogue, between the player characters in particular, is cringeworthy and stilted.
Nothing much to say about the story. I like it. The unsung heroes fight a battle against an enemy that could have turned the tide against the main heroes. I dig it.
I gave this game a "Yes" because, despite all the ranting above, most of it can be dealt with. Dialogue can be skipped or tuned out, the consequence-free dialogue wheel can be ignored by just hitting "enter" on the default answer. And up until chapter 6, the combat isn't as horribly unbalanced. The combat itself is fun enough, the enemies are fair, and the story is decent enough to hook you in for the ride.
No numerical rating. Play this game if you love the Lord of the Rings. Peace.

I'd recommend this game for the battle system, which I found really interesting.
(Really, really long blocks of text ahead. Sorry. TLDR at the end.)
The story was meh, I felt it was a little confusing at times, and not particularly gripping. However, I'm really not one to follow the plot carefully in RPGs (what am I doing playing RPGs then? haha, you have a point...), so I've probably missed some parts that would've prevented the confusion and maybe even foreshadowed the ending. Still, not a tale that grabbed my attention.
The battle mechanics were what really drew me in. It's brilliant! I've put in way more hours than the recorded 15. Once you run through the game fully, you get to start a new game in hard mode which is a whole other challenge (worth the torture, in my opinion).
As plenty of people below have pointed out, combat is turn-based and rather than controlling single characters, you can fight with 'unions' of characters. At each turn, you give general commands to each of the unions, and the AI picks the different attacks/spells for each of the union members (you can see what gets picked, but you can't change this specifically during battle). And that's one fun part of the battle system- it might seem like all their actions are out of your control, but careful union setup with suitably trained characters makes a HUGE difference in the sets of commands you get. You even get to fine tune the kinds of attack/spells each union member can execute by blocking some of their learned skills. This helps increase the chances of the AI picking up the attacks you want, since you've removed the ones you didn't need, even if it's just for a particular battle.
You're free to set up your unions as you wish- have separate unions for offense/tanking/healing/debuffing (like most sane people), just have an army of attackers slashing through monsters (this may actually end badly...), maybe, like I usually prefer, have self-contained unions capable of looking after themselves in battle so that you can forgo a healing union altogether, or all of these at different points in the game. You'll need a bit of care with how the unions are set up and how members are trained, otherwise the commands generated during battle can be really useless and frustrating. There's a lot of flexibility to this system, which becomes clearer as you progress further into the game and begin handling more unions; if you've trained your characters decently enough in their roles(warrior/thaumaturge/mage/warrior-mage/whatnot), you can swap them around a lot and calibrate their skills to try different kinds of union set-ups, and this allows you to try out any number of strategies for tough battles. That said, there will always be few hiccups out of your hand. Veeery few, if the unions are decent.
The other fun part about the battle system is that once you've worked out a few stable union combinations, just hit the spacebar and the AI does all the gritty work really well, and you can focus on your overall battle strategy/approach instead.
Stat increases are not random, their general direction of growth will depend on how you use the characters. Spam spells all the time and you'll see your characters' INT levelling far quicker that STR, and finally ending at a much higher number. But this is as far as our immediate control over stats gets, as far as I'm aware.
There is a 'morale bar' on every battle screen, and the gauge changes depending on how the battle's going. Maintining a decent morale in your favour can have a big impact in boss fights especially.
The game does have a strange levelling system, where grinding is not always rewarded (there are a couple of tricks to super-powering your characters early on at specific spots in the game via grinding, but that just really sucks the fun out of the whole experience). This, I feel, is a good thing; gives you more time to just explore the world, kill all the monsters, loot all the dungeons. Contrary to what's mentioned often, you don't have to skip -all- battles at first or be excessively wary about over-levelling. I have a habit of clearing out every new map, which is just what I did for my first playthrough, and ended the game at a Battle Rank of 144. Some of the boss battles were hard, but not too hard (except the Lost Remnant, maybe), and certainly not unbeatable. The hardest point in the main storyline in that playthrough was the part called 'The Nest of Eagles'- took 4 tries to finish it at ~BR 60 (considered a fairly high BR by most for this part of the game), but the fight needed a whole lot of re-organising on my part, and this made the win even more satisfying. Basically, the higher your Battle Rank, the more challenging the fights can get, but they rarely become insurmountable. I personally love the lack of intense grinding here, it just let me play the game to the end casually the first time around.
There are several classes you can train each of your characters to get into, depending on what skill sets they can acquire, and which ones you focus on. The Wiki is a great place for all the information you need on classes (and everything else). There are lots of weapons to choose from (a plus for me), each with different upgrade paths. Lots of scope for crafting. Nice loot from the bosses.  With the game config files as is, however, you can only change your main character's equipment. The others have set weapon paths, and you can only choose their upgrade focus (combat/mystic/balance).
There are lots of sidequests to complete; the bulk of your time will probably be spent on these. So if you become friends with the battle system, this can only be a good thing.
The DLC battles are great, in my view. My favourite part of the playthrough.
Graphics are cool, but this point is probably very subjective.
I've had no issues running this game, performance-wise (on a system with recommended specs), and have been able to run this on a system with specs slightly lower than the minimum suggested (significant lag, but that's where I finished my first 3-odd playthroughs, and I loved the gameplay enough for this to not trouble me!)
If there's one major complaint I have, it's that far too many playable characters come too late into the game, and are much weaker than your current set of characters. If you don't watch the BR, this difference becomes even more stark.
Or sometimes they're really cool, but you're almost at the end of the game so what's the point in hiring them.
TLDR; the battle system is very intriguing, give it a shot! Especially if you like battles. The game seems to be perpetually discounted on here anyway.

This JRPG has one of my favorite battle systems in any JRPG. It's not perfect, by any means but it's very fun to be able to recruit a mercenary army and go to town on an entire squad of enemies while still having a turn based style system.
I'm not really a fan of the Battle Rank system which doesn't make much sense. Basically, the enemies in the game scale based on how many strong monsters you kill, so grinding actually hurts you. So does... killing pretty much any mobs apparently, unless they are incredibly weak. That said, it's interesting to have an RPG that -encourages- speedrunning instead of requiring you to grind a lot!
It also has one of my favorite JRPG soundtracks with some incredible battle and area music. The game would be a lot more boring without its stellar soundtrack adding some personality to the areas.
These days the graphics look a little dated. The art design is somewhat generic, with many of the enemies having a stereotypical look to them, though I do like how many different sentient species there are in the game's world. The character design is hit or miss, though some of the characters do look pretty badass. Hint: It's probably not Lord Davide.
The storyline is just enough to make the game interesting, but isn't amazing. The main character, Rush, behaves really weirdly like he has the personality and impulse control of a 10 year old, which can break suspension of disbelief. There are more interesting and cooler characters in the game though, like Davide's generals and Emma Honeywell. The overall story about the Remnants isn't explained too well, and the Remnants end up feeling like big Macguffins with no rhyme or reason to their existence.

The game satisfies a certain itch and anyone who likes the gameplay genre or space games in general would be crazy not to pick this up on sale.

What can I say about Grimoire Manastorm? The idea is perfect, ever since I was nine, playing on my Gamecube and Wii, I've wanted a Wizard game just like this. Running around in first person (or third) casting spells at other wizards. If you're looking for a good singleplayer mode, it's not for you. There are lot's of interesting enemies including (and limited to) Skeletons with swords, skeletons with no arms, skeletons that snipe you with lightning from across the map, (Reminiscent to the Jackal Snipers from Halo.) skeletons that shoot fire balls, giant trolls, and giant ice trolls. If you can't tell I'm being sarcastic. The main goal of singleplayer is to defend a church, and the harder difficulty is to defend a path, so yeah. I was done with that real quick. Multiplayer mode is better. It's just what you'd think it is, running around and shooting spells. There is a problem though, if more than four people are fighting at the same time, good luck trying to see what the hell is going on. The screen turns into a lagging mass of red and purple, and then you're dead. It also doesn't help that the only map that a lot of people play on is the Marketplace, the most headache inducing map I've ever played on. The snow is brighter than the sun and everything is fuzzy. That with the lagging mass of colors flashing on your screen is not good. If this map wasn't the only one with more than four players on it, I would never play on it. It's not really the devs fault everyone plays on the worst map, but it is their fault it hurts to look at it. Please remove the snow! Also If you've ever played Fallout New Vegas, you'd know that the enemies are complete bullet sponges. Multiply that times two, that's how this game feels. Once I casted a spell that threw dozens of meteors onto an enemy, and he didn't even flinched. Even worse, his health hardly went down. A game that handles this great is Half-Life 2. Blood spills everywhere as you shoot up your enemies, and when they die, they ragdoll, onto the floor, or tumble off the side of a cliff or building. (My personal favorite is blasting the Combines into a wall with a shotgun.) But with this game you get none of that. Have some blood, and maybe an animation that doesn't resemble a death animation out of World of Warcraft. It's a fact that all gamers love that satisfaction of ending their opponents brutally. Also, if you start up this game for the first time, don't expect to win. At all. You're attacks do nothing to more experienced players, and I think it's because the game doesn't give you opponents of your skill level. I'm going to give this game a thumbs up, becuase I think it has a lot of potential, but for my review to stand, the dev is going to have to fix up the maps, indication that you're hurting someone, and the singleplayer mode. Other than that I love it.

To put it simply: this is one very decent JRPG if not for the combat system, which although quite novel can be excruciating at times.
Story: meh.
Nothing exciting happen and the plot goes far too slow to be enjoyed. Kinda funny for a  game titled The Last Remnant when most of the time the remnants only appear as uninteractable background objects.
Characters: okayish somewhat
Most of your party characters are mercenaries who have no contribution at all to the main plot. Some of them are (awesome) unique characters with nice side quest tho. It's hard to beat a 4-armed catman armed with dual halberds.
Music: okayish somewhat
The battle theme is nice to get your blood boiling but it get repetitive after a thousands battles
Gameplay and Mechanic: revolutionary? Yup. Frustating? Hell yeah it is
At first you'll be presented by a bunch of combat mechanic (deadlock, flank, rear assault, etc) that sounds awesome on paper but hardly useful on real battle. Most mooks are weak enough to be killed from just a simple deadlock while enemies who truly need strategy to be downed HAVE a high deadlock threshold to even be flanked.
This game also has one weird level scaling (kinda like TES IV: Oblivion) wherein your enemies level growth is high. The more you grind the more unkillable the enemies are until you can't do anything beside restarting the game. So, minimize your grind.
And the most frustating thing is the combat command. In this game, you can only give your squads vague ideas about what they're supposed to do next ("Use combat  arts!!!" "support them!!!" etc) and the ai will pick his action from his assorted abilities. The problem is it's fuken random, as in at critical time the command you need won't even appear.
Example:
You need to heal without breaking the deadlock?  Nah, this time the game only giving you an option to break the deadlock, heal, get raidlocked by enemies, BAM your squad downed
Let's use some strategy! Squad A to tank the damage while squad B attack from afar -> the command "Attack from  afar!!!" on squad B does not appear + the idle command does not appear  -> Your weak defense, high magic squad must fight the giant behemoth head on -> squad B downed.
Technical wise surprisingly (compared  to other SE jrpgs, at least. *cough *cough* FF XIII series) this game has a superb port. Nice graphic options (not just simply low, medium, and high), good translation, good keyboard support (mouse support is meh but you don't really need a mouse for this game), and most of all no random CTD.
Buy this game if you love JRPGs and can't stand not to play one. If you're not, only buy it when discounted.

This game looks pretty, has a pretty positive rating, and has an interesting battle system, but that same battle system is also what killed any interest I had for this game.
In the game, when you win a battle, you have a chance for something called your Battle Rating (BR) to increase in level. This sounds good, but just wait.
The game alters the difficulty based on your BR. This is especially true for bosses, who can become impossible to defeat if your BR is over a certain number. Meaning that, if you decided to go out and grind a little, thinking it wouldn't hurt, you may very well be doing away with any chance you had at defeating an upcoming boss.
How do you make the game playable? That's simple: You avoid every battle that you can possibly slip past. No random encounters, no mobs in the field, nothing. You can't even grind unless it's in certain parts of the game, and at certain times, unless you want to risk ruining your chances at progressing. That keeps your BR at a low number, which means bosses become 'easier' (I say it this way because, really, they're still ridiculously overpowered).
"But this game has so many positive reviews!" you might be saying, as your cursor hovers over the BUY button. That would be because most of the people who have played this and beaten it are either 'hardcore', don't know the difference between a poor design choice and a good one, or are just masochisitic. You can sink eight hours into the game, and find yourself unable to even beat a single random encounter, simply because you wanted to level up your party members.
Unless you've got some sort of demented craving for an overly difficult game, or you're seriously wanting to spend money on something you may never play, my advice to you is this:
Stay. Away. If you value your sanity, you'd do well to give this game a wide berth. It's not worth spending hours trying to even understand how or why this game is even out on the market.

I was 14 when I first played the original Bioshock when it first released back in 2007 and since then it still has remained as my favorite game of all time. I've beaten this game more times than any other game I can recall. I loved everything about it; the atmosphere, the story, the art, the gameplay. It has always been a 10/10 in my book.
When I first heard about Bioshock being remastered, I lost it, I couldn't wait to visit rapture again. Yes, as some of the other reviews have stated, there are some issues from the classic bugs that plauged the original game, mouse sensitivity issues, etc. but those issues didn't stop it being a masterpiece then and it doesn't stop it now.
The graphics are better than I remember from the first time I played it 9 years ago and now being remastered, it was like re-experiencing Rapture for the first time all over again. The game runs SO smoothly on my GTX 1070 (like they should), no jittering and a constant 150-200 fps (from what Geforce Experience was telling me depending on what was going on on the screen) on my 144hz monitor.
In terms of some of the other issues most reviewers have come across (game crashes, texture popping, and "unspecified" bugs) I have not come across them. The only thing I noticed is that there is more lighting than before which does take away from the game's original dark atmosphere. BUT like I said, these issues still don't stop the game from being the great story driven, atmospheric, immersive experience it has always been.
If you've never taken a trip to Rapture now is a better time than EVER. If you call Rapture your 2nd home would you kindly pay it a visit?

You have to beat an AI before you receive a win.
Plus, there seems to be a bug where your visible gold total doesn't update if you gain gold from more than one source at once, which is just shoddy coding.
If you want a cheap way to get in a few games of Magic, the price is pretty hard to beat. You can manage to get ~10 boosters from doing the tutorials and the story mode. But in a day and age when Hearthstone is showing everyone how to do an online digital CCG right, this is just a sad showing.

I received this game once upon a time because I had purchased the original Bioshock a couple of summer sales back. I thought it would be better and got really dragged by the achievements, inexistent on the original. However, I didn't get what I expected.

If crashes don't upset you [a lot] or you don't get them at all either because of a patch or you're lucky as heck, I'd say give this copy a try because of the achievements. But if you don't care for achievements or crashes are a no-go to you, I'd say stick to the original copy.

I started my Saints Row experience with
and I quickly fell in love with it. Everything in this game was so much over the top, but in doing so it was funny, and, moreover, incredibly entertaining. Still I was sceptical towards
; I read some stuff about it that I did not like. But I was wrong. Having superpowers was a great addition to the game series. So it was no question whether I would want to play
.
Despite this game has really no story, it is even more badass than its prequel. I mean, now you can now really fly and **** it, you can punch Satan in the face! Nice.
And when I say "no story", I mean it. Before starting the game, I as usual took a look at some reviews. Many of them stated that this game has no story, but I could not believe it. But now, after finishing it I can tell that it
does not have any story.
Why did I still like it? Because it exactly focuses on what I loved about its prequel: The superpowers and the weapons. Gat out of Hell is absolutely only about mastering challenges, which were, at least in my opinion, only a side-thing in Saints Row IV. But this is not even bad, because many of them are fun. I disliked only some of the challenges, e.g. the ones that were related to some guns that felt strange...
To sum this up:
+ Focus on entertainment: Blow the **** out of hell and its citizens
+ Related to the previous point: Be a badass superpowered hero
+ ~20 hours of fun, iff you do the challenges
+ Good gameplay; actually the same as Saints Row IV
- No story, just side-quests
- Some of the challenges are really annoying. I still don't know what the hell this Last Supper weapon is good for. For me this gun is completely useless.
- Compared to the sequels: No customization: Neither character, nor cars (but the car customizations already started to be useless in Saints Row IV)
If you like what the Saints Row series has become with Saints Row IV, you will also like this part. And if you liked Prototype, you will also like this game. But do not expect too much. Saints Row: Gat out of Hell is rather a DLC to Saints Row IV than a stand-alone game. In addition, I would not spend 15 bucks for it.
If you liked the story of the previous Saints Row games and want to know how the Saints' story continues, then pray that there will be another sequel, because this game has no story at all.

Hatred is a game where you play as a psychotic killer and murder kill death every thing in your line of sight. that's the long and short of it. I haven't played the game long, but i can already tell that I've gotten a basic gist of the gameplay to write a review on it.
*Performance*
First off, Destructive Creations did a poor job of optimizing this game, I should be getting a constant 60 fps, but instead i'm getting a jittery 30-42, it is still playable, just not as enjoyable as it could be performance wise.
The performance gets a 4.5/10 it's not horrible but it's not great either.
*GAMEPLAY*
Regardless of my kneejerk reaction the first time I saw the trailer, joining in with the large amount of people demonizing the development team for making such a "horrid game," I now find this game very fun to play, although I can tell that the gameplay will become repetitive in time do to the fact that every level is just "Kill (X) amount of people to proceed." Where the gameplay starts to diversify though is in the side missions, whether it be crashing a house party or killing deer hunters, this small touch really makes the gameplay feel interesting, wondering what will be on the next level for side missions.
The gameplay gets a solid 7/10 i'm really enjoying the gameplay and look forward to what cool side missions there are.
*GRAPHICS*
The graphics in this game are very interesting, it's black and white as to hark back to older horror films and it gives the game a very old timey, gritty feeling. But there are colors in this game, explosions are, well, bright and...explody, all the blood shed from police and innocent civilians is a lighter shade of red, and the Lights on the cop cars flash red and blue in a blinding fashion (in a good way). I feel though for all the extensive graphics options, the black and white filter of this game doesn't let the graphics shine in a way I feel they should have, don't get me wrong, the game looks nice, just not as nice as it could without the filter.
I give the graphics a 6.5/10 They could of been better, but they still look nice.
*STORY*
You all could of seen this coming, the story of our long haired, disturbed protagonist is no where to be found, while this can be looked at in a negative way, I look at it differently. The game starts out with (Noname) saying that he's going to kill as many people as he can and that he always wanted to die violently. The way I look at the story, the lack of story almost leaves itself open for more creativity, i.e. what could his name be? what happened to him as a child that spawned this dark cloud of hatred inside of him? But, i'm rating what story is here, which is none.
I give the story a 3/10 there is no story, but in a way it makes (Noname) more mysterious and creepy.
*OVERALL*
In the end I think we all got what we were expecting, a shallow, but extremely fun and interesting game about a psychopaths life ending rampage. I say if you have the money to spend on this game and have an interest in playing it, or have had one for some time, get it, I don't think you will be disappointed.
I give Hatred a 7.5/10 very fun and worth a try.

I so wanted to like this game. But the designers really dropped the ball on this one. Here are three big misses (among many):
1. Warfare is boring - What an amazing opportunity for the designers to dream big about what future warfare would look like. Are there robots? Drones? Devistatiing bombs? New defenses? No. Instesad they dumbed down Civ V combat by reducing all units to a few types (air, armor, ranged, artillerty, etc.) and only letting you upgrade these four levels. BORING!
2. Wonders are boring - One of the funnest parts of CIv (IMO) is building wonders. Civ V made them a lot of fun with varied bonuses, access to some only through culture trees, etc. Building a certain wonder could change the way you play the game. Again, what an amazing opportunity to dream about what future wonders on a new world might look like. Instead, we get generic wonders with no graphics or animation that provide lame bonuses. BORING!
3. Terrain is boring - Civ contained a myriad of resources that were interesting and critical to warfare at certain points in the game. BE certainly has lots of colorful resources, but none of them are particlularly interesting and none change the game play or warfare much. Where you land and which of the four key resources are near you will determine your victory strategy, which is a snoozer. It doesn't really matter, i guess, as the various paths to victory are so alike that one isn't any more fun than the other. BORING!
I certainly hope that the designers will take all the feedback they are getting and redesign the game. There is so much potential here, squandered by poor gameplay design.

Gameplay in Return to Castle Wolfenstein is your standard fare of arcade FPS fun, which is very similar to Quake III. Quake players should feel right at home, mostly because the game is based off the same engine, but we'll get into that later.
Gunplay in RTCW is solid. You will be delighted to see the game offer up a large and powerful arsenal. Ranging from a silenced SMG to a highly effective TESLA gun.  Same can be said about the enemies, as you fight your way through your typical Nazi grunts to something of a bloody terminator. This game is hard, really hard. Enemies can inflict large amounts of damage in a matter of seconds and a small squad could pick you off easily if you're not prepared. This gives the game a sort of tactical feel, as you start leaning and checking every corner while picking off targets more cautiously. There were multible times I felt like I was honestly playing a Rainbow Six game. Difficulty really ramps up by the end of the game and since there are no checkpoints, you should keep that F5(quicksave) key close.
There are moments in the game that are very cheap however. There were enemies that could zap you from across the room without once stopping to reload or enemies that could quite literally zap you to death from the floor below without giving you time to react. Moments like these make the game feel cheap, but luckily those moments are far in-between.

The atmosphere in Return to Castle Wolfenstein is excellent. While the music in the game isn't anything to really brag about, it works for the most part to keep the tone of the game right. Luckily though, the typical military music is countered with an insane level of map detail. Every level in RTCW is very different from the other- you'll be sneaking through a village one moment and fighting your way through undead vikings(?) inside a hidden crypt the next. The game really changes its themes a lot, which really help keep the game fresh. Not all is sunshine and buttercups though, as the aforementioned Quake engine has aged a bit and that can definitely be noticed in some of its maps.

Story wise, you play as the returning Nazi genocider B.J. Blazkowicz, as you uncover the dangerous and mystical project the Nazis are cooking up. The story feels a bit vague for my taste and the subpar cutscenes and voice acting don't help. But it is there for anyone who cares about the reasoning behind all the bloodshed. B.J stays silent throughout the whole game, but there are still some cutscenes that do make me crack a smile and be interested in every now and then. I personally feel the ending of the game was a bit off.

War survival game that is mainly about micro-managing the resources you obtain by scavenging, trading, stealing or killing. Good decision making and management of resources will allow you to survive. What is really engaging about this game is how the moral choices are hidden within the game itself. You can end up in situations where scavenging does not work, and you will be pushed to the edge and maybe, eventually you have to steal or kill to survive. The game also does a good job in making you emotionally invested in your decisions.
It is a fantastic game albeit a fairly steep price point, but I did buy the game from the humble store sale at 15% off. It has a considerable amount of replayability as you can try different ways to survive. You could also try different paths of human morality.

I've met the developers in real life. They are stand up guys who really care about their game, This is not more $60 shovelware, this is a passion project- that alone should be enough for you to consider it.

If you're expecting Beyond Earth to be a new Alpha Centauri, consider yourself warned. It is not. The game is ludicrously buggy for a realease. We're talking BSODs and units *just not doing what you commanded to last turn*. But, even that, is not the reason I hate this game. I hate this game because it is completely lacking any player connection. What I mean by this is, all of the cultures more or less feel the same minus a buff. It isn't like Alpha Centauri where every culture had a distinct ethos and they are all duking it out. I found myself caring little for any of the cultures in Beyond Earth as, with few minor exceptions, they were more or less the same culture with different skins and voice acting. Another problem is the lack of any real comprehension of the tech tree. Yes, what they *do* makes sense, but what you are *making* sounds like a bunch of star trek technobabble. It isn't like Alpha Centauri where it felt you were actually making units. All it feels like is generating buffs and passive bonuses.
This game is less civilization and more an excel spreadsheet. Don't buy it.

Sins never ceases to keep me entertained, even after a 10 hour game of tug-of-war with the AI. I think that's the strongest point of this game: the fact that it remains extremely fun even when playing with AI. Sure, you start to figure out some of the trends the AI falls into, but it never gets stale somehow. Even though there are common trends the AI follows, the events of the game do not feel linear at all. It's an open ended experience that truly adapts to how you are playing.
The multiplayer is where Sins really shines. Playing against a thinking, adapting opponent adds so much to the game. Strategies have to change quickly and become more creative when playing against humans. I've only played with friends, so I cannot comment on how the random online games are. The only problem with the multiplayer isn't even the game's fault: it's sometimes a bit of a commitment to complete a game since you're looking at multiple hours per game. Unless you have friends that you can come back and play saved games with, it might be a bit inconvenient.
Lastly, the visuals and atmosphere of Sins are something special. The soundtrack ranges from silent and mysterious to triumphant and aggressive. It fits in perfectly with the stunning outer-space visuals of the planets, ships, and skybox. All of the small touches really add up. The clean scrolling from the zoomed out strategic view to the up close cinematic view is fluid and makes the whole game feel like one cohesive world. Strategy games aren't usually known for atmosphere and feeling, but Sins has one of the most immersive experiences I've encountered.
Sins feels like an ever-changing, challenging, fleshed out strategy game that has the added bonus of great fit and finish on the atmosphere.

BioShock is set in 1960 in the underwater city of Rapture; the city's history is mostly revealed via audio recordings the player can collect during the game.Rapture was planned and constructed in the 1940s by Objectivist business magnate Andrew Ryan who wanted to create a utopia for society's elite to flourish outside of government control. Scientific progress greatly expanded, including the discovery of the genetic material "ADAM" created by sea slugs on the ocean floor. ADAM allows its users to alter their DNA to grant them super-human powers like telekinesis and pyrokinesis. To protect Rapture, Ryan imposed a law that no contact with the surface world was allowed.
Despite the apparent utopia, class distinctions grew, and former gangster and businessman Frank Fontaine used his influence of the lower class to plan a coup of Rapture. Fontaine profited by creating black market routes with the surface world, and together with Dr. Brigid Tenenbaum, created a cheap plasmid industry by mass-producing ADAM through the implanting of the slugs in the stomachs of orphaned girls, nicknamed "Little Sisters". Fontaine used his plasmid-enhanced army to attack Ryan, but reportedly was killed in the battle. Ryan took the opportunity to seize his assets including the plasmid factories. In the months that followed, a second figure named Atlas rose to speak for the lower class, creating further strife. Atlas led attacks on the factories housing the Little Sisters, and Ryan countered by creating "Big Daddies", plasmid-enhanced humans surgically grafted into giant lumbering diving suits who were psychologically compelled to protect the Little Sisters at all costs. Ryan also created his own army of plasmid-enhanced soldiers, named "Splicers", which he controlled using pheromones distributed through Rapture's air system. This Remastered version of Bioshock is beautifully done it will be an awsome gem in your library of games.

Quest Based JRPG with an unconventional Battle System and drawn out plot.
The plot is unique in that it's about political turmoil and backstabbings. Which isn't anything new, but certainly new enough for JRPG's. I enjoyed it well enough, but I can understand if the lack of drama might keep others from being interested in what's going on. Most JRPG's are character-driven, and here it's written with the main actors really being the states and the powerful remnants that reside within each (and the conspiracy fabricated to take control of them all). The title starts out with the simple task of you rescuing your sister, but it becomes quite evident that something much larger is at play and in rescuing her you become allied with a Duke (Nukem) and embroiled in his objectives. Some might get a little confused with some of the political bable and the various actors, but it's an easy wiki to get your mind back on track.
That aside, this game is all about the battle system. A battle system the game doesn't bother to elaborate on.
The short end of it is that you have unions each with a max of 5 members each. They're basically party members put into small companies that make a mini militia. The enemy is very much the same way, and battles play out between these companies, but since the company has one unified healthbar they're, for all intents and purposes, one ''unit'' in battle and its units attacking units trying to get their HP to 0.
You don't control the units in the unions directly (max of 5 per union), rather you give commands to the entire union, like ''Hang in there!'' and ''Attack from afar!''. You can see what these commands will lead to, so it's not too bad. But it can be aggrivating not being able to prioritize what attacks come out with limited AP (regenerates every turn). You might choose for a union to go into heal mode, but the one unit that has a massive AOE heal ignores the command and attacks whilst the other two that can only use herbs that heal for a miniscule amount do the healing. Generally though the game does a really good job at making this a painless way to control your units and I never felt cheated.
The game provides many options in setting formations for your unions, with varying effects for each. The problem is that they're not really explained in-depth and, according to most of the community at least, they're not required to play through the game. It's a nice addition but not required to get a grip on.
Most of the side-game is doing quests that lead to new union members or simple money rewards, with some resulting in new weapons. There's two things about this game that are bull♥♥♥♥ though:
-some quests disappear if you progress too far into the story. There's no warning of this.
-You don't gain XP, but you gain Battle Rank (BR). There's no ''BR'' bar to show how close you are to your next rank, but gaining BR is bad as it makes the enemies stronger; lower BR increases stat gains per battle which makes your units stronger faster and it makes it a less grindy ordeal. In a game where you get party members as the game progresses this is bad, as they start out weaker and weaker the higher and higher your BR is and it becomes harder and harder to level them up.
The second critique is this game's huge achielles heel. In many ways you're persuaded not to engage in battles until the midway point of the game where you will have most of the party members available to you. Whilst the entire party shares a culminative HP; the units can still be targetted and fall to instant KO spells or killed individually. If a party member is dead at the end of battle they gain nothing from the battle. Apparently this aspect of the game was rushed as they had to get it out. The fact that this isn't explained thoroughly in game is another sore point on this title: there is a severe lack of documentation. Seriously, some aspects of the game the community isn't fully sure of because it's not really explained. I have over 100 fuc*ing hours in this game and I'm still COMPLETELY IN THE DARK about some things. There's this quest where you get different rewards and people aren't sure what the HELL you have to do to get the best rewards. Something tells me the devs didn't really care if the player knew about some things or what exactly the mechanics or effects are and didn't think you needed to know. It's fine if you don't care but aggrivating if you do.
Aside from that, with 100 hours in, it's a generally ''new'' feeling game for its story and how the battle system works. It's not ground-breaking and I wouldn't say it's a must-play, but it's not offensive and does tries enough different things for a JRPG that I'll give it a recommendation. I'd say skip it if you don't care for RPG's, but give it a shot if you need something to play/a JRPG and are feeling adventurous in how 'new' you want the experience to be. If there was ever a proper sequel with some fixes I'd be there in a minute.

This review will be a comprehensive, detailed summary of my experiences whilst playing the remastered version of Bioshock; I will mainly be speaking in terms of glitches, graphical errors, and bugs that I have found and will be updating this review as many times as needed so that, in the instance I experience a new bug/glitch, or if something is patched, I may edit those parts, respectively. This review was started after the December 20th patch, fixing plenty of already known issues. After this patch, I would definitely say that this game is in a "playable" - meaning bearable more than anything - state. From a gameplay standpoint, even with the issues I am about to mention below, the game is still fun and enjoyable both with a keyboard and mouse as well as a controller.
To start out, I should give my system specs; I'm running an Intel-i7 processor at 3.4GHz, I have 12GB of RAM as well as an R7 390 GPU. Currently using Windows 10. For my in game settings, for simplicity's sake, I've all of the graphical settings on "Low" or its equivalent, while V-Sync is enabled.
Furthermore, I would point out that I did in fact recieve this product at no cost to me whatsoever for simply having Bioshock and Bioshock 2 already in my account. So I can't really "complain" for receiving something for free, but I can understand the anger that those who had purchased the item would have. This list is merely something that I can edit easily for both consumers and developers alike.
GRAPHICAL ERROR: Screen Flickering (I)
-Details-
The main source of my screen flickering now comes from using my Electro Bolt plasmid. To elaborate, I will - for instance - shock an enemy using the plasmid, and strike them with the wrench, killing the enemy; however, while looting and getting close to the corpse, I will encounter screen flickering. This seems to be at its worst when the enemy is dead and is during the animation in which the corpse violently twitches with electricity. There also seems to be some moments where, instead of flickering, I will experience "black bars".
GRAPHICAL ERROR: Screen Flickering (II)
-Details-
This issue mainly comes from environmental objects, instead of plasmid usage. This first time I've encountered the issue was during the first few moments of the game when
. Looking back on it now, there were sparks of electicity during the in-game cutscene as well. From the evidence that I've seen, both with the plasmid issue as well as the environmental issue, I can assume that, for some reason, whenever any sort of electrical texture is in the player's LoS, it reacts horribly with the environment and causes object flickering and black bars.
SYSTEM ERROR: Alt-Tab
-Details-
This issue is small in regards to the other issues listed, but I feel as though I should still mention it. As the title probably suggests, Alt-Tabbing while in game crashes the system and forces the player to relaunch the game.

Do not listen to negative reviews from people with 20 minutes of gameplay - that's roughly how much time it takes to realise that you can't win by just holding down the left mouse button.
That is when some may start nit-picking about animations and optimisation in a FREE PRE-ALPHA made by an independent studio.  The game runs better than battlefield 4 on FX 8350 + GTX 770.
The premise is amazing, the movement is fluid and non-restrictive, and combat is fast-paced and deply satisfying.
Easily one of the most innovative FPS titles I have seen recently.
What really sold this title to me though is the low-cooldown magic spells.  They make the combat so much deeper and skill-dependent.  Unlike in Paladins, you are not stuck using your main attack while waiting for your skills to recharge.  Unlike in Unreal Tournament, you are not at a disadvantage because the enemy was milking a weapon spawn area, or simply got lucky with the pickups.
I would love to see this game fluorish and am ready to make this one of my go-to FPS titles.  The only real and very serious flaw I see in the game is the average mouse sensitivity customization, and the fact that mouse sensitivity randomly changes mid-game.  It's almost game-breaking for people who want to keep their aim consistent across games.

Now, Gat Out of Hell is by no means bad. Its just not so much Saints Row, not even Saints Row 4.
The concept is simple. The Boss was abducted by Satan and now Gat needs to take over hell. The problem is that its basically the bare bones of Saints IV. There's almost no story progression, no planning or really making alliances. The story is summed up in one sentence over and over: "Make Satan mad, so you can shoot him in the face".
On top of this, there are no cutscenes, just still images with voice overs. There's no line of story quests, the entire thing is just "do side missions until the end boss opens up". The problem with this is that of the 5 districts of town (each with their own boss) you only HAVE to ally with 2 bosses to get the finale and there's really no indication that it is the finale until you're already there.
Instead of quirky loyalty missions to unlock superhero costumes, this time... there's nothing. You can't call on your companions, theres no conclusion to the loyalty missions, its just... eh. It feels like Volition finally ran out of steam or it could be because the entire budget was spent on a single musical sequence.
The other problem with the game is that a lot of the new weapons and powers are just effects. There's a shotgun that makes people dance, there's a gun that makes people eat eachother, superpowers that make people worship you, two super powers that makes peopel freeze. The problem is that none of the new weapons or powers are as good as the Saints 4 Bling and Chain reaction powers. On top of that, even though the game has made new side quests for vehicles, there's no reason at all to drive them, even less of a reason than Saints 3.
Additionally, even the achievements are pretty lackluster, most of them (and most of the in-game "quests") are just grinding. "Kill 1000 people with this weapon", good. Now "kill 200 people with this superpower" etc. etc.
I had fun for a while, but I just can't recommend it.

This stand alone expansion is made by a different studio and you can tell, it is bare bones to the extreme, the second you start playing it you can immediately tell that little to no effort was put into the development of this title.  You can tell this was done with limited everything by the lack of any meaningful voice acting and cutscenes everything is portrayed through still images.  There is no interaction between Kinsey or Jonny they are just clones of each other in game with no variation between the two.  Your homies are pretty much nonexistent unlike how they were in SR4 so have fun not getting attached to them at all, since there is no main ship you can interact with them that way either so again pointless.  There is no driving force behind the "main story' you just continue to do activities until the arbitrary amount have been done, forced and clearly done as a cash out in order to garner just a bit more money just because it's a Saints Row title.  There is no variation for the population of Hell just the same husk, again adding to the empty or hollow feeling of the title more showing off that it is simply at mod for Saints Row 4 but a very poorly made one with the original voice actors in it.
One of the major selling points makes a big deal about you helping out major figure heads of Hell, historical figures who ended up in Hell and so on but there is no tangible connection between the player and those NPCs, unlike SR4.  Thus this makes doing quests for them completely pointless and nothing but wastes of time.
When you look at your activity and quest log you'll understand what everyone means, there are literally pages of lines worth of these "quests" and after doing a few of them or heck if you did all of them in previous games then you will get very tired of them VERY quickly thus making this game a complete waste of time.
I kept looking at the sheer number of “quests” that the game had listed and realized how little there was to this game, if any which made me reconsider even bothering to fully play through this stand alone SR4 expansion.  This is a shame because I enjoyed 4 quite a bit, it had it’s low times as some of the activities are rather difficult especially alone but at least you had something that was story driven, but this……… no there is zero story here and I really don’t even care enough at this point with my meager one hour and forty minute play through but I just can’t push through the ridiculous number of pointless activities just to increase my “Satan attention bar” beyond what I have now.
I can not suggest this; to me this is not really more of the same Saints Row rather it is just a skin covering a title that revolves around doing activities as it’s main source of gameplay.  If you enjoy doing SR’s activities that much then go for it, otherwise……just stay way.  This will be one of the first games that I just can not push myself to beat and I will be attempting to get a refund because there is really nothing to this title and it’s very sad.  This title commits a major cardinal gaming sin, which is making the player feel like he/she is doing busy work rather then progressing through the game through activities and quests.

This game is certainly worth the 8 bucks it usually goes on sale for, and I feel that some criticism of the game is misplaced.  That having been said, it has a host of problems.
The game starts off in media res, and doesn't share its backstory until a few chapters into the game.  This makes it easy to get confused about what's going on and what the stakes are, especially since this game has a TON of proper nouns getting thrown around.  Lucille, Gran Pulse, Cocoon, Falcie, it can get jumbled up pretty quickly.  The game does have a index that you can read to get a summary of what's going on which I'd advise looking at the second you can - it does a better job of explaining the game's starting point than the cutscenes.
The gameplay is a mixed bag.  Personally the worst thing about it was only having two useable party members at a time for a large portion of the plot, especially because adding a third member gets you a large increase in your available strategies.  This is something the sequel fixed but this iteration can be rather boring to play until you hit the later chapters.  It's still flashy and fun to watch though.
The plot is interesting.  It does a great job at certain points and a crap job at others.  It's all about coming to terms with crapsack destiny and the way the different characters respond to it.  I'd highly recommend using the Japanese voices - the English ones lose a lot of emotion and while some of them are okay, others are just awful (Lightning's in particular).  Speaking of which, you might think this is a game about Lightning based on advertising.  It really isn't - it's about the party as a whole, and everyone gets some time to shine (some more than others).  The worst part about it is probably Snow - he gets his subplot carted off to the side for a good number of chapters and as a result some of his development feels a bit rushed.  One of your latter party members is barely in the game, which is kind of disappointing given that she winds up being critical to the whole story.
The game's ending is just baffling unless you play the following game 13-2.  Even then, certain parts of it won't make much sense (how did they know they could even do that?) but at least it hits the right notes emotionally.
The map design is linear.  Personally I didn't have a problem with this - it reminded me a lot of X - but unlike X it does a poor job of disguising it/changing up the pace.  While X had stuff like the Cloisters and Blitzball to shake up the progression, 13 is just a straight shot to the end until you hit Chapter 11 (where the game gives you an insane amount of freedom). There's this weird mechanic where you can ambush enemies by running into their rears on the map, but this is rarely usable and feels kind of pointless.
Overall, an okay game with a much better sequel.

Decent title, I enjoy it.
Essentially it is on a 2D plane, as others mentioned, but I find it not important in this case, since you are flying only large ships anyway - looking at Starpoint Gemini 2 (which fearures large ships only also but in full 3D) movement anyway more or less doesn't revolve around the 3rd Dimension so much, as in a game where you'd fly dogfighting little ships.
Which brings me to the namedropping of Freelancer, I see al lot.
It's not like Freelencer for me, for the same reason as SPG2: no fighters, no dogfighting, so you don't have the fast paced, zooming flight feeling as in Freelancer.
That doesn't have to be a bad thing, it's just different.
Graphics are shiny, combat is more fast paced than SPG2, although ship classes are comparable.
Another namedrop is the TV sries Firefly, which I instantly associated too, but this vibe is mostly because of the music score - i guess with other custom music, this Firefly vibe would be gone.
Setting is rather standard free roam space sim, with missions (quite some different ones with time and "levelling" curve), trading, mining(which I found very useless money/time wise, except at the very start, maybe there are good spots somewhere though...), a decently interesting main story and so on.
The gameworld is mostly randomly generated each new game.
The star systems and their availlable equipment are organized in tiers, comparable to SPAZ or Freelancer, at the same time there seems to be a different scaling for missions, which seems to depend on your overall equipment level.
What I instantly liked, is the freedom you have in approach:
You can pirate trade ships via dialogue options (you can shoot them too of course).
Contrary to Freelancer, you can actually really play as a pirate affiliate and do the story at the same time.
Or so is my impression at least, since once I had pirate affiliation, a "mirrored" main mission did pop up, I'm pretty sure i could have followed that main story strain instead.
I didnt, because sadly the military faction will drop to hostile, once you are not hostile with pirates anymore and I didn't want to go that route... maybe in another playthrough.
The title, as I understand, is from an experienced indie team, which shows at times - it is not as polished as some triple A titles, but it is solid and I didn't encounter many glitches, no gamebreaking bugs.
And it's around 20 bucks, not 40-60...
Some people said keyboard+mouse won't work well, but I personally don't have problems with that so far.
You can remap the keybindings and using the mouse for aiming, controlling the camera angle works fine for me.
The two most annoying things for me are:
- the rather barebone save system. You can choose a save slot for your playthrough, so not to overwrite an older one, but the rest happens only per autosave and it uses only this specified slot, overwriting it constantly, like Far Cry 3.
It saves each time you undock from a station, which works fine.
And it saves when you leave to main menu - this is problematic, if you don't know this and save this way in a hopeless fight ending up in a dead end situation, where you can't escape nor access an old save.
(I personally expect, or hope, this will be patched some time, to give more control over the saves, because it is really bothersome).
I suggest to backup the save files (in "MyDocuments" for me) regularily.
- the one moment, I really miss the 3D movement is, when trying to avoid obstacles. Semi-quoting futurama, in this dimension you can't step over something, you only can step around it.
Other than that it's definately a nice time killer.

It's difficult for me to appreciate all the negative reviews after I installed this game. To be fair I'm installing X-Rebirth after a number of major patches and I didn't see the game in its initial form. However, considering what Egosoft are doing here, I'm surprised at the amount of negativity surrounding what is an enormous amount of innovation by Egosoft. They should be highly commended for what they have done here. The custom engine is doing things that I'm surprised I've not seen addressed in an industry paper about 3D engine technology. The graphic design and overall artistic direction is beyond outstanding. Egosoft have created a genuine hint of what it might be like to be thrown into a strange alien universe that can be compared to the SciFi series FarScape. My reaction to the game reminds me of John Criton's reaction to being thrown into a starship of strange aliens and having to quickly, and somewhat painfully, adapt. This is all communicated in game by the overall atmosphere that Egosoft create. Another game that is doing this kind of thing very well is Wolfenstein New Order. I think both these games show the maturing story telling and atmospheric immersion of these new "next gen" games. As I understand it Rebirth maybe missing some of the features that attracted fans to previous "X" games, but I still think Egosoft should be commended for not playing it safe. The world needs bold new creations such as Rebirth ! Some of the furore surrounding the initial release reminded me of the situation when Codemasters released a game under the Operation Flashpoint name. Where that game did ultimately flounder, here Egosoft seem to be doing a better job of fending off the detractors and sticking to their guns. If Rebirth somehow manages to "stick it to the man" probably depends on how much you think space exploration is an important part of our evolution. But at one point I was flying down a warp tunnel ("superhighway") and the radar had the words "Far Out" emboldened across the top. Just so. Rebirth can be like some kind of acid trip, something that does not go unnoticed by Egosoft with the ship called "Albion *Skunk*" and at one point in the campaign the pilot says (after a weapon installation) ... "The Skunk seems to be really working now". Need I say more ?

Recommended: "Sort of".
It is a nice JRPG, that tries to do something different with its battle system. But it is deeply flawed in the following ways:
1. Graphics optimisation is poor. Textures pop in a lot, which is annoying. Sure you can mess around with certain files to fix it, but most people won't want to bother doing that.
2. You really do need to force V-Sync outside of the game, otherwise expect some messy screen tearing.
3. The plot is generic enough, but it does the job. Where it sort of falls away is you could probably blow through it quite quickly. The real meat of the game seems to be over the other side, with side-quests. And there's a ton of them, lengthy ones, quick ones, and so on. A few of them get closed out reasonably early on in the game, so if you're a completionist, you'll be spending lots of hours getting through these at the expense of the main story.
3b. The main story progresses at lightning pace. Honestly, sometimes all you have to do is go to the main story location, watch some cutscenes for 20 minutes and then maybe have a boss fight, and repeat. (At time of writing I've got to the halfway point with 30 hours, about 28 of those hours were doing side-quests and travelling imho.)
4. Battle system is interesting but horrendously flawed and frustrating. Basically you create armies or battle groups of up to five people per unit. And they all share the same health pool and action points. You give them commands to attack certain enemy units. Usually you want to keep physical and magic users separate so they can all use either physical or magical attacks together as mix and matching doesn't always allow characters to act together.
Also, you generally put a healer in the unit so they can heal when they get hurt. Here's a ridiculous example of a frustrating battle:
I fought a battle and ended up with 1 unit left vs 1 boss monster. They were far apart, so couldn't attack each other. My unit had just beaten everything else on the battlefield, but it had a mere 90 hp left out of thousands. That unit had several healers. The enemy unit was almost dead. All I needed to do was heal, and own it. But the game refused to show the heal command, instead my choices were close in to attack next round, or wait. So I waited three times. No dice. The game then took away the command to wait, and forced me to move in. I had lots of Action points, at least three of my characters in the unit knew how to heal in various ways. In the end, the game gave me one choice; Attack physically (or attack with physical skills). No heals. So I attacked, and I died.
Here's the kicker, when you die it is game over. So reload time, wait through cutscenes all over again and retry the bloody fight. All this could have been averted by healing, but the game stubbornly refused to allow me to do so. And this is exactly where it becomes so frustrating, here is another hour to be wasted fighting the same battle, a particular pain in the butt if it is a difficult one anyway!
5. Levelling is apparently a no-no
Every guide out there suggests avoiding to grind, as enemies scale somewhat and will just ruin your day. Although it's not as bad as people make out, it can add to the frustration.
I realise this sounds like a very negative review, and really, I wanted to give this a mixed rating. There's a decent JRPG in here. Probably one could argue that The Last Remnant was an early warning sign of Square-Enix overcomplicating their games and making them somewhat silly. Still, it is a workable game, it just requires a lot of patience. Worth taking a risk for fans of the genre, but it certainly isn't a JRPG for the JRPG-newbie.

I was very surprised by this game once I delved into it. Made by a very small team, I knew it wasn't going to be a long game, but what I didn't know was how much fun it would be. There's something to be said about the fun one can have being able to slice and dice nearly every visible object in the world. Thanks to this very addictive mechanic, creating your own path to the objective is both fun and challenging. Not only that, but an entire "cuttable" world gives great possiblity for the existance of secret paths and items, of which there are a plenty.
The graphics are reminiscent of Borderlands but have a certain original quality. Gameplay is fairly straightforward and simple; along with standard platforming, players are to able cut, push, grapple, and attach rockets to objects. The music is varied and enjoyable, ranging from a jazzy trombone quarted to electric music to spanish drums and guitar; it's very rare I actually stop playing a game to sit and listen to the music.
With every good there must come the bad, but thankfully there aren't that many here. With more funding, perhaps the game could have been longer, as well as had more challenging levels. Being that it is such a short game, the devs have put in the all too common completionist achievements such as collecting every single "boring rock" in every single level. Not something that appeals to me, but perhaps other people would enjoy it. The controls are a bit sensitive, to the point where I've fallen off ledges when simply tapping a key to turn a certain direction. The last gripe I have is with the title. Only once you have played through the game do you understand why it is titled as such. Whether this is an attempt at being deep or creative, it falls short of achieving this goal and only serves to give the impression the devs were throwing darts to pick a name.
Other than these few, small complaints, Tiny and Big has a real charm to it; definitely worth a playthrough. Hopefully, we will see more gameplay mechanics like this in the future.

Okay so as someone who I just checked has over 500 hours in this game...  I think that qualifies me to write a review on it.
With that many hours I like the game.  I will break it down into the pros and cons for new players deciding.
Pros
Hands down my favorite large scale battle system.  It balances controling multiple squads facing off against armies without being to micromanaging and yet with still a bit of flexibilty.  Their are some frustrations and a steep learning curve to it though.  You rely upon the computer to bring up your selections and there is a lot of mechanics that go into it from your class, to your formation to your party leader.  Outside of combat selections and even your party build up can dramatically effect your combat.  But when you do finally get the hang of all that you can lead your forces into some truly epic looking and feeling battles.
Scenery is lovely in the game and has held up well.  Some areas get repetitive when you are still hunting for rare monsters but usually the areas themselves look pretty.
The leveling system i enjoy but it might not be for everyone.  Basically when you begin the game you get to decide how to equip your main character.  The rest of your party you can only choose one of three focuses so they are less customizable. But overall I like the fact that one game I can make him an assassin leading an army, the next a ninja and a combat hog, and a third game an epic healer magic user, and if you have enough patience you can master them all.
Negatives
The main character truly has an annoying voice and personality.  How can i play a game so much that I hate the main character?  Well because I truly love the epic battle system it is relaxing and a lot of fun and it gets better and more epic as you go through the game.  And the first time you pull of a synergy or you start busting out the remnants it truly does have an epic feel to it unlike many other games. So just suffer through the main character and enjoy the fights.
The storyline.. This game was built to have sequels.  It does not to the best of my knowledge have any in the works yet.  Would love to explore more of the world.  This one has a lot of potential.
The learning curve...  You will hate or love the game for the first few hours.  At about hour twenty your going to find someone trick in battle that you didnt realize you could do and things will be easier.  And then youll starting finding combos you can use for end game.  Or formations and specializations.  So the learning curve on this game sucks.  At a hundred hours your still going to learn new tricks and techniques to make the battles more interesting or fun.  Yet while it sucks to take forever to learn it means that there will always be a new little trick you can pick up that will help you later.  Or someone to add to your party in a combo you didnt think of.
So the grind is what will get most people though.  Doing all the side quests takes time.  And the first time you have to run across the great sand sea you will appreciate ground transportation that other games have.  This one you have your feet.  No way around it sorry.
Overall seems like there is a fair bit of negatives with the postives.  So why do I recommend it so highly?  Because like legend of dragoon the combat is interactive.  The effects in it have stood up the test of time and truly capture the chaos and epic feel of army combat.  Some games will capture that but this lets you control your army in a more fluid manner.  I wish other games had a similar UI. Basically even after 8 years since its release...  The game is still unique in its play and fun to engage in.  Hope some others will give it a try.  That they will be able to suffer through the learning curve and the challenges and find some enjoyment  in it.  And if enough like it hopefully they will make a sequel one day.
Thanks for your time and the short novel read.  Have fun my friends and best of luck to you.
