First thing is first.  This game is rather boring.
The game has a monotone color that saturates it entirely.  This may provide some of a contextual view on the mindset of the player character.  After all, he deems himself the executioner of the human race, therefore he already sees them akin to maggots.  The color unfortunately doesn't work well with the actual game play.  People blend in with the environment, everyone runs when you shoot, but they run in random directions, stopping themselves when they leave your point of view.  That makes them appear like they're leading you, only briefly pausing to make sure you're still shooting at them particularly before resuming their "frantic attempt to escape your massacre".
Police tend to arrive after a period of time, but they're not exactly any better than targets to shoot for free ammo.  I had a fair amount of time simply trying to play through until I die.  It doesn't really work well when you try that.  :T The targeting cursor you're given doesn't exactly help matters, I found myself shooting wildly at anything within the general direction of my intended target.  Cycling through my weapons after I ran out of ammo until I was just swinging my knife around.
Ultimately, I just don't care for this game.  I wish I could, but there's better games that do the theme of "killing with style" or "with awesome grotesque flair" better than this.  Manhunt comes to mind, Postal is another excellent alternative, and for more recent titles...  GTA and Saints Row.  Any of the recent releases.
If I could give any constructive tips, I would just ask that the makers of this game should work harder in making the humans more entertaining to kill.  Explosions and destroyable environments are nice, I really enjoy blowing things up, but when you make the environment altering aspects of a game more enjoyable than the killing aspect...  something might need redone.
:<  Killing doesn't have its visceral impact...  first person would have done so well in this game.  Give more substance in bludgeoning someone's face in, shooting their chest with a powerful blast of your shotgun, and the like.  I enjoy these sorts of games not for gore, but for immersion, to briefly have the sense of power, dominance, and destructive aggression.  Even if it ends in me dying horribly to the police, there's a poetic justice and retribution in that.  The inevitability in that once you start, you're simply trying to kill as many as you can until the bitter end.
It can be improved...  it can be better than it is now.  I just can't recommend it like this.

Dead Rising 2 is an interesting game. The premise, while differing from the first one, presents the exact same kind of gameplay structure. You're thrust into a big locale filled with zombies from one end to the other, and your playground is stacked to the brim with items that you can pick up and either use as weapons or consume for health.
One big problem the game has that very ironically cripples the game's fun factor is the constantly running time, with relatively strict time limits placed on every mission in the game. From what I could glean, there is no way to turn this off. Even if they don't want to abandon the intentional rushed feeling of being stuck in a city filled with zombies, the time limit could make some concessions, considering it keeps running during almost all missions, even after you've initiated them, which might leave you to randomly fail a mission that, for example, involves carrying a wounded woman back to the safe house, a trial she survives with no problems if you don't waste time running to her rescue at the beginning of the mission, but for some reason "the truth is lost forever" when you take time to make a few Painkillers and create some combo weapons beforehand and then go take her, and the timer runs out mid-mission.
Another gripe is the game's limited save system. This was a huge criticism levied at the first game, and maybe the decrying of the first game was pointless, because the Dead Rising series seems poised to retain its rushed, dangerous and desolate feel of tight time limits and very sparse save points, that lead you to being unable to save a huge majority of the survivors, and make you reload earlier saves often to save time while doing the main missions.
Overall, though, the game is a delight. Chuck Greene starts out as a boring alternative to Frank West, but quickly becomes endearing, especially with the addition of a good co-cast, and a sporadic, but nonetheless touching, relationship between Chuck and his daughter, who periodically needs Zombrex, medicine that keeps her from turning into a zombie, due to a zombie bite gained prior to the game's events.
The combo weapons are fun, and once you get the hang of the game and start instinctually knowing where maintenance rooms are and memorizing the combinations, you'll feel naked using regular weapons (except for the firearms, and a few others, like the broadsword, which would be ridiculously fun if only it lasted for longer), which is a good sign in my opinion, because the joy of creating a cool combo weapon is satisfying to no end, especially with the discovery of some of the better ones.
The psychopaths are tons of fun to fight (once you gain a few levels, 'cause in the beginning they're impossible) and have varied fighting tactics which, coupled with the different environments and weapons you have and their relatively high difficulty, provide variety in tactics that you have no choice but to experiment with to prevail.
The storyline throws a few curveballs at you and doesn't throw too much monotony at you, which is more the domain of the tedious survivor rescues. Even though not too emotionally gripping for most of it, there are a few moments in the plot that can really get to you, especially if with the hardships you have to go through with so many gameplay limitations, you feel magnified emotional connections to some of the characters that you co-operate with, look after and occasionally save.
All in all, there's not much to say. Chuck controls very well, and there's a certain "meatiness" to his turning and his hits (with the feeling of smashing through a crowd of zombies with a sledgehammer being my favourite), and with the exception of the annoying time limitations which sometimes don't even make logical sense and the still-annoyingly sparse save points, the game is a fun romp that makes you feel both powerful, and hopelessly weak, that controls with little fault, and oozes personality through the graphical presentation and the colourful characters.

Saints Row: Gat out of Hell is a Open World, Third-Person Shooter developed by Deep Silver Volition and released in 2015. You will probably fall into one of two camps:
or
.
If you were not a fan of the Saints Row Series, you very well might utter the phrase "Burn in Hell Saints!" ...that or if you were eavesdropping on Roman Emperor Nero.
Well this game is the almost literal manifestation of that phrase.
The saints started out as a simple street gang, became public figures, became
you very well might be asking "well, where else can they go? What else can they do?" Enter the Super Natural.
Just between you and me, I feel like Gat out of Hell is more of a collectathon then "third-person shooter" or "open world", but you don't NEED to collect all the things, there's just a lot to collect to 100% the game. Basically you land in Hell, need to screw around, blow up all the things, do some activities... really you can do whatever you want to♥♥♥♥♥♥Satan off, once you've♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥him off enough you can enter the final confrontation, and tada, games over!
Being an overachiever, there's more to the game for me: I need to unlock all the achievements, get 100% completion, all of that jazz. So for completionists whom enjoy open world games, or just liked the Saints Row IV style, this game is enjoyable.
The controls are the same, the powers are almost cookie cutter, (the colors are anyway), you have a thrown super power, a summon super power, a stomp super power, and aura super power. The most notable change to this game is the addition of flight. Instead of "jumping" upgrades, you get wings and get to fly around.
I happened to have "must play flight simulator game" in my blood at the time that I was playing this, so I would fly around and make airplane noises and got quite a bit of enjoyment of trying to fly as fast as possible and dodge obstacles like a drunk buzzard flying a 747.
Most of the achievements in this game are easily doable, although some require a fair bit of work. Naturally you have your typical "unlock while you play" or "you can only miss this if you refuse to play normally" achievements.
You also have the "conditional achievements" which require special events, none are really noteworthy, the descriptions are all very self explanatory,
Thankfully there's no "sync your character with our website which didn't work for the last two years", that was a load of
, but this seems to be a pretty doable 100%, I'll get back to you once I finish getting 100%. the toughest achievement seems to be "Complete ALL of the Challenges".
Update 03/16/16: I successfully completed all the achievements for Saints Row Gat out of Hell, and my final conclusion about the achievements is "yeah, this is kinda what I expected".
The final few hours were rather boring, but I had already milked the game for all it was worth, thankfully I was able to pop a few extra achievements in between grinding sessions.
Saints Row: Gat out of Hell is priced at $14.99, those of you whom know my price/value model, I want an hour for every dollar, or at least a comparable substitution of replay value or enjoyment. To get 100% city take over and finish the game I spent 7 almost 8 hours.
That's close to matching the value, the best gauge is to ask yourself "did you like SR4" if the answer is yes, ask yourself "Do you want to play more SR4... but as Johnny Gat", if the answer is still yes; this game is for you.
Hey, there's an achievement for spending 20 hours in Hell. My point is that I'll definitely get my monies worth out of the game. Oh wait, this game was actually gifted to me by Angfucious, so it's actually HER monies worth
Questions to ask yourself: Did you like Saints Row IV? Do you like Johnny Gat? Do you like Kinzie Kensington? do you mind if the game is just about them? Do you have 7 hours to play through a game? If you say 'yes' to most of these then you'll enjoy Saints Row: Gat out of Hell.

Think Elite Dangerous, but with naval combat and a good story.
The naval-style combat deters a lot of people, but it actually works quite nicely with the single-plane orbit everything has in every solar system.  That means you can't fly up or down, only left or right.  However, smaller fighter planes and asteroids can fly beneath or above you, requiring your ship's turret placements to be more strategic.
You can trade, mine, steal, join factions, make factions hate you, help people in distress, escort ships, fight every time, flee every time (depending on ship speed).  You can play as good, neutral, or evil, or jump around and do whatever pays the most.
The game allows you to easily put your own music into it.
You can resell every ship or item for 100% retail value.  This means you can test out ships, weapons, defenses, etc. without fear of wasting money.  This is a nice way of getting around the fact that you can only own one ship at a time.
I think this game is definitely worth the price.  As of writing this I have played 32 hours.  I'm not done with the main story line, and I don't think I will be for a while.  There is too much money to be made, and too many ships and ship upgrades to buy.

You would be wrong.
Playing X:Rebirth is like when you're out by yourself and nature calls in a bad way, you must go NOW... and all you can find is a porta-potty. Apprehension sets in, like you're sitting on a huge heap of human waste separated only by a flimsy board and the cheapest possible plastic container.
You summon you're courage, heading in and you flip the knob from open to unavailable. “This might not be so bad” you think... Just like you'll think in X:Rebirth. You start going about your businesses then, out of nowhere... <WHAM!!!> the world is spinning! You're falling forward, some unspeakably evil human being has knocked the porta-potty over on you and not only that, it has landed on the door!!! You're trapped in a sludge of brown, blue and black which is now raining down upon your prostrate self, covering your naughty parts with unmentionable filth.
The guttural sound that emerges from your now agony and rage filled self is how you'll feel when you realize you paid MONEY for this game. They didn't even pay YOU but you paid them. At least if a gorilla throws their excrement at someone, that person has an interesting story (and a dirty face). With X:Rebirth, there is NO redeeming value.

If you are looking for something LOTR related and do not have anyone to play with or wish to play alone, you could grab this. When it is on SALE that is.
As to if you want to play it with your friends? In that case you will encounter two things that will devastate your enjoyment of this title. Those two things being disconnection issues that completely wipe ALL your progress in the level that you are playing with your friends, along with ALWAYS ON VOICE-CHAT. Now there are ways to go around that Always on voice-chat, but it is NOT worth the hassle.
As to the disconnection issues: You lose all your loot, all your levels and all your skillpoints you gained in that level / session. The loot in your inventory / what was equipped on your character does not get saved. The moment you rejoin, those things are gone. Period.
As to the always on voice-chat: Extremely crappy audio quality, no way to change mic levels or audio levels of other players, and no way to turn it off or mute others. Workarounds include using another microphone and setting it as the primary audio device and then muting it but let us be frank here. How many of us actually have another microphone, and do we really want to connect another microphone / headset JUST for a single game? I dare wager only few of us are willing and able to even try that.
In other words, an okay single-player LOTR game for 5 bucks of less. For 20 bucks (19,99€) though? No. Absolutely not worth it. Especially if you are looking for something fun to play with your friends. In that case, the sale price is not worth it either.

It’s Not That Bad
Some might say BioShock 2 feels very “same-y” to the first BioShock, but I think that it holds its own.
Gameplay
The gameplay is much improved from the first game. You can now dual wield, plasmids in one hand and guns in the other. The weapons are all new ones. None of the guns feel like any of the guns from the original game. I never really used the wrench that much in the first game, but I used the drill as much as I could. It’s just a lot more satisfying than the wrench. The hacking gun makes for some very interesting strategies. You can now hack things from a distance and cause trouble easier. The hacking is changed too. Instead of a pipe dream clone, it’s more of a simple timing game. Now when you hack the world doesn’t magically stop for you to finish hacking. You now have to hack while there you are being attacked. There are lot of protection missions to the game. When you rescue a little sister, you have to protect them from waves of splicers. It was cool the first couple of time, but one might find this very repetitive. There many little sister to save, so you will be doing protections missions a lot.
Graphics and Sound
It looks just as good as the first one. Maybe a bit better. The problem is that it look a lot like the first one. One could say that the developers got lazy and just recycled the assets form the first game. There weren’t any new graphical flares that separate this game form the first one. It still has that underwater creepiness to it. It’s not as atmospheric as the first one was, but it did serve its purpose. It made us feel like we were back in rapture. The sounds were very recycled form the first game. I felt like I had heard all of the sounds before. Some of the splicer voices also sounded like the ones form the first game. All and all, it looks and sounded adequate. Nothing to write home about.

Story
The story is defiantly a bit of a week point. The plot is ok and the characters are ok. The idea of playing as a big daddy kind of set the tone of a very week story. Sofia Lamb is a good villain. She is just not as good as the other villains in the first game. All of the side character you meet are also fine. None of them are as interesting as any of the character you meet in the first game. The only side character worth mentioning is Gilbert Alexander.
The Moral Choices and the Ending
The Moral choices are back. Now you have the choice to adopt of harvest little sisters. If you adopt, instead of getting the Adam right away you need to do the protection missions three times. Then after you do that, you can rescue the girl or harvest her. If you harvest to begin with then she’s dead. After you harvest or save all the little sisters, a big sister will come to attack you. It’s strange that they attack you even if you go through all the trouble to not kill the little sisters. There are three moral choices you make for three of the side characters in the game. There are two choices: You kill them, or you don’t. The only difference you get is the kind of ending you get and what statue you sees before the ending. The ending to BioShock 2 was actually good. I wasn’t a huge fan of the first ending, and BioShock 2’s ending was much better and more satisfying. It doesn’t end abruptly with a montage, so props to BioShock 2.

After a year of bug fixes and added features, this game starts to come nearer to an entity like it's predecessor, but in it's own right.
It's now playable, I haven't gotten the game breaking save bugs and other random crashes that were plaguing my initial attempts to play this game.
(Edited with later game experiences within parenthesis)
The Goodish
I myself personally enjoy acting like a commander of a large fleet sending my ai companions into battle to kill off or be killed off by large xenon and pirate capital fleets. This is where the game shines to me in comparison to previous X games. If you don’t enjoy watching things unfold from the sideline and only enjoy the flying around capturing new ships to use part of the old X games for yourself I’ll stop you here and not recommend the game to you, unless you like having them alongside you then by all means proceed.
Mining is vastly improved though! <<< Like really a hell of a lot better mining system. (still not required for a successful game experience, highly recommend it when you have the extra cash, at least from an automated standpoint when you need to supply your own stations with materials. Otherwise continue stealing freighters)
Fewer menu trees (though it’s only good in theory because the automation isn’t there so you just have to hope there is a command you need in whatever situation you got into… if you’re doing combat mission don’t forget to remove your mining ships from your squad)
(I’d of prefered more menu choices with less of a hierarchy from X3 so that they weren’t hidden away.)
Space Graphics… don’t look inside unless you want a dollar and old toffee candy.
The Disappointing;
The bad things that I see in this game are mostly from a lack of automation available to the player in the old X games and missing fleet commands that really weaken the whole spin on having one ship through the whole thing. --If I have to spend 10 min sending orders to trade out, that’s not a better trading system in my book it’s a depreciation of something that was much better in the old X games.
Player Stations I’m really disappointed that they are limited to defined areas within zones, the ability to set-up outposts anywhere in X3AP was so cool and satisfying that as I write this I almost feel like hopping over removing tubes and starting a real empire. That being said I do prefer the new player station system as a whole, but the lack of freedom here brings it down to a level below it’s original roots with station complexes. (After getting more hours into the game and scaling up my own economy, I really must say that the game falls way short here, I like the scaling of the stations but the building and expansion of improvements takes far too long and I don't feel like running my computer for 7hrs+ just to have a single section build waiting on supply bottlenecks because my other stations and traders are busy)
Earning cash as a whole just seems so backwards in this game that I can’t even begin to describe my disappointment in this area. In what sense should I have to spend 7-8mil to buy a ship that does an actual economic activity only to make 250k an hour when I can just go long range scan for 15min get lucky and make 1.5mil off 100 crates of station trash items. (Adding in there are really only 3 things you can do for cash, long range scan, board ships, and board ships. For a game speaking of economy as an integral part of the gameplay experience there seems to be a lack of reward for doing the most basic economic tasks in the economy, the way it is currently set-up owning mining or trading vessels is a waste of cash and you must essentially own your own economic empire to even think of making a penny from station building since you can't make a profit because of what for me seems to be a set demand basis from the other factions with their preset number of stations, they need to build more stations in zones and expand against you and other factions)
Conclusion
Anyway I don’t recommend Re-Birth over X3AP or over any game really for that matter at this point. not worth $50, but if you could get 75% off or something huge go for it.
(After putting a good solid playthrough at 50hrs into the game and scaling up to the point where I had multiple combat fleets the game just feels stale, There isn't the threat of a true pirate menace, my biggest woes are managing an economy between my personal stations and assets through a few god awful menus, or commanding a fleet to jump in or out of combat zones as I wreck, or get wrecked, by the npc faction I feel like killing at any moment. When the ships do get into fights it's a pretty beautiful light show, but that's about all it has going for it at this point. It's fun for a bit, but after the first few station sieges and capital battles you're just grinding in a single player game to grind. You can't effectively manage the systems you take and you can't produce new factions  of resistence to your mighty fleets.
----I'm quite peeved that I can't command Xenon I's which I consider the most beatiful ships in the game and the producers of some of the better laser light shows when carriers and destroyers jump in.
What Would Improve it!
AI
This game could be better with an overhaul to the menu choices and npc faction ai, micro and macro level ai combat and economy, something that allows for recognition of a certain asset level allowing for new diplomatic options with the factions as an equal, or something to that extent, allowing for a scale up of fleets sent at you or to assist you in zones that you have influence over determined through % assets in system
Better Ship Designs --- Why are "half" the ships that are flyable freaken  flying Y's that's great and all but I like where the designers went with the xenon I sleek and tons of guns. If I have one ship I better be getting one helll of a show.
Less congested menus, maybe even more of them just less hidden trees of menus, I don't know, but as it is now it's rather annoying. pricing sliders solves this issue

I want sliders for automated purchasing amounts of drones and ammo with fleet managers that have accounts, as it is now I can only manage one fleet at extremely  poor efficiency time wise, literally takes me 2hrs to get all my ships repaired, stocked, and all while making sure they are in the right places.)

With the release of X Rebirth 3.0 the game finally reached the state it should have been in at its initial release in 2013. There are still a few rough edges and design decisions that some might find mind-boggling, but overall it is a great space game that can be polished with the use of a number of mods, some of which bring back 'classic' X features such as automated galaxy traders and miners. (as of the 14th of March 2015 some mod makers are still updating their work for the new moddable UI, some mods are temporarily out of action).
When considering buying X Rebirth is important to keep in mind that Rebirth is a fairly ambitious game for a smaller studio, as such there are always going to be the QA problems relating to small teams that have the ambition to make big games, like bugs working their way in, and lacks of resources meaning change doesn't happen as fast as gamers would like. To give Egosoft credit, they have adopted extensive community beta testing for each patch so the game is tested on as many different rigs as possible. On my most current playthough started at 3.2 I haven't found a single plot stopping bug, in more general freeplay I rarely find a bug, let alone one that blocks me doing what I want to do.
There are still some annoyances in the game such as expected bread and butter features missing from the vanilla game (a lack of FOV adjustment is a pertinent example). But these things, as illustrated by the addition of a great new gravidar, new menu system, and external camera system, seem to have been identified, working their way back into the game as Egosoft move from bug squashing to remedying design oversights. You can now do things like transfer freight and drones between ships, and build stations in empty space, creating a new zone with 7 build points that you can rename. Now, many modders seem to be finding their feet. As the engine is tweaked for performance, and bugs are squashed, it looks like X Rebirth might be headed towards a golden age of modding (if current offerings are anything to go by). The Teladi Outpost DLC brings back more classic exploration, kind of like exploring some of the rim sectors in Freelancer which is a welcomed addition to the X Series. Also the new music in Teladi Outpost is awesome, 1980's inspired synth-pop goodness, perfect for a space game.
The AI can still be a bit flakey at times, but is improving with every regular patch. Commands for capital ships are still a bit limited: You either set them off on an automated task, or give general orders such as "attack this", "fly to zone", "fly to my position", "patrol" etc. The closest I can think of is it operates a bit like Nexus: The Jupiter Incident (without the GUI)—you give the commands to an NPC captain through comms, or if you use the Co-pilot conversation mod, through keyboard shortcuts. There are a number of significant mods in alpha state at the moment that look to improve AI behaviour (in addition to Egosoft's on going work in this area).
The economy is running well. New trade software means you can lock in more trades, and a mod like Yorrick's YAT (yet another trader), adds the option of automated galaxy, system, and cluster traders and miners. These all seem to run fairly well with a miniumum need for any micro. The economy is simulated but not 100% real, so the AI still makes use of a number of crutches, but this really doesn't affect the game much, at most it means the player can no longer make obscene profits for doing not much at all. That said, I still make plenty of credits in my most recent game start to keep expansion running smoothly, and the economy is flowing along well. However, if the AI using a crutch is a big deal to you there is a mod that removes the wares from ships spawned by the AI.
One part of Rebirth that I enjoy is the set up: slowly building an empire, amassing stations and capital ships, setting patrols, essentially minmaxing an empire. If anyone remembers playing with lego as a kid, it's kind of comparable to that: you set up a cool base, build lots of vehicles, get a crew together, then muck around - it is a similar kind of ethos involved in the X series but with the level of interactivity we expect from PC games.
At the moment I have about 10 stations that all support each other while producing wares to keep the galactic economy running, I have top of the line freighters and miners assigned to each station, and defense fleets that patrol my territory protecting my assets. I have named each ship and station individually with all the most well crafted names I could think of (and some stolen from famous Sci-fi and fantasy), prefixed with Iain M. Banks designations of GSV, GOU etc with a few of my own new designations. The little things like setting up an empire in this detail are what makes games of the X series fun.
If this kind of empire building appeals to you then you will like Rebirth. While my empire is building, I do missions, capture ships, place trade agents on stations, increase my rep with factions, get achievements, role-play and so on. With Litauen's 'Capital Ship Bridges' mod I often sit on the bridge of a frigate ordering profitable trades as it escorts one of my galactic freighters. Then at other times it's just enjoyable to sit back, parked up in one of the zones occupied by my stations and watch the empire hum along. Personally I think if you are expecting a straight-up fighter combat space sim you will be a bit disappointed (there is still lots of fighter combat but it is not the primary focus), the wider aspects of Rebirth such as the empire building are where this game shines.
Even if you decide to not follow the plot the feeling of flying around in space just exploring, seeing new places, and observing the galaxy going along with its business around you is incredible. A number of mods can improve this experience such as 'Ency's mod'* (link at bottom of review) that modifies planets, and adds nebula to create breathtaking vistas and lighting.
Personally I get okay performance, my set up is:
Nvidia GTX 760
Intel 4670K
8 gig of ram
24" IPS @ 1920 x 1200
I run adaptive vsync at half refresh on max settings in game, including all the driver side bells and whistles from Nvidia control panel, it sticks at 30fps. Some people might like higher frames but as long as the framerate is consistent and the game looks pretty I'm fairly happy.
A good idea when approaching X Rebirth is to embrace modding. The support of Steam Workshop means you can easily pick and choose features, removing things you don't like about the game and picking up new features generated by modders. Check out my curated collection of mods below for a number of improvements that save time and improve the game by adding handy new features, immersive changes, and the removal of annoying ones. One mod I can't support enough is the capital ship bridges mod—simply brilliant.
Remember there is no such thing as a "modified" tag in Rebirth, modding doesn't ruin achievements and Egosoft intentionally made the game easy to mod and added Steam Workshop support, they almost expect us to mod our games and personalise our experience, this means Egosoft can realise their artistic vision of what Rebirth should be and the gamers can have ours—we all win.

This is a promising step in the right direction for the world's most successful collectible card game.
It's clearly a direct response to the success of Hearthstone, and it is, while at it's core Magic: The Gathering, it does offer a few changes that stop it from being a direct copy of the paper game.
It does use the same core rule set, and builds on the previous entries in this series, but has evolved from being just a game, to being a platform which they intend to release additional cards on.
A few major differences:
1) The rarity of cards now also change how many of that card you can use in a deck. For example, only one Mythic rarity card can be used in a deck. Two rares, three uncommons and the full playset of four for commons.
2) You can purchase packs of 6 cards using in game purchases, or through farming gold by completing daily quests, or winning games.You get three commons, 2 uncommons and one rare/mythic card. It's worth noting that you cannot get more cards than you can use. Meaning that if you buy enough packs (with money or gold) you are guaranteed to get a complete set since you will stop opening rares you have 2 of, mythics you have one of, etc.
The card pool is custom designed for this limited format, and the card choices are understandable and allows for you to explore a number of archetypes but limits the impact of combo and control decks.
The interface is slick, and once you get used to the timer, entirely serviceable - significantly better than you get from the professional level reproduction of the paper product, Magic Online, which is quite terribly designed.
Will this allow Magic to compete with Hearthstone in terms of streamers adopting this version? No. It won't. but if you want a really nicely presented, casual interpretation of Magic: The Gathering that will continue to expand and offer you a relatively fair way of getting an online collection of cards and facing online competition... you can't go to wrong with this free-to-play game.

Original review
The time has come to post my review of this game... I think I've played almost every entry.
A while back I read that the person in charge of the Duels games had changed. The person who provided a really cheap way to enjoy powerful "casual" constructed decks, and my favourite, the challenges, was out, and a FTP MMO person was in. Well, there has never been stronger evidence of their direction than the latest, "Magic Duels: Origins" entry in the Duels series of Magic games.
Without further ado, the pros:
Accessibility. This game has one of the cleaner UIs of the series, it feels nice, the music and cutscenes are pleasant, and the introduction for total newbies is very smooth. This might be the best "babbys first" Magic game ever.
Story. I really enjoyed the single player campaign, particularly Chandra's. I got to experience the origin stories without having to (shudder) read the official material posted on the Wizards site. (Not that there's anything wrong with that).
Balance. You get to make sweet Limited decks. The sweetest Limited decks ever, with two planeswalkers! And as many sweet commons and uncommons as you like! Jokes aside, this is Limited, not Constructed, and I really enjoyed the Origins format, so it's a treat to get to design the most synergistic Reknown deck, or see my opponents go off with Evolutionary Leap or Sphinx's Tutelage.
Ladder. Yeah, this is a pro. It is a very nice feature to have some kind of progression other than card unlocks.
Now the good stuff: CONS!
Grindiness. According to my math, you unlock less than one card per game. This is just really cheap, the cheapest ever. Yes, you can just pay for unlocks, but the rate seems very bad. If you could unlock all the cards for ten bucks, I'd do it, but it seems overpriced with the current regime.
Bugs. Yeah, they're always here, but this one cost me first "super" unlock with two planeswalkers. I guess I could contact support, and maybe I will, for all the good it'll do my life. I also seem to randomly not get unlock points.
Design. There's some glaring holes here. The quest system seems to want me to play the garbage "archetype" decks no matter how bad they are, just to get them out of my quest log, which is clamped at three. The PvP lacks chat, which leads to some hilarious situations: a teammate of my opponent plays a creature, then the other opponent plays a sweeper. OK, so we can't trash talk; we also can't concede GG, or comment on a cool deck an opponent made, and make new Steam buddies. It also seems odd that if an opponent concedes, you have to play it out vs the AI, and if you lose, neither of you get the win points. GG.
Lack of content. No new challenges, no interesting new game mode, no cool combolicious cards (despite the sweet Limited decks). Very little incentive to grind out with the AI, since it gives less unlock points, even though the AIs sometimes have sweet decks (even in Magic 2015).
Conclusion:
OK, so we have the worst Duels game in the history of the series. Am I going to play it? ... yes. Shameful, I know, but the game, Magic (that is), is good enough. It's almost impossible to ruin completely. It's an official venue to play without having to play for money, buy cards, with the enjoyable Origins Limited format. It's a pretty faint recommend, because if you're an experienced Magic player, or even a seasoned novice, this might not be the game for you.
Bottom line: if you don't want to spend $350 on a playset of Jaces, or deal with the pressure of playing for stakes, it's a somewhat palatable option.

This game is interesting and very unique. I am still conflicted about whether I really recommend it or not though. To be honest I have not finished the game yet, and am only writing the review now because I have stopped playing the game for now. There are many things to love and hate, and to be fair I recognize that this is a game that was made on a game engine that was brand new to the development team at SE. To put it briefly, for everything I liked about this game, there was a part of that feature that drove me nuts.
So here's the deal, things to love about this game include the diverse and culturally rich world with lots of different characters that are all pretty cool. The graphics are awesome (as expected from an Unreal engine game). The story is captivating and enjoyable. There is plenty to do in this game. The battle system is a must see and is almost worth buying just to experience it because it is so unique, or at least it is not like anything I have ever seen before.
Now, things that will get on your nerves... (unfortunately it is often easier to say more about the negative, but that doesn't mean the game is more negative than positive)
While the world is amazing there not as much revealed about it as I wanted. You see many different races of characters and they all live together apparently peacefully, but why? They have diversity, but don't really use it very much in the story. The characters could have all been human and it would have made little difference. Their attributes in battle are not even that different.
The story is great, but admittedly hard to follow (not a surprise from a JRPG really). It was easy to get lost because there is not always indication of where to go to advance the story. Side quests offer some fun side stories, but can be terribly confusing even when using a guide.
The graphics look awesome, but the non-movie animations are awkward. Even some of the movies have parts where the voice acting do not line up with the expressions and movements (translation problem, maybe?)
The battle system is very impressive in concept, but nigh impossible to figure out. After 60+ hours of gameplay I still don't know what I am doing. Simply stated, it is a convuluted mess that is overcomplicated and chaotic. There are so many variables and things to adjust that I was just overloaded and gave up trying to figure it out. Even forums of experienced players can't make a lot of sense out of it. It seems most players ignore the majority of it and for good reason. You can recruit from a huge assortment of characters, use over a dozen different formations, assign leaders, occasionally be given the choice to have them focus on magic or combat, all of it makes little sense though and possibly little difference. It is essentially information overload in an attempt to give the player the choice to devise their own strategy. Speaking of strategy though, actual battle gives you little control at all. You simply give a general command and the characters choose which moves to use themselves. This can be super frustrating because what you want to do is sometimes not an option. Also, there are so many different variables in battle that you could fight the same battle twice using the same commands, and you might lose terribly the first time and win by a landslide the next. So much for all the strategy... I used a stat grinding trick for about 6 hours from a guide I found online and my characters grew incredibly, but still I have battles that just end badly. Luckily there is an autosave feature on PC, but you must turn it on first. It is off by default.
The character progression makes little sense. You know battling monsters makes you stronger and it would appear the stronger the monster, the greater the growth. Things like exp points are absent or invisible. Stats are shown on character views, but no indication of how far along the progress is or how to increase it. Each character also has a unique stat that no one knows what it actually does. There is a Battle Rank which would appear to be synonymous with Level in other RPGs, but it is not really explained what it means. Guides actually show that Battle Rank is better the lower it is because the battles get harder the higher it is. Monsters are stronger the higher your Rank is, which happens to be a feature of some RPGs that I absolutely despise because it makes all the time battling and grinding completely unsatisfying. Final Fantasy 8 works similarly, so if you have played that you might be familiar with it. As the story progresses you increase the number of characters you can use in battle, but you don't reach the max until late in the game, so your characters will end up heavily imbalanced because only characters you use will grow.
Sometimes what I like most about JRPGs is the soundtrack. I will say this game's is a rather generic fantasy one though. It is ok, but nothing to write home about. Certainly not one I would listen to outside the game. I actually find myself playing on mute though, listening to my own music or watching a show while I grind.
All in all, I give it a 3 out of 5. I stopped playing because I lost interest and after reading a ton of guides and forums I decided it is so unnecessarily complicated that I don't care to figure it out. I just want to see the rest of the story and have it be over. I guess I will recommend it because if you haven't played anything like it before, it is an interesting experience. I bought mine in a Final Fantasy bundle, so if you can find it in one of those for cheap, it is worth buying.

TL;DR - The beefier your rig the easier the game is to recommend ,and when performance patches help stabilize the game for lower end hardware it gets a must buy recommendation. Continue to check in here for updates to performance on medium power rigs.
A mechanically solid twin sticks shooter, sporting spectacular lighting effects and a robust physics system that even the frostbite engine fails to compare to. The difficulty sine waves all over and the checkpoint system makes for some keyboard smashing moments, but as a seasoned Souls series player I seem to crave the frustration. Levels are well laid out and fun to traverse and explore. Mission design is simplistic but has left me wanting more. Unfortunately...
The only true gripe about the game is the performance. I currently run a slightly modified ROG laptop, as my new tower is under construction, with a GTX 765M and can barely maintain 30 FPS one medium and low settings with a 1600x900 resolution. Since I acquired the game the morning of launch day, there have been 2 patches totaling around 150 MB, but the performance is still suffering. With no logs on the steam page as to updates its hard to understand what those patches did but I have faith that the game with be improved in the days to come.
In short, the game is a solid if under-performing twin stick shooter boasting tight controls, fantastic effects, and seriously impressive physics. However, with aforementioned performance problems on my mobile rig the game is a tough sell to those with weaker rigs. Otherwise the game gets a must buy recommendation for the art style and gameplay alone. Grimoire: Manastorm has a very simple premise to begin with. You only have to survive 10 minutes, after which the host of Validus Wizards arrive to eliminate the threat. You have everything that you need, and all that you need to do is to make full use of your arsenal of spells so you can remain standing until your comrades arrive.
Your main weapons are your spells. They are divided into five types. First, you have your Primary spell. This consumes the least amount of mana and does not require a cool down time. However, this is also the weakest attack that you can make against your undead enemies.
Next, you have your secondary spell. You can unleash it on your enemies by pressing the Right mouse button. It slightly more powerful than your Primary spell, but requires a cool down time.
Your third offensive spell is your Class Ultimate attack. This unleashes the most powerful attack on any group of monsters that you target it to. Think of it as an artillery attack. However, you have to aim carefully; since your targets are moving, you may end up hitting nothing at all with this devastating attack.
Your last two spells are support spells. One is the Utility spell, which casts a shield around you. The second one is the Mana Step, which boosts your movement by consuming Mana. This is very useful when you want to keep your distance from your enemy.
Movement is very important here in Grimoire Manastorm. You must not stay still, or you will find your self dead very quickly.
So on to the graphics, they a good, but not prefect, what we must remember that Grimoire is still in alpha stage and it looks like this will be a good looking game in the end.
Most of Grimoire’s combat is centered around each players base spells: four active skills and one passive skill. Each player also has two selectable spells: 1 Movement and 1 Utility spell which can be chosen from a pool to customize each class.
Combat is also highly mobile and reactive. By using Manastep (W,A,S,D + Shift) and movement spells players can dodge incoming spells, move around the map quickly, gain high ground on an opponent, escape from a bad fight, or charge the enemy. The default movement spell is Teleport and can be used by pressing F and is perfect for doing any of the above.
Utility selectable spells especially are designed around reactive gameplay. A couple examples include using Spellshield to block incoming damage from one spell or Stoneskin to absorb the effects of an entire meteor storm ultimate. You can lure enemies into Chains of Binding to trap them in place making them a prime target for spells. Or block a huge amount of damage from one direction with Fortify.
You can see from what the devs are doing, they are trying to make a great game, they are around on their discord channel most of the time and are quite happy to join in a game, and there is also 4 playtest a week. So far the game has promise, a lot of promise.
At this stage i can say i can give Grimoire a 7/10, if they keep this up they are going to have a good game, i can only see 2 problems at the moment, 1 is they are going to need a loyal fan base while in development, so when the game goes fully live, there is people there to play, and secondly, this is not a big problem, just one i could see help the game, that is that if they had a single player story mode, this would help peeps come to grips with the game more and also ground the game with a story, which most gamers luv. I will be keeping an eye of and on, on grimoire and posting vids of the gameplay at its different stages, but why not go and try the game folks and see for your self and become a mage warrior

You get to play as Gat or as Kinzie, which is... okay, but you can't change them, or what they're wearing. The NPC's all look exactly like each other. This game feels like a cash grab.
I tried to spend as much time on this game as possible, I spread out my gameplay throughout days, and I still only got 6 hours through. Yes I haven't done all those....activities... *shudders* just too many of them, incredibly dull and boring. Spent most of the time flying around lol.
Now for the good points.
It's playable, there's lots of fighting and good gameplay.
You can use your wings to fly all over the small map.
Lots of activities (which is literally the whole game, but I've already mentioned that...)
New weapons and upgrades.
The dialogue is okay, what you would expect from a Saints Row game.
Overall this game is disappointing, it's not to Saints Row standard, in my honest opinion, I would only recommend this game if it was cheaper. The game has dropped its price since I bought it, I paid £15.99, and now it's £10.99, but I wouldn't even pay that now.
I rate it 5/10, it's good if you got nothing to do, and try to not complete all at once because you will feel disappointed and angry at how terrible the story is.
I'm sorry, it's a fun game but with that poor optimization i just can't recommend it right now.

First of all, though my general opinion of the game is neutral, I cannot recommend it in its current state.  I do plan to revisit it in the upcoming weeks to see what improvements have been made, but it is still marked as an "alpha build" when it is scheduled to be released later this month.  At this point in time, it should be in the latter stages of being beta tested, which seems to be what state it will be after release.  I certainly would not recommend purchasing any of the DLC at this point in time.  However, it is worth giving it is try since it is F2P.
The game itself reminds me a bit of "Lichdom: Battlemage" with less polish and a multiplayer focus.  Gameplay is semi-enjoyable, though controller support really needs to be improved, especially since gampad controls are not specified in the tutorial.  Option settings do not always save properly, and bugs are very evident throughout the game.  The game is playable in its current state and is worth a try, but quite a bit of work needs to be done before I would consider it a "completed product" by any means.
I purchased the DLC some time ago to support the game, as I felt (and still feel) it is has great promise.  That being stated, it has a long way to go before it is truly a finished product.  With over 20 years of personal experience as a software developer, I understand the difficulties Indie developers face, as well as the misconceptions they may have going into the field.  Being an Indie developer means not only understanding the software engineering side, but having a development plan and business model.
Offhand, I'd give it 50 out of 100 right now, as the developer clearly intends to put more work into the project, so it doesn't appear to be "abandonware" at this point.  Nonetheless, a lot of work still needs to be done, and whether or not it will be (and within a reasonable period of time) is another matter.  It is not a "bad" game, but it looks and feels very unfinished at this point and a few weeks are not enough to complete all the work that needs to be done.
I still feel this game could have a good future if work continues and I will certainly update my review to a positive one if it evolves into a more solid, stable, and complete game.  As F2P, it is still better than many Early Access titles I've owned, but the DLC is a waste of funds in the game's current state.  Nonetheless, time will tell whether or not this game becomes one of my regular favorites, or ends up uninstalled.
Personally, I would really like to see this game be successful and popular, and truly hope it reaches its potential!

This game was a pleasant surprise for me!  It offers intuitive and fun space combat, a decent story (so far - I am not finished), and a great atmosphere.
Rebel Galaxy reminds me a bare bones, super-simplified version of Eve.  It has nowhere near the complexity of Eve, but that is not a bad thing.  This is meant to be a casual, single player experience and this game more than delivers on that goal.  There are plenty of different ships and upgrades to choose from and nothing quite beats the feeling of upgrading to the latest, greatest ship after saving up from either mining, pirating, blockade running, or playing the market.
After about 20 hours in, I will admit that the combat has grown slightly stale, but I still enjoy it, overall.  The enemies have continued to remain a challenge and there is always a chance that they'll drop some valuable cargo when destroyed, so that has helped keep things interesting and worthwhile.  There are also quite a few different star systems to explore and each of them have a least some variations and new ships/upgrades which helps keep things fresh.
With that said, I highly recommend this game.  For a simple, bare bones action RPG, the developer really nailed this one!

Even to this day, Bioshock 1 is a tough act to follow for any complex RPG-FPS hybrid game, and it was clear from the outset that Bioshock 2 had a lot to live up to if it was going to carry forward the legacy of its universally acclaimed predecessor.
I feel that Bioshock 2 delivered. The combat is vastly improved, and the combat interface just feels smoother to use. The plasmid upgrades are a lot of fun and really shake up combat. The story is truly beautiful, and takes a distinctly different direction Bioshock 1. Whereas Bioshock 1 was more about exploring and learning about Rapture, and the failures in building a Rand-ian Utopia under the sea, Bioshock 2 has a more personal feel to it, exploring the lives of the common people of Rapture, the people who built Rapture and how it came to be. We also learn more about the Little sisters (which leads us to a great, unique sequence in the later game) The game continues to be as thought provoking as the first Bioshock, exploring ideas of the consciousness (as someone who has studied the neuroscience, I was captivated by the psychiatrist antagonist and her speeches), religion and love, very atypical subjects to tackle for a major FPS title, and this is where I feel Bioshock 2 pushes the envelope and really stands out.
Bioshock 2 is visually and aurally sublime, through its great sound track and voice acting and gorgeous graphics.
Playing as a big daddy really adds variety to the game play, through the use of the drill, ability to combine plasmids for special effects and underwater exploration scenes which really pronounced the ‘city under the sea’ idea.
Due to Bioshock 2’s exploration of the history of Rapture, and the backstories of Rapture’s founding fathers, I found it actually served to enhance the story of Bioshock 1, further succeeding in its role as a sequel. Bioshock 2 will forever live in Bioshock 1’s shadow due to Bioshock 1 bringing so much new stuff to the genre. Bioshock 2 doesn’t do that, but it doesn’t need to. It succeeds in telling a compelling story, and making you care about the characters. This game is a must for any Bioshock fan, and I feel this game is criminally underrated by most.

Super-exciting, highly skill-based arena brawler. An absolute blast to ladder solo or to play with friends. A bit of a cross between a fighting game and a MOBA, it rewards those who are willing to put in the effort to get good, but is still lots of fun casually. You can expect to win pretty consistently if you are better than your opponents, but few matches are ever totally hopeless.
The characters have pleasing visual aesthetics, good sound design, and completely unique playstyles. Nobody should have any trouble finding a character they really enjoy either through taste or mechanics. The music is pretty good but unexceptional.
The loot system is like if Overwatch's wasn't terrible. It has chests and a currency given generously for quests, achievements, and duplicate drops. F2P players can expect to have access to a few starter heroes and a rotation until they have played a few hours and can afford to buy one. There is a bit of a grind, but I'm not exaggerating when I said they give you lots for achievements/quests etc.
The flaws that are here are pretty minor.
The balance is very good in 3v3 arena but does suffer a bit in 2v2s depending on your matchups.
Queue times can be long if you aren't in a really large skill bracket, but this is likely to change once the game actually launches!
The community can be vitriolic, but no more so than wiith any other competitive online multiplayer game (and it sure isn't League or DotA!), but most players are of a pretty good sort.
The Devs are willing to experiment with things and, although nearly all the changes are good, they are quick about addressing community complaints and concerns when they misstep. They have also mentioned that any drastic changes were likely a product of the Early Access and so any people joining up when it launches will not have to worry about any of that. Keep in mind that this is nothing like what LoL players have to put up with, though. The balance and mechanics are pretty finely tuned and so the odd rework and tweak are a far cry from the bi-monthly rollercoaster of emotions Riot Games puts its playerbase through!
The roster is reasonably large, but it is not expansive. What we have is GREAT, but the 4+ new characters arriving in the next few months are certainly welcome additions whenever they show up. The same goes for game modes. The base arena gameplay is super good, especially 3v3s, but it is still very focussed. The brawls and special events have all been fun. The new MOBA-esque mode is also fun, but there is still some variety that a highly casual player may find lacking. That being said, we can likely look forward to more and more frequent events, and something like Hearthstone's Tavern Brawls with a weekly/biweekly rotation of new and old event gamemodes would be a strong inclusion.
Overall, this game is a ton of fun and well worth your time. I got way more than my money's worth during my time in early access, and I would highly recommend it once it launches as a free-to-play.

I'm not a die hard LotR gamer, though I do enjoy the online game and I'll get into the Mordor game eventually. My first play through was filled with glee upon meeting several of the main story's listing of well known characters. I enjoyed the options for conversation with other NPCs, though I'd have liked to be able to speak to the AI party members about certain topics as well. Unfortunately, unless you get a couple friends to play along, not going to happen.
Another small issue is not being able to view the gear, inventory or stats of the AI's, as well as the fact they don't do their tasks, such as picking plants for potion making or finding secret loot areas specific for their character. The fact I can't switch characters at any time is another annoyance factor, at least for me. Waiting til the end of the stage, then not being able to switch til the end of the next stage, this is frustrating. If I could switch out anytime, I could get the special secret locations opened with one, then switch to get the hidden loot location with another in this secret area. The only way to get access to all the secret loot locations is to get two friends to run through with you.
Now besides this forced option, the single play through is okay, but the AIs will often sacrifice themselves to come heal you if you're down. That means that one isn't drawing the enemies away while the other comes to your rescue. You want strategy, get a couple friends who get it cause the AI's don't. True you can run to a spot, call them too you with Z and then C for attack. Then run to the location, such as a crossbolt set up or in front of a door to defend it from any enemies that get past them. It's tricky and you've got to figure things out fast solo. I can't wait to play this again with a few friends.
The other item that was rather disappointing, was discovering that all those other locations were for lore information only. I really hoped that I would be able to go to all those other places, if only to see the area and walk about in it - no quests needed. I just wanted to visit them, but alas there is only two challenge areas to go to besides the main storyline available.
All in all, I did enjoy the game play through, I'm going through it again with the Mage which I'm terrible with so far. Never did like getting stuck as a healer. Then I'll play through it a 3rd time with the dwarf to see if I can get a fair share of the achievements. I will likely still have to run through it with a few friends to get the last few as there are some that need a complete player party to pop up. It's a rather too short, in my opinion, game adventure, but for some it will prove to be just right.
I recommend playing it, but definitely believe the experience would be far more enjoyable with a couple pals to help out.
Hope you enjoy it and that this review has been helpful.

If you follow what the narrator says, you go through a very cliche story that, to be honest, isn't amazing. What makes the game great is when you defy the narrator's instructions. Where this would break a normal game, The Stanley Parable adapts to your choices and the paths you take, Personally, I wouldn't buy this game at full price, as I think there's only a few hours of gameplay and for £10 that's not great. I picked it up in a sale for £2.50, and I don't regret it. A good buy if you're looking for something a bit different.

I have played many indie games since my startoff on PC, and mostly it's sorta sad how a lot of the indie titles usually now a days try to do either a cheap Horror game which are usually based off Slender's success or games that try to be like Minecraft clones and so on.
Now this game isn't anything new in the indie market but that's not saying it's anything bad, on the contrary it's actually quite a lot of fun! The game itself reminds me of them goofy THQ Spongebob platformers when it came to the atmosphere and the characters you come across is well, the Main Character, A Radio that talks to you and mostly gives you the tutorial advice and the Over the Top Jerk that mostly stole your pants and basically leaving you to battle him to get them back.
The Level designs for this game are nice to look at and leaving you to sometimes retrace your steps when trying to find the right path to your journey. The 3 tools you get to have in this game are a Laser tool that is usually one of the most used to help cut things down so it can be used to your advantage to get to Point A to Point B. Next would be a Grappling hook like tool that helps you pull items towards you and helping you move things into position or out of the way. Last tool you get is a Rocket tool which can be used to fire a rocket that attaches on a object leaving you to shoot that item across an gap which starts to get more useful later on in the game.
The gameplay was quite nice and refreshing for a change for me after playing countless games that just pretend to be like other games, However the game is quite short and at the moment crashes on me after getting pass the second fight with the Over the Top Jerk which is really disappointing since of how much fun I was having with this little unique gem.
----Overall Verdict----

Rivals of Aether is a Smash clone that accurately replicates its core mechanics while making some alterations that still sets it apart from its predecessors. This review covers the game from the perspective of a semi-competent Smash player.
Movement is integral to any fighting game and Rivals has been able to take what made Melee's movement great and use it for itself. It's fluid and responsive and retains tech like dash-dancing and wavedashing which increase the skill ceiling. It gives the player snappy control over their character and doesn't have an excess of turn animations like Smash 4 which give the movement a sluggish feel at times. Those who enjoy Melee's movement should find Rivals to be to their tastes.
Combat at its core is the same as Smash aside from two main changes: the replacement of shields with a parry and the removal of the ledge mechanic. These changes are not necessarily bad but simply alter how the game is played. The roster while small is varied and each has their own playstyle with some familiar moves returning from Smash. The character balance is well done with no character feeling unviable unlike what often occurs in Smash titles. This is due to each character having a balanced kit with none having a crippling weakness. Perhaps an advantage of a small roster is that there is enough space to have different feeling characters without resorting to gimmicks to differentiate new characters.
The game's singleplayer content features an arcade mode style story which is I believe is fine considering most players will be looking for a competitive experience rather than story. It also features Abyss mode which pits the player against waves of weak enemies. More importantly, the game includes a tutorial that will teach players important tech skill in the game. Even though Smash's reputation as a casual game, in my experience most of its casual players are unaware of its deeper mechanics. It features remappable controls along with other general quality of life features. Bots are available to the player at various levels of competency, however like most games, these bots don't play like humans do and are prone to taking unrealistic actions which can lead to developing bad habits which only work against bots and not human players.
The game supports 4 players but only in specific configurations online due to how the P2P connection works only allowing communication between two systems. Full four player FFA and teams works offline as expected but online is either 1v1 or 2v2 with two players at each system. Finally, online matchmaking. I live in Australia and have never connected with someone that has less than 250ms ping making matchmaking practically impossible. If you live in a low population area, be prepared to drag your friends over into the game if you don't want to be stuck playing against bots.
This game is a great option for someone looking for a competitive Smash experience but cannot or doesn't want to play Smash for any reason. Just keep in mind that this is a still a small game with a limited playerbase.

A dying father, a sinking city, and a utopian ideal gone horribly wrong. This is BioShock 2 at its center. After a brief, violent glimpse into Rapture before its fall from capitalist glory, players are sunk into the boots of Subject Delta, a big daddy with a bone to pick with the leader of Rapture's newly-mended society, the Rapture Family. The gameplay still has that zap-and-whack feel that gave the first BioShock's combat so much appeal. The blood on the walls and viewable acts of brutality also remind the player where they are: Rapture.
In Delta's hunt for his Little Sister, he'll run into some familiar faces, and new ones. Tenenbaum has returned to this leaky ship, Ryan's posthumous voice is audible via recordings, and even Dr. Suchong and his grisly fate come to light. A whole host of new characters awaits Delta here, each of them interesting and memorable. Seldom are new Plasmids, but old weapons have been repurposed (and in some cases, replaced) for use by the protagonist Big Daddy. Deliberating over a Little Sister's fate is just as agonizing as before (even moreso, considering the player's role as a Protector), and pulling off a perfect plasmid-weapon combo is still a very, very satisfying experience. If you liked BioShock 1, you'll find nothing wrong with BioShock 2.

One of the best 4X space strategy games I've ever played, proven by my 250+ hrs of gameplay.  The game offers excellent balance, interesting factions that, while similar in organization, offer enough degrees of difference to allow for a variety of strategies in gameplay.
The software itself is solid, but one of the features that makes SoaSE so sustanable is the developer and distributor supporting, wholeheartedly, the modding community.  Just when you thought you were growing weary of the Vasari's dark fleets, or the TEC's economic supremacy, you can download any of several well-developed mods to suit your favorite sci-fi franchise.
The utter collapse of Kerberos' Sword of the Stars II left a void in the 4x genre that Sins has continued to fill with ease.  What the game lacks in the finer points of empire building, it more than makes up for with good macro-economic management tools.  But the brilliant tactical and strategic engine is what makes Sins the standard in current space-based strategy games.  If you were a fan of the Galactic Civ franchise, Masters of Orion, or Sword of the Stars (the original), this game is a need-to-have part of your collection.

A purely great game. Taking place 3 years after Dead Rising: Case Zero, in Fortune City, Nevada the outbreak hits again. You play as Chuck Greene trying to escape the city. And the game has so much unrealism, but that's what makes it fun! Just like the first game, you can kill zombies with nearly everything you can find! Trust me, let's not get into logic, because you can make lightsabers in this game. Well, they're called Laser Swords, but people refer to them as Lightsabers. So I'd rate this game... an 8/10. -1 for the pyschopaths because nearly all of them were seen killing survivors, and a -1 for a short game, but the first one also took 3 days. It's a great game. Get it. Now.
Must watch if you want to have some good laughs.

If you love the team fight aspect of your favourite games but hate the grinding and items / snowballing, this is the game for you. Battlerite strips all that crap away and is only arena combat, using WASD to move and most every spell/move is a skill shot, thats right no stupid auto attacks, all skill.
It plays out much like a MMO PvP game, with less crap in the way. You can't be healed back to full health, rather your healthbar is capped for "recovery health" which shrinks if you take more than allotted dmg without being healed back up
I have over 600 hours on this game and it's still my favourite game and game of choice
It does have a learning curve but if you're willing to learn, and not get frustrated and 100% blame your team mate(s) (its not usually them anyways) you will be a good player in the long run

The problem with Hatred is that it traded on controversy, and for many it worked. This game, while having the possibility of being unique and interesting, ends up with a character you don't care about, wonky controls, and a mild bout of motion sickness.
While the art style is interesting and offers up what would look appealing in still screenshots, the bottom line is that without color, it becomes very difficult to discern who is what against backgrounds. "Where am I standing?" is a common question as it isn't always in the middle of the screen. "What is shooting me?" The dark uniformed officer's clothes blend well with the natural ground and even worse, they see farther than you can typically.
The executions are.. disturbing but only because htey're strangely disconnected in such a way that they don't really make you want to cringe. Maybe I'll apply my pokey device, maybe I'll just shoot them from a strange angle, and then I'll let loose some sort of insult for now reason.
The game is a bore. They had a great chance to do something, and there isn't anything they did to take that chance.

This was supposed to be an improvement over previous versions, but other than the graphics, soundtrack and the return of a visible and usefull cockpit it does not live up to the expectations, nor the X title.
First of all your immediate surroundings look cramped, and I'm not talking about the ship interior... It used to be a lot more spaced out and felt more of...well...space... The upscaling of the stations certainly did not do the game any good as well, as it only contributes to that same feeling. It really feels as though your in the middle of a concert than in space.
Second, the controls...I don't know what came over the developers when figuring this out, but after all the hard work they put in the X3 engine I really expected more. I found it near impossible to target a station to dock with, not to mention it being counter-intuitive; While you could click on a ship in the distance to target, get info, whatever, on stations that simply doesn't work. The menu system was a lot sleaker and less cumbersome as well, it reacted a lot faster without all the fancy animations / transitions and the general feel complemented the game as a whole. And although I like the idea of a board computer that gives that feeling of your character actually interacting with a computer, unless you run at a very high resolution it is very difficult to actually read what it's displaying (played on 1280x800).
Last but not least, the lanes...why...why not have sectors overlap eachother so you don't need all that fancy stuff, or load based on the ships radar distance...there are so many alternatives to using jump gates (if that was the goal) that are not so much of a nuisance.
I have played every X game, and have loved every single one of them, regardless of the terrible characters and all that; That somehow became part of the charm. But I seriously believe this to be a big mistake made by EgoSoft. If they wanted to make an engine / game that looked and felt so immensely different from the rest of the X series, they should really have experimented with some arbitrary new title that has nothing to do with it; A once off game that may have the potential to grow into an entirely new series, or merge with the X series at a later time, whatever. It would have been a lot better than take a succesfull series and throw it down the toilet like this.

A violent flesh orchestra of non-stop blood chilling slaughter where every scream is a tempting siren song to more psychosis endorphin heights of orgiastic carnage.
Execution cams are grim and brutally dazzling in their excellence of shocking impact on the level of extreme gore movies such as WIZARD OF GORE, TEXAS CHAINSAW MASSACRE and STORY OF RICHIE. Butchering innocents is unnerving and harrowing and eerily satisfying in its macabre death soaked delivery like seeing a train wreck and looking when you feel as if you should not.
The black and white graphics enhance the feeling of being a character who has completely crossed over into a world of death where all other pleasures except vengeance and malevolence no longer exist. Physics are a nightmarish marvel of architecture annihilating madness where interior walls are shot out, doors shattered into eye piercing splinters, exterior walls explode into a typhoon of limb crushing bricks, cars detonate into blazing fire balls consuming flesh in a fiery caress of unequaled inescapable agony. Animations are wonderfully done as bodies flail about in terror and react to flesh shredding weapons impact. Dying bodies slowly slump against signs and slide down.
Audio is a funeral dirge shattering the facade of normality awakening the senses to a realm of murderous adrenaline heart thumping terror where civilians see their sanity ripped from their minds as they beg for their lives or in fear sweat soaked flesh attempt to fight back only to fall and fall and fall into the darkness the sweet escape of nothingness.. the death beyond knowing as the sound of a living environment is transformed into a desolate wind swept graveyard. The sounds of bullet impacts piercing thin walls and doors floods the air with mind numbing fear. Bricks sound like bricks..hurtful bricks. Explosions are all enveloping audio kisses of BOOM! Weapons have depth and a sense of power like a sledgehammer to the chest in their audio design.
Music is well paced with a 1970's John Carpenter horror movie ambiance. Check out the credits for some delicious head banging Death Metal euphoria :)
Game play is kill kill kill with set goals that are visible on a mini map such as wiping out a hotel full of guests taking down everything and everyone while destroying the landscape which will give you points earning you a respawn along with STEAM achievements. Doing executions will replenish your health.
If you crave for something dark and sinister.. something with that morbid magic of the first POSTAL then HATRED shall be your salvation my virtual murderous brothers and sisters. Enjoy the fantasy cause that's what games are all about.
Update- SURVIVOR MODE has been added into this grim work adding in more senses shocking violence to the original blood soaked layer with new characters who are disciples similar to the ones in the SAW movies including a pscyho cop and a female femme fatale among others. New maps to unleash murderous payback have also been added which are just as incredibly well designed as the originals where the enemy ai really stands out making them feel more lifelike then ever before.
Thank you and Hail DESTRUCTIVE CREATIONS for this miraculous work of mayhem beautiful and free in all its ways!
