incredibly enjoyable, content filled and cheap space action sim. that is probably the only thing i have to say to get the right crowd to buy it, oh and if you liked AC Black flags boat combat and was bored with the other parts, like me, then this is an even better fit for you.
the game is a bit grindy and can be repetitive at times, but the gameplay (which is AC black flags boat combat but in space and way better) is so fun and more importantly customizable. there are a plethora of different ships, weapons, shield types, boosters and other things i am sure i have not even unlocked yet that you can create anything from a super fast, manuverable smuggling vessel that can dance circles around enemy ships to a giant slow dreadnaught with enough guns, missles and protection to tear apart entire factions.
speaking of factions....yeah they have no personality. this is the only negative i have so far and its actually more damaging then you would think. its a space sim where the different aliens, human pirates and militia all act and do the same things, even the pictures for each faction whenever you engage them only have two faces, male and female, in the case of aliens only one potrait. you will fight six broad categories of enemies, each of which has a different sets of sub group customizations. there is the dreadnaught, battleship, missle ships, standard cruiser, light ship and fighter from biggest and slowest to smallest and fastest. I often don't know who or what i am engaging until the name pops up on the ship and by then i don't care since you only have to care about one of two factions, the pirates and the militia. the reason you should care about them is because depending on who you make as your primary enemy will determine which ports are safe and which are not. this is incredibly important because ports supply you with all your needs from repairs to selling/buying materials for trade.
the one positive thing about the factions is that they are always doing something. space is big, but even then i run into asteroid fields that are being actively mined by some korians or finding the militia fighting pirates and deciding whether i should help or not. hell the factions will even siege spaceports causing rising prices in certain materials and unlocking a host of missions from doing smuggling runs to that port for big bucks to destroying the commander of the siege in order to free that spaceport. or you could not even bother with the missions and go in to free the spaceport yourself by destoying every siege ship, looting whatever they drop, or abuse the fact that this port is under siege and buy all thier resources (which are incredibly cheap during a siege) to sell to a different space port for big bucks, and i mean♥♥♥♥♥♥tons of credits. there is endless variety and always things to do in this game.
what really makes this game enjoyable is how difficult it is. the tutorial is short and sweet (even to short in my opinion), and after you get out of the first space system its open game. you could come across anything from 2 little fighters that you destroy in 2 seconds to accidently warping near 5 enemy dreadnaughts that use draining missles on you in order to force you into a fight that you will lose. be anything from a heartless smuggler, to a bloodthirsty, to even the peoples hero, the game makes a point that this is your story so do whatever you want. i cannot recommend it enough.

Ah, the Final Fantasy Series! A beautiful story from each and every entry given to us by Square Enix. Whenever I play these games, I look back on previous entries of this series that I've played. Namely, FFIV, FFV, FFVI, FFIX, on consoles, and FFX on PC. I remember the wonderful stories, the characters, the worlds that were created! It was true bliss and one of the games from my earlier childhood.
Then we have Square Enix's attempt at bringing a new flare to the series with the introduction of a heroine (first time), and glorious CG. However, wary should be the Final Fantasy Fan who actually dares to approach this title, as it won't be like the previous ones.
With that, I shall begin.
Starting off in a beautiful introduction, two particular people are being transported in a train across a track over some interesting landscape. The train then enters a tunnel, where it reveals a fierce battle between two forces is taking place. Thus begins the interesting tale of our main heroine: Lightning.
So how does this story pan out? In comparison to other Final Fantasy stories, it isn't as good, nor does it have the twists or turns that previous titles had. However, the characters are quite interesting, and it's more of the "Journey to" that counts in this title.
When Introducing a character or supporting character into a story, I expect them to have some aspect of background to them. Thankfully, the game fleshes out these characters rather nicely catering to a variety of individuals. Although, it is quite easy to see some stereotypes inside and some predictable outcomes.
The Voice acting is Superb! Each character with their own unique manner, voice, and of course, stereotype. I thoroughly enjoyed the VA. (except for one or two parts with whining...ugh)
One issue I did have with the game's rendition of "story-telling" is that many side inquiries about various places, people, and things have to be read in the game's dictionary. So unless you're willing to spend time reading about these places and people, you will not completely comprehend the story. Because it forces you to stop and read instead of perhaps explaining it in a short cutscene...? It lost some of it's points for that.
Since what "was" supposed to be has been thoroughly discussed and disected by various forms of media, I'm only going to talk about what is here and now.
The Battle System for this game has both a pro and con to it. The pro being that you don't actually have to wait for your Battle Bar to fully fill to use a command which is SO nice. The characters are actually also moving around now, so certain moves like basic attacks which move you closer, or ranged abilities which move you farther back, can help mitigate some enemies damage. Sadly you cannot directly control where they are.
The main con (and this is a huge one) is that you can only control your MAIN party member! The other party members, though controlled by relatively smart AI, cannot have preset "do this" or "do that" put onto them, and instead is read for only what the game thinks is the "smartest move". Another large con is that if your Main party member (the one you control in-game) dies, it's game over. It doesn't matter if your other AI are alive, it's game over period. This alone adds artificial difficulty which had me foaming at times.
Now on to the the unique aspects of this battle system. Unlike previous battle systems, this has an interesting aspect with "roles". These roles range from Commando (normal fighter), Ravager (mage), Sentinel (the tank), and more besides. Each role is uniquely different with various abilities that can be learned by focusing on leveling up a certain skill crystarium. You'll find yourself at times having to arrange and micromanage consistently what roles you're going to use to what end in certain key battles, as you have to be VERY prepared in some areas and constantly abusing the instant full bar gauge with switching. This I think is a very nice change of pace (if you've played previous FF titles) and I enjoyed it.
Eidolons (Summons) thankfully are not OP and won't break the game, and they've all been given a unique design spin. I don't want to go into details here, but they're SO much fun to play around with :3
An interesting aspect of this Battle System is that certain skills can only be used using what's called Technical Points (TP). These are used in a variety of ways, but it'll mainly be used for two things: Libra (scan) and Summoning. I never found myself using the other skills ever.
I've been talking about the Battle system so much I haven't even mentioned the world!
As FFXIII was the first step into "the future of CG" for the Final Fantasy series, Square Enix wanted to bring it all in, and boy does it look BEAUTIFUL! What you see in the background, the character models, and the animated short movie clips makes me drool.
Now about the not-so-nice part of this entry....It's very, very linear. There's only 1 place in the entire game which one could almost consider Open-World and the rest is not. This is a large drawback for me and I despise this level design. At the very least, it's nice to look at.
Here we come to a close on this review. Did I like it?....It's hard to say. I have a love-hate relationship with this game. It did things that no other Final Fantasy Title had yet to try, and yet it hurt it in ways that I just cannot excuse. It did however, not entirely disappoint, so I give brownie points for that at least.

This game was a huge problem at the beginning. I bought this game sometime around November 2014 and gave up on it until the developers fixed the windowed 720p resolution sometime around December 2014. As of writting this, it is around June 2017. It took me a week to figure out what was causing the sudden studder of frames.
My machine's specifications:
Windows 10 Home edition
Intel Core i5-6600k
Asus Strix nvidia GTX 970
2x8 GB DDR4 Corsair RAM
2 TB Hard Drive
The problem of the sudden frame studder was from Windows 10. In the (Device Manager > Human Interface) I disabled all the HiD-compliment devices. Removing the HiD devices allowed the game to run at 1080p on a 1920x1080px60Hz(1080p at 60 Frames Per Second) Toshiba TV. I guess it has something to do with Windows 10 Hid devices causing Final Fantasy XIII to take up CPU or RAM to search for new devices connected to your computer.
Detailed Instructions (Should also apply for Windows 8, 8.1):
In Windows 10, right-click the "Start" menu and select "Device Manager" using left-click. In the "Human Interface" header/ option, expand it. Select each individual device with the prefix "HiD-compliment".
In Windows 7, open Control Panel from the "Start" menu. Open "Device Manager" then expand "Human Interface" header/ option, expand it. Select each individual device with the prefix "HiD-compliment".
I also tried the GeDoSaTo method to try fixing the frame studder, but that was completely Windows 10's fault. I would recommend anyone that has a TV or monitor that can support more than 1080p the GeDoSaTo third-party program to enjoy the higher resolution.
The frame drops only during intense battles/ spells/ ravager casting, but that is the game's fault. Other than a couple of frame drops, I would totally recommend this game as this is my first Final Fantasy game. Also would recommend it to anyone that likes long grinding RPG games or decent graphicial cutscenes.

Let's be honest here, this game is one of the best game I've ever played. It clearly deserves a perfect and non-ironic 10/10.
I bought this game almost a year ago (2nd January 2015), and I first played it back then and, because I failed my first playthrough, forgot about the game for a while after making a first review which was this summary of my first experience with it. I decided that for this winter holiday 2015 that I'd give it a second shot, and I managed to survive ! With my brand new eyes, I decided to make a full review of this awesome game that is
.
You are a group of survivors during a fictionnal civil war that tries to survive and get through it. During the day, you are in your shelter, and you can build a lot of useful stuff like beds, furnace, radio, weapons etc. There are some random events where for example a trader will com to your place and you can trade your items for some other supplies. During the night, you visit (not so) deserted places to try and find some more supplies, such as material, woods, weapon parts, food, medicine etc. In this time, your shelter can get attacked, so you'd better keep someone away in your home, if you don't want to get robbed or killed in your own home (note that you don't control anything, it's done automatically).
This game has a lot of strong aspect that I'm going to discuss here.
The graphics are really appealing to me. I loved the pencil-like texture applied to the whole game. It's dark, but it puts you in this civil war athmosphere.
Another aspect of the game design that I liked a lot is the characters you control, because they really feel like civilians, and you can relate and connect to them. It's done through their bio and their reactions, that feel really human and plausible.
While I'm at the reactions of you characters, this is what make the game really sad and heartbreaking. Your characters will regret killing and robbing people, as much as they'll regret when one of them dies or is sick. You feel the need to help and protect them, and this type of reaction is something that really breaks your heart.
In addition to the character's reactions, the music is another aspect that is well done. It's melancholic, it's accoustic, it's perfect for this game.
Let's talk about the gameplay. It's a point and click game, you play it entirely with your mouse. You have a lot of actions to chose from for every situation, the mechanics are well-crafted and pretty strong for this game.
Other things such as the radio programms or the places you can go at night add to the immersion, as they are realistic for a civil war.
My final positive point for this game is the DLCs and the game in itself: every benefits made from this game go to charity for War Child, an association that helps kids around the world where they face war on a daily basis, providing food, supplies, schools and much more to them. Just for that aspect, I even bought it in a shop where I found a physical version of the game. I may have paid twice this game and chosen to pay the DLC 20 bucks, but I regret nothing, as I know it's for a good cause. I think more charity groups should do games like this: they are great games and a great way to donate to charity, a way where everyone wins something.
The question here would be "has this game any weakness at all?" because it's a strong game in every aspect you could imagine. Well the only negative point I would make is the fact it's not that kind of game you can play anytime you want just for fun. It's not a funny game, but is the subject a fun one? No not really, so it's understandable that it may be a depressing game. That's why I don't play it often, because it's sad and tragic.
All in all, this game deserves to be purchased a hundred times. It's a well-crafted survival point and click game with a really deep and sad athmosphere where you can relate to your characters. It's sad, it's well-done, and it's for charity, so I don't see any reasons of why you shouldn't buy this game.
In a whole, the game is almost perfect, it may have this flaw where you don't play it often, but otherwise it's one of the best game I've ever played. It's an intriguing and tragic experience that everyone should try at least once in their lives.

Tiny and Big: Grandpa's Leftovers is a unique game, that takes a fairly familiar concept, and takes it to a whole new level.
The jist of the game is that you can cut almost everything is a level with your laser, and then pull it with a hook, or push it with a rocket. Simple enough, heh?
Well, it works really well! Each level is fairly large, and everything is huge, when compared to the size of your character. Then, it's about discovery and exploration, which this game certainly encourages!
The story is a bit silly, but if you look past it, it will reveal a deeper story of power and civilization. It's put very simply, and it's clearly not something you should obcess over, but it's nice that it's there, and it adds a bit of depth to an otherwise very silly game! (Don't worry, it's still very silly as it is!)
You play as Tiny, and you're off to collect the only thing your late Grandpa has left you: a pair of pants. Why pants? Hell if you know. But it's the last thing he has collected, as a spelunker, so it should be worth it.
And you're off, into a very empty desert. Then you have an accident, and you'll soon discover a new world in that seemingly empty desert. It's you and your radio on a mighty quest! For... pants.
Presentation wise, the game is simple, but it has its own style. I reminded me a bit of Psychonauts, which I know is a plus for many people.
Everything seems hand-drawn (even the textures). Everything seems rough, but it fits the whole style of the game, in my opinion.
Then, each time something falls, it'll make a noise, and will also drop a big "BAMM" or... "SMURTLES", in addition to the sound effect. It's nice, it's a cool little detail.
Another cool aspect I really enjoyed, was the little hints present in the world regarding its civilization and its lore. It goes a long way into making a world very enjoyable to explore, and feel lively rather than empty.
There are also secret levels that place you inside an old gameboy, with graphics to match. Only in 3D!
Overall, everything has a very unique feel to it, it's pretty good.
The
was also really good! It's hard to classify it, but it fits the barren wasteland where you are. Since you're on a journey with your radio, the music isn't necessarily continuous. You're free to switch tracks around with a single key, and just listen to the tracks you want.
I usually prefer the music to be tailored to the situations, but as the sandbox game that this is (mostly), I think that it works better in this way.
Along with it,
is also very good.  Since you're mostly cutting huge stones, everything will soon start to break, with a big impact. Both the sound effects and a small screen shake will give you the impression that the world is literally falling apart around you. I may or may not have tried to dodge rocks myself from my comfortable chair. Immersion is a strongpoint in this game!
Now, how is gameplay?
Well, it's the shining point of Tiny and Big!
As I said, the mechanics are very simple. You have a
, with which you cut the environment. You have what it essentially a
, to pull objects towards you. And you have a
, that you attach to things, and send them flying.
And with these 3 bad boys, you can do anything, really.
There are 6 levels (one of which is a Boss Fights) only, but you can easily sink at least one hour into each, in your first palythrough (and you're likely to miss secrets, which are worthy going back for).
The scale of the game is awesome, with very open areas, generally, and lots of places to reach. Of course, you can't just climb stairs... if you want, you'll have to make them. You'll cut pillars, mountains, doors, ... you name it. Chances are, if you can see it, you can reach it! Somehow.
Finishing the level isn't really the point here. Than can be done very quickly, and very easily. And all things considered, it won't be worth it. But, the game has a bunch of secrets areas to explore, and a few collectibles, if you're in for achievements. There are also or challenges, if you want to limit your toolkit.
If you're into more sandbox-y and exploration games, definitely give this one a try!
You'll find yourself trying to climb everything, cut the world in two (or, you know... in 50), looking under every rock (well, mountain)... you get the drill.
One very good thing, is that the game never really punishes exploration, at all! Once you reach somewhere important, the game will auto-save. That way, even if you die, you can just get back to it. It's a very good thing!
There are God figures to find, rocks to collect (just for the achievements, generally, and also encouraging exploration even more), there are Music Tapes, to add to your collection and there are also Arcades! Each arcade is essentially a "challenge" level. Some of them were very easy and straightforward, others were slightly more challenging. It's just a nice addition to the game.
There are also Easter Eggs spread around the world. The room where the band made the game's music, for example, with posters referencing other games, and the such. These are certainly nice to find.
The
, weirdly enough, are also a good thing, in this case. The developers knew that the game was all about exploration, trying different strategies, challenging yourself, and as such, they've implemented achievements accordingly. All of them were made to encourage you to explore, rather than just try to finish it. And it's a good thing, it's nice to see it for a change!
One issue that I have with the game, is the dialogue. Not because it's bad, but because of the way it was presented. In the cutscenes, everything was fine, and it made me grin a little. During gameplay, however, it has a big problem. In order not to obstruct the player's vision, they've kept the dialogue in the corners. The problem with it, is that you're very, very likely to miss it, amidst the chaos. The whole world is falling on you, so it's understandable you'll miss the little dialogue in your peripheral vision.
It's not a deal breaker, at all, but it's still a flaw, I'd say.
Another thing, is that the game is quite short, if you're into repeating levels, which I can understand. 5 levels is a bit short (I'm not counting the Boss Fight), even if they are varied. I've spend from 40 minutes to 1 hour in each level, roughly, by trying to explore as much as possible. I still missed a couple of things, which I'm likely to go back to, but you may not be.
But, all things considered, Tiny and Big: Grandpa's Leftovers is a genuinely great game! I hadn't felt as immersed in a game as I have with it, in a while, and that's all due to the freedom it gives you.
It's like a puzzle-platformer, without the genre's main flaw, for most people, which is that the solution are somewhat limited. Some people don't like those kinds of games, simply because there are very limited solutions to those problem. Well, that's not the case with this game. There are countless ways of traversing the map, all equally fun and valid!
You'll just lose yourself in each level, experimenting with each rock, cutting and pulling, trying to reach something that looks interesting.
Give this one a try, it's definitely worth your time!

This turned many people off because they expected a completed game with every single bell and whistle they desired. Those bells and whistles were not in at release, but they are here now. The graphics were initially buggy, and the game did crash several times when I first started playing- I have an NVIDIA GeForce GT 760M. But the Steam Community was able to determine that the touch screen keyboard function for Windows 10 was the source of the problem and provided steps to disable it. With the game working well, I was able to see and admire the detail of graphics put into this game, which certainly has held up over the years- the detail and articulation of the great eagles were well done.
Overall, I would say that if you are a fan of LOTR, this is a simple, fun purchase though I recommend picking it up when it is on sale (which it frequently is).

NOTE: I dont play MTG In meatspace as it were, so all of my experiences should be seen as someone who has little knowledge of the game and that im coming into this after playing Magic 2012/ 2013
This should be seen as more of a first glimpse into the game for now, I may revisit this if my opinion changes.
For a start, I had no issues loading the game at all, booted the game up, worked absolutely fine.
The interface for the game is pretty standard MTG game fare, but theres no need to fix what isnt broken. And the developer seems to have gotten this down to a T at this point.
I loaded up the campaign, and after rushing through all of the tutorial stuff, I got to my first matches in the campaign.
I have not yet started any of the campaigns barr the first one, however I sincerely hope that the difficulty raises, as I did not have a single match in which I dropped below 18, but overall the game ran absolutely without a hitch. I have seen bugs and errors in other peoples reviews that I have not experienced my self, but without a more complete scope of how the game is, I cannot comment on their issues one way or another.
After completing the campaign I went into the deck builder to see what that was like and I was pleasantly surprised to see an assisted deck builder. Of course the builder follows certain deck archetypes that arent neccesary for the higher class players, but for scrubby little noobs like me, it helped me build a deck I was comfortable in using that seemed to work well enough against the easy and medium AI.
So overall the game is good.. However there is one major bugbear that I have.. Microtransactions.
Of course I understand this is a free to play game, and the developer needs to make money one way or another, and thats fine.
To get new cards through booster packs, You need gold, you can earn gold by doing the daily quests in game (In a manner not dis-similar to hearthstone) Winning matches and doing the campaign.
My problem would be that the rate of coin earning seems far too low to keep someone who has no intention of putting any money into the game playing to earn new cards. Infact, if I were to want to spend any money, I would want to spend it on cards in real life.
To summarise. I would say that this is a good game for beginners and newbies to MTG, and in this way it serves its purpose to teach how to play the game and to show what the game can be like.
The downside is a fairly restricted microtransaction for cards system, which could be fixed with tweaking to the ammount of coins you get for completing tasks, or lowering the price of boosters in game.
Would recommend to New players, but am aware that there are better options for more hard core players of MTG, such as MTG Online.

Firstly the game does'nt do a very good job of explaining most of it's mechanics, google is almost a necessity if you really want to understand the game mechanics. The second major issue is the randomness of combat. Sometimes the combat can feel really random especially early on in the game where it feels like you're at the mercy of the enemy AI units and your own ally AI units. I spent 4 hours trying to fight this one early boss called the fiery idol whic you will face an hour or 2 into the game depending on how you play it.
The Fiery idol was pretty frustrating even after completing all the side quests I could find and upgrading my weapons to a good degree. If the boss decided to use its powerful AOE firebomb that chops 70% to 60% of your health on turn 2 the you're certainly dead and havve to restart fight. This is the boss that made me give up on the game. No matter what choice I made in fighting this boss it eventually boiled down to RNG deciding my fate. Will the boss use its ultimate on turn 2? will my AI companions who I can't order randomly heal me? It felt really infuriating. I finally did manage to defeat the boss and I reloaded the game to see iof I can replicate by making the same decisions but I had no success.
If you are somebody who isnt frazed by a "healthy" dose  RNG you might actually be able to enjoy this game. But, for me its not probably going to happen an Im deleting it from my PC.

TL;DR The game is good but needs some fixing and more cards, but it's playable in it's current state.
If you're not able to play Magic IRL like myself or don't want to spend your whole life savings on cards, Duels will suffice.
The game has it's share of problems. Some of the daily quests are broken, the ones where you have to win a number of games using a specific color combination deck only registers victories when using a deck made in the deck builder tool
and not when using a custom built one.
There are about 300 cards in the game making the pool of viable decks very small. Mirror match-ups are common, and the PvP matchmaking is swarmed by elf decks which are not easily countered due to the limited cards. I imagine as time goes on, if the game has a player base, more cards will be released.
The singleplayer component is short but fun. 5 campaigns with 5 missions each will take you a few hours to beat depending on RNG. Often, you will be stuck on a mission simply due to not getting any useful cards from the prebuilt deck and be forced to restart the duel. The singleplayer awards 750 gold in total which is enough for 5 booster packs.
The price of booster packs is not very high, considering how much gold is won from duels. A single booster pack costs 150 gold, a victory against a real player awards 20 gold and playing against the AI awards 5, 10 and 15 gold respectively according to the difficulty of the AI.

Fun? Yes. Would I pay 15 bucks for it? No.
Story:
Satan has kidnapped the president of the United States and it’s up to Gat and Kinzie to go and rescue them by punching Satan in the face. On the way, you meet pretty much everyone from SR2/3 and kick some♥♥♥♥♥ Pretty much up to SR standards.
Gameplay:
It’s SR4 with a hell theme pretty much. You can fly, stomp, shoot guns, and mess around. It’s almost exactly the same but the flying now requires you to keep up momentum and has a limited use. Think Arkham type gliding. I did feel like there was more of an emphasis on guns this time just because you have a lot of flying enemies and demons tend to crowd you but other than that, it's the same shooty-superpower-affair as SR4.
In terms of story progression, you have to do side missions until satan gets♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off enough to face you. Some of the side missions are the same like the goddamn insurance fraud one and some are different but they are all meh except for the flying one. Overall, this system isn’t bad but if you go and do everything in ¾ of the game, you can get to the final mission without even meeting one important member of the game.
Graphics/Performance (with a 970, 4790K, 16GB of RAM, SSD):
It ran at 60 on the highest settings and didn’t dip. Some of the menus and cutscenes ran at different frame rates but they weren’t all that often. SR isn’t known to look really good and it shows here. The details aren’t there and it has a cartoonish look to it. But it’s charming.
Final Thoughts:
If you liked SR4 and want some more, play this and have fun for a few hours. If you are a completionist, have fun because there is just so much content for you to get through. Get it on sale and enjoy some of it.

TL:DR at the bottom
Well, I think its a pretty common consensus to consider BioShock 2 the worst of the current 3 bioshock games. Well, having played them all, I have to agree.
But that doesn't make it a bad game.
While the story isn't as riveting as Bioshock 1 or Infinite, its gameplay is solid. Playing two is fun, it feels good, and its mechanically superior to the first bioshock. Remember in the first bioshock,  when you had to pick between a gun in your hand or a plasmid? Well Bioshock 2 lets you use both, one in each hand, just like infinite. So while its not "better" than the first game as a whole, its a solid game.
So should you play this game?
YES. Especially if you like the bioshock universe! its worth a playthrough. Bioshock 2 lets you wander through rapture for a little while longer as a big daddy. The writing is pretty good, the backstories are worth listening to, the plasmids are always fun, the guns are still good, this game is by all accounts a good game.
TL;DR
Give it a shot, especially if you have avoided it after playing the other 2 entries into the series. If this is your first bioshock game, you'l discover how eerily cool the underwater city of rapture is, and how captivating the series can be with its enviroment.

What a great game. I originally played Bioshock one on the Xbox a few years back and I had the sequel sitting in my library for a few months because I had forgotten how fantastic these games are. After picking it back up, I haven't been able to put it down with whatever free time I have left.
Pros:
- Very fun gameplay, the combat sequences are easy to get into and there are different ways you can go about exterminating the wannabe meth addicts aka "splicers."
- Incredible story line. This really hit the spot I love games that have a very in depth story that draws you in like a good novel or movie and this game certainly delivers with a very powerful story line.
- Visuals. The game is a few years old but graphically it holds up very well. I'm running it maxed out and, while it doesn't hold a torch to titles such as metro or crysis, the unique style of the game more than makes up for the aging textures.
Cons:
- It's a touch linear. This is a fairly linear game and it holds your hand throughout your play through. In certain areas this is very helpful, in others it sort of takes away from the immersion and individuality that I personally crave in video games. There are options in the menu that allow you to minimize the hand holding, but they don't completely remove it.
- Sometimes repetitive. When you are taken to a new area and you have to back track to get this item to open that door to get that item to find this guy to open a door in the entrance can become rather tiresome. However, it isn't so bad that it ruins the game completely, sometimes it just become a bit tedious.

So, I have never written a review for a game before, but I think that Battlerite deserves a good one. The game is quite fun and takes all the boring parts  out of a moba and keeps all the good parts. It is quick, intense action that only lasts for a few minutes so you don't have to commit an hour+ of your time to a single game. The community is somehow nowhere near as toxic as other team-based action games. I can probably count on one hand the amount of people that I've reported in my time played.
That being said, there are some things that I'm not a huge fan of: There are very few characters. It feels like every game you see the same 3-5 characters. I've also experienced some fps issues despite being well over the recommended system requirements. As someone who has bought early access, I don't know how fast currency gain is going to be in order to unlock new characters. I remember for the first 20 or so hours is felt incredibly slow and took quite a while to unlock characters, but I'm not entirely sure if they've changed that.
Overall the game gets a solid 7/10 from me. It is fun enough to keep me coming back every other day or so, but it isn't that addicting drug of a game that keeps me here for 8 hours straight like some other games could.

Return to Castle Wolfstein is one of my most unforgettable video games when I owned a PC 10 years ago. I was completely fascinated by the game-play and walk-through. Wasn't sure what to expect coming into this game. Now, less than an hour played and only 5 days in, I've robbed a man whose daughters were slaughtered, helped a man whose brother was shot by a sniper, been caught stealing by a group similar to mine, been victimized by the theft of all my food and water, and my 3 members are all exhausted, sick, wounded, or hungry. This game is, quite frankly, nerve racking and quite terrifying to think about when put in context with the horrors of war. Definitely a step back from the jingoistic, ball-busting action of most war games today.

This little gem is a strange mish mash of elements that work. The setting is space frontier, the music - is awesome!! i never realised i enjoyed blues rock or whatever you call it.
It's a sandbox game - 2 guilds, a couple of factions and 21 ships at the moment. There are reputation gains. You're pretty much free to do as you please from the start.
Maneuvering and combat is done on a 2D plane, although everything is rendered in 3D. Space station interactions is done via menu's quite similar to freelancer.
The premise for combat is that you're piloting a capital type ship - so frigates, corvettes, destroyers etc. So no barrel rolls or fancy schmancy flying. It's a lot more like sailing a naval ship with broadside blasting and turrets/missiles.
It all seems quite simplistic on paper - yet it works. The game seems a lot deeper than it appears. Hopefully Double Damage keeps working on this title and add more modules to this action - space - cowboy - sim!!
Definitely well worth the 20 euros.

This game really is a masterpiece and if I had a top 10 list of 2014 while this wouldn't be number 1 it would be pretty close.
PROS:
This game is stylized and I personally liked the look of the game  however I could understand if some were turned away by the black and white cell shading, I like it even more because it captures the atmosphere of the game which is dark and depressing. If you are looking for an uplifting game, don't look here. Completing this game will generally mean you get some blood on your hands, whether it is innocent blood or a bandit's is up to you. The gameplay is very nice as well, you have to be very vigilant in managing your finite supplies of food, water, and other materials used for building different additions onto your base. This management is difficult to learn what will be optimal for your survival, however once you achieve a good understanding of mechanics it is extremely satisfying to master, thriving in the war torn hell. There is also a randomized element in the game from random people coming to your door to offer you jobs or to ask for your help. This brings up your morals as some of the jobs you're asked to do might be....well let's just say nefarious in nature and it's completely up to you which tasks you spend your limited time completing. From multiple playthroughs I've seen different loot spawn in different places so that is also randomized to an extent making for even more replay value. There are also many different characters present in game that can show up to your door and join your group, all with different backstories, attitudes, and each have unique abilities that will help you in  your fight for survival. For the most part the looting and combat is intense and interesting. You can choose to stealthily creepy around buildings looting or go in guns blazing (if you manage to aquire a gun) the choice is yours on how you want to play the game.
CONS:
The soundtrack isn't very good, in fact there might not be one present in game as the only music I recall is when you tune your radio into different music stations. Combat/looting also has some quirks, nothing horrible but sometimes when you stealth kill an enemy others across the map will seemingly hear it and come rushing towards your position, this only happened to me twice in my gametime so it's not frequent but it definitely can happen. The characters in game are also not very interesting, each has his/her own backstory and if you pass an event their biography will update with their feelings on the situation. I personally didn't get very attached to any of them and when one died I was more concerned about who was going to go crawling through the dirt for food rather than sad about their passing, even a simple re-naming system for the characters would heighten my caring for their lives.
VERDICT:
I whole heartedly recommend this game as a fan of management, building, and looting games. If you purchase this game however beware that this isn't an easy experience and you most likely won't beat the game your first, or even second playthroughs. If you do manage to beat the game quickly not only are you better than me but the game has enough replay value where more runs are also very entertaining. I'm not much for number value reviews so I'll just say this game is definately worth adding to your library.

Rebal Galaxy is a space game similar to Freelancer set in a procedurally-generated quadrant of the galaxy that hits all of the points of the genre and hits them very well.
I've played a lot of space sims and this is one of the more entertaining.  It has all of the standard features of a space sim.  Dynamic trading?  Check.  Bounty hunting?  You bet.  Mining?  Sure.  Missions.  Yeah.  Upgradeable ships with progressively better tech components?  Plug it in. Factions with specialized ships?  You betcha.
The basis of the game is that you are a lucky guy with a mysterious aunt.  Your aunt has two distinguishing features:  She speaks like she swallowed a polecat, and she leaves you a space ship.  A basic one, but it flies (ship; not polecat).  Naturally you set out to find her.  Mysteries involving ancient technology, trecherous aliens and suspicious cops ensue.  In the course of solving these mysteries you will travel through 14-16 (not sure exactly) star systems doing story missions, all of the above fun things and killing other people and aliens who speak like they've swallowed exotic animals.  16 star systems doesn't sound like a lot, but each star system supports dozens of space stations, nebulae and other locations to explore.  (I'm not counting planets.  Naturally, being a space sim, you can't actually land on planets.  Obviosly all races evolved in space and planets are just those things you dodge trying to get to where you can dump your cargo).
Compared to other sims I have played (Elite Dangerous, the Starpoint Gemini and X series', to name a few) its taken some steps to simplify things.  But that can be a good thing.  I never understood how spacefaring races would design a space station where you have to hit a glide pattern then stop on the center of a landing pad - whether you are flying a shuttle or a dreadnought.  Or worse, they make you fly through a tiny keyhole and stop on a dime inside cargo bay.  Then they get mad and put a bounty on you when rookie pilots overshoot, ram stuff, or accidentally hit their boosters in the middle of their shiny space station.  This game dispenses with that.  You get near a station, press a button and you are docked.
The combat is also straightforward.  You have broadside weapons that fire -- broadsides.  A simpler version of the ship fighting in AC Black Flag.  You also have secondaries -- usually press-a-button to fire and forget weapons like mines or missiles.  Finally, you have turrets which can be set to preprogrammed fire (i.e. fire at fighters, fire at my target, fire at capital ships, etc.).  Each type of weapon has a variety of weapons you can select for a loadout.  As you upgrade to better ships, they will fire more shots in a their broadside, have more turrets, etc.
The decisons to make the game simpler were done to make it fun.  Rebel Galaxy it succeeds in this.
I do have some minor quibbles.  I tend to trade and mine a lot, and the trading could use a few more products.  Also, since you are stuck to flying level but rocks and fighters are not, sometimes its hard to bring your mining lasers on target.  Also, I'm only on the second system and the weapon types are starting to get a little limited, with "Mk 2, Mk 3 and Mk 4" versions on the same weapon types purchasable at most stations rather than whole new systems.  Maybe I just haven't found them yet.
As a final note of caution - you will see a lot of people comparing this to Firefly.  Well, its not.  If you think these comparisons mean you will get to defend a brothel on a frontier planet or rob a maglev train or engage in witty banter with your crew -- or any of those things that make Firefly Firefly -- just no.  The comparisons are due to the accents of the npcs and the soundtrack.  The soundtrack is very good, however.
Bottom line, I recommend this game to anyone who is a fan of the genre.

I really wanted to like this game as I enjoyed games like Final Fantasy VI, VII, and Tactics as a kid/teenager, but I sadly cannot recommend it.
Unlike some other reviewers, I thought the story was fine. It's more or less what I'd expect from an FF game. Yes some of the characters can be annoying at times, but it didn't persist throughout the whole game. The battle system was fine and an interesting twist on the old ways. I can't say it's my favorite, but it's satisfying to learn over time how to best manage your paradigms and party make up in order to win. The cast of characters was smaller than I'd like and, like many RPGs with a wide character selection, some characters end up being mostly useless to the point where you'll only want to use them when the storyline forces you to.
As for the bad, I was disappointed in the lack of interaction with characters outside the main party (you only have any real conversation at all with maybe 10 people total in the course of the game, and many of those are brief). I also found the shops (shopping is completely done "online" in the context of the game) mostly useless outside of the early game where I felt like I needed to grab a few extra potions. That said, I've played plenty of RPGs where there is almost zero need to ever buy anything from an NPC vendor so take that for what it is worth.
The worst part of this game was the linearity. Yes, other FF games are pretty linear, but generally reach a point where they "open up" and give you some freedom to roam around, do side quests, find easter eggs, etc. In contrast, FF XIII will railroad you into going exactly where it wants you to go and doing exactly what it wants you to do. Yes it "opens up" a bit in chapter 11, but the side quests there are all given by inanimate stones and are all "please go kill this monster for me." There isn't much extra story to be had.
Finally, a minor bad point is that this IS indeed a buggy port. That said, it's not too difficult to overcome the bugs with a little research online and making sure your graphics drivers are up to date. It's definitely playable and the graphics aren't as bad as all that (though I'm not scrutinizing every pixel on screen).

Return To castle Wolfenstein is the next chapter following the classic Wolfenstein 3d, Our good old William "B.J." Blazkowicz is on a mission after some Nazis and Magic artefacts, and he's once again imprisoned in Castle Wolfenstein.
RTCW (Too long to write) is a classic FPS, with few little innovation, and the engine is essentially a heavily modified version of the trusty Quake III Arena Engine: iD Tech 3. The most evident modifications are lightning and Flamethrower effects wich for the time really were an incredible innovation. Level structure is always linear with various settings, from castles to citadels, big large buildings, catacombs, hills and laboratories. In other words it has a large variety of ambiences, both inside building and open air.
The game structure is a classic "shoot-everything-breathing" but there are few sections where the mission requires your discretion, so you must use a stealth approach.
The story involves much more the occult side of Nazism, infact Helga von Bulow (one of your targets) is after some artifacts and as a consequence you will face some revived corpses.
Anyways AI is something quite odd as I've noticed that soldiers and enemies in general can sight and shoot you with millimetric precision even at the longest distances which is something really ridiculous especially for the stealth sections.
Your arsenal presents some interesting innovations and a very big variety of weapons. There are 3 kind of rifles, 2 sniper rifles, grenades, Panzerfaust and a Powerful Experimental Tesla Cannon, not to mention the Efficient Flamethrower.
I would like to point out the possibility to play in Co-op (which is how I've played in this run) through a very good mod, you can look into it in the always useful Steam community.

I have played Final Fantasy for a very long time, and 13 holds up many solid aspects of the series. The game itself was actually a commercial success but the company deemed it a failure after the negative fan response.
The game itself is quite enjoyable with a solid cast of characters, a great story that was supposed to over arc into what is now Final Fantasy XV and Type-0.
There are 2 major flaws with this game.
1) the game is very linear, you practically run through a figurative straight line for the first chunk of the game, that can be 24-30 hours of gameplay since you want to fight EVERY battle and watch the cutscenes first time around.
2.) For some reason somebody thought the auto-battle feature was a good idea. Litterally press 1 button to have the most optimal ability selection played each time. This takes away from the experience of figuring out for yourself what best to do. ( You still need to use abilities like scan for auto battle to know an enemies weakness so it is not all done for you in one button)
Other than that the game has an amazing story, and sets up what should have been a great sub series within the Final Fantasy series.
Pros:
great Story
Mostly likeable cast
visually stunning still today
Cons:
Super Linear for first half

I bought this game in an atempt to get into Final Fantasy. I've never played any other games from the franchise, so bear with me because I don't know what to expect from a FInal Fantasy game.
So I decided to pick up this game after many many years of seeing people go crazy over final fantasy at conventions like PAX and recently E3. So I looked for the latest single player version (I refuse to pick up any more MMOs) and found this one. Bought it despite of the mixed reviews.
I'm a few hours in game, and this is what I think of so far.
Pros

-Story, seems good, easy to follow. If you don't understand something, you can read up on most things in the game, such as places or people in the menu.
-Cut scenes (in game cinematic cut scenes, not gameplay cut scenes) are beautiful and very intersting to watch, really draws my attention.
-Combat is straight foward, I skipped through all tutorials and still mastered the combat in mere minutes.
-Runs like a charm, 60 fps the whole time (i5 4690K @ 4.3 Ghz with a GTX 1070).
-Really really love the style of the game (scenery, clothing, weapons, etc...), it's something that has always caught my attention with Final Fantasy (Advent Children).
CONS
-Next to no options in menu. Meaning no sound control, Graphics, and look sensitivity, all the basics basically......
-I HATE THE CAMERA MOVEMENTS IN MOST JAPANESE GAMES, INCLUDING THIS ONE! Horrible camera movement and control.
-Not really a con, more of a personal pet peeve, Turn Based combat from the 90s. I mean yeah it's a bit quicker and in real time, instead of the really old school turn based where you have to wait for the enemy to finish his move. But this is the main reason I stayed away from the franchise all these years. (a friend misinformed me and said Final Fantasy didn't do turn based combat anymore LMAO, which is why I bought the game)
-Very very limited exploring. I get it, it's not an open world RPG game, but having me run on a small little path for most of the game seems kinda bland.
Overall I'm enjoying the game so far, more pros than cons for me. I believe I may turn into a Final Fantasy fan after I finish this game, too soon to say though. Thumbs up from me.

This game is strangely compelling, given that in its core it's pretty much a mediocre brawler-type, corridor-driven action "rpg".
I'm playing it in local coop, which undoubtedly adds to the fun factor.
What probably provides the most fun for me are the random lore tidbits you find out through dialogue with the various less-explored NPCs like the Great eagles and the random Dunedain rangers you encounter all over the game world. The dialogue is okay, with characters sometimes directly quoting the movies/books.
The story is actually fitting the lore strangely well, dealing with a secondary force of Sauron stemming from the cold north and preventing an imminent attack on Rivendell (if I remember correctly, Gundabad was always an Orc nest, and was never really explored/explained in the source materials).
The fetch "quests" are as basic as you can get, including one painfully tedious quest at the beginning of the game where you literally go tell a girl that a guy is in love with her, and then go back to the guy to tell him she also loves him... I mean, wow, go tell him yourself, he's standing literally twenty meters from you, and you're both doing absolutely nothing!
The loot system is bland and basic, as is the skill "tree"- with a total of maybe three or four skills per character. Your "skills" are extremely basic, especially with the ranger class, where you get a "skill" to strike hard at one guy and a "skill" to swipe your weapon through multiple enemies. The combat is actually not bad, all things considered- you have your roll dodges, block, various defensive options including a magical anti-arrow barrier that also heals the party, and the enemies can be relatively varied and requiring different approach methods to defeat. Still, everything seems a bit basic and unenthusiastic, especially compared to something like Shadow of Mordor.
The loot system is made so that everything is completely separate for every player (a la Diablo 3), but that also includes experience- it seems that kills made by one player only award experience to that player- leading to the relatively support-oriented elven Loremaster ending up underleveled compared to attack-oriented dunedain Ranger and dwarven Champion and having to replay some levels to gain enough experience to buy better equipment.
The graphics, while pretty and completely in-line with the movies' visual design, are nothing to write home about. That does provide a benefit of working well on older hardware, though!
Overall, I'd recommend getting this game while it's on a heavy sale (75% off or more), especially if you're able to play it in LAN coop with a friend or two. It did keep me playing for a relatively long while, and I plan on completing it, so it gets a thumbs-up from me.

I have 10 hours + I finished it on PS3 once and have played almost all FF games.
This is aimed at those who have played FF and comes with an expectation of similar gameplay:
Instead you have a similar 'role-level' system as found in FFX and FFXII with the Grid System.
After each battle you get AP which is used to unlock new 'nodes' in your Role. You get more AP with a higher score.
Despite new names the Roles is similar to DPS, TANK, STATUS EFF. and HEALER.
I found the 'Paradigm system' to be very entertaining and it is fun enough to sit and pick what you want to unlock next.
While I really like the old-school basic level up system in past games, the 'Paradigm' more than suffices.
Yes it is true... Yet I accepted it and found it alright. I won't call it a Pro, nor a Con.
You still manage the whole team's paradigms, equipment and roles. Yet in battles you control the leader only.
So before battles it is important to set up Role-Sets which can quickly be switched between in battles.
Imagine a Role-Set as this: DPS - MGC - MGC is used for pure damage until you need healing.
Then you switch Role-Set to: DPS - HEALER - TANK and get healed up.
It works and is entertaining but far from classic FF battles.
Yeah it is FF quality. Yet for some reason the eyelashed on Lightning is messed up on my PC.
It looks really fun and is obvious a graphical error. She looks so funny. It only appears in the 'low quality' cut-scenes.
She honestly look like the young teenage girls who fails so hard at putting on make-up and looks like a drag-queen.
Everything is top notch when it comes to the high quality cut-scenes.
While the story is not anything close to let's say FFVII, FFXI or FFX it is 'entertaining'.
You won't cry because of Vivi. You won't begin to wonder about life after listening to Bugenhagen.
Yet the story is not bad. It is just not epic or super deep. At times it tries to be but fails imo.
It can even get too much at times where I feel like a 5 year old little girl doing cute emotion I learned on the Iphone.
It just get TOO girly at times, where most other FF titles had a fine balance.
It reminds me a bit of FFXIV at times where they laugh like small kids and get all 'happy' together.
I need some action, blood and big swords. Which the game ALSO delivers, so all the girly stuff is acceptable.
While the world IS pretty and beautiful it just was too unrelateable for me. Most FF titles mixed fantasy/sci-fi/reality in a very well balanced way. They managed to make you feel some what familiar to the world, even though summoned dragons and magic was flying around in the air. FFXIII however fails at this. It is just PURE futuristic fantasy world and half of the time I had trouble keeping up with where I actually was.
Some places however was really well made and I enjoyed exploring them (exploring.. haha).
However it was and is still just too out-there for me.
The game can only be classified as linear. Most of the time you walk a clear path and it is on these walks you meet dangers or find poorly hidden chests. I can understand you might get a bit dissappointed if you came expecting The Witcher 3 open world. Yet it did not bother me at all.
I knew it was linear before buying it on steam and bought it for that reason.
Just for once I felt like laying back and just chill without too much exploration and stuff.
I have been on every inch in FFVII and Gaia in FFXI to either get KotR or eat Dead Peppers at bubbles in the water.
So this time I found it okay to just relax. Do not expect huge open world elements. Just jump in and enjoy the ride.
Also, the game is PACKED with cutscenes. Sometimes you might only walk a short distance, doing nothing at all and then a another cutscene starts. I like it, as I could lay back and pick my belly button while enjoying the movie.
So once more: Yes it is linear.
I heard alot of people say Lightning is boring and like a machine with a pretty face.
She is a machine, but not boring at all. It is just that while the rest of the party has VERY outgoing and particular personalities, Lightning is like the AC version of Cloud. She clearly has her issues.
That said, she def is not boring but very machine like. Yet if you pay attention to story you will understand why.
While it does not beat the major FF titles out there the game is good. It is worth the playthrough.
If you can accept the things I've mentioned, the game does deliver a decent FF experience with familiarities.
The combat IS somewhat challenging but can get easy -> But c'mon in what FF game can't u just 1 hit with strongest magic when u get high enough level? Unless ofc it is those damn Yans...
I recommend it but expect alot of auto mechanics and do not expect a new 'best FF game'.
Buy it on sale if you think the price is too high.

Plus Side:
+Story Mode uses real decks.
+Close to real MTG rules.
+Looks pretty.
+A couple cool story matches.
Minus Side:
-*Close* to real MTG rules, for instance sometimes tokens don't have summoning sickness.
-Stupidly long load times.  I mean really, how long does it take to digitally shuffle two decks?
-The grind is too long to open a pack of SIX cards. As opposed to the 15 you would get in a real pack.  If you manage to complete the 3 quests you get you probably can get a pack, but that's the next point...
-The quests suck. They basically so far have been 11 quests to win with their terrible deck builder wizard, 1 to target an opponent directly and 1 to win with my own hand built decks that CAN win.  Oh and by the way you can only abandon one quest a day.
- Poor starting cards, hard to get a decent theme going to even have a chance to win even on easy.
- Awkward timing on play. See each hit against the opponent one by one, but when it's time to counter a spell you cant click fast enough.  Of course you get a timer each time the opponent plays a card even if you can't actually respond with a spell.
- Deck building has very basic filters.  Needs some keyword searching or something.
- Deck building is unintuitive.  Not even a 'save deck' button.  They're really pressuring the deck wizards that can't deliver early game.
- Story opponents are frequently given the perfect counter deck on non-final bosses.
- Edit: Oh forgot to mention, after finally getting a completable quest, completion did not award gold, hence the review/uninstall.
Altogether, rather play Yu Gi Oh on Game Boy Advance still.

I will not sugar-coat this, X: Rebirth was absolutely terrible at launch, but the reason why I still recommend it is because I think now with all the updates, it has become a
. If you don’t want to read the whole thing, then just go to the last paragraph on the bottom.
First of all, let’s consider the price. I think the current price of whooping 50€ is unjustified; it wasn’t justified at launch and it still isn’t justified now. What I would recommend to people thinking about buying this game – wait for the
. I’m sure XR will be on sale this December, so even if you don’t like the game, you will have not spent too much money on it.
Many people already familiar with previous X games will say XR should have been X4. What you have to consider is that the developers never intended to make X4, they wanted to create a whole different game with different mechanics. The biggest problem here is that they (over)
XR to appeal to wider audiences. This is the sole reason why XR does not feel like X4. They reduced the game complexities and I believe that cost them more than they thought it would. Many features were completely stripped from the game; the most debated being able to fly
reduced to
in XR. Some features have been added now with patches though, which I find this ridiculous as they should have been in the game from the very start.
As I mentioned before, at launch the game was riddled with bugs, crashes, and whatnot; it was completely game-breaking. But I believe they fixed quite a large amount of those and the game is slowly shaping up into a decent game. For players thinking about getting this game, you should be aware that XR is
. The developers wanted to make space exploration and economic empire building to be as realistic as possible, so even simple operations like ordering your ship to trade some wares, takes a while. They justify this by saying, “while you’re waiting for the trade to complete, go do / explore something else”. But after a while, this becomes terribly tedious and annoying, especially if you opt for building stations.
Building stations for your trade empire used to be much simpler and faster in previous X games. Now it just takes forever, and to top it off, it takes a vast amount of money and resources. Again probably to make it more realistic. Fleet control is hardly on par with X3, there’s less races, less star systems, trading can be grating at times while you’re waiting for something to happen, travelling times are longer, the plot is not really that great, the interactive menus are badly designed (improved with v 2.50), and the NPCs just suck.
BUT despite all this, I still invested 300+ hours into XR because I enjoy space simulators. The vast
they designed are stunning and gorgeous to explore, the universe really does feel alive, capital ships and freighters are also badass and I enjoy capturing and collecting them, watching your stations expand and earn you more money feels good, manoeuvring around stations at high speed looks awesome and your choices can really affect the universe.
Hopefully with the release of XR 3.0, new features/improvements will make the game more enjoyable.
In the end, it’s all a matter of taste. If you enjoy space simulations or you’re a hardcore space gamer, I think XR would be a good game to try. But if you are a casual player not looking for slow and complicated in-depth gaming, then you’re better off playing a space shooter or fast-paced strategy game.

This War of Mine is not a fun game. If you are one of those who think games ought to be fun, turn around, walk away and pretend this doesn't exist.
TWM is a harrowing, depressing experience which puts you in a war torn city, with a small group of truly ordinary citizens. A math professor, a football player, a fireman, a thief, a gourmet chef...
One of the very first things you realize is you are not playing this to win. This is war and war is hell, there is no winning. You are simply trying to survive, to keep on going for one more day at a time, hoping for better times.
You start out in a heavily damaged house, with holes in the walls and barely any food or materials. Over time you try to improve your living conditions, by making beds, chairs, stoves etc. If you are lucky, maybe you can make some rain water collectors, or maybe even a moonshine distillery?
As the days pass and the war keeps raging on, resources become scarce and everyone, the military, militia and even ordinary citizens become more and more violent and depraved, all in the name of survival. Whereas you could trade a few gems for a ton of supplies in the early days, you could end up trading your shotgun for a few pieces of rat meat in the cold and unforgiving winter...
In a world where we are all too quick to dismiss the wars in the Middle East or Ukraine with "not my problem", turn down asylum seekers based on our prejudices of race, religion and ethnicity, This War of Mine provides us (especially the Western audience) with a fresh perspective and maybe even a lesson in humanity...

While not the flashiest game around, and deceptively simple with its side action scrolling display, This War of Mine is a game that can be both riveting and engrossing.
This isn't a game for those looking for tons of action or a shoot em up.  This is a thoughtful game of resource management mixed with sneaking around while on scavenging missions.
You start with anywhere from 1 to 4 characters (randomly generated initially) and your goal is to survive the war.  The length of the war is random (25-45 days), and there are numerous randomly generated events to make every survival experience somewhat different.
Some of the random events include illness, attacks by night time raiders, the onset of winter (and extreme cold), and snowstorms and combat making some areas inaccessible.  Aside from this the locations you visit have more than one version.  You might enter an area that is free of hostile forces.  On another playthrough they can be filled with soldiers, rebels or thugs.  The locations are also not all available at the start of the game but are instead unveiled throughout the game over time.
Throughout the game you are confronted with moral decisions.  Do you help someone or not?  Everytime you help someone requires a sacrifice that can cost you in the short term either in terms of time, resources, or risk of injury and potentially death.  However, turning away all requests for help can lead to negative consequences on morale.  And if someone wants to join you do you value the extra pair of hands more than having another mouth to feed?
Similarly, you'll be presented with opportunities to make hard choices on your scavenging runs.  Do you take advantage of the weak?  Do you kill innocents?  Do you confront those doing wrong or let it happen?
Adding to replayability the resources immediately available to you are also randomly generated.  On one play through you'll find you have more than enough wood or parts, on another you'll struggle to find electrical components, weapons or food at your starting location.  As the game continues you'll find you never have everything you want or need which forces you to prioritize what you want to build and when.
On top of this your scavenging runs are further constrained by a fixed amount of backpack space.  Depending on the character doing the scavenging the amount of space can range from 8 spaces to 17 spaces (1 character), with most having around 10 to 12 spaces.
Similarly, the status of your starting characters are slightly randomized.  Sometimes they can start as ill or wounded (slowing you down and forcing you to manage your people more carefully as well as consuming important items like medical supplies).
This is a very good game that will appeal to most but not all.  It has solid replayability and multiple ways to win.
One warning, this is a somewhat unforgiving game with a steep learning curve.
There is no "save" option other than a daily autosave (in case of a crash) which is automatically updated upon a major event (like a character death).  In other words, if characters die you'll have to keep the group going in spite of the repercussions on the team.
That said, the first time you "survive" the war with no team deaths you will feel like you've accomplished something.

I'm not going to lie, after seeing some reviews of this game, and comparing it to Civ V, I was not thrilled by it. But this free weekend has allowed me to experience Beyond Earth for myself, and I was actually quite impressed! My only point, is that this would be better suited as a higher-priced DLC for Civ V, as it runs off of most of the same features.
They have made a lot of improvements to the old Civ V to make it seem quite different, and they have added some completely new features which add to the enjoyability of the game. Sure, it may not be AS GOOD AS Civ V, but we have to wait. Civ V became so much better with the arrival of DLC, especially Brave New World. This game shows so much promise and with DLC it could be loads better than it already is.
Positives:
All of the improvements to Civ V (inc. Tech Web and City States)
New factions to play as and starting bonuses are a nice touch, giving each player the chance to be equal to another, so there are no over-powered factions.
Generally fun gameplay. I enjoyed played single and multiplayer, the features are largely the same as Civ V so I could adapt quickly to understand and enjoy the new features.
Negatives:
The colour scheme. It's so dark and, I suppose, dank. There aren't any vibrant colours which stand out and it makes the game feel glum and morose. I hope a DLC can change the colour scheme, such as Brave New World did for Civ V.

Bioshock 2 is an older game now (nearly 4 years!) and has been reviewed many times; I'll repeat one thing that was common to a lot of those: If you liked Bioshock, you'll like Bioshock 2.  It doesn't have _quite_ as much impact as the former, largely due to the change of protagonist.
As Jack, even spliced up, you felt small.  Human.  Vulnerable.  There was a mile of freezing seawater between you and escape, and the lunatics had free run of the asylum... and drowning was something you would have no problem doing.  As Subject Delta (or, in Minerva's Den, Subject Sigma), you feel like a Big Daddy.  A little ponderous, but armoured, tough, and more than capable of beating a few splicers to death.
The story isn't quite as brilliant either - in the first game, Rapture was new (to you), and everything was exploration of Andrew Ryan's ruined dream.  Well, in 2, Rapture is just as pretty, just as fascinating... but not quite as new.  There's a certain sense of familiarity for those who've played through the first game and spent quite a few hours in the slowly decaying city.  It's worth noting that as with the first game, the art assets for Bioshock 2 are stunning.  Post-apocalyptic art deco and water effects make for a feast for the eyes.
Some of the new Plasmids (plus the ability to use guns and plasmids at the same time) make for some real fun, mechanically, and even if you're feeling like a nice, tough Big Daddy, the Splicers haven't been sitting still either.  There are some real challenges at the higher difficulty levels.
Overall, if you don't have it, but have played Bioshock, get this game, and play it.  If you don't have it, and _haven't_ played Bioshock, get Bioshock.  Then get this game and play it. :)

I have 10 hours + I finished it on PS3 once and have played almost all FF games.
This is aimed at those who have played FF and comes with an expectation of similar gameplay:
Instead you have a similar 'role-level' system as found in FFX and FFXII with the Grid System.
After each battle you get AP which is used to unlock new 'nodes' in your Role. You get more AP with a higher score.
Despite new names the Roles is similar to DPS, TANK, STATUS EFF. and HEALER.
I found the 'Paradigm system' to be very entertaining and it is fun enough to sit and pick what you want to unlock next.
While I really like the old-school basic level up system in past games, the 'Paradigm' more than suffices.
Yes it is true... Yet I accepted it and found it alright. I won't call it a Pro, nor a Con.
You still manage the whole team's paradigms, equipment and roles. Yet in battles you control the leader only.
So before battles it is important to set up Role-Sets which can quickly be switched between in battles.
Imagine a Role-Set as this: DPS - MGC - MGC is used for pure damage until you need healing.
Then you switch Role-Set to: DPS - HEALER - TANK and get healed up.
It works and is entertaining but far from classic FF battles.
Yeah it is FF quality. Yet for some reason the eyelashed on Lightning is messed up on my PC.
It looks really fun and is obvious a graphical error. She looks so funny. It only appears in the 'low quality' cut-scenes.
She honestly look like the young teenage girls who fails so hard at putting on make-up and looks like a drag-queen.
Everything is top notch when it comes to the high quality cut-scenes.
While the story is not anything close to let's say FFVII, FFXI or FFX it is 'entertaining'.
You won't cry because of Vivi. You won't begin to wonder about life after listening to Bugenhagen.
Yet the story is not bad. It is just not epic or super deep. At times it tries to be but fails imo.
It can even get too much at times where I feel like a 5 year old little girl doing cute emotion I learned on the Iphone.
It just get TOO girly at times, where most other FF titles had a fine balance.
It reminds me a bit of FFXIV at times where they laugh like small kids and get all 'happy' together.
I need some action, blood and big swords. Which the game ALSO delivers, so all the girly stuff is acceptable.
While the world IS pretty and beautiful it just was too unrelateable for me. Most FF titles mixed fantasy/sci-fi/reality in a very well balanced way. They managed to make you feel some what familiar to the world, even though summoned dragons and magic was flying around in the air. FFXIII however fails at this. It is just PURE futuristic fantasy world and half of the time I had trouble keeping up with where I actually was.
Some places however was really well made and I enjoyed exploring them (exploring.. haha).
However it was and is still just too out-there for me.
The game can only be classified as linear. Most of the time you walk a clear path and it is on these walks you meet dangers or find poorly hidden chests. I can understand you might get a bit dissappointed if you came expecting The Witcher 3 open world. Yet it did not bother me at all.
I knew it was linear before buying it on steam and bought it for that reason.
Just for once I felt like laying back and just chill without too much exploration and stuff.
I have been on every inch in FFVII and Gaia in FFXI to either get KotR or eat Dead Peppers at bubbles in the water.
So this time I found it okay to just relax. Do not expect huge open world elements. Just jump in and enjoy the ride.
Also, the game is PACKED with cutscenes. Sometimes you might only walk a short distance, doing nothing at all and then a another cutscene starts. I like it, as I could lay back and pick my belly button while enjoying the movie.
So once more: Yes it is linear.
I heard alot of people say Lightning is boring and like a machine with a pretty face.
She is a machine, but not boring at all. It is just that while the rest of the party has VERY outgoing and particular personalities, Lightning is like the AC version of Cloud. She clearly has her issues.
That said, she def is not boring but very machine like. Yet if you pay attention to story you will understand why.
While it does not beat the major FF titles out there the game is good. It is worth the playthrough.
If you can accept the things I've mentioned, the game does deliver a decent FF experience with familiarities.
The combat IS somewhat challenging but can get easy -> But c'mon in what FF game can't u just 1 hit with strongest magic when u get high enough level? Unless ofc it is those damn Yans...
I recommend it but expect alot of auto mechanics and do not expect a new 'best FF game'.
Buy it on sale if you think the price is too high.
