Hatred is a top-down twin stick shooter where your goal is to kill everybody that moves.  The game takes place over 7 distinct areas where you can free-roam (for the most part) and do objectives as you wish. The game does have requirements to move on to the next stage, mainly "Kill X amount of people" or "Get out of X". There are several side objectives that mostly involve killing the majority of people in a given area. Completing these side objectives gives you respawn tokens to use if you die. If you die and you're out of respawns, you have to restart the level.
You yourself play as an edgy misanthrope who has long hair, wears a black trench coat, and spouts one-liners. You are controlled with WASD by default, and there is a sprint mechanic that you can use to vault over small walls, a crouch mechanic that makes you harder to hit and increases your aim, an aiming mechanic that allows you to precisely aim as well as aim higher or lower to compensate for the top-down nature, and this spidey-sense type mechanic that highlights living enemies on your screen as well as equipment pickups. You can carry up to three weapons at a time, from about 10 weapons There is a health system, where you can only regenerate a bit of health by executing 'not-quite-dead' enemies. It sounds all horrible, but trust me, you get used to the same 'stomp the guys head in' or 'shoot the guy in the head' animation after a hundred times. The player character does sometimes get caught on hard-to-see level geometry or a tiny chip of a wall still standing which can be pretty irksome if you're trying to get away from a firefight.
You aren't just shooting innocent civilians, you'll be fighting police, weapons dealers, vigilantes, hunters, SWAT, and the army. Even unarmed civilians will sometimes pick up a gun and start unloading on you. They aren't pushovers, either. On higher difficulties, SWAT can take three shots with a shotgun and still be standing, and you'll often be forced to retreat and find some civvies to execute. The AI has a lot of room for improvement, but I let it slide because it's not really something you ask for in an indie game.  An annoying features is that enemies can shoot you from beyond your maximum view range, forcing you to rely on your (inconsistent) minimap to find your shooter.
The gunplay is solid and even the 9mm pistol manages to actually do something rather just being the equivalent of spitballs against tougher enemies. The physics engine is great and it's a lot of fun to play around with, though it can be pretty CPU-intensive. Speaking of graphics, I'm a fan of the style, where everything is grayscale except red, blue, and explosions. It can give me a headache playing too long, though.
It's a pretty short game, I beat it on hard in 3 hours, but like I said, they're free-roam areas and I was mostly just rushing objectives. Unless you want to screw around with the levels you liked later or get achievements, it's not a game that you'll replay a lot. There is workshop support and multiplayer/coop planned down the road, which would add a breath of fresh air to the game.
Finally, the moral panic. The game is not a fourth as bad as the trailers made it out to be. It's actually pretty tame. Like I said, you get jaded to the executions, and there's not really a lot of over-the-top gore except for bloodstains, blood pools, and some limb removal. I honestly don't see how this got an AO rating, it's M at best. For the tone, it gets pretty clear the game is parodying itself. The over-the-top one-liners by the player character (who is called the Antagonist by the developers) includes a line from the POSTAL DUDE. An important code for something later in the game is 666, for god's sake. Don't be offended.
Overall, I'd give it a 6.5/10, above average. Make sure you buy the game if you like it, not just to stick it to the people who don't like it.

If you want as much Magic practice as possible, then this is the game for you. If you don't need that, then you might prefer dueling with an actual person.
The cards offer a wide variety, though not all of them are powerful. You have plenty of opponents for practice, but some strategies (and the ragequits) get old fast. The more annoying problems are in the interface. I’ll give a few tips to dodge those.
If you want to build a stack, it works fine on your turn, but the opponent’s turn doesn’t yield priority during their upkeep or draw. To do some pre-battle sabotage, I either have to hope the opponent starts a stack first (I get 2-3 seconds), or wait until the combat icon begins to light up (also 2-3 seconds, and there’s no sound effect for the end of the main phase). Of course, the AI prefers to cast spells in the second main phase when possible.
The game has had some glitches with storing cards/coins. Tech support helped me, so feel free to ask them. (They gave me this prevention tip:
If you actually know how to use that info, then more power to you.)
You can run the entire game with a mouse except for two parts. One, you need a key binding to choose which lands to tap. Otherwise, the game chooses the payments on its own -- though it’ll do an okay job. The Options menu has the controls.

But the second headache is hitting multiple blockers. If the enemy gang-blocks your attacker, the screen zooms in on the battling cards. Use your arrow keys or scroll wheel to choose the first victim, THEN click. There is no undo button here, so sucks to be you if you fight the wrong creature first. Even worse, these zoomed cards cover up the rest of the battlefield. If you had another attacker, you only had the split second before the zoom-in to see if that attacker is headed for trouble.
The content isn’t half bad. There are tutorials everywhere, but almost all are optional, and each one you pass gives some coins that you’ll want later. The one required tutorial is Gideon's Story, and it's a fair test of skill. If you know how to pick your battles, you'll pass.
Your graduation prize = a few packs of Origins cards + a truckload of other cards. These starter cards are maybe 50-50 for winning duels. I like those odds. The free cards will give you dual lands in every combination, plus beatsticks and ammunition in every color, so if you pull just one or two lucky boosters, then you can stitch together at least one working deck. (I’ll come back to boosters in a minute.)
The other planeswalker stories have some intriguing flavor, none of them scripted like Gideon. The player decks are mono-color, as are most of the enemies. If they used my color, they tended to be pretty frickin’ good at it. This was my intro to the five basic styles, and having to outpace a same-color enemy meant picking up ideas from their cards as well as mine. That was pretty cool. Of course, the MTG folks don’t write a simple story, so the later rounds get a wide variety of enemies, colors, styles, and sabotage. Remember, it only takes one win to succeed.
The stories give one-shot coin rewards, enough for one booster per story. Most of your income will come from online battles or (more reliably) daily quests. (I'm not paying real money for coins, ever.) You'll never unwrap a fifth copy of any card, and any card you own can be used in infinite decks you build. That's fine by me. It means my collection can only improve. No, I didn’t like getting an overkill second copy of a seven-drop. But when I got that first copy, I saw space for it all over the place.
Which brings me, last and not least, to the deck-builders. There are two: freestyle, and assisted by a wizard. The freestyle one is great. You can sift your whole collection for color, mana cost, and card type, and it measures your mana curve and your creature-land-other card count. No more having to memorize those numbers.
However, the wizard has problems. Many of the daily achievements (your meager income, remember?) involve using decks of certain colors. Right now, only wizard decks count for that. Good news -- the wizard's smart enough to give you cards in three categories: damage from a themed strategy, fuel for the themed strategy, and other support. Bad news -- those cards come from your limited supply. If you plan to swarm and buff an army of weenies, but your collection has a distinct lack of buff cards, you're screwed.
Worse news -- the wizard doesn't let you pick from your whole collection. It gives you a five-card menu. You pick a card, it fills the gap, rinse and repeat for each of those three categories I mentioned. If you know you own a card that would help, but the wizard didn't feel like including that card, you are also screwed. Tip: at the end of each category, if you give an unwanted card back, the menu refreshes itself -- maybe with different offerings. Try it, and hope your do-over digs up something better.
Overall, this game isn't a
game. Money-wise, you can't beat the price. Hundreds of free cards that I might never have gotten to test drive otherwise? Count me in. A free mulligan on every duel? Also count me in.
Time-wise, the system doesn't always cooperate. Frustration sucks. Not being able to cast an effect in time sucks. A steamroll from a *medium*-level AI with two planeswalkers
sucks. If you want to practice, I guarantee this game can teach you to wring every last point of success out of every opportunity.
But if you want laughter with your fun, you're better off playing in person. Here, you can always send a friend request to someone who played an excellent duel. It's just won't be the same.
I've stuck with it, and if I duel you, I promise I won't quit. (Yes, people do that a lot. But now, the winner gets the coins and a rank up no matter what. Done deal.)

I've actually got over 60 hours in this game but almost all of it has been played in offline mode.
The downsides have already been pointed out by numerous people, but even so it can be a fun game as long as you don't go into it expecting to be able to do much besides the main story without extensive use of the wiki or walkthroughs as many sidequests have very specific, odd, or just plain "wtf" level triggers like having to find the right NPC as well as the actual quest trigger not always happening when you do talk to the NPC.
This is most notable with recruitable characters. Many of them have a series of conversations and sometimes a quest to gain a stat boost for them, but if you aren't using a guide you'll probably never get any of them because the conversations very rarely show up unless you spend an inordinate amount of time entering a town, checking the character, then exiting the town and re entering to see if the next conversation trigger has shown up.
Unlike most RPGs, extensive grinding will only hurt you in the long run because the rare monsters and many sidequest bosses "level up" as your battle rank increases, so the fights only get harder as you get stronger instead of easier like you'd expect. This is honestly a TERRIBLE design choice and I can't understand what the devs were thinking when they made the game this way.
To compound this you can't give individual orders to your characters, you just throw them into groups and during fights each group has a few different options each turn which may or may not even be what you want. Have a group that's close to dying? They may not even have a "heal yourself" or "defend" option show up. Other groups will sometimes have a "heal them" option pop up but will rarely take their action in time to save a group with low HP and will end up wasting their turn.
I could go on but I won't, because honestly I don't think it's worth it since there are many other reviews that explain the game's faults in detail. But I will say this, if you do decide to get this game then I HIGHLY suggest downloading the trainer for it, you'll probably need it to lower your BR if you end up fighting too many enemies and overlevel.

This game is the sandbox space sim we've been waiting for since Freelancer. Elite: Dangerous too fiddly for you? Loved AC: Black Flag for the ship combat? Enjoyed Firefly? Tired of waiting for Star Citizen to get to a release?
Then you're gonna love this game.
You fly a capital ship in a somewhat open universe. Trade, pirate, privateer - the choice is yours. Fighter pilots? Pah! I fly a ship that launches broadsides, son, and obliterates your little X-wing knockoff with my Flak.
The country and western soundtrack and Southern accents for some of the characters bring the Firefly references in so nicely and casually without explicitly resorting to Firefly-like dialect or setting, making it a subtle, valued tie-in.
The game suffers from the procedurally generated fault of being a 'lifeless'-feeling open world. There's also some minor Quality Of Life issues with trying to be a trader - finding out (last known) prices is a bit fiddly. Free trade is also unfortunately not very lucrative, compared to the Mission Boards (which will post trade missions that ironically make FAR more than you could shipping the goods without a contract, after you've gone into the game a bit). But at least the mission boards make the Trader path remain viable along with the plainly-intended Privateer path.
You also navigate and fight solely along each systems ecliptic and ignore the third dimension, to a much larger degree than Freelancer or its other wannabe successors. But let's be honest with ourselves - this genre was never about the third dimension.
This game is also very well optimized for the technical side.
Get this game. It's the game we've been waiting for, and it came with no fanfare.

A thoroughly boring, soulless experiment in charging full price for what should be an expansion pack. The vast majority of touted features are simply concepts from Civilization V mildly tweaked, such as Social Policies simply being reorganized into new hierarchies, Barbarians having barely-noticeable changes in aggressiveness based on how many of them you kill over a certain time, and the ability to pick a few token bonuses to expedite your victory progress ever so slightly.
The degree to which the game's elements have been copy-pasted from the complete Civilization V is most egregiously highlighted by whole lines of text, textures, policy and faction bonuses, and sound effects being Ctrl+C, Ctrl+V'd throughout the game, particularly in the even more lifeless than ever diplomacy screen, where the AI has exactly one new trick, and that is to offer "Favours" in exchange for its ridiculous requests for half your economy. The Miasma, a poor man's version of the Mind Worms and other hazards from Sid Meier's Alpha Centauri, amount to nothing but the seldom-seen Fallout effect from Civ V with the ability to turn its damage per turn into healing once you advance enough through one of the Ideolo- I mean Affinities.
Actually, that isn't fair, as Affinities are one of the few interesting expansions on their parent concept from V. They allow you to access a few unique units and determine the statistics of existing ones as they upgrade, as well as having threshold requirements for building certain mid-late game structures. The problem with this, however, is that this has come at the cost of losing unique units and buildings for individual Civilizations, resulting in a net
of variation, and contributing to the deficit of interesting content.
One of the things that influences Affinities is technology, which largely remains unchanged by the move from linear Eras to the web. The high cost of outer techs is the same barrier as all previous Civilizations' tech Eras, as beelining is indeed possible, if even less advisable outside of extremely specific strategies. The Technologies themselves suffer from the same problem as most other elements, though: They are not interesting due to being conveyed as little more than a wall of text and permission to build a few new things. This isn't different from past Civ games, but whereas previous games' technology was recognizable, real-world tech, there was a degree of familiarity that allowed you to intuitively know the nature of your Civ's advancement and be able to immediately relate the new options to the concept, with Sci-Fi tech, this isn't the case, and withoug well-done contextualizing, the techs become as lifeless as most of the rest of the game.
City States, Wonders, and Resources have all been rendered less versatile and engaging, with no City State diplomacy game to be played, nor bonuses beyond their trade yields, bland Wonder yields that lack in-game models beyond the game winning ones, which have admittedly added a bit of strategy to victory progress, albeit almost insignificant, and less Resource management strategy due to only Strategic Resources limiting or influencing construction options, with the others being nothing more than tile yield modifiers, rather than certain ones being prerequisites for buildings like in V.
Warfare is still as much of a chore as Civ V, with large-scale combat being a tedious process of maneuvering dozens of units over terrain while being pelted by ranged units. Combat promotions are all but gone now, as the only options are to Heal Instantly or add 10% strength to the unit. With the lack of units such as Paratroopers, Bombers, and Melee and Submarine Naval units, this
limits the variety on offer. The reintroduction of at least partial unit stacking, perhaps a limit of 3 military units per tile, would remedy this, but it isn't the case here.
It's clear that some effort went into the "lore" and background information, but the vast majority of it is burried in walls of text within the far too slim Civilopedia. This would not be a problem for richer Sci-Fi settings such as Mass Effect 1 or, indeed, Sid Meier's Alpha Centauri, but here there is no impetus to read any of it due to the complete lack of personality in the characters or intrigue in the world. The biomes are less fleshed-out conceptually than Minecraft, displaying little in the way of biodiversity as was mentioned in some preview material, not even going so far as to retexture bright green Wolf Beetles when on a blue-grey fungal planet.
Cannot recommend at all. If you want Sci-Fi Civ, I can only suggest acquiring Alpha Centauri.

Although released 15 years ago, Return to Castle Wolfenstein still packs a punch. Do note, however, that installing the game is not enough to have it run properly under newer systems - there is a guide available on Steam that tells us what patch to download and what files to overwrite. Once it is done, RoTW can be enjoyed even in the HD resolution!
The story of Wolfenstein has always been about Nazis and the occult. Blazkowicz, our hero, now faces some pretty gruesome monsters - beside eliminating soldiers we have lots of undead warriors here, plus, we get to see how Wilhelm Strasse's Übersoldat project unfolds. The Lopers are pretty nasty creatures - they are cyborgs whose lower body has completely been amputated and replaced with some sort of generators. Thanks to them and the undead creatures encountered in the labs, crypts, RoTW's atmosphere becomes great and creepy at times.
This is a classic shooter i.e. you shoot first then ask questions later. There are no keys to collect - just shoot everybody in your sight in order to proceed. Classic also means there are several hidden areas with lots of golden bars and chalices hidden throughout most of the levels. Finding all of them can be quite the challenge! While the game is old and has dated graphics the environments can still be appreciated. I still remember how critics marvelled at the flamethrower's effect which was one of a kind at the time.
I only have two complaints about RoTW - first, it misses a shotgun. There should at least be one weapon that is efficient during close encounters. Second, there are some levels where the emphasis is on using stealth playstyle. This is not executed very well always - sometimes you do not know what the reason was for the Germans to raise the alarm.
RoTW is a classic and should be played as such! Thanks to the great community there are means to run it on modern PCs and reminisce during its roughly 8-hour long campaign.

When I was first set loose in X: Rebirth's vast universe, right after it's release, I was convinced it was going to be amazing.  But I quickly realised that this was, in fact, a colossal supernova of bugs and ♥♥♥♥♥♥ game design that refuses to let you have any fun – and I really tried. I forgot about the game for a while, and came back to play the 2.20 update, hoping that the game would be fixed by now. I was disappointed, again.
First problem: you only get to pilot one ship, the horribly named Albion Skunk. You're able to explore it using a first-person mode, which could have been fun if there were more than two rooms to it, and if anything was even slightly interactive. The cockpit is cluttered and restrict your vision horribly, and it took me a good while to find some of the most important HUD elements, such as the speedometer. Which isn't that well done either. Eventually I found a guy that sells different cockpits, ehich there are four of. And so, I was saved from the horrors of the stock cockpit by bying the very open, combat-oriented one.
If I remember correctly EgoSoft said that there's only one ship to incease immersion and that they couldn't have made the capitalship gameplay fun while keeping the mobility realistic. Well, changeing ships has worked just fine in the other games. I would've paid extra for the ability to change into something with more than one gun. Even if it was just a frikin' shuttle.
Then there's your co-pilot, Yisha. For a character you spend the entire game with, and who's almost constantly talking, you'd think they would have hired someone with some basic acting ability to speak her lines. But while you'll eventually grow used to her awkward delivery, you'll never stop cursing how useless she is. Case in point: if you're piloting a drone, and enemies start attacking the Skunk, she'll just sit there dumbly. Couldn't you, like, move, or fight back, or something? Not to mention her, and everyone else's, bad animations and ridiculous outfits. Oh, and a boob-window on a spacesuit. Because logic.
Second problem: The voice acting. Oh god, the voice acting is absolutely horrible. It has to be mentioned multiple times. I could rate this game negative just because of it, but there's so much more. The game has a big problem with humans in genereal. On stations – which all look identical – you'll talk to NPCs, who are terrifying, slot-mouthed, dead-eyed mannequins. While space itself feels nicely alive, teeming with traffic and huge ships lumbering back and forth, the interiors feel lifeless and boring. In a nightclub I hear the ambient sound of people drinking and laughing, but it's empty except for two people standing motionless by the bar. Thankfully you don't really have to enter stations anymore, you now can do all interaction straight from your ship. But since it's done as a video conversation with the character you're speaking to, there's no escape from the animations and voice acting.
How about something positive for a change? Stations aside, Rebirth fares much better when you're in space. Ignoring some messy shadows, it's a good-looking game, with colourful nebulas, asteroids, planets and star. The combat is like jousting in space. Ships make passes at each other, firing a volley of shots when they get close and hoping some connect. Or you can use heatseeking missiles. Hit the spacebar and you can strafe, FPS-style. Hit it again to steer with the mouse. The movement feels nicely weighty.
Except that the Skunk can only mount one weapon at a time, which are all extremely underpowered compared to the fact that enemies can mount multiple ones, and have near-perfect aim. Missiles are nice, and one of the only ways to make combat work for me. The other is to fly to a station and hope the turrets kill the hostiles before you die.
Third problem: you have separate ships for trading that follow you around and have to be given orders. You couldn't, and still can't, buy any trade-goods with your own ship, everything has to be done with slow and dumb freighters that can't even fight pirates reliably, despite the 20 turrets that are mounted on them. You can't cancel an order without editing your save file, and sometimes the freighter just refuses to move, breaking the entire save and preventing the plot from progressing. It's like I'm dragging a badly-behaved toddler around a shopping centre. Thank god they've fixed most of those bugs by now, but the trading UI is still slightly confusing at times and the ships are still ridiculously dumb.
The UI... It's confusing and mostly useless.It's designed to work around a controller, on a PC-exclusive title.
There's so much done wrong with this game, even this full A4 page of text is just the beginning. No matter what happens with stability and bug-fixing patches, its poor controls, awful interface, and dull pacing ensure that X Rebirth will remain unpleasant for all but the most forgiving, die-hard space jockeys. And oh god, the voice-acting...

This game is NOT Hitman 2: Silent Assassin or Hitman (4): Blood Money... however, it is a great game in its own right.
Where the previous titles had you setting up a kill in a large sandbox like environment where you could approach from a whole bunch of angles/ideas, Hitman: Absolution (I'll refer to it as 'Abs') compartmentalizes each level into smaller parts.
What this does is make the game more directed (or forced). Pros: Story driven gameplay, Cons: You lose the feeling of suspense that one mistake could ruin your whole scheme.
Since this is also a more story driven game, it takes place basically in the United States (Chicago, and South Dakota). So if you liked going to Italy, Columbia, Russia, etc in previous games, don't get your hopes up. Moreoever, there are no levels that stand out like the ones from Blood Money (the winery/secret cocaine lab, the opera job, Mardi Gras, playboy mansion in the rockies). However, I will say that the levels are crafted with detail and care in this game.
This game has many great moments, and each level, although broken down into parts, can still be approached from multiple ways.
Where the older hitman games were pretty much mandatory stealth (due to poor-ish shooting mechanics), this game kind of ends up being the opposite.
Not only is the stealth option somewhat worse (a downgrade in many respects), I have to complement the shooting in this game. I ended up playing many levels like a Max Payne/Splinter Cell type game, mixing stealth and full out gun fights. There are so many guns that feel good, so many interesting weapons you can pick up (scissors, prosthetic arm, etc), that it is hard to ignore it. They even give you a slow down time and plan all your shots mechanic so you can take out a whole room with your pistols. I mean, it feels like you can painfully try to sneak around for an hour, only to get busted and restart, or just whip out your gun and go to town on all the guards and walk up to your target like the Terminator.
The thing that converted me was *minor spoiler* a level where a place full of nuns is massacred by a bunch of goons wearing the pantyhose masks (ala "Cobra"). And they want me to sneak around finding fuses? So I can cleanly kill their sadistic f*&# of a leader? No thanks, I think I'll take these dirty syringes and put them into this guard's eye, then take out my TMP and give them a taste of their own medicine (not a syringe pun).
I'll have to complement the game for these things. Again, they are: great story, great shooting mechanics, good stealth, interesting levels (despite being stuck in the USA), lots of variety, some degree of replayability. On its own, I can say that this game is great.
However, for a "Hitman game", it's good. Despite the PS2->PS3 general improvements (graphics, cover, shooting), Hitman Blood Money still nailed it for the "go to a cool unique place, search for the target in a large complex, plan a kill while you sneak around that large complex, execute a plan, escape".
Considering this game ends on somewhat of a cliffhanger, I hope they go back to the direction Hitman Blood Money went, while still getting the polish that all newer games receive.
TLDR: Good game in its own right, BUT I hope the sequel goes back to the STYLE that blood money went for.

"Would I recommend this game" is a difficult question. The game itself is good. It may be the weakest installment in the Bioshock franchise to date, but the weakest installment of an amazing series is still pretty great. The reason I decided to say "no" is because of the amount of crap I had to go through just to get the game to play. I have about 16 hours of playtime logged, and I'm willing to bet a good half of it was spent troubleshooting, checking to see if various fixes worked, replaying segments and sometimes entire levels... it got old, fast. For a game that's been out for so long to not have a single fix for everything is pretty inexcusable, especially one that you're expected to pay for. I ended up looking up various guides on Steam and 2K's support forum to get the game to work, uninstalling and reinstalling the game twice, uninstalling and reinstalling programs on my computer, tinkering with files, settings, and compatibility modes, even editing the .ini file itself. The most prominent issues I had were it constantly crashing shortly after starting the game (just when you get the rivet gun), on the loading screen to Siren Alley, the loading screen for Fontaine Futuristics, and near the end of the Fontaine Futuristics level. All of these required multiple attempts on my part to fix and finally finish.
On the other hand, my closest friend also has the Steam version of this game and reports not having the same problems. But for any game to give anyone this much problem, I wouldn't recommend spending your money on a roll of the dice to see whether or not it'll work (for the record, I had no problems with the original Bioshock, so don't assume that just because you played through that with no problems, you won't encounter issues here). It's truly upsetting that what could, and should, have been a pleasant, fun gaming experience turned into a frustrating nightmare, and as soon as I got to the ending, I uninstalled and washed my hands of it. Multiplayer? Other endings? Achievements? Forget about it, not worth the grief.
If you do decide to give it a shot (in which case I recommend a console version), here's what I thought, issues getting the game to run aside: like I said, it may be the weakest link in Bioshock's Great Chain, but that doesn't mean it's a total waste of time. A lot of the gameplay was simplified from the first game (such as hacking, researching, even the Tonics all being in one area instead of being in four categories with different slots you need to open), some undoubtedly for the better (it's telling hacking and researching didn't appear in Infinite) and some for the worst. There is the mechanic of carrying around Little Sisters and guarding them as they gather, akin to the ending of the first game only much faster and less frustrating (with tonics to maximize ADAM and speed up the process becoming available fairly early). However, there's up to three Little Sisters per level, and each one can gather up to twice. It's really up to you how you decides to handle them, as in the original, but the fact remains you're still going to have to throw down with a Big Daddy and you're still going to have to deal with them somehow if you want ADAM.
The main point that this game got a lot of flack for was the story. The game was, admittedly, a cash grab/attempt to keep the Bioshock name alive while Ken Levine and Take-Two/Irrational were working on Infinite, farmed out to 2K Marin. I, personally, think they did a decent enough job with what they had. The story lacked the symbolism and social commentary that made the first one so powerful, and a lot of the mystique and creepiness that Rapture had during the first outing is absent here. I won't even claim the story made total sense in the end (you pretty much need all the supplemental materials, including the dubiously canon novel Bioshock: Rapture by John Shirley, which did have input from Ken Levine, to make it close to solid). And, to quote the venerable Yahtzee, the original Bioshock's story didn't really need a direct sequel. But I wouldn't say the whole thing is a wash, either. For one thing, there's at least two moments in this game (I won't give spoilers) that I personally felt were some of the most powerful in the entire series to date.
It really seems like when they were at the drawing board, whether intentionally or not, 2K Marin got it in their head that in making a game that wasn't basically an exact rehash of the first, they needed to make it as different as possible, and ended up creating the original on Opposite Day. WHAT FOLLOWS ARE SPOILERS FOR THE FIRST GAME!
Whereas in Bioshock, you play a man that starts out with nothing and gradually finds his purpose throughout the game, in Biooshock 2, the main character has lost everything, including his identity (he's a Big Daddy), and is on a desperate journey, whether out of compulsion or genuine concern, to reclaim the one thing he had left. Whereas Andrew Ryan was a staunch objectivist who constantly extolled the value of looking out for yourself and acting in your own self-interest, the main villain of this game, Sofia Lamb, is a collectivist, with a cult built around being utterly selfless and willing to lay down your life if it would better serve mankind as a whole. Throughout the first game, you're guided by a man who seems kind, helpful, and sincere, but ultimately betrays you and reveals you were an unwitting pawn in his grand plan all along. In Bioshock 2, you're largely guided by a man who is a confessed and mostly unrepentant sleezeball, who makes no secret of the fact that he's mostly using you as a means to get him out of Rapture as well so he can profit off of the technology there. As he knows his plans hinge on you achieving your goal, he's willing to play ball. And let me add that 2K Marin deserves some major props for making a character that is so slimy, yet ultimately charming and likable.
All in all, it's a fun game. You won't miss anything for skipping it, especially now that Infinite is out, and I personally wouldn't blame you if you decided to give it a pass and not bother with this slightly subpar installment in the franchise. But with 2K Marin now in charge of the franchise as a whole, it might be worth it if you're a fan of the series just to see how they've handled it in the past. Just, for the love of little yellow duckies, play it on a console and don't waste your time, money, and possibly hours of frustration trying to play the Steam version.

Never played the PS3 ver so this is my first time beating this game. Let me get to the good things first.
+ Graphics. Just look at those sample screenshot. The entire game is pretty much like that.
+ Soundtrack. Not the best but still good. This thing depends on taste so don't vouch me on this.
+ Characters. To be honest I hate almost all of them (sans Sazh and his chocobo chick) at the beginning. I grow fond of them as the game progress.
+ Beautiful world and character design. Just look at that. Sometimes makes me just want to stop and appreciate the view in Grand Pulse.
+ UI Design. Simple and elegant.
+ Gameplay. The gameplay is more of building your party and playing with strategy in the middle of battle. I was disappointed at first, knowing that I only got to control one character in battle. With auto-battle even more. But this system gets pretty interesting from around the middle part of game where I need to actually switch out Paradigm to beat the enemy.
Then the bad things. Mostly sum to simple story, a bit bug, being kinda easy, lacking world exploration, and the fact that the sequels exists.
- Story. The story is too simple for my taste. There's struggle, but no big plot twist or any plot twist at all. Even the bad guy stay the same from the start through the end.
- Bug. Game crashes at Nautilus. I read it in forum and it seems it's a  common issue. The reason why this is not fixed after all these years goes beyond my head.
- Difficulties. Pretty easy to beat. Seriously. I only spend a few extra hours to grind out of curiosity and pretty much avoiding battle as much as I can towards the ending and I still beat the final boss in one go. And there's no option to go beyond Normal mode.
- Items are useless. Why use item when you have unlimited use of Curasa and Raise?
- Equipment. Start upgrading Lightning's first weapon and Hope and Sazh second weapon around midway in the game and use it until the end. Never touched those weapons I got later in the game. Accessory are just things I grab along the way and upgrade when I have extra money. Never really bothered about them since I still could win anyway.
- Summons are useless. I never use any of them in the battle. Never got cornered enough to use them.
- World exploration. They only have this thing in Grand Pulse. The rest of game are spent running through one way road. No tricks or watnot, just keep running straight ahead.
- Sequels. There's sequels and not in the way I hope of.
Conclusion: This game is not the best, but still pretty good and I didn't regret buying this at all. Recommending to grab this during sales or when you have extra money and in need of something to play. 7/10

seta r_mode "-1"
seta r_fullscreen "1"
seta r_customwidth "1920"
seta r_customheight "1080"
seta r_customaspect "2"

This game isn't as bad as they say, it's even almost acceptable, but it doesn't deserve to be named as "Final Fantasy". Its graphics are very good, and it has an acceptable soundtrack, although the later can result repetitive at times and isn't as good for a Final Fantasy title. The story is very confusing and it's just vomited at you, you're just vomited lots of information which is never explained, I had very serious trouble understanding what was going on for about the first half of the game. It's so linear you can hardly get lost, though. I've played it on Intel HD Graphics, 3.2 GHz CPU and 4 GB RAM. I haven't had any important FPS drops but I had a crash during the first cutscene on chapter 8. In order to get past the crash, simply play in windowed mode. Fortunately, all cutscenes are skippable if you pause the game first.
The battle system forces you to abuse potions until you're allowed (or rather, forced) to use "formations". Potions are so underpowered, as they only heal 99 fixed HP, while phoenix downs are so overpowered, they heal over 50% of your HP, making death often preferable to healing, which is messed up. You can only control your party leader and if they die, it's game over. Running away has been completely deleted in this game, so it's either win or lose. "Formations" consist of changing your characters' roles in battle, and it's the only strategy battles involve since the only other thing you have to do is spam autobattle. This game consists of excessive grinding once you reach the end of chapter 6, which is annoying and desperating. What makes it even worse is sometimes you can't come back and grind, so make sure to have multiple save files.
To finish, the final boss is almost unbeatable. Not only does it have insane HP, but it has attacks which instantly kill your party leader (game over), apply stop on your whole party, or apply "useless" on your whole party, not to mention poisonga, and it casts doom on your party leader once its HP hits 50% (Doom cannot be removed) The best from this game: its graphics and the fact that you (almost) can't get lost. The worst from this game: its grinding and the final boss' deathly attacks, not allowing you to beat the game.
if you are a hard working individual like me looking for a competitive game this is the game for you. Short burst of andrenaline and fun.

One of the best RTS 4X strategy games out there.
This game is about pure survival, you will try to use whatever tool necessary to make sure your empire sees another day.
It offers the four mighty Xs, Exploring the darkest corners of the solar systems or entire sectors. Expanding your empire by colonizing all kinds of different planets, asteroids and stations. Gathering basic resources which you need for your empire's growth and most importantly eliminating rival opponents in both single or multiplayer matches.
One of the greatest features of this game is actually the option to zoom in onto even the smallest objects in the space. Therefore you can enjoy some really beautiful sights of awesome ship and building models and space battles.
You can take control over large amount of ships which you can even asign into custom fleets to ease issuing commands.
The game's soundtracks are one of the best I've listened to while playing any kind of strategy games, simply marvelous.
Both single player and multiplayer gameplay is really smooth and solid. All the base game races are surprisingly well balanced. Every race has its pros and cons, but they share a kind of a basic setup from where the different specializations start off. What really surprised me about this game is that you can actually host a multiplayer match on a public IP with an access to your router's port-forwarding rather than crating LAN or Official lobbies.
There are few things that actually dissapoint me about this game.
One of them is the lack of any sort of story based missions or a campaign, which is really a shame, because the littly backstory of this game is really interesting and is surely worth pointing out.
The other, but not the last thing is about the not very efficient AI difficulty levels.
Using increased income bonuses and faster research as a buff for higher difficulty AI is in my opinion wrong move and it is nearly impossible to defeat highest difficulty AI in a regular match just on your own, without anyone else to balance the enormous pressure on, because the enemy's economy overcomes you in just few minutes into the game.
Other great thing worth pointing out is the support for mods. There are plenty of awesome mods out there, which can really spice up the gameplay of the base game or add an entire new experience with something new, using conversions.
As of the DLCs, If you find yourself enjoying this game at first, and you kinda get into it I certainly recommend adding both of them into your game as each of them adds some minor things and tweaks that can really improve the overall gameplay experience of every match you play.
I've played this game for more than a thousand hours in total off-steam and I enjoy every battle I manage to win or lose decisively or just by a pure luck. SoaSER is love, SoaSER is life.
Without anything more to say, I would rate this game by 9/10 for how awesome it is.

Unfortunately, I'm not recommending "Bioshock Remastered."  In a nutshell, it's tedious and buggy.
In more detail, apparently, I'm one of the lucky ones who didn't suffer  through the bad graphical defects and crashing of the game.  In my case, I had only one crash (at the first Gene Bank in the game) and no graphical issues at all.  So for me, that was fine.  The thing that put the game on the border of recommend/not-recommend was the tediousness.  There's a boat-load of things (vending machines, locks, security cameras, security bots, turrets, safes, U-Invent machines) that we should hack and it just breaks up the flow of the game (yes, we can use auto-hack tools, but we can only carry 5 of those).  Similarly, there are tons of containers of various types to open (not necessarily bad) and an awful lot of them are totally empty.  Heck, there are toilets to flush and sinks to use -- all for no purpose -- they never do anything unexpected.  Along with that is how we get the backstory:  the audio logs.  All 122 of them.  There's got to be a better way than ONE HUNDRED AND TWENTY TWO audio logs.  But, the final thing that pushed the game over into not-recommend territory is the bugginess of the Achievements.  After about 33 hours of tedious, detailed play trying to get various Achievements, the game refused to give me three of them that I had actually finished.  In one case, once I progressed to the Medical Pavilion in a New Game Plus mode, one of them just popped up by itself.  But, I'm still missing two (and possibly three) others.
So, I'm sorry to say I'm not recommending the game.

Think of a cross between the original Elite, or perhaps Frontier (if you're old enough to remember them) coupled with an amped-up version of the combat from Sword of the Stars 1 and you've pretty much got the barebones of Rebel Galaxy.  Throw in a distinctly wild-West, frontier ambience driven by the look of the ships (most definitely in the Solo-esque tradition of "she may not look like much, but she's got it where it counts") and the pumping country-rock backing track and you're close to what Rebel Galaxy is all about.
The biggest single bone of contention people seem to have with this game is that it's a space sim that doesn't allow movement in any axis.  For me, this really isn't an issue.  The combat is deliberately designed with an emphasis on broadside-heavy battles.  This simply wouldn't work well across 3 axes.  As I mentioned at the top, combat in this is something akin to Sword of the Stars 1 on steroids - and for me it works beautifully.
I would imagine that the greatest strength of this game could potentially be its greatest weakness: much like the original Elite, there isn't really a great deal of hand-holding; yes, there are storyline-driven missions to follow, but equally you're free to indulge in any of the time-honoured space-game traditions of trading, bounty-hunting or piracy.  From what I can make out, most players (myself included) seem to eschew the story and focus on doing our own thing.
In terms of negatives; well, there is undeniably a 'grind' aspect as you're generally striving to get the next best ship or increase your reputation with somebody but as yet I haven't found this to be a problem - it's a mechanic that is always likely to be present in games of this ilk, as Elite: Dangerous proves.
All in all, I think this is a brilliant, absorbing game that's an absolute steal at the price.  It puts many AAA titles to shame, especially, as if I've heard, the development team is only two strong!
9/10.  Wholeheartedly recommended.

Rebel Galaxy is a good-looking and fun space action game with a kickass soundtrack. It plays more of an arcade game rather than a space sim so for those looking for the latter might want to look somewhere else. What this game has is a procedurally-generated, sandbox solar systems set on a 2D plane where the player can explore right from the start.
For starters, the player's ship can't roll, pitch, or yaw (sorry, no
manuevers here) - only forward movement, and left/right turns. This is because the game’s combat is designed around the broadside naval engagements similar to
. Basically, you line up your ship (think of it as a space boat) against the enemy ship for a firing solution, and then unload your armaments to see some fireworks. It might sound easy but it has its share of tactical positioning and maneuvering - each side of your ship (front, rear, port, and starboard) has a hull and shield rating. After you eat through a ship’s shield face, you start hitting its hull to do some serious damage. You can spin that damaged side out of the line of fire to regenerate your shields and retaliate or simply retreat and fight another day.
The game has a decent selection of weaponry, ships, and ship upgrades. You can also choose to align with different factions but sadly, they have no personalities to speak of outside of the nicely animated talking avatars they have.
There is a main quest you can follow, or ignore it and set out in any direction you want and be a trader, a miner, a bounty hunter, or space pirate. You can get missions from space stations that can earn you currency to buy ships/weapons/ship upgrades, as well as alignment points to factions. The said missions can get pretty repetitive after a while, but the gloriously huge space battles keep me coming back for more.

Exploration in this game is fun and is rarely dull. It has the same relaxing feel as doing cross country delivery jobs in
. There are asteroid fields, floating space junk from the ruins of some old battle (which may contain some sweet loot and military grade weaponry), nebulae of different swirling colors, planets, moons, and of course, stars. It will take a few minutes to fly from point A to point B, but there’s usually some unidentified signal, a distress call, or just a random fleet of space bandits to keep things interesting.
The game’s soundtrack is really good. It exudes the same vibe as
with its guitar heavy tracks with twangs. The devs also included the most phenomenal custom music support I have ever seen in a game. There’s nothing like
from
kicking in as I enter combat. I have Cage the Elephant, Clutch, Johnny Cash, Darren Korb (Bastion OST), Queens of the Stone Age, Yoko Kanno (Cowboy Bebop), Vitaminless (Cowboy Bebop), and Bear McCreary (Battlestar Galactica) on my custom playlist. You can sort and assign them as combat, idle, or title music. Your custom music can also be merged with the game soundtrack for more variety.
I definitely recommend this game.

One of the best war-themed games one can buy, This War of Mine incorporates numerous risk-reward mechanics that adds an deep level of immersion to the game; damn near every action you make affects EVERYONE, and I mean EVERYONE. Beyond the obvious pros and cons of who's staying in your shelter, one must heavily weigh the priority and necessity of they need to get set up from deciding to upgrade your metal workshop to make your own weapons and equipment to deciding to upgrade your home workshop to make your shelter more secure and self-sustainable.
Even when you think you're doing great at the moment, the game throws various curveballs to completely shift your priorities such as bands of looters forcing you to constantly guard your shelter and the brief but severe winter weather that forces you to heat your shelter constantly or succumb to illness. When you go out to scavenge at certain locations, you may be presented with various challenges that can affect the morale of your fellow survivors i.e. assisting distraught civilians, using equipment to access better supplies, or dealing with hostile NPCs.
Overall, the game does an excellent job of setting the mood of a war-torn madhouse that...frowns upon the adrenaline rush that is war, to say the least. You'll rarely have situations where you aren't forced to cutback somewhere and maintain an all-time high moral standing; you're gonna have to do what you must to survive, of course. Just keep an eye out for your survivors...you don't want them to mentally succumb to the hell they're in.

I used to say this port was "Serviceable at best" but recently I've noticed something and found a few changes in its performance that jarred me so much I felt the need to recommend it in a review.
First off, the build I've used - to put some things later in the review in perspective:
GeDoSaTo, a common graphics injector, has a plugin for the game, but I'll get into that later.
On release, this port forced 720p, had no AA or shadow options, but unlike consoles, raised the framerate cap to 60FPS (Which does the game loads of justice, honestly).
They HAVE fixed this. Resolutions up to 4K are supported, AA (Likely FXAA) up to 16X, and shadows up to 8192p are now supported. Still capped at 60, but that's alright.
What this port on its own has no fix for currently are control rebinds, and 2D GUI components being upscaled from 720p without any anisotropy - they all scale and get a bit pixelated in the process, but this is acceptable in my humble opinion.
Before the evening I wrote this review, I found that the game's performance was horrid (30 to 40 FPS avg with 2X AA and 512x512 shadows) for absolutely no reason, and on top of this, it had this remarkably annoying stutter every second or two, to the point I flat-out could not play.
I tried playing with GeDoSaTo, which allows higher resolutions, supposedly a higher framerate cap, and has anisotropy for the GUI. The result of this was that the stutter was gone, and I got 60+ FPS in the overworld, but anytime a 2D GUI component would display my framerate would tank to mid-30's, with or without anisotropy. I found this bizarre.
But a friend told me they bought the port today and had no issue - stutter, performance, everything was okay, default. So I was confounded. I tested it tonight and thought "Okay, maybe they're using default settings". Went windowed, 720p, 1024p shadows and 2X AA, got 60FPS and no stutter. I figured it made enough sense.
Then I tried 1080p, fullscreen, 2048p shadows, and 4X AA, just to test waters and see how that scaled, and had no issue whatsoever.
"Alright then", I said. "Let's crank it." 1440p, 8192p shadows, 16X AA, loaded an endgame save to ensure I had more than enough nonsense onscreen to really bench it.
60FPS, no drop, at  all.
Only difference between any other time and now is perhaps a few months (With no updates to the game on Steam!) and now I'm using a controller.
10/10, forgot plugging in a controller rewrites DirectX code, overclocks, nitrogen-cools and plutonium powers all of your PC components.
Game itself is pretty rough around the edges - the actual good, explorative bit with an overworld and missions and lots of neat mechanics is like 20 to 30 hours in, buckle up. Writing is lacklustre, but the music and gameplay are nice. I've played it three times, so I guess I like it.

Unfortunately, I'm not recommending "Bioshock Remastered."  In a nutshell, it's tedious and buggy.
In more detail, apparently, I'm one of the lucky ones who didn't suffer  through the bad graphical defects and crashing of the game.  In my case, I had only one crash (at the first Gene Bank in the game) and no graphical issues at all.  So for me, that was fine.  The thing that put the game on the border of recommend/not-recommend was the tediousness.  There's a boat-load of things (vending machines, locks, security cameras, security bots, turrets, safes, U-Invent machines) that we should hack and it just breaks up the flow of the game (yes, we can use auto-hack tools, but we can only carry 5 of those).  Similarly, there are tons of containers of various types to open (not necessarily bad) and an awful lot of them are totally empty.  Heck, there are toilets to flush and sinks to use -- all for no purpose -- they never do anything unexpected.  Along with that is how we get the backstory:  the audio logs.  All 122 of them.  There's got to be a better way than ONE HUNDRED AND TWENTY TWO audio logs.  But, the final thing that pushed the game over into not-recommend territory is the bugginess of the Achievements.  After about 33 hours of tedious, detailed play trying to get various Achievements, the game refused to give me three of them that I had actually finished.  In one case, once I progressed to the Medical Pavilion in a New Game Plus mode, one of them just popped up by itself.  But, I'm still missing two (and possibly three) others.
So, I'm sorry to say I'm not recommending the game.

So what's Hatred about, I hear a lot of people asking. What's with the hype? Does it hold up?
Well, no. Not really,
. But I'll explain why.
So you're playing the guy, humorously named
by some Steam Community forum users, in whom is just.. Fed up by Humanity and wants to "cleanse" the world of it, before cleansing himself.
And that's really it. That's all you need to know.
Think of the game's story as Unreal Tournament 1-3, Quake 1-3, Doom, Postal 1 or GTA I - II. You kill because you want to kill. Nothing else.
But, instead of monsters or demons, as in Doom for example, in Hatred, you kill cops and pedestrians.
Just like in Postal 1 and every GTA installment. Nothing extra ordinary here.
Mr. Nod is *p e s s e d* off, and starts his killing spree.
Hatred is your average run-off-the-mill twin-stick shooter.
You mow down pedestrians and innocent civilians with various weaponary.
Bazookas, flamethrowers, rifles, shotguns, pistols and the like. Even stunning grenades, molotov's and HE grenades.
You can even drive around in cars if you like, but I'll get to that in a bit.
On your holy crusade of killing, you come across cops, SWAT teams and military. Even civilians are able to take weapons laying on the ground from fallen law-enforcers to defend themselves. Some of them even have them equipped in their homes.
Which leads me to a hardpoint..
Hatred is notoriously difficult at times. Even pretty unfair, which makes some people FUBAR RQ
. I were close at some points, to go said FUBAR RQ.
Hatred has three difficult settings. Easy, Hard and Extreme.
Hard would be considered Normal in this occasion, right? But no. It's actually pretty hard. It's even a challenge for me at Easy. At least at later levels.
So the unfair bit is... The levels are long, there's many civ's to kill and if you get killed, you restart the whole level. Well.. Kinda.
The game has Respawn tokens. At most maps, taking out some points (shown as icons on your mini-radar-thing) earns you one Respawn token. Most maps has three at max.
Imagine getting to a point deep into a level. Imagine you almost feel it's at it's end. You've used all your respawn tokens up, and you can't get any more. And then.. You get killed by a rain of bullets (which happens a LOT in the later levels because of the amount of law-enforcers around you) or getting run over (in which kills you instantly). Yeah.. FUBAR RQ.
Fear not, though, because Mr. Nod Emportent has the ability to regenerate health by the help of executions. Either a single shot to the head will be showed, or if the engine thinks there's nothing going on, it lets you in on a mini-cutscene-execution. Which can be tiring and annoying after some time.
Good thing there's options for that, though!
What you get for your money is a GTA-Slash-Saints-Row-Killing-Spree-Only-Edition. With a twist, I guess.
Hopefully mod support will add some much needed spice to this game.
Lastly, to the Devs:
Rating: 7/10,

Magic duels is a really good card game because it is based on the paper sets which is designed with amazing care and has been improved over the years. It has a decent portion of the paper cards, but only of the newest sets of 2015.
The magic rules are well implemented, I did not witness many gameplay bugs.
The game is free to play.
You begin with tutorials quests for each color, doing a bit of storytelling and explaining how the game works, and giving you the currency of the game as a reward.
You are also given the standard starters decks of each color and you can build your deck entirely as you desire between 60 and 100 cards. It has additionnal limitations from the paper game on deckbuilding, the limit of 4 times the same card has been deviated to further reduces the amount of copies of rare cards you are allowed to put in the deck. For example you will be limited to 2 copies of legendary creatures.
Winning matches in versus will earn you the game currency against Ai (5-15g) or human (20g) with a limit of 200g per day. Then you can buy boosters for 150g. Boosters will not give you duplicates of a card once you have reached the maximum amount of copies you can fit in a deck. There is no trading cards available. So you will be able to get 6 new cards every day for free as long as you can build a decent deck. You can check magic forums like nogoblinsallowed to get ideas if you are new to this. You will be able to build some solid decks with the basic offered cards.
You can also buy the game currency with real money to unlock a lot of boosters immediately.
gameplay problematic:
The starter decks are extremely limited, you will lose a lot of matchups against human oponents that have farmed the game from the start or that have purchased the booster, wich means that you will need to grind a lot of matches to be able to get to your 150g daily gold to buy a booster, which gets quickly dull.
For example the toughest green creature is a vanilla 6/7 for 7 lands, which sucks for a green creature, and especially when a wealthy player will face you with a 6/6, renown 6, for 5 lands, nuke your board with chandra's ignition, and can drop gaia's revenge a bit further down the road.
You better play agressive or midrange, because ramp is much better with booster cards.
Now the painful part:
Magic games have been around for a while, and the matchmaking is still painfull to go through, it is long and buggy. In 2v2 mode you need to reset the match  2/3 because one player was not connected properly and was replaced by AI. That is especially bad compared to the newcommer of the genre Heartstone. And that hurts a lot more when you know that your deck could be much better and you are not that confident in the actual fight that will happen.
The passing of turns and interupt mecanisms forced in the game add a lot of downtime compared to paper magic.
Don't get me wrong, the game is a lot of fun, you can use it to learn how to play magic and get a good idea how to build decks, staregy and tactics, for free. And you can also play it anytime, anywhere as long as you are connected.
But I'd rather recommend playing paper magic with your local community if you live in a city, or buy the boosters ASAP to get you to the fun decks adn spare you the painful grind.
So actually the game is more around 32€ if you want to enjoy it.

Well. While I loved the concept, admired the art style and was looking forward to the script (I bloody love Infernal War) this is leaving me cold. It's clunky, unresponsive, badly written, buggy and has all the gravitas of an Amiga PD game from 1992. The art style leaves much of the game obscured and difficult to make out, occasionally The Antagonist seems to forget what grenades are and the words uttered after the (quickly repetitive and dull) executions are laughable, if never quite as bad as, say, Spill The Dirty Blood Of Jesus.
I *do* recommend this game, as I'll likely play a lot more (I'm hoping for some patches and performance improvements) and in my own brief correspondence with the team responsible they seem like decent guys, even if they hadn't heard any Deathspell Omega.
Put quite simply, if you're 14, have greasy hair and think Cannibal Corpse are the greatest death metal band in the world, this is likely to be your favourite game. For the rest of us, it's a broken but daft mess that will raise a chuckle in the same way a Troma movie or Rompeprop CD will. Take it for what it is, don't expect to be hugely impressed, and have fun!
Oh, and for a twin-stick shooter it's *abysmal* to play with a controller, which is unforgivable. I'll personally fight the next person who compares this favourably with Robotron...

I've been playing this game since it came out and I even invested around $50 in real money for the booster packs, but I am done with this game.  It has both serious bugs and a serious lack of features seen in prior games that make it more frustrating to play than fun.  As far as bugs go, there are two major flaws that are ruining the game for me, both of which are related to Two Headed Giant play.  First is that trying to invite a friend to play with you works less than half the time - you either get a connection timeout error, or the game ends up sticking your friend on the opposing team!  The second bug issue is that whenever you are playing against random opponents and they quit/concede the game because they are losing, the game will usually hang when attempting to let the AI take over, and you are forced to concede the game and take a loss - this happens in about 35% of the games I play.
As far as lacking features - there are two huge ones missing.  First is an in-game chat system.  It is a huge pain to play Two Headed Giant when you cannot strategize with your partner.  This problem would be "resolved" if you could invite friends to play with you and chatted through the Steam app, but since that rarely works you are left with no chat options.  The second major lacking feature is that you cannot choose the lands you want to use when playing spells.  This is a huge problem.  You might have enough land cards to play two spells in your hand if you tap mana in the right combo.  But the game will auto-choose for you and do so in the wrong order and you end up only being able to cast one spell.  This makes or breaks games all the time.
Magic 2014 worked flawlessly and had these missing features.  I don't know how WotC screwed up this version so badly but they did.  I am uninstalling and they will not be getting any more money from me.

Magic with a Hearthstone UI, minus the charm and the part where the actual gameplay is suited to such a UI. It may be useful for teaching someone the basics of Magic, but for veterans it's probably not worth the download time.
Default settings will pick the damage distribution for you when you block with multiple creatures, and
. It's horrible, especially in story mode decks that absolutely require doing this to play effectively (and the AI does it even if you can't).
This might be because of the (on by default) Auto Resolution setting, which is described as "Automatically resolve effects of many spells and abilities". I guess combat damage is a "spell or ability" now.
The short countdown timer on phases is terrible. You'll either be forced to wait around on phases you can't do anything on, or you'll be suddenly shoved off to the next phase because you didn't mash the "pause timer" button in the 5 seconds or so from when the phase started. Trying to squeeze in an instant or ability in the opponent's End Phase? Nope, it's your main phase now! Stop looking at your cards for so long, sheesh.
Gameplay issues aside, the only way to grow your collection beyond the starter set is through random boosters (there's just one kind of booster in the entire game; the "Store" just lets you buy 1 pack, 2 packs, 4 packs, etc...) and you can't really make a decent deck in most of the deck wizard archetypes with the starting collection they give you.
It can be fun to dabble in the Story mode for solo play with prebuilt decks (when the terrible phase progression system doesn't cost you the match), but for actual deckbuilding and multiplayer, just pick up Magic The Gathering Online. It's not pretty and it's a little less streamlined, but it's a faithful reproduction of every aspect of the physical card game and gives you full control over your play. You can buy cards from WotC's shop in all the same packs/decks as the physical editions, or just trade / buy individually from resellers if you know the excact cards you want, build decks in Standard, Extended, or any other format, play normally, 2 headed giant, etc, participate in the same sorts of events/tournaments as physical MTG, literally everything except single-player against AI. So here it is-my Rebel Galaxy review. Full disclosure-I'm friends with the devs and got an advanced copy of the game. That said I've done my best to be impartial.My Tl'dr opinion? I  love it and was well over 100 hours in before I took a break from it. This is so many things about space games I love rolled into one.
The Setting.
The game goes for a Firefly/Wing Commander:Privateer/Freelancer vibe. The solar systems in this game are on the wrong side of the galactic tracks and haven't had a bath in aeons. They're rude, crude and filled with rocks and junk. Rebel Galaxy features an interesting cast of characters. It's one of the games unfortunate downsides that you never really get to know any of them very well. It's loaded with the kind of wink/nudge humor you'd find in TV series like Farscape or Firefly-for example one of the commodities you can trade is called 'Narco-cola' and it is just that. Powerful narcotics in the form of carbonated beverage. If you're a fan of stuff like Hitchhikers Guide to the Galaxy you'll appreciate the humor.
The Story:
Length 30-40 hours (20 if you're an old hand at these kind of games).
It ain't deep but it gets the job done. Like I wrote above the characters all have interesting personalities but those personalities are shallow and you won't interact with any of them very much. It's a shame because they are just interesting enough where I wanted to get to know them more. By the time I got past the 'Hello, nice to meet you, may I help you kill this troup of troublemakers?' bits their role in the story was done.
This becomes even more disappointing by the end of the story. It's a great lead up but the end is a bit of a letdown. I'll give DDGames credit-despite my not liking how it ended I've played through it numerous times now.
The Sound:
If you're into down and dirty southern-fried blues rock this will be right up your alley. It helps add a lot to the atmosphere and makes you feel like every space station bar serves oil pan shots and barbed wire biscuits. The sound effects are another matter entirely-voiceovers can get a bit repetitive to the point of tediousness at times. Some of the audio isn't mixed well-radio chatter clips/distorts a lot and I don't recommend you use expensive speakers or a subwoofer if you plan on blasting this.
Voice acting isn't bad for an indie game. This is one of the things that lends a lot of personality to the characters. It was done by the devs themselves (with the help of the always amazing Lani Minella). I dare say it's better than in most Bethesda games I've played. Even though Travis does numerous voices they sound different enough where it's not that much of a drawback.
Ships:
There are 21 playable ships you're able to buy throughout the game. Some of these require money and some require you to build a positive reputation with various factions (pirates, merchants guild etc). Each ship is upgradable with a wide variety of weapons and components. Lasers, missiles, shields, hulls-you can customize your ship to beef them up and match them to your playing style. This wide variety and manner of acquiring and upgrading ships means there's a lot of replay to be squeezed out of the game.
I did find it unfortunate that you're not able to access all ships. Certain ships belonging to certain races seem to be inaccessible which is a real downer in a game that revolves around the very notion of collecting every ship you happen to come across.
Combat:
Combat takes place on a 2-D plane. That means it's more like naval combat in games like Assassin's Creed:Black Flag or Sid Meiers Pirates (the 2004 edition) or the auto combat in Mad Max. Thanks to the variety of components and weapons in game no matter what your playstyle is you can adapt your craft to it. Upgrading certain components helps with your survivability. You can also hire a merc to accompany you which is always a smart move as some of them are extremely lethal. The one down side of using a merc is that you can't upgrade their weapons or ships.
It would have been cool to see something closer to the pets in Torchlight or Companions in Diablo III-especially considering all the weaponry that drops from capital ships. Being able to give my mercs better gear early on would have helped a lot as the best mercs aren't available until late in the game.
The main downside to combat is that difficulty seems to be very imbalanced at the moment. It's a lot of fun don't get me wrong but some missions say they're difficult when they're not and vice versa. It's also pretty spinny. Enemies run but they never run -that- fast or far which  means there will be times when you spend  battles going in circles. That said the effects are glorious and when combat is good it's really, really good.
The other stuff:
Mining-It's a pretty zen-like experience. Cruise up to some rocks, scan them then go up to the ones full of ore. You can buy a fault tracker early on that paints red circles on asteroids that have more than one piece of ore in them. Blow it up that way and you get multiple ores. It's a pretty relaxing experience unfortunately unless you're very good at the market stuff, explore a LOT and very patient you won't be making a ton of credits mining.
Commodities: Stations sell commodities. Buy low/sell high type stuff. Different stations have different events that effect the rest of that systems economies. You can also read the in station news boards or ask the bartenders/merchants for info.
Hackable transponders that give tasty info, random cargo containers that contain nice loot (sort of like the outer space version of barrells in an rpg) and rescue missions aplenty are some of the other bits of content you'll find in this game.
SUMMARY:
Rebel Galaxy is a fun, arcadey naval-game-in-space that provides some of the trappings of a space-sim while ditching most of the complexity and time-investment required of more traditional space sims like EVE Online or Elite:Dangerous. It's great for drop in and play for a half hour or so sessions. If you're the kind of person who spends hours playing space games just for the sake of the atmosphere and love blowing stuff up with enough lights to build a discotechque this will scratch that itch for at least a little while. Personally I'm 100 hours in and haven't gotten bored yet.
Those looking for a deeply engaging story you're not going to find one but the characters have tons of personality and give the setting a very lived in feel-just be ready for the ending to be a bit of a let down. Those into trading should be happy though the game feels like it needs a bit of tweaking since not all professions feel viable. The accent is on combat so expect to blow up a lot of ships if you're looking to be one of the galaxy's richest space truckers.
Despite its flaws this is an impressive first game from Double Damage Games. The developers put a lot of heart into this and it shows. This would have been a solid deal even at $30 but at $20 it's way more than worth it.

Let me preface by saying X Rebirth is quite possibly the most amazing-looking space game of all time. My complaints run the gamut, but graphics are not among them.* X Rebirth's developers built on a massive scale appropriate for space -- this isn't a space sim where the universe feels small, or where stations are half-hearted efforts to give players a place to dock their ships. The stations in X Rebirth are glorious affairs, with Blade Runner-esque lights and signs, intricate manufacturing modules where you can see machinery sculpting products from raw materials, nooks and crannies to hide your ship from hostile forces, and often jaw-dropping detail -- when you do a slow fly-by around space farming stations, for instance, you can see every leaf of the vegetation growing beneath massive domes, and machines strafing those spacegardens with water jets.
Likewise, the devs clearly paid attention to planetary scale. When you're in orbit around a planet, the planet should be almost incomprehensibly massive. It should dominate your field of view. And in this game it does, providing an amazing backdrop for pitched battles and ambushes. The designers also did a fantastic job of increasing visual immersion with the way the Albion Skunk's cockpit is rendered -- the ambient light in the cockpit changes with the light source from outside. That means if you're headed toward a station close to a star, your cockpit is bathed in vivid yellows. If you're in deep space, the cockpit's hues are subdued.
Still, I can't recommend X Rebirth. Lots of people have reported problems with framerate, even on high-end systems. This has been acknowledged by the developer. Personally I have not had that problem, but the problem is, it's nearly impossible to tell if the game will run appropriately until you install it on your own machine. Secondly, there is merit to the complaints about inscrutable menu systems and unnecessarily complex in-game tasks. Getting your fleet's ships to dock, refuel, and take on cargo can be a nightmare, and the difficulty is apparently arbitrary. Sometimes it works flawlessly, sometimes you're waiting an hour until you fly in to inspect the problem yourself and see that, for some reason, drones are not off-loading cargo.
Likewise, there's a difference between hand-holding and obscuring features beneath menu layers that make it difficult for players to get their bearings, nevermind figure out how certain tasks are accomplished. This is a game that can't be played without an open web browser to help get through frustratingly, needlessly complicated tasks. You'll also need the web browser for figuring out how to progress, because the game doesn't always make it clear if you're prepared for certain zones or missions.
Conclusion: Save your money. If X Rebirth plunges to $4.99 or $9.99 in some future Summer Sale or flash sale, it's worth picking up just for the joy of exploring the game's systems and starbases. And maybe, after the better part of two years, the game will be smoothed out by then. We'll have to wait and see.
* Caveat to praising the graphics: The space station interiors are pretty awful. All of them are nearly identical in decor and visual style, if not layout. It makes little sense that a civilization cut off from the rest of humanity would build stations exactly like everyone else, but there you have it. Let me get this out of the way that I am a long time fan of the series. That to you means either of 2 things: 1. That I mindlessly support it as a fanboy. To which I'd respond: No, there are a handful of them that i don't like. or 2. That I am one of these who believe anything done after 6 or 9 is bad. No, my favorites are the most popular ones: 7 and 10.
So, now that you have enough material to judge me, let me say: This is a good game. Yes it is a tunnel simulator. There is not much choice or moving around in an open world. But I never understand why those things are important. I don't see much value in replayability in this kind of game so the only thing choice can bring for me is emotional involvement. I'd prefer that to be done through dramatic art skills known to us since ancient Greece rather than shalow choices like a. kill him b. befriend him. And for open world I go out. It is just as boring but far more diverse in graphics and sound.
The game is a bit hard to relate to. My guess is because Lightning, main character, although appealing as a hero, has not been developed quite well. She stays a bit machine-like throughout.
Gameplay? It's meh. Not the best of the series and not the worse. Music? Not Uematsu but hardly any worse than rest of he game. Story? meh too. No big twist. You get involved in it but you won't remember its details a couple of years later like you would do for 7 through 12. Graphics? Absolutely fantastic. Characters have the beauty of Japanese game characters. They are not cartoonish anymore but they are not realistic humans. The balance should have been hard to get right and I think they did get it right. Animations are not that good but still good.
Recommend it? If you like the genre and you are not really obsessed with moving around freely in the world or making choices that create 7 different game endings, yes. If you want those things, move along.
