I'll preface this by saying that my negative recommendation is conditional: if you strongly enjoy Peter Jackson's film version of The Lord of the Rings, and your computer doesn't use an ATI video card, and the game is on sale, then you should buy it.  It will be worth your while to play through it at least once.
This game gets some things right.  The story and voice work are good.  The art design feels a bit over-wrought and generic at times, but for the most part it does a good job of maintaining the feel of the Jackson films.  It's also clear that the developers were careful to ensure that the game's events do not contradict Tolkien's work.  These aspects of the game are all much-appreciated.
Where the game fails for me is the actual "game" part of the game.  War in the North feels as though it was developed by people who have a general idea of what a hack-and-slash game is, but don't understand any of the nuances required to make a GOOD hack-and-slash game.
For one, dodge-rolling: does it have invulnerability-frames, or does it not?  I'm honestly not sure because it seemed like even odds whether it would allow me to actually evade an attack.
For another, stun-locking: it often feels as though every hit sustained by the player causes you to be staggered.  Scoring hits on enemies, however, rarely ever interrupts their actions.  Some late-game enemies combine flurry attacks and staggering in such a way that you can't really fight back.
Hitboxes and hurtboxes: this game has some of the sloppiest hitboxes and hurtboxes I've seen (essentially, invisible regions in and around character models which determine whether or not attacks connect).  Even when playing as the game host, I frequently found myself taking damage from hammer strikes and sword strokes that very visibly missed my character model by several feet.
Lack of impact: this one isn't as severe as the above problems, but the combat lacks any sense of weight when attacks connect.  When fighting enemies that don't stagger you every other hit, the only indication you have that you've been hit is a sudden reduction of your health bar.  It took me a moment to realize why it felt this way, and I eventually realized that the game doesn't have hit-frames (I think that's what they're called).  Dragon's Dogma (a significantly better polished hack-and-slash experience) demonstrates this pretty well: when an attack connects in DD, it's often accompanied by your character's animation hanging for an extra frame or two at the instant of impact.  It gives the impression of your weapon colliding with the enemy (or the enemy's weapon colliding with you!).
If the gameplay exhibited the same high production values as the art design and voice work, then giving this a thumbs-up would be a no-brainer.  Unfortunately, War in the North's gameplay ends up being the worst thing about the game.

But I still think this game is going to get better and better with time.
Issue 1. Barely any communication for the company making it. It would be nice to know when a new set is coming out or maybe even a note that they are working on things like bugs.
Issue 2. No reason to replay the story mode, ever. I get that if they gave full points then some one could just do a battle over and over on one they found easy and get easy coins. (Not counting the 20 from first online battle win or whatever you get from daily quests) Ocassionally you will see a community quest that calls for a certain story mode mission to be beat by the community a certain amount of time. Issue 4. I have played all the previous games and all those cool modes. I hope that one day they will make more then just multiplayer two headed giant. I am not huge on online play. Why not some of the cool modes from previous games such as planeswalker or arch enemy. I know that this stuff takes time to program and maybe they will have it in the future, but its not as if the company is ready to hint at any developments.
I still love the game though cause I am a Magic junkie. I just hope they get stuff smoothed out in time before the less patient half of the people playing give up on it.

BioShock 2 lends very few innovations to its predecessor. Wielding a plasmid and a weapon at the same time is a welcome change, but you won't find too many new plasmids here. The drill you receive is super fun to use, but unfortunately burns fuel (yes, you need fuel) rather quickly. You will find yourself in tight situations - be prepared.
As far as the story goes, there isn't much difference between this and the original. You'll rescue or harvest little sisters and the ending will be influenced.
The game doesn't really have anything poignant going for it until the very end, with a *very* interesting mechanic that could have been more thoroughly used. Overall, the game is mediocre compared to the original, and rubbish compared to Infinite. But you'll still find some play value in it, and those who have played Infinite will notice certain... commonalities.
In short, buy it if you are lore-hungry or an achievement-hunter. But be warned: if you've played Infinite already, you probably won't want to play this past the first 20 or so minutes.

Fantastic game, loved it on Xbox and on PC even more. Like the Saga games, the mechanics are unique and poorly explained or not at all, and considerably more complex than a standard JRPG like Final Fantasy or Tales. But once you get to grips with it all, it's SO satisfying.
It provides a sigificant challenge, in fact, if you don't understand the mechanics and play it like many people tend to play a regular JRPG  - i.e. lots of grinding - then it can become much more difficult, possibly overwhelmingly so. Essentially this is an ANTI-grind JRPG, but actually you can grind if you wish, you just have to do it in the right way.
Thankfully there are a number of experienced and helpful players and a comprehensive wiki, so if you're prepared to spend the time to learn, then you'll discover one of the most satisfying JRPG's i've ever played.
Story; the usual JRPG nonsense. The main characters aren't particularly interesting, but they aren't annoying either, a feat many JRPG's can't manage. But there's a huge roster of support characters some of whom are endearing and memorable.

This game is a little odd to place for me, its sort of like an arcade version of eve online... something like a sci fi biker story set on a space frontier.
It took me a little while to get used to how the game wanted me to do things but once I did I really started to enjoy it. I think I sort of cheated myself out of the full experience though. I found a story mission early on that I was getting my♥♥♥♥♥kicked on several times.. i would go in and fight a bunch of stuff nearly die so I would run away... didn't realize that each time I did I was just building up a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of cargo floating around the combat area near the mission. When I finally did beat it I looked at my map and it was literally covered with loot from my previous attempts.. some of it quite valuable. I went from having sub 100k credits to having several million.
Naturally I picked it all up and sold it and went and bought the biggest, baddest ship I could and mounted it with the best guns and equipment I could. I then ended up just coasting through the remainder of the game completely decimating it. The missions just keep giving higher and higher rewards and I was so far ahead of the natural equipment curve that no matter what I came across I was 1-3 shotting even the super dreadnaughts and destroyers I was coming across.
I decided to just keep plowing forward fully expecting to get to a point where my gear would finally just be barely enough.. but then the final mission of the game happened and it was a cake walk.
Naturally there is still a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of game left and according to the map there are SEVERAL places I could still go that are marked as very high risk and such. But still.. i completed the "main story" in just under 4 hours because of what I guess is a flaw in the loot mechanics in the game letting my 5 or 6 failed attempts at a big fight just stack up loot that was somehow on the higher end of value on the trade market in the region giving me massive profits.
Due to the procedural nature of the game I suppose the market prices are a part of that as well and I just got lucky.
I am not sure how much more time I will spend with this game but I feel I probably could of easily of gotten 15 or 20 hours out of the main story had that not of happened to me. I might still go back and try to finish up the achievement list but I am not sure.. lots of other stuff coming out soon.
Another thing this game does very well is its soundtrack.. something about biker road music set in space is quite appealing and it matches up perfectly with the combat they have going on here.
Anyways its a cheap game with fun fight mechanics and some pretty damn deep ship customization when it comes to gear and weapons. Easily worth the money they are asking for it and a nice little diversion for a few days while we are waiting some of the bigger titles to come out in the upcoming weeks... I am looking at you fallout 4....

One of the best war-themed games one can buy, This War of Mine incorporates numerous risk-reward mechanics that adds an deep level of immersion to the game; damn near every action you make affects EVERYONE, and I mean EVERYONE. Beyond the obvious pros and cons of who's staying in your shelter, one must heavily weigh the priority and necessity of they need to get set up from deciding to upgrade your metal workshop to make your own weapons and equipment to deciding to upgrade your home workshop to make your shelter more secure and self-sustainable.
Even when you think you're doing great at the moment, the game throws various curveballs to completely shift your priorities such as bands of looters forcing you to constantly guard your shelter and the brief but severe winter weather that forces you to heat your shelter constantly or succumb to illness. When you go out to scavenge at certain locations, you may be presented with various challenges that can affect the morale of your fellow survivors i.e. assisting distraught civilians, using equipment to access better supplies, or dealing with hostile NPCs.
Overall, the game does an excellent job of setting the mood of a war-torn madhouse that...frowns upon the adrenaline rush that is war, to say the least. You'll rarely have situations where you aren't forced to cutback somewhere and maintain an all-time high moral standing; you're gonna have to do what you must to survive, of course. Just keep an eye out for your survivors...you don't want them to mentally succumb to the hell they're in.

It's hard to recommend FF XIII. On one hand, I adore the graphics and battle system. On the other, it's very linear, too combat focused and paced poorly.
The story is a mixed bag since I love the concrete/real conflict among the characters but I don't really like anything about the rest of the world. More specifically, I don't like how it's presented, because after I finished the game, I read the lore on various sites and found it interesting but in-game wise, I think it's poorly presented.
Music is also very weak since it's too subtle, none that really stands out and doesn't feature any from the previous games except for the chocobo soundtrack. I do like the song during the ending credits though.
The combat is the only thing I can say I really love about the game. It's one of if not the best I've played in an RPG game. Still, it is quite cumbersome to learn and again, the pacing of the game might turn people off since it takes quite some time for it to really shine.
Overall, I don't recommend it unless you can withstand poor pacing in terms of story and combat and don't mind relentlessly long corridors that doesn't have anything visually attracting. If you can, I would definitely recommend it. Set your expectations low, and you might just enjoy it even more.

Saying Kung Fury is bad is paying it a compliment, so it seems counterproductive to criticize it. That said, it's 30 minutes of stupid and it's free. Would it still be the highest rated film on Steam if you had to pay for it? Possibly, I'm not sure if this is actually the case, since I'm not from the US. Some countries have access to Mad Max films, but I'm not one of them. I can mostly pick between Devolver Digital films. Lucky me.
Thankfully Kung Fury has its moments, some nice one-liners, cool effects and cool music. It's a fitting homage to the 1980s. It fell short of its feature film funding goal, which is probably for the best, but that's just me. It's better that it exists in 30-minute form than not at all. I would recommend Turbo Kid over this any day though, which has tons more personality. Kung Fury is the film equivalent of someone uttering a sentence that has never been said by anyone ever, because it doesn't make any sense and it's not supposed to. Alternate history films and games are fascinating to me, so I recommend it for that reason alone. The 22+ million views it has on Youtube is not surprising, cos this is the generation that grew up watching '80s action films. It's harmless fun.

I finished this game and I can honestly say that the hate this received is unwarranted.
I've played most of the Final Fantasy games as an avid fan. The last one I played was almost 8 years ago which was XII so I played XIII with fresh eyes and just after a gaming hiatus.
I can say that the battle system of XIII is really the best from the series so far (i cant speak for XV yet though) but it really made you think and create strategies. Let's be honest, if you could control every party member, you'd end up what other teammates are doing with their paradigm roles. It's a rational response and I think XIII really mastered that.
About the characters, I don't understand when people said the characterization was weak. Sure Lightning isn't the main star of the game but that's because every character is a main character. XIII managed to make every character play an important role in the story. There aren't any feelings of a side character because every character gets justice. Their character developments are also amazing so I'm honestly baffled seeing why this game got these kinds of remarks.
In terms of linearity, sure it is linear for the most part of the game. But FF X was also linear, it just had blitz ball. In fact chapter 11 of XIII is really open here. The only criticism is that this game requires a lot of grinding post-game. But I feel like it's the intention of the creators which wanted to give the players something to dwell about while waiting for the sequels. But yeah, if you loved FFX, i find it irrational to hate on XIII when the two have pretty similar ways of storytelling.
Finally, the soundtrack is incredible. The ending is also glorious. Like sure, it had a slow build-up story-wise but once you get halfway, you see characters develop and seeing the characters have more purpose and you get sucked into the story.
Is it a perfect game? No. But did it deserve to be called the worst Final Fantasy game? Most definitely not!

FF13 excels in many of the areas that Final Fantasy games are most well-known for, providing a thrilling cinematic experience through deep worldbuilding, cutting edge animation, and compelling storytelling. Unfortunately, not everything lives up to what the name implies. While most Final Fantasy games are known for being repetitive, as are most JRPGs, FF13 is especially so (for the brief moments not watching a cutscene, that is). The thing more horrifying and disgusting than the dying online review sites describe this game to be, is how badly they're going about trying to sound like they're "too good" to play this game.
On a 3 year old computer, with every setting set to Ultra at 1920x1080, the game keeps a solid 50-60 fps. The action is intense, visceral, and never scripted. The destructible buildings and walls create ever evolving fire-fights as you duke it out with the police. Cars and furniture go flying as explosions rock the screen, walls crumbling away under a hail of bullets, providing new vantage points and evolving battles in ways Battlefield could only dream of creating.
The mostly black and white palette sets a mood, but is never hard to read. If there is ever a moment of doubt as to who is shooting at you or where an item is, a simple press of left alt (or whatever button you bind it to) will highlight enemies, items, and civilians on the screen for you for ever easier reading.
The controls are tight and familiar to anyone who is old enough to have played a twin stick shooter, something most of the reviewers (including unfortunately Total Biscuit) apparently never did in their lives before. For those new to the genre, you will master the movement and gameplay (duck, rolling into and out of cover, throwing flash bangs around corners before taking out the stunned enemies) in minutes, providing a solid strong twin-stick shooter.
The game lets itself be self aware of how grim-dark it is trying to be, being a self aware B-Movie from a tiny indie studio. Pathetic how many professional reviewers try and spin this game as taking itself dead serious.
If execution animations grow annoying they can quickly be turned off in the options menu.
A strong solid shooter with very few bugs and plays like a dream even on lower end models. Ignore the dying gaming press trying to act like they're better than this game. At $20 it's a steal, and with an infinite number of ways of going through each level the gameplay stays fresh and exciting even after a several hour marathon of play.

This is one of the best games of the sapce RTS genre.
3 races are available humans in the form of the TEC, upgraded humans called the advent and the alien race known as the vasari, each race is divided between loyalist and rebel faction, so a total of 6 factions are available each factions has its own specific cons and pros.
The game is just beautiful, you can see wonderfull planets, asteroids and stars, zoom in/out from seeing just stars to a single fighter flying around, watch how your planets come to life whith ships flying around trading and all, its just amazing.
The game functions as many RTS with resource gathering, create buildings, research tech and build units, there is a black market where you can buy/sell extra metal or crystal, there are pirates that attack players who have a bounty on there empire and make a random attack on their space holdings.
You get general control of the planets and of its civilian aspect and a much finer control over military aspects. asteroids  and planets colonized have a limited number of upgrade points and building slots all dependent on the type of world it is, this allows you to gear some worlds as defense points, fleet builders or resource gathering depending on their base capacity.
your fleet is made of a mixture of capital ships, frigates, cruisers, fighters and one titan (if you can get it on space). Capital ships and the titan have a certain rpg element, they get experience and can unlock powers that can then be leveled up as they destroy stuff or if they are present at the destruction of an enemy. The rest of the ships are just cannon fodder or muscle to augment your big ships power. there is a fleet cap, but you can upgrade the cap so you can field more ships, the con of having bigger fleets is the upkeep cost, which becomes a more severe penalty as you get bigger fleets.
There is something that has to be said about gameplay and that is this games is only a skirmish and multiplayer game, there is no storyline campaing, i have not found this to make this game any less enjoyable but if you are into just the lore of things then it is a factor to consider.

It's a hard toss-up between recommending and not recommending Bioshock Remastered. I haven't had as many crash issues as other people, but there's definitely enough to affect my enjoyment of the game. I have to obsessively save the game every time I pull up the map, since loading the map seems to be what crashes my game the most. It lags every time, too, so it's always a gamble of "did it crash, or is it just taking forever?" Loading a new area, pulling up the map, checking a hint or old voice recording, all of that seems to be most likely to trigger the game to freeze so hard I can't even alt-tab out, I need to force shutdown my computer.
I seem to recall having random crash issues with the original, however. It's been over 3 years since I played it, so I can't say that I remember it well enough to compare it to the remaster, in regards to crashing, changes in graphics, and other added features.
That being said, the game behind the technical difficulties is very good. The atmosphere alone is reason to play, in my opinion (though I may be biased, because I love anything ocean and deep sea related). The creepy elements are done well - it's not quite an outright psychological horror as, say, Silent Hill, but it's enough to give you a sense of unease while wandering through Rapture. If you somehow aren't familiar with the story and the major plot twist, I would say that it's worth at least giving it a try, if your game crashes at a frequency that's tolerable. My game crashes about once every 3-4 hours, which I'm not too happy about, but I can tolerate it.
I feel it's also worth mentioning that the remasters of Bioshock 1&2 both have Trading Cards, despite that it's not listed on their store pages. The Trading Cards, the addition of the acheivements, the atmosphere, and the story are enough for me to say that it's worth trying it out.

Bioshock is widely regarded as a classic and is critically acclaim. I can see why.  tl;dr: ASIDE GAME CRASHING (SAVE OFTEN), the gameplay, atmosphere, story and story telling techniques are incredibly well designed. That said, it's a very lonely and dark game. Some horror included.
Gameplay:
Weapon choice is plentiful, be it plasmid, tonic or gun. You are given wide latitude to choose how you build your character. The only downside to this is that because the discovery of all the items is staggered, you may have committed to a certain playstyle by the time another one reveals itself. No detrimental bugs in gameplay besides crashing.
Atmosphere:
This is where the Bioshock series excel. The game is linear, so it's pretty easy for the devs to tell a narrative, but how it's done and what the narrative is are most important. The surroundings, the dialogue, the music, the level design all demonstrate how well thought out the game is. When the game wants to send a shiver down your spine, your spine dances. When the game wants to blow your mind, it makes you set the bombs without knowing it. Then, BOOM.
Loneliness:
You never get close to a regular human. They're always behind doors or scampering away. Logically, this is probably to prevent you from wacking everyone you see, but it still gets lonely. I hadn't known that the game was a horror one, which also explains the loneliness, but sometimes it gets to you.
Throughout the story, you do actions without question. Then, you're forced to question everything. 10/10

The Last Remnant is an amazing game. There is so much content and combat is fluid. I will not lie, this game is not noob friendly. Spent quite a few hours in the game recently and thought Id post my thoughts on the current version (1.3)
While yes it does have issues that are likely to frustrate many players, the overall game and the challenge of it more then make up for those frustrations for me and it is incredibly fun to play and even just to explore all the mechanics of it.
The core issue in the game itself is its balencing. The balencing is unequal between the dinos and humans, and goes against what you would expect. Classes that should do high damage dont, classes that should have low defense have strong, and similar issues along those lines. There are a lot of tricks to get around these problems that you will quickly learn by playing the game on various maps and learning techniques you can use to help overcome the bad balencing.
Otherwise, technically the game runs very well, there are a few of the usual Unreal Engine errors, but certainly nothing game breaking or enjoyment stopping. The game feels VERY smooth to control, and I don't get any motion sickness like I usually do with FPS games, although it is worth noting that setting up a controller is incredibly difficult and not doable from just in game.
So yes while it does have a few issues I find the game itself incredibly enjoyable. The satisfaction of taking out a Rex, or dealing with a bouncy raptor is great, the same as you get as a dino when you manage to sneak up on a human and kill them or set up a run to do mass damage to a group at once. Turning around and seeing a dino charging at you is terrifying, helped by the great sense of scale that the devs have used model wise, and being killed across the map by a human with great aim really keeps you on your toes as a dino.
While its not the most spectaular looking game, the graphics and assets they have used work very well together. Flora moves when you touch it, which means keeping your eyes open is very helpful, and the maps are well spaced, and often have unique balencing across various areas of the map itself. There is also a nice variety of map styles that you can play, if you can find servers using them.
I do highly recommend the game, and it is great deal of fun, although if the balencing is likely to extremely frustrate you, you might be better off waiting for the v2.0 thats being worked on.

Civilization and I have a long and checkered history. I've always loved the format, the complicated build trees, the diplomacy, even the combat system, which has made leaps and bounds since Beyond the Sword, though I still count that itteration as my favorite. All of these things, Beyond Earth does well, even the opening cutscene is wonderfully made. The combat is quick and well calculated, continuing with Civ V's introduction of the before combat analysis, a helpful tool. The factions are diverse and complicated, offering various routes into their good nature, including the additon of favors, which you can gain by giving a faction a certain resource and can be cashed in later, for ample benefit. The game itself is beyond pretty, offering a vibrant and living world, full of danger and opportunity, alien life taking the place of the barbarians of the other games. Beyond Earth also introduces Affinities, or ideological specializations for your civilzation to aspire too. On this note, as you level up in a certain Affinity, upgrades for your basic untis become avaliable, Soldiers become Marines, Rangers become Gunners, and so forth, each Affinity offering different and powerful units the more invested in it you become. The only real drawbacks to the game, are the limited number of factions to play as, though the Steam Workshop is taking care of that right quick, and the taking of cites, as cities have been able to defend themselves since Civ V, but perhaps I just have yet to find the proper formula for the offensive. All in all, Civlization: Beyond Earth, is a refreshing look at the series and a brand new way to play strategy games.

One of the best war-themed games one can buy, This War of Mine incorporates numerous risk-reward mechanics that adds an deep level of immersion to the game; damn near every action you make affects EVERYONE, and I mean EVERYONE. Beyond the obvious pros and cons of who's staying in your shelter, one must heavily weigh the priority and necessity of they need to get set up from deciding to upgrade your metal workshop to make your own weapons and equipment to deciding to upgrade your home workshop to make your shelter more secure and self-sustainable.
Even when you think you're doing great at the moment, the game throws various curveballs to completely shift your priorities such as bands of looters forcing you to constantly guard your shelter and the brief but severe winter weather that forces you to heat your shelter constantly or succumb to illness. When you go out to scavenge at certain locations, you may be presented with various challenges that can affect the morale of your fellow survivors i.e. assisting distraught civilians, using equipment to access better supplies, or dealing with hostile NPCs.
Overall, the game does an excellent job of setting the mood of a war-torn madhouse that...frowns upon the adrenaline rush that is war, to say the least. You'll rarely have situations where you aren't forced to cutback somewhere and maintain an all-time high moral standing; you're gonna have to do what you must to survive, of course. Just keep an eye out for your survivors...you don't want them to mentally succumb to the hell they're in.

Gat Out of Hell is the same activity-filled, over-the-top open-world comedy sandbox game we've come to expect from Saints Row, but it doesn't offer anything new or interesting above Saints Row IV. That is fine given that it's an "expand-alone", but unless you are short on games to play or haven't played Saints Row IV, you're not missing much. There is no character or vehicle customisation but that's fine for a game like this. There's still plenty of side missions and excuses for blowing things up, flying around and collecting orbs, hurtling a ragdoll into traffic and so on, as well as the typical RPG elements for upgrading your character's abilities and weapons. But when it comes down to it, the game's main story is extremely short. There are lots of side activities but these get repetitive and chances are you're not going to get to use all of the 7 new "Deadly Sin" weapons without completing a substantial amount of them. I finished the story at 84% total game completion and still had 3 or 4 of these weapons unobtained. There's also no music in this game, if you're into soundtracks.
Don't get me wrong, the content that's there is still on par. The comical value, whacky characters and story do entertain, it's just a shame that there's not more of it. I'd rather have had a longer story and fewer side activities. Still worth playing if you liked Saints Row IV but only if you get it very cheap.

The mercenary guild (which has a station in each system after the first) gives out random kill/protect contracts - just as the merchant guild does.  After playing through several of these to rank up my standing with the mercs so I could buy a new ship, I noticed that I get a lot of missions that pit me up against system militia and other 'good guy' factions, with no warning in the briefing whatsoever.  On one mission in particular in the second system, the enemies generated for my mission were also mercenary's guild - which resulted in a huge net loss for faction for completing an assignment from that guild.  This makes ranking up the mercenary faction very difficult and frustrating - after tweeting the devs on this, I heard back that it's working as intended, and the only option to get around this is to abandon the mission, fly all the way back to the source, and get another one - which may or may not present the same problems.
So I would wholeheartedly recommend Rebel Galaxy - but with the caveat that if you do pick it up, save yourself the frustration of trying to rank up with the mercs and just go with regular civilian or merchant class ships instead.

I have always been a fan of the Civilization franchise, so when Civilization: Beyond Earth had a free weekend, I decided to try it out. I played it for a few hours, long enough to get a grasp on the mechanics.
Beyond Earth is a sort of remake of Sid Meier's Alpha Centauri. Sort of. The same basic idea (Civilization IN SPAAAAAACE) is there, the planet is still filled with horrible aliens that are not happy about your colonization, and one of the victory conditions is exactly the same as in Alpha Centauri. But this game is no Alpha Centauri.
Beyond Earth has some pretty good ideas. I like the Affinity system, whereby you can customize your colony's philosophy along one of three lines. This ties in with the system for upgrading units as well, as your colony's Affinity determines what units can upgrade into. The tech tree has been replaced with a tech web, which allows for more freedom of technological development. The factions and their bonuses are diverse and all of them are useful, even if they don't seem it at first. A good example of this is the ARC, or American Reclaimation Corporation, who have a bonus to espionage activities. Espionage is a much more important part of Beyond Earth than in other Civilization games, and thanks to the ARC's focus in it, I was able to build up my energy reserves and my military force without firing a single shot, all by having one of my agents steal energy (the game's currency) and recruit defectors from one of my rivals.
But here is where we get into what I dislike about Beyond Earth. Firstly, there are those self-same factions. The leader of each faction is given just enough background information to make them seem deep, but they lack any real personality. A lot of this is so that the player can tailor their playstyle and Affinity choice without worrying about it seeming out of character for their leader and their colony to do so. But the leaders of Beyond Earth seem like cardboard cut-outs compared to the ones from Alpha Centauri.
Additionally, I never felt like Beyond Earth had any of the "magic" of other Civilization games. A lot of the fun of, say, Civilization 4 came from seeing things that could never happen. Romans with machineguns! India engaged in a nuclear war with the vikings! The Zulus inventing flight! With Beyond Earth, you don't get any of that. It wasn't as much of problem in Alpha Centauri, as the technologies you invented always had some sort of philisophical discussion or thought behind them; there's barely any of that in Beyond Earth, beyond the overarching question of "what does it mean to be human".
In short, Beyond Earth is fun, and it had some enjoyable ideas. But it doesn't FEEL like a Civiliation game.
I'm reccommending it cautiously; if I were you, I would wait until it's on sale for about $10 or so. And in the meantime, go find a copy of Alpha Centauri.

I am a huge fan of the X series, having played hundreds of hours in both X3:TC and X3:AP, however I was very dissapointed with Rebirth on releaes.
Game had an absolutely terrible launch, completely broken and buggy, but coming from a small studio I suppose its to be expected. However its been almost a year since the game has launched and Egosoft has been steadily updating the game and improving upon it. With the 2.50 patch which is currently in open beta, I feel the game is finally reached a point where it is of a an acceptable release quality.
The game runs very smooth now, and the AI is much better than launch. Bug fixes and many new features have been added, such as small / medium shipyards, adding shields to all capital ships, new squad management hierarchy for commanding your fleets, ect ect.
One of my biggest gripes about the game, was how easy it was. With the addition of difficulty levels and a complete combat rebalance in patch 2.0, you can no longer solo capital ships with the base ship. Even a small swarm of fighters can overwhelm you if your not careful. The game is steadily moving in the right direction, although I still feel the universe and number of sectors is too small compared to previous X games. Also the skunk still is not as customizable as it should be , considering its the only ship you can fly.
Overall, I like what egosoft has done with the game, and am excited to see what kind of future paid expansions or DLC content may bring to the table, its just a shame it took them so long to make the game fun and playable.

I can totally see how people would get turned off by the aggressively linear level progression of the first 20 hours. It’s not exactly thrilling roleplaying when you’re merely walking along a set path. But I also have to contest that this was the first game in the series that did it like this, because X was also pretty damn linear and even the more open games like VIII and XII were only open in the sense that you could deviate somewhat from the path for a few sidequests, and even then, the progression as a whole was extremely linear, so it really isn’t that big of a deal to me.
What bored me in prior attempts at playing the game later on was, ironically, the part where the linearity stops, where you get to Gran Pulse and the game opens up and gets more MMO-like. So this time, I just headed for the main quest marker on Gran Pulse and discovered that you can entirely bypass that section of the game that people usually call the point where Final Fantasy XIII gets good. Because I really have to disagree on the fact that Final Fantasy XIII gets good when you leave the “hallway” and get to explore an open map. And if you fear that you won’t be able to withstand the later parts of the game because you didn’t do any grinding, don’t worry. You’ll get a chance to go back to Cocoon right before the final stretch of the game, because the dev’s anticipated that you’d be underpowered. At that point, I simply said “fu
ck it” and knocked down the difficulty to easy, because I didn’t want to grind and beat the rest of the game without breaking a sweat.
But what made me finally get through this game on my second attempt was something I rediscovered about this game that I initially forgot. And that’s that I really like the character interactions in this game as well as the group dynamics. Now don’t get me wrong, I don’t want to claim that any of these characters are brilliantly written, not by a long shot. They also weren’t in prior games. But I still have a soft spot for these types of characters and how they interact with the people around them and there’s a silly but endearing quality to them. The only disservice the game does to this is the fact that it repeats so many conversations almost verbatim for way to long stretches of the game. The initial conversation about the group turning into “cursed” beings and their need to figure out how to break that curse is rattled off a dozen times and it never really seems to progress anywhere. That, and Hope can just die in a tire fire.
This is also one of the problems the early game has. It takes way too long for the story to make any meaningful progress. You’ll be traversing any given landscape for hours with very little to actually do while you’re in there, outside of combat. And the combat encounters that are put in here feel a little to gamey. Let me explain: Since your path is so linear, there’s basically no point in having random battles anymore, so you can actually see all the upcoming combat encounters on the world map itself. And how these encounters are designed shows very clear patterns. In every area, the designers introduce new enemy types (read: Palette swaps with different elemental stats), so you’ll typically be fighting a single one of those new enemies the first time around, then a group of the same type of enemies and after that they’ll usually introduce another new enemy type, have you fight against a group of those and then finally they’ll just mix them all together, once you’ve learned how to best deal with any given enemy. It just feels like a lazy way of progressing these levels, because during large parts, the story basically grinds to a halt and you’re forced to do this entire enemy encounter rigmarole over and over again.
This problem is only exacerbated by the fact that the group often splits up. And I feel that this isn’t done out of some desire to tell an epic story, but more because it represents an easy way of stretching the story to make room for more content. I would’ve respected the game more if it didn’t drag out its runtime with endless amounts of identical fights and just clocked in at 20 hours or so.
Because as much as people have railed against the Paradigm system, I think it was actually a neat idea with some potential. I don’t mind not having to manually input all the commands and let the game do that stuff, because this system isn’t designed for micromanagement. It’s meant to give the player strategic options to deal with the variety of challenges that it presents to them. In that regard, it’s not entirely dissimilar to old CRPGs, where combat wasn’t so much you giving individual characters specific attack orders and more giving them roles to play in any given fight without much input from the player. It’s a classic job system really. The unfortunate thing about FFXIII is that as the game progresses, it ceases to be challenging because you end up using the same strategies over and over again and fights only get longer because enemies tend to get way more health and status immunities. Way too large groups of enemies can be defeated by a general arrangement of characters without needing to switch them or the job combinations you give them out for anything else. The bosses on the other hand tend to be on the exact other side of this approach, giving you an incredibly hard time until you figure out the precise combination of characters and jobs that make their fights pi
ss-easy. What would’ve actually made this system way more interesting would be an option to actually switch out characters mid-fight or change the job combinations during fights, since if you lack the specific combination you can just hit the retry button. Or, you know, they could always get away from that nonsensical tradition and have every character you have in your party also take part during the battle.
The story is hot garbage and really not worth further elaborating on. It’s nonsensical, since you end up doing exactly what the villain wants (and yet he somehow still hinders you at every turn) and the final catastrophe is merely averted thanks to a deus ex machina.
One criticism I’ve heard a lot against this game was the fact that there aren’t any towns or stores and that you tend to have very little interaction with NPCs in this game. Now for the first half, this certainly makes sense, since you’re fugitives and nobody on Cocoon would want to deal with you in any way. What I personally found to be a missed opportunity is the fact that Gran Pulse is also just a desolate wasteland. Now I get that the implication here is that the people who did inhabit Gran Pulse died out centuries ago, but it just felt weird to not see any human settlements on this planet. It reeks of laziness, since they designed the systems for Cocoon in a way that didn’t mesh well with those on Gran Pulse and as such they just decided to make everything the same.
And that’s really the biggest criticism that I can lob against this game: It’s samey. To the point where it feels no different playing the game 4 hours in to playing it 40 hours in. This game just feels like an empty vacuum to me, it’s indistinct and featureless. Which explains why I haven’t mentioned the Crystarium (upgrade tree) or weapon and item crafting, because they’re just there. And hell, even during writing this review, I completely forgot about the Eidolons during my first draft. You know, the monsters you can summon to help you during battles that were part of every game in the series since III? Yeah, they’re completely useless and I ended up never really summoning them.
In the end, this game is just terribly insubstantial and the things I liked about it are both in a clear minority and at the end also don’t survive the entire runtime of the game.

Despite all these positives, the game comes with many flaws. You just walk down corridors all game, running into battles. So here we are with Hatred. I bought it because.....well........of course I did. The best way I can describe the game play is a darker, slightly more complicated, slower paced, more open world (Im almost done I swear) poorly optimized version of Hotline Miami.
Its a top down shooter. 3 levels in and its not particularly difficult thus far. Controls are a little clunky at time of release but Im sure that will come about. Something I have found is a common problem is getting caught on corners that extend too far. That may be a combination of user error and visuals though.
As I mentioned its not particularly well optmized (release day I know). My GTX 970 SSC got up to 48 degrees playing and that was at 60% fan speed on the new ACX 2.0 system. Im sure this will improve shortly though.
The thing this game is SCREAMING for is co-op. You and a friend in this would add a great deal more to the strategy and action.
As for the "controversy." The game is extremely violent but not particularly gory. What I mean that is this game and its context is horrific, but none of the violence is particularly realistically animated. You shoot someone point blank in the head and blood splatters but you dont see an exit wound or brain matter hanging out.
Honestly for $20 its a little steep, but I am curious to see where the game goes from here and how it evolves, particularly the possibility of multiplayer in the future.

2K has tried to resolve some game crash issues which for some is frequently every couple of minutes to others who seem to only crash occasionally or when saving or loading a new area. This does cause frustration and contempt as you often have to go back and redo portions of the game. For us this only occurred twice yet the specter of a crash loomed over our gameplay and resulted in a lower overall score. If you receive BioShock Remastered for free, then it is worth giving it a shot.
The controls are responsive and easy to figure out. Some will find only being able to use a plasmid or weapon at one time annoying as you have to switch between the two. Being able to freeze the game to select your weapon is a nice perk but also destroys some of the immersion. The graphics themselves even remastered seem a bit dated and there are occasional texture and graphic glitches. The game offers four difficulty levels but with the ability to save anywhere this is made to be a bit of a joke. The AI itself becomes predictable and each type of splicer is dealt with in the same way.

The pace of the game is great, only a few times did I feel I needed to backtrack or look around pointlessly for the collectibles the game was asking for. The voice acting is one of the strongest of any game to date. The characters are alive and draw you into the world. The ambiance is also spectacular with the old 1930’s music only adding to the creepy feel of Rapture.

BioShock excels at building the world of Rapture. From the start, you feel like you are inside of an actual city built under the sea. The crumbling dystopia feel is only enhanced by the gradual unfolding of the plot as you discover what happened to Rapture and why you are there. The final fight is straightforward and relatively easy to be honest. The game offers two different endings depending on if you saved or harvested the little sisters. We felt the ending was satisfying as almost all loose ends are tied up.

A fast, deep, and well-balanced platformer-fighting game with interesting departures from the mainstays of the genre. Character design is top-notch and all the character feel unique and fun. There is enjoyable single-player content, but the game shines in its multiplayer. The online services feel a bit lacking, and there is some noticeable lag that occurs regularly, leading me to believe that there are issues with the netcode or servers rather than both players connection speeds. Local multiplayer however is truly an amazing experience and I see myself playing this game with friends for years to come.

The Last Remnant.
It's one of those rare games that compel you to keep on playing. A one of a kind JRPG created by Square Enix that focuses on skill based tactical combat rather than simple select action>hit enemy with playable characters as in the FF series. With several Hero characters & a lot of generic soldiers to choose from,each with their own styles & weapon sets,the amount of replayability is quite high while trying out the different teams & formations. Plus the ability to control the flow of battle by raising morale,inflicting status effects or simply bludgeoning through the enemies is an added bonus.  Plus there are guild tasks which can be completed to earn new formations,items,money & new certificates that unlock even more tasks & prizes.
One drawaback of the game is its tendency to get repetitive as it heavily depends on grinding to build up skills & find materials to upgrade weapons & accessories. Plus monster spawns.especially the rare kind are randomly generated & sometimes it gets extremely frustrating to get a monster spawn at a specific area to get it killed & unlock new items & magazines that helps in getting previously unavailable monster drops.
Overall,It's a great game to have for both RPG & JRPG fans as well as tactical gameplay lovers. The bosses are great & have a few hidden bosses(DLC) that are extremely tough to beat & requires careful planning & approach.
It's also one of those few games that I have played & possessed as a torrent download,a disc & finally a digital distribution.
My rating for the game will be a 8-8.5/10.

I really, really wanted to like this.
However, I was no great fan of Civ V, and this is, when all is said and done, just a reskin of Civ V with a few bits and bobbles added. So ultimately: If you enjoyed Civ V, you'll probably enjoy the gameplay here. If you didn't like Civ V, nothing is improved here whatsoever.
When Civ IV did a total conversion with a few new mechanics, new graphics, but ultimately the same engine underneath  -- with "Final Frontier" and "Fall From Heaven: Age of Ice", both tucked away as part of the mods for Beyond the Sword -- it was just an added part of an expansion pack that gave you more in Civ IV itself.
With Beyond Earth, I'm expected to pay the price of a new game for it, and I cannot deny I am disappointed in what it adds, and more importantly, where it fails to live up to its spiritual predecessor, Sid Meier's Alpha Centauri.
The Virtues system seems like it could've done so much more, but instead it's just power-ups with no tradeoffs. The Affinities are clever, but ultimately fail to end up truly drawing you in. (A tiny suggestion there: it would've been nice to see your own leader as he or she is transformed by their affinity, just as much as it was interesting to see the other leaders transformed!)
A bizarrely minor gripe: the tech descriptions are all read by one voice; even though they are frequently attributed to the leaders, who are voice acted. Why not pay the VAs a bit more and get them to read those things? (Heck, could we have had the voice actors actually read the lines for their dialogue in the diplomacy screens? Nah, not that either.) It would have done a great deal, as with Alpha Centauri, to help make the leaders seem more alive. CEO Fielding isn't even in the same ballpark as CEO Nwabudike Morgan.  These leaders didn't feel like actual characters, and I managed to get through an entire playthrough without a single one of them declaring war against me, despite numerous threats.
In summary: I wanted to love it. I don't. I can't recommend it at the price it's at.

BioShock 2 is many things. It's the black sheep of the -Shock series, and for good reasons. It was not made by Irrational, which has made every other -Shock game. It doesn't really add anything innovating to the combat, just simplifies it, which is nice, but not groundbreaking. And, the worst part, the story is...dissapointing. However, BioShock 2 is not a bad game. By far. It's just when it's compared to the other -Shock games is when it falls flat.
Like I said before, BioShock 2 is not a bad game. In fact, I liked the direction the developers were going, but I think they didn't go far enough with their changes. They gave the morale system an overhaul which is a huge improvment over the last game. Depending on not only how you deal with the Little Sisters but also if you kill people you find in your journey or let them live, your ending will change drastically. However, I feel like they could have made it even better. Maybe during the intro cutscene you could try to fight the Big Daddy plasmid and you could, I dunno, fight Lamb and maybe cut her arm off or something? Then when she is in the water and <SPOILER> Eleanor can save or kill her she would drown even if Eleanor tried to save her and she would become mad that you cut her arm off. I dunno. That would be cool.
The combat in this game is also improved. Now you dual wield plasmids and weapons instead of switching between the 2 like in the original. But 1 thing I find odd is that you are a Big Daddy, right? So why do you take damage more easily than a dude in a longsleeve shirt when you are in a FREAKIN DIVING SUIT? That makes no sence. I do like the changes with the Little Sisters, but then everything in the 1st game is reversed. In the first the Little Sisters ended up not taking as much time to deal with. All you had to do is kill the Big Daddy. Now, you have to kill the Big Daddy, adopt the little sister and go through several waves of splicers while she gathers ADAM. Then you can cure or kill her. After dealing with every little sister, you then have to fight the Big Sister which is tireing. It just seemed to me like half of the time I was playing the game I wasn't even continuing the story, just dealing with the Sisters.
The worst part of this game without a doubt is the story. Lamb is nowhere NEAR as interesting as Andrew Ryan and there really isn't a huge twist at the end that makes you think about life and philisophical stuff, which sucks because that's always a highlight in a -Shock game. And all of the endings, even with the multiple endings, are still kind-of bland and dull.
Now before people ask, no, I haven't tried the multiplayer or Minerva's Den because A. My computer glitches out whenever I try out the multiplayer, and B. I don't feel like buying it.
Overall, this is a solid game, but it doesn't live up to any of the -Shock games. Just don't compare it to the others. Then you will be dissapointed. If you just think of this as an averageish game, then you will enjoy it a lot more. It's like the Godzilla movie from 98. Don't think of it as a -Shock game, and you'll be fine.

I must say that this game has won a place in my heart as a great multiplayer. This game flew under my radar for quite a while until a friend of mine brought it to my attention. I was a bit skeptical, but I ended up getting during one of the Steam sales. I have played it off and on ever since. The balancing of the teams can be equalized by limiting the number of the giant walking tanks (the T-Rexs), but even then, it seems like it is still tilted to the dinosaurs. Do not get me wrong though, playing as a human is a very rewarding. The multiple classes you can choose from have different playstyles and abilities that are unique enough to make teamwork a necessity, especially when taking on a T-Rex. Playing as the dinosaurs is fun and has a unique feel to it, but there is not much to compare this game to since it is so different. All in all, I would recommend this game just on the basis that it is different from your average multiplayer in terms of playstyle. The gameplay mechanics might not be different from any other type of multiplayer, but the game shines in a coat of paint that is called "Giant dinosaur FPS".

So I've been playing this game for a bit and read some of the reviews, finally deciding to write my own. TL;DR - Do I recommend this game: absolutely.
I've read a few negative reviews, where people compared this game to Privateer, and were disappointed by it. Personally, I think they're half right and half wrong. Is this a Privateer clone? No. Absolutely not. It's a little faster-paced, but not as much depth. It's gorgeous, intuitive and fun.
Yes most of the systems and stations can get a little redundant. Yes the combat can get repetative, but keep in mind this is a $20 title not a $60 one. This is the type of game that I love to pick up, bang out a few missions in an hour or so and turn it off.
The exploration feels great. I love cranking up my speakers while flying around the galaxy. SideNote: Sound Track is f-in' phenomenal. Some of the planets, stars and nebulae are nothing short of beautiful.
Rebel Galaxy boasts a pretty impressive array of weapons, defensive capabilities, and of course a myriad of ships. Ships come in a few different classifications; from Corvette-class striking ships to much larger, lumbering yet powerful Dreadnaughts and Cruisers.
Again, I wouldn't compare this directly to Privateer. It's isn't as much of a sim. Combat is much faster, as most of your weapons have some sort of auto fire. But there is strategy as well. Find yourself swarmed by fighters? Attach some flak cannons as your secondary. Want to go and blow up some colossal chunks of ice for some water to sell? Slap on a mining laser. Find yourself getting bombarded by enemy missles? Upgrade that Deflector.
In short, if you're looking for an inexpensive, polished and fun $20 title that gives you the freedom to do whatever you want out in the vastness of space, look no further.
Thanks for reading. Hope it helps your decision!

One year after buying(/preordering) this game (Well, 2 weeks short of a year) I got to play it when my friend finally bought it.
I had some expectations, mainly because I heard that the only story are the side activities from previous games - and how the game is extremely short. Indeed, I think game completion was 7% after half an hour of playing.
It took us a bit over 3 hours to finish the game.
But... Those three hours were amazing, it was the most fun I've had this year. The flying works perfectly and there are couple new side activities and the old ones work a bit differently. It didn't feel like three hours. Sure we kept joking about how fast the game completion % was going up as I saved the game and how we had only played for so little time.
But I didn't feel like the game was too short. I had fun for all those 3 hours. I didn't feel sad or angry when the game ended, even if the last boss is kind of boring, at least in co-op. I loved the whole experience.
And what I'd call the most fun sideactivity from SR3 and SR4; Insurance Fraud, was probably my least favorite from the side activities here. Still fun though. (SR2 Fight Club was best :V Or spewing♥♥♥♥♥♥ unfortunately, neither of those appear here. Some people from SR2 do though)
The humor is the one you're used to from the Saints Row games. I think it goes more to the SR3-crazystuff humor than the parodies of SR4.
I had one of the best laughs in a long time while playing.
(This game is a true Disney musical)
The game has multiple endings, so there is some replayability, though, the 3 hours before those endings would be the same, so maybe pick the ending you want and then go check the others on youtube or somewhere.
The game also checks your files or something and drags your player character from Saints Row 4 into the game. I was actually a bit surprised when I saw my President in the cutscene, and I loved seeing him there.
I fully recommend this game, especially on sale. Though I recommend either having someone with you when playing to laugh and joke about all the stuff going on - or even better, have someone else playing with you through the game on co-op.
If you enjoyed the previous games, especially their humor, I'm pretty sure this will have you entertained for the few hours it lasts.

Those were the last words a sick old lady told me as I slowly walked towards her to finish what I started, my group ws starving and injured and we needed what they had inside the house. "How did you get in here? Please, leave, unless you have medicine, my wife is sick she doesn't need to be bothered."
I hesitated, then in a desperate fit to get food for my starving group, I punched him square in the face.
"BANDIT, HONEY, GO HIDE DOWNSTAIRS."
The old man tried to run, maybe for a weapon, but I must have staggered him since he fell over at the foot of the stairs, I quickly caught up to him and finished him. "Please.. don't hurt my wi-" He didn't get to finish as I beat him where he lay, I quickly went downstairs to find the wife.
I went back upstairs into their bedroom and while scavenging I found a letter, I don't remember the exact words but it was to their Grandchild, how they were comforting his concerns on the state of his grandmother's health, how Bernard, the old man I murdered downstairs, was going to fix his swing when he visited later.
Soon after I managed to find the supplies I needed, and once I was done satisfying my hunger and bandaging 2 of my friends, I sat down and remembered what I had done... I wish I didn't need to do it, I want this nightmare to be over, "It's alright" Bruno told me, "you did what you felt to help us survive, now get some rest."
Pavle after standing guard all night, mumbled to himself as he laid in bed "Why'd you have to do it Marko? You'll never forget what you've done after the war is over."
This was only 5 days in and we were raided 3 nights in a row.

I am a monster.

So, I'm a fan of space sims.  I love X3, X3 Terran Conflict and X3 Albion Prelude.  The sheer scale of the open world in the old games was incredible, play as a mercenary, military officer, pirate, trader or entrepenuer.  The choice was yours.  So, when I heard that X Rebirth was in the works, I was over the moon.  I was right up there excited about what was promised to be the most immersive X game yet.  The reality is quite different.  If you want the short version, skip to summary.
I'll start with the positives:
The game is, astetically beautiful.  Ripe with amazing models, seemless transitions between sectors and the freelancer highway system, the effects, reflections and graphical detail are incredible.  Adding further to the immersion is the ability to walk around your ship and talk to crew.
It also had a tutorial that put a nice ease on the learning curve.
Now the negatives:
Now I mentioned walking around your ship.  Yes, this is cool.  Unfortunately, the only ship the player can control is the Pride of Albion.  While the ship is able to recieve upgrades, the real beauty of the X3 games (for me) was the ability to fly nearly any ship.  You could fly a fighter, a bomber, a cargoship, a transport, a megafreighter, even battleships and fighter carriers.  As far as I'm aware, you can't even use mods to change your player ship (or if you can, nobody has bothered to create one).  The hidden beauty of the X3 games was their moddability.  Ship models are availiable for download (for free) on egosoft's forums for the older games.  For me, I view this as a real missed oportunity.  They were able to extend the projectile distances in the new engine by quite a ways.  This meant that capital class vessels really could initiate gun based artillery duels.  The tragic truth is that without the ability to change ships, you can witness these battles, but you can't directly control them.
Summary: At the end of the day, I feel that Egosoft missed the mark.  Instead of polishing gameplay and their gem, customization, Egosoft took the root that so many gamers are frustrated with: shiny coat of paint on a mediocre game.  As Minecraft and Sword of the Stars II have shown, the game itself is what makes a game successful.  Gameplay is more important than the shiny ships and pretty explosions.  You can have a great game with 8 bit graphics and it will still sell.  But you can't have a  dodgy game in 1080p and expect many good reviews.
Addendum: I am looking at this game as a fan of previous X games.  I think as far as sapce shooters go, it's alright, but it is a bit of a departure from the previous games.

2K has tried to resolve some game crash issues which for some is frequently every couple of minutes to others who seem to only crash occasionally or when saving or loading a new area. This does cause frustration and contempt as you often have to go back and redo portions of the game. For us this only occurred twice yet the specter of a crash loomed over our gameplay and resulted in a lower overall score. If you receive BioShock Remastered for free, then it is worth giving it a shot.
The controls are responsive and easy to figure out. Some will find only being able to use a plasmid or weapon at one time annoying as you have to switch between the two. Being able to freeze the game to select your weapon is a nice perk but also destroys some of the immersion. The graphics themselves even remastered seem a bit dated and there are occasional texture and graphic glitches. The game offers four difficulty levels but with the ability to save anywhere this is made to be a bit of a joke. The AI itself becomes predictable and each type of splicer is dealt with in the same way.

The pace of the game is great, only a few times did I feel I needed to backtrack or look around pointlessly for the collectibles the game was asking for. The voice acting is one of the strongest of any game to date. The characters are alive and draw you into the world. The ambiance is also spectacular with the old 1930’s music only adding to the creepy feel of Rapture.

BioShock excels at building the world of Rapture. From the start, you feel like you are inside of an actual city built under the sea. The crumbling dystopia feel is only enhanced by the gradual unfolding of the plot as you discover what happened to Rapture and why you are there. The final fight is straightforward and relatively easy to be honest. The game offers two different endings depending on if you saved or harvested the little sisters. We felt the ending was satisfying as almost all loose ends are tied up.

DR2 is a completely different game, in almost every way. You have a RPG-styled character with upgrades and perks. You have hundreds of 'weapons' you can use to annoy or wipe out zombies. Stability wise, the game is not friendly to alt-tab, and the co-op play is also bug ridden with random disconnects. If you can stay together, it's a fun time battling missions, sharing weapons, building awesome combo weapons, driving new vehicles, and of course... killing zombies. This is definitely not a BAD game, I just wouldn't recommend it. Online is really hard to play not because of the game's complexity (You can definitely play Melee on Netplay and the complexity is kinda the same) but because it's really hard to find a match outside a big region, so you can't actually enjoy the competition this game is trying to create unless you're from said big regions. Singleplayer has barely any content, that added to the fact the roster is pretty small and getting the DLC characters is super close to buying the game again, and before you say it's pretty cheap and complaining about this means you're broke, think there are more countries and realities than US/EU.
And before you say my opinion sucks because I only invested 8.6hrs into the game, I'll say I've invested way more time in the game this is based on (Melee, another game that I wouldn't recommend unless you have people to play with) and I didn't feel the same motivation to keep investing time, specially with characters behind a paywall (idc if they're not "top tier", it's still matchups you have to learn and understand otherwise you'll get cheesed) which also was one of the reasons I grew tired of Smash 4. I'll now just add my personal impression here when it comes to mechanics, I completely dislike the way the game limits your defensive options (parry instead of shield, I know they had to deviate from Smash in some way but try parrying something consistently with +160ms) and some mechanics just feel off for me (no ledge grab + being able to use another recovery special after touching the wall). Also I find some character design to be pretty questionable, but that's an opinion so personal it doesn't weigh on the review that much as the other points.
Can this game be fun?
Under certain circumstances, sure it can be. But if for any reason you can't meet them, you'll probably be in disadvantages and the game can get boring fast.

Rating 6.5/10
Overview: Third Person Action RPG
The Good:
+ Choose between three separate characters each with their own unique passive and active abilities.
+ Story, dialogue and voice acting are solid and do a great job making the lord of the rings universe feel alive.
+ Lots of different locations to explore within the LOTR universe
+ Challenge levels
+ Great sound design
The Average:
Not the best-looking game, some areas look decent while others are bad. I would have liked better use of colors as most areas seem to be a mix of brown and green. Certain textures seem lo-res as well.
Characters give great details about side quests which help flesh out the universe, the problem however is that every side quest is a collect-a-thon.
Plenty of loot to find and the loot itself looks great when you equip it however the items you find are not very exciting. The only stat you will be looking at is whether it increases damage/armor.
Combat, although controls well starts to feel very repetitive half way through the game.  The character skills are not diverse enough and the combat isn’t deep enough so gameplay starts to drag out.
The Bad:
- Terrible, terrible technical performance. Framerate drops, stuttering after major events, graphical glitches etc. This seems to happen at very odd times. Most of the time the game will run smoothly but then for some odd reason the framerate will drop drastically, the game will start chugging even though very little is happening. The worst was at the very last level where I was getting 1-10 fps even though nothing was happening. Setting everything to the lowest option seemed to have fixed it however.
- Multiplayer is dead which may not be a bad thing because playing co-op tends to cause game breaking bugs.
Conclusion:
I believe this was Snowblinds last game. Like most average games there was a lot of potential here but failed to live up to it due to lack of time and money.  If you love lord of the rings, this is a good game to play however the numerous technical problems and average gameplay hold it back.

So I originally played the console version of this game, and got nailed by the game-breaking coding. Not a bug, just a somewhat infamously poor design choice that could easily render the game unbeatable halfway through. Hearing that that was fixed, I decided to try the PC version and get the game's full experience. And I just can't; the aforementioned flaw overshadowed the more important fact that this game is BORING. I like the story, but the presentation and setting are rather lackluster, alot of obvious questions are never asked, the pacing is weird, and the main character rivals Tidus for being just an annoying, foolish lead. Really, that highlights the most noteworthy aspect of this game; it's JRPG as you can get, in the worst way. Even as a lifelong fan of the genre, my favorite one, there are things that are just irritating in it, and this game seems to take them all and magnify them. Everything about the game feels so RANDOM. The damage you deal, and receive, jumps around tremendously, I mean by literal orders of magnitude. One guy, with the same attack stat, can do 30 damage, and the next one will do several THOUSAND, no lie, no hyperbole, that is what happens. You have no direct control over characters, instead issuing vague commands to character clusters and hoping for the best (good luck getting them to heal, it seems to be the hardest thing to do). And there is some requirement for you to command the battlefield itself, choosing which enemy units to hit, but with no rhyme or reason to the order of who gets to attack, you can often find yourself being intercepted when trying to attack a group of enemies literally three feet in front of you by another group of enemies 40 feet off. What? And while damage to the character groups is pooled, mostly, it is still possible for you to lose individual members of the group for no real reason, drastically hurting your potential. You have a morale meter in battle, which increases your damage and decreases the damage you take, but it always favors whoever is winning the fight, meaning the better side gets better and the worse side gets worse; in the end, what it means is that you absolutely dominate already easy opponents while getting creamed by powerful ones you might otherwise might have had a shot at. Increasing your party's power simply involves finding them random items from monster drops that they just keep and somehow use on their equipment, or occasionally carrying around equipment and hoping they eventually ask you if they can use it. There are no straight levels in this game, instead playing like Chrono Cross where every fight will probably give at least one character some minor boost to a stat, like 2 HP or something. However, leveling isn't much use, since enemies level with you, more or less. You also have this little guy who can mine for resources for you, but only so many times, and it's very random.
It's very difficult to fully describe this game's issue without giving detailed explanations of every mechnanic, but let me sum it up; if you are not a fan of JRPGs, run away from this one, you will hate it. If you are a fan, ask yourself if these are the kinds of mechanics you like, where you basically require a guide to play effectively, everything is very random, and the game involves lots of repetivive grinding through the same tiny areas against the same 3 kinds of enemies for hours just to get certain drops or to do the 5th quest in the same location. I was hoping to enjoy this game all the way through this time, but I'm even less tolerant of it's problems today than I was 6 years ago. It's just too annoying and repetitive to play, causing controller-busting frustration over the game's predominately AI controlled combat acting really stupid. In a way, the best comparison I can think of is Enchanted Arms; both have servicable if predictable plots with typical Japanese tropes, both have unique combat systems to try and hang their hat on (and failing), and both are so plagued by mechanics and randomness that don't make any realistic sense and lack any reason to exist that it makes the games simply un-fun. If it had a traditional leveling system without monsters leveling with you, higher movement speed, higher drop rates, more info giving to you, less randomness and more control in combat, I could enjoy the game, even with it's flaws. But it's just too slow and plodding and annoying to enjoy the decent parts of it, and novelty of the combat system isn't enough to carry an otherwise mediocre-to-poor title. You better be a total JRPG fanatic to play this.

If Saints Row 4 was a love letter to the franchise, Gat Out of Hell is a postcard. If SR4 was a game you enjoyed, go ahead an get this one, it's just as wild and crazy. The Boss has been kidnapped by Satan and taken to hell to marry his daughter, so Johnny Gat and Kinzie Kensington go after him/her. To get Satan to confront the duo, you have to destroy hell to get his attention.  A pretty thin story, but it works well as an excuse for raising hell all over hell.
A number of old characters return, like the DeWynter sisters (SR3) and Dane Vogel (SR2). There are some new characters too, like Vlad the Impaler, Blackbeard, and Shakespeare. Oddly, though, they're not recruited as homies, only as “allies.” Single-player Gat Out of Hell is a solitary effort. And short. Others have claimed 6 hours for completing the story; I took 8, but that's still a quarter of the size of the other Saints Row games (maximum level is 20). If you want to bring the game to 100%, getting all the collectibles and completing all the activities, there's a lot to do, but the game devolves into a collect-a-thon at that point.
Super powers return; Stomp, Minion-summon, Aura, and Blast each have three elements to choose from. The geography of  hell is new. Most of the activities are back, though in some new forms. Insurance Fraud is now about removing years off of souls' sentences in hell; when Adrenaline Mode is active, there is an explosive fire effect that can really heat things up. One of the best parts of Gat Out of Hell is the flying, which is good because you'll be doing a lot of it. The weapons are also a highlight; shooting frosting at enemies to make them attack each other? Yes, please. Shooting love dust at enemies to make them break into a sexy dance (even the titans)? Oh, yeah. If there is a downside, it's that the game is easy, even on the hardest difficulty.
I had fun with Gat Out of Hell; Johnny was missing for most of Saints Row 3 and half of Saints Row IV, so this game was like catching up with an old friend. No, you're not playing as the Boss, but “Who wouldn't want to be Johnny Gat?” - Johnny Gat.
Note about Kinzie for single-players: you can play as Kinzie throughout the campaign and switch between her and Johnny whenever you want; you just have to return to the Ultor lobby to do so. For the final boss battle, though, you will play as Johnny; Kinzie enters the room, Johnny shows up, they high-five, and you play as Johnny for the boss battle. It is called
Out of Hell, after all.

If you want dogfighting in space, there are more superior alternatives to X Rebirth, since dogfighting in this game is very rudimentary and isn't the focus. But for space enterprising, you'll currently find no better modern franchise than the X series. X3 and X Rebirth are the best wholesome space sim games out there. You will build massive station complexes, amass great fleets and compete with NPC factions in both capitalism and glorious combat.
Pros and cons between X3 and X Rebirth? X3 is starting to show its age, especially compared to X Rebirth. But its age is also its biggest advantage. X Rebirth can't hold a candle to X3's universe and economy simulation, but X Rebirth is constantly receiving updates and is inching closer to being a reasonable alternative to its older brother other than in the eye candy department.
As of right now, the economy in X Rebirth simply is not working. The game cheats in order to mask this up, so everything you do ultimately feels inconsequential as the game just does whatever it wants anyway. X3 is no different in that the NPC factions will cheat back their destroyed stations and ships, but there are mods out there to rectify this. The economy in vanilla X3 is fully functional.
The story in X Rebirth is no masterpiece by any means, but it helps to get you to the meat of the game; cultivating your personal empire. The story also attempts to introduce you to and explain the backstory of the universe you now occupy, if this interests you.
Both X3 and X Rebirth are officially gamepad supported, but in both games you will inevitably spend a lot of time navigating menus regardless of what control scheme you pick. Such is the nature of economy-driven games. Keep this in mind.
X Rebirth is also very performance heavy. Once you get the proverbial snowball rolling, there will be a LOT of things in the game for your computer to keep track of. You'll need parts well beyond the recommended specs to enjoy a smooth experience.
Despite its issues, this game will easily hold you over for a good 50-100 hours before any of the showstoppers rear their heads. Though once everything has been ironed out, X Rebirth will be one of the go-to singleplayer space sim games of this generation.
