I've played every game in the civilization franchise, and I like this one too.  Yes, it uses the civ 5 engine and cannibalizes parts of that game.  But Beyond Earth's differences make it a unique and thoroughly enjoyable 4X game every bit as good as both its predecessors and contemporaries.  This game may have fewer mechanics than Civ 5 with all its DLCs, but I can't help but feel that this base game is probably one of the most balanced 4x games I've ever played.  There will probably be DLC extensions, and I'll buy those too.
A lot of reviews I've read suggest that folks stick with Civ 5 given you can buy it and all the major DLCs for less.  And if you don't have Civ 5 I suggest that too.  It's epic.  But it too started out as a base game that eventually required 2 major DLCs in order to fully realize all of the complexity and mechanics of its predecessor.  And honestly the Civ 5 AI never really satisfied me as an opponent.
But if you've played and loved Civ 5 then check this out.  The AI isn't *much* better than Civ 5 but the improvements make single player games far more enjoyable (at least for me).  And the balance of tech, resources, units, diplomacy, exploration, and trade is a huge step forward.  I look forward to when DLCs add even more complexity to this game.  For now I'm content playing the excellent game as it exists now.

RTCW is a fun game and has aged well.
The premise of the story is very interesting. It centers around the Nazis' interest in the occult during WWII. While the story isn't the game's strongest point, it is satisfactory and never takes away from the gameplay. I appreciated the various letters that you find lying around during the game; they really add to the game's atmosphere.
Despite the game's age, the graphics are still good, in my opinion. By 2001 standards, they are exceptional.
The Quake 3 engine not only provides decent graphics, but, more importantly, makes for an awesome FPS combat experience. The weapons are great, and your character's movement is smooth. Combat is the game's main focus and without a doubt its strongest point.
The enemy A.I. is tough. I played the game on Bring em on! (the "normal" difficulty) and died several times during my playthrough. However, my deaths were never frustrating; I always felt as if each of my deaths was due more to my own shortcomings/poor play than by any cheapness from the A.I. I was forced to keep multiple save files and I recommend the same to anyone who isn't an expert at these sort of games.
The level designs are great. Plenty of hidden spots with loot for the players that appreciate that sort of thing in a game. I've  heard complaints about the stealth missions, but I found these levels to be really fun and a great change of pace. My only complaint is that some of the levels were a little too dark for my taste. They made it difficult to see enemies who have no problem seeing and shooting you in the same poor lighting.
The game's music is good as well. The sounds of the game really add to the atmosphere, and in some parts the game is downright creepy. You also stumble on conversations between Nazis who are unaware of you presence. These conversations often add to the game's story, and a few of them are hilarious and memorable.
It took me about 6.5 hours of total playtime to beat the campaign. At the end I was more than satisfied. I highly recommend this game to anyone who likes fast paced FPS games.

A strange and unusual game when compared to its peers.
This
game was released in the late life of the seventh generation of consoles i.e. Xbox 360, PS3. (Blood Money was released in the early life of the 7th generation)
As such you can probably guess what gameplay and graphics are like.
Graphics
improve if you have a higher spec graphics card (but won't be anything like 8th generation games). In fact, cutscenes rendered by your own machine will look much better than pre-rendered cutscenes.
Gameplay is rather intuitive, although AI can be a bit dopey at times. You must proceed along areas where the objective is mostly to pass through an area undetected, using disguises and distractions to aid you.
When the game finally does get you to eliminate targets, things get interesting. You can make things look like an accident and watch as the NPCs are shocked and scared, or you can take firm action and garrot, stab, bludgeon, shoot or blow up your target either quietly or as loud as you can get.
The game's focus on stealth does sometimes fail itself, as certain missions are next to impossibe to complete quietly and would require you to go loud to take out as many hostiles as possible.
As a third person shooter, it's relatively solid, but as I've said the stealth can sometimes fail and going loud won't be an option. NPCs can't see you at a cetain distance, but can see you if you're garroting a guard or otherwise. Certain actions will raise suspicion, others will not. Crouching is considered suspicious, as is running and so is pressing up against a wall.
The story of the game makes little sence and often involves elements which have probably been thought of by some deviant at IO Interactive (I am referencing the Agency BDSM nuns with one RPG to share, and other weird stuff), but that's not really why you're playing a
game.
The contracts feature does bring the game back to its firm grounding where it's as simple as just eliminating a target in the best way possible.

The idea of this game is good. It's a Lemmings type of puzzle game where you have to save a number of fish each level using a variety of tools. There are several modes of play: adventure, free and survival. In the adventure mode you play through each level in sequence, in the free mode you can replay any level you've already finished and use extra tools which you buy using coins you find in each level. In the survival mode perma death is introduced. You start with 100 fish, but any fish that get's killed means you'll have less fish at the start of the next level.
I have a number of problems with this game. First of all it's not been optimized for mouse based play. Instead of giving you icons on screen to open up the menu or fastforward the game you have to use the keyboard. My second problem is that there are often things happening at several parts of a level, since water tends to collect whenever there is a bottle neck and many levels have several at different parts of the levels. And you can't keep track of what is happening because you cannot pause the game, nor can you divide the screen into several parts (like in commandos) and there is also no mini map. So I often have to frantically move the camera up and down, left and right in order to keep track of different parts of the level, opening and closing snails (which act like faucets) or waiting for the right moment to use a specific tool. In similar games like Lemmings you often get enough tools to try out different solutions. But in this game, you get the bare minimum of tools necessary to finish a level. And while I've sometimes managed to find a creative solution, most of the times it's clear that there is one specific solution you have to follow. Which strips many levels of any creativity that makes these type of games intereseting. You could argue that you can return to these levels in free mode and buy extra tools so you can try new solutions. But since the amount of money is limited, spending too much money on one level will make it impossible to experiment with other levels. My final problem is the wonky physics. The water doesn't always behave in a consistent way so a solution that works once might not work (the same way) the second time. All these little problems together make for a game that is fun in concept and looks pretty, but which is frustrating to play in practice.

What would the world of gaming be like without Crysis?  It's a Concorde moment in the history of gaming and the gold standard for first person shooters and as far as I'm concerned, the greatest FPS ever created.
Every aspect of Crysis is at the highest quality imaginable, especially for 2007 standards it was way ahead of it's time, from the graphics, the music, the sound effects, your character and nanosuit options, the weapons, the vehicles, the massive size and scale of the environment that creates a non-linear gameplay style, your characters ability to interact with the environment, the uniqueness of the maps (like a weightless environment) that create new options in approach every time the game is played, F5 to save as you deemed fit, believable AI, and a story that transports you and engrosses you to a new time and place and constantly propels you forward.  There's really no weak link, other than when it first came out, it shut down everyone's computer and burnt out your graphics cards!! (Melted the fan of my ATI Radeon X700 and forced me to buy an Nvidia 8800GT!) It really is the large scale non-linear high quality interactive environment that puts Crysis in sharp contrast to all the other linear FPS games that have come before, and sadly, ever since.  There's no FPS competitor to the non-linear gameplay style created by the big maps of the original Crysis, and it still rests in a league of its own in that way.  Also, it's graphics easily hold up to today's standards, 10 years later!
My only critique is that I found the VTOL jet level frustrating and too difficult for my adrenaline junkie brain.
Crysis Warhead should've been a part of Crysis, as it tells the side story of Psycho, which I thoroughly enjoyed.
Crysis 2 and Crysis 3 chose to go down the cramped rabbit hole of the linear small map checkpoint style of gameplay like COD:MW to cater to console gamers so EA could make more money, and although extremely fun, those games lost what I liked about the original Crysis, especially F5 to save, and having to pick up weapons and ammo instead of just walking over them.  That being said, no FPS game before or since has ever looked as nice or with as high of graphic AA and AF as Crysis 3; it's truly in a league of it's own that way, and I've probably replayed certain levels of Crysis 2 more than any of them, so there's something for everyone in all of them.
The steam version of Crysis works great for me, I have no issues, so I'm surprised to hear people are having so many various stability problems with it. No idea.  I have the graphics cranked to very high on an ASUS G74Sx-3de ROG laptop out to a 27" monitor, without a blip in framerate, it's stable and beautiful, so I don't know what to say to anyone having problems other than perhaps, reinstall?
In conclusion, I like the designers minds behind the original Crysis and the effort placed to create such an incredible benchmark in the history of gaming.

Looking back, now that I have actual cards from the game itself, and knowing how broad and interesting Magic can be, I can see just how limited and flawed this game is. The card-set is very, very small, which severely limits what you can do with the decks you make. Often, you see the same strategies used because of this. And earning any cards at all is a hassle, simply because you get so few for how much gold you spend to get it. This, of course, is besides the numerous bugs and glitches the game has.
With all of that being said, I can't reccomend this for seasoned Magic players. However, I can fully reccomend it for those who, like me once, have no access to Magic cards. The game is perfect for those of us who have never played before, and just want to learn how to play the game. Since rules and tapping cards is all automated, you can see exactly how cards are supposed to play out, and you get a full understanding of how things work. And once you get the understanding, you can build up your deck however you want and use the card set they have to really see what kinds of things you can do.
Beyond this, I have to give the game credit for having every aspect of it be fully unlockable. There is no content that you NEED to pay for to get. Paying does get you an advantage, of course, but it's not so much that you'll be completely lost without having to pay. Enough time spent will, slooowly, get you everything the game offers.
Is the game good? Well..no. It functions rather poorly, glitches and bugs happen, grinding DOES take way too long (though, again, you can still unlock everything), and the cards are limited when you compare it to the true Magic the Gathering experience. But, for anyone who wants to be introduced to the game, this is the perfect way to start. Tutorials, some variety of cards to play with till you get used to them, fully unlockable content..and all free! Just remember that, if you enjoy this, there is so much more waiting for you if you can find the means to get some real cards.  And if/when you do, just abbandon this game and go enjoy the full Magic experience.

This is Wizard's poor attempt to ride the reigns of Heartstone's success. The only problem? It's so much a Pay to Win scheme that it's sad. I mean I have no issue with the pay option to get boosters, but the rate to acquire them are just plain atrocious. If facing against AI opponents, a victory garners 15 coins, a booster pack is worth 150. That's an average of 10 duels for 6 cards. Really? You guys couldn't just give us more to work with? The AI are jacked with decks with strategies that clearly outclass you in various degrees. Maybe it was my luck, but playing the same AI through story mode 10 times is not what I call thrilling or enjoyable.
But I will say there is one aspect I deeply enjoyed, Planeswalkers. Finally, it has only taken so many years to get this point. The custom deck builder is fun and user-friendly, but not the deck wizard, it's an abomination of a deck building alghorithm for new players.
Not only that, these Quests (which are like daily things) where the Archetype ones involve using decks from the deck wizard are utterly annoying and not fun at all. But they give you free coins if you can just grind through them. It becomes a chore especially when they are using color combinations where you have not so great cards in those areas.
There is also one other feature I really was ticked about, in the older iterations of Duels, you could stop and pause the clock as an actual setting feature for every phase. Now? They got rid of it. You literally have to have the spazziest hands on this planet to hit either the Space Bar or the Mouse button on the hourglass icon. It's upsetting and while I understand that it streamlines the experience it really takes it away from the more experienced players who want to not worry about missing a chance to react to an effect or spell.
I know I do not have alot of hours logged into this game, but that's because I play physical MtG. And this game does exactly that, it frustrates or inspires players enough to actually buy real booster packs and play the actual game. It's sad when you know that at the end of the day, that's the true aim and goal of this game's current incarnation. I just wish they had actually done some more material with actually more card options besides just Magic Origins. It's a good game to teach new players, but to keep tormenting yourself for enjoyment? No thanks.

Let's talk shop here. I have played the original Sins of a Solar Empire, long ago when it was just a disk game for the PC, long before Steam was even a thing. I was amazed at the flexibility of the game. I loved how you could choose how to play and win. Sure you could be super agressive and just go out and kill the enemy, or you could be super slick and just flood the enemy planets with your culture and just wait for the inevitable. And there were many other routes you could take. This has transfered over amazingly well to Rebellion. I have been keeping my eyes on the series for a while now, and while I may not have been able to play the other itarations (all of which I hear earned star studded accolades) I will say this about SoaSE Rebellion... this game is the quintacential space RTS. They developed a winning strategy with the original Sins and have only perfected it over the years. With stunning visual quality for a RTS, a delightful soundtrack (also the use of a dynamic sound playlist), robust AI's (playing on anything higher then hard is still almost impossible for me), humorous and interesting voice acting, and DLC that actually warrents its price tag... Sins of a Solar Empire: Rebellion is a must have for any RTS fan. The addition of Titans is the most interesting and rewarding part though. With their immense size (and cost) the feeling of accomplishment when they are finally constructed is palpable. So, let's talk about multiplayer.
Like any good RTS game, the fun does not stop at the single player level. The community may be small, but there are players out there who love to play against one another on Sins, and I must say, teaming up on a cruel AI or against one another is supremely satsfying. Although, there is something that needs to be noted... the difficulty of setting up a  lobby on the game is notable. Beware, if your computer is not very amazing, you would be best to just join a game.
Final Verdict?
8.5/10
Insanely fun, and plenty hard. (though a bit too hard for the more casual gamer)
If you like space, or RTS's... you need this in your collection, hell, go back and play the first one, it will blow your mind at how old it is and how it's still so good.

I have been playing "Magic" for 10 years by now and these are my thoughts on the game for both experienced players as well as beginners. If you don't feel like reading much, skip to the conclusion.
What is "Magic"?:
"Magic" is a deeply tactical trading card game which exists since 1993.
If you don't know anything about the game, check this out first:
Earning new cards:
After a mandatory tutorial-like campaign, which allows unexperienced "Magic" players to understand the gameplay easily, you earn a proper stack of basic cards and a lot of boosters, which contain six cards each. Boosters cost 150 gold which is earned by winning against an enemy (20g) and completing quests, which you can have three at a time, like "attack five times with five or more creatures" (40g). Gold can also be purchased for real money but all cards can also be solely earned without paying money, which of course takes time but in my mind in an appropriate speed. At this point it has to be mentioned that it's not possible to buy single cards but only draw them from boosters. You will however not draw cards which you already own four times, so you won't get hold of unusable cards. At the moment the stock of cards is limited to the "Origins" cards which implements a balanced setting but I'm sure they'll add more expansion sets.
Building a deck:
There are two options to create a deck: You can either build it freely or choose your colours and let the system suggest cards promoting a matching strategy (It's actually well done, not just random cards of the chosen colours). The free deck builder allows well picked filter options which reduces the effort of looking for the right cards to a minimum. Basically you can choose any combination of colours since an adequate amount of dual lands is included in the basic cards.
Unfortunately it's only possible to fulfill a colour-based quest with a deck created with the "Deck Wizzard", not a freely built one.
Gameplay:
The gameplay sticks to the common rules of "Magic" with the only difference being that you can take the first mulligan whithout losing a card (which I personally like). During the progression of a match the phases are clearly arranged and the game even surrounds usable cards in red which is great for beginners. Quick timers run off at each possibility to cast an instant or an activated ability. These can be stopped and you will have time to think about using it. The only negative aspect about the gameplay is that sometimes it takes longer than necessary. Concerning balance it's close to the original game: Slightly luck-based (like every card game) and ofc you have an advantage owning better cards (like in every trading card game) but usually you face enemies with a stock of cards similiar to the strength of yours.
Interface:
Cards drawn, damage being dealt, etc. is nicely animated (which can be disabled) and all in all the interface is satisfying and easily comprehendable.
Conclusion:
- So far the best implementation of "Magic" as a computer game.
- It's easy to comprehend the mechanics of the game and get into it. Of course it takes some time to figure out all tricks but you will stand a chance to win as a beginner.
- It's possible to invest money into the game but there is nothing that can't be achieved without.
So far I can't confirm the bugs people are complaining about. Sometimes it takes a view attempts to find a match but usually it doesn't take me more than 30s and my game hasn't crashed once. The only bug I personally experienced so far is that the gold, earned after a quest, sometimes just appears after a restart.
Caution!:
At the moment the game data created on your PC or iPad/iPhone are stored on different servers and aren't synchronised with each other so therefor you won't be able to use cards unloo´cked cards on your PC on your iPad and vice versa.

Where to start?
TLR Is a prime example of a unique and interesting idea executed poorly but even so, It's still a decent game if you can ignore all of the issues.
The isn't much beyond your typical JRPG style here and this is both good and bad. Firstly the music, oh my dear god what fresh hell is this? It's as if square have taken the old school way of "Just repeat 5 seconds of music over and over" from their old FF titles and thrown it in to a modern (at the time of release) game.
There's really no variation in it. The battle music is the same no matter the enemy or the area, it is always the same and after a couple of hours you get so damn sick of hearing it. Every area has its own music while exploring but don't expect anything memorable or creative because these little pieces of music are the same five seconds stuck on a seemless loop that quite frankly drives me insane to the point where I had to turn the music volume down to 0.
The voice acting is about what you would expect from any square game really. The voice actors were quite clearly ripped from older titles and some random anime by the sounds of it, the dialogue is cheesy (Who doesn't love a bit of cheese?) and you hear the characters talk in combat too. That in itself is a neat idea but that dialogue is as repetative as the music they are talking over but luckily square give you an option to disable the combat dialogue all together, thanks square.
The combat is the unique idea that was executed poorly. It could of been so much more than what it is. You feel like you can do so much but the reality is you can't really do anything at all other than sit there with your fingers crossed hoping the enemy you encounter will have an option for you to use a specific attack.
You group your characters in to units, you attack with a single unit by selecting an enemy unit but you have no controll over what attacks the characters in said unit will use which is pretty damn stupid when in order to "Level up" it's the "Gain expereince by doing" approach so the more you use a skill, the more powerful it will become.
That's awesome and all but doesn't have much merit when you have no control over what skills are being used in the first place. You have to wish that the enemy unit you have selected lets a character use a specific attack. Healing in this game is also pretty redundant to be honest because if you want to heal a lot you have to break off from your engagement. You'll get max health back but then an enemy unit will ambush you in to a "Raidlock" which means you take more damage and the enemy unit does more damage making all of that healing you just did completely pointless.
Why have I given this game a thumbs up even though I have all these issues with it? Because it's still fun.
The world they drop you in is interesting, you can tell there's a decent amount of lore there but you'll never learn any of it. It does feel like an old school JRPG in a modern style with a unique but somewhat pooryl executed combat system. It's cheap as hell so I say give it a go and if you don't like it? Steam refunds are a thing.

A fantastic "Space Trader" game.
I preface this by saying that I never played the other X games, don't often like straight up flight sims, and usually play with a controller. This review is coming from that perspective.
After reading the reviews of this game, I was convinced I waould hate it. Even after the 2.0 patch, I remained uncertain. I'm glad I took the plunge.
Go into this game expecting a classic "Space Trader" game and you will be blown away. Even with the remaining bugs, lack of variety in ground maps, lack of any real ship interiors, and a steep advancement curve, I have quickly fallen for Rebirth.
It's essentially the ultimate space ship sandbox game. You have a ship and some cash, go play. The standard "merc, trader, pirate" options are there. However, due to the MASSIVE scale of this game's physical universe and socioeconomic simulations they feel more like "Han Solo, The Emperor, and the head of the Orion Syndicate."
You literally go from running small amounts of cargo between stations in your one little ship to operating a massive empire of ships and stations that spans a space so large it can take hours (of real time) to traverse... from your one little ship. This also makes projects immensely satisfying when they eventually finish. You go from "crap, how am I ever gonna get enough cash for this station?" to "Damn, there are a ton of supplies involved in building a station and it's gonna take forever!" to "Cool! Those cargo drones are actually building my station!" to "Wait... this wasn't here befo... oh wait, it's green, this is MY station!"
It is a slow and methodical game (unless you just want to shoot things then you go do that while the game slowly and methoically reacts to what you're doing and changes the unverse in response) but a very rewarding one.
Now, don't get me wrong, many of the gripes people have with this game are valid:
Ground maps are very repetitive, you only get to fly one ship and it really only has one room (technically two but one is just a waiting room/hangar bay that you spend very little time in), the dialogue is fairly generic and repetitive, and there's a lot of waiting around or traversing huge distances.
But, as of 2.0 it's thouroughly enjoyable if you know what you're getting in to and worth buying, ESPECIALLY if they do another (hopefully better timed and received) sale.
Everything I've read about this company and this game leads me to beleive that there will be a 3.0 and it will probably be free, there's no damn microtransactions, it's not an MMO, and it's not procedural (don't get me wrong, procedural worlds are awesome, but a hand crafted universe of this scale is rare and usually amazing) so this truly is a unique and incredible game in the current industry. Some people will genuinely hate Rebirth with good reason but, knowing what I was getting into, I have found it to quickly become my favorite Space Trader in a very very long time.
So my advice is this: if you think you might still want this game even after reading about the downsides... yes, you REALLY do!

It's quite short, but the over the top action and humour of the franchise will surely pay out.

I recommend this game to anyone who enjoys economically realistic time-taking strategy. The game's overall concept of gravity wells and phase jumping definitely enforces a strategic concept that isn't found in most RTS games. The combat grows more exciting as the fleet sizes increase and more factions partake. The pirates are also a nice addition as well! (Even if they become pesky sometimes.)
The rebellion expansion to this game is cheap and worth getting. The added factions have their own little special titans and abilities and I like that. Keep in mind that this game does NOT have a campaign. It is solely skirmish-based. At first I kind of frowned upon that a bit, but then realized that this game doesn't really need a campaign in the first place. Simple games can last hours upon hours and require delicate attention throughout the majority of it.
All three factions (blobbing rebel factions together with their loyalist ones) have their own pros and cons. Some of these make these factions very deadly! The advent's culture is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ but useful. The Vasari eventually can see wherever anyone is phase jumping, at any time. The Tec can cause rebel insurrections to pop up on just about any planet, plus their novalith cannons do not feel good when they smash into a planet's surface.
The AI become increasingly manipulative and difficult as you raise it, and I find that definitely valuable. (But the in-game AI do like to blame you every time one of their capital ships is destroyed! The nerve!)
But regardless of all that, despite this game having no campaign.. I'd rate it a 7/10. Definitely worth playing!

Snowblind are known for putting out some great arpg's-Baldur's Gate: Dark Alliance. Champions of Norrath: Realms of EverQuest, and Champions: Return to Arms are some of the best Diablo-style arpg's to have come out on any system. They helped made the PS2 one of the most memorable console's ever and copies of all three fetch anywhere from $20 to $150 on ebay. That's why it baffles me how they messed this one up. It's just not a good game.
The main issue with it aside from the story not measuring up to the material that inspired it is the combat. If you're playing it single player prepare to face infuriating balance issues. You'll be yawning while button mashing as you overpower scores of enemies and then all of a sudden you'll have a cave troll or mini-boss constantly overwhelming your AI companions. When AI are able to reach you they'll be constantly knocked back by enemies. Added to the frustration will be gear. Good gear is rare and when you do get it nothing you get scales well. This isn't quite as bad early on but as the game progresses it ends up making it difficult to reach the end of the story by yourself.
The story itself is weak. While some of the characters in this are in Tolkiens works and the films they're more like celebrity cameos in a bad 70's holiday special. The main characters in this lack any kind of personality or defining trait other than being generic representations of their assigned class. Dialogue is terrible with bad cliche's all throughout and cutscene's that act as filler to pad the games already short playtime.
Performance and art-wise it performs just fine even on older systems. The art however while reminiscent of Lord of the Rings online's Middle Earth mixed with elements form the films feels looks just as generic as the characters personalities. The game is an on-rails grind fest through a series of uninteresting settings that evoke none of the ancient melancholy, ethereal beauty or ominous dread the novel and films do.
To sum up this is a game from a company who once made some of the best arpg's around who seem to have forgotten how to do just that. I would not advise picking it up.

The Last Remnant introduce you to many unique systems when it comes to combat, party management , crafting & loot. Non of them and I mean NON works right. At the beginning everything seems okay and understandable but at the moment you get in with the rhythm of the game, it leaves you alone without even explaining any necessary part of any RPG game like crafting for example. And you say to yourself: OK I'll get hold of it the more I play. But you wont. The game will be more complex and you'll feel lost. Sure you'll keep pushing forward finishing a quest after quest but you feel that there is something that you don't quiet get. When I found myself in this position I decided to read some guides in order to understand what I'm doing wrong. And then it was easy to realize that even the people who made those guides (that are mostly helpful) does not understand many sections of the game.
Take me for an example. I'm 50 hours into the game. I haven't bought anything from any merchant. I haven't crafted a single item even though that I have tons of components. I don't know what does a characters class means. I don't know half of the stats that my characters have like love, luck or courage because there is no way to monitor them. The game is vague about everything it has and it is not willing to show you anything so you have to treat it like Dwarf Fortress and go and read pages after pages of info that the game should have taught you at early hours of gameplay (if it was a good game).
Let me tell you about level design. If you are exploring one of it's small and peaceful towns or a natural place then it's okay. But the most parts you will be running through castles, caves & temples that are designed like a really boring and empty mazes. I was once into a castle to do a side quest. I miraculously managed to find my way to my target without a map with everything explored except for a small hallway near the end of the level (you always find the map in a chest somewhere). So after I reached my destination and finished the side quest the game automatically takes me out of the place back to where I started it. Then I got curious maybe I'll find something useful at the hallway that I did not explore. So I decided to get back to the castle battle the stupid respawned enemies and waste half an hour just so that I find a map of the place that I have no business in no more! This is how stupid the level design is in this game.
One of many pointless ant totally worthless side quests was a guy telling me that he lost something and this "Something" has been broken into six parts and I have to search for those parts and bring it back to him! even a 6 years old would have the imagination to make a better side quests than these.
I could spend all night writing about every single bad thing about this game from it's uninteresting pokemon-like companion (which is called mister diggs - lack of imagination again) to it's bad looking enemies with their repetitive moves to it's boring and disgusting grinding and leveling up system.
I could tell you about everything that I encountered and diminished my enjoyment of the game. But I guess that is enough. You can still give it a try because it's cheap but I don't recommend doing it.

So, this game is awesome. A really well made title, the graphics are bright, colourful and convey the lay of the land easily. At no point have I felt confused by an overcluttered UI, or even a lack of a helpful one, the UI is designed *just* right as it conveys what you need to know and what is useful to know without hiding important information.
The ship design, while by no stretch unique, is striking and follows easily identifiable paradigms, no matter the faction A Frigate is A Frigate is A Frigate, so to speak, which allows for easy identification of targets and thus target priority.
Weapons are cool, different types are covered; Projectile, Laser, Pulse, Missle, Flak, EMP, Mines, any combination of them is allowed AND the controls for them are simple (certainly on a controller, which I would recommend.)
Overall I've found, so far, that this is a solid game with a nice twist on the Space Sim genre, no longer controlling the fighters and the one man craft, this is the big leagues! Corvettes, Frigates, Destroyers, Haulers, Dreadnaughts, Battleships, Cruisers.
My only complaint is the lack of a player based Z-axis, so while the enemy craft and allied ones) dance around you, up and down, you are stuck on the planetary plane, but honestly there could be much worse faults!

This is an interesting take on the puzzle/platformer genre, and it is fun, but the reason I don't recommend it is because the game is far too short for the price; I was able to beat it in just over two hours. The game's framerate also drops occasionally for no apparent reason (possibly the engine not being able to handle the physics calculations). There is also an apparent lack of quality control in the writing: I lost count of the spelling and grammar erros in the dialogue.
As I said in the opening sentence: the game is fun. The game requires you to cut apart and move parts of the level to progress with three different tools, and the game makes good excellent use of that concept. As a puzzle game it is somewhat lacking in any brain-busters and as a platformer there are only one or two points that are a challenge, but the lack of difficulty doesn't detract from its enjoyability, not unlike Kirby's Epic Yarn or Scribblenauts Unlimited.
The game is indeed very short, but there are collectibles in each level (rocks and audio tapes) that allow for a level of replayibility, as well as statistics on the player's performance which are shown upon completing a level. If hunting down collectibles and beating previous level completion times is your thing then you will get more out of Tiny and Big than I did.
To sum up this review: the game is fun and creative, very short albeit with some replayibility, lacking in polish, and is rife with spelling and grammar errors. The game is well worth getting during a sale but not at the full asking price.

DR2 is a lot of fun, it's my kind of zombie game slaughtering large groups of slowly moving zombies in creative ways. None of that  fast moving zombie garbage.

Capcom did a terrible job of porting it to the PC though.  You are more or less stuck with the default control scheme, there is no way to re-bind the keys inside the game.  You can hack an INI file to change the bindings but it's a little buggy.  Even after changing all of the "move forward" commands in the INI when pushing a cart I have to use the default "W" key.  Likewise, the on-screen prompts will still use the default key which can make it difficult to figure out which one you really need to push for quick-time events.
You can use a gamepad, but the ONLY one that works is a XBOX 360 wired controller, any other gamepad including the wireless XBOX 360 controller won't work.

The Last Remnant is a whacky six-year old title from squenix, in which you will find yourself confused for a large portion of the game. You will be dumbfounded by the combat mechanics, as well as leveling systems, which tend to go for the different-must-be-better approach. Likewise, you will find dialog cliched, and wierd game flow ideas tossed in to mix it up. For example, after a main quest mission, you get insta-ported back to a castle. After you walk out of said castle five seconds later, you find an NPC right outside that tells you to go directly back to said castle to progress the game for no real reason. Not once, but multiple times in succession.
There are numerous faults with the game, and I defy anyone else to say otherwise. But, it's still kinda fun. It's certainly worth the five bones I spent on it, and the six hours I've put into it thusfar have been relatively enjoyable. It's definitely different, and quite possibly could have turned out brilliant were more time and effort expended developing the game -- especially the plot, combat tuning, leveling, game flow, etc.
I doubt if I'll ever get around to finishing The Last Remnant, which is charming because of its interesting approach (if flawed), and is still way more fun than Final Fantasy XIII, the closest thing to a digital lobotomy I've ever experienced.

When I went into BioShock 2, I had heard so many negative things about it. I know it would be hard for lightning to strike twice, especially when the first had such an amazing plot twist that actually made you think of what you were doing the whole time, but I at least give it a shot to find out what was so bad. And I would be lying if I said I didn't like it. Playing as Subject Delta, at first feels weird because early in the game you're a bit weak for such an awesome creation as a Big Daddy, but later on when you are at maximum power you truly feel like you are in Delta's diving suit. Anyways for the story, while not matching the same level as the original, BioShock 2 stands on its own as this time you are against Sophia Lamb, the new leader of Rapture who has links to Delta's past and as you continue along you learn more and more about her. It is also pretty cool to see Rapture again after the downfall of Andrew Ryan, especially now that barnacles and other sea-life are starting to grow around some of the area in Rapture, as well as interesting new areas such as a kind of Disney-esque theme park attraction made to educate about how horrible the parasites on the land are and how safe Rapture is. The gameplay mechanics remain mostly the same, but with a few new weapons, plasmids, and splicer enemy types thrown in for a wider variety than the first game. Little Sisters are back, looking more human than the big, wide-eyed little girls from the first game, and are more adorable than ever making it way too hard to harvest the little darlings, especially after having one ride upon your back and right after you incinerate a splicer hearing her say, "Mmmmm, marshmallows!" The only complaints I could really find are that some of the quests that you have to do end up being fetch quests, which can be a bummer. And in case you are wondering, the multiplayer is alright, but not the best, but that's just something you have to test out for yourself. Overall, I would say BioShock 2 is a solid sequel that 2K handled well and isn't as bad as some fans might say. So would you kindly buy the game and see it for yourself?

The concept behind this game sounded pretty sweet, but in practice, this just feels like an incomplete Civ 5 with a fresh (and confusing) coat of paint. The base mechanics are all the same, only renamed to sound space-y and futuristic and barely any of the improvements brought by the Civ V DLC are here. Whatever new mechanics are added, they feel poorly implemented at best, like they know they're gonna release 30$ DLC in the future to rework them (as is likely the case).
-The Affinity system looks interesting at first, but it's entirely reliant on the the tech tree (or rather "web"), so if you're not focusing solely on producing Science, you're not gonna get anywhere, fast. -Everything depends on Affinity now, from Victories to Unit upgrades, and unless you're devoting yourself to one Affinity, you can't do anything productive.
-In fact, apart from Domination, all the victories are basically differently flavoured Science victories now, as Diplomacy and Culture have been all but removed.
-The new Tech Web also seems interesting at first (a common theme with this game, it seems), but it quickly loses focus, because you have to go for the Affinity-adding techs, wich are spread seemingly at random on the Web. So on one hand you need to concentrate on Affinity, but that means randomly picking different techs... It quickly becomes a mess, considering the next point.
That new tech-y coat of paint... The great thing about Civ was how quiclkly you could get into it. The Units, Buildings, Leaders, even Wonders - you took one look at them, you knew who they were and what they did. Now, it's basically stabs in the dark. You have no idea what each unit is by glancing at the name (like when you're deciding what to Produce next), the Leaders are completely interchngeable, the Wonedrs are basically random bits of words stuck together to random effects... And since you can't help but to compare this to Civ V (and you have to, because the gameplay is identical), it looks just awful.
-Oh, and the worst part - instead of Spock's (or at the very least Spock's sound-a-like) soothing narration you get something that sounds like a teen girl, narrating random quotes by the fictional "leaders".. Yeah, actual quotes from actual people have been cut too....
There are good points - the Espionage system is expanded and the new Quest and Decision systems work really well. But that's all, really.
Most of all, this just feels like a big new scenario for Civ V. And if that's what it was, instead of a full price game with several full price DLC coming soon, that would be pretty awesome. But now, it feels like a big step beck for the franchise, not justifying the full price.

First of all, I was among those that pre-ordered X-Rebirth, and it's safe to say the game was beyond atrocious when it was first released. It was more like an early alpha state, full with bugs and tons of other issues. It was a fest for facepalms, especially after all the promises made in the Trailers. I had a rather unfavorable review up for those years, even after trying the game again upon 2.0 and 3.0 and editing the review many times. And I stand by my opinion back then, the game wasn't worth half its price.
With 4.0 I can finally overhaul and change my review to be somewhat positive. Nowadays I can recommend X-Rebirth, but only very, VERY carefully. It gets like a 5,1 out of 10. There's one last disclaimer, if you're interested in these kinds of games and have not played X3, start there. Seriously. X3 is still better than X-Rebirth in almost any conceivable way with only a few exceptions.
So here's what I think about X-Rebirth nowadays, and I will compare it to its predecessor:
Pros:
-Acceptable dogfights, though still not as nice as in X3
-A pretty fun boarding mechanic, much better than in X3
-The systems and sectors are beautifully crafted, giving actual depth and perspective to systems and sectors, far better than in X3
-Highways and the boost mechanic give a nice feeling of mobility
Cons:
-Mediocre and rather uninteresting economy
-Somewhat shallow story
-Absolutely atrocious NPC models (grandmas in space and lots and lots of copy-paste people where one looks like the other) and super awkward 'smalltalk'
-Speaking of smalltalk, some of the minigames are shallow at best and outright annoying at worst (see drone hacking for Rising Tide)
-Going along with the point above the depiction of the people and races (aside from the Argon/Terran of course, sigh...) is incredibly shallow and stereotypical to the point of being insulting. Only female Teladi are present and they all talk about business all day long, only male Split are present and they talk honor and war all day long, Boron and Paranid are missing completely aside from some references, and actually the Argon/Terran females all come across as emotionally unstable nagging hags
-To further add to the point above, Xenon are present in X-Rebirth again, just like in all X games before, but to my greatest dismay they're for the largest part just about the most generic cannon fodder enemies you could think of. There's so much more depth to the Xenon, indicated in the books and partially even shown in the previous game, as they're not just mindless machines, yet that's how they were implemented in X-Rebirth, and it just makes me sad
-The UI has been severely improved over time and is quite usable nowadays, but it ought to be nicer still
-You get much more depth in ship modification, but you also only get one ship to fly
So... the list of cons is still overwhelming and the most pressing issues in my eyes haven't been really addressed. The game in terms of mechanics is kind of okay nowadays and it can kill a few hours of time, but it's still nowhere near being worth investing thousands of hours into as with X3.
I don't think those issues will ever be addressed, as they are too deeply ingrained in X-Rebirth, and as such I just hope that Egosoft learns some lessons and starts making X4 soon.

I wanted to like it.  I gave it a good try (and $50), and I just can't take it.  I've been scouring the internet trying to find ways to make the game fun, playable.  There's just no hope.

Survival, looting and crafting. Yup, tiga kalimat ini udah jelas banget ya. Misi utama lo adalah survival ditengah peperangan. Lo musti bertahan diri dari panggilan alam (lapar atau sakit), bandit, bahkan teman lo sendiri. Nah, untuk bisa memenuhi kebutuhan lo, mau gak mau lo musti looting. Pertama kali main, gak akan ada tutorial. Jadi lo langsung muncul dengan 3 orang karakter dan sama sekali gak tau musti apa yang dipencet atau apa yang di klik. Duh... Nah, ketika lo udah berkenalan dengan control, mulai deh. Hal yang pertama kali lo musti lakukan adalah looting markas lo sendiri. Lo bisa search di lemari, meja, dsb lah. Begitu udah cukup resource, segera buat workshoop dan toolshop. WAJIB BUAT SHOVEL DAN CROWBAR karena itu adalah 2 tools untuk looting. Setelah itu bebas deh mau buat apa.. ini review ya bukan tutorial jadi you figure it out lah.. okay balik maning, setelah lo looting dan crafting, lo musti cari resource lagi ditempat lain. Begitu end of the day, lo bakalan memanage tugas karakter lo. Satu disuruh jaga, satu disuruh tidur, satu disuruh scavenge ya itu terserah lo. Nah begitu lo menyuruh scavenge, gameplay bakalan masuk ke tempat lain dan tugas lo adalah looting. Ingat, lo cuman punya waktu 1 malam untuk looting. Lo musti pulang sebelum matahari terbit atau ada kemungkinan besar karakter lo mati. Begitu karakter lo kembali, do that crafting, cooking, sleeping and stuff.
This War Of Mine adalah game bagus yang bener bener niat. Game ini menekankan gameplay sebagai senjata utamanya. Harganya juga masuk akal kok dengan fitur yang ditawarkan. Fair price. Kalau lo suka survival looting dan crafting dengan spek komputer standart, ya lo bisa coba lah game ini. Gue jamin, lo ikutan galau. Jujur, butuh tingkat pemikiran dan daya filosofi yang lumayan untuk main game ini.

In my opinion this game is a wonderful creation and all I could ask for in a digital MTG medium. The card collection system is the crown jewel of Magic Duels. Cards are unlocked by buying boosters with Coins won through Single/Multiplayer duels, campaign missions and daily tasks. The booster packs are not cheap but for me this only adds to the exitement and anticipation of opening a new pack of cards. Just like in real life, cracking open a booster to find that card you've been waiting for to perfect and tune your deck is an exhilarating and rewarding experience.
I have only recently begun playing Magic in the past month or 2 and because of this game i have increased in skill and understanding of the game rapidly and exponentially. It familiarizes players with the rules, key words and tactics used in constructed MTG play. The deck building wizard isnt my favorite because it turns the art of fine tuning a deck into a mash up of vaguely connected cards. Although i'm not fond of the deck wizard method of deck construction all is made right through the ability to maually constuct decks from scratch. Being able to build decks without the hassle of sweeping through a thousand cards to find the ones i'm looking for is one of my favorite parts of having a digitally organized collection.
Finally if the developers follow through with the release of digital content that coincides with paper releases (such as the Battle for Zendikar cards that were released on October 2nd) I think this game would be one of my favorites of all time. I've currently logged over 40 hours into the game and have no intention of taking a hiatus.
In conclusion I would say that this game may not be for everyone but if you love MTG and you want to step up your skill in deck building as well as tactful play then this is a great game. It's been getting some negative feedback but i thought it important to throw the other end of the spectrum into the limelight as someone who really enjoys the game.

There is potential in a game such as this, but the design destroys all hope of quality.
The Bad :
- Campaign mode forces you to play matches with terrible utterly useless decks from the second fifth on. Against opponents whose decks are very effective against the utter crap you have to work with. If you know what you're doing you will win when the game chooses to give you a match that is mathematically winnable. Thing is, this happens rarely. That is not difficult, it's just terrible♥♥♥♥♥game design.
- The AI is too "good". Even on the easiest setting the AI executes everything flawlessly with relentless aggression. Meaning If the game is not winnable mathematically in the beginning, it never will be, because the AI never ever makes a mistake. And will obliterate you. Again, if the game gives you a winnable game and you know what you're doing, you'll win. This once again happens rarely. That is not difficult, it's just terrible♥♥♥♥♥game design.
- The Deck Wizard is the biggest joke in the history of Magic. It is a "help tool" that more or less creates a deck for you. Thing is, it creates super slow utterly useless decks with some sort idea of "strategy" that never actually materializes. It's so bad it goes as far as NOT GIVING YOU ENOUGH LAND. If you make a deck that has more black cards than red ones, it gives you significantly LESS swamp cards than mountains. And you can do nothing to change that. That is terrible♥♥♥♥♥game design.
- The easiest way to gain coins, with which to buy boosters, is to do Daily Quests such as "win 4 duels with black/red archetype deck". What does "archetype" mean? It means a deck created with the Deck Wizard. So you are actually asked to win matches... that are stacked against you to begin with... with a "deck" created with a "program" that seems to be specifically designed to create the worst, slowest, most useless, borderline unplayable deck in the history of mankind. Sound fun? I can tell you it isn't. What it is, is terrible♥♥♥♥♥game design.
- The card pool is too weak to make the game interesting even from that front. Also the means of getting boosters is pretty weak, since actually playing the AI is a lesson in frustration trying to get a game going that isn't unwinnable from the word go. That is terrible♥♥♥♥♥game design.
The Good :
- The tutorials are pretty OK and I like the idea of giving some currency for completing them. I also found the first fifth of the campaign to be somewhat decent and fair.
- One on one duels against a friend can be fun.
- The actual card gameplay seems to work fine and that creates small echoes of the fun this game could have been.
Conclusion :
A game such as this has lots of potential. If the campaign and solo battle duels would be better designed to avoid constant mathematically unwinnable matches and the card pool would be widened, it would be a much MUCH better game. Also the Deck Wizard needs to be either fixed to work properly and give much more freedom, or be removed completely and let the daily quests be completed with user-made custom decks that don't involve the wizard. Also I have to ask. Who is this game for? Pro players will scoff at the limited card pool and the bare-bones approach in general. Newcomers will learn the basics from this but will be utterly turned off Magic by the aforementioned constant unwinnable starts to duels against the flawlessly murdering AI. How does that help anyone get interested in Magic, I ask?
If you absolutely need a free option to play duels against your friend, or you want to go through tutorials to learn the basics of the game, this might be for you. Otherwise I can't recommend this until all the mentioned problems are fixed, which would require essentially rebuilding most of the game. Do not spend money on this at least.
EDIT : I have to update this with my current experience. At some point, I'm assuming after opening something like 15 boosters, the game _always_ creates a deck for the AI that has a planeswalker. Regardless of whether or not you have even one in your collection and regardless what sort of utter useless crap you have to use to get your archetype daily quest done. Also the game cheats. It can have two Legendary Creatures of the same name in it's collection. You can't. The game creates decks for the AI that you can't build. I know in rules of magic you CAN have 2 Legendarys of the same name in a deck as long as they are not on the battlefield at the same time, but what I mean is you can have ONLY ONE in this game, and in the last duels game _in your collection_. Also this leads me to suspect that the game creates the AI decks on a turn by turn basis. I Countered the Legendary Sphinx Allhammaret in my match to the graveyard, and 3 turns later the AI played another   Allhammaret. The only way this makes any sense is that the game simply generated a new Legendary of the same name into the deck the moment I countered the first one, since making a deck that has two of same Legendarys makes zero sense otherwise. Cheating ♥♥♥♥♥.

Alrighty, real review:
Honestly, I wish the story was longer. Obviously, with a title like "Hitman", you aren't going to go too deep into a story. But some of the plot simply didn't make sense. I enjoyed the combat, and it had excellent graphics (especially considering I'm running this on a laptop on low settings... and still gorgeous). I enjoyed the control layout, the classic Hitman Franchise "sneaking around", and the fact that one mistake can lead to a whole lot of trouble.
PROS:
- Graphics
- Great Interface
- Sometimes hilarious costumes (LOL - Chicken Suit!)
- Nice change of scenery
- Comes with Hitman: Sniper Challenge!
- Solid ending. Very enjoyable.
CONS:
- Story is... eh.
- The game honestly wasn't very long. Took me two-and-a-half days. 8 hours, maybe? I wish the story went on a bit longer.
- The "Contracts" part of the game is totally horrible. Honestly, total crap.
- Sneaking around is difficult. I feel that NPCs catch you too much and discover who you are when you are in disguise. Are other people in the real world honestly that attentive? I kind of dislike the need for combat situations whenever someone "finds you out."
Other than that, I thought it was great. I got a kick out of it! I just wish that the story was a bit better! The biggest negative for me was the "Contracts" section of the game. I like the idea of a challenging others/accepting challenges. The only problem is that you need lots (and I mean LOTS) of Steam friends who play this game. And for me, I have zero. The second thing is that there is no tutorial on how to create contracts. You're kind of left totally clueless about it.
Absolution though... beautiful.

I was almost about to say Zachary Hale Comstock when recommending this game for the “Villain Most in Need of a Hug” Award but, nah, the nod must go to the original villain of the Bioshock series, Andrew Ryan, the visionary capitalist run amok, whose astonishingly beautiful underwater utopia is a continuing delight to behold and play in, through two wonderful games, even in its “fallen” state.
I’ve read in various places that Ryan is supposed to embody an Ayn Randian antihero but if that’s the case then it’s a very simplistic view of objectivist philosophy (Big Bad Capitalist run amok). However, gamers don’t play Bioshock to gain philosophic insight, at least this gamer doesn’t, but to wander through one of the most breathtaking worlds in all of gaming while rescuing pitiable “Little Sisters” and sending demented  Splicers to their eternal rest. Now that’s memorable gaming!
As for utopia crumbling into dystopia, we are playing in Ryan’s playground, his dream of a better world, and, well, if his dream turned into a nightmare then we can revel in the nightmare, and if we speculate at all, perhaps it would be to ponder the vanity of human wishes.
Just so happens I’m 60 plus years and I would recommend the entire Bioshock series to other “seasoned gamers”, with the caveat that if you have a heart condition like me, you’ll want to play on the easy setting. As in all action role playing games there are jolting surprises as you journey on. As for eyesight issues, there is not a lot a lot of small print in these games and the lighting is adjustable in the options panel. The Bioshock games certainly stimulate “les petites cellules grises” to borrow a phrase from Hercule Poirot and while requiring some manual dexterity the game allows for planning as opposed to mindless button mashing.

This entry in the BioShock series is, to me, a polarizing experience.
Standing on its own, this game is incredible. The art design is absolutely mesmerizing, complemented with a sensual soundtrack and astounding voice work. The gameplay is quite intuitive as well; guns feel distinct and your entire arsenal is an equillibrium of diverse offense. Plasmids feel unique and the inclusion of traps allows for a meticulous, strategic approach when protecting Little Sisters' and their harvesting. BioShock 2 succeeds in these aspects, though it falters in others.
Comparing this game with BioShock 1, however, proves much dissonance. While BioShock 1 provided enough backstory to support necessary explanation for things in the universe, BioShock 2 unloaded an excess- it feels forced, uninspired, and ultimately like fan fiction. The new information given in BioShock 2 doesn't mesh very well with what BioShock 1 established- the tone of the subject matter feels radically different between the two. The story of this game feels as though it lacks true progression of any sort, and ultimately hinders in pacing and character development. To make this game feel more as if it didn't belong in the main canon, it was entirely neglected in both episodes of Burial at Sea for BioShock Infinite- no mention of any characters, foreshadowing of any sort, and even entirely negates some of things established in BioShock 2.
BioShock 2 is a love/hate game- on its own, it stands quite fine. When compared to BioShock 1, it feels entirely unnecesary and unfitting.

The story is a bit weird and complicated, and the plot well.. the plot too.
It's quite a depressing storyline and frankly, the uppity-haha-lighter moments that every FF has, are hard to find. Some cringeworthy characters are tossed in the mix, special shoutout to mr. Estheim. I don't want to spoil anything, but this kid has some serious issues, and the others let him get away with it bigtime. Really, his issues are solved for all the wrong reasons. Because of this, whenever I could, he wasn't selected for my battle party.. I am pointing out that Hope Estheim (among others) is a believable annoying character. One you would like to have a seat and talk to, and he starts screaming in your face and it's all your fault and you have to calm him but you can't and the only thing that calms him is to play along with the lie he's been telling himself (BAD MOVE SNOW! Now he thinks he's right, you a-hole). Phew.
As for the game(play), it's a Final Fantasy alright! I've played FF5 and up, and it belongs amongst the FF series. The game is for most of the story fixed on a path (as in, no free roam), which deviates from most previous FF's, although in all fairness you couldn't just go freeroaming in most other FF's. The gameplay unlocks very slow, I believe it was chapter 11 of 13 total, where you get to pick your own battle team and set up your preferences. It was chapter 11 that made me realize I actually was playing a Final Fantasy game, broad maps, lots and lots of side dishes, and monsters that snuff you out in seconds. Chocobo's finally make an entrance, and you get an introduction to one of the cooler features: Missions. To be able to wield the best equipment and beat the biggest monsters there is a lot (let me emphasize: A LOT) of grinding involved, which I like. This is on par with other FF's, the endboss of the game is laughable compared to some optional quests (missions) bosses. Next to powering yourself up (crystarium level up system, meh), you get an Eidolon per character. I barely used them at all, they change into vehicles once dismissed and that was something I found stupid (they have legs, some can fly for gods sake, no need for a vehicle). I really miss Ifrit too, although he probably is happy Square didn't turn him in a motorboat or bicycle or trike or whatever.
The meat of the game is the grinding part for all equipment (Treasure Hunter trophy isn't for the lazy to obtain, and this is how it should be, some easy trophies and some you have to work for) and the missions. The missions (64 in total) are ranged from easypeasy to how the hell am I going to beat this guy, and the difficulty exceeds the endboss' by far. Which is good, you only unlock the complete power up grid AFTER beating the game and you choose to 'git gud' and go for the mini-bosses and trophies, or choose to be satisfied and quit playing. If you choose to quit, you're missing out on some of the finer battles of the game, as well as the bigger hits and stronger teams (999.999 damage is fun to dish out).
So, it's slowwww going, annoying characters (yea every FF has those), weird plot, kind of a serious approach (I actually wouldn't let young kids near this game because of the heavy themes without lighter moments), for endgame there's a good deal of grinding and farming involved and reoccuring FF characters are missing (Wedge, Biggs, Ifrit, etc). Still, I like and I don't know why :).

Bioshock 2 provides an interesting second look at the world of Rapture, expanding on the story set by the first game. The gameplay is arguably improved a bit from the first game, with a broader weapon set and extra polish, as well as some tweaked plasmids (Security Command is a fun one- lets you summon flying security bots wherever you are). However, the storyline feels a bit grindy and aimless, with the main character's goals feeling relatively unmotivated compared to those in the first game Yeah, he's dying, but for some reason it just doesn't feel compelling. You never actually meet two of the big characters in the game- Sinclair and Sofia Lamb- in any major role physically, so they just feel like voices in your head for most of the game. Also, this game is as glitchy as the first, if not more, and will probably crash you out to the desktop more than a couple times. Quicksave will be your best friend.
Reservations aside, I highly recommend this game, because the slight complaints I have are well worth sticking through for the experience of the game as a whole.

Short review: If you really want to try this game, either (A) wait for a great sale (at least 1/2 off) or (B) buy X3 Terran Conflict and Albion Prelude.
Long review:
Simulation games, especially space simulators run a very tight rope. They must be open enough to allow the player to experience the universe, but structured and formatted well enough to ensure the experience is a fun and pleasant one. Anyone who has seen 2001: a Space Odyssey knows that simulating space exactly would be maddening, boring, and above all, not really a game. In the past, Egosoft has managed (with a great deal of modder and community help) to make an enjoyable space sim. They managed to balance the openness of the universe with (albeit a bit buggy) mechanics. Although the learning curve was steep, the rewards were worth it when you found yourself the ruler of an interstellar empire.
For X rebirth, Egosoft decided to sprint full speed ahead, oblivious to that balancing act, and fell off that rope before it even managed a single step.
Pros: (1) Graphics update, (2) Capital ships have subsystems you can target strategically, (3) Boarding and training marines are more straightforward, no more chasing marines in space or waiting for them to train. (4) I managed to finish a full length novel and download another on my kindle while waiting for things to happen.
Cons:
(1) You have 1 ship. Which wouldn't be bad if (A) you could actually customize it beyond 1 upgrade for each option, (B) you could actually customize the ship itself, beyond changing the glass layout in the cockpit, (C) your AI ships weren't braindead or hell, even (D) if you had a copilot that did more than argue with the computer and
(2) almost half my total play time was spent wasting time doing NOTHING while I waited for (A) NPC trade runs to complete, (B) trading to complete, so that construction could continue to complete, (C) follow/escort missions to complete, (D) scripted events to start, (E) scripted events to complete, (F) NPCs talking to themselves, especially during D and E, (G) navigating menus while listening to NPCs flirt with me about their "wares". (I even managed to finish an entire novel in the time I was waiting! I kept it close by for these times)
(3) The design, and trade menus are awkward to navigate, having been designed for xbox360. There is no depth in the commands, options, or details of the ships. It is nearly impossible to compare ships or their capabilities without using Roguey's site, and even then, there's no real reason to choose a different AI ship because
(4) AI is terrible. Normally this would mean that your other ships were on equal footing. However, based on the design and lack of command options, your ships will not attack unless you yourself are attacked, or you navigate three menues to command them to attack a target chosen from the map screen while you are under fire. They also love to run right next to enemy ships (especially the capital ships) instead of using long range weaposn.
(5) Repairing capital ships is a giant waste of time, and takes forever; repairing any non-capital ships is impossible without a mod. In other words, anything less than a capital ship is useless.
(6) Everything requires an AI NPC, that you must carry around in the back of your ship to transport. Built a station? Needs a manager and a rare speciallist that you must find in a wild goose chase.  Just capped a ship? Better hope you already have a captain, defense officer, and engineer sitting behind you! While I get the idea that capital ships need officers, there is no way to have a "transport" ship keep these NPC's around for you. And god help you if there are no suitable candidates with the skills you need in nearby stations, or you've run out of space for freeloaders in the back.
(7) NPC skills have no visible or explained effect. My 5 star all around captain/defense officer combo is equally as useless as my 1 star duo. On the same ship. In the same fight...
(8) You must visit every station, constantly, in order to trade. Want to trade somewhere you already visited? TOO BAD! Since the two minutes you last docked there, the trade offer is gone. Note: the trade offer is still there, but you have to revisit to remember it is there!
(9) Voice issues and translations: while I understand there are translational issues, a single english speaking person could have cleaned up 90% of the voice over issues. Heck, I might have preferred their native speakers to voice it, with subtitles, as opposed to hearing terribly performed, gramatically incorrect gibberish.
(10) If there is a "story" in this game, it is hidden behind hours of waiting, incoherent english, bugs, and useless interface.
(11) I'm pretty sure the game is about some guy named Ben who found a laser space skunk and trained it to fight "the man" (and then robots I think?) alongside a pair of breasts in a skintight suit with a strategic breast window. They are named Isha and Terran.

Good music and beautiful space vistas are the strongest aspects of X Rebirth. Unfortunately, that's where the "good" ends and the "bad" begins.
Despite all of the bugs and glitches (which have mostly been addressed in the 2.0 update), there are fundamental flaws in the basic game design. The X series has been well known for its deep economy and combat systems. X Rebirth took most of that away. The X series has been touted for providing a large universe to explore and secrets to discover. X Rebirth took most of that away. The X series has been a staple in the space simulation genre for its meticulous attention to detail and giving the player immense amounts of freedom. X Rebirth took most of that away.
As you can see, X Rebirth is a mostly step backwards rather than a revisitation--or "rebirth"--of the series. I purchased the game on release day and have been regretting it ever since.
The biggest flaw that stood out near the time of release is the fact that you are limited to a single ship; to make matters worse they called it the "Albion Skunk", a ship that was once known for its prowess (and went by a different name) but was later found in ruins and scrapped. Having only one pilotable ship should have been the first sign to me that this game would never live up to expectations. Because of this limitation, major mechanics that are considered "norms" for the genre, like trading, are handled by pilots you hire who can fly other ships. This limits you to focusing almost completely on combat. There are a handful of missions you can run, but they mostly consist of bounty hunting.
One of the key aspects that was announced before the game released was the ability to step out of the cockpit and walk around stations. The concept was fantastic and it has rarely been done in the space sim genre. Sadly, X Rebirth failed to make that as exciting and innovative as it was made to seem. There are basically two types of interiors that you'll see. Every station uses one of those two layouts and tried to make them unique by blocking off certain sections for each station. It's fun and interesting to walk through the stations the first few times, but it quickly becomes frustrating when you have to go through a maze of corridors to get to your destination to talk to a vendor or mission contact. Additionally, the stations are almost completely devoid of life. There are maybe 20 people in any given station, and all of them stay in the exact same spot and do absolutely nothing. Which leads me to my next point...
Character design is terrible! Other than the few key characters in the tutorial campaign (such as Yisha, your copilot), every other person you see is just a copy. There are maybe four unique character designs: human male, human female, and roughly two alien humanoid species. They are then copied and pasted throughout the stations.
There are many other examples of poor design and rushed development that I could continue to list (such as terrible UI, bad voice acting, etc.), but I think my message is fairly clear already. X Rebirth essentially attempted to make the X series more streamlined and accessible, but it seems like their answer for that was to make the game more casual-friendly by ditching fundamental space-sim mechanics and to change the focus on the series and genre completely (You don't even have 6 degrees of freedom! Everything has an UPWARD orientation which makes absolutely ZERO sense in space!).
However, X Rebirth doesn't fail completely. There are a few things that stand out and are worth mentioning. As I stated earlier, the music is good and the space backdrops are gorgeous. Additionally, activity outside of the stations actually makes the areas feel populated. Each stations will have hundreds of ships flying around, traffic heading in and out of docking bays, police ships scanning and chasing criminals, military cruisers fending off attackers... There is no lack of visual fidelity when it comes to the station exteriors.
Unfortunately, the few things that X Rebirth does right are too few. With the space sim genre coming back to fruition with games like Elite: Dangerous and Star Citizen in development, it's very, very difficult to recommend or praise X Rebirth.
