As most everyone knows, X: Rebirth was a horrendous mess at launch. It was fettered with problems: a horrible optimization that led to unplayable framerates, gameplay elements that at best were buggy, and at worst were completely broken. It was a game that screamed it was totally rushed to market. Egosoft was pelted with so much bad publicity that the Metacritic score was a complete embarrassment at 27 at its lowest point. That being said, Egosoft took some time, listened to the community, and did a complete overall with the 2.0 update. The big question you should be asking yourself is: is X Rebirth still the unplayable mess, or is it worth purchasing now that the 2.0 update has been released.
I scoured the Steam and Egosoft forums for a true, balenced answer to whether or not X Rebirth was worth purchasing since the 2.0 updates. Unfortunately, I was unable to find a true endorsement for buying the game. The weird part was, I wasn't able to find a true condemnation of the 2.0 updates either. Everyone seemed to be mired in hurt feelings over the initial release, and angry over gameplay elements they deemed as stupid. In truth, the more I read, the more I realized that these people were angry over the fact that the game wasn't Terran Conflict. Frustrated with my inability to find a straight answer about whether or not the implemented fixes made the game worth playing, I remembered back to when I bought X3 at launch. That game, too, was a complete train wreck of a launch, but over time was patched, modded, and ended up being one of my favorite games in my collection - a staple that I kept coming back to. So, I took an attitude of let the buyer beware, and dived in to purchase X3 Rebirth to form my own opinion on whether or not it was worth buying.
I've been a huge fan of the X series since I first played X2. Bear that in mind, because I'm going to qualify a lot of what I'm saying through that lens as I write this review. The long and somewhat rambling preamble is intended to make you understand that I'm writing this through the eyes of someone who holds the X series near and dear to their heart. I'm not an Egosoft fanboy, nor am I an X fanboy. But I do think that since everyone gave Diablo III and SimCity a fair shake, despite their disastrous launches, X Rebirth should get consideration for the changes that were made as well. So, this review will only consider the game post-2.0.
----
First, it's important to note that X Rebirth was clearly a game made for the XBox 360 and PS3, and the design philosophy makes it clear that the PC release was an afterthought when some elements were designed (such as the map system). This doesn't mean it didn't translate well to the PC, it's just very clear that the game was really designed to be played with a controller. I don't play with a controller, and play with a mouse and G13, and it works very well. However, fans of joystick/throttle combinations will be very disappointed, as the game really wasn't designed with flight stick enthusiasts in mind.
The main fix that was impleneted in 2.0 was the optimization of the graphics through making it 64-bit native, making more use of RAM and multi core threading. I don't have a superpowerful rig, and I run a single NVidia GTX 560 Ti and an I7 Quad Core @ 3.4GHz and 8 GB of RAM. The game runs silky smooth for me, even in sectors with tons of traffic, and I'm running the game on higher graphics settings. It's safe to say that if you're running a halfway decent computer, you'll at least be able to run the game on medium settngs.
The game looks absolutely fantastic - with rich, dense sectors that are reminiscent of Blade Runner or Fifth Elemnt. The character models do look somewhat strange, and seem to be kind of a secondary element, but they're not so awful it ruins the experience. The voice acting is extremely mediocre, but again, it hasn't distracted me from enjoying the game. The station designs are pretty much the same four or five models, with extremely little variation, and the novelty of getting out of your ship to meet someone in a station wears off extremely quickly. The stations don't feel alive or vibrant, and there was definitely a missed opportunity to create some variation. The game really shines, however, when you're in your ship, flying around space (which is what you'll spend 90% of your time doing).
The game drops you after the events of X3: Terran Confict, and you're dropped into the Albion Skunk, the last and only prototype of an Albion battleship. You pick up a mysterious technician, and events conspire to ruin your status as a neutral party in the galaxy, forcing you to take sides in a conflict against the Plutarch Mining Coproration. The crux of this story, however, is what brings the unique (and sometimes reviled) aspect of X Rebirth that begins to seperate it from other X games - you are only able to pilot one ship through the entire game. You buy or gain other ships throughout the game, but they're micromanaged to take on tasks you set (such as escorting you or trading at stations). This micromanagement can become tedious, but honestly, no more so than X3: Terran Conlfict. There doesn't seem to be any autonomous trading options as there were in X3, so you will have to constantly micro your fleet to take care of tasks to earn you income or fight your enemies. I don't feel like this is game-breaking, since I manually ran trading in X3. There is also a new highway system in the game that allows you to fast travel between sectors without using a time compression mechanic.
Unlike previous X games, the game is very forgiving to the newcomer, introducing you to gameplay elements in the campaign to acclamate you to how the universe functions -  from controlling your ship, combat, controlling other ships, hiring crews for those ships, boarding and capturing other ships, etc. It presents gameplay (in my opinion) in a much more accessible way.
A main issue you're going to have if you've never played an X game before is relying on community support. The X games have always had an incredible and active modding community, and Egosoft has always done a good job of supporting their games long after launch. The general community (what's found on the forums), however, is an absolute terrible disgrace. They are generally extremely rude to those not intimately aware of the X Universe, and simple questions on how to do things are met with general trolling. As a fan of the X games, I am a bit ashamed that I love a game with such a horrible community that's founded on exclusivity and keeping the "average" gamer out of their space (because, trust me, you're just not hardcore enough to play an X game). There are, however, a ton of X resources on the internet, and once you get past the outright indignance of the community over the launch of X Rebirth, you'll be able to find some decent resources to help you figure out how to do things.
So, should you buy this game? That depends. If you're looking for an experience comparable to what you had in X3: Terran Conflict or Albion Prelude, you should probably look elsewhere. This is a totally different game. It's not different in a bad way, though. It's a fresh take on the universe with some issues. This game is far from perfect. There's still some bugs under the hood that need to be hammered out, the sameness of stations gets tiresome, the outright rage of the community over the game is kind of depressing, waiting for your ships to get to their destination to complete a task can be kind of annoying if there's no missions around to complete while that task is being completed can get tedious, the map system can be really unintuitive until you get the hang of it, and the voice acting could be much better. All of these things pale when you see what this game can be, though. I'm having a lot of fun with it, and I'm glad I ignored a lot of the venom that was spit over the game's broken release. Recommended.

First, I'm probably biased in this review, since Bioshock is my all-time favorite game.  Despite this, I think that, after the updates, Bioshock Remastered is worth getting.  It's the same incredible atmosphere, game feel, story, and mechanics as the original with a fresh, and very pretty, coat of paint.
Everything that made the original great is here.  Without spoiling too much for anyone who might not already have played the original, the plot is steeped in philosophy and weird science, acting as an excellent critique of Ayn Rand's Objectivism.  It's always easy to see that it's building up to something, and the plot twist towards the end is legendary.  The plasmids, while not as necessary as they might seem at first, add an interesting aspect to combat, and this is one of the first games I personally played that uses its environments in clever ways during fights.  The trailers do plenty to show what kind of atmosphere the game has, and while not the scariest "horror" game, it does have some great creepy moments.
Unfortunately, a lot of what was wrong with the PC version is still wrong with the remaster, even after updates.  The game runs for me, but I often have to reset my graphics settings, and I'll occasionally see glitches like texture pop-in and physics objects floating on air to a corner of the room.  The developer fixed a few things from the original, such as the strange ragdoll animation, and in a post-launch update they fixed the FOV issue that has plagued the PC version since its original launch, but I still see a lot of mistakes that I can't help think could easily have been avoided.  I also had one of the better experiences with the remaster, as it seems some people couldn't even get it to run.
I can only speak based on my own experience, but I would recommend this game, especially to anyone who got it for free if they had the original in their library already.  It's a classic, and I don't see it getting old any time soon.  There's a reason this was exhibited in the Smithsonian.

Magic: the Gathering itself is great, but the advantages of this computer game start and end with the tutorial. Story Mode is fair since AI uses real libraries with random hands unlike it is in Magic 2014, for example. Unfortunately, there are poorly designed decks like the one in infamous Liliana's campaign. As for common duels, progress with collecting cards is extremely slow and too luck-based if you don't buy gold for real money. If you play with AI, the choice of difficulty doesn't affect your opponent's library, so you might easily win on Hard but encounter an opponent with four mythic cards on Medium when you don't own any for your deck. There are archetype decks which are much easier to build out of the starter set than the others, but it quickly becomes boring to farm in-game gold with the same strategy. In personal quests, you often get tasks like winning 4 games with a weak deck and winning 2 games with a decent one, and both have the same award. Community quests that last for several days are usually completed within first 24 hours and then just occupy the slot uselessly. Sometimes there is an impossible goal to achieve, and once there was a quest that didn't work at all, having 0 in its counter for the whole time being. Developers just didn't give
to care about it. Also, there is no in-game chat (even in two-headed giant games), no any awards for two-headed giant victories, and network games just get stuck from time to time.
I highly recommend playing real MtG and maybe spend some free time in Magic 2014 to have some practice. Magic Duels, however, is pretty poor.

Surprisingly Fun Game Mechanics -
Look, if you've never played a Lord of the Rings  action brawler, stop what you are doing and go get Shadow of Mordor
For those that have already conquered Mordor then this game is worth checking out at the right price.
It definitly shows it's age, the charecters look like they all have glass marble eyes that sometimes slips♥♥♥♥♥♥eyed. The Textures are on the lower end even when maxxed.
But in spite of all that it does provide a fun Action RPG romp through the war of the one ring. You can chose 1 of 3 charecters (Ranger,Elf,Dwarf) and there is some basic custmization as far as appeareance goes. What's cool is you change to another charecter at the start of any new Chapter, so it gives you the variety of being a mage, tank or warrior at your choice.   There is a decent skill tree system that pertains to each charecter's strenghts,  I personally went with a dual weilding ranger. The action is more on the level of pre Arkham brawlers but still ton's better than you find in most arpgs as far as having direct control over your charecter.  This is not a game where you just queue up commands and watch things play out, you will be activly dodging and hacking your way through the Orcish hordes.
Story wise it's a mixed bag, to the plus they do take to iconic scenes from Trilogy, including running intoo Aragon at the Prancing Pony while he waits for Frodo and Co. to show up. The down side is the voice acting can be pretty bad at times. Controls are responsive though and being and older game if you have any sort of even marginally decent gpu you ought to be able to run this at 120 fps easy.
Despite the dated graphics and stilted voice acting, once the action starts you tend to forget all of that and can have good time  slashing and dicing the baddies.
In Conclusion:
If you are a fan of the Lord of the Rings Trilogy who has already beaten Shadow of Mordor then this is a decent shot of Middle Earth goodness. If you have played SoM yet, then whats wrong with you? Go get it. After that come and chill with the War in the North for a fun ride.

Okay, so, I spent an hour writing out a lengthy review of this filled with insight, in depth information, pros, cons, and fully described aspects of the game with no spoilers. Then Steam decided it was going to not going to let my review go through, then proceeded to crash before I could copy what I had written (lesson learned: type out the review in Word or Notepad before copying it here).
Because I don't have the energy to write out that lengthy of a review anymore, we're going to shorten what I wrote down to the important aspects of it.
Rating 3.5/5
-0.5 points for Difficulty scaling
The game has a co-op feature for up to three people. I beat the final boss in less than five minutes on the first try, yet other battles in the game took me an hour because I was playing solo. The game shouldn't punish me for playing solo. I shouldn't need to cover two different sides of a battle with hopeless AI that can't do it for me when solo playing.
-0.5 points for Combat/Mechanics
I chose to play just the dwarf for the entirety of the game rather than switching in between missions. Perhaps sticking with one character was the wrong choice because the combat is overly repetitive. Once you unlock some of the skills, it becomes a tad more varied, but then quickly goes back to repetitiveness. Atack, attack, dodge roll, attack, skill 123, attack, rinse and repeat. Nothing special. Also, there is no jump but instead a dodge roll, which is fine. However, there are many aspects of the game where the designers definitely made it seem like there was a secret on a ledge, but lo and behold, you can't jump. A few bugs where you can't attack, or can't hit a crate, or can't move around an object were present, but didn't take away from the experience.
-0.5 points for Miscellaneous
Lack of a save function other than visiting a shop or travelling to a different place. And my biggest gripe is the inability to compare weapons when trying to buy something. I shouldn't have to look at my gear, memorize the stats, go into the shop, look at the boots there, realize I forgot the stats of my equipped item, back out, and do it all over again. That is beyond tedious. And the last miscellaneous complaint is the challenge missions. Much like any game like this, there are challenge missions where you have to defeat multiple waves of enemies. Unfortunately, after spending 30 minutes on a challenge mission, you get nothing for beating it other than the experience from killing the monsters. I went through 20 healing pots and didn't get a single reward for my troubles?
+1 point for Visuals/Voiceover
The game isn't anything spectacular visually (it IS five years old), but it has a certain charm to it and does what it can to honor the world of Middle Earth. The voiceover work was a real great point of interest for me as a voice actor. Most of the voice over was well done with fantastic casting.
+1 point for Lore/Story
For any fans of the books/movies, this game definitely does a good job of immersing you into familiar territory. There will be quite a few familiar faces, and a whole myriad of new ones. There are familiar locations like Rivendell and Bree, and a few new ones like Nordinbad (a Dwarven city).
+1 point for Skills/Gear/Leveling
This one was on the fence for me. I was afraid the system was going to be too simple, but it turns out it's rather nice. Leveling up grants three points to be spent in either Strength (melee damage), Stamina (health), Will (mana), or Dexterity (ranged damage). Then you get to put one point in your skill tree. Each character has three active skills you can unlock with respective trees underneath those skills. Unfortunately, each tree has randomly thrown in skills that often don't have anything to do with the skill you unlocked. The gear isn't visually impressive. Finding a new sword won't WOW you visually, but a clear stat difference can be seen when using it in combat. I could go into more detail, but, the entire system is just meh, but I don't have many complaints on it.
Overall, the game isn't too bad. The replayability is pretty good because once you beat it on normal mode, you unlock heroic mode where you can play through again but stay the same level so you can unlock more things and get better gear. I would recommend playing it with a friend rather than going solo.
tl;dr
Not bad. Not good. If you're a fan of LotR, give it a try. Play with a friend.

Game that has been released halfway through development. Would recommend only to die-hard Final Fantasy fans but they already have played this game.
The battle system has a lot of potential and can keep interest up for the game. Unfortunately the game suffers from unsufficient testing and being published too soon. There are many points in time that that you end up wondering "what on earth were the developers thinking when they did this?" If this had not been a Final Fantasy game I would have stopped playing much earlier but I thought that when the problems surfaced were just lone hiccups.
Quite often you find yourself losing a fight with no idea what you did wrong. This happens even if you have your party leveled up as much as they can be at those points. You simply have to google what to do. Even then you might be left wondering why the solution you googled worked.
The final straw for me was the final boss. The fight was going completely fine and was taking way quite some time as the final battles tend to do until I suddenly just lost and I didn't understand why. I had to google the last attact the boss had used (one it had used couple of times during the fight). The thing is the final boss has an attack that has a 50% chance to kill a party member. If you party leader dies, you lose the fight. Having 3 party members this means every time the boss uses that attact you have a 15% chance of losing the fight.
I really like the game and I look forward seeing it on multiplataform multiplayer someday. =)

Been immersed recently in Rebel Galaxy, though the game lacks the ability to move up and down, it makes up for it in the following ways.
1- The Music is perfect, every time I go into space combat in EVE or STO or any other space game; Star Citizen, Elite, etc. I always have to patch into Pandora and set some rock and roll or techno. This is the first space game I never touch Pandora in, the music is perfect for the combat and for the moment.
2- The variation of ships for a game at this price point makes me wonder why its not more expensive. To me this game's value would have to be set at 39.99 or 49.99. I have seen games at a 60 dollar price point that has less content and less hours of gameplay than this. Everything from frigates to Dreadnoughts are in the game with unique and epic designs to be found in each one.
3- The Story for me is actually interesting, without making any spoilers, I am very interested to see whats next. While doing these missions it reminds me of firefly pulling into a space station and checking the mission board for any missions I can make a few credits on. Get some munitions or better weapons.
4- The graphics are quite good, the explosions are beautiful the weapon designs are stunning. Coming from someone who is an avid player for Star Citizen, to say I'm actually quite pleased with the graphics of this game speaks a lot for itself.
5- Some may not see this as a plus, but you cant just get carried away in combat, not paying attention to your shields, not using your deflector shield and rotating your ship can lead to some frustrating moments when you see your ship explode from damage. I got so into the combat that I didn't realize my ship was taking critical damage and suddenly... BOOOOOM SPOOOSH BA
Only negative I see for this game is the lack of 3 dimensional movement. However I have played games that don't have a jump function and they are amazing. The guys who developed this game did an astounding job making it, and it is a must have in anyone's game library that even remotely likes space ships.

Honestly this game wasn't even on my radar mainly because there are so many space games on steam I generally pass them by. However this game was different after I actually saw some gameplay. It shares many similarities to games I love like Sid Meier's Pirates, Assassin's Creed IV Black Flag, etc. It shares that similar formula, there are many places in the vast emptiness of space where you can trade, take up mission for many different factions, etc. The economy is very in-depth but not complicated when it comes to trading. You can fully customize your ship with many different weapons and modifications (or even buy a new ship). Complete openness as well as many different enormous Solar Systems you can travel to and from. The most unique part of this game though, is the music. The music is very odd for a space, sci-fi oriented game however that just makes it even more epic with its t'wang of country or southern-rock-inspired music. I also have not come across any glitches or crashes yet. I would easily give this game a 10/10.

Review update [July 2014]
Note: I am currently playing on an Xbox One controller rather than trying my old flight stick setup because the game had problems with detecting and configuring it at game launch (though I have heard Egosoft has added official *working* support for joysticks). Will be interesting to see if it actually works. Too lazy to set it up at the moment.
Devs have addressed a lot of the initial problems at launch (Free Update 2.0), making this game tolerable so far. Mods help push the current release into some pretty good territory. AI still sucks sometimes (which was always a problem with the X series) and the equipment selection is still lacking (I'm sure mods and official parts will be coming in after they close off the rest of the major bugs/UI problems), but otherwise very playable. New official cockpit modifications are nice.
TLDR: The game has improved a lot since day one, to the point where it is very playable. Still a lot that needs to be addressed. You'll probably want to use a console controller, however, as the game was designed for that at the get-go.

After playing a couple of hours of Civ Beyond Earth, thanks to the free weekend, I really felt it diffcult to like this game at all. As an avid fan of Civ 5, over 350 hours played, I wanted, really wanted to like this game, but it was just too difficult.
The biggest problem with Civ beyond Earth is... the future. The great thing about History and historical technologies is we can relate to them. For instance I know instantly that a rifleman is better than an archer or Infantry is better than gatling gun. But in in beyond earth I haven't a clue if a roaming rover is better than a Marine or a "soldier". Speaking of relating to these units, its the same for buildings and wonders. They are so difficult to relate to as they are made up seemingly out of thin air. A barracks in Civ 5 I know what that will do but a repair facility... meh not a clue.
Other Cons:
UI - Why have they turned Civ 5's easy to follow UI upside down, buttons like "Return to map" move all over the place and making a UI flat and boring is not "the future".
Research Tree, if you can follow this then your one step ahead of me. This confusing map of clickable icons is awful. Please go back to the horizontal research which was simple to follow.
To the Sid Meier's team, I wanted to like this game, I really did but please, stick with history or at least combine the two, the future isn't all it's cracked up to be!

Most reviews lately have been negative due to the bug-filled innitial release of this game. However, I can positively say that as of the 2.0 release, almost all of the bugs many people complained about have been fixed. Thats not to say that there are no bugs, as there are still a few, but the majority of them that damaged gameplay have been resolved. Anyone who is a fan of previous X series games would love this game. In addition, there are many mods out there that also enhance gameplay, and make the game easier or more interesting, depending on how you use them (I.E the "no fuel cells for player ships" mod and others).
To those who have the game, i've noticed that many people complain on the difficulty of completing the main story line station construction mission, due to the fact that the only stations that sell most of the materials needed for station construction at that poin of the story line are hostile towards you. I found enjoyment in this fact, as I spent lots of time hunting down ships carrying the needed resources, and had to spend time creating plans in order to raid the enemy ships, bring in ships to collect the resources, and safely transport them back to my station construction area. To those who dont want to spend time finding the resources, or want to simply create their own empire with numerous stations and ships, you can easily modify your save game files using notepad ++ or other XML editing software, however notepad ++ is much easier to use. Any information in regards to modifying the game files, simply look online, there are many topics about it, especially since the initial release of the game occasionally needed this to work (but as I said these problems have been solved since the 1.25-2.0 release).
To those who wish to get into the X seriese games, or are new to them, my recomendation is that you start with the previous ones, like X3 terran conflict or albion prelude, before starting X rebirth in order to understand some of the backstory that (at least to me) is very interesting. For those who have experience with the X series games, I recomend this game 110%. But people must realize that while it is an X seriese game, it is not an expansion of X3. It is its own stand alone game that expands the story of the x universe. People trying to compare it to its predecessors does not give this game justice, as it has many fetures that i found were missing in previous x games, that makes this game feel more lively. not to mention the universe itself is absolutely gorgeous and stunning graphic-wise. My recomendation to those having trouble with the game, mess around with the controls and commands, and you will see how simple some things are that once upon a time seemed difficult and unable to work.
I hope this has helped all those thinking of buying this game, and all those who had it, but chose not to play it due to previous bugs and problems that might have been fixed since the latest patch. All this being said, i look forward to egosofts next update, and hope they expand the main storyline with new stories, missions, AND THE ♥♥♥♥ING BORON!!!! I MISS MY SQUID ALIEN FISH THINGIES! I WANT THE BORON TO COME INTO THE GAME LIKE GENGHIS KHAN AND SAY YOLO TO THEIR PEACEFUL WAYS DAMNIT! :D happy xenon hunting everyone:)

As most reviews say, this is not the Hitman you know, this is very different. The levels are not as big as some of the previous games, but if you ask me, they are way more detailed and more options than the previous Hitman games. You don't get to much of an open world anymore, but more a, get from point A to Point B style. i was skeptical about this at first, but grew to love it, even though it's a From point A to B, you still get alot of diversion and ALOT of choices on how you wanna get there. The new disguise system is 50/50, i love how it adds to the realism. The cop will know you are not one of his colleagues, but how is the civillian to know that you are not a cop? It is a bit to sensitive though, even though you are standing with your back to a guy who is 6-7 meters away he will still notice that you are not one of them, and that is a bit to much. You don't get to choose what weapons and equipment you wanna use anymore at the start of the game though, but i think this adds to the fun, and it works well with the story, this also means that you don't have a pocket filled with thousand coins anymore, instead you gotta find objects around the world, that you can use as distractions/weapons, this is also a welcome change.
The story is also a big part of Absolution, in the previous games. You got your mission and then you executed it, however you felt like and that was that, and that was good, cause that's why you played it.
I felt alot more motivated to keep going in this one, cause of the story and what happend in it, and even though i mostly try to do it stealth with none or a few extra casualties , there was just places where i went in guns blazing cause i didn't think the ones i was up against deserved to live. I also had some really heartpounding moments, cause i was so focused on killing my target for one reason or another and that rarely happens to me.
On that note, it also alot funnier to do fire fights in Absolution: When you empty your 45 cal. UMP magazine into a guy and you see him spasm all over the place as he falls to the ground, feels really awesome.
All in all I will give this game a 9/10 it is a great game, but with a few things i would like tweeked, but these things are so minor that they can be looked through pretty easly. Don't expect the next version of Blood Money, but a deeper more involved game.

The Last Remnant is a game of questionable ideas and fantastic gameplay. The plot is decent, the writing is horrendous and the main character is an idiot with retard strength. But if you can get past the story portions of the game, the game will reward you greatly for your time. I'm not even past the Disc 1 portion of the game and already sunk 25 hours while doing the side quests and searching for the rare monster fights, it is just that satisfying to run around and explore.
The game relies heavily on explorating and grinding monsters for stuff. You cannot directly control what your team mates equip, but you can control what skills they use and if you get the resources they want, they will upgrade their own gear. You assemble your team in groups that attack together at the same time against other groups and give loose orders on what they do. Because of that, it is highly encouraged you disable skills you don't want your units to randomly choose.
The grinding of monsters can get tedious, to the point where I would skip monsters to finish quests faster. The good news is you can save anywhere, anytime outside of battle, and even autosave after fights in case you forget. That alone makes the grinding bearable since you can take breaks without needing to skip monsters if you want to loot the area clean.
Besides the story I previously mentioned, the biggest downfall to this game is they do not at all describe what the stats do in the game. If you get gear that gives +1 to sword, there is nowhere in the game that tells you how big of a boost you can get. Thankfully, people datamined the game code and found out the exact stats, so you can utilize that in the wiki website for The Last Remnant. Makes the game at least have some sort of sense. It plays like Saga Frontier (also made by SquareSoft) in that way where all you need to know is high stats are good, right? Maybe? Perhaps?
If you want to play a tactical turn based RPG you can play for a long time, I recommend this one quite a bit. I got it on sale for $3 and was worth the price so far. I reckon it'll be another 50 hours before I beat the game. That be a lot of messing around, I tell ya what.

tl;dr: This is good game. Cheap for what you get, lots of mods. Good optimization, much pretty. Music nice, gameplay nice, must play for space RTS fans.
Sins of a Solar Empire is a space RTS with no campaign, but endless replayability. Every game, the universe that the game is played in is randomized, or selected from a premade map (which offer specific challenges to make the game more interesting). There can be many stars in one universe, and each star can have very few or very many planets, asteroids, wormholes, etc.
The game offers a very nice blend of combat, research, and dimplomacy. But research really trumps everything, which leads into one of Sins' flaws...
. This game will kick your♥♥♥♥♥if you are a newcomer to the RTS genre, and even if you are a veteran, you will find a good challenge. This game is not for the easily frustrated, because going against AI, or other players, can really pump up the blood pressure sometimes.
The game itself runs very well for my system. I'm running it on an AMD FX 6300 Processor, NvidiaGTX 660, with 8 GB of RAM, and it runs perfectly fine. It is very well optimized and looks beautiful. The backgrounds of space look phenomenal and the ships look pretty good too. Watching the space battles can be so nice to look at that you forget to make sure they are actually doing alright.
Anyway, This game is worth the $40, but I would also cash in for the DLC, because they are very good for the price. The modding potential for this game is amazing as well. If you ever get bored of the basic game, you can just browse the giant selection of quality mods on Moddb. If there is a popular movie/TV/game/book series taking place in space, there is a good possibility that there is a well made mod already created, or being crafted of it.
Thanks for reading, if you got this far, and I hope this review helps, although the fact that there are already 1,000's of positive reviews made for this game should be a clear indication of the quality of Sins of a Solar Empire: Rebellion.

Crysis 1 can easily stand the test of time.
It's graphics are still nice to look at. The landscape is amazing and you will find yourself lost for minutes just looking at the environment.
In it's core Crysis 1 is a sandbox shooter.
And yes there is a story but the game isn't about it.
Story summary:
USA good!
Aliens bad!
North Korea worse!
Where Crysis 1 can shine is in the sandbox like levels. Most the time you will start in an open landscape with a primary target and one or more secondary targets. And that's where the fun begins!
The level are so open and allow you to solve the same mission in almost infinite ways and this is because of two reasons:
1. Your suite. The nano suite you are using has a lot of different powers. It allows you to jump extremely high, run faster then most vehicles, armor up or even cloak (which is overpowered as hell!). By combining those skills you can use completely different strategies on each map.
One time you will use cloak and play the level as a stealth game. You kill out of the shadows and kill dozens of enemies without ever being seen.
The next time you armor up and use close range fire arms to go in all guns blazing.
Or you get a long range sniper rifle kill a few enemies from a high point (by using your jumping skill for the nano suite) use the run ability to get away to the next sniper point and start sniping the next few enemies.
Or you let them spot you but prepare with a few mines or some C4.

Rivals of aether is a smash bros like game with different characters for the pc. But it isn't just a smash bros knock off its a good game with a lot of potential but I do not like a few things about the game.
1. DLC Characters
so you get a very small collection of characters (only 8) but each one all has individual playstyles and there own ways to be played so its pretty interesting playing them all and finding out how you can play them. But even still 8 characters isn't a huge amount. So they released 3 other characters each costing around 5$ each (apparently you can buy them all for 9$ but I can't seem to find it). While that is annoying for characters to be so expensive even rivaling Super smash bros, the real issue is the unfair advantage they recieve. So all characters have there own playstyle and seem evenly balanced but the dlc characters have special things that no other character can do which is understandable but its not fair when they are better than the base characters. Like take Clairen he has a parry (which is a lot like the standing block which stuns the other character) but instead of stunning the other character it creates a huge area where no projectiles are useable which is obnoxious in itself but clairens parry is far longer than the basic parry every other character has. Another example is Rannos bubble stun thing, Ranno can apparently stack a debuff on you maxing out at about 5 I believe which increases the time of his stun that he has (A yoshi like move and incapacitates the opponent by putting them in a bubble and allowing Ranno to attack the opponent). This would be completely fair except for the fact that another character has a move that can also incompacitate the opponent which is etalus, but its much harder to use and easily dodge-able while Ranno's is very fast easy to use and doesn't leave you open to an attack afterwards which Etalus's does.
2. Online fighting
So online is hard, so hard it makes me not want to play. Why dont I just "get good" right? It just doesn't seem worth it to me every time I que I either am physically unable to touch the opponent or completely roll them. There should deffinentely be a ranking system where it ranks peopel vs time played rather than just tossing you into a match with a pro that doesn't even let you touch them. I wouldn't suggest purchasing this game to anyone that doesn't have friends that would also play with them.
Also an added note it seems dumb that there is no real 4 player mode only 2 local vs 2 local Hopefully they update this in the future.
3. Campaign
The campaign is rather bland and a bit confusing at times and ultimately just short (You can beat it in about a half n' hour if your fast) with 2 other characters never introduced and to not have them in the campaign is a bit odd. I also feel that you should be able to unlock a character for completing the campaign.
All in all Rivals of aether seems like a game that has some passion but falls short in a few areas. I would only suggest this to you if you either hate yourself and wanna punish yourself in online play by being beaten over and over or have friends willing to play with you.

This War of Mine is not mainly focused on destroy this, beat this, or finish him, but more focused on other elements of surviving in the middle of a war like... how are you going to eat? Mainly, most of this leads up all up to two main things in the game, survival and your humanity. It's also about the type of person you become after or during the war. Are you a bandit? Are you a vigilante? Or are you just someone who just wants to survive? You want justice to all the bad people in the game? You have to bring justice yourself, there is sadly no other way in this game. Also, the game also points out another thing, you aren't a soldier or some super hero, you are only human. Which means you can't go with guns and just expect to take down 5 people with a pistol when they have assualt rifles and shotguns. Which means your best combat option is usually a stealth kill or a backstab. This game shows you a lot of terrible things about war, this may conflict within you like the supermarket girl, if you haven't played the game before be warned of the spoiler up ahead,
You can maybe just say, "It's just a video game, it's not real life", but if you do or when you play this game, treat this like its real life, this game is here to make you question your own beliefs about what is right and what is wrong.

Magic Duels is moderate entertainment if you don't mind a huge grind or don't mind throwing money at the problem (in this case, the problem being a buggy game). I don't recommend it because there are glitches dealing with the currency system -- honestly, currency that is purchasable with real money is the LAST thing a game should have problems with...
However, I personally do not recommend it. Here are a few negatives:
(1) In the many hours I have spent in this game, I have never encountered an AI that didn't play a land in their first five or six turns. I don't know if the AI "cheats" but I suspect so. I have been land starved after 4 lands in about 20% of my games using the decks given to me -- surely the AI is using similar compositions. Which leads to #2...
(2) Get used to hitting the "Restart Game" in the Story Mode (to grind the currency a bit faster than head-to-head games). After completing the entire story mode including all the tutorials, I had enough currency to ... (WAIT FOR IT) ... buy six booster packs. The only thing sadder is that this is *significantly* faster than grinding in head-to-head games.
(3) I have completed quests, seen the 40 gold checked and move towards my currency total, and then had no currency added. This happened to me most recently just a few minutes ago, and after wasting time creating a new deck to finish a quest, and then not being rewarded, I can safely not recommend this game to nearly anyone.
I have played earlier Magic titles, and surprisingly... wait, no, *UN*surprisingly from this company, this is the worst one of them all.

PROS:
-Familliar interface to fans of Duel of the planeswalkers 2013
-Earning coins via victory means eventual free boosters and incintive.
-Big player base, never left waiting too long day/night
-Freedom to build and use custom decks, much more lenient than 2013 (whish only allowed preset decks in online)
-Just like the real MTG!
-Wonderful art, nice enough soundtrack and neat stories involving the planeswalker's origins
-F2P! Though paying is encouraged it's not at all required, Boosters can be earned by in game objectives alone. (but take much longer)
-Updates! They say that this game will update along with the real card game meaning new things are always on the horizon.
CONS:
-Definantly easier for people who pay for coins/boosters. You get a nice amount to begin with but better cards remain hidden.
-Game can sometimes have connection issues when trying to join a friend to play, either kicking the invited player from the room or placing them on the wrong team.
-Matchmaking seems like it ought to try harer to match you closer, might be for lower wait times but the skill difference can be seen.
-No coin rewards for two headed giant victories with friends.
-Even the easier difficulties seem a bit rough, discouraging new players.
-2HG dosen't seem to have a text chat for team/opponents like 2013 did, it supports headsents but this can be inconvenient for those who cant/dont use headsets.
In total MDO is a mixed bag that is overall good. It could be greater than it is with some minor polishing but for being F2p for the most part theres no harm in trying. If your a real MTG fan then i reccomend trying it out and even buying some boosters to get a more unique deck. (the starter decks are very simmilar) Overall if you want a MTG game with plenty of opponents and constant updates on par with the official game, then look no further.
3/5 Stars!

Although I only spent a little time playing this game, I was unfortunately disappointed. I was very excited to get a Smash Bros. clone with original characters and fighting styles. I grew up on Sega Genesis and enjoy seeing 8-bit/16-bit games appear from developers.
My biggest gripe is that the controls feel clunky and difficult to maneuver. I have been played countless hours of Super Smash Bros. and Super Smash Bros. Melee which I use in comparison to the controls included in this game.  While I do recognize that this game is its own entity and an exact replica of the controls is not realistic, Rivals of Aether seems to fall short here. I played with a Xbox One controller and immediately noticed the jump function was defaulted to Y, which feels very odd in a game that primarily uses buttons for attacks. Fortunately, You can change the controls to use Up on your joystick if you want a more classic feel.
Rivals of Aether has well designed retro graphics, but lackluster character design. The moves associated with characters are fairly predictable; however they are unique to the genre. As for the bizarrely short story mode, each character has a "story" in which they fight through several matches (5 I think?) before reaching the end. In my short time playing, I was able to complete two "stories", even while fighting with the controls the entire time. It is tough to recommend this game, though I feel there are some who may enjoy it.

What makes me sad is that Bioshock 2 has been treated like the illigitimate child of the Bioshock series for far too long.  There is a certain beauty found in playing this game, and it has by far one of my all time favorite written DLC's that I have ever had the pleasure to play.  If you're on the fence about playing this game or simply don't know enough about it to jump here's my top reasons as to why this game is worth the second look:
It shows you parts of Rapture you could only dream about.  At the end of the first Bioshock we turned ourself into a "Big Daddy" to complete our task and bring resolution to the "Rapture nightmare" but did you ever think that perhaps there was a much bigger story left to enjoy? Sure you could play the first game over and over again, combing through each audio diary but there still felt like there was more story to tell behind Rapture.  We never really got to experience "Big Daddy-hood" for its true raw nature, sure we wore the suit but what did we do with it? Nothing except use a sister to obtain our goal.  In Bioshock 2 they took that experience and gave us a more indepth look at the relationship of the Big Daddy and Little Sister.  We could explore outside of those collapsed tunnels, walk the ocean floor (while finding some Adam slugs on the way), and use the weapons we only dreampt about before.  We finally learn what it is like to care about the Little Sister as she gathers, and we are given more weighted consequences in our actions.
The environment is still very much the Rapture we knew and loved from the first game and is filled with a wonderful cast of characters that really gives the game a new meaning.  Sophia Lamb is an enigma we just love to learn about, did she truly love the daughter she created or was there more behind her legacy than even she knew? Each plot twist lovingly crafted, leaving us at the edge of our seats until we reach the end and see the fruit of our labor.  How did we craft the daughter we may not have wanted? Our actions are given true meaning with every step we take, every moment we interact.  Now I'm not saying breaking a lamp has a tragic consequence, but the people we meet, the sisters we save or harvest, each one is weighted with a consequence.
The DLC, I will always mention Minerva's Den when I talk about Bioshock 2 because it is really one of the best stories game-wise I have ever had the pleasure of playing.  We are subject Sigma, and our story takes place in the paralell of the main events of Bioshock 2.  As Tennenbaum said herself, "there are others I must save before the city drowns," this is what she meant.  In the final part of this game we learn about "The Thinker" the central hub of Rapture, the only thing capable of helping Tennenbaum reverse the "Rapture Nighmare" once and for all.  This DLC put the lid on Rapture once and for all, tying up any loose ends that we may have felt were left behind when Jack took the bathysphere to the surface with those little girls (err good ending anyways), and if you're the type that enjoy's a good "feel" from your games, this DLC really slams it home.
Finally, though I could keep going forever about how much I love this game, it's a game that gives you many options on how you want to face the end.  There is no right or wrong way to play this game, much was the way with the first game.  True there are certain objectives you must complete, but there is no right or wrong way to achieve them.  You can be as thourough or as fast paced playing this game as you'd like.  It's a game that can be run in an hour 25 minutes or can be run in several hours, it's up to you.  I find I always get lost in the story and so I take my time, but others will run this game for the sport of it (as it will be run at the 2014 SGDQ), there is not right or wrong way to enjoy it, just so long as you have fun playing it.  So get up and grab your keyboard and mouse (or your favorite controller) and give Rapture a try, would you kindly?

If I could give FFXIII a neutral review, I probably would. But I enjoyed it, and at the end of the day that is all that really matters. There is no arguing that the game has serious issues, but if you take it for what it is, and not what it isn't, it is still solid. Treat it as more of a cinematic experience, rather than whatever your preconceptions of what a JRPG should be. Of course, the issues of it being hugely linear are not to be discounted just because of that, but viewed through that lens it makes more sense.
What you think of the game will ultimately be decided on how you feel about the combat system. I like it well enough, but I can understand hating it. I suggest watching a video or two if this would be a deal-breaker.
There is also an issue of performance, and lemme just say that the game can't hold a steady frame rate. Pretty sure it is a porting issue, and it does take away from the experience. I never had a single crash, though, so there is that.
Also, I originally played the game years ago on the Xbox with English voices. This time I played with Japanese voices and had a better experience. If you aren't allergic to subtitles, I suggest you do the same.
The biggest point in the game's favor is actually the price. This is a classic example of being totally worth it for $10 but highly questionable at $60. You could make many a worse purchase than FFXIII if you catch it on sale.

Yet, it has drawn a lot of criticism from gamers. I think the main "problem" of Beyond Earth is that it carries the legacy of not only one, but _two_ immensely popular games (Alpha Centauri, and Civ 5), and it cannot really pull ahead of either of those.
BE borrows most of its mechanics directly from Civ 5. They just got renamed - "happiness" became "health", "gold" became "energy", etc. Most mechanics of the Civ 5 expansions were not included in BE, which is a problem for many Civ 5 players, who tend to think that the expansions were what made Civ 5 enjoyable. BE does try to add some new things: The tech web allows very flexible research strategies. The victory conditions are new ideas, fit the setting, and are mechanically solid. The "orbital layer" adds tactical depth (but seems underused). So the innovation _is_ there, but only in some details, so veteran Civ 5 players will still get the feeling that they "lost" the Civ 5 expansion content and are basically playing an elaborate mod of the Civ 5 base game.
BE borrows most of its _setting_ from its spiritual predecessor, Alpha Centauri. It can't use the exact same setting due to legal issues, but the parallels are obvious. Unfortunately, the setting is BE's weakest point. Where Alpha Centauri featured interesting characters, an overarching story of the planet's exploration, and a clash of ideologies that permeated every fiber of the game (down to leaders providing voiceovers with ideologically colored, well written comments about researched technologies), BE feels surprisingly bland in that regard. It feels as if the devs didn't even try to flesh out the setting, but just took some civs from Civ 5 and reskinned the leaders. Coincidentally, there is currently another 4x game on the market (Endless Legend) which has its strengths exactly in the lore and atmosphere aspects, which makes BE's shortcomings in that regard all the more obvious.
Unfortunately, BE also fails to correct that one major flaw of "Alpha Centauri" - the weak AI. The game sticks to the "one unit per tile" paradigm from Civ5, and the AI still can't handle it. The AI is incapable of positioning its forces efficiently, it doesn't read the terrain well, and it still cannot plan ahead simple movements. I've seen units being sent into certain death because the pathfinding insisted to send them through miasma tiles when other options were available. I've seen the same unit going back and forth a dozen times when I simply opened or blocked a passage. I've seen AI units sitting uselessly on the same spot for ages. I've seen the AI sacrificing a dozen planes to my interceptors instead of using the "sweep" mission just once. I've seen an AI from another continent first sending a colonist to mine, then settling there without sending any units, and then (after I conquered the outpost) asking for peace and offering me one third of their empire: a full-fledged city on their continent, that I hadn't even discovered yet, so I posed no threat to that AI whatsoever.
That said, if you strip away the legacy of Civ 5 and Alpha Centauri, then BE is quite a decent game. It still has complex gameplay (just don't focus on what was "lost" compared to the other games), it still has an interesting setting (just don't focus on how SMAC's setting was much more enticing), it does bring interesting new things to the table. It _is_ very enjoyable as a 4x game, the mechanics are solid, and it's not as bug-ridden as new 4x games tend to be.
Since the game itself seems decent, BE's "not being able to escape its legacy" issue would probably not be much of a problem _if_ the game were priced accordingly, at perhaps 30€. With an initial price tag of 50€, though, I think people started focusing on what BE is not, instead of appreciating what it is. Coincidentally, it's on sale for 30€ now, and I believe that it's worth that. It would probably have received a much warmer welcome if it had been offered for that price from the start.

To be very honest with you, I don't know why people are complaining about this game. My only lead on it is that the others have played the previous CiV games, but in this case, I have not. So this is coming from someone straight out of the series!
And I really enjoy it so far!
Yes, the game gets really confusing for the first 20-30 minutes of playing. But after a while, you start to get what everything does and it just clicks in.  I've been playing this for a good while now to give some opinion on it.
Pros:
+The game itself is VERY pretty.  When I saw the opening cutscene for it, I just almost floored.  If you hate this game, you can't diss that it's visually appealing.  Throughout the game it manages to keep that way as well!
+Detailed Actions. What I mean by this is that it gives you a full explanation of what you are doing. Not tutorial wise, but just how everything is set-up and how it will work.
+Addicting. Yes, the game is very addicting. I can't seem to get off this thing! I don't know how the CiV series compares to this one, but I'll have you know that this will keep me in my chair for a couple of days if I'm getting deep into a game.
Cons:
-Confusing. As I said before, the game will start to make sense after a while. But the tutorial itself isn't really a tutorial.  All it does, is point out a few things you should know and just sets you off free to figure out what you are doing. This is a good thing in most games, but it is not for this one.
Opinionated:
-+Very slow. This is a game that requires a lot of patience and stragety. If you are not into either one of these, then I suggest you're better off looking for another game.
Overall Review:
I was really surprised when I played CiV:BE.  Most of the people that have played the previous installments would disagree when I say that this game is actually really enjoyable to play.  If you've played the other CiV games, I might say to pass on it, even though you should give it a shot. But if you were like me, who hasn't played any of those games and is new to this genre in general, then you should give it a try. It might just surprise you and keep you in your seat!

Very upset to say, this game is not what I expected. Luckly I purchased this game at a much later date when it was being sold for 50% off. As much as I want to recommend a game that developers put a ton of time into, I just cannot do it with X rebirth.
Here are the reasons why:
1.) We'll start with the campaign; One thing I like about Syfi games is immersion. If you can make me feel like I'm in living breathing world with things to do at ever corner, you've done a good job. Now I must admit they almost had me but when I found out that NPC's in the game where not actually doing anything they're simply there for cosmetic purposes, that killed me.
2.) Voice acting, simply put, if I wanted to go see or hear talentless actors, I'd watch Twilight. The voice acting is absolutly, (ABSOLUTLY) atrocious. Coupled with bad resolution NPC models which a player would easily see that they all look simlar to one another, like a universe with a obvious incest problem.
What I don't understand if you would go to the lengths to make the outer world beautiful, and unique. Why not apply that same work when you're inside the station walking around? Keep in mind AAA graphics is not the bread-and-butter of a game, but keeping graphics the consistant through out definitely helps.
3.)  I've played the earlier installments of the 'X series' and enjoyed them very much, personally one of the things I enjoyed the most was being able to switch ships around for bigger and badder ones. Although piloting a ship is one-hundered times better in X Rebirth, you are limited to one ship. Many people will aurgue this, but point blank if you're going to compete with today's space sims this is a feature your game is going to need.
The good:

1.) With all that said, the game does have it's good side. One, being piloting the ship and navagating through menus is awesome, takes some time to learn.

2.) The "outer world" (when you're flying in space, near station (ect...). Is beautiful! And very futuristic looking.
3.) The game does offer things to do being: Minging, Gas harvesting, Station building, Trading, and exploring.
4.) I'll give it to Egosoft, they know they fu(ked up. But are working to impove the games mechanics, and any game braking issues. Hopefully the game will have a birghter furture, we'll see.

I'm not good at reviewing games, but I figured with a childhood classic like this, it would be good to tell those who are new to the old Wolfenstein games what this game has to offer. This may be long, but worth skimming if you're interested in buying.
As a child, game mechanics, wonky controls, poor story and bad graphics were completely ignored and off our radars as young, fresh gamers. I remember my dad playing this game on our Windows 98 desktop. We had the Game of the Year edition which I own to this dad, but sadly got corrupted, so I bought the Steam version. My dad and I were blown away by the destructable objects, hidden areas and terrifying enemies. Now, coming back to it a decade and a half later, the novelty as not worn off. It feels the same and thinking about it critically makes me more impressed at how well this game has stood the test of time. Coming back to older games, I find myself thinking "This looks like crap" "how did I let that cinematic go and not laugh at its stupidity" "these controls are terrible". Coming back to this, I found myself amazed at the fact that I was only saying "This is still terrifying" "I don't remember that secret room" "Woah, that's awesome."
This game had impressive graphics for its time and gives the same Doom/Quake FPS feel that most early FPS players are accustomed to. What makes this game unique is its level designs, enemies and believe it or not, horror-themed atmosphere build ups. Each level makes you feel like you're in that place and gives you a real sense of presence that other old FPS games completely ignore. The story is great too, though its no Metal Gear Solid or other intricate storylines, but it gives you a goal, an enemy and context. You really take on the role of an OSA agent fighting advanced Nazi technology. The action unfolds around you where in modern shooters it would be in a cutscene free from your control. The music and ambience doesn't get old and adds to the experience and sounds (although silly, like falling bones or collapsing bodies) are superb.
Should you get this game? That's up to you, but not only is this game a pinnacle moment in gaming's "Golden Age", but it is still enjoyable and entertaining to this day. For those new to the Wolfenstein series who may have come in through "Wolfenstein" in 2009 or "The New Order" I highly recommend you check out this stepping stone in the series. Don't get it so you can say you've played it, get it because you will like it.

UPDATE: With the new editor, this game can also double as Baltimore Simulator 2015.
This game is basically Ukraine Simulator 2015.
The Good:
- There isn't really a tutorial, which helps to create an atmoshpere of caution as you play through the game. You get relatively few characters to use, each with their own benefit, so losing even one may have dire consequences.
- The gameplay has the right amount of challenge to it. If you play smart, you should be alright but if you do not, you will not survive. The fact that the game is unforgiving also helps to evoke the sense of desperation present in the characters' situation.
- The environment. With the right tools, you can begin to destroy things like cabinets to scavenge them for parts.
- The art style. The way the game handles shading, and your characters' field of vision, is great.
- The game evolves as you play. Did you leave a pile of wood in that rubble, for later? Getting back to it may suddenly become impossible, between the fighting and the snow. And if you do get back to it, there's no guarantee it'll even be there, if the area you're going has people at it. It makes the choice between that can of food, or that bunch of planks, all the more important.
- Your characters give you feedback about the choices that they make, and their feedback can have tangible results in gameplay. Generally, the more horrible you are to your fellow man, the sadder your little group becomes, which seems to effect how quickly they move, or perform tasks.
This game is very immersive. If you were a fan of the Fallout Series, but also enjoy a more "serious", even dark, atmosphere, this game is definitely for you.
The Bad:
- The game gets repetitious, during the day cycle.
- "Realism". This War of Mine does a good job of drawing you into the setting, but at the same time there are a lot of little things that break one's suspension of disbelief. The way the game squishes time means that it can take your people a half an hour to climb two ladders and walk a hundred feet to answer the door. In a game focused on gathering and survival, there are a lot of things that you can't scavenge. Doors, and the planks barring the doors, I'm looking at you. Papercuts also generally don't require rolls of bandages to combat. And closing doors doesn't seem to increase the temperature in your shelter any, when it starts getting cold. Also, why I have to purify my water before I boil it, I'll never know.
- The game's "Good choice/bad choice" moments are pretty generic "do the good and inconvenient thing/do the bad and helpful thing" survival choices. Where the decision making really begins to get murky, is with the internal choices such as "Who gets to eat?" (Sorry I let you starve Bruno, but the irony of the cook starving was too amusing).
- The level of interaction you have with other people is limited in comparison to games with similar themes.
- There is no tutorial. This is also in the Good category. This is also bad because the game does not explain how combat works, so the first few times a situation goes sideways you will probably lose due to figuring out what does what.
This is a slower-paced game. If you are a fan of flashier/shooter games, and not a fan of micromanagement, this game probably isn't your cup of tea.
All in all? I'd rate this game a solid 8.5/10.

People seem to be comparing this £15.00 (or equivalent) game to a Triple-A title. Fifteen pounds, that's the equivalent of a meal in a restaurant - hell.. less than a meal. You can't compare this to GTA, you can't compare this to Battlefield, you can't compare this to Witcher. Why would you? Big-budget organizations vs. a small Polish games company with a considerably lesser budget and experience.
The game isn't perfect, the A.I. is buggy at times, the performance isn't superb, and aiming with a controller is ridiculously difficult. That being said, you have to appreciate the game for what it DOES do right (and it does a 'lot' of things right).
The art style is superb, I'm sure I'm not the first to compare it to something like Sin City, but I'm going to anyway. The game is predominantly black-and-white, with certain items and effects being in colour. Sirens flash blue and red, explosions are shades of orange and yellow, and blood is purple. No, I'm just kidding, it's red. Very red. The destruction system is superb. You can shatter glass windows, blow holes through walls, drive vehicles THROUGH buildings, it's phenomenal. The whole feel of the game is incredibly sinister. Sure, you can do these things on GTA, but it's not stylized to be a rampage 'sim', if you will. Hatred on the other hand, represents indiscriminate murder for the sake of it. The screams of innocent people as you slit their throat, set them on fire, shoot them through the head, all sounds so real.
People also argue the game was made to be 'edgy'. I hate that word. The developers set out to make a game of their choosing, and they did so successfully. They didn't need to advertise the game, because the media sh*tstorm that occurred as a result of such a game did it for them. People criticize that, whereas I praise it. It might seem like a simple premise, so why did nobody do it sooner? Destructive Creations had the balls to do it, and it paid off.
I wouldn't say the game has huge replay value. That being said, it's not pretending to be something it's not. If you're willing to sacrifice a meager sum of money for a few hours fun here and there, I'd highly recommend it.

I wanted to recommend this game because, at hour 4 of gameplay, I found it to be very entertaining. However, the hours I spent playing after the 4th began to show its flaws, and there are many of them. What This War of Mine delivers is a fantastic idea for a game genre: A civilian-based point of view of war/disaster survival. What it does not deliver is a well-executed game to back up the hype surrounding it.
To start things off, it has a few very distinct separations from reality that make it far less immersive. For all of the worry about food and sleep for the survivors, there is zero concern for water consumption. In a survival situation, the human body can go for several days without sleep and, depending on the body type, a week or more without food. However, the human body, in a survival situation, cannot go for more than a day without water before serious problems begin to arise. There is also no difference between each character for how much food or sleep each needs to survive. Everyone takes the same time to sleep and the same food to sustain operation. Another aspect of reality that is lacking is the inability to send out multiple scavangers. The game quickly becomes a food/parts farming game, which is made more difficult by the fact that only one person leaves the house at night. In a survival situation, everyone has a job. If there are 4 people in a house (which can happen in this game), that leaves 1 to sleep, 1 to guard, and 2 to scavange. This limiting factor contributes to the linear point of the game. A linear game would be fine, in this case, if it had any replayability. This is my major gripe about This War of Mine: It is only good for one playthrough (maybe only a half) before it becomes dull.
In its advertisement, this game was described as having a "randomized world and characters every time you start the game". There is painfully little truth to that statement. There is only 7 possible starting character combinations, and the "Random" button does nothing but pick from one of the 7 preset character combinations. In fact, there are only 12 different characters to play in the entirety of the game, and each is very one-dimentional. If a person could pick a starting group of characters or even have a random character generator built into the game (an easy task with such simple characters), it might be more interesting for another couple of hours. However, there will need to be more than even that to help it live up to its hype.
There are also only 9 different NPC characters that show up at the house during the day, and every one of their stories / side missions is identical from game to game. The night-time NPCs don't fare any better, as each is set to a specific location within each scavanging scenario. That's right, the scavanging scenarios aren't randomized, either. Each of the 21 different (not hundreds, not dozens, but 21) scavanging scenarios is identical from one playthrough to the next. The only thing that is slightly randomized is the loot, and it's only random as to the type and general location of the common loot within each scenario. The NPC movement is not randomized, either. One can memorize the patterns they use and easily avoid NPC detection with a little time. The starting locations even lack randomization. There are also only 2 possible starting shelters to use as a home base, and each is set up in exactly the same fashion with the exception of starting in winter (at which point a woodstove is placed in the shelter and a consumables are added to the loot piles). The only thing I've found through the course of the game to be random is the starting loot in the home base shelter, and even that loot contains the same number of common vs rare items during each start. Even the war length (game time) is hard set at a specific length, which goes to hurt both the replayability AND the realism of the game.
This War of Mine is a horrible execution of a fantastic idea. If it was actually built as a random-generated survival game, it would be one of the best titles that I've played in ages. It could have been something fantastic, but it is either A: unfinished; or B: a linear game being marketed as a replayable survivor sim. As it sits, it is not worth the $20 price (or even the $15 sale price that I purchased it for).

If you're looking for a space pew pew lazorz game, just buy it. Right now. What are you waiting for? Stop reading these words and go buy it.
You're still reading? Fine I'll put more words here that might mean things about stuff. Seriously, though, this game overdelivers its $20 at release date price (or whatever you can get it for on sale). There are plenty of other reviews speaking to what's great about this game, so I won't beat a dead horse. However, I would like to speak to some of the negative comments that I've seen.
"Missions are repetitive." - this is true, but that hasn't reduced my enjoyment of gameplay. Sure the missions are repetitive, but each encounter does have variations within it. There are at least 3 major variations with each mission: mission type, types of friendlies, types of enemies.
There are escort missions (follow a friendly around at warp speed and defend them from attacking hostiles that pull you out of warm), defend missions (move into an engagement and prevent friendlies from being destroyed), destroy missions (fly in guns blazing until everything is on fire, including you), snatch and run / fight missions (fly into an area teeming with hostiles, grab some cargo, and gtfo), delivery missions (get some cargo and deliver it to another station, while being pulled out of warp multiple times from hostiles trying to take your cargo). There are also other types that I haven't done yet (pirate missions).
The other aspect that changes missions are types of friendlies/enemies. Sometimes you're fighting multiple cruisers with minor fighter support, sometimes you're fighting a dreadnaught with tons of fighter support, sometimes you're fighting waves upon waves of fighters - and yes these do require different engagement tactics. Good luck charging into waves of mine layer / bomber fighters with a cruiser and winning.
I also feel like I need to point out that repetitive side missions aren't a new thing. How many times have you collected herbs as a side quest in some other RPG?
"2D space combat" - When I read this before buying it, I wasn't sure how I would feel about it. After playing the game - I just don't care that it's not 3D. I don't feel like it being 3D would make it any more fun, especially with the "broadside" style gameplay (which I do enjoy). The 2D movement environment plus broadside style combat provides enough complexity without making it over-complex. You can still use tactics to use a smaller vessel to take down a larger one. I've used my quick cruiser to take down multiple dreadnaughts by getting behind them so that the only damage I'm taking is from their rear turrets and the occasional heat seeking missile, and they can't turn fast enough to broadside me. Plus with a fast vessel you have enough maneuverability to be able to zig-zag between your broadsides (shields don't depreciate as a whole - but each side is separate, for a total of 4 shields) to be able to keep your shields up, all while staying out of the main line of fire. Or you could just buy a huge ship, get ramming deflectors, AND RAMMING SPEED EVERYTHING TO DEATH. Twice.
"Main Storyline is [insert words]" I'm not sure why people are complaining about the main storyline. At the time of writing this I've had 26 hours in the game and still haven't finished it. Sure it's nothing especially fancy... but it is engaging, and seriously it's a $20 game. I'm not sure what you expect. I've played plenty of single player RPG-style games (ones that ONLY have a main storyline) that I've cleared in under 30 hours, and those were $50-60 at release.
"Soundtrack something or other" I also really enjoyed the soundtrack with it's Firefly vibe, however I would have to agree that it starts getting repetitive. I also have an easy solution. Turn off the music. Play your own if you really want music. Again, for a $20 game the soundtrack exceeds what I would expect.
Final thoughts - the depth and enjoyability of the game overdelivers as a $20 price tag, making it a worthwhile purchase.  I would also like to see (and gladly pay for) some DLC/expansions to further increase the depth of the game (greater variety of missions, more ships, more weapons, more factions, expand main storyline, more musc, online co-op play)

In theory, Grimoire: Manastorm is an interesting idea - a multiplayer shooter with wizards and sorcerer taking the place of futuristic super soldiers. In practice, Grimoire: Manastorm is a low-budget, unpolished shooter that does nothing at all new
Magic schools (of which there are a whopping six) act like a combination of class and weapon. You have frost railguns, fire missile launchers, wind plasma guns, and the like. They're extremely uninspired, and they pretty much are a 1:1 recreation of a couple of archetypal weapons and their secondary fires crammed into a single school of magic with four applications, except slower and with the interesting effects on a cooldown. You can occasionally rain meteors on an opponent, turn him into a rabbit or create an healing tree, but most of the time you'll be running around playing a bad reskin of a futuristic shooter. The effects are cheap, weak and really ugly to look at, and worst of all, they hardly feel like they even have any weight or power behind them at all.
You can also choose a random utility spell, which boils down mostly to various forms of defense, like placing down a very ugly looking shield or becoming temporarily harder to kill, and a mobility spell, like a teleport that literally pops you 1000 units forward with no real effect on your sight and a ping sound that feels like it should belong in a puzzle game, or a wind bolt that's basically a non-damaging clone of one of the Fire spells. They feel just as bland and uninteresting as the combat spells themselves.
The graphics are subpar even for indie games in this day and age and they lack any kind of charm or uniqueness. The setting is null and void, generic fantasy at its worst, and the sound design would be alright for a very bland puzzle game.
There's a free for all mode, and an objective mode that's every point capture mode ever made. Despite the game currently being free to play there's a grand total of 10 servers up, all of which are mostly populated by extremely stupid bots.
it is currently a Early Access title, but considering the developers are tossing this out as a Free Weekend, I have a hunch they feel like it's getting close to release. In its current state, there's very little redeeming about Grimoire: Manastorm to latch on and have hopes for. At its best, it's generic and uninspired, at its worst, it's just plain bad. It needs a serious conceptual, technical and promotional overhaul for it to even be worth considering.

I always rate games the way you are supposed to rate them. "Is the game fun?" Is at the heart of every good review. It looks gorgeous, the battle system promised more than FFX-2 and Lightning looks kickass on the trailers. I do not take the term "boring" lightly. It means the creators messed up somewhere big time.
