A pretty enjoyable old FPS from the early days. I once played this game a few years ago and got bored in the middle of going through the Ancient Burial Site at the beginning. But that was a younger and more foolish me that we don't refer to in conversations anymore. I've returned to Wolfenstein II: Return to Castle (An odd title, but whatever), to look at it professionally as an adult.
For what it's worth, RtCW has a solid story. It's not entirely as clever as saaaaaay.... Half-Life, but it gets it's job done. It's actually quite similar to the style of story that Star Wars: Dark Forces has. You're a gun-toting manly man where the only bit of personality he has is "likes to shoot guns" that goes on a secret mission and slowly uncovers more information on this secret of an evil government and getting tons of huge guns as you finally get to the humongous boss. The plots are pretty identical, when you look at it in that aspect. But what Return holds over Dark Forces is it's more subtle craft of telling it's story. Sure, it has too heavy of a reliance on cutscenes where the information is so thick it might as well be your mum trying to spoon-feed you double-fudge cake (Where as Dark Forces had a little file you could read... well, I can't see that as much better. I guess it's moot point then).
What I mean is... there are points in the story that are crafty. They tell you what's going on without any words at all......... Like Half-Life. BUT they're still commendable! For example, near the end of the game you encounter the Nazi rite ceremony and the Nazis that are left behind have to fend for themselves against the crypt's guardians... and they're sucking at it. By telling how their skins look and the scripted event that happens in-game, it tells you exactly what you need to know without directly telling you.
In fact, there are a few moments you can read letter (though I'm sure most people ignore them because who reads in video games, am I right?) And I ended up reading a few, and I came to a conclusion. Return has a good sense of humor. The little small-talk between Nazis is enjoyable to listen to before you inevitably splatter their brains across the floor, and sometimes it's funny to cross a letter in a top-secret lab where the priority message being send out is for an emergency delivery of chocolate. The game had me laugh at a few parts, I won't lie.
The level design in this game is good, too. It really has a good color-palatte that shows a lot of variety to it. Some scenes make you feel stealthy, some make you feel like you're trampling on unholy grounds, and some make you feel like the next step you take could be your demise. Because this game is very hard. Very hard. It's hard as balls. Well, it's not the most difficult game, but it still is hard. Some of the most irritatingly difficult enemies I've ever faced in an FPS (The Nazi women, the Uber Soldat, the Electro... spinner... thingies) are found in this game. If you like a nice ramping difficulty curve with good level design, here you go.
However, there are some faults in this game. The sound certainly hasn't aged well. Crumbling rocks sound like soundbites from... Half-Life, and some of the voice-acting is a little less that what it could be at parts. But the guns sound fine, and the majority of the voice actors are very decent. And perhaps the best sound is that of your flamethrowere and you move it in circles. THAT is a good sound effect. Another downside is that while the level design is good, it has this vague side to it at times. Where you'll be running around and realizing you missed one small corridor or room because some doors and hallways blend a little too well with the rest of the background and after seeing someone else do it on a walkthrough makes you slap your forehead like you're an idiot or something.
It's not a perfect FPS (Like Half-Life), but Return to Castle Wolfenstein is still an excellent one, that I'd recommend to anyone who wants some great game design and a pretty decent story.

I tried this game when it came out and found it boring since I was playing alone. Figured now that it's aged I could pick up my own copy for cheap, I also got a copy for my girlfriend since she's a LotR fan and coop would spice it up.
Good news is that it was much more entertaining coop but the rest of the game is still pretty bad in my opinion. The game only supported a few resolutions so I had to use a 3rd party program to get it to run at a resolution that didn't look like crap, but it may have been do to this that in some areas of the game I would get screen flickering every so often though it wasn't bad enough compared to how it looked at the wrong resolution so oh well.
The game is buggy, some enemies would teleport to different places even on the hosts screen. They would occationally get stuck in these strange staggered animations loops when hit by a critical attack next to an object. Their bodies would occationally slide on the ground after they'd been knocked down or rotate. It made getting finishing blows pretty difficult. Also enemies bodies would sometimes disappear as soon as they were killed, and seemingly sometimes before they died. There were a few occations where I would use a finishing blow on an enemy and my girlfriend would comment that she couldn't even see the enemy anymore and assumed he was already dead.
The attack animations are pretty repetative. Ranged attacks have a strange auto lock thing. When you fire a shot at an enemy it may decide to hit the air that somehow counts as an enemy that's closer to you. Trying to shoot over a different enemies head will almost surely hit the person you're trying to shoot past. This is super annoying when trying to take out archers, you aim at them but it decides to say you hit the nearby melee enemies instead.
Npc's are crap. This game is clearly meant to be played with 3 people. The npc went down constantly. They make it a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to use their skill points to give them abilities (since they don't seem to level on their own). They body block you all the time making it a fuster cluck just to get through some hallways if you have to turn around. At least 2 times our npc ally didn't even follow us and got stuck on a ledge in the level leaving us to fight alone till we got to another checkpoint.
The story is a bit flat as well. It seems like a good premise, you three are tasked with foiling the plans of a servant of the dark lord trying to conquer the north and helps distract from the presence of the main fellowship trying to destroy the ring of power. Dispite this you end up feeling like you did almost nothing. *Small spoiler* It turns out that at almost the exact same time you kill saurons servant, the one ring was also destroyed, so their army would've fallen to pieces anyway, and saruons death could be the reason why the last boss of the game dies anyway. This isn't the only time where something like this happens either. You befriend one of the great eagles early on, but this freaking eagle steals all the glory it can. There are a few fights where you do all the work, then it turns out that the enemy isn't totally dead, and then in flys Mr. Eagle, getting the killing blow. This would've been find had it not happened multiple times. This is even an option in the last fight which we didn't take since we wanted one boss to our own but then the ring ends up being the reason for his death anyhow.
Lastly the map design. I HATE the way the devs did these maps. There are invisible walls everywhere in this game. The maps are designed to look more open than they are. This makes sense since even in a linear game you want people to feel like they're in a world not walking down a glorified hallway. That said, there are little detour areas where chests and such are usually hidden. These two things do NOT work well together. You get detered from even checking other paths because alot of times an area that looks like a side path has an invis wall that you smash into. Then you assume that another place is just walled off and it ends up being a chest area. So you spend a great deal of the game smashing into immersion breaking walls of solid air. If a dev doesn't want you going somewhere it's almost always better to put a natural looking barrier in your way like a fallen tree or cliff face, but even worse is sometimes these barriers would exist and there'd be an invis wall right in front of them. In Mirkwood there's a stream that has fallen trees in it that would stop you from going that way, but there's an invis wall probably 10 ft in front of those trees so you can't make it to a more natural feeling barrier. Also in Mirkwood there's a tree with an invis wall stopping you from getting right up against it but there's a loot pile there so the wall makes it hard to pick the stupid thing up. Also the game uses  tiny cliffs that you have to walk off but can't get back up since there's no jumping in this game. These serve no purpose at all other than to stop you from walking backwards, this makes no sense to me either since all this does is make it impossible to go back for chests you missed (as happened to us twice) when combat happens to bring you over the ledge. And the checkpoints/loading screens aren't hidden at all. They're big glowing blue barriers you can't pass till all human party members are near them. And sometimes these could be passed as soon as you pressed E meaning they weren't loading anything they were just there to stop you for a bit for no reason at all, and again they're all over. More than once a checkpoint would give us access to a room that had a checkpoint on the exit as well.
If you're a fan of LotR and this game is super cheap you could still check it out, but this was pretty poorly executed in my opinion.

Have you ever wanted to go down to hell just to punch Satan in the face? Well this might be the game for you.
If you have played either of the last saints row games then you have already played this one. It is literally the same as 4 but with a new shiny coat of pixel, now this is not a bad thing in my opinion, but I just wanted to say that before I begin.
So the president has been kidnapped and it is up to Gat to get him/her back from the evil clutches of Satan and his rather cute daughter Jezebel. Kinzie is also there but no one cares about her so moving on. So following the president down to hell on a rescue mission you go about causing the largest amount of havoc as you possibly can whilst making a few friends and allies in the along the way.
The main meat of the game is its rather large and very well detailed open world filled to the brimstone with diversions, side quests and things you just want to killerize. I had a lot of fun with everything that was thrown at me, from speed flying to tank rampages the game has it all but as mentioned it’s not much different from previous titles so if you are into those activities then you will have a great time
The world is awesome in my opinion, I loved just floating around and gawking at everything, the hellish landscape fits the theme perfectly. Flowing magma falls from floating islands that just hang in the sky like clouds before cascading into the giant glowing lakes of fire that litter the ash filled city whilst hapless damned souls wonder around doing what the damned do on their daily routine, to me it seems like bursting into light when you shoot them is the highlight of their day.
Now weaponry, the good stuff, I am not going to spoil it. You of course have the standard guns, all with a hellish theme, but when you eventually get hold of the seven deadly sins you know you are going to have a great time. A hammer that shoots lightning, a reclining chair that fires missiles and a sentient revolver all await you in your hellish arsenal of goodies.
And I can’t talk about weapons without mentioned super powers; they are back, but this time its arcane magic. You can super sprint your way around the city and destroy all the cars that get in your way or take to the sky with your own pair of fallen angel wings, just a side note flying with those is awesome, when you get used to them and have a few upgrades under your belt dashing through the sky is phenomenal. Then there is the offensive magic, 4 spells each with 3 different elements changing them completely. Not going to ruin them but you can summon imps and suck the life from people, enough said.
Over all this is a super fun game with enough to keep you busy for a while. The plot is thin at best, but the world and everything in it is enough to entertain. I would recommend this for sure if it’s on sale and if you enjoy this sort of game then full price then it’s still a deal.
Oh and one more thing, play as Gat and use unarmed melee… trust me.
Have fun ^_^

While Egosoft is truly devoted to the genre and their past games have been great niche games (go check them out, buy the X Superbox), this time they took more risk than they could handle. Not only the engine has undergone dramatic changes, if not even being rewritten from scratch, the whole gameplay was redesigned and changed. This results in huge performance problems even half a year after release - and yes, still in version "2.0" - as well as tons of bugs and lack of polish. The game still feels like a beta version at best. The graphics are shiny (except for the NPCs, they're creepy old-people dolls with dead eyes), but on many systems you won't get even playable FPS. If you think your rig is top notch - this doesn't matter. Look at the forums.
In terms of the gameplay, they have not yet reached the complexity of their older titles. Important features are currently missing, like the ability to create a closed ecosystem when you are building a complex of stations and want them to only buy from your own supply chain. The UI still is uncomfortable, but to be fair, the X games always had that problem.
Personally, I had not much of possibility to play the game due to unplayable FPS. I am not sure if I like how they changed the universe to be much more dense and brought the action close to the stations. From what I have experienced, the universe feels too small for my taste. It's more like being in a giant space city, but the feeling of the vast space just doesn't appear. I think I would prefer a mix of the old X3 Reunion and Rebirth. Back to a sector based universe with lots of empty space to travel, but the stations as big and complex as in Rebirth. But I would leave out the NPC interactions. The idea of having to interact with NPCs to get tasks done might have good intentions, but it annoys me. Especially when they are as ugly and static as in X Rebirth. I prefer the good old ship computer and menus.
So. Would I recommend it? Not in version 2.0. Maybe in version 3.0 or 4.0, what I want to say is: when they have fixed the game. Keep an eye on it, stay informed. Egosoft always has supported their games for an extraordinary long time. It surely is an interesting title, but it currently has way too many issues in performance, bugs and polish to recommend it. Go get the X Superbox and play the older titles, they are awesome space sandbox goodness.

The thirteenth installment of one of my favorite series of all time. This game does a lot of things right, but it doesn't end up flawless.
This game's biggest advantage is its storyline. Even though it seems confusing at first, it is nonetheless highly engaging and it kept me motivated to go on through countless enemies again and again for hours upon hours.
Graphics are, as it is usual for the FF series, absolutely fabulous. Though I have to say, the mix of CGI cutscenes, with ones recored using the game's engine, and an in-game dialogue, is a bit awkward to look at sometimes. It is an eye candy, but you see a very stark difference between some cutscenes and the gameplay.
Now to the flaws.
The biggest flaw this game has is the still unpatched controller bug. If you play this game and experience frame clipping every couple of seconds - you are not alone. There are two solutions I've found: 1. either turn off the HID-compliant devices in your device manager OR 2. plug in a game controller\joystick. The latter solution worked for me, when I plugged in a PS3 controller into my PC.
You may experience other technical flaws, such as game crashing as you launch it, or a low framerate. I have only experienced crashing a few times when I started the game, but overall it worked out well, and it is usually fixed by trying to start the game again and again.
The second flaw is the gameplay. The enemies are numerous in quantity but not in quality. Actually, the developers kept recycling the same enemies but using slightly different textures. It is cheap, in my view, and does not add to the enjoyment I get from the game. Furthermore, many enemies can be easily avoided, with you only sacrificing some XP (or 'CP' - crystal points), which is a mixed blessing in itself.
Levelling up is unnecessarily confusing. You level up by moving direction buttons and holding ENTER or SPACE, which allows you to spend your CP in a wrong direction on accident.
I would give this game 7/10. It is a great engaging story and an eye candy, but otherwise a pretty mediocre game. However, the former reasons are good enough to buy it, especially if you are an FF series fan. However, be prepared for some bugs, and make sure you have a spare gamepad ready to stop the game from searching a controller every few seconds, which causes lagging. Depending on your PC and your system, other bugs may surface due to flawed porting. But if you can manage those issues and you have a decent PC, I do recommend buying it just to enjoy a good storyline, if nothing else.

I've got 350+ hours logged in Civ5.
Civ:BE? I still haven't managed to bring myself to actually see an entire round through. I always get bored and start a new game.
As other reviewers have noted, the only thing this game has going for it is looks, and even then it's still not the prettiest game out there. The gameplay is boring and lackluster, the tech web is a complete mess that typically doesn't even give you the slightest hint of which direction would be most beneficial for you to go, the aliens are like barbarians but even more obnoxious and irritating (which, I will give them credit - I didn't think it was possible to get more annoying than Civ5's barbarians already were)
This game is, at BEST, a mod for Civ5. The factions are a joke, the unit selection is god-awful and the only way to get better units is to mindlessly jump all over the tech web trying to get affinity points because it is literally the only way you can upgrade your units into better, stronger versions.
Oh and there really isn't much in the way of superweapons from what I've seen. Need to knock out a group of enemy units halfway across the map in order to save the unit that's about to get zerg-rushed by aliens from every side? Forget it, they're dead. Oh and your fancy new orbital items that you can deploy? They only have a certain range that you can deploy them away from a city. And you better make sure it's where you want it when you first set it up, because in spite of the fact this thing is literally orbiting around the planet and should be able to move in literally any direction, once you set it that's it. There's no way to move it somewhere else if needed.
Thank you Steam for doing a free-play weekend of this game, because you've saved me from wasting my money on such an absolute clusterf-ck of a game. How Firaxis/2K thought they could get away with this is absolutely mind-boggling. Again, this isn't a standalone game, it's nothing more than a mod for Civ5. The content is not there, the gameplay is not there, the graphics and music aren't there. There is literally nothing about this game that qualifies it to be a standalone title like it is, yet they're still milking people for $50 (USD) a pop unless you buy it on sale. It's on sale at the time of this writing for $30 USD and I STILL can't be bothered to buy it.
This is in no way, shape, or form a sequel to Civ5. They took all the best parts of Civ5, cut out half of them, slapped on a pretty new coat of paint, and sold the exact same game. Praise Cthulhu this has Workshop support, otherwise it wouldn't have even warranted more than one game.
Caveat emptor - stay the h-ll away. Do not buy unless you've got at least 1,000 hours put into Civ5 and have literally run out of things to do. Even then I would recommend Pandora: First Contact with Eclipse of Nashira over this piece of garbage.

This game takes a familiar concept and presesnts it in a refreshing way. The atmosphere of the ruined city, buildings and people feel very believeable.
The premise consist of three survivors who are living together in a decrepit old buiding, each has their own unique skillset, and you must control all of them to accomplish task, build useful survival tools and keep warm and well fed. If you fail to do so you'll have to start dealing with more complex issues like illness, depression and even worse.
In This War of Mine, the day time is when you stay in your shelter and manage your living conditions, which is in itself interesting and suprisingly well delivered, but the true gameplay starts at nightfall, when you choose which survivor is on looting duty, who is going to guard your base against looters, and which weapons to give out or leave behind. You then choose a location to loot and use stealth to loot as much as you can carry. The mechanics of the game work very well. A blurry overtone marks the areas where your character can't see or be seen from. The only complaint I can have about this aspect of the game that when it comes to combat, it works great most of the time, but I have been in some instances when I was unable to perform the attack I wanted. This was due the tedious manner in which you switch your weapons, requiring a physical click on a specific on screen button to change from "Scavenging" to "Combat" which is suprisingly difficult when your getting attacked.

In someways, even though were not told too much about the characters at all, it is easy to feel invested in them. For example, one of my survivors, who goes by the name of Pavel I believe, is an expert scavenger, on one of my early playthroughs he died around day eleven. By that time I had not only viewed him as a valuble asset, but as a character i cared about, I felt personally sadden at his loss, seeing his empty bed, and no longer having a scavenger with fifteen slots.
The best parts, ones with some real shock value, I refuse to write about because it took be by such suprise that I wouldn't want to lessen the impact of when it happens to you, if it ever does.
To top it off I would have to highly recommend this game, it's a shining example of what an indie game should be: Polished, thoughtfull, and worth investing some real world time and money into. 9/10

Defy Gravity is a pretty solid platformer based around device that shoots gravity and anti-gravity wells to assist with making progress. Honestly, the game is fairly unimpressive, sporting the look of a mediocre flash game - Ugly textures, plain effects, detaied sprites that look good on their own, but forgettable amongst the game. It's a simple "jump to the end" game with a unique mechanic that will only entertain gamers who like platformers AND very challenging physics based gameplay. Being physics based, Defy Gravity plays a bit floaty, since you need to manipulate gravity wells to pull you in or push you away to jump on objects to bounce off of and reach platforms. Defy Gravity has an almost "Super Meat Boy" like quality: Having instant kill gameplay and failure being the players fault versus the game being cheap (except for the jerks that shoot deadly stars at you).
My goal was to finish Defy Gravity as it is a short game, though somebody who has problems with "color switching" mechanics like seen in Ikaruga, will make this game take forever to complete.

It's not a BAD interpretation of MTG. I just can't recommend it for anyone that actually plays the real thing.
Good
-MTG anytime, by yourself or against a random player online
-Possible to unlock all the cards for free
-Nifty ability to stop the timer and do what you want in response, sort of like in real life (assuming you're not playing a complete jerk) you can tap lands and do something
-Origins is a pretty good card set to start with
-The Quest system. Pretty fun, gives background on the planeswalkers, has enough challenge to make it enjoyable without being super frustrating. Also teaches the game mechanics very well.
Bad
-The online MM is TERRIBLE. Someone leaves? Penalty for not wanting to play out against the AI. Someone drops? Penalty. The wait time is rather long (at least it has been for me) and prepare to get wrecked by people who have dropped the money to unlock as many cards as they can.
-The guided deck builder is just plain bad. Instead of putting up a bunch of dreck, how about providing a list of one drops, two drops, three drops, etc and saying "Hey, you should have this many of this kind of drop."
-The grind to unlock cards. Seriously this right here is killing me. I don't expect it to be a waltz through the park but it's so agonizingly slow and the quest system just doesn't work right. The need to use the awful deck builder to do half of them makes it even worse, as custom built decks (y'know, ones that aren't complete crap) don't count.
-The AI in solo battles. Again, not expecting anything to roll over and die but it seems very much like it already has all the cards unlocked, gets perfect draws 90% of the time, and is overwhelmingly blue. Blue is for people who have no friends and smell of wee. Not just whining here though, the AI really is quite bad at the game. I can kind of understand giving them certain advantages, but maybe teaching it when to trade, when to flunge, and when to cast certain spells (do not drop your +1/+1 all creature AFTER the attack step for example).
-The turn order can be kind of screwy and this leads to some frustrating situations. Abott of Kerral Keep is completely unusuable, as it just exiles, and unless you have another card to cast AFTER you drop it you can never drop the exiled card.
-The button positioning. Put the Skip Attack button UNDER the attack all button. DO NOT have a big finish button for graveyard/triggered/death effects that cancels the effect, label it PASS or CANCEL or LET EFFECT RESOLVE FOR CURRENT RESULT. That gets really old, really fast, especially if you're in the middle of something and you misclick.
Most of these are based on a crack packer's attitude, but some of them really should be addressed. The wonky quest system for instance. If I build a Black/White deck that doesn't suck, let it count towards the Black/White victories.
If you've never played MTG and have no desire to get into the physical game, give this a shot and have some fun. If you do crack packs, this will hold your interest for a little while but Wizards will get your money anyway and it's not going to be through this.

Day 9 and all is going well for the four survivors. They've got some barricades up, they've got some building materials, weapons and decent items for trade but they're short on food. Night falls and one of them decides to investigate an apartment that they discovered the night before. He thinks his pistol and four bullets will get him past any hostility. They don't. Day 10 and the three remaining survivors are depressed as they discuss the loss of their companion. They get through the day and send another of their number out to scavenge for food. It's another house this time. When caught breaking in he lashes out with his crowbar and before he can grasp what's happening, a father and son lay dead at his feet. He's mortified, but he takes everything they have because he knows that their deaths are for nothing if he doesn't. On the way out, a shotgun blast from another family knocks him off his feet. He's dead. Day 11, and the two survivors left have not had a good night. There's been a bandit raid on their base. One survivor is badly wounded, the other has fallen sick. Their bandages and medicine were stolen in the raid. Both are now starving to death, because there's still no food.
TWoM is a mixture of emotive story-telling and rage-inducing changes in good fortune. Surviving requires a good deal of patience and discipline (or luck). The mechanics are simple enough and the game does look and play beautifully. In places it's frustrating - you'll spend ages gathering supplies and you will find that minor mistakes in judgement can get you killed very quickly. Note that there's only one (auto) saved game permitted, and it's cloud based (if you have this enabled) which means no backing up before a risky raid. On the plus side there's bunch of different survivors that, as you probably expect, have different abilities. After playing with the default three for a bit you get the option to start with different combinations of the 8 or so available. Any of these may also turn up at your door seeking refuge during a given playthrough. Each attempt also randomly generates the locations you can visit and will have different "events" as the days roll on.
TWoM won't be for everyone, but I'm definitely a fan.

"This War of Mine" is a beautiful yet brutal, unforgiving game that will hit you right in the feels. It lures you in with it's simplicity, and then BAMM! before you know it half your group is sick or wounded, food is short, bandits hit your shelter night after night, and you genuinely care about who lives or dies, you find yourself sending the weak out to scavenge so that the strong can persevere. you find yourself judging people not on who they are but what they bring top the group, who cares about a lawyer when the little girl of the group will straight up murderise people to bring your group the food they so desperately need.
For me this game gives a real insight into the harshness of war, and not from the soldiers perspective, but from the civillians, who didn't choose to live in a war zone, had this forced on them. The game will make you question your values, how far will you go to survive? Too often in a game it is easy to make the "right" choice, stand on the moral highground, "This war of mine" offers no such opportunity, if you take the moral high road, you might find that it brings nothing but your death. Sometimes however you make your choice and are rewarded for your humanity in such an inhumane situation. As the games webpage states "in war there are no right or wrong choices, only survival" and this game holds very true to this.
As for the game itself, multiple starting groups/locations, random elements of the game, and the very changing nature of the situations themselves give a high level of replayability. The simplicity of the control system aids the immersiveness of this game, without hindering the experience of gameplay and allows the lack of tutorial mode to work. The fact that this game essentially throws you in at the deep end with no real hints as to how to proceed, really adds to the games overall experience. You actually have to listen to your group to understand there needs and wants. With a learning curve that is spot on, allowing new players to get to grips, yet not punishing experienced players by making them sit through endless exposition and explanation, this game really reminds of game from my own childhood where gameplay and story are paramount.
In short, buy this game, it is immersive, enjoyable and rewarding

There don't seem to be many detailed reviews, so I will try to write one for everyone. Though I feel it is going to get thumbs downed a lot because I am not a die-hard LOTR fan and I don't kiss the franchises♥♥♥♥♥
Its a good game, but I thought there would be a lot more to it. The ending and the entire story really feels irrelavent to the actual story.
I was also expecting the story to be much much longer, seeing as how it would play in the timeline of the 3 movies, but instead the game didn't take long to beat at all, or at least not as long as I had expected.
This game took me 11 hours to beat, and about 8 hours of that is gameplay, while the other 3 hours is storyline.
Seeing as how you meet the fellowship before they depart, I thought you would be a group that played a part in the movie, but were more in the background, sort of like you had a part in the story that the books and the movie didn't show.
The in-game map shows all of the locations of the LOTR, Helms Deep, Mordor, The Shire, etc.
I thought we'd take part in the battle at Helms Deep, that maybe we would fight some Orcs/Goblins that had followed Frodo and Sam, without their knowledge, as they were about to destroy the ring. I thought we would be able to explore places like the Shire and some of the other major places in LOTR. But instead, you go everywhere EXCEPT those places.
By the end, I feel like the War in the North and all of what is done in this game is irrelavent. Like it played no part in the main story, like it added nothing important to it. You have this "right hand" of Saruan, Leader, but I'd think that if he was that important, powerful, and in charge, he would've been mentioned in the movies or books, so adding this enemy seemed pointless.
- The gameplay is quite annoying, feeling clunky and based on button mashing.
- You can tell the game was built on the purpose of co-op. seeing as how everytime you switch characters, your previous characters gear is changed to a default kind of gear, so you cant set other characters gear unless you are playing as them.
You also cannot switch characters as you please, you can only switch between chapters, so you may as well stick to 1 character throughout your entire solo playthrough.
- The Orcs all feel the same, like a bunch of brutes, and all take 7-10 hits to kill, EACH. Which makes it frusterating and boring when you're fighting large groups of orcs.
- There is no build with any of the characters or their friendship. They are simply 3 travelers who decide to fight the war in the north.
There is no character build, no relationship built by the 3, and all of their personalities are the SAME.
* Remember how Legolas and Gimili had that funny relationship where they would have a contest of who would kill more orcs in a battle?
* Remember how Legolas and Arigorn had a brotherly kind of relationship?
* Remember how Arigorn and Gimili had that semi funny moment where Gimili asked Arigorn to toss him over to the bridge at Helms Deep, then said "Don't tell the elf!"?
* Remember when Gimili tried to jump across a bridge, that he thought he could make, while a demon was chasing them and when he jumped he almost fell, and Legolas grabbed him to save him and Gimili yelled "not the beard!"?
The point is, there was relationships built within the fellowship.
Here, there is NONE! No relationship, no friendship build at all! You will end the game not caring at all about ANY of the charaters, except maybe the birds.
I was looking for the dwarf to have that battle-thristy personality, the elf to have the wise personality, and the human to have the smart and careful personality. But instead, they all have the same, bland, boring, personality.
- Your AI teammates can be quite annoying when they are struggling to revive you or your companion, or when the elf wont heal you when you're 1 hit away from death, or sometimes they will not follow because of 1 single enemy so when you run into another group you'll be left struggling while they sit back with their thumbs up their♥♥♥♥♥trying to kill this 1 single orc archer that they cant hit or kill and once you are down they will take forever to actually reach you since they are now the prime targets of the group of orcs that just murdered you dead.
- Its semi-fun to play. I played it solo, so its probably better with co-op.
- Its cool getting to meet most of the fellowship before they leave onto their quest.
- The leveling up system is pretty nice, like any other RPG game.
- Has NG+ so when you start a new playthrough, you don't lose all your gear or your level(s).
Maybe my expectations were too high, maybe my standards were too high, but I am very bummed out about how this game turned out and how it ended and the time it took for me to beat it.
I recommend to get this game while it is on sale. Maybe its because i'm not a die hard fan of LOTR and I am not an♥♥♥♥♥kisser to the franchise, but to me, this game is a MAJOR disappointment, and not worth $20. Tolkien and Peter Jackson fans alike should enjoy this game.  The game characters bear a remarkable resemblance to Peter Jackson's film characters. My PC game however was prone to crashing and at one stage I lost my save game, although it was luckily early in the piece. I'll be ammending this review if it happens again as I'm now at L14.
Crashes aside, I enjoyed the simple combat system - essentially mashing the mouse button(s) whilst maneuvering and choosing when to invoke special actions. It reminded me of the combat in the Batman game series. Plus you get to sit back and watch your avatar hack, slash and behead Orcs and Goblins in various interesting ways. I think there's an option to tone down the gore but seriously, hacking Orcs to bits is a major theme in the books and films.
There were numerous cut-scenes which made it feel like the game was one big interactive movie. The background scenery and music was well done, as were the character voice-overs. Then there were the standard RPG features: quests, side quests, secret caches of weapons, equipment upgrades, buy/sell at vendors, NPC interactions, choices to make, skill trees and character builds etc. All the psychological stuff to keep one interested.
I'm playing solo with 2 other AI characters and they do a pretty good job at staying alive, attacking enemies and at times reviving me. So hats off to the developers for not creating dumb AIs. These AIs handle their own skill tree and attribute upgrades plus they equip the best gear they find automatically.  Another special mention goes to the dialog with Gandalf (I think) where you ask the question all LoTR fans ponder: why not send in Frodo on the back of an eagle to begin with?  Play the game to find the answer :-)

I find that the game has quite a few positive qualities.
Free to play is always a good entry point. Good soundtrack, I really enjoyed the music which made the multiple and long loading screens more bearable. I also liked the art style, it felt true to magic and was well executed. From what I saw from the story in the tutorial mission the plot, while somewhat cliche, is fitting to the purpose of a young planes walker raising up to be a hero.
However...there are 2 big elephants in the code that can't allow me to give this a thumbs up. One - constant crashes. One peculiar example is a specific card play order on the last tutorial mission will ALWAYS result in a crash. Loading screen - crash, check options - crash, click a button - CRASH! In the 2 months since release I fully expect those basic issues to have been addressed by now.
The 2nd problem for me is the general interface and the tempo of the turn stages. By default the game puts in place some odd arbitrary presets such as automatically end phase if you can't play a card or automatically pick the order of blocking creatures. Seems like a good way to make the mechanics more accessible to new players but the options don't allow near enough customization to make it an efficient system. For example no option to extend or pause timer automatically if you have an instant in your hand you can play. I have to constantly hammer on the space key in hopes to pause the timer in the ridiculously short timer during an opponents attack phase.
I find these mechanics EXTREMELY frustrating and after about an hour of battling with the interface and crashes I am giving this one up.
Ever want a more accessible melee with balanced characters yet still has much depth? Look no futher!

I've got 350+ hours logged in Civ5.
Civ:BE? I still haven't managed to bring myself to actually see an entire round through. I always get bored and start a new game.
As other reviewers have noted, the only thing this game has going for it is looks, and even then it's still not the prettiest game out there. The gameplay is boring and lackluster, the tech web is a complete mess that typically doesn't even give you the slightest hint of which direction would be most beneficial for you to go, the aliens are like barbarians but even more obnoxious and irritating (which, I will give them credit - I didn't think it was possible to get more annoying than Civ5's barbarians already were)
This game is, at BEST, a mod for Civ5. The factions are a joke, the unit selection is god-awful and the only way to get better units is to mindlessly jump all over the tech web trying to get affinity points because it is literally the only way you can upgrade your units into better, stronger versions.
Oh and there really isn't much in the way of superweapons from what I've seen. Need to knock out a group of enemy units halfway across the map in order to save the unit that's about to get zerg-rushed by aliens from every side? Forget it, they're dead. Oh and your fancy new orbital items that you can deploy? They only have a certain range that you can deploy them away from a city. And you better make sure it's where you want it when you first set it up, because in spite of the fact this thing is literally orbiting around the planet and should be able to move in literally any direction, once you set it that's it. There's no way to move it somewhere else if needed.
Thank you Steam for doing a free-play weekend of this game, because you've saved me from wasting my money on such an absolute clusterf-ck of a game. How Firaxis/2K thought they could get away with this is absolutely mind-boggling. Again, this isn't a standalone game, it's nothing more than a mod for Civ5. The content is not there, the gameplay is not there, the graphics and music aren't there. There is literally nothing about this game that qualifies it to be a standalone title like it is, yet they're still milking people for $50 (USD) a pop unless you buy it on sale. It's on sale at the time of this writing for $30 USD and I STILL can't be bothered to buy it.
This is in no way, shape, or form a sequel to Civ5. They took all the best parts of Civ5, cut out half of them, slapped on a pretty new coat of paint, and sold the exact same game. Praise Cthulhu this has Workshop support, otherwise it wouldn't have even warranted more than one game.
Caveat emptor - stay the h-ll away. Do not buy unless you've got at least 1,000 hours put into Civ5 and have literally run out of things to do. Even then I would recommend Pandora: First Contact with Eclipse of Nashira over this piece of garbage.

I tried, BE.  I really did.  You're CIVILIZATION, IN THE TWENTY FIFTH-AND-A-HALF CENTURY!  Sci-Fi Civ, with nifty technologies, a new way of managing unit upgrades, and a space layer!  But you have less replayability and strategic depth than Civ V did on release, fewer options than release Civ IV, less... EVERYTHING than Civ II.  Worse, all three BE games I've played have felt very much the same.
I conquered the planet, settled the Earthlings, and conquered Earth.  Those should be three very different experiences (Pure military might, territorial expansion and defense, technological focus respectively) but they weren't.  I didn't feel that "Just one more turn...." draw that has made the Civ series rightfully famous.  That last part is a travesty, because it has been there from Civ I (C:/Civ/Civ, run civ.exe) all the way through Alpha Centauri, the Call to Power games, and Civ V.  But it isn't here.
Less prose:
Pros:
+Hooray Sci-Fi and Futurism.
+True innovations in unit upgrade management.
+The aliens (barbarians) are a large factor, rather than occasional nuisance.
+The space layer and space units are awesome.
CONS:
-Very low replayability
-Very low tactical depth.
-Wonders are bland and uninspiring
-No wonder movies.  WAT.
-Clunky interface.
-Unbalanced trade mechanics.
-No character to factions or units.
-No more "Just one more turn..."
With at least an expansion pack, this might pique my interest again, but for now it's just a 15 dollar game that I paid 50 bucks for.

First off, why do they put GBs worth of Japanese audio in the game and then fail to include what must have been mere KB of Japanese subtitles. A real disappointment from the start.
The game itself is really good. I know it is not anything like all the FFs before it, I know all the hardcore fans are probably disappointed and having played earlier FF titles later on I fully understand why. For me however this was the first FF I ever played so I started the adventure with absolutely no expectations of what was to come.
The epicness of every fight, the characters and the entire story was the main thing I absolutely enjoyed while playing the game. They managed to overshadow the many shortcomings the game admittely has. The story is really complicated at first and you will probably only understand the very first scenes on a second playthrough. It has some twists, some emotional bits and it is really long, so it basically has everything a good storyline need. The storytelling itself could be improved as well by making it more chronological with less flashbacks. You start off on the 13th day of the events and the game will give you snippets of what happend before throughout the first hours of the game. This is clearly done to avoid an overload of information right from the start I just think there could have been a more elegant solution.
The characters are likeable (except maybe Snow and Hope) and have a clear personality. There personal stories are told throughout the game and the are one of the main points why I like this game.
The fighting system is not complex, it's more action-oriented. You only need to make the basic decision what each character role should be (healer, damage-dealer, etc.) at any given point and the auto-battle function will select the most appropriate moves for you. This can be seen as a good or a bad thing but you will always have the option to make the decision manually and even with auto-battle the game is still sufficently challanging for most players.
The character progression system will give you a lot of very useful skills but there is no real customizing. With about 30 min of grinding after every boss you will be able to max out your characters up until the very end of the game. It's a real shame since all of your playthrough will be more or less the same this way.
Well lastly there of course is the most negative point of the game: linearity. It's basically one big corridor. Later in the game you'll probably be amazed to see a huge open area which will turn out to be just an extremly wide corridor. Normally that's an absolute dealbreaker for me but the story and the characters had me invested from the start so this is one of the few games where I can overlook linear game design.

This game is one of the smoothest Hitman games I've ever played. Nearly every movement is fluid and natural. Even Blood Money, for the masterpiece that it is, can be a bit clunky at times. The added takedowns and cover system really help you get into that assassin mood. The disguise system is weird but it works, in that guards actually NOTICE that you're not their longtime friend Bill. You can bypass this however by using the Instinct feature, which helps in a multitude of ways. Not only does it show where enemies are at/headed, it also slows down time so you can check the surrounding area without taking up too much in-game time. These features add to the overall efficiency of your kills. After all, that IS what being a hitman is about. The biggest downfall in my opinion was the weak story. It didn't quite feel like it held up as much as previous entries. But while this game is no Blood Money, I can without a doubt say that it is definitely a Hitman game.

1) The night time scavaging is VERY fun and unique.  One map might be strictly used for trading, another for worry free looting, and another will require sneaking around guards.... 2) Looting is done well and it is a constant struggle to pick and choose what you want to carry back with you.   Do you take the extra wood to build something, the extra ammo to protect your home, or some alocohol for better trade?  You decide
3) The game flows like a rollercoaster.   For a few days you might be struggling to find food, and then your next struggle is to find wood OR medicine. They removed many of the inventory and 'crafting' issues i have with other survival games. This game takes a familiar concept and presesnts it in a refreshing way. The atmosphere of the ruined city, buildings and people feel very believeable.
The premise consist of three survivors who are living together in a decrepit old buiding, each has their own unique skillset, and you must control all of them to accomplish task, build useful survival tools and keep warm and well fed. If you fail to do so you'll have to start dealing with more complex issues like illness, depression and even worse.
In This War of Mine, the day time is when you stay in your shelter and manage your living conditions, which is in itself interesting and suprisingly well delivered, but the true gameplay starts at nightfall, when you choose which survivor is on looting duty, who is going to guard your base against looters, and which weapons to give out or leave behind. You then choose a location to loot and use stealth to loot as much as you can carry. The mechanics of the game work very well. A blurry overtone marks the areas where your character can't see or be seen from. The only complaint I can have about this aspect of the game that when it comes to combat, it works great most of the time, but I have been in some instances when I was unable to perform the attack I wanted. This was due the tedious manner in which you switch your weapons, requiring a physical click on a specific on screen button to change from "Scavenging" to "Combat" which is suprisingly difficult when your getting attacked.

In someways, even though were not told too much about the characters at all, it is easy to feel invested in them. For example, one of my survivors, who goes by the name of Pavel I believe, is an expert scavenger, on one of my early playthroughs he died around day eleven. By that time I had not only viewed him as a valuble asset, but as a character i cared about, I felt personally sadden at his loss, seeing his empty bed, and no longer having a scavenger with fifteen slots.
The best parts, ones with some real shock value, I refuse to write about because it took be by such suprise that I wouldn't want to lessen the impact of when it happens to you, if it ever does.
To top it off I would have to highly recommend this game, it's a shining example of what an indie game should be: Polished, thoughtfull, and worth investing some real world time and money into. 9/10

You even control the rate at which things get built, resources earned, how fast ships travel, and speed of many other attributes to the game, using settings, if you choose. If you love random replayability where one game you can win, but the next with all the same settings, but game developed differently from beginning, becomes a little more difficult and you lose; this game is for you!
If you enjoy production genre of space shows, like; Star Trek, Star Wars, Battlestar Gallactica, and other scifi shows/movies about Galactic control, this game is for you. Everything I mentioned, I enjoy! I also enjoy Sid Meier's Civilization Series, Empire Earth, Command and Conquer, Galactic Civilization II, Age of Empires series, Master of Orion series, Star Craft the original, and many more. To give you an idea of this game compared to some of my favorites I listed... SoaSE:R (or SINS for short), has kind of a Star Craft three different races feel, mixed with the massive galactic control and Diplomacy of Master of Orion, and a fast pace strategy set of Empire Earth and Age of Empires, however to experience the unique faction diversity set between each of the three main Races, their is no real comparison... you just have to Experience Sins of a Solar Empire: Rebellion for your self.
I personally love the Vasari Loyalist; Their unique ability to create their own phase lanes and travel between stars as they see fit, with their Kostura Cannon attack of defenses on a target leaving its own Phase Node behind, matched with the Titan's powerful warship and ability to terrorize enemy forces jumping around inside planet's Gravity Wells, as well as around the different planets, are some reasons why I enjoy the Vasari Loyalist!
However, nothing can match the Cultural power of the Advent, and their ability to manipulate the culture across the Galaxy with their super weapon Deliverance engine casting a massive culture bomb behind enemy lines. If timed right, having a powerful armada close to a target for culture bomb, and the right research, Advent forces can get a huge combat bonus within your own culture, in side the enemy bases if fighting within the culture bomb influence. They also have many power mind control abilities to take away many ships!
Nothing compares to the Massive economic power of the TEC (Trader Emergency Coalition), and their ability to expand fast and cover the cost, and earn much more power through commerce compared to the other two. TEC also can coerce the Pirates factions, and all natives across the Galaxy to side with them, creating an unwavering force of friendly support  across the map, and cause relentless waves of mild assaults by unforeseen pirate raids among different Enemy bases!
If played right, any of the three races, and the split factions within, can become a powerful force to be reconned with! Can YOU build an Empire, to Stand the Test of SPACE and TIME?
If still interested, feel free to check my steam profile... I have many screenshots, already posted... and more going up all the time!

As is, it's a game with solid base but one that fails to do anything with it. Likewise, this game is like any other 3D puzzle platformer. The graphics are pretty cool, but that's not what most people play games for. The puzzles are repetitive and dull, and don't ever seem to use Tiny's arsenal to its full extent. The controls are awkward and almost broken, and it is riddled with glitches. All in all I bought it on sale for 99 cents instead of $9.99. I really wish Steam gave more options than just a thumbs up or a thumbs down for reviews. Crysis is one of the best and most fun games I've ever played. Everything from the suit you wear to the environment you play in is make this game thrilling to play every time. And despite the fact that it came out 10 years ago in 2007, it still has breathtaking visuals and graphics, and the mechanics are better than a lot of modern games. I bought it recently on Steam because I remembered playing it with my dad back when it first came out and how much fun it used to be. I can happily say I was not disappointed. It's just as awesome as I remember it being. My problem with it is that apparently it has no support for 64-bit versions of Windows, and I'm using the 64-bit version of Windows 10. It would almost be forgiveable considering the game is 10 years old, but considering how popular it is and how many people still play it, you'd think they would have patched it to run on 64-bit systems. The only way to fix it is to download a 64-bit version of one of the game's files from a questionable download link and replace the original. And once you do that, Steam won't track your game progress. That's obviously not a huge deal, but it is annoying. The bottom line is that I would absolutely recommend this game, but it's disappointing to have to deal with these problems in order to play it.

Super long harsh review following, but first I'll start with the good points. (Final score: 7/10 an okay game)
This game has great music, the setting is very intersting, and the game imports some of Civilization V best mechanics.
Technically, I think this game will run even on the crapiest config out there, especially with the Mantle API that makes it run like breeze on an AMD system (I don't know of its effect with an Nvidia GPU). Though, it's still the same old engine, if you change something in the config menu you have to restart, and it's still slow on booting up, but faster. It's Civilization V, in space, on an alien planet. Go read the background on why humanity gets there, it's really intersting. The atmosphere, this game gets it right. And spying, the spying mechanics of this game are really fun, as for the rest of the gameplay....
After a game in half (around 10h gameplay), the game fails to compel me to play it instead of its predecessor Civ 5 or last year indie entry in the genre Endless Legend. The interface is somewhat confusing, especially the tech three which doesn't explain much about what does what except for what unit/building it unlocks, and the quotes are quite bad when you finish researching a tech; I understand that it's fiction but the writer is pretty bad. The map is a bit hard to read, I don't know if it was a design choice for the player to feel like it's an alien world, but there's almost no visual difference between an hill and a plain, unless your read the tooltip. The units look and fight pretty much all the same from each development stages, during most of the game, they play like Civ 5 20th century units with limited range.
As for the economy and resources management, trading is the main engine for "energy", the game's currency, generation. It makes sense, and it's well implemented. But the strategic resources, their usefulness is based on what affinity (more on that later) you're investing into, and that's limiting. The enviroment will sculpt your civilization based on what affinity-based strategic resources is near you, well that is if you want to make your life easier and not try to conquer half the map in the 50 first turns to get what you want; though the map itself won't let you. It's quite an intersing concept, but the lack of diversity in affinity is, again, a limiting factor. Also, health, that thing that replaces happiness and modulates your growth, you can mostly ignore it. That's bad, especially since luxury resources are gone with no analogues, you can't make it go high without spamming a bunch of building that are unlocked in the end of the tech tree. And, because of that, this stat has been completely nerfed, a sign that the game has been rushed.
However the native alien species of the palnet, they're a real faction, they're even smarter than the main factions of the game, they'll give you a run for your money; this planet is HOSTILE.
Speaking of faction, even if the background of each civ looks awesome their actual civilization bonus do not differentiate them much. Even if humanity converges in the future, it's no excuse for this lack of character.
The main differentiator in the game is your affinity, which effectively reduce the number of civs to 3. Cyborgs, Purists, and Alien melders. The AI doesn't seem to want to win, if one of them is near a victory the neighbours will not lift a finger to get the victory instead, unless it's you who is winning. It makes the end game less dynamic whereas if it were human players they'd all band up against the one with the winning conditions. Since now, victories are "interceptable", that's a mechanic I was expecting. At least the AI is less schizo than Civ 5, but your alliances will fall apart if you have divergent affinities. The Leader screens, they're boring and feel rushed unlike, well, Civ 5. Actually, the whole game feels rushed, as if 2K/Firaxis didn't have much confidence in the game and cut the budget before the dev actually made something truly interesting with great set they had. There are various visual bugs, but thank god, no game breaking one.
Even if this critique has been harsh, it's mostly because I love this game series, and that this late adittion has a lot of potential. I'll be waiting for the expansions, they made Civ 5 from a good game to a great game. But this one it only gave me an ambivalent feelings. It's an okay game. Great if it were just an expansion. I'll be playing some more.
Score 7/10

Civilization BE is more like civilization 5 DLC, not standalone game. It looks like Firaxis/Sid cheated on you changing planet texture and research tree (stealing idea from endless space, huh?). I also personally expected new, modern Alpha Centaura. People who played original game would understand me. But it's not Alpha Centaura. You don't have terraforming or underwater cities here. There is no prototyping. No aliens race. Many things that stuck in my mind for years from my childhood are missed here.
Pros:
+ new civilization look&feel
Cons:
- cut version of civilization
- not even close to original Alpha Centaura
- unjustified very expensive
If you didn't play civilization 5 you might like BE. If you don't see original Alpha Centaura you won't probably miss it. But if you have a choice what to buy civilization 5 or civilization BE - grab civ5, it's much better now. I don't say here that BE is a bad game, no. I say that this game is not ready, it requres a lot of DLCs and your money, of course, to make it a civilization 5 level.
There are many good games I can play and wait for years until they release all DLCs, make complete pack and push it with a good discount. Save your time and money and enjoy playing cool games!

The entire thing is optimized terribly and even in my high-end machine I could barely break 20FPS at the lowest possible settings. And I mean lowest. Don't be fooled by the screenshots on this store page. They don't reflect anything I ever saw with 12gb RAM, GTX 760 and a Core i7. It seems like when you walk around on foot the game is not only simulating, but rendering all of the activity outside of the station which causes it to run like complete trash even when you're standing still, doing nothing.
Now they are rebranding as "X Rebirth 2.0" but don't be fooled, it's the same game with the same♥♥♥♥♥♥optimization. In the 7 months since launch they fixed a lot of the mission bugs and added the ability to not bother leaving your ship to go out on foot.  I think they also added some new cockpits and some different start conditions. But, maybe the worst part about the game is that even with all the bugs and optimization fixes, I don't think it was very good as a game... I only completed the tutorial so I don't have a great perspective but from what I played it was slow, clunky, and not fun.
Cherry on top: The price of this game hasn't dropped a dime since release. They are still selling it for $50. This game is not worth $50. If I could get a refund I would. That 33/100 metacritic rating doesn't lie.

Slow linear progression

; get to an objective while killing off Nazi forces and abnormal looking enemies to keep alive. The game gradually gets tougher as you progress through the missions where new enemies who unnaturally aim better and have more powerful guns will start coming in.
It could just be my computer but I get severe & random frame drops every now and again despite most of the game going at 60-90+ FPS.
The maps in the game are both linear with a few very small paths to find secrets & supplies & whatnot
somewhat open where objectives may have you do some bothersome backtracking. The backtracking really can be a bother since there aren't usually any visible indications on where to go next for anything. In some relatively open maps I had to do some running around to find where I had to go which I'm usually fine with until things like locked doors that have been passed by minutes ago only become unlocked with very little to no indication of the door being unlocked after an objective is reached on another side of the map happens.
Although the game is generally straightforward with its shooting there are stealth mechanics in the game, which seem pretty weak. At the very least it functions; crouch or walk up behind an enemy and use a suppressed gun or backstab with a knife to silently kill them while avoiding enemy detection. The problem is that it seems a bit out of place for a game that's generally all about being fast and shooty. The stealth is optional in most missions and I think for the most part there are times where detection is unavoidable.
After an enemy spots you it seems like headshots become almost non-existant when all enemies are aware of your presence. They don't die instantly when taking in a headshot or the spreadless-shots hitting the body instead of the head despite the reticle aimed at the face. There are objectives where you can't allow the enemy to hit the alarm if you've been found which in this game is more annoying than it is fun. Fortunately objectives like those are incredibly minimal in number.
There are a chunk of weapons you can have in the game almost all practical one way or another. The only guns in the game I found to be useless are the two available pistols which all shoot very slowly and are generally weak
I could be observing this one wrong but the hitboxes for anything look like they go all over the place. When firing something with incredibly little spread aimed aproximately two feet away from an enemy they seem to take damage anyway.
Out of the 7 missions in the game (split into 3 or 4 parts each) there are only 2 boss fights (3 if you count that upgraded version of another enemy). All of them are incredibly easy to kill and are very anti-climactic when defeated, even the final boss.
It's still an overall simple and relatively short fast action Wolfenstein game (at least when you let it be that) so there's definitely fun to be had.

It pains me to write this review. I am a big fan of square enix and of the games produced by them. When I saw this title on steam, i thought 'ah, cool. An rpg by one of my favorite video game companies.'
After playing for about two hours, my initial reaction was completely turned around. While the game does have 3d animation comparable to the time it was produced, the remainder of the game is sub-par from what I have seen of other titles by square enix.
The battle system is extremely boring and repetative. While it is easy to learn, it doesn't make sense. Instead of controlling a single character or issuing commands to multiple characters, you issue orders to squads, or "unions" as they are called in the game. And the types of commands are limited to the circumstances of the battle, but are limited to [basic attack], [special attack], [magical attack] and even more rarely [heal]. Once you give the orders, the characters are pretty much left to their own devices, attacking whichever creature they so choose and in whatever fashion they want, which can and has in my case not gone in favor of a winning battle. Not being able to plan and strategize a battle plan with all your characters makes fights far more difficult than they should be, given all that you can input in the commands.
I could have seen past the battle system if the storyline and/or voice acting/dialogue were good. Sadly, that was not the case either. I felt like I was watching a really poorly written anime. The main character, who is perhaps 15, I am guessing, meets an important nobleman and suddenly becomes part of the army, fighting shoulder to shoulder with top level generals and no one raises a fuss. The characters seemed very stiff, almost no emotion going into the dialogue. The bad guys are easily spotted and are cliche'.
Overall, I am dissappointed in this title.

UPDATE: In-depth video review is now up, in 2 parts.
I bought the game for the sole purpose of wanting to give it a chance, and probably will do a full video on it later. Despite all the negativity surrounding it, how 'tasteless' it seemed, and by god, the controversy... I just wanted to see how it fared as a game by its own merits.
After playing through it, I can say that it was not worth the money, even if you can get past the awkward, probably disturbing themes to some. But even that wasn't all that disturbing. Death and murder comes so frequently, with so little consequence, reason, or realism that it's barely even worth mentioning.
The Antagonist's dialogue is amazingly terrible, and I'm torn as to whether or not it was done as a parody. Some of the lines are just so stupid that it's hard to imagine it being taken seriously, but.. who knows.
The game runs pretty terribly, usually hovering from 38-45fps on a GTX770, with some settings turned down even. It dipped as low as 20fps in a few parts, and frankly, the game's graphics don't justify it at all. The destruction of the environments was impressive at times, admittedly, but it was usually then that the framerate tanked the hardest.
The game is very short, it took about 3 hours to beat.. probably less if you're not terrible at the game like I was. It's extended through an archaic 'respawn point' system, where you earn a respawn by completing side objectives (kill more people or blow something up, that's about it), and each time you die, you'll spend a point to come back.
If you run out of points, you're put back at the start of the stage. This wouldn't be so bad if the way you recover health was by executing people.. and to do that, you need to shoot someone, or kick someone, enough that they fall down, but aren't quite dead. Then you execute them by pressing 'Q', an animation plays, and you recover some health.
With how difficult the final 2 stages can get, you'll find yourself dying and having to restart repeatedly. It makes the entire thing frustrating, I was just hoping that it would finally be over. Finally being after 2 and a half hours of game time. That's not a good sign.
If you're a fan of gore or excessive violence.. play something else instead.

As much as i\'d like too, i can\'t really find a good reason to recommend this game. Last Remnant brings some interesting ideas on the table, but also have some very serious flaw that drags him down. The unions battle system doesn\'t really deliver the strategic feeling it should; too much RNG screwing up battles, sometime in your favour, sometime not.  You can\'t command action freely for every member; RNG will decide if you get a good command or not. You can\'t decide when and if the QTE for critical strikes will trigger; RNG will decide if you get a chance for a damage increase or not. Same thing for the special attacks that certain characters can use. Heck, you can\'t even freely change any of your party members equipment! There is simply no excuse for this, it\'s just bad design. For the majority of the game, the outcome of every battle that is not faceroll easy will be decided solely on rng dodges, rng parries, rng crits, rng special commands, and so on. As a result, you will not find any form of satisfaction within the gameplay, not even when you win.
As for the rest:
Video: visuals are nice considering the release date, but level design sucks, with the same halls and corridors that repeat themself over and over. Every location has it\'s flair of course, but just one, with almost zero variations within it. Animations works fine within battle and in most of the cutscenes, outside of them tend to be kinda crappy and unrealistic. The game also presents some technical problems: costant screen tearing (you can turn the vsync on editing the .ini file, but it will not work regardless) and texture-popping are the most noticeable. There are some partial fixes around the web, though.
Audio: OST is good but without any kind of personality. Also, many locations have shared music.
Narrative: the story is nothing special - but good enough to grab your attention \'till the endgame, even if some part of it seemed like rushed, some almost absurdly so. Characters are generally well designed, but the protagonist can be very, very annoying at times.

You need a spreadsheet to do the combat correctly, and simply grinding to attempt to become powerful will backfire and you'll be unable to effectivley fight, because you'll have made the monsters too powerful.

If you have a masochistic strain of autism I'm sure you'd love this game, but if you just want to have fun with a modern JRPG, this isn't the game for you.

This is a great survival game for many reasons.
1) The night time scavaging is VERY fun and unique.  One map might be strictly used for trading, another for worry free looting, and another will require sneaking around guards.... OR killing them if you want.  There is randomization to the maps aswell and some scripted events that change as time goes on.   Parts of the map also become unavailable at times due to fighting and winter....  So your MUCH needed hospital might be unavailable for 5+ days.. what are you going to do now?
2) Looting is done well and it is a constant struggle to pick and choose what you want to carry back with you.   Do you take the extra wood to build something, the extra ammo to protect your home, or some alocohol for better trade?  You decide
3) The game flows like a rollercoaster.   For a few days you might be struggling to find food, and then your next struggle is to find wood OR medicine.   Things get really tense when you have multiple problems on your hand.   It got so bad on one playthrough that i ended up loosing 3 people within 2 days.. and i STILL completed this playthrough with only 1 person for over 13+ days.
They removed many of the inventory and 'crafting' issues i have with other survival games.   I hate having to craft sub-items in order to create something new... in this game, everything is straight forward and items are categorized at a high level and they can be used to build whatever you need.... an axe? a heater for food, or an upgrade for the house?

This game takes a familiar concept and presesnts it in a refreshing way. The atmosphere of the ruined city, buildings and people feel very believeable.
The premise consist of three survivors who are living together in a decrepit old buiding, each has their own unique skillset, and you must control all of them to accomplish task, build useful survival tools and keep warm and well fed. If you fail to do so you'll have to start dealing with more complex issues like illness, depression and even worse.
In This War of Mine, the day time is when you stay in your shelter and manage your living conditions, which is in itself interesting and suprisingly well delivered, but the true gameplay starts at nightfall, when you choose which survivor is on looting duty, who is going to guard your base against looters, and which weapons to give out or leave behind. You then choose a location to loot and use stealth to loot as much as you can carry. The mechanics of the game work very well. A blurry overtone marks the areas where your character can't see or be seen from. The only complaint I can have about this aspect of the game that when it comes to combat, it works great most of the time, but I have been in some instances when I was unable to perform the attack I wanted. This was due the tedious manner in which you switch your weapons, requiring a physical click on a specific on screen button to change from "Scavenging" to "Combat" which is suprisingly difficult when your getting attacked.

In someways, even though were not told too much about the characters at all, it is easy to feel invested in them. For example, one of my survivors, who goes by the name of Pavel I believe, is an expert scavenger, on one of my early playthroughs he died around day eleven. By that time I had not only viewed him as a valuble asset, but as a character i cared about, I felt personally sadden at his loss, seeing his empty bed, and no longer having a scavenger with fifteen slots.
The best parts, ones with some real shock value, I refuse to write about because it took be by such suprise that I wouldn't want to lessen the impact of when it happens to you, if it ever does.
To top it off I would have to highly recommend this game, it's a shining example of what an indie game should be: Polished, thoughtfull, and worth investing some real world time and money into. 9/10

Original review was as follows, most of it is void though:
"A good way to experience Magic for the first.
As my first in-depth encounter with the trading card game, Magic: Duels offers a lot of help and lets me experiment with different decks and game-mechanics from the get-go. So as a "gateway game", this version is perfect - the fact that you can accumulate cards pretty easily and relatively fast helps this free-to-play model a lot.
There are a few bugs I've encountered, but none too game-breaking for me to get angered. The worst one was with me logging in from a different computer and losing my cards to a bad steam sync. But customer service was prompt to answer, and even over-compensated my lost cards to me. I can stomach technical difficulties of a starting-out game pretty well, so that's that.
But what I really applaud the makers of this game for, aside from the business model and the intro to the wonderfully deep game, is for the overall feel of the experience. Good music and art-work (though they should have some extra cosmetic items in the in-game shop), nicely done campaigns, with a very nostalgic sense of fantasy writing to it, and a decently intuitive and good-looking interface make for a pleasant game.
Main gripes would be in the AI crudely taking over when a player disconnects or concedes and in some connectivity issues. These are pretty significant problems, but I do expect them to be solved, as there are many who play the game and the game just came out.
All the gripes don't null the fact that in this game, there is actually lots of variance in play-style and the likes, and that it actually allows me to get decent cards. All points in which Hearthstone loses horridly, even though the latter *is* more twitch-, and youtube-friendly and gets points by that.
Overall, I enjoy the game (much more than Hearthstone) and recommend to all newcomers."
