Overall:
Good Game - although not as good as Bioshock 1. Enough was done right in this game to recommend it.
In my opinion, both Bioshock 1 & 2 are must plays, even for people who do not like FPSs (e.g. I am not a big fan of FPSs, yet I loved the Bioshock Series).
I also highly recommend "Bioshock Infinite" if you played and enjoyed the first two games.
Even If you do not like Bioshock Infinite, its two DLCs "Burial at Sea" Episodes 1 & 2 take you back to Rapture (the world of Bioshock 1 & 2). I highly recommend those DLCs as well.
Single Player:
It is Good. It borrowed a lot from Bioshock 1 and the story was not as interesting, but I still liked it.
They definetly did not put as much love and polish into making this sequel.
Multiplayer:
I Hated the Multiplayer with a passion for four reasons:
1) The Multiplayer is not fun - I think most people will agree with me on that
2a) It takes forever to level up your MP Character. Boosting is made very difficult, so you will most likely be stuck leveling legit.
2b) The Single-Player Trophies/Achievements are hard enough, so I do not understand why they thought it was a good idea to make the Multiplayer Trophies/Achievements so time consuming.
It Forces you to play to the point that you completely despise the game, just to get your 100% trophy/achievement completion - I am a perfectionist, passionate about in-game collectibles and game completion percentages so it might not bother others as much as it does me.
3) Adding Multiplayer took resources away from the Single-Player.
The SP could have been much more polished, innovative and closer to the quality of Bioshock 1.
They nearly made the same mistake with the third Bioshock installment "Bioshock Infinite", but decided to scrap the Multiplayer. They did however put resources into "Bioshock Infinite's" Multiplayer before scrapping it. So just imagine what could have been if all resources had been devoted to Single-Player only?
FYI Regarding my Reviews of Multiplayer in General:
I generally I do not like Multiplayer at all, but do like CO-OP Multiplayer.
I only play multiplayer when I am forced to because they are tied to and unlock PSN/Steam Trophies/Achievements. Rarely because I think a game's multiplayer is any good.
So I must admit that I may be a bit biased in my review of  Multiplayer in General.
Lastly this game is newer than Bioshock 1, but somehow the graphics seem to not have been improved in the sequel. It seems on par with Bioshock 1, but the Sound is not nearly as good as it was in Bioshock 1 (e.g. the dreadful sound of a Big Daddy approaching).
I remember the days when Bioshock 1 came out and everyone was astonished at the graphics, physics etc. and then everyone (including my friends and I) ran out to buy a better graphic card in order to be able to play it. This was not the case with Bioshock 2 because it was not innovative.
- Play the classic "System Shock" games.
- After that, play all three Bioshock Games + their DLCs (the SP DLCs are good). Play the games in the order that they were released.
- Each time you beat each game,  Read/Watch a few analysises of the story/plots twists/ending/morals of each game before moving onto the next.
DO ALL THIS, AND YOU WILL GET THE MOST OUT THESE WONDERFUL GAMES - NOW GO PLAY, YOU CAN THANK ME LATER!

Return to Castle Wolfenstein is a sequel to Wolfenstein 3D fo sorts. Well, of prequel. Or reboot. After 9 years or so and technology advancment you shouldn't expect things to be same anyway. It's a WW2 shooter from 2001, made by id and Gray Matter and Nerve Software (one handled singleplayer, another handled multiplayer), it runs on Quake 3 engine. And well, was released in the beggining of those horrible times when every second shooter was WW2 themed.
There also was Enemy Territory, a sort of stand-alone multiplayer expansion pack that is free. It's not included there, but you know, it's free.
It also had XBox and PS2 version, both with additional prologue level and new shotgun as weapon. XBox even has 2-player coop as far as I am aware. Worth tracking down.
Surprisingly, for id software title, this game on Steam works pretty fine. It just doesn't support widescreen, which I think can easily fix through config files or so. Check guides.
Well, if forget that multiplayer portion still tries to use master server that was shut down times ago. In all honesty, I didn't bother fixing it, I doubt that it has active enough player base nowdays. Multiplayer the main reason people were praising this game, but with free Enemy Territory around, I don't think anybody will be playing this now.
In this game you play as agent Blazkowicz, noted for his ability to infiltrate bases and infiltrate every nazi he meets. And you have to Return to Castle Woflenstein!
If forget that you already start inside it and it's not as pretty as your rose-tinted nostalgia glasses were telling you, so now you have to Unreturn to Castle Wolfenstein!
All while learning about occult stuff on your way out, which then excites people at headquarters enough to send you to every Nazi evil project in the world, to learn more. And to sabotage every possible invention that Nazi came up with. Which is fun, no complaints.
As for game itself, well, it's an early WW2 shooter. It was past Doom times when your movement was your defence, since pretty much every attack here is hitscan. It was also before regenerating and cover systems. It's just an early realistical FPS where your main defence is how fast can you react by headshotting soldier and where you can get into unfair situation where you randomly die due to random hitscan bullets and you can't do anything but to reload quicksave until you luckily pass it.
Thankfully, this FPS is one of those 2000s shooters that mix stealth and action instead of fighting straight on. You could lean left and right to peek around corner. You could just walk to sneak onto enemy. And you have knife that instakills if used on the back of unaware enemy with stab stab stab animation. You will also get silenced weapons that will help you. Oh yea, and pistols in this game are useless, don't bother.
Just don't think that Stealth is all that goodly done. It's on a weak side, somewhat, just enough to vary action up, to remove some soldiers before main action starts. It's not often required, outside of two mandatory stealth missions, that aren't as hard as worst examples in some other games. Just don't expect it to work well, you can always get noticed seemingly randomly.
And then once alarm goes on and everybody notices you, or if it was straight action mission to begin with, you get to shooting part. And well, it's mostly reaction game. Enemies who aren't exactly aware what and where are you don't react so fast, but once they do, they can be pain. Now, you can easily outshoot common enemies. You can even effectively snipe them at long distance, and it's fun. Or you can use grenade around corner, fun too. Awesome music helps.
Game gets to worst when you get to straight fight, when you can't sneak or ambush or take advantage of enviroment much. These are bad moments of gameplay. It gets worse if you meet tougher enemies in such situation. Unlike, say, enemies from Rise of The Triad, game that handles crowds of hitscan enemies, soldiers can shoot with no problem back while being shot at while screwing your aim off. And then game can have unfair situation, especially when you are on low health. Like, getting ambushed right while crawling up the ladder. Or second boss, Das Ubersoldat, immeditly hitscan-attacks you even before you can take cover or even check where you can take cover. Unless exploit his AI, mhm. Or just getting shot at by sniper in a foggy valley, where sniper is only barely visible from the fog, is placed behind tree, is on the hill somewhere on the side, and keeps dropping your aim off by shooting you succesfully. All yay quicksaves.
But hey, outside of shooting itself, game has nice exploration feel to it, despite being linear. Small detail spread over realistical, yet not painfully gray, levels. Secrets are placed through levels, nicely hidden. First mission, castle Wolfenstein, is especially awesome with all the secrets hidden. Graphics are nice. It also has plenty of less generic guns, like flamethrower or tesla gun.
I also didn't mention the very few parts of a game where you handle undead. It becomes something more simple here. Not great by itself, but helps to vary up.
Bosses aren't great. First one is good, second is hitscan bulletsponge, final one is bulletsponge that has harder time to kill you than anybody else.
Soundtrack is also awesome, improving atmosphere and actually helping you to get into mood required for playing this game.
Return of Castle Wolfenstein is pretty good when compared to other early WW2 shooters. It's a mix of not-so-strong stealths and not-so-strong action, which will give you fun when both of those are present. When it comes to parts with straight action, it gets as frustrating as expected, though.
Still better than Wolf3D. It is however amazingly overrated, while being more of meh.

Day 9 and all is going well for the four survivors. They've got some barricades up, they've got some building materials, weapons and decent items for trade but they're short on food. Night falls and one of them decides to investigate an apartment that they discovered the night before. He thinks his pistol and four bullets will get him past any hostility. They don't. Day 10 and the three remaining survivors are depressed as they discuss the loss of their companion. They get through the day and send another of their number out to scavenge for food. It's another house this time. When caught breaking in he lashes out with his crowbar and before he can grasp what's happening, a father and son lay dead at his feet. He's mortified, but he takes everything they have because he knows that their deaths are for nothing if he doesn't. On the way out, a shotgun blast from another family knocks him off his feet. He's dead. Day 11, and the two survivors left have not had a good night. There's been a bandit raid on their base. One survivor is badly wounded, the other has fallen sick. Their bandages and medicine were stolen in the raid. Both are now starving to death, because there's still no food.
TWoM is a mixture of emotive story-telling and rage-inducing changes in good fortune. Surviving requires a good deal of patience and discipline (or luck). The mechanics are simple enough and the game does look and play beautifully. In places it's frustrating - you'll spend ages gathering supplies and you will find that minor mistakes in judgement can get you killed very quickly. Note that there's only one (auto) saved game permitted, and it's cloud based (if you have this enabled) which means no backing up before a risky raid. On the plus side there's bunch of different survivors that, as you probably expect, have different abilities. After playing with the default three for a bit you get the option to start with different combinations of the 8 or so available. Any of these may also turn up at your door seeking refuge during a given playthrough. Each attempt also randomly generates the locations you can visit and will have different "events" as the days roll on.
TWoM won't be for everyone, but I'm definitely a fan.

Over the past few years, I have heard many complaints regarding Bioshock 2. It was not as good as the original, it was not innovative, and the story was not as well done as the first game. While I agree with some points made, Bioshock 2 is a great game and definatetly worth the time of any Bioshock fan.
Story
You play as Delta, one of the original big daddies who has been seperated from his little sister, Elenor. Your task is to find Elenor and escape the ruins of Rapture.
Overall, I thought the story in Bioshock 2 was not as good as original, I think 2K Games did a good job making you feel for the characters and their backgrounds. Lamb is an interesting character who's views are very religious as she tries to take over Rapture. However, I personally enjoyed Andrew Ryan as the antagonist more. Ryan's past and motives are more of a mystery when compared to Lamb's. The one aspect of Bioshock 2's story that I throughly enjoyed was how it closed loose ends of Bioshock 1's story. There were multiple audio logs from Andrew Ryan, Fontaine, and Atlas.
8.5 out of 10
Gameplay
This is the area of the game in which I thought Bioshock 2 really improved on. Weapons and plasmids are dual-wielded leading to faster gameplay and more intense firefights. There are also a few new weapons and enemy types. Plasmids and weapons can also be upgraded three times - just like the original game. The one thing that I disliked about the gameplay was that you could not pause the action and select a weapon or plasmid. You were able to do so on consoles and in the original (not sure if this feature is included when you plug in a 360 controller). All the weapons and plasmids are now hot-keyed which lead to me selecting a plasmid or weapon that I did not want to select. Regardless, I still had a great time shooting my way to get to Elenor.
9.5 out of 10
Audio
Everything from the weapons to the orchestral score sound great. Had a few instances in which audio would cut out much like the original. Even with a Creative sound card, this is extremely annoying. It does not occur much, but when it does it can cut immersion. Overall, the audio in this game is solid.
8.5 out of 10
Graphics
This was probably the hardest part of the game to review. At points in the game, the game still looks stelar. However, there are some levels in which the graphics do not look as good as the original Bioshock. Muddy textures can occur taking away from immersion, however this only occurs when you really look hard. In general, certain levels look better than others. The game still creates an amazing environment to explore and get lost in.
8.5 out of 10
Multiplayer
Multiplayer is a new addition to the Bioshock series and is done pretty well. The setting takes place during the civil war in Rapture, and it is great to return to locates from the original Bioshock. The weapons/plasmids are balanced and provide a lot of room for experimentation. My only gripe with the multiplayer is that it uses a peer to peer connection system. If you or the host have a crappy interent connection, the server will just lag for 10 minutes. With the multiplayer community not what it use to be, this can be very irritating. I really wish this game had dedicated servers - it would have had a much bigger community for it really is fun.
8 out of 10
Conclusion
Although not as impactful as the original game, Bioshock 2 is still a great game. You learn more about the failed underwater utopia, the origins of little sister and big daddies, and much more. The multiplayer is fun and refreshing, and the gameplay exceeds that of Bioshock 1. Definitely pick this game up if you are a fan of the Bioshock series.

Example Elite dangerous looks amazing, but all the traveling and trading, and lack of major battles turned me away after a month (yes i know alot has changed)
But Rebel Galaxy dosent have these faults. Its not an exploration game in my opinion because there isnt much to look at. The game looks ok but i feel its lacking alot of visuals for a space game, there is to much emptyness, when i travel nothing really catches my eye pluse the map is short. WHICH IS A GOOD THING. you dont spend  more than a min. or 2 traveling which is great for players like me. And while traveling alot happens in those 2 min. U get ditress calls, ambushes, unknow signals, and battles which u can stop at.
Battles are a strong point in this game. Fights are for the most part done in realitvily close combat which allows you to see the details of the battle. something other space game fail to capture. You can always have a wingman on you so your not fighty alone which was a huge plus for me. And larger fleet battles are intese with alot of visuals.  my only gripe about battles is u are stuck on a 2d axis while the AI isnt. This makes aiming anoying at times. But i can forgive it.
Theres not alot of ships but hey...its indie. you can customize your ships with different engins and weps, its basic but gets the job done. cool feature- you can set what each of your weps targets. example. i manually control broadside weps, turns attack anything near by, and i set one missle launcher to hit capital ships and my other launcher to manual only to no waste the limited missle ammo.
You can trade in the game if u want to, there a trading system with a flux market, random evnts like random wars and disasters effect trade. I cant go much into detail since i hate trading in games but it looks like a simple version of eleite dangerouses trade.
you can stick the main story or branch off to side missions, they game doesnt force u to only sitck to the course.
There is also reputation, it allows u to play the way u want. U can choose to help the militas and goverments or side more with the outlaw factions. the reputation also is based on how u play. example 1st mission. u have to get some good from a trader.... well u get there and have a choice...pokect the money the guy gave u to buy stuff from the trader for him and just kill the trader and take his stuff.....or complete the transaction. if u kill the trader, u make money but now the system is upset, it effects where u can dock, if u get attacked, and if they help u in battle, etc
I want to see some more features in the game for battles, but overall i like it.

This game marked the end of an era for me. Gone were the days of simplistic levels and stupid AIs. This was like nothing I had ever seen before the level of detail was amazing. The water effects and the moon lighting made me grasp for the first time the future of gaming was coming faster than I could have imagined. When I started gaming Wolfenstein 3D was the most advanced game available. Most people were playing NES for kicks and Kurt Cobain was still alive. The media had advanced so quickly gone were the days of playing Quake on dialup. This was for the first time a sleek, smart and realistic at least in appearance representation of WW2. The levels were so cozy it was a fun little trip through time with clever Germans in period clothing with even the right uniform markings for rank and branch. You respected those AIs at least you did after the first grenade to the face. It was interesting and entertaining even adding side conversations you could listen in on. The men smoked, drank and coughed sometimes laughing or listening to music just like any real person would, It was amazing. The story was good to begin with escaped spy on the run from the nazis. But then half way in you get blindsided by the cult zombie storyline it was perfect. You got a lovely dose of midevil gameplay with the creepy mummy knights and WW2 gameplay on top of it. The whole thing came together without a hitch it was one game I will always remember -SEF

Paying over $10 for this game will leave you with severe buyer's remorse. If you just want facts, skip the next 2 paragraphs.
To begin, I'll state that if you've played X3: Reunion/Terran Conflict/Albion Prelude and loved them, this is not a sequel, spiritual successor or anything along those lines. X Rebirth falls under the "inbread abomination" category. It borrows heavily from the lore, but not from any of the concepts that made the previous titles fun to play.
Don't be fooled by the positive reviews, half of them aren't even consistently deluded. With comments like "10/10" then individually listing the areas of the game as followed "Sound: 6/10, Graphics: 8/10, Gameplay: 4/10. Totally loved it" it's as if the positive reviews came from people either associated with the company or from people so dissapointed that they decided a drunken review to sucker more people out of their money was the best alternative to admitting this game was a flop.
Graphics: Nothing special here and if it runs on your computer properly it can be very pretty at times, about 50% of the uses are consistantly reporting massive framerate issues even after 6+ months of release. It uses directx 9, which is several generations old at this point and most believe this was due to it's, all but confirmed by the devs, origins as a console port.
Sound: The voice acting is mediocre to bad, it's repetitive too so there is really no way around listening to it.
Controls: Severly limiting, more complicated than previous "X" titles due to a complete failure to streamline them into a simpler form. No initial support for flightsticks on a space sim, the menus you use to navigate and control your *cough* "empire" *cough* are obviously designed around the limitations of a primarily controler driven interface, they took the menus from previous titles, removed them, then added in even more awkward and convoluted replacements that are twice as hard to navigate and produce half (if even that) the intended results.
Gameplay: If you like ultra repetitive minigames where you ping the map then blow up space debris for money, you'll love this game. If you like reflex minigames where you get to hear horrible voice acting, repeated over, and over, and over etc. you'll love this game. Your ship, The Albion Skunk, is essentially invincible and overtuned to the point that it's almost not fun. The ships in your fleet can't be directly controlled, they can only be given very, very basic orders and they often decide the best thing to do is follow you instead of completing those orders. These ships die or just dissapear because they're probably as sick of this ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t game as you are at this point.
Don't waste your money on this game, the only thing they did right was hyping the hell out of it to sell copies and even then it's arguable if that truly was the right thing. After this stinker, I'd be hard pressed to see how Egosoft expects to sell another game in this franchise to anyone.

I try to like this game. As a fan of the final fantasy series ever since the snes, I feel I'm required to cling on to the franchise and ignore the fact that it's turning into something I don't like.
I played through the game on xbox back when it was new. I bought it again now on steam and restarted for the sake of actually getting the story. And seven hours in, I feel that I really don't care about the story. Yes, final fantasy games have hardly ever been at shakespearian levels of character motivation, but we don't need that. We just need some reason _at all_ to go into the world, be it because your imaginary boyfriend might be real after all, robin williams told us to scrag his wife, or because our childhood girlfriend has a great rack.
Lightning has none of this. No reason at all known to the player why we should move forwards. Which is a shame, since moving forwards is the only gameplay available. Har har.
And so, with no further info than the fact that she's angry at something, we follow clip-clop through the world. A beautiful world full of rich details, wonderful landscapes, and a massive backstory. None of which makes any real impact. We don't know why clip-clop does what she does-. We don't know which external harddrive is on our side and which aren't, and we don't know why it's so imperative that we complete our quest. We wallow in the world, letting things flow over us, but not really absorbing anything because we have no starting motivation we can attach further knowledge to.
I'd say that the story is bad. I'd say that the world is bland. I'd say that the characters are badly written or hard to emphasize with. But really: the setting and the story is just wasted effort. A whole ton of writing and design which goes unappreciated because we have no reason to pay attention.
What we are left with in the end is a pretty picture, a combat system which is a good take on the job&paradigm systems of previous games but ultimately so disconnected from the story it might as well be skipped altogether, and a whole lot of backstory which is basically getting in the way of trying to figure out the story.
Bonus points for the game: It really is a beautiful game, and it runs nicely on older hardware. Even my busted up old rig can handle the 30fps cap on 4k resolution. Clip-clop punches the most dislikable character in final fantasy games since Gilgamesh. Shiva has turned into two hot chicks who scissor into a motorcycle on demand. The battle system is different from previous games, and actually somewhat balanced for once. There's a whole lot of gaming hours for the asking price.
I tagged the game as not recommended, but really; for its flaws, it's a definite maybe.

Fifth Hitman in the series, following a completely new path in comparison to previous installments. Without spoiling anything for those that haven't yet played the game - you are not just leading assassination after assassination. Its different. Agent 47's role isn't just being a Hitman, its also to protect.
As much as Absolution takes a completely different slant on the normally-expected storyline, I hold high praise for IO Interactive & Square Enix (Publisher & Developer). In simple terms, it worked brilliantly. For future titles, I would be disappointed if this was now normality. As a one-off, Absolution places you in different situations then Agent 47 is used to. The silent assassin now requires to look after not just himself, and must think on his feet quickly to the change in environments. Do expect linearity in missions.
A new and slightly frustrating feature in this game, although realistic, is the enhanced disguise function. Normally Agent 47 would be able to wear any type of uniform to slip past guards/security with ease.. not anymore! The AI isn't as thick as what it once was. Now you have the detection meter, so you could be wearing a police officer uniform - walk towards a police officer on duty - and get immediately alerted as a target. Time to be careful! You might be wearing the correct uniform, but people know who is on duty and who isn't. Therefore through this new feature, you can use your stealth meter to "hide" your face, so walking past guards isn't a problem. The problem however is the stealth meter runs out very quickly, so look to fill this up as quickly as possible when depleted. There are numerous times where you will be spotted a f****** mile away and it will annoy the sh*t out of you, but you'll learn the system and begin to appreciate it.(or, if you really really do hate it, there is a way of turning this feature off, google it!)
One other point to make which at first did annoy me, then became quite comical.. was that 9 times out of 10, a uniform which you expect Agent 47 to wear WITH the attached headgear/hat/mask... he will not. And it began to make me laugh because I thought the most deadliest, ruthless assassin in the world.. who chooses not to wear any form of headgear and runs around with a barcode on the back of his big bald head! Go figure! No wonder they keep spotting me damnit!
Jokes aside, I loved Absolution. Last time I played this was in 2012 on PS3, but was great to play again and fully complete, whilst trying to remember some of the routines! It has a very unique style of play and an interesting storyline, but for me personally I hope they don't make this the "new" gamestyle and instead focus on the roots that made Hitman the iconic series it is today. Well worth anyones time!

This game... I really can not understand how this game could get so many positive reviews. It failes at so many levels. First of all it features the most annoying male protagonist ever. And that really isn't a good start for a game when the character you start the game with is causing you pain just listening to him.
It also features a horribly random combat system. Not just is the order in which characters and enemies got to take an action random. Also the actions a character has available at his turn are down to randomness. You desperately need to heal? Well, you can only pray that in the next turn the game gives you the option to heal as one of the available actions.
I lost a lot of fights not because of doing anything wrong, but simply because the random number generator decided to not give me the option to heal when I would have needed it. Terrible design.
Another prime example of terrible design would be the leveling system. It's probably the most counter-intuitive leveling system ever featured in an RPG. Rule number 1: the less you fight the easier the game is. Getting a higher battle rank in this game is NOT a good thing. It will make basically all encounters harder up to the point that some become outright frustrating thanks to the randomness of the combat system.
The easiest way to play this game is to just run through the areas and avoid fighting as much as possible...
I never finished the game. The combination of meh story, painful main character, and the terribly random combat system extinguished my interest in completing the game fairly quickly.
I really can not recommend this game to anyone. Both gameplay and story fail to deliver.

This is such an un-sung game by such a mainstream company. So many things about this game are great!! I would attribute its obscurity to the fact that, not only did it come out on XBox first, I've also read that there were many balance issues and annoyances with that release.
The PC release seems to have corrected those issues, and what you get is an RPG with a very unique battle system (never seen anything like it), tons of characters that you get to really know through the story and MANY side-quests, a very fun resource gathering system, EXPANSIVE multi-purpose dungeons (the maps of which you have to find first!), beautiful graphics, and amazing music!
My one caveat is that if you are very attached to being able to micromanage in an RPG, this is not the game for you.
- You can not order units in battle specifically. You give them a general strategy and objective each turn, although you can see what their intended action will be. This could change however, depending on how the battle unfolds! Sometimes your groups will be intercepted or flanked! Sometimes characters will re-assess their action to do something more useful! In my opinion, this actually adds to the immersion and attachment you feel to the characters. I love watching the battles unfold.
- You can't even equip your other characters directly. Instead, they'll ask for equipment you find and craft, and they'll ask for components they need to improve their own gear! Again, I think this is great, the feeling that your characters are autonomous people with minds of their own really adds something to this game's experience for me.
All in all, definitely worth the price. It feels like I've just scratched the surface of this game, and I know that countless hours await me with all the side-quests, monster hunts, and exploration.

Crysis is a game that gets talked about more than it deserves. This is of course, because of the graphics. They still look pretty good in 2017, let alone 10 years ago. However they are not optimized well at all and the frame rate is as consistent as RX 580 stock. The sound in this game is ok. The effects are good and the soundtrack is fitting, but very forgettable. The voice acting isn't amazing, except for the British guy. I could listen to his gravelly voice say ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ all day.
The gameplay is conflicting for me. For the first 5 hours the game is a competent open ended fps that lets you tackle objects however you want. The nanosuit has some cool powers but isn't really done to its full potential. The games ai is also a bit ridiculous as even crouching within 100 metres of them will get you spotted. Instead of trying to make line of sight actually fair the developers just give you invisibility mode with your nanosuit; this feels like kind of a cop out but it is fun to dominate guards with. Then there’s the other half the game. In the first half you fought North Koreans in a combat sandbox. The second half of the game is just crap. You go down linear levels fighting bullet spongy aliens. Its pretty crappy stuff compared to the first game.
The reason I haven't mentioned the story is that it is impossible to care about. The main character has so little to say he may as well be a silent protagonist. The only good character is the aforementioned British guy, he feels like he is from a different game. What is a Britigh guy doing in US special forces anyway? But just like the plot, who cares.

Return To Castle Wolfenstein is a first-person shooter reboot of the Wolfenstein series which much like its predecessor focuses on fast-paced gunplay with a number of improvements made to compensate for the new engine technologies available at the time.
Firstly, unlike Wolfenstein 3D, the developers actually tried to implement a compelling story to a franchise known for not actually having a “story”. To some degree, the story in this game, at least from a concept point of view, brings something new to the table by adding elements of occult. The plot revolves around the American soldier, B.J. Blazkowicz, trying to impede the Nazis from discovering and extracting a serum hidden in an ancient tomb capable of augmenting soldiers into “Dark Knights”, an evil undead army from the 9th Century. Nazis and occult? Absurd ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, but what’s not to like. However, while the concept does enhance the single-player campaign, the story itself is mostly ignorable since it generally feels like it is there to fill in the space. Blazkowicz, while a total badass, still remains one of the blandest protagonists in existence. He takes orders from his superiors like a puppet with no remorse or personal motives. Even when the Allies want to give him a medal for his efforts and persumably a well deserved break at the end, he is somewhere outside still kicking Nazi butt. Boy, he sure is souless; born with only one scope in life: to kill Nazis for eternity. Plus, it is silly how the Allies' solution to most problems is to send a "one-man army" to take down Nazi headquarters single-handedly without even breaking a sweat. But that is Wolfenstein after all; it purposely does not need to explain how Blazkowicz does it -- and hey, some ancient voodoo magic is involved, so anything is justifiable, right? Fortunately, the story did manage to create the cool villain by the name of Deathshead, who later becomes the franchise’s main antagonist.
The gunplay in here is hasty but satisfying, reminiscent of older games such as Quake, Doom and Unreal Tournament, and unquestionably the strongest point of the game. While it all boils down to sprinting and shooting enemies in quick manners, the game does offer some moments of straightforward stealth where you get to sneak behind enemy lines. Additionally, there is an adequate variety in enemies from the deadly female squads in tight leather uniforms (those butts though) to juggernauts like the Über-Soldats. Different weapons are at Blazkowicz’s disposal too, with the Tesla gun being the most fun one to use, even if the MP40 probably becomes the most practical throughout most of the game, thus making pistols pretty redundant. One problem with the weapons though is the fact you never seem to run out of ammo. Retrospectively now, the gunplay does feel very basic, but mostly thanks to its fast paced action killing waves of enemies does not get dull, surprisingly enough.
The level design has the mentality of most shooters back in the late '90s and early noughties based on maze-like corridors and paths, essentially allowing the player the freedom to pick whichever route to travel back and forth within the somewhat confined space. Exploration is also encouraged and rewarded by finding secret chambers filled with collectables, even if these give no gameplay advantages to the player. Graphically, at the time, the game looked great but as time went by its visuals sure look dated today. On the other hand, the same cannot be said to its soundtrack which even to this day remains memorable and rather ageless. When you can recognise a level/map by a specific track from the soundtrack, then you know the soundtrack left a good impression.
Boasting a strong single-player campaign, (wherther you take the story seriously or not), many probably remember the game for its multiplayer component which at the time was very popular and considered by many superior than the campaign, even as far as being regarded one of the best multiplayer components in a game ever. I cannnot argue with that, although it was not until the highly acclaimed free standalone Wolfenstein: Enemy Territory came out that the multiplayer component peaked in popularity. Featuring a class-based gameplay similar to Team Fortress, two teams (Allies and Axis) fight each other to complete objectives on various maps. Personally, I spent far too many hours in the multiplayer alone when I was younger because it was balanced and had a very enjoyable experience. Currently, the multiplayer from Return To Castle Wolfenstein seems dead. Rest in peace.
In conclusion, Return To Castle Wolfenstein still remains a classic in the eyes of many, including myself, who played it in its heydays online and/or offline, and a milestone on PC. But it definitely lost its relevance and appeal to the general public as years have passed due to more ambitious and realistic shooters showing up years later. More old-school than modern, it still is a solid shooter, nevertheless, which does not spoil the player with today’s regenerative health and cover-base mechanics and can still provide enough hours of fun mindlessly killing Nazis. Pick it up only for nostalgic purposes or if you are curious to see how fast-paced shooters were like more than a decade ago in case you never grew up with them.

Despite having played a few hours as of now, I feel I can already review Return To Castle Wolfenstein on Steam since I played it a lot with my dad many years ago, when I was still a child (don't let mom know about it!).
So I already have decent understanding of the story of this game. Heck, I know the whole story in general. The story is good: during the Second World War, you play as an American agent of some secret service who investigates certain activities of the fictional SS Paranormal Division. You operate behind enemy lines, your mate has fallen and the service refuses to send reinforcements; therefore, you stand alone. The story fits nicely in the whole Wolfenstein saga, and gives a nice thrill overall.
Graphics are good for a game which is roughly 14 years old. Gameplay doesn't have any serious shortcomings either; it is just your average first person shooter. Only thing I miss is the possibility to aim down the iron sights of non-scoped weapons. The setting is an extra plus for fans of the WW2-genre, with a touch of fantasy attached to it. Bonus points for feelings of nostalgia.
The only serious problem with this game is the initial inability to set the resolution higher than the default setting. Although that can be fixed by downloading and mounting a non-official patch of the game (link:
. Patch can be found under 'DOWNLOADS'. Extract all files in the ZIP-file in the Return To Castle Wolfenstein folder under SteamApps > commons.), it is an issue which prevents jumping right in, which some may find irritating, and should be adressed accordingly by Steam.
One more important thing: make sure to save your game regularly, as the game doesn't save automatically even after completing a level. Got me back to the beginning after three levels.
This game is okay and deserves to be recommended, but enthusiasts of nostalgia and the WW2-genre will find something valuable in Return To Castle Wolfenstein.

You got problems captain.
You just came out of warp. Your screen fills with red icons as criscrossing missile trails and cannon fill your vision. Seems this station is under attack by a rather nasty group of pirates. You can see your turrets taking aim and firing as you aim for the station itself. The system militia seems to be doing well, but the pirates just got reinforcements. Torpedo bombers and enemy frigates are starting to get real close. Too close for your liking. You activate your flak cannons and watch the fighters pull away from you. Unleashing a broadside into a passing enemy frigate, you idly wonder if maybe you should just take that mining laser off of your rear turret. Maybe get another tachyon turret? Your ship shakes violently as a mine slams into your hull, and with growing concern you hear your ship calmly relay the fact that your engines are slowing down. Hitting your deflectors you absorb a few torpedo hits as your shields try their best to recharge with the brief respite you have given them.
Best shields in the sytem you had thought to yourself as you happily pressed the buy button after trading all that juicy ore you mined. This situation probably wouldn't have been a big deal, if you hadn't of been ambushed on the way here. Apparently when the mission board said 'deadly ore delivery' they had meant it. That fight with two massive heavy frigates had ripped most of the armor off of your hull. Then your hull had been beaten something fierce. Emerging from that fight with a mere 20% hull integrity had been rough.
That was before the distress call. Sure, you could have ignored it, after all in your experience sometimes it was a trap. Yet sometimes it was a trader in need of help. You had come out of warp with all of your weapons singing. The friendly trader barely expressed his grattitude before handing over a handful of credits and jumping to warp. Sure, you could have ignored them and kept on trucking, but that aint you, is it outlaw? Frontier folks gotta stick together.
You sigh as you realize you just fired on a militia ship. It was gonna be a while before you could build that rep up. Luckily, the station was in full view, and you hit your boosters and your deflectors to make up the remaining distance.
As you dock, you smile as 31,900c goes into your account, and the repair costs of your ship are covered by those alien artifacts you scooped up coming in.
You have heard rumors of other galaxies. Starpoint Gemini 2, X3 Terran Conflict, Evochron Mercenary, Freelancer, but word in the space bars is that all of those where missing something. As you replace your flak cannon arrays with EMP grids, you can't help but smile once more.
Yeah, you got problems captain, but that's the way you like it.

So first off, let me say that I have not played any of the previous entries of this game. But at the same time I LOVE a good space sim. With that said, I went into this game with no preconceptions of what it should be overall. I think that is kind of a problem sometimes with people that go into a game that have a long standing series that they played most of and they feel like it should conform to what they have played before and thats ok too sometimes though and can be helpful to people also but, this review I think could be helpful from the point of view of a person coming in fresh to the series.
I did watch some youtube videos of gameplay prior to buying this game. My intial thoughts, afterward, were that I MUST have it. Now, after getting into the game a little bit and playing through the story some, I think that I stand firm with my intial thoughts for the most part. I like X Rebirth a lot. Its a great game with a lot to do. I love that it breaks up flying around space with a little on foot things to do as well. I believe that lends to immersion and that it is an easy game to really project yourself into. Also, with workshop support there are many different things you can add and change about/to the game that can add enjoyment or tailor to the way you want to play which is a very big plus imo.
As I have said, I played through the game a bit now and with that I have also seen some of the bad parts of it. There are missions that get bugged and prevent progression. It is nothing but a google search and some notepad++ action to remedy it usually but it still is unnecessary steps for a game that is supposed to be finished (out of beta). Optimization is not the best either. But, as for the above mentioned topics it really does seem like Egosoft is working hard to patch and update the game to fix these problems while adding more functionality and gameplay to the experience. On a more opinionated note, I found that except for story missions and the occasional 1 line there is no verbal interaction between the pilot (you) and the co-pilot that sits next to you. I would've liked to seen more dialog between them when just flying around for more immersion and to learn how those characters relationship evolve and more about their history.
While I did and do recommend this game and feel that it is definately one worth playing if you like the genre, I dont feel like in its current state that it is worth the $50 price tag (as of 2.10). So if you're really wanting value from this I would suggest waiting on a sale or just waiting in general because I get the impression that they will continue to work hard to fix some of the issues with this game to make it an even better experience. If you're not that concerned about the price tag and want a good space sim and are willing to deal with some generally mild problems then my recommendation is to give this a shot.

First, regarding all these people complaining about that update, a new patch went live 2 days after that and added casual mode again, so these complaints are obsolete.

This game is an arena brawler (going Free 2 Play on Nov. 8th). The gameplay is... pretty unique really, I don't know any other game that does something like that (although many people seem to refer to BloodLine Champions, by the same developpers, but I have never played it). Think of it like a top-down, very nervous PvP game (in the like of Ragnarok Online's PvP, if that helps). Here's a game with progamers if you want an idea:
It has 2 arena modes, 2v2 & 3v3, and a 3v3 mode called Battlegrounds that adds some objective-based elements (while still remaining as nervous as the other ones).
The artwork is very appealing (character design is a big + for me), the music is fine, the community is nice and helpful, the devs are very attentive to us players and pretty hardworking.
What I absolutely love with this game is how it is 100% based on skills (at least for the arena mode). No items, no shop, no skills to unlock, no levels, no objectives, no minion farming or whatever - simply raw, intense action-packed battles where your only assets are your skills and your teammates. I personally don't know any other similar game, and I enjoy both playing and watching streams of it :D (if you want these other things, you can still play Battlegrounds though, it has some of them)
To sum it up: great game, I recommend. And I personally like to believe it has some room to become bigger :P
PS: No, I do not know any dev and I am not paid for this xD

Okay. Let's face it: you've heard quite a bit about this game. "There's nothing to explore.", "The characters are garbage.", "You can just hit 'auto', and it'll play itself."
That's... well, that's pretty much true... if you don't play long enough.
From the surface, Final Fantasy XIII looks pretty shabby. And as someone who is playing all the way through for the first time? I'm not really lying when I say that around 20 hours in, I was dragging pretty hard. I stepped away from the game for a while, because it really was ONE hallway after ANOTHER hallway.
But if you have the patience to labor through around 25 hours... the game starts to give you more freedom, less cutscenes, and quite a bit to do.
After (your mileage may vary) 18 hours or so, the game quits holding your hand, and you can now assign classes to all six of your characters (it's also, conveniently, the first time all 6 characters are in the same room as one another... how's that for building up backstory?). After around another 7 or so hours (YMMV... grinded quite a bit in that 7 hours), you also get to the part of the game that most people are thinking of when they say they like this game: Chapter 11.
The game is divided into 13 chapters (Final Fantasy 13... makes sense), and the "half way point" of the game is roughly when you beat chapter 9. So when you get a little bit past halfway through the game, you make it to Chapter 11, where you're just plopped into a huge open world to explore. Not only is there main story, but there's roughly 65 (or so... don't know exactly know how many, as this is where I'm at right now in my playthrough) side missions. These range from "go 20 steps behind you and kill the glowing blue pile of plasma" to "go across the gigantic field, head to this optional area, and beat the insanely hard boss at the end". Your reward? Anything from items, to weapons, to even a double-xp item that makes post-game much, MUCH easier.
In this open world, everything goes. When you first start an encounter, you have no idea if you'll survive, or not, as the multiple enemies running around in this open world can be pretty low leveled, or some of the hardest enemies in the game (as believe it or not, story bosses aren't the hardest enemies). This makes it somewhat annoying, but considering a "game over" screen kicks you right back to the second before you bumped into an enemy (and gives you around 3 seconds of i-frames to allow you to decide if you want to give it another go or not), you don't lose much if you die. It makes it a low-risk, high-reward game, but considering how long some of these tough battles can be, I don't blame the devs for not wanting to cause too much rage.
The game itself has aged extremely well, considering it's initial release (HUGE props to the devs for bringing this game to PC 4.5 years later. it took them awhile, but PC finally got it). The cutscenes still hold their own with a lot of current-age video games. And the gameplay visuals themselves are pretty stunning until you get to the open-world stage, and can actually see the render distance and horizon textures start to show their age. The game doesn't suddenly look horrible, or anything, you can just tell that it's a port of an older console game.

For those who want to explore more Final Fantasy after playing FFXV, I say "go for it". The rest of the series is fantastic, and a lot of the stories in these games are iconic (looking at Final Fantasy IV, VII, and X as the most highly regarded). If you've never played Final Fantasy, this isn't a bad place to start, considering it's availability on pretty much everything but the PS4 (it's no longer on PS Now, I believe).
But go in knowing that this part of the series isn't perfect, and Final Fantasy XIII, XIII-2, and Lightning Returns have really divided the fanbase. These games are great, but only if you have the patience to really see the games in their entirety, and not everyone is willing to do that. That, and these 3 games changed too much in some die-hards' opinions, leaving a bad taste in the mouth of the community for everyone involved. Those who praise the game are annoyed by the haters, and those who hate the game are annoyed by those who like it. It's a lose/lose situation.
Those who want to explore this game thinking it's like Final Fantasy XV... I don't recommend this game. It's completely different. And Final Fantasy I - XII aren't going to scratch that itch, either. Final Fantasy XV's combat revolutionized the series, and was a major turning point, even from the kind-of-almost-but-not-really related Final Fantasy XIV: A Realm Reborn MMO. The over-the-top fast-action from XV isn't here. So if you want more the WORLD of Final Fantasy, check it out. Just don't think it's going to play like XV.

Okay so having finished this game at a 100% completion with over 400 hours invested in it (I played it on X360 too, years ago) here's an actual non-biased review.
Pros:
The UNIQUE (and by unique I mean nothing compares to it in ANY game whatsoever) combat and leveling system.
Not only do you have to keep track of the classes (which, by the way, are in a very large amount), but you keep track of your stats (obviously), weapons, abilities (arts)...
Every weapon leads to different styles, different arts, different stats, different gameplay..
The customization possibilities are virtually endless. I really like the graphics of the various spells you cast, the combat is really fun to watch, and sometimes the game can get really, really hard (i.e. DLC bosses omg). But hey, I finished it at 100%, and I'm not some hardcore gamer. There's SO MUCH to learn about that when you realize how in-depth and complex the game mechanics are, it can get overwhelming and you might end up quitting.
The wiki for it has a plethora of information, so you can't really "get lost". But there's so much to do that a 100% completion, played casually and just exploring without really being sure what to do... That's gonna take over 150 hours, most likely.
NEW GAME +. oh yes, starting the game with large amounts of cash, and a few other things that I won't spoil.
The units and leaders: So. many. possibilities. You dislike a guy? Bench him forever. Want to make a party of only chicks? Go for it. Don't like the main toon? Don't play him. (But he can kinda do everything so worth using).
Ah, also. Beautiful story, I really enjoyed the graphics (I mean I played it 7-8 years ago) and the universe you play in is quite large, there's a ton of quests to do.
Cons? Sure there's a few.
Kinda flawed, a little redundant sometimes, the main character is not the brightest guy..
Magic isn't as strong as you'd want it to be, sigh. S
ome bosses are super annoying and are tough to kill regardless of what you try.
The items for your companions, well you can't really choose what they use. Some have unique items, and to properly "equip" them, you kinda have to learn how leveling works... which is very complex. Not complicated, complex.
Overall: for it's genre, a turn-based JRPG, I'm honestly giving it at 9/10. I don't see what could possibly make it have a bad score. The bad reviews are mainly because of people not taking the time to understand the in-depth mechanics.
IT. IS. COMPLEX. But really, really, really fun.
TLDR: Very complex game. Unique leveling/combat mechanics. Endless customization. There isn't a lot of information in-game about how everything works (you need the wiki, srsly). But if you like RPGs, and turn-based rpgs, (enchanted arms, lost odyssey) you're gonna love this. It's freaking 13 bucks (to me at least) and has all the DLCs. Until Lost Odyssey gets to PC, I'll be playing this often.

Melee is one of my favorite games ever, especially competitively. Rivals is probably the closest any other game has gotten to it that I've played without feeling like a bad knock-off.
This is a really solid platform fighter, where you knock people off the screen to win just like in Smash. Movement is very fluid and fast and I never feel like I'm fighting the game when I want to do something. I enjoy playing most of the cast and every character feels unique, which helps when there isn't a huge roster to play. The music is great and the art is very clean, free of overly flashy visuals that could be distracting. There's a good variety of stages plus the ability to play with competitive and casual versions of every stage, turning stage hazards off or on.
Rivals does make efforts to differentiate itself from Smash, though your mileage may vary on whether that ends up being for better or worse. The complete removal of ledge grabbing is a pretty radical change although recovery still feels fun enough without it. Things I definitely miss however are shields and grabs/throws on every character. It just feels like there's less depth in the game now without that, and parrying isn't a good enough replacement for regular blocking IMO.
Story Mode is probably the weakest part of the game. It's basically just a slideshow with fights spread out along the way that don't even match up with the story for the most part. It's nice that it even exists at all I guess, but it's no Adventure Mode or Subspace Emissary. I would have liked something more substantial to build up the world at least a little bit. Abyss Mode is thankfully really fun, it's just a shame that Abyss Versus is local only.
I want to highlight the tutorial which is miles ahead of anything Nintendo ever bothered to add in any Smash game. It's very in-depth and perhaps more importantly guided and interactive, covering everything from the basics to advanced topics. There are even character specific tutorials. It's a really great resource for getting started with the game if you aren't familiar with how a lot of the deeper Smash derived mechanics work.
Overall I think Rivals succeeds at capturing a lot of what I enjoy about Melee even if it doesn't quite reach it, which unfortunately means that it has to live in the shadow of a different game for me. That still doesn't erase the fun evenings on the couch with friends getting hype for the sick combos. This is where the game really shines, and in that sense it was more than worth it.

Rivals of Aether is a platform fighter, much like Super Smash Brothers or Brawlhalla(among others). If you enjoy those games, especially if you enjoy the high skill ceiling they have, pick up Rivals. It's made by a small, dedicated team of individuals who continually update their game, and are incredibly involved with their community, both in the casual, and the competitive scenes. Below are my thoughts specifically on Rivals of Aether and what makes it stand out from its ilk.
Super Smash Brothers has a sort of 'character triangle' when it comes to top-of-casual or low-competitive play. It is most evident in the newest entry of Super Smash Brothers, for the Wii U/3DS. The basic logic is such:
Reflector > Ranged > Counter > Reflector...
This logic has basis in low-competitive levels ONLY, and is not applicable to higher levels of play. Low-competitive is essentially what you would see in the For Glory mode of this game, generally. Counter-Based characters are beaten out by Ranged as their specials are all but useless when they are being ranged out, but those projectiles are useless against a Reflector-based character. But as Reflector-based characters generally have no or very slow projectiles, they can easily be killed by counter-based characters. Obviously this does not hold true for all characters(Mewtwo, for example, is for all intents and purposes Ranged and Reflector in equal parts), but is a general rule when counterpicking(the act of picking a character more suited to beating your opponent) is concerned.
Rivals of Aether does not have the same triangle. Every character is every single type, except for a few exceptions. Every character but Clairen and Forsburn have ranged attacks, but the parry(used the same way a spot-dodge is in Smash Brothers, or just by dodging with no directional input on the ground) is both a reflector and a counter, as it stops the enemy if you are hit with a melee attack up close and makes them vulnerable to a strong attack, or sends projectiles back to where they came from if used to block those, while alos granting a small amount of invincibility to help you close the gap and get in a quick hit. There are still metrics for the characters(as Dan Fornace himself put it, there are characters more geared towards rushdown tactics as opposed to spacing, and vice versa), but every character is viable and every character has no obvious counterpicks. This makes Rivals infinitely more interesting to the low-competitive player, and puts an emphasis on predicting your opponents' next move(commonly called 'reading').
Rivals also has much larger amounts of hitstun(the moment when you cannot move or take an action after being hit and launched into the air) than Smash Brothers, allowing for a more fluid and forgiving combo game that values that first hit even more, and not what comes after it as much. As long as you know what direction your opponent will DI(move away after they are hit), you can easily land a follow-up.
In closing, Rivals of Aether is a heaven for people tired of Super Smash Brothers' limited combo game, tired 'true' combos, and restrictive character balancing. It is much more fluid, fast, and relies more on the players' strength when it comes to reads, as well as creativity in mixing up their approaches and attacks to keep their enemies on their toes. It's made damn well and runs like a dream, and has a lot of Quality-of-life improvements over other fighting games(such as the ability to see how good your connection is with another player exactly BEFORE you enter a match with them.
Also, Dan Fornace's twitter is amazing. Seriously, look it up.

I hated this game...not everything, but most of it.  Let me first start with the positives.
Pros:
Battle System - The battlesystem is more action-oriented than previous incarnations of Final Fantasy series.  While I prefer the old-fashion ATB style Final Fantasies, I think the Paradigm battle system does make the fight sequences less of a drag and keeps my blood pressure slightly elevated.  The Paradigm system simplifies and streamlines the commands of the party and keeps the fights engaging.
Graphics - As of this writing, Final Fantasy 13 is nearly 7 years old since worldwide release.  The performance enhancement provided by the PC port gives the game an extended lifetime as far as visuals go.  Oddly enough, the FMV suffers the most and looks grainy compared to the smoother in-game graphics with the port.  There's no denying Final Fantasy 13 is a gorgeous game.
PC Port - I was concerned that the porting of this game from the console would result in many bugs and glitches that would hamper my enjoyment of the game.  Surprisingly, there were few bugs that I found distracting.  This is a terrific port as far as PC ports goes.  As such, bugs and glitches did not hamper my enjoyment of the game...the enjoyment hampering was the result of a multitude of other issues which I'll discuss next.
Cons:
Story - Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥..the story is convoluted!  Even until the very end, the story didn't straighten itself out much.  So the basic premise (from what I understand), is that the floating world of Cocoon (which is essentially a moon with a big hole on its side) and the larger planet, Gran Pulse are at odds with each other.  The deity-like entities, called Fal Cie, appear to be warring with each other...though it is never made clear why they're not buddies.  Although the Fal Cie do have tremendous powers, they are limited in the manners they able to wield said powers.  Just think of a dragcar attempting to go down a 25mph residential neighbohood.  In other words, they're powerful beings that are trapped in their respective worlds.  The Fal Cie can, however, directly influence humans.  Once such way is to give human's a "focus"...aka task.  Upon completing their focus, they are awarded immortality by being converted to a crystalline form.  If they fail their task, they are then turned into these miserable, mindless creatures called Cieth.  This is the Fal Cie's way of getting around their limitations.  The Fal Cie are limited in what they can influence, but humans have no such limitations.  Humans can do anything they want.  The Fal Cie realizes this and exploits human freedom of choice to enact their own agendas against the other's world.  In comes Lighting, Snow, Sazh, Hope, Fang, and Vanille.  The main plot revolves around the six of them as they try to figure out what their focuses are and how to complete it.  The game explores several themes, but the biggest recurring theme is free will vs. destiny as they try reconcile their own interests, the interest of the people of Cocoon, and the interests of the Fal Cies.  So that's the overall, broadstroke gist of the it all.
Like I said, I hate the story.  I found it hard to connect with the characters.  The voice acting didn't make it easy (I think Sazh was the best voice-acting in the bunch).  I thought the motivations of the antagonists were really esoteric and not very compelling.  I didn't feel the comraderies and bond between the characters...and that's not for a lack of trying on the writer's part.  The characters have their own set of baggages and there was plenty of story built-in to cement those relationships as they resolve their problems together....but it was never quite convincing or compelling to me.  Most of the time, I found the characters were just down-right annoying.  Worst of all, the story was confusing to me...and just when I thought I had some of it straightened out, a new plot twist was tossed in to make it more muddled!  After about the 10th hour of the game, I just didn't care anymore and rushed the rest of the game to finish it.  I've played every single Final Fantasy game (except part 15), and I have to say...this is one of the ♥♥♥♥♥iest story for me.  I liked part 9, as far as story and characters go, the most...just to give you a sense of where I'm coming from.
Character progression - The character progression is kinda crappy.  To make your characters more powerful, Final Fantasy 13 gives you the Crystallarium system.  You collect CP when dispatching monsters and then, in turn, you use the CP to move along this grid to reach the next status, spell, or itemization upgrade.  The system is not very deep, and doesn't provide much in the way of variability of your characters.  It's simple, just collect a lot of CP and apply it to the Crystallarium grid.  There some choices that the player has to make when using CP on the grid...do you apply your points to the Commander grid or the Ravager or Medic grid?  There are some forks in the grid, but it's not a big deal because if you earn enough CP, you can get the skill or stats of either fork.  There's no real consequences for picking one path over another because nothing gets locked out.  They may as well have just stuck to the ol' tried and true 'gain xp points to level up', because this system has about the same amount of depth.  It's very linear and not fun to play with.
Exploration - Or rather...lack thereof!  The game is reputed to be an RPG corridor...I now understand why.  There's no real exploration in the game.  There are no towns or dungeons...or even NPC to talk to!  The game is very linear and plays as if it were on rails.  The options are few and obstensibly, the outcomes are the same.  The closest the game comes to an open world is at chapter 11 where you finally make it to the world of Gran Pulse....or a small section of it I should say.  On Gran Pulse, you can pick up missions from these Cieth Stones (people who have turned to Cieth and then subsequently to stones.  These Cieth Stones asks that you complete their focuses for them.  The missions are fairly simple...find monster X...and then kill monster X.  There are various rewards for completing the missions including items, weapons, and weapon upgrade materials....but ultimately, by the point in the game, I didn't want to do any of them if it required backtracking.  As I mentioned earlier, I just wanted to be done with the game by hour 10.
Overall Feel of the game - I might have been fine with the game if were called something else other than Final Fantasy.  For me, FF13 didn't feel like a Final Fantasy game.  The world, although beautiful, did not feel alive and interactive to me.  The signature icons of Final Fantasies made appearances, but none of them in the manner they appeared in other FF games.  The Chocobos were just a part of the Sazh's plotline as he resolved his issues with Vanille and his son.  The Moogles didn't really make an appearance, but instead is a part of a menu on the save selection options.  Some of the creatures were familiar...like the Behemoths and flan....but most of the creatures were reskins (how many sabretooth tiger skins can there be?!?!).  Although, I must admit the Adamantoise was pretty cool.  Lets see...oh yeah, the equipment management was really shaved down...but I think that's been the trend since FFX, I think.  There was no vehicle travel...going from A to B was all on foot.  The world isn't too big, so travel time isn't much of an issue...it just doesn't feel right.  Even FFX had an airship at the end where you can land at preselection destinations.  No such thing in FF13.  The game's feel was too much of a departure from what I knew and love of the Final Fantasy series.  As such, it's hard to recommend this game to fans of the series....but at the same time, if you're a true Final Fantasy fan like I am, you'll suffer through this game like I did.

Back in the day, when Sins of a Solar Empire first came out, it was already quite apparent that what Ironclad Studios had made was unique. Then the Entrenchment and Diplomacy expansions came and changed the game entirely for the better. Ironclad was content to let it be after that, but when a dedicated group of fans started churning out optimization mods, the Sins team took notice and decided to give us exactly what we needed: Rebellion! With a fully custumizable interface and with more than fifty high quality mods (not to mention the ability to create your own maps in the Galaxy Forge), Sins of a Solar Empire: Rebellion has some of the highest replayability factor in any game I've ever played. The online play is intense, and while there is the occasional crash or two per game, the real time tactics and deep character behind every aspect makes it more than worth playing through. If that's not enough for you, there are some excellent mods that can be easily installed. I would highly suggest using the E4X Mod, the Star Wars Interregnum Mod, and the Epic Scale Mod. However, if Star Wars isn't your thing, then you might be more interested in the various Star Trek, Babylon V, Stargate and Halo Mods! Nothing is impossible with this game; I've actally made a few private mods and skins myself, it's that simple. Next time it comes on sale, I highly suggest you buy it along with all of the DLC. You won't regret it.

An experimental game from Square Enix. Essentially it's a squad based semi-tactical JRPG. Why semi? Because unfortunately it heavily relies on RNG component rather than real tactics. You'll command a mini-army of 18 characters (units) divided by 4-5 squads, the problem is that you can only give them a set of commands (like, "attack with all you've got", or "help the others") and which skills/spells to use they'll decide on their own, for example if you want to bombard a certain enemy with a certain spell than you'll have to rely on luck, your units may decide to use them, use something else or even just simply attack with their weapons. There are few workarounds (essentially just having 3-5 people in a squad with a desired spell will boost chances of casting it or switching targets to get another set of commands) but sometimes it could lead to a very unfortunate results in your battles. I think it's the main reason why this game was not very well received.
Despite all that it's still a very fun game to play, there are a lot of everything in this game: characters, weapons, skills, equipment etc. Believe me - quantity of everything is just enormous. Skill system is pretty complex but once you get a grip over everything you'll be pretty satisfied. There are also a lot of customization options for your army, you can hire generals, soldiers, make different formations, farm rare monsters for materials to upgrade weapons of your soldiers or simply craft them yourself.
I guess you have to try it to understand whether it suits you or not, cause you wont be able to answer that question for yourself by watching related media and at this price I can certainly recommend this game, especially if you're into JRPGs and not afraid to try something new.
My final score is 7/10.

One of the magazines (IGN, I think) said that this was the war game that we've all been waiting for.  Not only do I agree with that statement, but this is probably the survival game that we've been waiting for.  No zombies, no sci-fi post-apocalyptical scenario.  This game does a great job at communicating the realities of trying to survive in a very real situation.
I just started my second playthrough, having survived only 27 days in the first run.  I haven't noticed anything "special" about the interface or anything technical about this game.  The graphics are simple, but smooth, but I like the nice touch of having the photo on the bio card blink every once in a while.  The music is also basic, but it fits the genre and situation.  Some variation to the score would have been much better.  There isn't anything that really stands out in terms of gameplay when comparing it to other games of its kind, even Flash-based survival games.
What truly sets this game apart is the realistic scenario.  It is so easy to ignore the realities this game reveals when they are explored through the safe medium of Zombie Apocalypse.  In most other survival games like this, there is typically a common enemy that the surviving humans have to fight against and allying with other humans to beat them is the only way to win.  In "This War of Mine," there is no such enemy.  Hunger, disease, depression, and hypothermia are the only enemies in this game.  The other humans you encounter are also trying to fight these enemies on their own terms just like you are.  It truly begs the question - what will you do to survive when War comes riding through?  A question that most - if not all - players will never have to answer in real life.
Many props to this developer for making this game!

Sequals usually fall flat when people play them. Not very often does a sequal come by that impresses and wins over an original games audience. Lets face it,
is a cash in on the success of
. Despite this, it does not fail as game, nor as a sequel.
The overall gameplay of this game is far superier to that of the original. The weapon variety maybe not as diverse, and the weapon designs do not change drastically like the original, but still good weapons nonetheless. I mean, what other game can you play as zeus in a metal diving suit, with a gatling gun? In addition to this, the balence is better, the research process is better thought out, plasmids are not stupidly OP anymore, and you can actually get some neat tonics and upgrades to your Big Daddy. The little sister and escort sections are not tedious anymore either, they offer a nice break from the monotony of the main story. This is broken up with some nice tea parties with  former co-workers of yours, and some swims in the community fish tank. The games pacing is fluid from beginning to end, and does not chug at any point, unlike the original.
Originally, my main criticism of
, is that it did not have that "AHA" moment the original had. Well lets just say that the DLC Mirvenas Den solves that problem. Everything I thought
was lacking, that DLC contained. What it did, is offered that "AHA" moment that made the original so good. At first, I thought the DLC ending would be generic and terrible, only to find out the big plot twist at the end. This twist, along with the ending area/cutscene, offers a conclusive end to the rapture experiance. It finally wraps up the city in a satisfying way, something, neither game alone could do.
In short, this game improves upon even facet of the original, maybe not to a shine, but certainly to some degree, and offers a conclusive ending to the original Bioshock series/Rapture. Giving this God-Forsaken underwater dystopia, finally a sense of peace.

As I look back, there are a lot of LOTR games for a single setting that is. War in the North is a 1 to 3 man co-op game. It is played in 3rd person and at its core is a Hack ‘n Slash. Your character choices are a Dwarf Axe wielder, Human Ranger, or an Elven Magic User.  The game can be entirely soloed but for a complete more enjoyable and manageable play through I suggest teaming up with 2 friends.
Combat Monotony: So this game’s simple system of Heavy Attack Light Attack, Roll, and Block really took its toll on my attention span. I would not go as far as to say I was bored with it, but it was very repetitive. Coming from a history of very grindy, time consuming titles, I was fine with this.
Weak Story and Characters: So the story without ruining anything runs parallel to the LOTR Books/Movies. That is to say Sauron is still trying to rule the world but you’re after his Lieutenant or something. It’s that unmemorable.  In fact I don’t remember getting all the achievements for this game.
Bland is the word I’m going to use here. It’s all I have. No innovation.
Beyond that it has your typical RPG Elements with Skill Trees and various weapon upgrades.
The Visuals: The most memorable part of this game for me was the Visual look and feel of the world. It has a movie like feel and has the graphical strength that should have been applied to LOTR: Online MMO.
Final Thoughts: Die hard LOTR Fans will still enjoy the bits of story that crossover from the rich world Tolkien created. Always play with Friends and never forgot to call an Eagle to fly you home after a Hobbit Feast.

Crysis. A landmark title in PC gaming history and the spiritual successor to the first Far Cry. Make no mistake here, this game looks great but is doomed to be remembered for its graphical prowess and the meme surrounding it, while the game should instead be remembered for the open ended gameplay it provided.
The first two thirds of Crysis has the player exploring large nonlinear levels that encourage player freedom and exploration, and the game is at its best when you're taking out enemy camps in your own, creative way. The variety of gameplay is facilitated by the nanosuit and its powers, letting the player choose between silently killing enemies from behind to grabbing them by the neck, jumping 10 feet into the air and throwing the helpless ♥♥♥♥ into a shack that collapses under the nanosuit's might. You even can throw explosive barrels at helicopters, shoot them, and watch as the explosion causes the helicopter to explode as well. Although it's great, there are a few small nitpicks I have with the gameplay, such as the snail-paced walkspeed outside of the speed suit power and the AI that manages to be dumb but infuriating at the same time, sniping me with shotguns from a fair distance.
However, the game takes a turn for the worse as you reach the 4 hour mark. I have never experienced such a baffling, dramatic tone shift in a game before. The large nonlinear levels are traded for linear ones, the enemies are changed from North Korean troops to boring aliens (that you can't grab by the neck and toss around) and the story is prioritized ahead of the gameplay itself. It's mediocrity from here on out as you ♥♥♥♥ about with a confusing alien base level, an escort mission, a turret section, a flying section, a 20+ minute walk-here-walk-there story mission, and then a boss fight that requires a weapon that you are not forced to pick up, allowing for certain players to be stuck until they replay the last mission.
Overall, Crysis is definitely worth checking out for the first two thirds of the game alone, as it provides a unique experience among first person shooters of the time and even today. You're not going to get the most interesting story or many memorable characters but it's a fun romp through its iconic tropical landscape. The expansion, Crysis Warhead, is also worth checking out if you like this game, as it is full of open ended level design from start to finish. But, for the love of god, don't play the sequel.
