Final Fantasy 13 (XIII) is one of the most polarizing main numbered titles in the Final Fantasy franchise. Every part of the game has been streamlined, from how the story progresses to combat to even how your characters get stronger. I may have Stockholm Syndrome, but I think much of it has changed for the better, removing some annoying hiccups in the process, while some resulted in the pitchfork emporium running out of stock.
FF13 is a good but not great game that tries a lot of new things, many of which are good, but don't mesh well together, with a good story, decent characters, and simple combat system that has some flexibility. 7.5/10
Final Fantasy 13 is the first entry on the PS3/Xbox360 generation. It takes place in the cyberpunk super hi tech world of Cocoon, overlooking the much larger wild planet of Gran Pulse. There are 13 chapters within the game, with the first 10 being entirely linear (no side quests, no extra areas to explore, just a main path to the objective with a few short paths for treasure) and the world opening up for extra stuff in chapter 11. Progression is through the crystarium system, which keeps you from becoming too powerful too fast by only unlocking more stuff and certain junctures, including after beating the game.
Combat uses a modified ATB system, where you control one character; if they die, game over. Using paradigms, you can manipulate what your party of 3 is capable of doing, from tanking damage, to debuffing, to buffing, to healing, to dealing a crapload of damage, to increasing the amount of damage that enemies take.
One of the biggest changes is in how the story is told; more specifically, how the game is basically a corridor for 15 hours and you have no choice but to progress with the story. Personally, I don't think that this is that big of a problem. The story is one of the best parts about the Final Fantasy series, and this one is no exception. The main party are pretty whiny in the opening chapters, but there is a lot of character growth through the middle and latter stages of the game, especially with Lightning and Hope.
The big problem is that they just open it all up in chapter 11 by shoehorning it in. Oh, we've been building up our story for several chapters and now you have a very short period of time to complete your focus? Let's just throw that pacing out the window and let you go kill a bunch of stuff! The game was pretty good (maybe not up to Final Fantasy hype standards, but good none the less), but it feels like the developers wanted to do a certain something with the game by having a lot of focus on story, but felt the need to include some classic side quests and world exploring that are part of what gives the franchise its mystique.
Combat, in short, is a "Press X" simulator. You have a party of up to 3 characters, with direct control over only one character. As it is still the ATB system, you have a bar that fills up to determine when you can make actions. To use the ATB bar, you can either select auto battle to have the game automatically choose what it thinks are the best actions, or go to abilities and select a chain of abilities for yourself. What's great about this system is that 1) it is good but not perfect, so you can auto pilot easy stretches of battles while having the normal flexibility that comes with a variety of abilities and 2) abilities are only constrained by how many portions of the ATB gauge they cost, and not mana, meaning if you fight a flan that is weak to magic and strong against physical attacks, you aren't screwed by a lack of mana. Other options in combat that don't use the ATB gauge are items and TP skills, which include stuff like summons, a huge team heal + rez, the only earth spell in the game, mass dispel, and mass stop. The whole TP system gets a bit complicated, but it's existence adds a bit of depth and limits summons in a unique way to the series that are otherwise extremely strong.
The progression system in this game is pretty♥♥♥♥♥ You have a Crystarium for each character that eventually has 6 paths (1 for each class) and 10 levels with a linear path to upgrade. Weapons and accessories are upgraded by consuming random junk that drops from enemies, meaning that there are very few treasures worth actually finding in the game that aren't components. The whole system is kind of like the Draw and Junction systems from FF8; interesting in theory, but really really tedious and, more importantly, removes a huge chunk of potentially interesting gameplay as you spend time grinding money to upgrade to ultimate weapons as opposed to doing interesting things to go find the ultimate weapons and accessories.
One of the biggest negatives I feel was
. The names we have come to know and love from the series are still there, but have unrecognizable names. Goblins have a giant gaping hole for a mouth and rollerskates, bombs are a floating piece of origami, and the list of strongest enemies in the game is a bunch of giant turtles that are common enemies. There are a handful of good boss fights throughout the game, such as Enki and Enlil, the Havoc Skytank, Barty round 1, and the Proudclad, but there is little to no fanfare around most of them. You just casually stumble across most bosses, bonk them, chapter over, no interaction other than beating them into submission. There are good fights, but the enemies have no depth from the story (other than Barty) and are just dust in the wind.
It's part of the story, but I'll just add this last part here. There really aren't a lot of characters in this game. You have the 6 in the party, Serah and Dajh, the 2 PSICOM colonels Jihl and Rosch, Snow's NORA squad of 4 (Gadot, Yuj, Lebreau, and Maqui), Cid Raines and his lieutenant, the big bad guy, a handful of 1 offs in Hope's parents and Lightning's sergeant, and... that's it. It's a really meager cast and takes away from the epic feeling of the game.

This is a great JRPG. At first, seems a sub-Final Fantasy title (and, concerning story, characters and the world, it certainly is), but the stellar combat makes it something special. Also, it's a +100 hours game, even if you don't do all the quests and guild tasks. I played it for 103 hours and got to level 92, without grinding or being too much of a completist.
It took me almost 10 hours to get the hang of combat, but after I understood its system, the game became really exciting. At first seemed like the characters were playing by themselves, but you start to realize how important strategy is. The most important thing is keeping a high morale, by flanking and intercepting the enemy and not letting him do the same to you. And, as the characters learn new "arts", you have more options and the battles get way more interesting _ specially when you "link" several enemies and becomes outnumbered. You can also enable QTEs during combat, to perform critical hits and to parry or counterattack _ it takes a while to get them right and it will make you curse at the screen, but it's great fun.
There were some boss fights that appeared to be impossible, but became a breeze after I changed strategy. This is a game that's not hard at all, but fair: play it well and you'll have a good time. Besides that, there's a lot of customization, from items to military formations.
It's a pity the developers didn't add achievements and trading cards. I'd also love a sequel.

"The black sheep of the series," "Skip it," "Ken Levine didn't touch it, so it's terrible."
These are phrases commonly associated with
.  You've probably heard them at some point, and when the game was released, that's all anyone ever talked about, at least around me.  Because of that, I skipped this game up until last year, a couple months before
came out.  I first picked this game up for the Xbox 360, mainly because it was still easy to find a physical copy, and it was commonly $8.  I looked at the box and remember the internet memes of the Big Daddy on the cover being an upgraded Bomberman; I even joked with the guy at the counter when I forked over the $10 I had in my wallet.  I looked at the back of the case, seeing "
the Game of the Year," and realized that this game was seriously just riding off the success of the first one, maybe everyone was right.  I came home, put it in my 360, and over the course of a week, I had finished a very fun, intriguing, and great game.
is the sequel to the game
, if you couldn't guess by the name.  In
, you played as a dude, Jack, that survived a plane crash and ended up in the underwater city of Rapture.  Rapture, a city meant to be the dream of its creator, Andrew Ryan, was in turmoil and literally falling apart.  People used the substance Adam to gain supernatural-like powers, such as throwing electricity from their hands, lifting up objects with their minds, and so on.  Plasmids were the name for these, and the addiction to splicing their genes led up to people generally going crazy and tearing the place apart.  There's more to the first game, but this isn't a review for that.  If you haven't played
yet, do yourself a favor and play that first.
uses the setting of Rapture, and doesn't have much of a connection to the first game outside of the setting.  There are some references here and there to characters and events from the first game, but
exists largely on its own (however, I'd still recommend at least playing through the first game, as the references in
will spoil key parts of the first game).  There's a completely new cast, a new antagonist, and tons of new areas to explore.  The level of detail, I found, in levels in this
title far excedes that of the first game.  If you love the world of Rapture, this game turns it up to 11.
So, what the heck is the story this time around, since the first game seemed to tie up the end of Rapture quite nicely? (Unless, of course, you got the bad ending).
puts you in the role of a Big Daddy, a person in a hefty diving suit meant to guard Little Sisters.  Without spoiling too much, the gist is that your specific Little Sister is the daughter of someone quite important (the main antagonist), and your Little Sister is taken away from you.  Due to the bond shared between you two, your Little Sister communicates to you and tries to get you to rescue her from her captor.
What many people knocked about
was that its storyline wasn't anything special.  You're a dad, trying to get your daughter, the end.  But, I found the story to be engrossing, and there's a bit more to it than that.  There's plenty of interesting characters you get to meet along the way, and they add to the overall story and atmosphere of the game.  In the first game, the moral choice system was merely if you harvested or saved a Little Sister.  In this game, there's many more choices that you can make, resulting in a bunch of different endings depending on your decisions.  However, I will note that there
any big twists and turns in
; you see everything as its coming.  Being that the first game and
both have those "ogodmybrainwhatishappening" moments, I will admit it's a bit unlike the series not to have some big twist at all.
Without a big twist, this game makes up for it in being seriously fun to play.  The first game's combat system was having your plasmid in one hand and your weapon in the other; there was no dual wielding of the two, so you had to pick one to have out.
fixes that by allowing you to using both your plasmids and weapons out at the same time (something that carried over into
).  On top of that, weapons have a plethora of alternate ammo types, allowing you to change up how you approach situations.  For instance, you get a cross bow that can launch rocket propelled arrows.  Your main gun can plant trap shots, which enemies can run into.  Ammo types can be switched out instantly, so if you're in a bind, the game reacts quite well.
The other main rub that people have/had with
, that I may or may not agree with, is the Little Sister harvesting missions for every area.  During the course of your trek to find
Little Sister, you adopt other Little Sisters along the way, and you have to perform harvesting missions.  These harvesting missions consist of your recently adopted Little Sister plunging her Adam collection thing away at a body on the ground, and an endless stream of splicers of all types running at her and you.  You have to do this twice for each Little Sister, and then there are usually three Little Sisters per area.  So, overall, you have to do this six times.  The benefit of doing this is that you gain Adam, the currency used to upgrade your plasmid powers.  I usually find these harvesting sections fun, since you can gear up beforehand, placing traps, turrets, summoning bots, and so on, and then take down the waves of enemies that come after you.  Though, I can understand why people don't like this aspect of the game, since it can be repetitive.
Here's a few other things that
, I think, did much better than the first game:
* Hacking.  Instead of playing Pipe Dreams, you simply stop a dial on certain colors.  It's far more stream lined, and there aren't cases were the hacking starts you in an unwinnable state like the first game did.
* Little Sister models.  I much prefer the models used in this game for Little Sisters than in the first game and

DLC.  But, that's just more of a personal thing.
* Research.  The first game had you take pictures of whatever you were researching to get upgrades against them.
does a video camera approach, where you focus on a subject, and your research score is determined by how interestingly you kill the enemy.
Is
a terrible game?  No, not by any means.  It shouldn't be skipped.  The team behind it did an absolutely fantastic job keeping with the spirit of the first game.
---
There's also Minerva's Den, the story DLC for
.  Just, just buy it.  It's absolutely wonderful, and well worth the price.
It also has that twist you're probably lusting after that was missing in the main game.
---
, however, is not without problems.  Specific to the PC version:
* The biggest issue you will have with the game is the audio.  It weirdly goes in and out, and some things don't get picked up by your speakers correctly at all.  This issue is a known one, unfortunately, and judging from the support topics over at 2K, it probably won't be fixed any time soon.
* Crashes.  I've had moments in this version of the game where I would simply open a door and the game would crash.  There are reports that switching to DirectX9 will fix the issue, but I powered through the game on the default setup and just remembered to save often.
* There were many times where the weapon/plasmid wheels in the game would just flat out disappear.
I haven't any real issue with the 360 version of the game, so if you have an Xbox 360 around and you're willing to sacrifice some graphics quality, the 360 version won't have the issues I just described.

Okay lets start with the positives.
The actual gameplay really does work, the cards available are mostly fun to play and you can build some quite nice, creative decks if you have some experience with the series.
The story campaign works as both a tutorial and a narrative. It doesn't bog itself down too much - and introduces you to the mythos of the series.
The planeswalker cards are reasonably balanced - most colours have a way of dealing with them, and there is enough board clear to make sure aggro isn't the only thing on the table.
The reintroduction of two-headed giant is welcome, even if it should have come with a chat feature. You Stainless, you don't have to cut a feature everytime you add one.
Grinding gold is easy. The currency system is more than fair - it is outright generous.
Now for the negatives, and why I rate this a no.
This is supposed to be an introduction to MTG. The deck wizard sucks, and whoever designed should never be allowed near another project. The trouble with it is, that it has no concept of curve, so if you are not an advanced player, you're going to end up with a bunch of 4cmc cards.
With 24 land in your deck constructed using the deck wizard - you will find a frustrating number of times when you have a choice between having 2 land in hand, or going down to 6 cards.
So a lot of the time you will lose, because you can't get to 4cmc in specific deck types. Which means if you're a new player, you often don't so much just lose with this deck wizard, you don't really get to play.
Which means it fails at its basic job. As daily quests often rely on deck wizard constructed decks - you will find generally that grinding gold is easier just ignoring most of the quests and building your own deck.
Playing against the computer, you will see this in action. Often the "hard" opponent won't play anything for the fourth turn, which means a fair chunk of the time winning is way too easy.  I am assuming the hard opponent decks, are designed by the same deck wizard, and they don't really work.
This isn't just a problem from a gamer perspective -we'd like hard to be hard- but also from the business side.
Once you have some pacy cards, you can quite quickly hit the game's gold limit playing against the hard AI, which half the time doesn't really fight back. From the devs POV, well I've got all the cards and over 5000 gold. At this rate, the expansion isn't going to net them much money because we all have the gold necessary to not have to spend actual IRL currency.
They should possibly add stuff we can do with currency apart from buying cards. Maybe different backs to the cards or something, just some tweeks to keep that gold from building up.
The other problem is the bugs. For example when I close the game and try to reopen it, it tells me it is still running. I know how to fix this by going through Task Manager, but I shouldn't have to. When the main game isn't running, there shouldn't be any of it left running.
Now a lot of issues are being dealt with by the devs, they are actively updating the game - but it has been a few months now, and this game was delayed like crazy at the start of launch. If it is this buggy a mess now, I can only imagine what IOS users went through.
The frustrating thing is, there is the skeleton of a really good game here. It is nicely balanced, it is pacy, it is addictive in its own way and I'm still playing it, so there is a lot to be said for it.
But I cannot recomend it to new players without a serious overhaul on the deck wizard, and some serious polish everywhere else.

Regarded as the ‘Big Daddy’ of world design and storytelling in video games, the original Bioshock in 2007 proved to the world that games should be taken seriously as art. And nine years on, the opportunity to explore under the sea has arisen again.
Bioshock Remastered is a free re-release of the original Bioshock for PC players who own the original game on steam. It was overseen by the studio Blind Squirrel Games and involves a revamp of the original game’s graphics and performance, as well as a new series of documentaries titled ‘Imagining Bioshock’ that explore the creation of the game with original key developers.
Considering the original game is now edging on ten years old, its a testament to how incredibly revolutionary was that it still holds up. The story follows protagonist Jack when his plane crashes into the ocean in 1960, only for him to discover a mysterious and derelict underwater city run by the enigmatic Andrew Ryan. This city, Rapture, is the soul of what makes Bioshock so incredible. Not only is it an amazing setting for a game, its created through world design that was unparalleled at the time of release. The cracking hull of Rapture is an intensely creepy and atmospheric setting. Mysterious shadows creep up the walls, water leeks across the floor, and its horrific citizens fill the air with blood-curling screeches of pain and madness. Its a place that is clearly descending into hell, and manages to convey so much with saying very little. Environmental storytelling is the main device that original developer Irrational Games utilised to tell its compelling narrative, and its astonishing how much story they can create from something as little as a tape, a teddy bear and a body in a drain. To put it simply, Rapture quite literally drips with story and is at the crux of what makes Bioshock so special.
The other pillar of the Bioshock experience, the gameplay, obviously cannot live up to the storytelling side but still manages to be compelling enough to happily see you through the 12 hour campaign. Jack uses many different methods to get through the treacherous corridors of Rapture, including basic gunplay with standard first-person shooter weapons, as well an assortment of different genetic abilities known as Plasmids. The gunplay, particularly after the progress videogames have made forward in the last 10 years, doesn’t hold up incredibly well. Its still enjoyable enough, but lacks the weight and punch expected from a modern FPS. This shortcoming is luckily covered by the Plasmids however, as they not only allow you to mix up combat in interesting ways, such as with lightning, telekinesis and hypnosis, but also add some much needed dynamism to the gameplay outside of filling enemies with lead. Outside of basic combat, there’s also the need to hack machines and explore the environment that must be contended with. The mini-game used to hack is simple, but effective and never gets old enough to the point that it becomes frustrating. The exploration of the environment on the contrary is a complete delight, as Bioshock‘s level design is comfortably on par with its setting. Each section of Rapture is distinct and offers many branching paths and hidden corners to explore.
So while its been established that the ‘Bioshock‘ part of the titled is incredible, its unfortunately the ‘Remastered‘ aspect that drags the overall product down. To get the good things out of the way, Blind Squirrel Games did a decent job improving the graphics to a solid level, and the additional documentary is likely to be fascinating for new and old fans alike. However, its the technical support on that is legitimately disappointing. At launch, the game missed a number of significant graphic’s features, several key resolutions and suffered from a whole swarm of frustrating bugs. Granted, many of those issues were fixed in a patch released almost a month later, but even after that I still continued to suffer from frustratingly frequent crashes to desktop. I estimate that I lost almost two hours of gameplay to lax saving and a subsequent crash. Its genuinely disappointing considering the quality of the game itself, and makes this remaster feel more like a cash-grab than a loving re-release of a modern classic.
That being said, this is still the best way to experience this masterpiece of game design. Certainly the technical side is a let down, but the sheer quality and richness of the experience on hand almost makes trudging through the bugs and crashes worthwhile. If you haven’t dived into Bioshock before, would you kindly purchase this remaster, because everyone deserves to go on this incredible journey under the sea.

“It's a dangerous business going out your door. You step onto the road, and if you don't keep your feet, there's no knowing where you might be swept off ... “
Hearken to me fair folk of Middle-Earth - are you a devouted follower of the writings of the linguistic, literary mastermind and father of modern fantasy, the one, the only - Professor J.R.R Tolkien? Are you ripe for adventure, lore-exploration and feisty combat? If so - then, The Lord of the Rings: War in the North is most certainly a game you would enjoy.
As a person who revels in the realm of fantasy and enjoys reading, watching and playing anything related with it, I am of course a loyal acolyte of Tolkien's Legendarium. Therefore, I have played almost all the Middle-Earth related games out there, starting all the way back with The Fellowship of the Ring (2002) all the way to this game. Seldom could I find a game that gazed it's lofty magnitude upon me and capture my thirst and love for Tolkien's world - as War in the North. While some might compare it to the works of legendary games such as The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim (my all time favourite game of all times), I find such thoughts folly, as The Lord of the Rings: War in the North, offers a far different experience: to put it frankly and to the point - 'tis a game for those who truly enjoy the vast amount of Tolkien's books (with references being pulled from works such as The Unfinished Tales, The Silmarillion and The Hobbit).
Yet, even those who aren't particularly die-hard fans of the series, such as a good friend of mine, could still find this game's storyline, it's quests and characters and the combat system itself, interesting. Character customization is limited, yet quite sufficient in my humble view, game combat is entertaining and fun, if a tad repetitive, the locations and plot are top-notch. The three character races you can play being: Dwarf, Elf and Man have their own unique playstyle (the Dwarf is  your tanky all-weapons master that can pretty much take on Sauron's forces on his own, the Elf being that vital link healer/mage that can provide your little band of heroes that so needed back-up support, and the Man being a sneaky, archer/ranger who can also duo-wield and perform sneak attacks. Additionally, I found it equally rewarding to play the game in single player and in multiplayer with one or two friends, for a true 'Fellowship' feel! And while, indeed the game has aged somewhat in terms of graphics - I believe it still remains an amazing testament to the power of Middle-Earth.
In short - I full heartedly recommend The Lord of the Rings: War in the North to anyone who wishes to further deepen his understanding of Middle-Earth and explore the largely untouched story of Sauron's attempted conquest of the North. PS: The soundtrack is so beautiful!

TL;DR: If you're a fan of Magic The Gathering (paper or digital) then at least check it out for yourself, it is free.
"Yes" recommendation is really hard for me to put as I'd like to say "Maybe" instead...read below to find out why.
As a long time veteran player of both paper Magic and the Duels series, this game is a very mixed bag.
One thing you may notice if you are an experienced player is the new set (the titular Magic Origins set) and how they did a pretty hard reset on card power and overall OP nature of creatures/spells etc. It's not overall a bad thing, I guess it's kind of nice to see a return to the more simpler roots of the game where a strong creature with no special powers of it's own can be enough to win you the game.
In regards to the presentation and interface...for a mostly 'online only' type of game, largely focused around multiplayer and the community, they really failed in my opinion with this game. As many other reviews state, there are large problems with matchmaking, stability of connection once in a match, certain game conditions causing freezes, and people not even able to launch the game at all.
The worst of the problems above have been addressed in a few different updates, but mostly the problems still pervade the experience and leave a bad taste in your mouth. Want to play the very popular 2 headed giant mode where 2 players go head to head with 2 other players each with their own decks but the teams share life totals? Well, unless you like random players who may or may not be familiar/skilled with the game then good luck. I have had about a 10% success rate with inviting/being invited to a partner's game. The netcode just seems to be garbage that can't properly place you in a match.
In addition to these issues above, there have been a lot of other glaring issues that are a confusing step down from previous iterations of the series. If you want to chat to each other, you either have to add the random player you are teamed with in 2hg for instance and steam message them back and forth (if they even accept your invite or you can find their name with the 2,000 other players of same names) or maybe do skype/Team Speak etc outside of the game. This is ridiculous to not even have an in game chat option in a game so focused around teamwork and strategy. There is not even a text chat box as in previous versions. This is a huge missed opportunity and hurts the experience a lot.
In summary, again, if you are a fan of the series or a noob just trying to see what all the fuss is about, this game is a serviceable introduction to the series. On the other hand if you are a seasoned vet, even of the digital games, you might look to some of the older versions for an overall better experience.
Score: 6/10 (hoping to improve this rating if they ever improve the game)

I am a couple decade long MTG player.  I had very high hopes coming into this with their new "we will let you build your own deck from scratch" comments.  I do not like the following:
-You cannot skip the tutorial - and presumably if they change it later so you can, you won't get the coins.  I have played all the previous MTG console games and play in real life.  Why must I suffer?
-They still have the issues of when an opponent leaves the game it not ending the match.  In normal MTG this is a forfeit and should be an auto-win for you.  Don't waste my time.
-The cards packages are a joke.  The amount you have to play to get any decent cards is disproportionate.  This is an obvious attempt to get you to drop money on coins.  If I am going to spend money, make it worth it - not like an IOS game.
-The single player campaign is a joke.  Particularly the Chandra and Liliana campaigns, you are always at a disadvantage.  With no control over your deck, you are forced to hope for a good draw (I found myself losing 4 times in a row even with no play errors).  MTG should never be based on a 'good draw'.  A properly built deck should have several ways to succeed regardless of draw.
-All builds are geared towards 3 completely different strategies in single player and how you are led in the game.  One single concept (tribal, horde, beefy, control, etc) would be far better, but they short you on cards for builds and the single player decks.
-There isn't enough variance in the cards yet.  Countless sets have already been released.  Don't be that company that only releases sets going forward - use some history.
I hope they fix some of these in the near future.  I didn't even get 15 hours out of this game.

Civ 5 had a lot of graphics in its interface which made it easy to navigate and find what you needed, and get an idea of what you were picking to study/build. It also looked very nice to see each portrait of each unit in the game, easily identifying ranged/flyng units. However, this game just has text. It feels rather lazy to not include portraits/icons like in the base game of Civ 5. It is also frustrating to navigate through 50 different options and trying to find which one it is I want. When everything also has some kind of alien inspired name, it adds to the frustration. Even with DLC or an expansionpack, the game wouldn't appeal to me due to the lack of graphics.
The leaders in Civ 5 all were very distinct, with appearence and how they responded to you as a player. You could easily identify their behavior and manage your strategy against them based on it. They would great you, insult you, apologize and declare war differently. In this game, I found the leaders basically looking different, but they respond in the very same ways. They have zero personality and after 5 hours of gameplay, I could honestly not remember a single name of the five leaders I played against. So whenever someone asked me to help them fight another, I had no clue who they were referring to. Sure Civ 5's leaders had a lot of strange names which took some time to get used to, but at least I had somewhat of a clue who they were referring to when I played.
The game also dosen't allow you to play as one of the leaders, instead you get to pick some perks and you are just some random civilization. The perks aren't very different either, making the game very samey on the second time around. I loved to try different leaders in Civ 5 and try to master the games with their differences.
Even though the game is newer, the color choice for the map is just ugh. It's like the color palette was deliberately chosen with the ugliest colors imaginable, everything starting with "Dark." Dark yellow, dark grey, dark green... you get it. Everything looks dull and very hard to tell apart from each other. I couldn't even identify the forest in the mess. Maybe I was just unlucky and got stuck on the ugliest map available, as I remember seeing some  screenshots with beautiful landscapes and vibrantly colored crystals.
Instead of Barbarians, we have Alien monsters running around on the map. I -hated- Barbarians in Civ 5 and guess what? I hate Aliens even more. They actually made me appreciate the Barbarians even more.
The problem with the aliens is that they occupy most of the maps around your starting area. In Civ 5, if you had the easiest setting on, the Barbarians were ridiculously easy to defeat. The higher the difficulty, the tougher the barbarians. With the aliens however, even on the easiest setting, start out with units that kills your soldiers in two turns. And they have these worm creatures that instantly kills any of your units. How is that fair? It's like letting the Barbarians starts with a death robot on turn one. You simply can't defeat that. You also can't send out any units to explore in the early game, because there are massive sea creatures that will destroy them in one turn. Even towards the late game on the easiest setting, some of the sea creatures were ridiculously overpowered. (those Turtle krakens)
However, if you do manage to kill one of the OP aliens (basically had my city shoot at the worm for 20 turns or so), then some other civilizations will hate you for it. I could understand if you could somehow preserve the aliens or convert them to your side, so that you could have some use of them, but no. They just want you to leave them alone while they basically trash any of your units with one or two hits. Imagine in Civ 5 if, on turn one, the barbarians were running around with a death robot and if you stopped it, the other civilizations would declare war on you. Why? The aliens were clearly killing the other civilizations units as well. In Civ 5, if you resqued another civilizations units from the barbarians, they would be thankful.
Another problem with the Aliens is that they prevent you from exploring, which confines you to a small portion of the map, unless you are lucky enough to get a big space of your own. It took away a lot of the fun from the game, in Civ 5, I enjoyed discovering hidden ruins and sending my units there.
The victory conditions in Civ 5 are very clear from the start and it's easy to take a path towards it. In this game, I found myself clueless as to how I was supposed to win. At a 0 money price tag (free weekend on Steam) this game has the potential to change your life.
One of the best ways to enjoy it is to install it and then go out and have a drink with your friends. Over time it may improve your social skills, expose you to new and interesting people, and who knows, maybe some of them will share great stories, or present you with incredible business opportunities. If you're not that into other people though, you could also install this game and then go out to the park, catch some sun (it's great for your skin and essential to maintain your vitamin D levels), listen to the birds and feel the wind gently caressing your face. You could also hit the gym and work on those flat glutes you got from sitting down all day, every day.
As a third option, if you really prefer being indoors, you can always install Civ:BE and then go watch a movie, read a book, perhaps even study for those finals.
However, if you REALLY want to play a strategy game, then you can install this game and play any other title within the genre, like Duck Hunt.

I must say I am a bit surprised i'm giving this game a go. I found myself at the 30min mark having a bit of fun then stopped to play something else. Come back to it now at the 1hr mark and I realize something.....this game seems to be getting a bit tedious. I stop again to resume another game and come back later. Looking at the Rebel desktop icon I come to the realization that even at this early of a start I can already see how this game will get boring quickly. Without even feeling bored I can already see it coming. I pause and think and decide to give it the ol college try and make it past and still nope.
Combat was "eh", mining I swear was going nowhere (and still don't care for it), trading wasn't a very good option since at the start if you so much as pebble your mighty ship was full in an instant and it all seemed so....not that epic? can't think of a good word. Literally came up on the 2hr mark and the time to decide if it refund or keep. I literally stopped playing for a day and pondered it because the game seemed like it had things going for it. Was absolutely lovely once I got the graphics settings right (gave a different resolution for some reason), combat was simple but effective, everything was flashy, the music and sounds were nice but it just didn't click. But I decided to take the leap and just go with it, and I don't regret it. I believe it was completely my thinking of the game. It's a relatively small download seeming more arcady and simple then anything so maybe I came in with a "rush, rush, faster" mindset. Once I put that aside (and a bit bored) I just pushed through and the game opened up for me.
Combat although really simple can be as deep or remain as simple as you want it. With ships having multiple turrets areas it's completely possible to play it smart or just brute force a lot of things.  Set some of the turrets for specific enemies or bigger ship armaments with targeting priorities. Play the smart way with shield specific turrets to take down protection then batter them down with the heavy guns. Get extra protection with deflector shields and anti missile armaments because lord knows there will be lots of missiles being shot at you. Outmaneuver enemies and separate them for easy pickings. OR do like me and just go in guns & lasers blazing allowing anything to target anything in a blaze of bullets, lasers, explosions while taking control of certain ones when needed. Now this may all seem glorious and may be revving your engines and fingers to buy but as I said before, combat can be as simple or deep as you want. There's mining but I mean it's mining so it's not rocket science. Although there are ways to help produce better results but I have personally not dipped too much into it. I will say blowing up space rocks is flashy and hasn't gotten old yet though. Trading is simple and straight forward, buy low sell high with different possible events happening to effect said prices.
At some point depending how fast you are you will be somewhat at the top of the food chain in not that long of a time but you can still get stomped at times if you get reckless. There are quite a few ships to get some feeling different then others and some unlocked later by doing or becoming apart of...things. Random map events, battles etc and small touches and details that I won't ruin. Overall I think this is a good game that hopefully gets better and in all honesty at some point will wear thin. This is no surprise as the space warrior can only go so far BUT the time getting there has been enjoyable for me at least. Getting that next ship, getting more turrets, better fire power, being able to go right into the fray just tanking everything and watching your lasers just shoot, blow up and just rip apart many a small ship as you focus on the big ones is a beautiful thing. Or just cruising paying no mind and seeing a kill happen all because an enemy got too close and looked at your turret funny.
I believe this game is good and worth a buy and what can ruin it is coming in thinking or expecting something it's not. This game isn't ultra deep requiring big management nor is it as shallow and simple as it seems at 1st. The best way I can think of this game is it's like the "Civilization Revolution" of the lot. Just deep enough to seem familiar and can get you to think a bit but not so overwhelming to put off more simple people like myself (although I do enough a deeper game at times). Do you research, watch a few vids, take it out for a quick spin cause i'm sure some of you will enjoy it.
ALSO! whatever you do, do NOT do swarm missions or things with the words "swarm" in them. If your not coming in prepared those ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s will rip you a new ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ within another ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥~

I feel obligated to share my appreciation of this game because I feel it combines two of my most favorite styles of game in one (and it does it well).  I adore trading sims; and I find broadside naval combat cathartic (ala AC: Black Flag).  It also happens that I deeply appreciate outer-space themed anything (although not huge into 4x games).
I have a crazy schedule and prefer the "pick up and play" type of games that only feel deep; but are, in reality, simple grind fests with a long goal.  After having only played for a few hours, I feel like I'm going to be logging hundreds by doing every last side mission available.  And when I'm done, doing it all over again.  The core gameplay is as simple as it gets - point, shoot, buy/sell, travel, upgrade.  The best part of the game isn't just it's execution with how tacttile everything feels though - it's the graphics.  I feel like I'm exploring a deep and untamed spacial universe ripe for the picking with dangers and all.  I needed this in my life and I've been hoping and praying for something like it ever since getting hooked on Sea Trader for the Gameboy Advance.  I have a feeling this title is going to hold a major place in my memories for years to come.  And in another 10-20 years when I'm playing the Playstation 6 and running Steam OS I'll kick back and think "y'know, I wish they would re-make Rebel Galaxy, there hasn't been another good trading sim ever since".

A solid enough twin stick shooter. Make sure your rig is somewhat beefy before heading in, the game has an intense destruction system/mechanics that can really take the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of a lesser PC.
The game plays fairly well and the controls are decent enough. The camera pans where you aim, and can be manipulated about as we'll as you'd expect with the isometric view. Weapons, lines, and animations are all at least passable, and have a nice amount of variety. You'll usually be able to kill a few dozen people before noticing repeats. The lines are lovably cheesy, and the whole game has a very Postal 1 atmosphere while still managing to take itself seriously to a humorous extent.
The destruction mechanics are interesting and fun to use, from driving a car through the front of a grocery store to using grenades to flush out soldiers by blowing down a wall it's but functional and fashionable. Vehicles can be driven and are like miniature race cars with paper-thin exteriors. They're fast, get you where you want to go, but don't expect to live long in it. The player is very mobile and can vault over objects, take cover, sprint, etc in an easily controllable and responsive manner, though it may take some getting used to in order not to get stuck on bushes and leap over cover.
The major flaws are the aforementioned hardware requirements, the isometric view being a pain sometimes (though adapting and using the minimap is a key skill in overcoming this), and the washed out colors making it difficult to see some enemies/locations (but once again there are in-game mechanics in place to nullify this, it's mostly a passive issue that simply requires some more attention to minimaps or using the highlighting key).
All in all if you enjoy a bloody, destructive romp, twin stick shooters, or edgy funtimes that make the politically correct♥♥♥♥♥♥their pants in sheer frothing rage, then this is your kind of game.

I'm rewriting my review after a year of this game being out.  I'm also going to consider it from a stand alone point of view.  This is only an X game from a story line point of view, it does not hold anything else in common with the preceding X games.
As a whole, the game is free from major bugs, expecially the plot breaking ones.  The biggest problems I have with the game, is that for a game set in space, the areas are both cramped and to expansive at the same time.  The massive stations, while full of detail, can really become a hinderance while fighting near them as there is no reprecussions for the ai if they accidentally shoot them, but as the player, if you shoot the station or some of the civillians running around, you get reported to the police, have a standing drop, and if this isnt' your first time, get to have some of the police joining the fight against you.
These stations aren't so far apart that it takes long to get to them, but finding your way around them to a specific docking port can take a while if you don't have something to lead you to where it is.  This has been helped alot now though with the ability to gain access to all of the people on the station from near one of the dock ports.  You can also trade and recruit without landing on the station, with a slight delivery fee.
The stations themselves, while each type being very detailed and different, are rather limited in numbers.  Station interiors and NPCs also fall victim to this.  There are only about as many interiors as there are types of docks.  While each one is changed slightly, it's kinda like just rearranging a house without changing the base layout, there's only so much you can do.  The NPCs are all very generic, detailed, but ugly people generally.
This type of situation is the standard for the game.  Excellent detail on the individual parts, but so few parts, they repeated to many times.
Your ship, the Pride of Albion(aka Albion  Skunk as the designers decided to name your ship without giving you a chance to rename it to something worthy of a leader's ship)  Falls vicitim to this detailed mototony again.  Your primary weapons, a variety of lasers, are all able to be equipped to the ship simultiously, though you may only use one at a time.  As your experience, and cash, goes up, you are able to purchase upgraded versions of these, but they are nothing more than more powerful versions of the basics.  The missile selection is a little more diverse, mainly attributed to  the latest patches, with a good selection to suit most suations.  The engines and shields are also limited in selection with an average version, then one version at each extreme.  3 "types" of engines/shields, and increasing levels of them.    Your "copilot" is probably one of the worst parts of the ship, she is repetitive, annoying and the choice of outfit just doesn't fit into the game.  While that's not usually an issue, it really does bug me for some reason, considering the amount of time she ends up on your screen. I'm all for hot space women with very little left to the imagination, but this one doesn't fit into that in any way, and the "boob window" as it is called, just annoys me.
Basic ship to ship combat is very standard, run of the mill.  Captial ships are large lumbering and pretty much push overs.  While they do support good shielding and hull hp, they only take time and very little effort to take down.  They have plenty of blind spots to hide in and recharge your shields while being pretty much invulerable.  One good example of this is the drone bays.  Wide open bays you can park your ship in, with no real way for the enemy to attack you.  Once you have recharged, you can pop back out and start taking out the turrets again.  They are very slow, and while they can jump from area to area, they are hard to manage on a large scale.   Trading with them tends to be tedious.
I do like the transportation system, aka highways.  they give you a nice view of systems,  balanced transit times, and are fairly well laid out, though it can take a while to memorize the network.  The improved maps in the latest patches have made finding your way around them easier, but I still think there is room for improvement on this aspect.
The missions and storyline are the one thing that really hasn't changed from the older X games or many other space games.  There are a couple set basic types of missions, and they are varied in difficulty by time, number of enemies, and such.  The biggest issue with the missions is that you have to wander around the massive stations looking for the icon to pop up,  there is no central place to find them, and you can sometimes take longer finding a mission than it takes to complete it.   I do like the story line and it fits well into the X universe and it's history.  The acting leave something to be desired of but on a whole, I do like this aspect.
The final part of this game that I'm going to cover is the sandbox.  Whether you start from the end of the story line or a custom start, this in my opinion, is where the game is most lacking.  I have found it hard to set goals that keep me playing the game.  Your ship is fairly limited in upgrades, so combat can quickly become monotanous, though boarding and capturing ships has become increasingly difficult with the latest patches.  Building stations is also a long and tedious process with very little return on investment, as well as the same thing with trading.  The main problem I have with all of this is that once you limit out your ship, the only reason you need any money is to restock your missiles, or build more stations and capitals.  Yes you can use it to fund large combat squadrons, and go around wiping out whole stations and zones, but since you can't seem to takeover/rebuild the stations, you are eventually shooting yourself in the foot trade wise.  This game just does not have the variations in the right areas to be able to set large, diverse goals that can keep you playing the game for extended periods of time.
In review, as a whole, this game has a large attention to detail in what it has in it, but there is just not enough general content.   The story is a bit of a grind at times, but worth completing I believe.  All in all though it is a pretty average game these days,  Excellent detail, severe lack of content.  On a positive note though, unlike a lot of the good indy space games that are out, this game has an attention to layout that prevents the confusion that many of this genre suffer from.  There are a lot of other games, that while they are much more diverse and open ended, suffer from a pieced together user interface that is cumbersome and hard to understand. This game is sleek well designed and easy on the eyes.
One more section to this review. If you have played any of the prior X games, do not go into this game with any expecations of it being like the rest.  You have been restricted to one ship, one race, even though there are 2 other races floating around, and a very limited selection of support ships.  From this aspect, they took the massive amount of content that the other games had, and removed it to provide high detail on a limited amount of content.  If they were to create DLCs that are X Rebirths for each race, and added them to the current standing game, not on their own indivitually, this game could eventually get much closer to the feel and playability of the original games, but I really don't see that happening.

Since this is my first review of a game, please give me some leeway for a bit of naivety. It will happen, I'm sure, because I probably have bias towards or against some things in the game. Now to get on with the actual review.
The Last Remnant is a game that I was skeptical about picking up at first. It happened to be on sale for $5, and I saw a few good reviews, so I decided to buy it, and I am so very glad I did. I love strategy games, and this turned out to be one of my favorite strategy games I had ever played, quickly knocking others down on my list.
First, the story: in terms of details, it's pretty good; ideas, the same description; in fact, it has a rather unexpectedly in-depth story for what I expected, as of some of SE's games recently (I looked at a few; the story in each drove me away). It takes you into the world and explores the Remnants, which are mystical/magical objects that randomly appeared out of nowhere on the planet and, when bound, can be used as anything from a weapon to a tool and just about everything in-between. However, this is just a subsection of the story, which has (as far as I have played) covered politics, war, rogue elements, many details on the Remnants, scientific researchers, and i actually forgot the end of the list because there were enough parts that I ran out of attention span while typing this. It can be a bit wild in progression, as the story-based events occur only when you go to the right areas, but the quests and tasks (which are basically the normal "side quests" and "fulfill-and-reward" ideas) also add to the information on the world. A few quests even explore personal areas on certain characters, and each character that is involved in at least a side quest has been carefully built. I was very impressed by all of these details, and from what I have read, I'm not even halfway through the game.
Next, the gameplay. Okay, so the first thing I'm going to say is this: there are way too many controls. Your battle controls, field controls, menu controls, and critical controls are many, and some of them overlap in weird ways. For instance, it appears that this game was set up to be used on controller, as you control sight/movement in the field with what is the keyboard equivalent of thumbsticks. Also, what you would think are the same controls in each area of the game are not. They may be bound to different things, i.e. camera movement controls in the field are camera/menu controls in battle (which, it is weird to move the menu and catch sight of your view moving in the same direction as your menu cursor) and a few other things. However, they are not impossible, and once you settle on a comfortable set for you, it doesn't take long before the controls seem natural, no matter how mixed up they seem at first. Now that I'm finished bugging out about that, let's move on to the rest of the gameplay. The Last Remnant uses a combat system that is unique in that I can't remember another game like it. I'm sure there was, but I'm at a loss to which it is. Anyways, you control unions (groups of fighters assembled before battle in preset positions) in a tactical battle setting, which is to say that although you take turns, where you wanted to go and what you wanted to do with each union may not happen. In the battle, unions move throughout the field and engage enemy unions in various forms. You also have to deal with morale, which increases and decreases according to your success in battle. I'll leave it to the game for an explanation, but suffice to say that it is an interesting fight, and no two engagements seem the same.
Now, on to other details. The music is quite good; a heavy beat gets you pumped for a fight, and the music changes depending on morale during battles, which in my case either sent me on a murderous rampage or had me fighting desperately for my life. It grabs you and drags you into the fight like no other music I've heard before, similar to the way that the Final Fantasy series often did in the past (case in point: 4-7, at least in my opinion). The characters develop a lot more than I suspected they would. I thought they would be plain soldiers with backgrounds and a bit of development, but they also develop some of the characters you get from sidequests, giving them background information, personalities, and putting much  emotion into the way they act. I find that I absolutely hate to lose units in battle, not just because they are useful, but also due to the emotions and their personalities that have burnt themselves into my mind and heart, and losing one means I lost a friend in the game. When that happens, well, take how you would feel if someone KO'ed your friend with a punch to the face when you were right there with them and apply it to the situation. That's my personal twist on the characters in the game, and I don't care whether you think I'm insane or not (I am, by the way :} ).
In conclusion, the story is pretty good, the music is epic, the battles are engaging, and the only cons you really have to deal with are the occasional slowdown at the start of a cutscene (due to high processing required and extreme details being applied, has occurred few enough times that I can count them on my hands) and the exceedingly rare random close out (happened a grand total of 3 times for me so far, two of them I'm pretty sure were because my computer was doing updates, the warning and the actual restart caused the game to close out).
In my humble opinion, this game is 10/10. I love it, am addicted to it, and will never say otherwise. ^_^

This is seriously a gem of a 2D capital ship space game. It has a very Freelancer feel to it with a story line that reminds you very much of Firefly. The sound track definately adds to the feeling.
Pros:
+Freedom. You can go almost anywhere and do anything. Want to be a trader? Go do that. Want to be a pirate. Go do that. Want to be Batman? I guess you could do that if Bruce Wayne built his own capital class space ship. He built a space station, twice, so why not? It's your imagination after all.
+Capital Ship Combat. Ever want to command a multi-ton vessel as is slides up to another massive craft and unleashes a devestating broadside? In space? With highly volitile plasma?! This is the game for you. Combat is 2D for you because you are in command of a capital class ship. Fighters and gunboats will still wander in all 3 directions but you don't care. You're in a gorram capital ship! You aren't here to dog fight. Barrel rolls are for poor people how can't afford proper ships.
+No Carriers. Sure there are some fighters and gunboats in the game but this game is about a giant mountain of steel doing its best to obliterate another giant mountain of steel with hot balls of light in a beautiful salvo of broadside combat.
+The sound track and sound in general. The music really sets the mood. And I say this as a person that usually turns off the game sounds after an hour or so. Not with this game. The music really immerses you that extra little bit to make playing the game without it a crime.
+Characters. The Voice Acting is great and the modeling of people is also good. Might be a little limited in variety but the characters that are in the game are their own entities. You can see the tediousness in the traders eyes as you trade with them in deep space. You can hear distain the local militia forces have for you as you ask stupid questions.
+Character Creation. There isn't one. This game isn't about you, it's about giant ships. As such, the character creater is limited only by your imagination. You can't find a more powerful creator with that many options anywhere else on the market.
Cons:
-Camera issues. With how big your ship is, and it takes up a glorious portion of the screen, this is a both a good and bad thing. It adds to the sense of mass your ship has, but also makes it really hard to aim or even be aware of your surroundings.
-Some of the UI could use a little work. The trade interface in particular could use a little tweaking to help you out some.
-The smaller craft in the game (fighters and gunboats) seem overpowered at the moment. I understand they are suppose to be some threat to the PC, but right now they punch way above their weight class. They are THE threat to the PC, not other capital ships. And they out range capital ships, which is pretty crazy.
-No Superdreadnaught or Titan class ships. Personal gripe. I always want bigger ships. And more guns. And bigger guns. I just want a flying gun with more guns on it. Is that so bad?
Conslusion: Get this game if you enjoyed Freelancer but wanted to pilot something bigger than a single seat craft.

Absolutely love this game! The graphics excellent, the AI can be very tough to fight on Hard difficulty alone (let alone the "Very hard" and "Unfair" diffulties!) and the variety in ships between the factions and their research and powers provides a continuous feel.
My main positive with this game though, is how mod-able it is! "Sins of a galactic Empire" (Star Wars full conversion), "Sins of the Prophets" (Halo full conversion), "Star Trek Armada" (Star Trek full conversion), "Dawn of the Reapers" (Mass Effect full conversion), are just a few of the mods you can find that are just mind blowing and yet keep the same Sins feel to them!
PROS:
+ Excellent gameplay
+ Excellent scenery
+ Great effects during conflicts
+ Huge numbers of ships can be recruited, giving potential to massive conflicts at a time
+ Love the music and sounds
+ Very mod-able, opening up a variety of other gameplays
+ Multiplayer
+ Large numbers of maps available to play with various sizes and star systems
CONS:
- Can be difficult to get used to some of the features and the pace of the game if your new to it. Give it some time and perhaps start on a small map to work out the controls and your style of play before taking on the larger maps and harder AI's (trust me, you'll get obliterated otherwise haha)
- [This is more of a personal con] - Wish there could be a bit more detail in wreckage. One thing I seem to keep missing when playing sci-fi RTS games like this is that when a ship is destroyed it explodes and then nothing is left behind. In this game there is only a small amount of wreckage left. If you have a big enough battle it's not such an issue, but more wreckage would add another level of greatness to conflict. However there are some mods and full conversions (such as Star Trek Armada) that address this.
OVERALL: Fantastic game that is a perfect addition to the RTS genre. If you're looking to expand your RTS collection or just add more games to your library list, this game is certainly worth the buy!

Wow, what an adventure.
To get to the nitty gritty, let me focus on a couple of parts of the game: the battle system, the story, and the ending.
The battle system:
The battle system of this game is unique and definitely improved the game in my opinion. If you are unfamiliar, you have multiple squads under your commands that attack in sets. If you've played Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic, it is somewhat similar, but much more smoothly executed and on a much grander scale. The battles feel huge in certain cases, and it really adds to the experience in that it makes it feel like you're fighting a war right off the bat, rather than just skirmishes.
10/10
The story:
The story was very engaging, and this characteristic is largely why I prefer RPGs to other types of games. Though it has a couple of predictable plot twists, the world is immersive. The side quests definitely add to the story and add to the immersive-ness of the world, as well as providing tangible advantages such as recruiting valuable characters and the acquisition of powerful weapons. There were a couple of problems, such as the ending feeling rushed, but I'll get into that in the next section.
8/10
The ending:
The ending was absolutely the worst part of the game. I think it's odd to feature the ending as a part of the review, but I felt very strongly about it. This game can be split up into two fairly individual parts (to the point where one could have actually been a sequel). The second half of the game felt rushed compared to the first part. I felt like, where the story had a comfortable and reasonable progression in the first half, I felt like I was barrelling through the story when I went at the same pace for the second. At endgame, the game really just kind of feels like it skids to an emergency halt. The final boss is scaled in difficulty to the progression of your character, which is nice, and the final boss did take me a few tries, but when I did actually beat it, I was for some reason a little disappointed. The ending cutscenes did give me a feeling that I was finished, but the satisfaction wasn't really there. For the reasons that the ending was sort of abrupt, but well written, I give the ending a
6/10
Overall:

I got it for @29.99 during a Christmas sale.  I was hesitant because of all the reviews I've read that it didn't work on many people's machines and that it wasn't fun for people who have played the more fully-orbed version of Civ V with all the add-ons.  But I figured I'd give it a go, and if it didn't work that they'd eventually fix it.  I'm pleased to report that it works perfectly fine in full graphical resolution mode on an i7 based laptop, as well as my desktop with an AMD 8 core processor.  No issues at all so far with how it runs.  I also have played Civ V quite a bit, and like it too. My only beef with Civ V is that the text won't display when I try to play it on Linux, so I have to boot into Windows when I want to play it.  I think both Civ V and BE are fun, and BE is worth the $ when you can snag it at $29.99.  A lot of people complain about the lack of depth, but I think that the first game that comes out in the series does this intentially, because even with the "lack of depth," BE and Civ V (without the add ons) are still pretty robust games in their own right with a big learning curve if you want to play at the more difficult levels.  Of course the add ons provide greater depth, but I actually preferred to start with the base package of Civ V, and then play the add-ons incrementally, despite having purchased them all at once to where I could have played the full-up version.  So, in short, if you liked the base package of Civ V, I'd give BE a shot.  If you didn't like the Civ V series until all the add-ons were released, then I'd recommend that you wait until at least the first add-on is released.

This is a quality online platform for MtG, I've been playing Magic now for over six years.
After reading some reviews I feel the need to set the record straight.
Most negative reviews will complain about the early bugs that existed in the game. These have/are being removed. I personally have not had any issue with bugs.
As for the game there are a few parts I'd like to cover.
The tutorial is mandatory, however it is fairly quick and easy to get through, and gives you a lot of easy coin (in game currency).
The rest of missions can be difficult as all the decks are designed to be played a certain way. As an experienced player I would have liked to see more copies of the cards that generate the win the deck is designed for. Apart from getting unlucky and not getting one of those copies all the decks are winning decks.
The game controls are fairly straight forward. The ONLY two cautions I will give: If you are running a multi colour deck, take your time and make sure the correct mana is tapped when you play your cards. Second: The "skip attack" button is in the same spot as "continue" a button you will be hitting a lot. I've skipped attack several times due to impatience.
The deckwizard is meant for unexperienced players, and having taught a lot of people to play I can see the deckwizard  working well.
The only other thing I would like to see, and it is entirely likely this will take place in future updates, is a larger selecetion of cards. You are able to get all the cards by playing the game without. You can buy packs with either real money or in game currency, the packs are the exact same.
If you like Magic the Gathering, I would recommend this game. Just be ready to build your card collection again.

I'd like to start off by saying that I purchased this game whilst it was on sale. 75% off, a bargain I thought, and with the mostly positive reviews and generally widespread praise, why not? I am writing today to tell you that, as much as I may have 'enjoyed' this game, I cannot recommend it, and I will not. Let me explain to you why, in the best, most detailed way I can. I will bring up an aspect of the game, and elaborate on my thoughts and experiences regarding it. I hope to encourage potential buys to have a more in depth look into the general feedback the game has received, not just on Steam, but other websites such as Metacritc, IGN etc. I aim to be as spoiler free as I can, should you decide to purchase regardless.
EDIT: Since posted, this review, I discovered the mostly clunky movement, mostly, was the fault of my keyboard, and has been returned.
Let's begin.
GRAPHICS:
Graphics are easily one of the most important parts of a video game. As video games are a visual entertainment medium, they heavily interact with your visual stimuli. The visuals of this game, resemble that of an outdated era. This game honestly looks like it's from the early 2000's, and would run on the original Xbox or PS2 consoles.
Textures on the main character models are somewhat nice (as they usually are) and the same can be said for very few select areas, such as Rivendell and Nordinbad. The remainder are rather washed out, muddy looking excrement pits. This is painfully obvious in the very area in which you start, Bree. It certainly doesn't help when the visual settings apparently don't function at all. Overall, very lacking in the graphical department, a bit of a disappointment considering the game released the same day as Uncharted 3, and 10 days prior to Skyrim.
MUSIC
Music is a rather under appreciated aspect of video games. It's the music which can stir emotions and fuel adrenaline. From calming orchestral pieces, to epic bombastic rapping of drums, from soothing synthesisers to eerie violin plucks. The soundtrack is half of the ambience. I was astonished at how forgetful the soundtrack for this game was, especially considering it was composed by one such as Inon Zur! (Responsible for the late Fallout games, Dragonage Origins, Company of Heroes, and much more!) The only really memorable piece is the main menu theme, in other words, the theme of Rivendell. I've never liked the term 'generic' when labeling music in video games, but damn, that's the only word that comes to my mind. A very big let down, expect nothing spectacular here.
TECHNICAL - ANIMATIONS ETC.
Not only does the game look old, but it feels old too. Animations and controls are clunky. Buttons sometimes don't work when pressed, and menu navigation can be tedious. Barely any character expresses any form of emotion, rather, they resembles zombies, or mannequins. The voice acting isn't too bad mind you, but overall the game just feels like a mess, like you're learning to use a controller for the first time. I'm not entirely sure of the Snowblind Egnine's capabilities, but I assure you, it is far from impressive. The game is also littered with bugs, for example, playing cooperatively, I could not revive anyone as the Dwarf, and was forced to put points into the skill that allowed me to via my War Cry, this ultimately became somewhat game breaking. The game also forces its own voice chat system, which resonates an obnoxious echo if you are communicating through the likes of Skype, or Discord. To fix this, one must minimise their game, whilst in the multiplayer lobby, disable their microphone, and re-enable it. A simple option to turn it off would suffice.
CHARACTERS - PLOT
Another downside to this game is the characters, both playable, and not. None are even remotely memorable, and hardly inspiring. You establish little to no connection to any NPC and the more you play, the more you realise the game fails to create any kind of bond with these characters. Dialogue is drawn out and becomes more of a nuisance than a benefit.
The story otherwise, doesn't try to break any serious barriers. It coincides with the plot of the Fellowship films, and tries to convince you that you were part of the reason they succeeded. At the very least, some new locations like the Ettenmoors and Carn Dum were introduced, but the game being entirely linear, does these places a disservice. You know when a game has failed to sell itself to you when you literally sprint through the levels.
"But Garth, what about the gameplay!"
"Gameplay matters more than graphics!"
Unfortunately, gameplay doesn't equate to much when the game poorly performs in every other aspect. One cannot deny that visuals and sound design are equally, if not slightly less, as important as the controls and gameplay.
This game focuses on an exp system in which levelling provides you with some skill points, and some stat points. It also randomises loot in containers and the surrounding world, and encourages you to search every nook and cranny to find items that may not even be useable by your class. Yes, I haven't much of an issue with this aspect, but the grind for better loot is ever so tedious, in such a small linear game. One positive factor to this is that items are randomised in containers from play to player, not everyone has access to the same loot, which encourages trading, which is done through a poorly designed menu. Storage for the junk items, which are the most common, is lacking, as you find that you will never completely fill the space given for weapons and armour.
This loot however, does visually change your character, and some of these armours and articles of clothing do indeed look nice and have an intricate design, but customisation is extremely limited.
There are side quests in this game, but most are simply fetch quests, and some are even subject to unseen parameters, such as a time limit. Which brings me to NPC interaction. You are given an extremely predictable dialogue system, where choosing the top most option always results in the best outcome. A somewhat complicated design for a simple minded game. The fact that there's no sense of morality in the game emphasises the the notion that such a system need not be present for this game, but props to the devs for trying, I guess...
Combat is rather, enjoyable. Mostly because most, if not all other LoTR video games feature very little violence, and this game compensates for that fact. Satisfying blocking mechanic, good button mashing. Overall, enjoyable, but it does become repetitive as the game drones on, and enemies begin to become damage sponges, soaking up even the mightiest of blows. Ranged weapons, are particularly overpowered, with the Dwarf's crossbow capable of dealing insane amounts of damage with a single bolt, never mind the classic shotgun shell sound as you reload it.
Movement is on the downside too. I found that my character barely if ever maintained a constant jogging pace, as the game seemingly could not register that I was holding down the W key.
Overall, a very clunky kind of game, with decent combat mechanics. But is this enough to sway you? I would hope not.
OVERALL
With all that I have said in mind, does this still sound like the game for you? Even at a heavy discount of 75%, I can't help but feel robbed of my time. An entirely lackluster, anticlimactic game, with extremely underwhelming technology, controls, and a heavily uninspired soundtrack. The ending felt rushed, and disappointing.
Being 100% honest, I cannot recommend this game at all. And I advise people to actually not purchase. Save your money for when a more promising LoTR game is released. There is no replay value in a game as tedious as this. As soon as you load the game up, you will as soon come to realise what a forgettable experience it is, and here we find that the term 'forgettable', is the sweetest thing you can say about this game.

To tell you the truth, I didn't really know about this game until this friend of mine told me that it was a nice coop title to play online. Well, not only that, but also that it had a major possibility of not working properly according to a review that he watched before (yep, kinda like having a "save game" break of synchrony, for example). Anyway, since we already had the game, we finally decided to give it a go (already expecting for something bad to happen). Well, we surely had to deal with some glitches throughout the way. Some of them were because of the game itself, while others were because of my friend's PC config. Either way, somehow we've managed to play it until the end and finish it. Overall, it was a really cool experience. One of the most surprising aspects about it in my opinion was the in-game microphone, which literally emulates this "echo effect" when you're inside of a cave, for example. As for the general aspects, the graphics, music and sound effects are ok. There're three different characters to choose from and you can even get to customize them (I've made my ranger look like He-Man's Man-At-Arms just for shizzles and giggles). The controls are ok too, you can get to play well on the keyboard / mouse and on a joypad as well. Since it's a coop game, there's definitely some replay value on it, just be careful with some weird glitches that you might bump into during your run (kinda like having an invincible boss to deal with, that wasn't cool at all).

You can see that I've given this a thumbs up well okay but let's get the bad parts out of the way first. Right off the bat this game is overrated by people new to the genre, who have had bad experiences with other games in the genre, are impressed by dev team responses in threads, are amazed that it's made by a two-man dev team, and love the soundtrack. New to the genre is self explanatory - it's a great and under used genre that has been a niche for far too long. Bad experiences..well a lot of the games of this ilk are either out dated like the greats Freelancer, DarkStar One, and the whole Privateer series, whilst the X series is notorious for being released in terrible condition and aren't patched to a high standard until usually the 3rd major patch. This doesnt make them any less worthy examples of the genre when they ARE finished but the initial buggyness and headaches tend to make people react so badly that the games are crucified before they even get to that stage. As for dev responses..I've not had one to my queries and even had one deleted from the threads altogether so no brownie points there fanboys. Whilst Double Damage are a two man team it is very rare for small or solo teams to do all the work themselves..they hire part-time fillers for artwork, coding..whatever is needed..I'm sure that's the case here - When was the last time you saw a credits list to ANY game that showed one or two names? The soundtrack IS great with its modern outlaw theme (very similar to some of the music in the Sons of Anarchy T.V. show) but great music alone does not make a game.
All this said, it's an accomplished entry FOR THOSE NEW TO THE GENRE who may be put off by something a lot more wide ranging and complex like Elite Dangerous; others may be put off by what can seem dumbed down and simplistic by comparison leaving a somewhat arcadey feel to combat. Regardless of how you feel in that respect it's a decent game that is certainly worth the asking price.

So I got Rebirth during the last dale. 1/2 off a X series game? Sure, why not? I knew well in advance of purchasing the game the gripes others had about the game, and to be honest I was fully expecting to play it once and never again.
