It has some issues. Like the fact that someone put targetting info over the RADAR screen (it could be GRAVIDAR, to obscured to know). And no SETA was originally a pain. But then I started to slow down. I'm not focused on GOTTA GO FAST. I'm actually finally flying my ship instead of using it as a robot courier.
The Skunk is also a decent ship. I really miss jumping into my capitol and watching the main cannons disintegrate targets, but the Skunk shoves you right into the action and even on the harder difficulties it's pretty easy to survive.
So would I recommend this game? It's made space gorgeous again. People keep talking about Freelancer, but I'll stick with X for as long as I can.

Rebel Galaxy is a fantastic throwback to games like privateer from my early child hood. Something happens your given a rust bucket from a family member and kicked out into space to do whatever you like. There is a story there if you'd like to explore it, but theres also a very large set of systems for you to get lost in. These systems start easy and quickly ramp up into fleets of doom that look like something out of babylon 5 or a borg invasion.
Graphically the game is very pretty. Each weapon type has its own effects and its easy to tell what your oppents are using once you get familiarized with the types. You'll know when your enemy is shielding himself from your attacks and able to plan accordingly.
Combat is a blast. Its a traditional "sailing" broadside system with a bit of a twist. There seems to be 2 types of ships. Broadside focused ships and turret focused ships. Turret ships have weaker broadsides so slightly less punch but they can hit in 360 degrees around their ship. Broadside ships usually have nasty blind spots at the front or back of their ships but if you end up on their sides your going to be sucking vacuum very quickly.
Gameplay is very open. You can do simply the main storyline and just enough side quests to up your combat effectiveness for the next mission or you can join one of the guilds. Partake in trading, Mercenary work, Pirating, and evening mining to pay the bills. All of these have their own supporting play styles, missions, and equipment.
Keep in mind that there are also factions in the game, so if you choose to start popping merchant ships for their yummy goodies expect to have to deal with that militia destroyer next time you hit a station.
Alternatively there are TONS of randomized seemingly procedurally generated encounters as you fly along towards your missions or stations. Merchentmen calling for help under attack by pirates, pirates trying to lure you in with distress calls, communication beacons you can hack to get some secret info for trading, mining spots, or loot caches, and of course the occasionally massive fleet battle from one of the many factions who's decided to take a crack at each other.
All of these features lead to making Rebel Galaxy on of my favorite games for the year and at a price point that is simply mind blowing.

SquareEnix released this game back in 2011 for PC (on Steam) and 2009 for the XBox360 - and it shows. Below is a comprehensive list of Pros and Cons, as well as some Middling views after beating the game.
PROS:
+ Story
The story is fairly simple, as is the main character, Rush. He's introduced running into a battlefield while two armies fight - anybody that dumb is surely the main protagonist I want to root for. But, all kidding aside, the story has the basic elements to make it interesting enough to grab ahold of your attention.
+ Graphics
The scenery is absolutely beautiful, and you can tell a lot of detail went into the water/background effects, the way that every city or town has their own unique architecture, and every cave or open area feels both wide open and yet closed off simultaneously, as if something is just over the horizon.
+ Music
While the battle music does fluctuate randomly (more on that below) the tracks themselves are very good at what they do. The sad music is appropriately tear-jerking, the Uh-Oh music is ready to make you panic a little, and the fight music makes you want to swing a claymore through somebody's torso at times.
+ Gameplay
A much-contested portion of this game, based on numerous Critic- and Reader Reviews online, is that the battle system is very interesting. I have to agree - "Interesting" being the operative word here. Some battles are over before they begin, for good or ill, and that makes some fights tedious but mostly it's fair enough to not have to re-re-fight something for the umpteenth time because that one character is too slow.
MIDDLINGS:
~ Travel
You start off the game by running through a cavern. And... that's the entirety of the game. At least, so it seems for the first hour or so. You run here, run there, watch a cutscene, run somewhere else, more cutscenes, finally explore a cave or castle and... more running. Thankfully, once you've discovered a city/cave/dungeon/area, you can just warp to the main entrance directly from the main map, so it's not a huge slog all the time.
~ Areas
The scenery is beautiful, but it's so empty. Every open field is huge - really, really big - and you feel so small. Great, right? Well... no, not really. You can sit and stare at the walls for so long before you want to get to where the story or the fighting is going on, but first you need to run down huge expanses of empty field or desert to get there.
~ Fighting
If the battle system is great, that means that something has to be wrong with the fights - they're interesting enough initially with a small number of people and a semi-large group of enemies (2-4), but that quickly becomes tedious. So they increase the amount of "unions" (groups) available, making the micro-managing element reappear in a shiny new suit. But it's still the Final Fantasy XIII method of winning most of the fights: Mash Enter/Space/X/A to win.
~ Music
The cities and towns share music. The dungeons share music. The only places I know of that have their own musical scores are the optional places to go visit, and even then the music is pretty bland after three hours of it. Battle music especially is annoying, seeing as how it jumps based on how the fight is going. Going badly? Bad music; good fight, good music. Bosses are notorious for this at times, with notable exception being the final boss.
~ Characters
Loads. Almost 300 named characters, each with somewhat distinct characteristics. That "mitra" (human) is a healer, this one's a sword-and-board fighter, and that one uses explosives. Varied and interesting enough for the Generals - that is, the Unique characters you can assign/recruit - to make it so you know who's who right off the bat.
~ Voices
The in-battle and after-battle dialogue is especially tedious after the 20+ hour mark. You really start to hate the way somebody says something about "needing the other one, the other one!" every time they level up. To be fair, hearing Pagus (a main character) give you a backhanded comment on how that spell was "effective" is a nice touch.
CONS:
- Grinding
This game is tiring, and that's because about 85% of the game is running around killing the same enemies hundreds of times for that one item you need to make the one piece of gear that's a slight upgrade to the piece you're already wearing. Not to mention Mr. Diggs (albeit the best character in the game) is necessary to acquire the ores/metals you need to upgrade or create most of the gear you want, so that's also a factor.
- Diggs
The aforementioned Mr. Diggs is a unique aspect to the mining process - a weird rabbit-like creature with huge pink round eyes that dances when it gains a level - but it only adds to the grinding nature of the game. You first acquire him with 5 digs available - he can mine grass or rocks 5 times before you need to exit to the world map and come back in. That, in of itself, isn't so bad; the bad part is that the digsites, and what you acquire from them, are randomized every time you load up the map.
- Crafting
No game from Squeenix these days seems to be complete without some kind of Creation gimmick, and TLR is no exception. The gear you make is better than what you buy, and what you buy is the base for what you make. So you've done your 3+hours of Digging and killing monsters and finally have enough materials to upgrade your weapon for a... +3 attack damage output. That's just ludicrous, and not in a fun way, either.
- Parties
You start out with a small party of about 3-5 people in it, reasonable enough when learning the game, but you don't actually increase the size of that initial party until a good two hours into the game. Seeing as how you go up against bosses and groups of enemies (6-7 groups at most, with about 3-4 enemies in each group) with your small team, it almost seems unfair the lengths you need to go to survive encounters.
So you've crafted that unique 2-handed sword for your beefy tough guy? Too bad, you can't equip it on him manually. Everything is done automatically for you, when the game decides it wants to let them have the item. And even then, without memorizing who's who, you may accidentally give that new weapon to your healer and not your damage dealer.
In combat, your main group could be near death and the others are at top health. There is no "heal me" or "heal them" option available unless the game decides it wants to give one to you. The micro-managing aspects that people said have disappeared from this game are what make it so annoying at the same time. There are times when yes, I really do want to use certain attacks by a certain character on a certain enemy, because I know it'll work really well - but the game decides that said character is going to try and level their fighting ability and not that healing spell I'm trying to increase.
- Combat
The game already takes forever in terms of grinding, and thankfully, the PC port has given us the ability to speed up the fights. It is wonderful - and yet, the sheer volume of fighting negates that entire wonderful feeling. You're going to end up seeing the same monsters again, and again, and again, for nearly the entire game. There is only one part of the main quest where Giants come into play, and only in that one section. The rest of the time, it's generic enemy models.
- Enemies (field)
As stated above, the types of enemies shown on the field are very few in distinction. What is very aggravating are their hit-boxes; the area in which they can start a fight against you. It isn't well defined or even shown, and a gentle tap from a flying enemy above you where you can't see it starts a fight where they get a free turn.
BOTTOM LINE: If the game's on sale, and you like tactical RPGs, go for it. Otherwise, just play Final Fantasy.

BioShock 2 is one of my favourite games. Some time after it came out, I saw it was getting spit on and dismissed, but I didn't really pay attention to that, as I assumed it was the all too well known kneejerk reaction of the smug fanboy portion of the players.
I got it and went in unbiased. I don't want to compare it to the others in terms of which I think is best, because I love them all separately and as a whole, but it does quite a few things better than the other two titles. What I can say is, I think 2 had the best combat out of the games, because there were so many possibilities, especially with the dual-wielding and the plasmid trap combos. That's not to say I think the combat in 1 or Infinite wasn't good; in fact, I liked it in both games, although less in Infinite. Of course, the latter had a variety of Vigor and weapon combos as well, but not nearly as big as 2.
BioShock 2 also improved on many mechanics like the Camera, plasmid use, hacking, Little Sister interactions, upgrading, as well as things like the visuals and more. However, what I most love about it is the bond I felt with Eleanor and how my actions actually changed her character and demeanor. I really wanted to help her, I wanted her to be safe. And seeing the statues of me rescuing the NPCs through the Little Sister's eyes really made me emotional, as did the whole Little Sister adoption and subsequent saving mechanics. It was so touching to see how playing a merciful, forgiving Delta changed how the NPCs reacted to you and pretty much established you as the most human character in the game, even though you were, as Sinclaire roughly put it, a "tin man". And who can forget the Big Sister fights? They were the ultimate test for your skills, weapons, plasmids. And the ending monologue Eleanor does for the best ending, as well as that pan of Rapture with the main theme of the first game and her saying, "And then, Father, the Rapture dream was over." Man. That was one of the several moments in the game where I teared up and felt introspective about the whole (at the time) BioShock world.
"The Ocean On His Shoulders". How fitting indeed.

This is perhaps the most divisive Final Fantasy so far.
I got this cheap and perhaps that puts this FF in a better light than if I'd  have paid full price. It's not a a bad game, but it carries the weight of the Final Fantasy name and ends up being the worst Final Fantasy experience I've had.
Story: Lacking scope, interesting hooks and depth of previous titles. I didn't care about anyone or anything. A far cry from other FF titles. Probably the worst part of the game.
Characters: Perhaps the most unlikable group of FF heroes at the start. Some limited character progression impoved things. Lightning grew on me and Fang is probably my favourite 13 character. I wanted to fast forward whenever snow and hope came on screen.
Combat: Too slow to introduce the more interesting aspects of the paradigm system and no reason to not just libra and mash auto battle for most of the game. The flow and visuals of combat are great and some battles really bring out versatility of the paradigm system. Ability to change AI behaviour of team mates and reposition during combat would vastly improve the things.
Visuals - Great sci-fi aethestic and still great looking graphics for it's age. Probably best thing about 13.
Linearity - Big issue, but second half of the game opens up and was enjoyable.
Localisation - The dialogue is fine for the most part and the voice acting is ok..ish.
40+ hours of content, which can be pushed up much higher if you complete post-game content and achievements.
Ultimately recommended if you like JRPGs and at the £10.99 price it's listed for on steam.

I love Magic. I have been playing since the late 1990's and this game is both amazing and infuriating. I love the concept of being able to choose every single card in your deck and the vast amounts of cards to choose from; however this game is painfully stupid in many ways.
Firstly, the concept of winning duels to gain coins to then buy boosters is a great concept for a free to play but you have win 15 solo battles to obtain one booster. Every game that you play will take at least 15 minutes to complete so it takes quite some time to obtain enough coins to even buy one booster through solo battles. Now the story mode does offer more coins for you to complete the planeswalkers stories. I actually find this to be an amazing part of the game, even if brief, giving background lore on some of these great cards, but with greatness also comes the worst aspect of the game.
This leads me to the actual gameplay mechanics and how infuriating the the AI (Yugi-oh with Heart of the Cards x10000) can be along with the terrible card selection (especially Story Mode). I have played numerous versions on Steam and Xbox 360 of the older Magic games have found the AI not to be terrible and at times quite good but they ain't got nothing on this bad boy. If you are a beginner at Magic I highly suggest you stay away as the computer will time after time destroy anything you put out or just swarm you (mind you this is on easy mode!). The game forces you to play through the first Planeswalker's story as a tutorial but it is very deceptive on the diffculty. I breezed through the tutorial thinking about how I was going to have 20 boosters in an hour but I soon found how wrong I was. After the tutorial they tell you to play a solo battle and create your own deck!!! Super pumped at choosing my new starter deck I picked a goblin deck for quick destruction and faster boosters and after taking 15 attempts to win that first solo battle I learned how painful this game can be. The solo battles randomly choose opponents so it is not like I kept running into the same roadblock but instead got decimated 15 different ways (milling, a 14/14 on turn 6 with trample, 4 2/2's by turn 3, burn/death/buffs spells every turn, etc.) The main reason for my losses? Mana shortage or mana dump. I would literally have games where I only drew land and games where I never drew a single land all of this coming from a starter deck (that you can't change the # of lands)! This problem is worse in the Story Mode (after the tutorial portion) due to the worst card selection and opponents ever. It becomes a game of reloading the duel until you are starting first or have the best opening hand you could possibly have and even then it is a crap shoot sometimes. Oh also to mention the AI never has a mana shortage EVER. NOT. ONE. SINGLE. GAME.
If you are an veteran of Magic and want a real challenge I suggest playing this game it is worth the time but will probably still make you want to punch your screen after the 5th turn of drawing a mountain.

It's got a good array of varied levels; some fast, some more strategic. Figuring out a level and executing it perfectly is greatly satisfying. The dialogue/story is a bit slow but I found it uniquely entertaining and fun. Also all of the
characters have utterly high-end delicious voiceacting and their different playstyles are good to explore.

They aren't terrible issues, but they can make longer levels infuriating. It feels like you lack the control to make the game truly snappy and fun. but maybe i should just get gud

Had quite a few crashes on level startup (so at least not at a bad time) - maybe about 5 in total in 8 hours.
Again, I did enjoy this game and will be getting the DLC for cheap (now that I've found it - the link doesn't appear anywhere but on the in game startup menu which is kinda funny). However I wouldn't recommend it, especially not at full price.

This game is surprisingly fun, even for someone who is not into the LOTR franchise like me.
This game is designed for 3 players, but can easily be played with 2 players aswell. If you are 2 players, I recommend nobody picking the dwarf, since he is too overpowered and you will just be brainlessly stomping through the game with him.

For example, the built-in voice chat is not mutable, and when restarting the game some of your preferences get lost (like the game's audio settings or the arrangement of the items in your inventory). I've seen quite a few other reviews mention alot of crashes and bluescreens, I never experienced such an occurence though.
If you can live with a few technical downsides like these, you can have a few great hours with this game. As reference, it took me about 25 hours to complete the game 3 times (once on each difficulty).

If anything, this game is immersive. You truly feel for the characters and their plights.
There are a few design decisions that I found questionable:
-A save system. I understand that by removing the save system, it would enhance the immersion, but  I see no harm in adding a different setting similar to that of X-Com's Iron Man setting. The downside for this would be a loss in immersion, but I wouldn't be dissuaded at playing for short plays.
- A secondary goal would be nice. Like if an individual character wants to leave the city and eventually leave the group, or if a character wishes to find a reletive that will eventually join the group. Or maybe it is implemented and I have not gotten that far into it.
Over all, the game is good.

I recommend this game wholeheartedly!

Third rewrite:
I've spent longer playing Rebirth by now, and I still can't recommend it. Egosoft seems to have tried to please everyone at once while giving themselves too much deadline pressure, and I also suspect they may have lost key people at some point; the vision that gave us The Threat is simply not present in this game.
Problems with the game:
Only one ship to fly. This is a big one. They knew it would be a problem, too, but instead of recognizing that and extending their deadline while they re-did the game so we could fly different ships, they tried to sell us a "drone" system. Well, guess what? Nobody's buying.
They still let us control capital ships, sort of, but they managed to screw that up too. We never get to see the inside of our wonderful capital ships; we don't even get to go to the bridge. There IS no bridge; just a little circular deck with no roof or windows that we have to share with our ugly, idiotically named player ship with a crappy theme; we can hardly see anything from it. I wouldn't mind a general "tell the captain what to do instead of doing it yourself" system if I could at least actually be on a nice bridge.
And if they're not going to let me go inside my capital ships, why on God's green Earth did they find it necessary to design a whole clunky, half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ poorly-implemented FPS interface for us to interact with stations through? What was wrong with just flying the ship into the station and using some simple menus? It worked for x2 and I really liked that system better. No, I didn't like x3's system; it was clunky and went too far the other way. They really had an excellent game in x2, and I played x3 and Rebirth expecting that they would have refined everything people liked best about it and added to that. Instead, they ditched it all, started from scratch, and did a crappy job at it.
I'm sorry folks, but it won't be enough to just wait for the patches. They'd have to completely rewrite the game to get it to where it needs to be, and I don't see them doing that. So, don't waste your money.

Hitman: Absolution is a stealth assassin game that is mostly linear but fun. Compared to similar stealth games, its controls are a bit clunky but it does offer some unique stealth mechanics.
I have only played the campaign on easiest (to save time), although I do have some stealth game experience in the form of completing Splinter Cell Blacklist and Watch Dogs on medium difficulty.
If you played the campaign like I did (easy ghost playthrough), you probably just want to feel cool and see the story, and for that purpose the game is probably alright. Like any AAA game there is a lot of variation in scenery and setting, and in any levels it offers you multiple methods of taking down enemies.
The things I liked about the game is that the style is good (although I would have liked the radar to NOT fade out when I'm using instinct), the graphics are pretty realistic and the campaign story is pretty fun.
The things I disliked about the game is that there is no way to overprepare for a level (the only way to gain skills is to complate a previous level to a certain score standard), and the game does not have a mechanic to customize your loadout during campaigns - it would have been nice to be able to use weapons you found, especially between levels that allegedly take place minutes apart at the same location.
Unlike splinter cell which has a last known location system to help you escape enemy tags, in this game the only way to escape an enemy tag is through changing clothes out of sight, or killing the witness which is all good and well if the game didn't punish the use of murder heavily, and you care about your score because it affects the skills you gain so there is an inherent imperative to being stealthy. While I understand that, I still do not like the game punishing you for violence, because in the game the score is not just a number - as I said before it affects the skills (ie. upgrades) you gain.
There is a minor issue with the game I have experienced, that during playing the campaign perhaps during unstable internet I would  be interrupted by a popup informing me that steam connectivity is lost and online functions are disabled, even though the campaign has nothing to do with online mode and I couldn't find a switch to turn off that notice, so beware if you have unstable internet.
The writing in this game is good, despite the game's gritty appearance it does have a lot of comedic dialogue in cutscenes and between npcs to lighten up the mood in between stuffing unconscious guards into closets, although given the epicness during the game the ending was a bit underwhelming. Take note that there are only like 6 songs (not counting sound effects) that are reused a lot, and they're not great songs either but thankfully its only during cutscenes, it seems that they may have cheaped out on the music licenses.

This is a game for players who love sidequests. The game is maybe 80 percent side quests and 20 percent story. There are the usual side quests of tracking down rare monsters and building new kinds of weapons. But there are also other kinds of side quests, such as collecting herbs for a scientist. The combat system is unique and original- it's not like any other Square Enix RPG you might play.
It is an immersive game that requires a high time commitment. A lot of the dungeons take a good long while to get through. This is offset by the ability to save wherever you want anywhere you can bring up the menu. The game accepts input from a keyboard or a USB controller. I've used both and found that in spite of twelve to fifteen keys being available for use, I only ever use five of them (besides my number pad).
The characters are mostly developed through battle. It's a little easier to tell what they're thinking when they vocalize in Japanese. The voice acting is original and accurate. There's a weird little frog man with orange skin and a high pitched voice. There's a bulky white whale person with a deep, gruff voice. And there's a female knight who doesn't take any crap from anybody. It feels like an old Super Nintendo game with better graphics. Highly recommended.

An excellent RPG, lite on the RP and heavy on the G. CGI is out of this world, with fantastic and almost unreal locations that you have to see to actually believe.
The basic plot: a group of heroes are given powers by godlike beings who have created a futuristic civilization above a primal and dangerous world. However, the powers they were given also cursed them, forcing them to run for their lives while trying to understand the serious and dangerous power they have unwillingly been given.

Objectively - looking at the facts - this is one of the best FFs since FF7.  Let's look at 6 key areas that supposed fans of the FF series cared about until this game came out:
1) Story - This game's story is convoluted and stupid.  So is FF10's.  In FF10 they tell you one story for 90% of the game and then the last 10% of the game they say, "Nope!  There's an immortal wizard casting a spell to make everyone believe that this is what's happening!"  Great story, bro.  FF8's story is objectively bad, too.  You grew up with these people and you don't even remember them?  And I LOVE FF10 and FF8.  But story is not some hallmark of the FF franchise that had been good until this one came out.  The story is no worse than many of the highly regarded entries in this series.  In fact, I would argue that most FFs' stories, when you actually sit down and plot it all out, are pretty nonsensical, and 13's fares worse because it is more recent and subject to higher standards.
2) Characters - This is completely subjective.  I find the characters in this game to not really hit any of the highs that we got in previous entries, and a few of the characters were worse than your average FF character.  While my opinion is that this game has worse characters than most of the FFs since 7, I'm also not going to ignore the Cait Siths, Quina's, and Rikkus that exist in other FF games.
3) Graphics - The graphics in this game are sublime, and compared to its 2009 competitors is every bit as cutting edge as the best graphical games of the series (and possibly better).  IMO, only FF7 was more awe inspiring (graphically) for the time it came out, and looking back at it I sometimes scratch my head as to how I came to that opinion.  FF13, in 2017, is a game that makes you say, "Holy...THIS game is from 2009?!"
4) Music - Like characters, this is something that's extremely subjective.  To me, this soundtrack is up there with the series' best.  While the series' best soundtracks likely had more heavyweight classic tracks, they also were bogged down by quite a few forgettable tracks.  And this soundtrack is the first FF soundtrack that I recall listening to where it felt like one cohesive vision.
5) Gameplay - This is the first FF that I am aware of where the term "high level gameplay" actually means anything.  Think about past entries - what is "high level gameplay" in FF7?  Setting up a couple of cute materia combinations?  What is "high level gameplay" in FF8?  Spamming your limit break?  In FF13, true masters of the combat system can accomplish things in seconds that even a seasoned FF player would take 10s of minutes.  Take one of the bosses in this game - Proud Clad II.  Most walkthrough videos on youtube beat this fight in about 7-8 minutes.  A world class player can beat that fight in 55 seconds.  And it's not just true for that fight - there is a huge skill gap between casual players (which includes most FF fans who bash this game) and people who actually understand the intracacies of the combat system.  And it's not just a matter of looking up the right paradigm deck.  You actually have to "git gud".
6) Endgame / Side content - This has been extremely hit and miss throughout FF's history.  FF7 pretty much hit on all counts - great optional end game content, optional bosses and areas, etc.  FF8 was hit and miss.  FF9 I didn't finish.  FF10 was mostly a miss.  FF13's sidequests include a series of 64 "missions" (boss fights), most of which are easy but a solid 1/3 are pretty difficult.  The hardest of these missions (and there are several that I would include in this category) are up there with any of the hardest endgame/optional bosses in the FF series.  In addition, in order to obtain all of the ultimate weapons you will need to grind a series of optional superbosses.  This is like grinding Ruby Weapon - it's not mindless...one little mistake and these bosses will eat you alive.  There are 3 of these optional superbosses to choose from.  I thought this was extremely rewarding - maybe not as diverse as FF7's optional content, but certainly some of the better optional content in the FF series.
On the whole, OBJECTIVELY, when you take the nostalgia glasses off, this is a game that is right at home in the FF series.  Be very wary of anybody who complains that this game is "press X to win" - instead of listening to them, feel bad for them.  It's like somebody who played through the first Mass Effect as a straight shooter without using any biotics or tech, or played through Bioshock with just gunplay (and no plasmids), and then complaining that the gameplay is boring.  Of course it's boring - you didn't bother to explore what was so interesting about it.

I love Magic. I have been playing since the late 1990's and this game is both amazing and infuriating. I love the concept of being able to choose every single card in your deck and the vast amounts of cards to choose from; however this game is painfully stupid in many ways.
Firstly, the concept of winning duels to gain coins to then buy boosters is a great concept for a free to play but you have win 15 solo battles to obtain one booster. Every game that you play will take at least 15 minutes to complete so it takes quite some time to obtain enough coins to even buy one booster through solo battles. Now the story mode does offer more coins for you to complete the planeswalkers stories. I actually find this to be an amazing part of the game, even if brief, giving background lore on some of these great cards, but with greatness also comes the worst aspect of the game.
This leads me to the actual gameplay mechanics and how infuriating the the AI (Yugi-oh with Heart of the Cards x10000) can be along with the terrible card selection (especially Story Mode). I have played numerous versions on Steam and Xbox 360 of the older Magic games have found the AI not to be terrible and at times quite good but they ain't got nothing on this bad boy. If you are a beginner at Magic I highly suggest you stay away as the computer will time after time destroy anything you put out or just swarm you (mind you this is on easy mode!). The game forces you to play through the first Planeswalker's story as a tutorial but it is very deceptive on the diffculty. I breezed through the tutorial thinking about how I was going to have 20 boosters in an hour but I soon found how wrong I was. After the tutorial they tell you to play a solo battle and create your own deck!!! Super pumped at choosing my new starter deck I picked a goblin deck for quick destruction and faster boosters and after taking 15 attempts to win that first solo battle I learned how painful this game can be. The solo battles randomly choose opponents so it is not like I kept running into the same roadblock but instead got decimated 15 different ways (milling, a 14/14 on turn 6 with trample, 4 2/2's by turn 3, burn/death/buffs spells every turn, etc.) The main reason for my losses? Mana shortage or mana dump. I would literally have games where I only drew land and games where I never drew a single land all of this coming from a starter deck (that you can't change the # of lands)! This problem is worse in the Story Mode (after the tutorial portion) due to the worst card selection and opponents ever. It becomes a game of reloading the duel until you are starting first or have the best opening hand you could possibly have and even then it is a crap shoot sometimes. Oh also to mention the AI never has a mana shortage EVER. NOT. ONE. SINGLE. GAME.
If you are an veteran of Magic and want a real challenge I suggest playing this game it is worth the time but will probably still make you want to punch your screen after the 5th turn of drawing a mountain.

Final Fantasy XIII is one of the few Final Fantasy titles I've played that I'm truly torn about.
First off, the story is incoherent. Now don't get me wrong, everything is explained and in detail. However exposition is janky and the pacing leaves something to be wanted. If there is one thing the FF series is known for, it's the rich stories. FF-XIII just falls flat in so many areas, you're eventually left to wonder just what is even happening at times. As for characters, many of them are truly forgettable. However I do feel this may be something of a cultural boundary, as the characters do represent the typical Japanese shonen style characters with flat personalities aimed at teens. But of course, many of the FF games do this, FF-XIII just seems to fail at even producing character arcs which other titles in the long running franchise have managed to produce.
Now in terms of graphics, this game really is beautiful. It's pleasing to look at with excellent art design. The combat is also interesting, though it may feel lackluster at first, with some playing around in how the system works, it really does shine when it comes to fast paced battles and using a bit of variance throughout the game as your forced to work with different combinations of characters. But then, things get tricky with how FF-XIII moves about. It's very very linear and this has earned the game a lot of complaints. The game does open up briefly about 3/4 through with a very large area to explore which can easily inflate the already short story of about 27-30 hours by another ten hours. But this relies heavily on the player having a strong understanding of the battle system, as this large explorable area is unique to only this part of the game and contains many powerful creatures which can wipe the floor with anyone left even just a little under prepared.
Now I will say, in spite of the story being lack luster, the final act really does help pull things together and nicely ties up loose ends so you're not left scratching your head in confusion when the credits roll. A nice feature is something of a new game plus of sorts, but you don't start from the beginning, but rather start near the end of the game with the option to go back to certain points in the game, specifically the large explorable area I mentioned, with the entire leveling system unlocked so you can really pump your characters up.
Just don't go into FF-XIII expecting your typical Final Fantasy game. You won't find that here.
Pros:
-Beautiful game
-Fast paced battle system
-A fair amount of customization for the battle system
-Appears to be a decently optimized port
Cons:
-Very linear
-Bad character development and arcs
-Very confusing and bad story exposition
-Controls for keyboard/mouse are bad
-Controls are more attuned for use of a controller
If you do love the Final Fantasy series, I'm sure you'll have plenty of fun with FF-XIII, but as I said you shouldn't expect your typical Final Fantasy here. As for it's linear nature, it is my understanding that Square-Enix felt the technical limits of consoles at the time of release couldn't support the usual large overworld featured in other Final Fantasy titles.

This game repeadily screws with you until you no longer want to play it. Doing side quests and grinding makes the game harder due to level scailing to the point where I can no longer progress because I never bother learning all the little intricacies of gearing every character in your party and leading the party members into the right skills. Since you can't manually do any of it, you'd never know what you were doing if you don't use a wiki, which I didn't which is why I got screwed. Why you can'd just equipe your party normally is beyond me. Pretty much everything is a chore to do since you can only tell a party member to focus on something and then they need to take gear from your inventory when they want it, at random. This wouldn't be so bad if the game wasn't so difficult because of the combat system.
The combat system is terrible. You can't tell your party to do anything you want, It's all decided by RNG. Every turn it's 3 options of attack the enemy, which all do pretty much the same thing unless you have the wiki open and know exactly what is useful against what enemies. Then you do the QTEs to win which if you miss you you lose most of your damage. Some times randomly maybe you get an option to heal which is always nice to have but they don't always give it to you when you need it. It's infuriating to be fiting a hard enemy for 20 minutes of attrition and then they just don't let you heal for a turn and you lose. WTF GAME?  You can't even defend and stand still because standing still means you lose all your morale if you get attacked, they punish you for not attacking. Positioning is next to impossible since you can't choose to move, only to attack someone and choosing to stand still is asking to lose if there is any enemies that aren't locked in combat. Attacking with multiple unions on a boss is also terrible a lot of the time since bosses get to attack every union that attack them. Which means they can hit you with AOEs more option.
The bosses will repeatedly do AOEs which can wipe a union in 1 hit and they can hit all unions in range. So since you can't move, you are at the mercy of the boss RNG of chosing to do the AOEs and how many of your units are in range because that is all controlled by RNG. I can't imagine how they expect people to approach the battle strategically when they give you no options in the battle. Every boss battle feels like flipping a coin because you need to dodge some AOEs or you'd lose. There is no other way arround it. The AOEs will 1 hit KO a full union if they hit.
Overall, the game just isn't for me and it pisses me off so much that it made my write this review. Mainly because I played more than 40 hours of it and I can't even progress any more. I am now stuck unless I want to cheat or something. I saved accidentally at a part I can't progress pass because the boss is too hard and I can't even leave because the game locks me from leaving the area until I beat said boss.
I actually enjoyed the idea of controlling a large group of units in an army like this but this game feels like it just want to screw with me every chance it gets. There is no logic to the combat system at times and it is all a long gind. Even with all that I would have been happy if I just got to the of the game but the game won't even give me that.

Final Fantasy XIII isn't all that cool, I guess.
You play as Lightning, someone who totally didn't give herself that nickname. Lightning picks up a black guy and embarks on a mission to save her sister who got herself into trouble and, much like my sister, makes it everyone else problem. Unfortunately Lightning is infected with the same cool tattoo problem as her sister and has to do some sort of mission not explained by the big stupid statue that gave her the tattoo and wants her to do said mission in the first place.
And so begins the adventure of Not Cloud and her stupid friends who all suck down the world's longest corridor.
I think my biggest gripe with FFXIII is that it doesn't really feel like an RPG. Like they wanted to make an action game but last second decided to screw everything up even further. Most of your game is spent in a place called Cocoon, which is a floating continent over a place called Gran Pulse, which is supposedly a hell on...Er. Pulse. Cocoon is actually a pretty neat place with it's own societies, cultures, and customs. The problem is you don't really explore any of these features.
Remember how in older Final Fantasy games you would journey from place to place, usually on an over world if you were playing one of the older games? You could find towns, dungeons, and other areas that have absolutely nothing to do with the game, like if you just followed the main story you wouldn't even visit any of these places. So you would discover new areas, meet new people, learn new things, and maybe even find a side quest along the way?
FFXIII doesn't have that, it has none of that wonder and mystery that other Final Fantasy settings had before it. Instead, for most of the game you just kind of follow a long corridor that leads you from one cut scene to the other. It's like being stuck at the world's slowest  DMV. And at the rare times when you are around other people they usually just make off-hand comments as you pass them. Even when you end up in a city or something
you still end up just following a trail until a cut scene plays and the story continues. The most glaring problem with all of this is that there is actual lore and back story to Cocoon and Gran Pulse, the problem is that its just shoved into your datalog as the game progresses. It just tells you that things are happening and there's stuff going on, but you usually don't get to see it for yourself.
I don't know if they were trying to appeal to a wider audience or something, but even a wider audience would find all of this bland and boring.
The characters are also a big flaw. The only character I actually ended up liking is Sazh, and even then he was just the Old Black Dad character with a bird in his hair. Lightning is about as bland as she looks, and her hostile lone wolf personality she had early in the game almost made me want to turn the game off. She has outbursts and other actual character developments, but they end up being more like moody teenage pouting than character progression. It'd be cute if she could stop trying to be the tough girl for one minute.
Snow is like the kid who ate paste in school. Who always calls himself and his friends “heroes” while constantly ♥♥♥♥ing up on a scale that would make an 80's cartoon villain blush. For instance he tries to punch the same character in the face three times, and each and every one of these times he gets knocked on his♥♥♥♥♥with the same move. Three. It's like routine.
Hope goes from a whiny baby to an angsty teenager, to a anime protagonist in the time span of about six hours, I can't really say anything bad about his later personality. Fang is Australian and the only reason Vanille seems to exist is to heal my party and make mouth noises. I don't mean talking she just kind of grunts and giggles a lot.
Combat feels like a kick in the nuts followed by a bill you have to pay for being kicked in the nuts. You have three options to choose from as well as the paradigm shift, which is a fancy way of saying class change. Instead of having the usual “Attack-Magic-Skills/summons-Item” system like other games you instead have Attack, Attack but this time you get to pick your attack, skill, and item.
Auto-battle is the first option, where the game chooses what you use to attack the enemy. Command is where you actually get to pick your attacks, skills has things such as Quake, summon, revive, etc, and items are items.
The fighting happens in real time, with your characters attacking when all of their action bars filled or when you press a button to attack with what bars you already filled up. Your best bet is to fill your enemies stagger bar and then break it, the higher percentage the more damage the enemy takes while staggered to that percent.
Paradigm shifts come into play when you need something to get the job done. Commandos hit enemies with a folding chair so their stagger meter doesn't deteriorate as fast, they also do the most damage when the enemy is staggered. Ravagers use magic to fill up the stagger meter faster as well as do damage, medics heal, syngerists buff, and saboteurs debuff enemies. You mixed these together to get better results, like 3 ravagers burn through enemies in no time, three medics make sure that nobody flat out dies, and commandos just kind of mug people.
This all sounds complicated but it really isn't. Basically you paradigm shift to maintain the stagger, shift to do damage, shift to heal, shift to play basketball, etc. The shifting itself is also kind of stupid, because a little cutscene plays the first time you do it where it has to take a few seconds to show each character change classes. In this time you cant issue commands but the enemy can attack you. So it's kind of stupid when an enemy burns through your HP, you shift to your healing paradigm, but your party takes the time to pose and lose even more HP during. I've actually die because of this.
It doesn't help that you only control your main party leader and you just have to hope that your other characters cooperate. Their competent for the most part, but a good number of times I've lost party members or flat out died because my healers refused to heal me and I couldn't handle healing 3 members at the same time.
It's also so damn boring. There's no real strategy to it, you just use Libra to find the enemy's weakness and then burn through his health with said weakness. If they have no weakness or all magic damage is halved then you can just fill their stagger anyway, only now it takes longer. There's some variety though, like you can cancel out your attacks and change them mid action if you have to. But that variety is like the dollar menu at a McDonald's.
It all looks different but you know its all still made out of homeless people.

As a former M:tG player myself, I was thrilled to see a FtP version of Magic with "Duels". That was one of only few good takeaways I have for this game. The other being the sheer easyness of earning in-game currency to buy boosers. If you understand the basics of Magic, games can go rather quickly...or at least seem that way.
The bad things (and I won't repeat the usual buggy reports most people are giving), do outweigh any good thing that I could come across. The one that sticks out in my mind is that nowhere can I find what edition of the rule book the game references either on Steam or the M:tG website. You know...cause that would come in handy when there's a question about the legality of a move/triggered ability/activated ability/etc etc (e.g. "When creature comes into play, tap target creature your opponent controls. That creature does not untap during it's controller's next untap step).
Okay, that's a pretty straightforward ability and nothing about that in and of itself raises any alarms. But wait...there's more!
We will take said example and apply it to a creature that I control, that is already tapped (due to attacking). My opponent, in this case, Artificial Retardation, targets an already tapped creature, thus it cannot untap now during my next phase. The way I remember it, and still it played in tourneys is that if all of my creatures were tapped, they could not be targeted because part of that creature's ability could not be met.
If i'm right, i'm right. If i'm wrong, someone please tell me then what rule set this applies to. Cause I do believe I have not ever seen this before.
Other cons: Lost coins, six card boosters instead of fifteen like the physical packs (could have at least made it eight cards), poor matchmaking, poor algorithim used in "shuffling" the deck (too easy to become mana-flooded even with as few lands as possible), poor online matchmaking.
Good thing this game was free, or it'd be a definite victim for the Steam Refund.

Bioshock might have been one of the best games of the last generation (of consoles).  It's an absolutely fantastic game that worked on every level and delivered a one of a kind story and narrative.
So why am I giving this game a negative recommendation.  Did they mess it up?
Yeah they did.  Bioshock remastered might be remastered.  But it's also got a HUGE number of problems.   First off I'm playing this on an Alienware Alpha with upgraded ram (16 gb of Ram) and a 500 gb Solid state drive.  Almost no other game has a problem with this set up.
Somehow Bioshock has an infuriating load time to pull up the MAP..  not the game itself, I mean literally hitting the select button to pull up the map.  Why is there a load time there?   And in addition I have seen soft locks.
Now Bioshock is old, there's really not an auto save so if you're working through a level and your game crashes, you're back to the beginning of the level *unless you quick save."  And quick save is not quick at all.
There's a ton of bugs, and something else feels "off" this is not the same game I once played.  I don't know if the graphical changes have greatly changed the world, or I already know the story, but this isn't exactly the same game I played almost a decade ago.  It's not nostalgia goggles, there's something wrong with the game.
Bioshock is a great game, but after playing this, I'd much rather play the original instead of the remastered.  I love Bioshock I love achievements, this should have been a slam dunk, but instead this is just painful.   What happened 2k?   Were too many people asking for another and you are trying to kill the fan's love of the series?  Because it doesn't work that way, we just learn not to trust your publisher.

Greetings, comrades! After playing the first game, I was excited to see where the next BioShock would take me. But it turns out we just went right back to Rapture, where the already abysmal situation has somehow been made 10 times worse. Don't try and make sense of it, it doesn't work.
Pros:
The Plasmid system was GREATLY improved. No more constant right-clicking to switch between weapons and Plasmids.
You get to play as Big Daddy! This means that the severely OP'd Rivet Gun from the first game is now your personal play-thing, as well as the gut-wrenching, face-mangling, skull-crunching drill that is the icon of the series. This... is... AWESOME!!!!!!
Also, there is a particular scene where you get to play as a Little Sister. That was rather impactful.
The Cons:
It's BORRRRRIIIIINNNNNGGGGGGAAAAAAAAAAA!!!!! If I stop playing a game after ~30 minutes, that's BAD! Literally, the "breaking point" for me was at ~30 minutes. The rest of the game was an endurance just so that I could say I beat it. It does nothing to keep you interested, as the environment is just a rehash of the first game, only slightly more decrepit. This is probably the greatest flaw in this game; there is nothing, ABSOLUTLY NOTHING to keep you interested. The plot is just dry and lifeless, and the whole game just feels like an endless slog. Take the whole "turn-yourself-into-a-Big-Daddy-for-no-reason" thing from the first game and make that the entire game. That is what this feels like.
The balance and pacing is just terrible! I can't do it justice here, much less explain it properly, but I'll do my best. Your weapons are over-powered, plain and simple, so balancing measures are expected (if not vital), and I'm fine with that. However, the handicaps placed on the player are rarely fair or intelligent. For instance, the drill is super-powerful, but you run out of fuel in a matter of seconds, making it not really worth pulling it out to begin with. The Rivet Gun was really powerful at first, and was balanced by an ammo shortage. That was fine. But later in the game, ammo was coming out your @$$, and it did a shameful amount damage. What happened? Did the Splicers find a "Resist Rivet" Plasmid or something? The .50 cal MG was the only gun that stayed constant, all the rest were variables (Heh, see what I did there? Ah, never mind.). The money is once again a problem, as I literally filled my wallet to the max on more than two occasions. That should NOT happen in a "survival-horror" game. The deeper effect of this hyper-deflation is that at that point you are never short on anything. Big Sister coming? No problem. Just run to the nearest vending machine and camp out.
This game commits a horrible violation of my cardinal rule, "never be boring". This, in my opinion, is the b@$tard sequel to a great game. I cannot in good conscience recommend this to anyone. That's what you get for turning the series over to someone else, Irrational. But I don't blame you, rest in peace. Thanks for reading and have an awesome day!

The X series has been a lot of fun.  This one, however, departs from that.  Space feels far too full of 'stuff', extremely generic and repeatative dialogue (In order to buy ANYTHING, you have to hear your character say "Show me your wares, please") with a total of maybe three or four voice actors for hundreds of NPC's.
Oh, also it's buggy and crashed out on me several times (In addition to somehow clipping inside an asteroid and having to force quit), extremely high amounts of video lag on all settings(partially from my older video card), lens blur from sunlight is insane and often comes through asteroids/space stations/etc, making me wish I could customize my character with a cheap pair of sunglasses.
Oh, and the 'soft shadows' is pretty awesome.  Until you realize that you're in the vacuum of space, the one place in real life that doesn't have random 'stuff' making the light scatter, and causing soft shadows.
The campaign is so full of plot holes :
- Oh, yeah, here, have some free guns.  It's cool.
- I just happen to have a massive freighter floating around unmanned, I'm sure nobody will steal it.
- Hey black market guy, over here!  I've got some illegal drugs to sell you!  Don't worry about that security guy standing next to me, he's not programed to care!
- Direct quote: "Steal anything that's not bolted down." from inside a station with no repurcussions. Heck, shooting a station a few times is just an 'accident'. But scanning that same station gets your reputation ruined.
I didn't get far enough to have anything other than the 'noob ship', but I have to assume it doesn't get any better.

I got the game as of patch 2.0, so I can not speak of the disasterous launch.
The combat AI in Rebirth is very similar to previous games, yet it can do something other than fly in a straight line at you like a cretin, and it will use evasive manouvers  - which means that the game is tough. Even a small 3 man raiding party of fighters can kill you easily. The universe is a dangerous place and you need to be prepared to fight, with missiles and crew - or be prepared to run. I could kill virtually anything in previous games with an M3 and a rear turret, not so anymore.
Despite what some people might tell you this is still classic X. The plots frustrating and perplexing. The visuals are stunning. The voice acting is relatively bad, yet you grow to like the characters. You will get confused, you will google, you will laugh and you will cry. If you don't understand the foibles of the previous games prepare to scratch out your eyes in frustration - but stick with it and you may grow to like and understand it.

This is an excellent little game for the money. At it's core, it's a somewhat simple spaceship combat game that sees you upgrading a little ship with a host of different weapons and defenses until you're flying a giant capital ship at the end that brushes aside entire fleets with its massive broadside guns.
It is especially fun for people who enjoy a slow, steady progression of upgrades. It is not for people who don't enjoy grinding, as that is most of the game. There is some depth in the choice of weapons placements and types, but nothing too drastic.
Facts
- Grinding-based, gradual upgrade game
- 2-D combat (you can't fly up or down)
- Single player only
- Multiple ways to make money
- Multiple factions with different ship types
Pros
- Well polished
- Good music
- Entertaining combat
- Satisfying and fun
- Huge returns for game cost
Cons
- Inconsistent difficulty curve
- Somewhat repetitive
- Occasionally bizarre behavior (A squadron of fighters can obliterate you in seconds, but a lot of times they don't)
- It is a little lacking in complexity, so don't expect more than a playthrough or two
- I personally feel the number of ships available is lacking somewhat. There are long dry spells where you use the same ship.

Not recommended... This is not the "X" game you are looking for...
Firstly, let me stress that I am a massive fan of the previous "X" Games. When I saw "Rebirth" was due to be released I immediately found myself looking forward to getting lost in another massive, bustling galaxy with lots to see, do and buy. I always found the massive range of player useable ships meant I could always find something new to work toward purchasing and upgrading.
Now, when I heard about Rebirth, and the ability to dock and walk around stations to trade, modernised graphics and a great new storyline campaign, I was ecstatic. I thought to myself "this is exactly the game I have been waiting for!".
Unfortunately, when the game was first relased it received such appalling reviews that I did't even try it. I guessed (correctly I suppose) that if I waited a while then game-breaking bugs would be fixed, and the price would fall. So, with the release of the latest update, "Rebirth 2.0" which claims to have recitified the majority of faults and overhauled the gameplay based on player feedback (combined with the Steam promotion which was running at the time) I thought Rebirth might be worth a look. I was wrong...
Visuals: Yes, it is pretty. Well... at least in space. Graphically this is a nice step up from the latest generation of X games, and is more or less what I had been expecting. However if you dock at a station, don't expect anything resembling realistic characters. Character models on the whole are grotesque, with extremely outdated visuals and horrible, frozen expressions. Stations themselves once you reach the interior, are simply cookie cutter copies of each other with very little variation at all. See one station, you've seen them all. At one stage of the storyline, an NPC aboard your ship exclaims "Wow, I've never seen a station like that before" (or words to that effect.) But as I clambered out of my ship, oh look it's the same docking bay/corridors/rooms as the previous 10. They're empty, lifeless, bland and generally uninteresting addtions to the game that in my opinion would have been better off ignored.
Gameplay: Well... Bland. That seems to be the most commonly recurring word I think of when trying to accurately describe the majority of the game in fact. At first, flying around in your ship is reasonable fun as you take in the view and fly through the highways. But it gets old, fast.
Firstly, the small to medium sized vessel you begin the game with is the only thing you will be flying. The "Albion Skunk" is yours for the duration. Sure, you can fit it with new weapons and engines as you'd expect, but you cannot purchase or fly other ships, even though you may own them and hire crew to fly them for you. And as flexible as this ship is, I can't help but long for the days of being able to pilot just about any ship I could find. I didn't get any sense of achievement or reward being stuck with the same, rather bland (there's that word again) ship throughout.
Secondly, the campaign itself. I admit, I completely abandoned this after around 4 hours. I kept thinking something wonderful would be just around the corner, however I spent the entire time flying through numerous sectors in which there was nothing to see, to numerous stations in which there was nothing to do. Once there, I would talk to one of the numerous copy/paste NPCs who would then send me to do the same at another station. There is no longer any form of time dilation to speed up travel, you're stuck staring at space.
On the whole, I think the biggest issue with this iteration is simply that there is nothing to DO... You spend your time floating meaninglessly through space filled with meaningless empty characters with no purpose. The large majority (and I'm really not exaggerating here) of NPC's will simply fly in circles without any concern for the world around them.
I really, really wanted to like this game. And I tried, I really did. Unfortunately, it just wasn't to be. I am sorely disappointed, even after going in with low expectations following other poor reviews. Take my advice, and spend your money elsewhere.

Including ship chassis. You're free to experiment with new types of loadout at will. No charge for resale at all.
There's a stat in the pause menu that shows your
, including your ship and all of the parts you have on it, what's in your cargo hold, etc. It's a great way to do a single-player space exploration game.
People complain a LOT about warping taking too long, but I don't find it a problem at all. You can get upgrades to your warp drive that increase the speed dramatically. As for hitting asteroid belts during a warp, you can and SHOULD watch for oncoming nebulae and asteroid fields. You can literally see them coming from a million miles away, and just steer out of the way. Snake around space for a better paralax view, so you can tell whether you're coming up on something big.
So, your turrets can hit stuff above and below you depending on their placement, and your side-guns are primarily for hitting the bigger stuff.
There is a surprisingly large number of ships in the game, I'd put my currently seen number at about 20. Each faction has their own set of ships on offer. I particularly like the trade faction's GIGANTIC verticall wall of shipping containers, bristling with turrets and cannons.
When considering your loadout, you spend a lot of time trying to strike a good balance between equipping anti-fighter, anti-cap, anti-shield, or anti-armor. Each turret and cannon has it's own set of attributes, and the jack-of-all-trades stuff is lacking a little in the numbers department. Over all, weapons feel good and balanced between types, with a slight leaning toward Mining Lasers at the start. I found them good for the first system, and switched out to specialized guns later.
The cowboy music aesthetic is nice, very firefly. I ended up turning it off after a few hours of hearing the same four or five tracks, and loaded up a playlist with all the Star Wars music from the original trilogy. Definitely a good choice.

itself in the game is very simple. Go to station, find merchandise that is selling low, travel around until you find a place to sell high. It's interesting, it's a fun and unique little spin, but... It's nothing we as a community haven't seen before when looking at the "CORE" game mechanics, i.e. what am I doing here. It's a shooter with very grim and macabre storytelling. It is original as a body of work, as a piece of art, and as a social statement that this sort of thing can exist and it really isn't that big of a deal. How? Read on, we come to the violence element.
The violence itself is not that bad as far as what's already out there and done. It's all about the presentation and how it's being spoon-fed to the audience. It's brutal because of the morality and horror involved in what you're experiencing. YES. It's a dark game. But, the actual ACTS of violence and gore when detached from these elements are nothing new. Purely as a visual, we've seen this before in countless other violent video games over the last decade. Again.. It's the total package in which the carnage is being presented that gives pause to controversy. However...
(**WARNING** the following paragraph addresses social implications, skip to the bottom to avoid topic)
It's an adult game, it's meant to be nightmarish in it's delivery. Take the movie Hostel or other "torture-porns." It's just another medium of adult entertainment. If this isn't for you, then it should be viewed no differently and approached with the same discretion as anything otherwise, parental or personal. The "go-to" kindergarten-country mentality just blubbering to take offense at this game is the same tired pile of self-important reactions they've always been. Agree or disagree, a contrasting  viewpoint gives no grounds to dictate what a video game can be as entertainment or what others should be "allowed" to play. That's why it is rated appropriately as AO.
But as a game to play? It's fun, but it's a passing conversation piece you'll be done with in a week and a half. Nobody needs to pretend big brother needs to be here. Have fun with it and let's not take ourselves too seriously,

Not what I expected from the Hitman franchise. I read all the reviews, saying how this game was a critical masterpiece, under-appreciated, etc. I didn't find this to be the case at all.
The game is gorgeous, and the controls are good. But the actual gameplay is extremely frustrating. The game gives you a ton of ways to deal with your targets; however, the save system and score system get in the way of this every time. If you actually want to enjoy the game, then you have to ignore the score system. While previous Hitman games encouraged experimentation, this game actively discourages it by giving you - maybe - one checkpoint in each level, at the most. WOTC has finally pulled the plug on this game (no further expansions from here on out) and going to stop polishing this turd of a game. Did they learn the right lessons, though? I'll summarized the reasons why I hate Magic Duels so they can do better for the next game:
1. Land Draw
Make the land draw mimic an actual real-life deck. How hard is that? All the Duels games from Stainless Games are notorious for mana clumping that will never happen with such regularity in real-life.
2. Hold Priority
Don't let the game skip phases automatically! How hard is that? Too hard for Stainless, apparently. Ironically, this is a new feature in Magic Duels. The previous games in the series did have hold priority.
3. Animations that prolong game time
Instead of removing animations that prolong a game, Stainless mangled the core mechanics of MTG with automatic phase skipping instead. This is not rocket science. Well, ok, it is, for Stainless.
4. Daily quests that punish offline players
Want to get more people to play the game? Then don't make dailies that can only be completed through online play against other players! Online players already get more rewards for winning a game, there's no need to reward them further and in the process alienate players who do not want to play online. This is, again, not rocket science.
5. Finding the card you want when deck building
There is no way to search for a particular card. This is not easy to fix, but it's obvious Stainless didn't even try. The filtering options are not adequate and if WOTC hadn't pulled the plug this problem is just going to snowball and gets worse with every new expansion.
6. Cross-platform
If only Magic Duels was cross-platform the same way Hearthstone is. Actually, I read that Magic Duels was unplayable on iOS for a few months, and is not available on Android. Can you say "minimum viable product"? I know Stainless Games can!
Here's to the next digital Magic game. Hopefully it will be a good one, but the track record so far has not been promising.

This is quite literally the most bored I've ever been playing any game ever. I have played Magic: the Gathering with meatspace cards for years but, since I have recently forsook the hobby for real life, I was excited to get involved in a free to play version of the game. Despite my distaste for the incredibly limited deck building available in the preceeding Duels of the Planeswalkers games, I was more than willing to let Magic Duels have a chance because I simply want to play M:tG again.
However, Magic Duels is convinced that everyone who will ever play has never even heard of M:tG before and thus need a step by step introduction to every concept in the game by a voice that sounds like the narrator for an early 00's corporate training video. The game, after it stops teaching you how to navigate its GUI, finally begins with a duel where both players only have the most basic kinds of creatures with no abilities. You must play the entire first duel with nothing to do but go through the arduously slow process of announcing and sitting through the animations of the games weakest creatures.  When the game finally deigns to give you a creature with the arcane and befuddling concept of a "creature ability" it interupts the duel in which you are currently engaged to load, then explain, a staged duel where you must use that specific ability. It does that in the second duel when it finally introduced "instants" then again for every new idea that ever comes across the board.
It took me an hour to play through 3 actual duels and had to sit through a dozen "Baby's First Spell" interludes and I had still yet to do anything more complex than boost the attack of the some of my creatures. I could not be more put off by a tutorial if it had uttered a racial slur under its breath. And it took the frustration of boredom quitting and probing the internet for people equally bored by this game to realize I could have slogged through the dozen pop ups it takes to get the game to let me start building my own deck and play without suffering the world's least engaging tutorial.
Once you get the game to stop holding your hand, it delivers the experience I expect from M:tG much better than Duels of the Planeswalkers with a much more in depth deck building system, Interesting decks for the AI players, and, despite the spotty connections that have been reported, lots of interesting decks by the human players too. This is a good game but in my frustration I cannot help but place this review as a warning to other veterans of DotP and M:tG in general that the game is difficult to get going but could be worth it if you're realy interested in the source material.

I picked up this game during the free weekend in January 2015 to try it out. I was hesitant to buy it when the game first came out so the free weekend was a godsend to demo it. I started up a game with a buddy of mine and we fooled around in a multiplayer game for four or five hours. There are some things I liked and some that I didn't.
-In Civilization 5, multiplayer games had pretty consistent desyncing problems. During our long game time in BE we experienced exactly two of the "reloads" that designate a desync, and they were brief. That's a huge step up in my book. If only Civilization 5 could do this.
-The artwork in this game is really wonderful. It's not overclocking, Crysis, realism earth-shatteringly beautiful, but I really appreciated the design of the units and the world. Watching my astronauts with assault rifles become hardened soldiers in power armor with lasers was a real highlight.
-The new quest system was a really cool idea! I loved reading the little pop-ups about how my new colony was adapting to the environment and technologies and what was being done. I also really appreciated the choices of customization, though some were distinctly better than others.
-Despite the misgivings I'm about to list, I did
.
-The Tech web is a good idea but with poor execution. It makes sense that technology would no longer be linear at a certain point and it plays well into the affinities, but... It was confusing. It was an information overload and the tactics I wanted to pursue were often spread out all over the place and required researching technologies that had absolutely no benefit to me. +1 to manufactories? Woohoo, I don't have any of those... But I need to sit for 30 turns just to unlock the research I need. Civ 5's techs always felt helpful in at least small ways.
-Aliens were also poorly executed. In the beginning they were far too numerous and too strong. By the end they were very annoying in that the alien nests would never permanently die, but were no real threat. They just kept appearing even after destroying them for the fifth or more time.
-My buddy and I pursued the conquest victory condition in our game. Kill all other civilizations to win. We had made each other allies in the lobby, so we shared tech and various other bonuses throughout the game. The biggest disappointment of my time with the game was this: after destroying the last civilization... The game didn't end. It still counted my ally's civilization as one I had to destroy. What? How do you break a conquest game type? I don't even...
I do not reccommend this game. I had fun for the one match I played, but that ending really killed it for me. I say: play a game or two during this free weekend and maybe revisit it when it goes drastically on sale. Perhaps by then this game will be better ... optimized?

TWoM is a very fun game, showing how 3 people band togeather and survive or die. Survive long enough, you will meet other survivors on the way, and get a bigger team. The bigger, the harder. Pavle, Katia, and Bruno survived...well, not very long. On day 1, Bruno was already sick, but we found enough supplies in our shelter to make a bed for Bruno to sleep on. We also made a radio, so we could hear what is going on, what♥♥♥♥♥♥is going down. It seemed to be the Rebels lost a valuable memmber. The weather would be warm, not very rainy for the next few days. I found a nice, good radio station that happened to play classical music, which was lovely with all the shelling and shooting in the background.
Night 1, Pavle went to go scavange, while Katia stood guard and Bruno slept to get better. Pavle found some usefull things, where he went. He found food, weapon parts, components, electronics, wood, etc. The building Pavle went to, well, it was vacant. No one lived there, so it was easy. The only thing that freaked Pavle out was the rats, which he thought were people walking around.
Day 2, the night seemed calm. Bruno seemed to get better, and Pavle got back with the resources. The three began to build a stove, in which they could cook better foods. They also made a metal workshop for better weapons. They did not have enough for any weapons, or enough for lockpicks. They did make a crowbar, and ventured further into the shelter, finding more items, making the workshop able to upgrade. They also made one more bed for Pavle to sleep, Bruno to stand guard, and Katia to go scavanging. Katia and Pavle went to go scavanging on different nights, finding foods, and resources, but no medication. This seemed to be going on for the next few days.
Day 3, not very exiting, some people to sell things.
Day 4, more news on the radio. More classical music.
Day 5, not very exiting.
Day 6, first robbery. We lost some food, even though we were very low on it.
Day 7, A man arrived to tell Katia about an aid drop. All the rebels took alot of it, but there were some in the no-mans land, the man said it was risky, but Katia went anyways, coming back with some food, water, and other resources, but she came back with some more wounds.
Day 8, not very exiting
Night 8, Pavle went to Sniper Junction, where he found good loot and saved a man's baby.
Day 9, not very exiting, more robberies, no-one went scavanging due to sickness and injuries.
Day 10, not very exiting.
Day 11, a women showed up and asked to join, and she was very helpfull because she went scavenging the next few nights.
Day 12, More robberies, everyone was injured but the new girl due to scavanging.
Day 13, The New girl died while scavanging.
Day 14, Pavle died from hunger and his injuries, Katia died from severe injures, leaving Bruno with severe injuries, sickness, and his heart broken, fearing for his life.
Day 15...Bruno couldn't take it anymore, and commited suicide.
***
Katia never found her parents, and when the war was over, her parents went to Katia's grave to mourn for her.
The New Girl(I forget her name)'s parents never showed up, maybe they died.
Pavle's family died during the war.
Bruno's family had mourned for Bruno, but never showed up at his grave, possibly due to the fact the town was just to sad to come back.
Bruno, Pavle, and Katia survived for 15 days total, but they all died as one, meeting each other in the after world, whatever the hell it is.
OVERALL, I seriously enjoyed this game, and nearly brought tears to my ♥♥♥♥in' eyes. I left some details out, mainly because I forgot about them. Katia did some bad things, Pavle did some good things, Bruno helped in every way possible, but didn't go out scavanging.
All in all, I rate this game a ♥♥♥♥in' 9.3/10, it's a very, VERY good game. It was thought and planned out very well, and I ♥♥♥♥in' loved it. Get it now, before the daily deal ends.
