Let me first say, Bioshock 2 is just as good as Bioshock 1. In fact, once I got used to the new Plasmid controls (tweaked slightly from Bioshock 1), I realized they had actually improved a few small things. So, now that you understand that I did in fact thoroughly enjoyed both games, I will list a few things that bothered me slightly about the story. These were not enough to detract from the overall enjoyment of the story, just some little things that were slightly *off* for me that I wish had been written to make the stories bend together better & provide more well thought-out continuity.
The following contains spoilers, so if you have not yet played both games all the way thru, you have been warned.
***********************SPOILERS***********************
The ending of 1 felt wrong to me.
----------------------------------
I loved playing both 1 & 2, the story had a great buildup and some nice reveals. When I got to the end of 1 and you suddenly made a clean escape from Rapture, it felt wrong. The ending does not affect gameplay, it is just a short cutscene after the fun final boss. But it did not feel like it really fit with the overall theme of the story.
So then I start 2 and find out that you are now a Big Daddy and I got my hopes up that they had changed the lame ending to 1. You did after all spend the entire last half of 1 transforming into a Big Daddy. So starting 2 as one felt right & I was intrigued.
I played the first 30% of 2 having a lot of fun, then spent the next 20% wishing it were shorter. That's only bc it started to get a little repetitive. No big deal really, just a minor complaint. Then suddenly just past the 50% mark, the story picked back up with a few big reveals about you. These alluded to you possibly being the same guy from 1. I was quite happy.
There was no final boss in 2
-----------------------------
It's true. Some people may argue that there is in fact, a very large final battle that counts as an extremely hard boss fight. This argument is completely negated by the simple fact that as soon as you start the final event, you can (& should, by design) immediately skip the entire battle and go straight to the ending. I won't give away specifically how of course, but will tell you that by doing exactly what they tell you to do, you will not fight a single enemy in the end. It's kind of a mild let down after the big buildup you just went thru at that point in the story. I say you should do this, & by design, bc the final battle in question is completely un-winnable. Again, by design. They intend for you to do exactly what they tell you to do and  move on to the cutscene. I did however like the way 2 ended. The cutscene this time did make more sense in the grand scheme of the story.
Sorry if all that rambling made no sense, just wanted to share my thoughts. None of this detracted from my overall experience of the games. I enjoyed both games and am very much looking forward to starting Infinite in a few minutes ;)

A fun little game where you manipulate gravity at will (using your gravity gun to shoot either a gravity field or an anti gravity field) to solve puzzles. Not very expensive so you can get it if you're interested. And a profit maker for steam cards
Gameplay
The main focus consists on using your gun to create gravity fields in order to solve the puzzles of the game (even if some do not require using it at all, but that depends on your skill). And in typical fashon of platformers the stages get harder each time you complete them.
The game has a fair amount of checkpoints so it won't frustrate you that much of repeating the stage, although depending on your skill you might need them or not.
It is interesting once you play it and while not 100% innovative it's interesting to play with gravity since the mechanics are solid and well made. And it can engage you in solving all of the puzzles. So this is by far the strongest point of the game.
Story
The story consists of you going to a certain place to face trials in order to become a gravitymancer. There's not really much to tell so it's story isn't important and not important for the game, so you can safely ignore the opening.
Graphics:
The graphics are mediocre, but they serve their purpose since they look very bland and uninspired in order to make the gameplay shrine. I've seen better models in other games but again, once you play it you'll forget about it and focus on the challenges.
Music:
The music is very good and does serve it's purpose on engaiging you in the stages besides hearing something pleasing. And considering that this game is cheap it does have a soundtrack that should be in higher priced games. As for how memorable they are, IMO they're not memorable, but you'll probably want to listen to them if you really like them.
Overrall
If you like platformers or puzzles and want an interesting game mechanic of using gravity then get this game, you'll not be disapointment and you'll probably get another game by selling the cards when you get in on a sale.

First I have to say that this is the only game in the "X"Series that I have not tested, and this was by choice for lack of time to truly give full attention to the game.
After reading most of the comments about the game, I saw that 90% of the comments were negative...it wasn't really encouraging, but since I have faith in Egosoft, I bought it anyway. For the life of me, I can't really find anything truly wrong with the game.
I haven't experienced the game crashes that others were complaining about, and I didn't get the impression that the game was unfinished in any way nor that it was still in beta form.
So for those people that were stating that the game was in Beta form or should have been an early access game, you obviously don't know the game your dealing with. The game is finished and complete. So either the people making those types of comments don't really know what their doing when it comes to testing or they really don't know the game and the history of the "X" series games.
Most of the complaints that I read were from the very first weeks of the game being released. Egosoft always has patches out for their games within 6 to 12 hours of release if there were final tweeks needed or even fixes to correct game breaking bugs, and all it takes is going to the website and downloading the patches.
On the other hand, Steam might not have the updates uploaded nearly as quickly, but thats a steam thing and not Egosofts fault.
I have to admit that after being an "X" series veteran since X-beyond the frontier and having been a member of the Dev Team from or since 1999, this game is a beast all its own. And seeing as I got it from Steam, I don't really have a ready manual right in my hands to help me along with some of the commands and some of the other facets of the game.
Piloting the ship is interesting, and I like the return of the cockpits, I was one of the mates that missed them when they were left out...so KUDOS!! for the return of the cockpits.
On the other hand, I really don't care for the way that the character walks through the station. I'd personally like a 2nd or 3rd person view of the character, on the other hand...I really might have gone a different way with the modeling of the NPC's on the station. I'd be willing to go as far as saying that if something was rushed in the game, it was the characters...I do however miss the POV look around. It was helpful but not a hands down needed feature.
There are a lot of things that are different in the game. Some of them facinating and other that could be infuriating...like trying to track down a specific person in the campain...but after I completely understood the nature of the game, it wasn't all that hard to find the others and it started to become fun.
So reading all of the negative reviews...I took a look back at them...intersting that their near or on the same day...and probably about the same time...but thats another subject for a different type of forum. I also noted that the same people that were complaining that the game was unfinished and crashed a lot had as many hours as 600+ logged playing the game...thats not a number that denotes there are "...lots of bugs and crashes"...and..."the game is a lost cause..."
Since I've only played the game for a cursory period of 3 hours or so, I don't really know much about the game play. I do know that I haven't encountered any of the bugs and or glitches that people say they have encountered...then again...I've only read where one or two people recently had trouble running the game recently as of the latest patch on 05/20/2014 and the bulk were more than a year old...so I'm guessing that many of the game breaking bugs have been fixed and dealt with harshly.
I do have to say, with any game, if your PC doesn't have the "kung fu" to handle the game, its not going to play or it won't play right if at all. So perhaps the people that are complaining about the game are running them on machines that truly can't handle the program...I'm not there...so I really don't know.
I myself am running a 3rd Gen Phenom 6 core...I run 2 and sometimes 3 3D modeling programs at the same time like 3DS Max and Maya while using photoshop and fireworks in tandem with adobe premier Pro, and I have no slowdown in performance...so my machine can handle the game and then-some...but someone else might not have a PC that can handle the game like mine can or anyone else that plays the game without problems.
My advise to people that want to buy this game...
1).  Make sure your PC can handle the game...graphically and processor wise as well memory wise.  Take the time to look at your machines specs and figure out if your PC can actually handle the game...as a tester (alpha and beta...and not just for Egosoft)  you should always make sure your PC can handle the programs you are running. Sometimes a system that can not handle the game will act funny while running it...that is IF it runs the game at all.
2).  If you've played the previous games and are expecting the same type of game...Don't...its not the same game...as I said before...its a beast all its own.
3).  Take the time to get used to the way the game plays. If you have a joystick, take the time to adjust it to the game...all buttons and movements etc. If you play using mouse and keyboard, get used to the way everything responds...learn the controls.
Perhaps I got really lucky and I can run the game because it likes my machine, but I really haven't found the glitches and bugs that everyone else is/was complaining about. My one and only complaint is that I can not find a physical copy of the game and had to get this through Steam. Its a preference to be honest, and I like having the physical copy on hand to make multiple instances of the game on my PC...its a tester thing.
All in all...I like the game. Its an interesting viewpoint for the game and an interesting switch up in the game world.
I will not however recommend this game to someone that does not have the time to invest in the game play. Its not a casual instant gratification game and never will be. So if you're looking for instant gratification, look for another game. Re-Birth takes time to play and it needs a good deal of time invested to truly get anywhere in the game...thats the way the game is designed.
Think - Trade - Fight - Build...and one more...re-learn what you have learned about the "X" series of games...You're not flying with the gate system anymore.

Even for 25$ this game is not worth it. Even I, a long term fan of this series cannot find enjoyment in this X game. It is true most X releases required a year or so of patching to get them in a good state but at least even without the patches for performance and bugs, the previous X games had something going for them. A huge universe filled with tons of interesting things and dozens of ships to fly and equip with countless different weapons. This itteration of the series makes the world seem small in my honest opinion. There are dozens of "sectors" but they are separated between a mere 4 systems and as such the scenery ends up looking the same in many sectors as opposed to X2 or X3 and that makes the world seem uninteresting to me. Another problem I have with Rebirth is the decision to stick you in one ship and give you a poor 8 choices of missiles and maybe 6 weapons. No longer can you fly what you want to fly, now you are in the Skunk and that is it. Even now after such a long time and so many patches I do not recommend this even at it's reduced price. The performance HAS increased but sadly the game itself remains dull and quite frankly boring due to all of the poor design decisions that were made. I will personally be waiting for the next game in the series (if it is to be) and hope they will return to their roots and give us a proper X with sectors by the dozens accross the galaxy and the choice of any ship that is present in the universe.

This is a post 2.0 Review. A lot of the problems listed in the overwhelmingly negative reviews have been fixed. This far, I've found the game playable, and even interesting, though admittedly I waited to buy it on sale so I'm not expecting Mass Effect meets X3: Albion Prelude.
The first thing I'd state is that this game is a simulation, not a traditional space sim. Thus far, the command ship I'm piloting flies like a drunken cow. Take a look at a contemporary aircraft carrier; that's what command ships do. But the world they've built here IS interesting, and at 10 hours into the game I'm starting to find ways to turn a profit and build myself into the trading system, as well as having a decent amount of fun exploring what the dev team built here.
If you're expecting to jump straight into the cockpit of a maneuverable fighter, or fight large scale space-operatic battles right off the bat, this is not the game for you. There are still some bugs here (learn to love quicksave), but the game is good looking and a genuine, immersive experience.
I'm going to say this one more time: THIS IS A SIMULATION. It's halfway between X2/X3 and Battlecruiser 3000AD. If you don't want or can't handle a steep learning curve and some of the frustration that comes with trading between genuinely different stations and not being the baddest ship in the galaxy (though you might just become the baddest fleet in the galaxy), pick up the old X3 games. Otherwise, you're in the right place, I hope they get the chance to finish polishing it.

As many people have mentioned already, this game is great with friends while playing alone does not quite grant you the same level of enjoyment. Your AI companions remind me a lot of Resident Evil 5 or early Gears of War companions - kind of just there for flavor, they have some uses like putting up a shield to protect you from arrows but don't give them your items and don't expect to customize their skills.
It's heavily loot focused - finding armor set pieces is the best way to capitalize on your character stats, but require that you grind out areas to find the pieces that you're looking for (unless you're looking for the Marksmen set, those pieces seem to be EVERYWHERE).
You'll always find yourself lacking in needed inventory space. Inventory sorting goes as far as you dragging and dropping items in the order that you want them, so if you like a neat-and-tidy inventory, prepare to have to maintain that yourself. Item stacking only goes so far... 10 potions per stack, and if you're making your own potions and hope to save them for a rainy day, prepare to not be able to hold anything else very quickly.
Of course, money doesn't seem to have a lot of value. Money isn't that hard to come by, things to sell are abundant, and there isn't much that merchants are selling that make you want to part with what you've already earned. Occasionally they'll sell a set piece you're missing, but otherwise it's just generic equipment or more potions you don't have room for. Money REALLY isn't hard to come by too when you find out you can easily duplicate items in coop sessions, but that's for cheaters, so you wouldn't do that now would you?
Sometimes when you give items to your friends, they'll just never receive it, so hopefully it wasn't too valuable!
But I think the biggest annoyance I have about this game is the fact that I have to change my computer's microphone settings to eliminate the in-game chat during coop sessions. There are no microphone options in the game itself, so if you're using another chat client to communicate with your friends, you have to do some adjustments that eliminate the echo you hear from both chat mediums.
All-in-all though, these are very nitpicky complaints. It's a great game to just pick up and dive into without having to invest a lot of time in understanding mechanics or the story (if you're not in the mood to listen - the story's not bad in my opinion). Combat is fun, investing in different skill trees feels rewarding and really highlights your character strengths, and artificially supping up certain stats through equipment so you can wear something you don't normally have the stats for is, in its own way, kind of funny. Timed slow downs during dismemberments feels really satisfying and certain combat animations when doing a coop attack or against particularly large enemies makes you feel really awesome afterwards.
Overall, pretty fun game if you just want to run in and hack and slash enemies. RNG's kind of "meh" if you're really looking to beef up your characters through equipment, and it's highly recommended to play with friends because the AI really isn't the best, but you can frequently find this game on sale, so it quickly becomes a game easy to justify having in the collection for "game night" with the pals.

I just love this game.
I don't know what the CryEngine 2 did differently compared to the other engines, but the whole aesthetic it creates for Crysis still looks better to me than most of the stuff I see today. A lot of modern games -- even the "realistic-looking" ones -- have this aesthetic that makes the game objects look soft and too polished. Objects in Crysis (especially vehicles, weapons, buildings etc.) have this rawness to them that makes it feel like they have weight. It's hard to explain, but a big contributor is probably the lighting and especially the fact that most objects are destructible, i.e., most of the environment reacts to your actions, something that's still absent in most games a decade later.
Another layer that helps sell the imagery is the incredible audio. Weapons have a real punch to them and the explosions are seismic (run away from those grenades!). The surround sound is wonderfully immersive.
The game is not all about the tech though, even if it's deservedly remembered because of it. It's a semi open-world game with very large maps and a liner mission progression. The open world maps invite different solutions and the nano suit allows you to pick between stealth and rambo mode. I've found that somewhere in between is probably the most rewarding way of playing, depending on the situation.
There's one mission in a beautiful valley where you have to drive a tank and push through the North Korean tank and infantry units which use rocket launchers. Without revealing more I'll only add that it is without a doubt one of the most epically orchestrated battle scenes I've ever played.
But keep in mind that it's largely a slow-paced game. You're playing a US special forces operative, not a world war soldier on the front-lines. It's an incredibly rewarding game if you take your time and find optimal solutions to each objective. The story can be a bit cliche, but I find it pretty satisfying to be honest.
With that said, it's unfortunate that most people (myself included) still have to go through the effort of fixing the broken executable file (securom seems to be the culprit). If you're playing on a 64-bit system, you'll probably have to find third party solutions (google "Crysis 64-bit fix") to even get in to the game.

The Stanley Parable. Besides what is superficial, such as its polished design, story, and a wonderful narrator, there is much to discuss of its nonlinear course of decisions for itself, which you take, and punishes, rewards, or humors you with. The game is obviously revolved around choices in which you form your own story, and this is why I highly suggest you replay this a few times, because different choices can lead to completely different scenes and endings. It's all about the seeming lack of choice, yet a clear option one may not always see. This is what makes it special. The story is the narrator's to control, yet in reality you have complete control over it if you decide you want to take a different route. Remember: fate is not real; you are in complete control.

I'm always skeptical when a game claims that it is a lot like Freelancer, but this one actually is and meets that high bar for me. Thematically it feels a lot like Firefly: the idea of a old western space cowboy where morality is questionable. Everything from the music to the characters to the dialogue choices are very well done and promotes that theme. It is the sort of game where you come up with a backstory for your character in your head and decide, "would I really do this?"
What struck me the most at first was that your movement takes place along a "galactic axis", in other words on a 2D plane. From a game mechanics perspective your ship including guns and movement operate much like a naval battleship. NPCs however can move around in any direction.
I thought it would be a hinderance and kind of lame not being able to fly in any direction, but the way it is done with enemies moving around combined with the camera it feels very natural. It gives you the illusion of flying in any direction with the way the camera works, but because you are actually on a 2D plane it means the controls are very easy to handle in the heat of battle.
It is a great balance between casual and hardcore space simulator while still offering many of the features of games like EvE or X3. Very highly recommended.

I was reluctant to try this game because Magic Duels of The Planeswalkers 2015 was so extremely bad - Bad design, bad marketing, poor stability, low performance - You name it!
However when I saw it was free (and realizing I had no money to throw at other games anyway) I decided to give it a go. While the game still suffers from the same problems as Magic 2015, it is nowhere near as frustrating.
However apart from the fundamental flaws inherent in Magic the Gathering (Grinding for cards, having to Mulligan, having to mulligan again, having to... ok you get the point) it features a number of new frustrations only available in the digital version such as:
1) Losing cards obtained through tiresome grinding.
2) Undocumated tax on in-game currency, as it vanishes into thin air.
3) Waiting for timers when neither player can do anything.
4) Flickering pixels until graphics settings are reset - on every damn game bootup.
5) Having a negative number of a certain type of card.
6) Being forced to go through "Skill Quests" when all you want to do is quit the game.
7) Phases changing before you have any chance to play spells/abilities.
8) Constantly being pestered about reviewing the game (even after doing so).
Well, the list could go on i guess...
So, would I recommend this game? For old MTG players like myself that have come to love the depth of gameplay in MTG despite it's obvious flaws: Maybe. For everyone else I'd say there should be better gaming experiences available, even at the low price of nothing.
Edit: The game has now been updated with Shadows over Innistrad. As expected the update brought some apparently much needed bugs to further frustrate the players. At this point I'm not sure if Wizards of the Coast loses or gains more players from having this digital version. But seeing how little/poor work is put into the game, I'd say they'll still be making lots of money on it...

- Great soundtrack
- Great combat
- Great universe

Finally its quite easy to break the game early on. There is nothing stoping you from (ones you buy the jump drive) to trade around in the starting system, get a lot of money and then jumping to a late game systemto buy the best weapons, ships, mercs etc.
Anyway, if you like Firefly, Star Wars and games like Freelancer and Elite Dangerous be sure to check this game out!

Over the last few days, I have been enjoying this game very much. I have seen people raving about the sound track, and while it is good, after playing for long stretches of time, it does get a little bit repetitive. I do appreciate the ability to implement your own music library. This feature solves that issue.
The gameplay is solid. The broadside mechanic works well, and once you learn to not shoot at targets that are too low or too high, wasting your charged broadside, you will become more and more effective. There is also an amount of strategy in how you approach the battles that you will inevitably be thrown into. If your ship is more maneuverable, you will end up using different strategies to what you would use if you had a heavier ship.
I have seen people complain about the warp system, but honestly it is one of my favorite mechanics. The main issue that some people have with the warping system is that you sometimes are pulled out of warp into battle from enemies that will happen to be in your way.
Theres a couple ways to avoid this issue:
Scan before you warp – if you are worried about warping into a far superior foe, scan your environment (press “f”) before you warp out. The scan has as relatively large range. Take advantage of it.
Maneuver while you warp – if you see a huge asteroid field coming up, don’t just fly right into it! Maybe turn left. Or you know, you could also turn right as well. That might work too.
One major point, and the reason that I am writing this review, is to commend the developer. I had an issue with my save. I lost around 14 hours of progress. After messaging the developer through the forums, I was delighted to find that they are incredibly receptive and helped me resolve my issue within 15 minutes of my asking the question.
Overall, I have enjoyed my time in the game so far, and I look forward to reaching end game on my current save, only so I can have an excuse to start another and try a different playstyle.

Summary: Deck construction!
Multiplayer: Yes
Completion: 4 hrs campaign
Cards: Yes (but cannot be "earned")
Cloud: No (saves online though)
If you played any of the Duels of the Planeswalkers games, Magic Duels will be overly familair. The overall interface is nearly identical and the game is largely the same. The campaign is remarkably short this time around, and they force you to use their preconstructed deck each time. I'm still praying for they day they actually make a comprehensive storyline for their games, but that's wishful thinking on my part. Oh, there's no puzzle mode either, but to be fair that's not the focus of Magic Duels. The focus is total deck construction and the ability to use the cards you earn in any way you choose in solo or multiplayer battles.
When facing the solo decks, I swear the difficulties on some decks need to be fine-tuned. Easy decks should probably not be packing planeswalkers, and Hard decks should not be easier than Easy decks. I don't particularly notice any difference in the AI. It still plays about as optimally as it can regardless of difficulty.
The daily quests tend to be annoying, as they most often require you to use the Deck Wizard instead of your own constructed decks, and the Wizard won't let you pick your nice cards half the time. I usually cycle out the ones that make me play 4 times because it's just boring playing those Wizard decks.
I'd really like an option to speed up animations to make them instantaneous. I've lost track of how many times I played the wrong card because I was in the middle of the drawing-a-card animation. Otherwise the graphics are fine. I still love the card art, and the rest of the painted images are pretty. The dueling table could make do with additional decoration, like various backgrounds and patterns. Wouldn't you like to duel in a forest or an ocean once in a while? The music is... there I guess. I don't remember how the songs go at all.
Probably the most irritating part of the game is how they made the grind even slower than previous DotP titles. Previously you typically got one card per duel (which is still too slow imo). Now you get 6 cards per roughly 8-10 duels, a significant drop. And since the cards you get are random, don't expect to get that one rare you want any time soon. Thankfully the game won't drop cards you already own 4 of, so that's a plus. Still reeeeaaally slow though. As of the time of writing, there are 251 cards available from the Magic Origins set. Assuming you wanted four of each card, that's a fairly lengthy grind.
The card selection is all right. Card power got rebalanced a bit. In particular, permanent removal and counterspells cost more for less bang. On the other hand, combo capacity is high, but since combos require actually having cards, it will be dozens of duels before you can make decent combo decks.
I can't deny the attractive price point of free. You could spend real cash on boosters, but that's no fun to me. Oddly, boosters are the only thing you can buy. Some cosmetics might have been nice, such as new portraits, backgrounds, and battle tables.
I put a fair number of hours into it, and I enjoy it enough to keep playing. I give this game a 8/10 (as a mostly solo player). Here's to hoping they bring back a game like the Microprose 1997 Magic the Gathering.

My favorite is that the quests don't work all the time: you have to use one of their crap decks to play them, investing time in a deck that will rarely win, then once you do win one (restarting 5-10 times to get out of a mana screw) it may or may not count, because of reasons.
Unbalanced. The computer decks even on easy are MUCH better than anything you can do. A naked attempt to milk money out of you to buy packs to get a CHANCE at getting cards that are worth a damn so you can play with decks that actually work.
Uncreative. It's just magic, but you get to play with commons against decks that routinely sport multiple rare powerful cards. The solo story mode was alright, but why not mix it up with other types of game play rather than just 1v1 or 2 headed giant. Why not quests or exploration? Why not challenge puzzles to solve? Why not bounties to unlock specific cards?
Time sink & money sink. You have to spend money to get cards worth a damn, then you'll only lose to those that have spent more money than you. Deck designing is tedious and takes too long. Playing games against those with less money is just a boring nub hunt and playing against those with more expensive cards is just a waste of time.
Mana screw. It never fails to amaze me how much programming MTG is messed up in such basic ways. Yes your interface looks nice, but if the ONLY reason I'm losing is because I get 3 lands for 10 turns or 10 lands in a row for 10 turns, you have a problem with your design! There's a simple way to shuffle actual MTG cards that doesn't result in these HUGE clusters of cards and makes the game actually fun to play. Drawing land after land because the devs were too lazy to do it right is just irritating. The goal is to ATTRACT players, not turn them away because some stupid random crap got in the way of them having a good time or being able to actually win a trivial game, except for the way you've made your game!
So in a short: a game rushed to release to get in on the candy crush micro-payment sweetness that's deparately unpolished in enough different ways for me to swear off of it. Grats Wizard's, this is exactly why I don't buy your cards or your crap software.

Interesting premise, and some visually interesting execution. Unfortunately, a few detracting factors combine to turn me off this game. (1) The limited application of randomness to a custom-designed platform-oriented world, while intended to add replayability, really just seems more to frustrate the beginner who has not yet learned which level contains which resources requiring which tools to be taken along in order to get them. (2) The apparent repetition required in daylight hours to get everyone fed and cheered up. This could be better automated and would make the game a lot faster paced. (3) The unpolished fighting mechanics. Since fighting is actually pretty inevitable, you'd think it could be made a lot smoother and less risky. Unfortunately, half the challange now seems to be whether the AI decides to randomly step left or right, thereby causing you to click incorrectly and sudden-death your character. Not fun as stands .. could definitely be improved. (4) Certain unrealistic things like manufacturing water filters from unlikely components, crowbars that break after a few doors, etc. (5) The lack of saves. OK, sure .. it can make a small indy game more of an on-edge thing ... but it also limits your audience effectively to people with enough time in their life to bother replaying something 10+ times over just to get to a slightly new piece of content. News: lots of older gamers find this boring, and according to Steam statistics that's where the money is.

This review has been a LONG time coming so let's give you everything you rightly deserve. I'm honestly having trouble concisely wording just how much I dislike it so I'll put forth my radical opinion plainly before I expand on it in usual [overly] long-winded fashion – I consider it rock bottom as far as core Final Fantasy entries go. There are so many ways this game has disappointed, but possibly the worst is that I could see glimmers of greatness in it.
As befitting my usual style I'll talk about the characters and story first. Or at least as much as I can in a mess like this one that makes you wonder how it even got approved in an actual development process where, I assume, there was a director of some sort. Our main character is Lightning herself, member of Guardian Corps, and we see her busting out of imprisonment on a moving train with her cohort Sazh in what is a very pretty cinematic. Why would she do this? To rescue her sister Serah who was taken away for being a l'Cie – beings branded by fal'Cie – and things kinda escalate when dear sis ends up being turned into crystal for “completing her focus”. Whatever that means for all you know at this point, but still serves as motivation. I do find myself wishing game didn't waste side characters like Cid and Nabaat as basically throwaways who just pop in the story at some point and then ingloriously disappear, though. You could make an argument the story in the background, about PSICOM, Guardian Corps and others would've made a much more fascinating tale to witness instead of what we got, but that's up to taste and par course for JRPGs. Remember what I said earlier about how it COULD have been a good game and there are glimmers of quality there? For the vast majority, like 80% of game time, game never really earns what it's going for. Emotional moments? Those usually fall flat on their face because of over the top voice acting that has to fill all dead air with grunts and sighs. Dramatic scenes? Exaggerated body language and cliché writing make sure your eyebrows rocket high up. Which is sad because you can see where some reworking could've resulted in a much better outcome. Scene where Hope and Lightning have a heart-to-heart talk about his dead mother and revenge against NORA is such a moment where you can tell game nearly had it, but then it takes a detour into drama central and botches it.
I have to roundabout here and comment on two vital points a lot of people have, somewhat justifiably for the most part, raised about the game in these years since original console launch; level linearity and combat system.
Former is most definitely true as those initial, well, 20-ish hours are linear as all hell and game drip feeds you tutorials at a pace and exhaustiveness that just comes off as insulting unless FF13 is popping your JRPG cherry. There is not a single goddamn thing that would warrant such extensive explanation while things that could use such a manual, like upgrades for example, get more or less token cliff notes to work with. To get away from that and back to linearity – it's true, but a lot of people have this notion game opens up when you get to a single huge zone later on. There's an insidious trap there, though. Up to that point game essentially has a tight leash on your character progression because you're going through corridor after corridor with usually unavoidable enemies unless you really make the effort to finagle around them, but that changes later on when you're given freedom and that very moment set upon by enemies you'll struggle a bit to get anywhere because you've been conditioned that everything
My latter comment from paragraph above, that being combat, is simultaneously more straightforward yet also somewhat divisive. It would be dishonest of me to deny how much I enjoyed boss fights in Final Fantasy 13 precisely because Paradigm switching system it went with suits them oh so fine. You see, characters don't really level up anymore as much as they earn CPs which you then use to progressively unlock nodes in the Crystarium for various roles such as Commando, Medic, Saboteur , etc where each of them fills in group roles you're familiar with like damage dealers, buffers, healers, etc. Familiar ATB system is here where each action takes up a certain number of slots required to execute, but your bread and butter when dealing with enemies lies in staggering them. What do I mean by this? Attacking them sufficiently so you fill their Stagger bar which makes them helluva lot more vulnerable and open to attacks. This ties into what I said about bosses because it's great to topple the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s and then do them in all violent like. It's a lot LESS fun when you realize it's also what you'll be doing in most fights against regular enemies until you're so drastically overpowered you don't have to anymore. Constantly witching between Paradigms, group role setups of three such as Ravager-Saboteur-Medic for example, becomes a chore very because it quickly devolves the entire combat system into a lethal version of Simon Says.
Final Fantasy 13's positives are really self-evident and on display so I'd just be doing the game a disservice if I had an agenda here and wanted to smear it for not [justified] reason. Game looks absolutely gorgeous. Somewhat less when you look at textures artists clearly didn't intend for you to have a gander at up close, but it's still amazing to behold and you can tell tremendous effort went into the project. You can't help but wonder where all this creativity even comes from when you behold just how detailed and elaborate levels are, even if it does come at the expense of entire game except for one huge area on Gran Pulse being comprised of just corridors. Which is kinda impressive on its own – you will go through high-tech, ancient ruins and natural locales, but there are corridors and ramps everywhere regardless.
I think game's biggest asset is its production value and all that entails. There are magnificent cinematics in the game that I couldn't believe they went through the effort to actually have in such quantity. Some are bit overcrowded and I didn't know where exactly to look at, especially when Eidolon's took front stage, but almost seamless switching from gameplay, cutscenes and cinematics in general kept me immersed like none other. Already mentioned VA is not bad or anything, I just can't stand the direction they went with, but I have to give props to voice actors regardless of preference because from what I could hear no one half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥it here. Soundtrack is also a significant standout, albeit perhaps not the best in the series and with a somewhat grating combat song. It sounds a lot more suited towards story moments Square Enix wanted to tell over simply setting the mood. It worked for me and there's certainly no lack of quantity here with 85 tracks to boast with.
My keyboard is yelling molestation here so it's probably time to stop. Fact Final Fantasy 13 was on my hard drive for couple of years and in all that time I didn't get past chapter 7 until very recently speaks volumes. I did not enjoy the game overall. There were no technical problems aside from some frame drops here and there, and game's visuals were outstanding as well as sound design, but it faltered in both story and mechanics department. Both felt convoluted and contrived when they didn't need to be to. It would've also worked in game's favor if it wasn't so front-loaded with needless assistance that just gets in the way of playing the damn thing.
The way it is I hope I don't see it any time soon and I wouldn't recommend to many people.

'Defy Gravity' is a platformer that uses physics (gravity). It has the usual jump-or-die and dodge-or-die mechanics, but you can also create two kinds of wells:
Add to that the option to switch on a body shield, which renders you immune to all gravity and anti-gravity effects, and you have some nice mechanics to play with.
I'm not a big fan of the platformer genre because I find standard platformers too 'twitchy' for my taste. But occasionally, I wil try a platformer game that has some special mechanics like the wells in 'Defy Gravity'. So you need to read the rest of this section knowing that I'm only a very casual platformer gamer.
I have to admit I liked 'Defy Gravity' and I had a lot of fun until the 'Grandmaster levels'. Judging from the Steam Achievements, that's almost halfway through the game. At that point, you get a warning screen letting you know that the game is kicking it up a notch and is about to get - and I quote: "much more difficult".
I noticed in the first 'Grandmaster level' that the game was no longer my cup of tea because it got way too difficult and yes, too twitchy for me. But I suppose for hardcore platformer gamers, the fun would only just begin at that point.
I would like to point out that all the footage seen in the demo video here on Steam is from pre-Grandmaster levels. I'm not saying that's a conspiracy on the makers' part or something like that, it's just so you know when looking at that footage and thinking to yourself 'that doesn't look too hard to me'.
The graphics are ok. They are nothing special but certainly good enough for a game of its genre. I invite you to take a look at the video and the screen shots to judge for yourself.
A lot of reviewers don't like the music. I can relate to that but personally, it didn't bother me and I have a low tolerance for annoying music and sounds. For the most part, I even thought the music was nice and at least fitting for the game. So it's clearly a matter of personal taste and let's leave it at that.
There are no options whatsoever for graphics or sound.
'Defy Gravity' has 5 Steam Trading Cards. You'll get 3 just for running the game.
The Steam Achievements are uninspired. They are limited to your classic 'pass x number of levels and get an achievement'. If you just play through the 'easy' part of the game, you'll end up with 4/8 so a 50% completion rate.

Very fun expansion/sequel to Saints Row 4. The game imaginatively casts hell as a dystopian city where Johnny Gat and Kinzie must travel to rescue the Boss when she is kidnapped by the devil. (Yes, "she", Laura Bailey is the only real boss).
Pros:
- Superhero gameplay is more fun than in Saints Row 4. Your powers are a little bit toned down, but you have wings and you can fly everywhere, which feels very satisfying since you can build momentum like in real flight. The wings also look badass in comparison to the "wingsuit gliding" look from SR4.
The special abilities are also more unique and cool feeling to use.
- The game also has ability orb type collectibles, but they are also more fun to collect since you can fly into them instead of having to land.
- Inventive plot featuring a bunch of re-imagined historical figures. (And a mini-musical).
Cons:
- There aren't a lot of story missions. The vast majority are generic activity missions with no plot. There are a lot of different locations where your character can comment on the surroundings but it would have been nice to be more integrated with the story.
- The execution of the story was disappointing due to how short the cutscenes were. I got the feeling that they ran out of budget or something, but the beginning and end of the game could definitely have used longer cutscenes.
- The garbage trucks constantly spew exploding garbage. Funny idea, but it gets annoying when you are constantly hearing explosions everywhere you go, drowning out the environmental FX and music.

Story and Concept: 4/5
Gameplay and Game Mechanics: 3/5
UI Design and Controls: 2/5
Art, Music, Ambience: 5/5
Overall Rating: 3.5/5
Review Summary: This War of Mine is a fresh, compelling take on the day/night cycling survival genre and is recommended as a must-play for serious survival fans. The story concept and art design are thoughtful, elegant, and beautifully immersive.
But while the economy and crafting aspects of gameplay are well-executed, other parts of the gameplay need serious refinement and fleshing-out; and the entirely point-and-click user interface, while simple and easy-to-use, comes off as clunky, ham-handed, and inflexible. It's an extroardinary concept and story and is a solid gaming experience as-is, but This War of Mine could benefit from a serious reimagining and overhaul at the nuts-and-bolts level, particularly with respect to the user interface and some of the more mechanical aspects of gameplay.
--- --- ---
Major Kudos:
- The game's economy of scarcity is expertly designed and balanced. It feels "real," which is no small feat.
- The crafting system is balanced -- adequate to the task without being too junky or circuitous.
- AI and general mechanics in scavenging mode are fairly realistic and transparent, especially the stealth system.
- Randomization of certain elements and the patterns of moral choice available make the game strongly replayable.
- The game's story is unique and emotionally compelling; even where the characters are two-dimensional, they get the job done.
- Art and sound design and execution are excellently suited to the story, concept, and gameplay style.
Serious WTFs:
- The flow of in-game time is so incongruous as to interfere with suspension of disbelief. For example, it takes only an hour or so to build a radio from spare parts, but several hours to clear a pile of refuse by hand, and it can take about 20 minutes just to walk from one side of the house to the other. This could be remedied by doing away with the real-time clock (hours and minutes) altogether, which, while probably intended to foster a sense of realism, actually has quite the opposite effect in practice. In terms of sheer pace, the pseduo-real time flow seems just right for the night scavening portion, but rather too fast for the daytime crafting portion.
- The point-and-click-only interface is not ergonomically uncomfortable, but it is clunky and awkward at times. The game could benefit tremendously from some simple assignable keyboard shortcuts, particularly in the daytime portion, where the ability to cycle through characters with a keystroke and to send them to various tasks with a keystroke would be extraordinarily useful.
- Certain crafting-related and home improvement activities should be assignable and automatable among characters the player is not controlling at a given time.
- Replayability could be enhanced by tiered difficulty levels.
- While I don't mind it so much, some people will have an issue with the inability to start a new game without overwriting the old one, a new and slightly annoying design trend in games.

Despite what's often said of this game, it's a great one. Interestingly, in the absence of Ken Levine, it really points out his abilities and flaws.
Expect a fairly simple, but quite effective story. There really aren't any plot twists, and evevrything pans out fairly nicely. But that doesn't matter, because the artists here masterfully constructs is so that you'd feel the full emotional impact all the same.
What not to expect? Do not be awed. It is not an "exceptional" game in the conventional sense. Ken has a way with pivotal "moments" which this game lacks. There's nothing amazing in here at all, which is a shame.
But Bioshock 2 is more than sum of all its part. Even the very predictable ending pays dividends, due to how well the whole thing has been setup. This isn't a game to make you awed and appalled like the original Bioshock, or pondering and thoughtful like Bioshock Infinite. I feel it's more of a sci-fi melodrama, and you'll find your sympathy swinging along with the main characters. Unlike the other Bioshock's the ending really feels rewarding.
Gameplay itself is not special. At least you can use both Plasmids and guns at the same time, and you also get a melee attack as well. Apart from a few new Plasmids to play around with, you'll be here for the same sort of thing as you had with the other games.
I can't comment much on the multiplayer. There are no servers, and you'll be playing on listen servers, i.e. other people's PC, so expect lag. I live too far away from the continents to play this very well, so I can't give a good review of that.
Anyway, it's a good buy, and I wholly recommend this to anyone who has 10 hours to spare.

Short review: I don't 'hate' it, but it isn't compelling enough to recommend either.
Hatred is a black and white twin-stick isometric shooter.  It's premise is simple: forget about story, here's a gun: now go to work.  I don't mind that, its par for the course for many bargain first-person shooters who similarly use terrorism as a lazy hand wave for genocide.  At times it even rewards a bit of critical thinking due to some difficult 'tasks' and a semi-unique health mechanic.  So why the lack of recommendation here?
The issue is that the killing just isn't that compelling.  While my biggest complaints boil down to the camera perspective and various aesthetics, let's just clear the air—there is an issue with the theme.  No, not wonton murder of 'innocents'.  Take another decidely violent twin-stick shooter, Hotline Miami, for example: the frenetic action coupled with contra-style vulnerability blends it into a sort of puzzle-murder simulator.  Part of the fun is trying to do it faster, better, more competently, etc...  It's difficult and morbidly rewarding to kill and Hatred has none of that.  There are no points to score, no kill streaks, no modifiers.  The action is adequate, and there are even flashes of a decent game from time to time, and maybe that's fine for some but I find it to be filler.  "Kill everyone here."  Why?  Is it more rewarding here than there?  And let's be brutally honest: shooting civilians really is the 'quirk' and while they do serve to recover your health, it's there in lieu of more interesting ideas.
But let's say you don't care about that, you just want to shoot.  Unfortunately I was left wanting.  The game is incredibly dark (no pun intended) and the camera perspective often obscures your firing lines making it difficult to both use the environment to your advantage or shoot someone right in front of you.  The game could benefit from some intelligent aiming to provide better cues or a smidge of autoaim.  For example, you cannot shoot downwards so any elevation difference between you and your target prevents you from shooting them.  At least a simple laser sight would make it obvious.  It might not solve the core aiming issues, but at least you would know where you are pointing.  In a game about shooting, regardless of target, this is a big issue.
As for bugs, I didn't experience many.  Jumping is a pain, mainly because it didn't always work—I managed to pin myself between a wall and a car for example—but the bad experiences were edge cases.  Besides, the little irritations are just blits highlighted by other, stronger issues I've already mentioned.  What it comes down to is Hatred a mostly competent twin-stick shooter that sans controversy would end up as a forgettable bargain bin title.  It's a difficult yet largely casual experience, and hardly more controversial than infamous Call of Duty airport level.  I don't 'hate' it, but it isn't compelling enough to recommend either.

Over the last few days, I have been enjoying this game very much. I have seen people raving about the sound track, and while it is good, after playing for long stretches of time, it does get a little bit repetitive. I do appreciate the ability to implement your own music library. This feature solves that issue.
The gameplay is solid. The broadside mechanic works well, and once you learn to not shoot at targets that are too low or too high, wasting your charged broadside, you will become more and more effective. There is also an amount of strategy in how you approach the battles that you will inevitably be thrown into. If your ship is more maneuverable, you will end up using different strategies to what you would use if you had a heavier ship.
I have seen people complain about the warp system, but honestly it is one of my favorite mechanics. The main issue that some people have with the warping system is that you sometimes are pulled out of warp into battle from enemies that will happen to be in your way.
Theres a couple ways to avoid this issue:
Scan before you warp – if you are worried about warping into a far superior foe, scan your environment (press “f”) before you warp out. The scan has as relatively large range. Take advantage of it.
Maneuver while you warp – if you see a huge asteroid field coming up, don’t just fly right into it! Maybe turn left. Or you know, you could also turn right as well. That might work too.
One major point, and the reason that I am writing this review, is to commend the developer. I had an issue with my save. I lost around 14 hours of progress. After messaging the developer through the forums, I was delighted to find that they are incredibly receptive and helped me resolve my issue within 15 minutes of my asking the question.
Overall, I have enjoyed my time in the game so far, and I look forward to reaching end game on my current save, only so I can have an excuse to start another and try a different playstyle.
So I must say this game feels like Hotline Miami meets Postal great game over Hyped no need for an adult only rating.

The possabilites are pretty big. Think player made factions and guilds fighting wars for resources or player made pirate groups raiding player escorted relief convoys that will effect economys in the game and the major factions relations and standing in the world.
Overall I would very much recomend this game to anybody who is a fan of si-fi and or western drama with its beautiful world and fun gameplay with a large choice of options and intense ship on ship combat.

I got this one on sale for 8$, and it's only barely worth that much.  FF XIII is definitely the worst game of the main series.
Let's get the good out of the way first.  The combat system is new, and serves to abstract the combat for the player.  Instead of taking a more direct role in commanding your people, you instead asign them roles which allow them to behave in different ways.  Healer, Tank, Damage Dealer, Buffer and Debuffer.  Success in combat depends on knowing when to use the right combinations of these roles.  It's not the most conventional system, but it works well and the fast pace provides a fair amount of excitement in battle.  Enemy diversity is good, and requires you to stay flexible rather than relying on a single formation.
...well, that's it for the good.  Now the bad.  For the most part, FF13 is a never-ending slog down a mostly straight tunnel that extends between you and whatever your current objective is.  The main story is confusing at times, often leaving you wondering why your characters are going to a certain place.  The very first side quest is no less than 20 hours into the game, and almost all side quests take the form of hunting special monsters, or "Marks".  The story provided for these quests is minimal and can all be summed up with the same sentence: a fallen warrior was unable to fulfill his mission and needs you to do it for him.  They aren't even given to you by unique NPCs... you take them from identically shaped statues representing different fallen warriors.
There are no towns.  There is no reason to talk to what few NPCs you may come across, and you will notice the functionality for doing so is quite stark.  All of your purchases will be done over the game version of the internet at your save points.  Essentially, the entire game is combat and cut scenes.  There is a minimal amount of exploration to be done down the short branches from the main tunnel to get some treasures, and only slightly more once you get to the side-quest region.
To sum it up?  Good thing the combat is ok, because that's all this game has to offer.  If you simply must have every Final Fantasy game go ahead, but otherwise steer clear of this embarrassment.

I came in to this game with the idea that "If you liked freelancer, you'll like this".  I liked Freelancer, I didn't like Rebel Galaxy.
I felt like the camera was always way zoomed in and at a weird angle, and during combat it's pretty much always facing at a right angle to the direction you're moving (because of broadside combat) so I run in to asteroids a lot.  My second time out in a combat zone I ran into an asteroid that had something else next to it, and my ship got stuck such that it couldn't turn, and you can't go backwards, so I had to reload to get my ship free.
It feels like you're flying through something far more viscous than water.  I can forgive constant thrust = constant velocity in space games if they at least let you cruise along for a while without slowing down super fast when you disable thrusters.  This game feels like a naval combat engine with space combat art resources.  I think the ship in assassin's creed black flag has less resistance from the water than your spaceship does in the vacuum of space in this game.
I also didn't like the weapons.  They auto aim at stuff, and you do broadside combat where you don't really have to lead or even aim close, your weapons all just kind of pick stuff and shoot at it.  The combat is very non engaging and easy, and if it were hard I'm not sure it would be anything but frustrating since there doesn't seem to be any strategy or skill involved.
The UI and the controls on keyboard and mouse are also not too great.  It seems like it might feel better on a console, but that's not much of a "consolation" on PC.

They seem to be similar to the barbarians in the normal civs, but they also have super strong units like the worm/leviathan that you still need to watch out for later in the game. it's a well balanced play, I would like to see maybe playable alien races incorporated in, but that might change the direction of the game too much. Overall, pretty good game if you like the civs, I wouldn't by it for $50, but $35 seems to be a good price for it in my mind.

I was eager to buy the game until I read some of the negative reviews, but do not be discouraged! This game is perfect, especially those who love to feel.
I started my game with 3 survivors, Marko, Bruno, and Pavle.
Marko was the scavenger of the group. That's where he was best. He did start out a bit sick though.
Bruno was the cook of the group. He made amazing meals for us - when we actually had the food for it. Before the war, he was a professional chef with his own TV show. He started perfectly healthy.
Pavle was a professional football player. He was quick, but didn't have much else to offer. Still, he was a nice guy with concern for the group, and he pulled his weight, switching guard shifts every other night with Bruno. He started out slightly wounded
Marko and Bruno were buddies before the war, and we found Pavle on the streets. Together through these tough times they became great friends.
But let me tell you about my first week of the game.
We started out nearly empty handed. I made one chair (in addition to our current one) and a heater. I made Marko scavenge this abandoned house for the first, say, three days? We found some neat supplies but not much food. We ran out quickly. The second day I built a bed so Marko could sleep during the day and Bruno/Pavle could have somewhere nice to sleep.
Starvation crept on my survivors, as well as sleep deprivation. We got raided on our second night, and bruno defended the house with his bare hands. Sadly, though he was slightly wounded in battle.
The fourth night I made my way to the ruined villa. Two people lived here, I had known them from my previous game. Emil and his wife. After searching their house for food, I was peeking through the door where his wife was. She started walking toward me, and I thought:
"I have to kill her, I have to."
So she opened the door and screamed "Emil! Someone is here!". I took a big slash at her with my knife and took half of her health. Suddenly, she climbed a table and jumped up to the next floor while Emil, armed with a knife, jumped down to attack me. I took a swing and took a third of his health.
"This is easy" I thought.
It wasn't.
He lashed at me and took a third of my health. I retaliated and did the same. "I can't lose more health, I don't have the bandages for it!" He took another slash at me and brought me down to a third of my health. "One more should do it." But I was too slow. He took the final blow and killed Marko. Quickly realizing what happened, I panicked and Alt+F4-ed the ♥♥♥♥ out of there.
Try again.
I go back again, but this time I didn't have my knife. I didn't make off with much on the fourth night, I only got a few supplies from searching the rubble outside their house and in their basement. She found me again and I sprinted to the exit. Didn't want a repeat of the previous game, except worse.
By the fifth night everyone was tired or hungry. Supplies were low. I managed to trade some of our electronic parts for food. Some woman came back and said she wanted Bruno's help with boarding up her house. I sent Bruno to her house (He didn't get any sleep or food, but I felt good about helping). I went back to the villa and that's when I scavenged plenty of supplies. While I was in the basement the girl came downstairs and I had to kill her. It was over quickly and she didn't fight back. I didn't have any lockpicks so I couldn't open their cabinets, but I stole some supplies from their drawers and all of their meds. For some reason the fridge did not want to open.
Sixth day, tired, hungry, etc. Bruno was very tired and hungry. I allowed him to sleep, and him and Pavle to eat the last of our rations. I traded, worked, and then set off.
The sixth night I raided. I found out that the girl was not Emil's wife. His wife had already died, and he was a wreck. She was a mere stranger whom he found on the streets of the torn war, wounded and all. He helped her back to health, and that helped him get over the loss of his wife.
Emil was torned by sadness, and thats when the feels hit. It was all my fault. I did this. I killed his only friend and took his only supplies. I raided his fridge finally and took the biggest surplus of food ever. I took so many things from him that night.
The seventh day was beauty. Marko went straight to sleep, only very hungry, sad, and very tired. His sickness had left thanks to Emil's meds. Bruno cooked us four nice meals to eat, and then traded to get even more supplies. Pavle did some work for us as well. Everyone was no longer hungry, Marko was only tired and sad, and Bruno only had slight wounds. Pavle was up to full health.
As for the game itself:

If you love Tolkien lore and hack & slash gameplay with small RPG elements, this game is a must have. If you love one or the other, buy it on sale. If you've got nothing to play and are interested, just buy it. If you have an AMD rig, buy it for console.

You choose one of three characters: ranger (melee/bow; agile), elf (melee/magic; support), or dwarf (heavy melee/crossbow; tank). You can switch characters at at the main menu or level beginnings. Your goal is to chase and hunt Agandaur, one of Sauron's strongest servants. You visit many popular locations (Gundabad, Mirkwood, Bree, and more). You can find and purchase various items like armor, weapons, potions, etc., some of which are upgradable through rune slots. You manage a skill-tree throughout, as well as a few main stats, e.g., strength and stamina. The
is simple, but it takes some thought and awareness if you play on the hardest difficulty (recommended). You have a light attack, heavy attack, and a ranged, as well as class abilities; the pace isn't quite God of War or Castlevania, but its close. You can command your allies' position, or of course you can play co-op. You'll mostly fight waves of enemies, but there are bosses and mini-bosses here and there. There are secrets and loot placed throughout. RPG elements are in the dialogue with various characters; it's organized a bit like Mass Effect. All-in-all just a great game, especially for LOTR enthusiasts.

If your PC is newish and AMD, it may be worth a try on sale; if you're Intel, go for it, you shouldn't have issues.

By all counts, I should hate The Last Remnant.
The battles are long, control over characters seems to be random, there are an endless amount of missables, you need to grind for items to upgrade character weapons...
And yet despite it all, I'm finding myself really, really invested in this game. The story is convoluted and I'm not sure I'm completely following the lore, but I'm enjoying the characters a lot. Even the side characters who don't show up in any major cut scenes, whose characterization can be condensed to five lines of backstory... even those, I find them to be rich and strangely well crafted.
I could, theoretically, just plow ahead, and play simply the story. But I am actually enjoying doing the many many many many sidequests, and I've been keeping track with an FAQ to make sure I don't miss any. And you will miss some, if you aren't paying a lot of attention to what you're doing.
If you have the patience for the game, if you are willing to accept that you will never understand all the systems, if you can handle the somewhat random nature of the battles -- then, yes, I absolutely recommend it.

This "game" if you can call it that, is still in Beta.  This shouldn't even be publicly released yet.  It's probably closer to Alpha or internal beta.  What are the problems?  Far too many to list, but I'll break it down based on my top gripes.
First, I'm stuck in the same ship.  Any X fan knows that one of the best parts of the game has always been the ability to pretty much fly anything in the game, including caps.  Not here.  No.  You're stuck with the "Albion Skunk" which was a hilarious joke to play on all of us, considering that the advert said the ship was called "The Pride of Albion", only to get in game and find out that "some joker thought it would be funny to rename the ship Albion Skunk" and of course, no option to change it back.  The ship model blockout for the interior looks like it was done in maya by a frosh graphics student in college.  Actually, there are better modders out there than what these guys made.  The textures are terrible and the character feels like you're playing ROTT or DOOM back in the 90's.  Not to mention the space station interiors, which leads me to the next point.
You have to land, get out, and go run through the station to go find someone to buy something from or sell to.  So, these guys have developed faster than light travel, but apparently can't communicate more than 2 feet away.  Ridiculous.  I know they said it was because they wanted us to go explore the station... all 3 variants of the same junk, while we load up our pockets with stolen stuff from lockers and boxes just sitting there while a guard, who apparently isn't guarding anything, looks on.  The character models look like something from the 90's too.  I've seen F2P MMOs with better character models than this junk.  Not to mention the interactions with the characters...
"Go boil yer head".  Really?  Who says that?  Is that some kind of norseman joke or something because I don't find it funny or quaint and I get sick and tired of hearing that... along with "nice chat... NOT" every time I exit chat with an NPC, as if the scripts were written by a 12 year old who thought Wayne's World was a good movie.  Not to mention the "token" co-pilot, who has this awkward accent like English is a second language and it's the first time she's voice acted anything other than badly singing in the shower.  Seriously.. was it really necessary to have her "cutout" in the front near her cleavage?  On a suit that is supposed to survive in vacuum?  I guess this is coming from that same 12 year old who still hasn't scored with a chick and thinks objectifying women is socially acceptable with gamers because, you know.. we're ALL nerdy pimply kids in our grandparents basements and the closest thing we ever get to scoring a chick is google images, right?
Next is the fact that pretty much everything is broken.  I started building a station.  I checked back a bit later, and nothing was done.. I kept checking back... nothing was done.  I let the game run overnight and came back.. nothing was done.  Let it run again overnight the next night, came back, and yay there's a little tiny bit of scrapmetal put in place.  Once that one was finally done after about a week of leaving it run all night, I started another station and, well, it's just sitting there waiting for people to sell resources to it and apparently it's just too far to have to go from the next block over to bring them.
Then there's the terrible ship management and UI.  It's clumsy and sometimes there are game-breaking glitches that happen with the animations which cause you to lose progress and have to restart the game.  Also, the fact that you get punished for having a high-end system, because apparently these geniuses decided that most of the graphics should be dedicated to the CPU instead of using all this incredible GPU hardware we have nowadays...  because you know, who needs graphics cards, right?
Then there's this "highway" travel thing, which is nothing like the highway we saw in the previous games, with what looked like a tunnel of accelleration rings.  No, this is just one snaky path of light that is somehow magically broken into tubes of "lanes" and everyone travels faster than you no matter what, which gives you reason to slipstream behind people to draft them and go faster.  Really?  drafting?  IN SPACE?  Who was the genius who came up with THAT miracle of physics???
I could go on and on but suffice it to say that this game in its entirety is nothing but failed promises and dropped balls.  This game is a slap in the face to everyone in the sci-fi gaming community.  I know that they supposedly fixed a bunch of things and added a bunch of other stuff too, but it is too little too late guys.  Fool me once....     there's a reason the metascore is 33, and honestly, I'm suprised it's even THAT high.  This is one of the worst heaps of scrap code that ever was labeled a game.

If there was a "maybe" that I could give, this game would receive it. The game is either entirely one-sided or not. In the like two minutes I played this, this is what I found.
1) The one-sided nature comes down to the skill of both teams. If one team has more than one player in one area then the team with more players will have the higher chance of survival, especially if they are dark casters.
2) The game starts in 1280x720. While this is nice for the larger 1080p or 720p monitors, my current monitor is a 1024x768. It's not my choice, I have to deal with it currently. It's not a gripe that it starts at this resolution, but the fact that I chose fullscreen and my native resolution made the game freeze. It wasn't anger inducing, it just froze. So I guess that's more of a bug report than anything.
3) The movement and attacks are way too slow for what seems to be a fast-paced game. It's actually a little annoying, especially considering this is a Capture-The-Flag type game and it doesn't appear to have any real combat going on at any point in time.
While these are my gripes, the game seems to be well made and can be a lot of fun with friends. The graphics look nice for the kind of game it is and it even has a "Low-End PC" option in the Graphics menu so even bad computers can run it.
Overall I kind of wish this game was better designed so I give it a "No". But that shouldn't stop you from trying it, it seems like it could be a lot of fun if you took the time to get into it.

The problem with most modern games is that people like to write about the things that offended them rather than actually looking at a game critically. Hatred at it's core is just a simplistic game that is designed to be fun, and the fact that many "professional" reviewers are actually taking it seriously, the fact that people think that Destructive Creations aren't obviously turning this game up to 11 on the edge meter just to make sales is baffling to me. Hatred is probably the text book definition of a concept that sells itself, you have the brain-dead gaming sites that take it seriously which boost sales, and the socially inept pocket of gamers that want to spite some invisible enemy that is trying to push some agenda on video games. You'd half expect this game to hand you the gun and line up a bunch of liberals for you to shoot at purchase.
If you look at Hatred as a game, and not some sort of weapon against decency, you'll come to realize that it's one of the more simplistic games to be released as of recent. Each level has you going around and performing various objectives, whether it be just kill a certain amount of people, or to escape a police ambush by hopping on a train. There is no complex leveling system or dialogue choices, just a straight forward goal of go to X and shoot Y, and they give you a decent variety of weapons that can be used towards said goal. The game is charming in it's simplicity, and half of the amusement I have received from this game is just reading the discussion forums and looking at reviews, I had a decent amount of fun playing Hatred just because I realized the game shouldn't be taken seriously. I recommend it if you want to have mindless fun for a decent amount of hours, but I think everyone has to look at the discussions about this game to get a lesson on how to completely miss the point.
P.S. Extreme difficulty is ♥♥♥♥ing hard.

It's Not worth your time!
First, the technical issues: Need third party software to make a playstation controller (or even normal input controller) work on this playstation game. And the audio is terribly out of sync in half of the cutscenes. Since beauty is really the only saving grace of this game, you can't even enjoy that.
Every time you save the game, it tries to get you to save in a new slot, so you have to always find the slot you actually want to save in. And save/reload have an extra annoying and unnecessary dialogue box that you have to close after it actually saves/loads.
You can't choose your party or even change the leader until you are over halfway done with the game.
I'm fine with classes only being able to use certain abilities, but only the commando can actually use a normal attack. which means you have to keep switching paradigms to heal-attack-heal-attack, etc. And switching Paradigms makes you sit through a stupid animation in every battle, while you are getting beat up by monsters watching the animation. And you have to watch that animation every time you switch, and you have to switch often.
Battles take a seemingly long time, and they aren't real clear how you are supposed to do many things so you don't really master the battle system until the end of the game. This means you will die constantly and pull your hair out trying to figure out what you are doing wrong (I've died more in playing half this game than all the other ff games combine). Toward the mid game, if you don't level up the right classes in the order the devs thought you should, you could be at a severe disadvantage. They give you the allusion of freedom to level how you want and choose your own strategy, but really you have to do it a certain way.
The battle system, other than switching Paradigms is boring. Just Libra the enemy and use autobattle to let the ai decide the most impactful abilities.
The leveling system is kinda stupid. If you have more lvl points than you can spend, you can't spend them until you unlock the next level by advancing in the story, which means grinding won't help you at all. As if you could grind, the game is so linear that you often have to save/load or walk long distances to reset the enemies. It's just not worth the time. And then the leveling map eats up random and seemingly unfair amounts of lvl points so you can never tell how much you actually need. And when you hit your lvling cap, and powered up your characters as much as you can, some normal battles (not to mention boss battles) are still ridiculously hard, or at least take a long while. And the game even gives you less than 5 stars to say that you didn't do it good enough and miss out on some possible rewards. This is stupid because it encourages players to save/reload to refight boss battles to get 5 stars. The game even tells you that you should avoid certain enemies (which you will never come back to fight) because they aren't worth it (so why put them in there in the first place). At least in ff 12, the powerful enemies had a place later in the game when you came back stronger. There is no real exploration, or customization. It's all "follow a straight line and level up how we think you should." Really all you are doing is watching a poorly audio-synced movie and pressing a few buttons inbetween scenes.
And then there's the chocobo chick chase, where you have to find a chocobo chick. But the game points you in the exact direction you need to go so all you have to do is walk forward after each cutscene. And there is no point to it. They could have easily made that into a quick 5 second cutscene and it would've been the exact same thing.
This game is so watered down and linear. And so restrictive and frustrating that I just did not have much fun playing it as much as I have. Really the only thing I enjoyed about it was the cutscenes, which I still didn't get to fully enjoy because the audio was out of sync for half of them.
This game was beautiful graphics ducttaped to a mediocre story, dumb character designs, lack-luster battle system, and terrible game coding. Even if you get the game on sale, I just can't recommend wasting your time.

I wouldn't buy it for full price, of course; it'll be discounted to $10 by this summer.
My only real complaint is that the Civ series has always been intriguing because of its main mechanic: you can watch your stone-age nation advance all the way through the modern age. There's a consistent sense of movement and advancement. Beyond Earth lacks that; a game can span 250 years, but nothing ever appears to change, no matter how much research gets completed. Still, as sci-fi turn-based strategy games go, BE is upper-tier.
