Hitman Absolution is a horrible game. It not only betrays the design philosophy of previous games, it also fails as a stand-alone without any expectations or standards the title on the box gives us. You do yourself a great service in avoiding this game at all costs.
Hitman Absolution is a pseudo-stealth game. Objectives range from "go from point A to point B" or "kill this target". Naturally, the best ways to accomplish these is to do it without witnesses, without getting caught, without getting shot at and of course, as silent and discreet as possible. Previous Hitman games essentially gave you a sandbox to explore and a variety ways to off your targets. Even going as far as to make it possible to make your expertly executed murder look like an accident meaning nobody even had to know an assassin was even present. At the risk of sounding pretentious, it's without a doubt one of the most artistic depictions of stealth in the medium. Hitman Absolution instead controls a lot more like a third-person shooter. Ghosting (minus the required targets) is still possible, but incredibly annoying to execute because of contradictory design choices. Let's start with the small problems and build our way up.
First off: the score system. In previous games, you were awarded with a certain amount of money based on how well you played. The higher your rank, the higher the prize. This could later be spent on upgrades, new weapons for missions etc. This time however, it's entirely cosmetic and borderline irritating. The scoreboard will constantly subtract or add points based on your actions in real-time during gameplay, but it's entirely pointless. Its sole purpose is for online leaderboards which really shouldn't be the focus of a Hitman game. I don't know about you, but I do not want to be reminded by a useless scoreboard that I'm playing a game every time I do a thing within said game.
This scoreboard highlights the shallowness of this game. For one thing, not only is creativity less important, you're often flat-out TOLD how to perform unique executions in order to get points so you can participate in the leaderboards. This ranges from routes, disguise options you can find across the map, weapons, weapon locations and even unique assassination techniques to make the murder look like an accident. The game constantly holds your hand and reminds you can do all of these things when all you want to do is be free and explore, hopefully without the extra grating tutorial voice that I'm hoping you've already shut off in the options menu unless you have already returned this game at gamestop where it belongs. Hitman is supposed to be a game about two things: 1. I should be able to plan my weapons and route with the help of a map and 2. be able to do some improvisation with the given location. You can only do the latter which is made worse by limited weapons, smaller maps, less options and ultimately less interesting/exotic locations.
So let's come right out of it. The gameplay is bad. For one thing, even though stealth should be the better option, fighting back with brutal force is strangely enough encouraged a lot of the time. It really shouldn't be like this, but with covers sprayed everywhere and the annoying disguise system which I'll get to later, making a few sacrifices is often your best bet at survival.
But the scoring system is what breaks this. The game is full of contradictory design choices like this. You're basically told to do complete a certain goal and you're given less of a score for doing something bad like killing or harming non-targets, getting spotted or letting bodies get discovered. Well, gosh I'm so sorry for not doing everything perfectly in my first run, IO interactive! Even stranger is that if you knock a person unconscious from behind and hide his body, you don't lose points but if you knocked someone out and hid the body after he/she spotted you you still lose points. This make some sense as he did see your face except not really when you realize he saw your face a couple of seconds before you decided to choke the living hell out of him from behind. This is made even worse by the horrible checkpoint system which does not save your progress but instead resets the entire level and only brings you to a different part of the map. This means that all of the bodies you put into lockers before hitting a checkpoint are now inexplicably walking around again. Not being able to save wherever you want is also very annoying and discourages experimentation.
And lastly we come to ever awful disguise system. The way you get spotted by enemies is simply awful. When you're in the sight of an enemy you'll see a yellow cone on your screen. Even worse is that their vision cones which are displayed on the the radar don't match the movements of their head on screen which is really off-putting. This will disappear when you move out of the way. Stay in there for too long and the guy will try to stop you and eventually he will become hostile unless you do what he says. You can reduce this reaction time with a disguise. A disguise allows you to enter locations that would otherwise be prohibited to get in or even interact with other NPCs. It doesn't work for people with the same disguise however. So if a police officer spots you in a police uniform he for whatever reason won't be fooled by it. Even when your face is entirely covered it won't stop people from finding you suspicious if they're part of the same group. You're probably thinking that this makes no sense, but it gets worse. There's ways to avoid getting spotted with a disguise. First off, you can move out of the way which makes no sense. If some guy spots you and you duck for cover he or she won't find that suspicious that all. Even worse is the instinct mode. Instinct mode allows you to see throw walls, highlight objects of interest, because Hitman is now Batman. It also allows you to maintain your disguise when spotted by depleting your instinct. How do I use this incredibly skillful technique, you inquire? Gather round and be sure to take notes. The one and only step is the following: you hold a button. That's it. Again, I have make this clear: with mostly linear levels and a horrible disguise system, most of the gameplay will consist out of moving forward and pressing X to not GET CAUGHT. This is what Hitman has devolved into. Other stealth game would at least add interesting uses of darkness or sound, but these staples in the stealth genre that were praised in titles like Thief or Splinter cell are nowhere to be found in Hitman. Heck even Metal Gear Solid, a series I despise, has interesting moments with its fast-paced arcadic gameplay. You're basically reduced to press X TO WIN when it comes to pacifist runs minus targets you need to kill. All redeemable factors from Hitmans predecessors like the sandbox elements, the explorations of multiple methods in assassinating your targets or the creative executions are all gone.
So if press X to hide sounds appealing to you then by all means go buy this game. Other than that there's very little to say about this game. There's a damsel in distress storyline with very little surprises but performed by mostly good voice actors. The original 47 is also back for the ride which is good because IO was originally going to use a Christian Bale impersonator judging from early trailers.That first casting choice rather reflects the soundtrack quite well which was mimicking inception with a hundred percent more BWAAAAAAS. Very disappointing when compared to Jesper Kyds compositions in Hitman Blood Money. As for graphics, the glacier 2 engine made this game look beautiful, but I'd rather have a game that plays well.
That's about all I got. If you like the type of kind of a third-person shooter, sort of a stealth-type of game then go for it. This just does not do it for me. Looking forward to HITMAN: THE APOLOGY.

This was the first Hitman game I played, and out of all of them, has been my favourite by a long way.  I know that veterans of the series would not pick Absolution as being the best, but my perspective is very different.
The difficulty scales well from very easy, through to incredibly hard, and the variety that the difficulty levels provides has kept me coming back for more.  There is something highly pleasing about mastering the highest difficulty level (Purist) and receiving the "Silent Assassin" rating, telling you that you more or less completed the level perfectly, achieving all objectives and weren't spotted once.
The graphics are excellent, for it's time period, and the sound design and music are totally awesome.  There are some nice humourous moments to break up the nerve-wracking stealthy-creepy-can-I-make-it-though moments, (tip, take your time to listen to what the npcs have to say about all manner of topics), and while I might not have bought this game at full price, I can can heartily recommend it to anyone who spots it on sale at a price that works for them.

I just finished the game and my overall rating is 7.5/10. Compared to the 1st Bioshock, BS2 certainly have some positive improvements in terms of graphics and game mechanics. Theres new weapons that can be improved to the point that they will have new abitlity such as heated bolts for the rivet gun. In BS1 you only able to improve the damage,clip size or recoil of a weapon. The plasmids also have unique ability at level 3 and the coolest plasmid is the cyclone trap which can be charged with other plasmids to give electric trap, inferno trap, freezing trap and many more type of traps that particularly useful when you are protecting a Little Sister gathering. There is also a long list of gene tonics to help your character depending on your playstyle. This game also have 6 possible endings depending on how you deal with the Little Sisters and other 3 characters. The storyline is also good and there is continuity between this game and the first one.
On the downside, I do miss the ability to craft items from scraps like in BS1 and the final battle is a bit boring. You also cannot backtrack to previous level like in BS1 in case you missed any weapons upgrade station or free plasmids along your journey. Overall, Bioshock 2 (and its series) is a one of a kind FPS game with unique backstory, gameplay and game design. Looking forward for Bishock Infinite...... when I have the cash.

RtCW is fun. It retains a lot of the corridor shooting fun of the original while still opening levels up to some degree. The graphics were good for the time and still look respectable. The facial textures still look surprisingly good. The game world did feel really empty as compared to modern shooters and even compared to the original Call of Duty that was only a couple short years after this. There's only ever infantry to fight. The level design was still good, though. It was mostly linear, but level layouts were never in a straight line. There was some light puzzle solving that kept my mind engaged. Fairly early into the game you start fighting skeletons that have come to life as the result of nazi experiments. One shoots fire and if the fire hits nazis, it turns them into undead fire monsters. It was pretty rad fighting the fire monsters. Unfortunately, that's about as interesting as the game got. From there it was mainly just fighting progressively tougher nazis, with the occassional monster boss battle. So, nazis are trying to ressurect some guy that was a bad♥♥♥♥♥1000 years ago. Considering that ressurected monster along with all the monsters it creates are taken out in short order by one singular guy, it was probably a waste of time to put so much effort into bringing him back to life. Both allied and nazi characters point this out during the game. While being a completely valid criticism for this games story, it seems like this criticism strikes at the heart of video game stories in general: they are highly unlikely and often extremely illogical. The weapons weren't all that great, except for the Sten machine gun. That was always a blast to use and  it always got my blood lust going mowing down the legions of goose-stepping goons. It can over heat so there's additional strategy to using it so as to not get caught in the middle of a fight with an unusable gun. Even after I got way more powerful weapons, I used the Sten as much as possible and it was usually just fine for handlin' business. On the technical level, loading games was kind of lame. When you die, it takes you back to the last game you loaded or the autosave at the beginning of the level. Further, you can't just pull up the load screen and load the most recent save. The game has to be quit and then the save you want to play can be loaded. There were some minor technical glitches, but nothing reloading a save couldn't fix and the game ran very smooth otherwise. It took around 8 hours to finish. RtCW was a nostalgic trip back to the dated past and it was fun.

In my short time with X Rebirth, I can say that I am, so far, 100% happy with this game. I know that the game had a rough (awful) launch and the following months weren't even remotely good either, but I believe update 2.0 fixed most of the problems players were having. The campaign is still a bit buggy with trade ships flying around for 40 minutes, only to leave the area without finishing the run, but restarting the game fixes that. If you're looking for a story, don't expect one. Play through the campaign to learn how to play the game, then jump into Free Mode, where the galaxy is yours to do as you wish. This is the space sim I've been wanting since childhood. This game is phenomonal in nearly every aspect. I say nearly only because of the facial models and some voice acting. Yes, some stations are copy/pasted, but I can look past that unlike most of you. To me, it feels nice to be able to freely exit my ship and talk to other people and aliens, and accept jobs or trade. This game is truely  what a space sim should be. Let's go a bit further though.
You only get to fly one ship?
Yes, but that ship is uprgradeable/customizable in nearly every aspect, including the cockpit/HUD
I heard the FPS dips to sh**
I've yet to have that happen, even during massive, 100 ship battles. Upgrade your POS computer.
What can you do?
Whatever you want, really. Go to bars, strip clubs, buy weapons, food, ammo, trade to ships/stations, bounty hunt, work for police, explore, pirate, anything!
This review is not yet complete and I will be sure to update as I play the game more, but for now, yes I 100% recommend this game to anyone who loves space sims.

I honestly think this is the best of the Bioshocks, gameplay wise: the mechanics are basically lifted from the first (if it isn't broken...), with some minor but important tweaks: for example, gone is the annoying hacking minigame, weapons have more impact and the new Splicers rushes and Big Sisters add a whole layer of gameplay around the once simple binary choice save/harvest Little Sisters.
The true stars of the game, however, are the levels. Sprawling, full of unique places and details that extend in all three dimensions, they succeed in the first goal of good level design: giving the illusion of being real (fictional) places, instead of game levels.
I think that the perspective offered by time may lead us to think about this game with the fairness it deserves: its prequel (itself a great game but far from perfect) may be a considered by many a milestone in gaming as art, but Bioshock 2 is a great game on its own merits.

Return To Castle Wolfenstein is a first-person shooter reboot of the Wolfenstein series which much like its predecessor focuses on fast-paced gunplay with a number of improvements made to compensate for the new engine technologies available at the time.
Firstly, unlike Wolfenstein 3D, the developers actually tried to implement a compelling story to a franchise known for not actually having a “story”. To some degree, the story in this game, at least from a concept point of view, brings something new to the table by adding elements of occult. The plot revolves around the American soldier, B.J. Blazkowicz, trying to impede the Nazis from discovering and extracting a serum hidden in an ancient tomb capable of augmenting soldiers into “Dark Knights”, an evil undead army from the 9th Century. Nazis and occult? Absurd ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, but what’s not to like. However, while the concept does enhance the single-player campaign, the story itself is mostly ignorable since it generally feels like it is there to fill in the space. Blazkowicz, while a total badass, still remains one of the blandest protagonists in existence. He takes orders from his superiors like a puppet with no remorse or personal motives. Even when the Allies want to give him a medal for his efforts and persumably a well deserved break at the end, he is somewhere outside still kicking Nazi butt. Boy, he sure is souless; born with only one scope in life: to kill Nazis for eternity. Plus, it is silly how the Allies' solution to most problems is to send a "one-man army" to take down Nazi headquarters single-handedly without even breaking a sweat. But that is Wolfenstein after all; it purposely does not need to explain how Blazkowicz does it -- and hey, some ancient voodoo magic is involved, so anything is justifiable, right? Fortunately, the story did manage to create the cool villain by the name of Deathshead, who later becomes the franchise’s main antagonist.
The gunplay in here is hasty but satisfying, reminiscent of older games such as Quake, Doom and Unreal Tournament, and unquestionably the strongest point of the game. While it all boils down to sprinting and shooting enemies in quick manners, the game does offer some moments of straightforward stealth where you get to sneak behind enemy lines. Additionally, there is an adequate variety in enemies from the deadly female squads in tight leather uniforms (those butts though) to juggernauts like the Über-Soldats. Different weapons are at Blazkowicz’s disposal too, with the Tesla gun being the most fun one to use, even if the MP40 probably becomes the most practical throughout most of the game, thus making pistols pretty redundant. One problem with the weapons though is the fact you never seem to run out of ammo. Retrospectively now, the gunplay does feel very basic, but mostly thanks to its fast paced action killing waves of enemies does not get dull, surprisingly enough.
The level design has the mentality of most shooters back in the late '90s and early noughties based on maze-like corridors and paths, essentially allowing the player the freedom to pick whichever route to travel back and forth within the somewhat confined space. Exploration is also encouraged and rewarded by finding secret chambers filled with collectables, even if these give no gameplay advantages to the player. Graphically, at the time, the game looked great but as time went by its visuals sure look dated today. On the other hand, the same cannot be said to its soundtrack which even to this day remains memorable and rather ageless. When you can recognise a level/map by a specific track from the soundtrack, then you know the soundtrack left a good impression.
Boasting a strong single-player campaign, (wherther you take the story seriously or not), many probably remember the game for its multiplayer component which at the time was very popular and considered by many superior than the campaign, even as far as being regarded one of the best multiplayer components in a game ever. I cannnot argue with that, although it was not until the highly acclaimed free standalone Wolfenstein: Enemy Territory came out that the multiplayer component peaked in popularity. Featuring a class-based gameplay similar to Team Fortress, two teams (Allies and Axis) fight each other to complete objectives on various maps. Personally, I spent far too many hours in the multiplayer alone when I was younger because it was balanced and had a very enjoyable experience. Currently, the multiplayer from Return To Castle Wolfenstein seems dead. Rest in peace.
In conclusion, Return To Castle Wolfenstein still remains a classic in the eyes of many, including myself, who played it in its heydays online and/or offline, and a milestone on PC. But it definitely lost its relevance and appeal to the general public as years have passed due to more ambitious and realistic shooters showing up years later. More old-school than modern, it still is a solid shooter, nevertheless, which does not spoil the player with today’s regenerative health and cover-base mechanics and can still provide enough hours of fun mindlessly killing Nazis. Pick it up only for nostalgic purposes or if you are curious to see how fast-paced shooters were like more than a decade ago in case you never grew up with them.

This game is 99% combat-based and the combat is uninspired.  Every turn, you only get five choices as to what to do and those choices appear to be predetermined.  This leads to frustration because, for example, in a boss fight your "union" (group of up to 5 troops) may lose half of their health in one attack.  Logic dicates you better heal up so you can survive another attack.  Game doesn't give you the option because your health isn't low enough.  Then there's random number generator (RNG)♥♥♥♥♥♥where the AI does their most powerful attack (sometimes capable of taking out multiple unions in one attack) repeatedly.  Game over, man, game over.  Even if you're leveled well beyond the enemy you're fighting, you may have to retry the fight many times before the RNG decides in your favor handing you a victory.  Games like this should be about knowing thy enemy and stratgizing, not random rolls.  In order to progress in the game without getting♥♥♥♥♥♥♥all of the time, you have to grind, and grind, and grind some more.  I'm asking myself why?  I've got two other games I'd rather play right now and it's not like this game has convinced me the story is worth finishing.  It's disjointed and explains little.  I started feeling apathetic towards the plot about 30 hours ago.  The only reason why I care about the plot is because it is the only way to command more unions and get more troops to put in said unions.
I could go on a long time nitpicking about lots of things from the bland environments (pathetic for a 2008 game) to the repetitive music (I think there's only one combat song and that only changes if morale gets to the bottom) to the quick-time-events (you want to look at health guages, attacks coming up, etc. but if you do that, you'll miss the QTE which could easily translate to losing the battle) to the inability to change troop equipment (they ask to "borrow" equipment from your unequipped inventory).
I suppose there's some people out there that love this kind of game but I am not among them.
Edit: The above was written after 37 hours of playing the game.  Because I was long past tired of the combat, H4X0R Mode Engaged! (one hit kills on unions) and the game still took 65 total hours to finish.  I think this would be a pretty darn good game if it ended in ~40 hours but the combat...just...drags...on...forever...and ever...and ever...  it gets in the way of everything else that is otherwise passable.

First review in a while, but this game deserves it.
I'll start out with the somewhat common "my playtime is inaccurate" speech, having played more than 200 hours of this and it's previous incarnations through Impulse.
Sins of a Solar Empire: Rebellion is truly one of a kind. This version basically combines the entirety of the 2 previous titles, Trinity and regular ol' SoaSE, so Rebellion truly has it all and more.
As such, this review is kind of both a Rebellion review and SoaSE in general review, because I've never reviewed the original or Trinity as there is no real story to this game, which makes it a difficult game to even explain to the masses who enjoy story driven games.
I tend to play a Single Player skirmish with 2 or 3 Hard AI players, however in the past have spent a great deal of time playing lengthy LAN matches, which were loads of fun, but ultimately one of the only major flaws of SoaSE comes out through such lengthy matches, even just playing against AI.
That flaw has been given a bad wrap in more recent times because of the evolution and adoption of Multi Core processor technology.
Essentially this game does not utilise multicore CPU's and unfortunately there is no fix for this, even after extensive research and optimisation mod trialling. But to their credit, those mods are great for getting the game to run on lower spec systems, laptops, virtualisation/steaming etc, but no mod can add 64bit or multicore support. That's the game's engine limitation, and it's not the only one around... I'm looking at you Cities XL.
It is important to note that at regular playing speed, this takes tens of hours of a single match to even be a problem, but on lower spec, lower (and older) GHz systems, this happens within about an hour give or take 30mins of regular speed play time with a couple of AI players.
With all that said, one of THE greatest longevity features for me is the ability to speed up the game time by 2x, 4x and 8x increments, even in a LAN match (host must change it).
Because of the vast expanses of space and [travelling] time at regular speed, this speed up feature can actually make for a much more challenging game, albeit much faster. Generally you will have to sacrifice micro management for macro at those speeds, but on large scale maps with only 2 or 3 players, with multiple star systems, the ability to speed up hyperspace travel from a distant planet to another is a HUGE time saving and action creating element and there is no penalty or lock down on the control of the game speed that you have, apart from it's 4 presets, so interchanging between them can be as fluid as zooming in or out and the speed controls can be remapped as well as basically everything else.
When I first discovered this speed up feature in the original Sins, it was, at first, not something I was looking for or really cared about, largely because I was still learning the controls and the game at the time.
When I was finally bored with the amount of time it took to setup, capture, defend, build and deploy, it would be too long for a single game session, and that bothered and still bothers me.
Command & Conquer (up until and including 3) had the right recipe for possible lengths of a single player skirmish battle. With Sins this isn't possible at regular speed, that is if you're interested in actually establishing a large empire of any sort instead of rushing with a dozen weak ships, which gets stale fast.
The camera controls in Sins are very fluid and quite unique, and once you get the hang of it, there really is nothing like it, some things are similar but the ability to orbit and zoom freely around any axis while fixed on a certain point is impressive, and the instant ability to track any of your fleet and zoom right in to the ship and it's details or zoom right out to galaxy level all in real time and fluid as your mouse can move. An RTS camera/movement system that IMO rivals that of what Blizzard, Westwood or EA have ever done is definitely worth a mention in this review.
The 3 original factions, the TEC, Advent and Vasari have been Loyalist-ised and given their Rebel counterparts in this final Sins title and have created many new ways of playing the game. I found that this is by far the most balanced of the 3 in the series mainly because of the 3 extra sub-faction additions, which also open up Role-Playing type elements of having say, 3 Rebel factions vs 3 Loyalist factions in a desperate struggle to take control over a strange galaxy.
The in-game Map Designer is also worth a mention, although it takes a fair bit of trial and error to get something you're happy with, and even then playing your own creations can sometimes backfire or surprise you in ways you never thought possible.
The only downside is the lack of manipulation you have on Planets and Stars. The "Map Designer" is basically a Map Generator.
If you've ever wanted to take on several hundred space pirate homeworlds in the one solar system then Sins is for you!
But in all seriousness, the Map Designer does a pretty good job once you learn how it works and ways you can create interesting maps just by changing sliders and numbers.
If you're really serious about designing your own Solar System or Galaxy then Ironclad have supplied everyone with their GalaxyForge editor which is used to create the many included Single and Multiplayer premade maps.
My Pros & Cons shortlist;
Pros:
+ One of a kind space-based RTS gameplay
+ Useful and informative dialogue boxes, hovering over icons has been given great attention to detail.
+ Massive tech tree
+ Awesome scale of real time space battles and large scale empire building.
+ Fine control over placement of your buildings, or for riskier, faster matches, an "Auto place" feature for Buildings which is also a +
+ Interesting and unique items, ships, power-ups, upgrades
+ The graphics scale really well across many many different types of systems, but the close up details can be a bit disappointing even at Ultra settings.
+ Inclusion of both a Map Designer & GalaxyForge editor.
Cons:
- Fairly steep learning curve and long match times
- Units (mainly Capital Ships) of the same type have to be upgraded individually, on a small scale this is less important then on a larger one.
- No minimap
- Left Planet, Structure and Unit tree can't be hidden. Capturing more than 10-20 planets adds much more time navigating and cuts any efficiency of the tree at all.
- Some tasks would be better left automated, such as the 2 scout ships that you start with should have their exploration ability Autocast set to on, not off. Also Metal and Crystal mines could be auto-built after you have captured a planet and have the resources to spare
- At regular speed it takes far too long to reach higher tech levels in a single match
- Can be boring in stages of early travel or exploration. Once you've seen the same variations of desert, ice, volcanic, terran and asteroids over and over, the excitement wears down over time (tens to hundreds of hours for me)
- Not just a con of Sins, but most RTS games really need the ability to 'mute' a certain Unit or Building you are queuing up and and creating 50 or 100+ of the same Units and the game wants to announce the successful creation of every single one.

Ok so there are a lot of high ranking negative reviews for this game, and there are also a lot of positive reviews for this game, so I'm going to do my best to explain why I do recommend this game, just maybe not for everyone.
NOT A HERO is a Devolver Digital game, and it fits the Devolver mold perfectly. It's hard, fast paced, has a ♥♥♥♥♥in' soundtrack, and is snarky as all hell. The gameplay consists of 2D sidescrolling combat and light platforming. The combat mostly centers around timing your movement in and out of "cover" (we'll get to that later) to shoot at enemies or rushing up and getting the drop on them before they can shoot first. The game features about a dozen characters which can be unlocked by completing additional challenges in missions to improve your overall "approval rating". The game is sort of reminiscent of Hotline Miami, placing you in the shoes of a random character employed by a larger organization to murder people that may or may not deserve it. All characters are voiced and their dialogue is appealing to listen to.
The gameplay is the biggest issue for most people here, myself included. Combat can be difficult with the "cover system" just being you leaning against a 2D wall, the only indication of this is a slight shadow coming over your very tiny character. Not only is this hard to see in combat, it's unreliable as hell, meaning you often have to run rather than fight and risk dying from the unreliable mechanic. Additonally, if you die at any point in a level, you have to restart. Unlike Hotline Miami, this game has no in-level check points, so it's back to the beginning of the level, no matter how long the level is. This is frustrating as♥♥♥♥♥♥at times, and can cause a certain level of fatigue from the gameplay. That said, the game is still fun. Alternate ammo types and bombs can give you an edge, and on those runs where you're just gunning it and killing everything, it feels awesome. I'd recommend this game at full price. The content is there, it's just difficult to get to. But that's nothing new from Devolver. Enjoy the music, enjoy the pixel citiscapes, enjoy the characters, and have a good laugh at Bunnylord's antics. 7/10

Story and Concept: 4/5
Gameplay and Game Mechanics: 3/5
UI Design and Controls: 2/5
Art, Music, Ambience: 5/5
Overall Rating: 3.5/5
Review Summary: This War of Mine is a fresh, compelling take on the day/night cycling survival genre and is recommended as a must-play for serious survival fans. The story concept and art design are thoughtful, elegant, and beautifully immersive.
But while the economy and crafting aspects of gameplay are well-executed, other parts of the gameplay need serious refinement and fleshing-out; and the entirely point-and-click user interface, while simple and easy-to-use, comes off as clunky, ham-handed, and inflexible. It's an extroardinary concept and story and is a solid gaming experience as-is, but This War of Mine could benefit from a serious reimagining and overhaul at the nuts-and-bolts level, particularly with respect to the user interface and some of the more mechanical aspects of gameplay.
--- --- ---
Major Kudos:
- The game's economy of scarcity is expertly designed and balanced. It feels "real," which is no small feat.
- The crafting system is balanced -- adequate to the task without being too junky or circuitous.
- AI and general mechanics in scavenging mode are fairly realistic and transparent, especially the stealth system.
- Randomization of certain elements and the patterns of moral choice available make the game strongly replayable.
- The game's story is unique and emotionally compelling; even where the characters are two-dimensional, they get the job done.
- Art and sound design and execution are excellently suited to the story, concept, and gameplay style.
Serious WTFs:
- The flow of in-game time is so incongruous as to interfere with suspension of disbelief. For example, it takes only an hour or so to build a radio from spare parts, but several hours to clear a pile of refuse by hand, and it can take about 20 minutes just to walk from one side of the house to the other. This could be remedied by doing away with the real-time clock (hours and minutes) altogether, which, while probably intended to foster a sense of realism, actually has quite the opposite effect in practice. In terms of sheer pace, the pseduo-real time flow seems just right for the night scavening portion, but rather too fast for the daytime crafting portion.
- The point-and-click-only interface is not ergonomically uncomfortable, but it is clunky and awkward at times. The game could benefit tremendously from some simple assignable keyboard shortcuts, particularly in the daytime portion, where the ability to cycle through characters with a keystroke and to send them to various tasks with a keystroke would be extraordinarily useful.
- Certain crafting-related and home improvement activities should be assignable and automatable among characters the player is not controlling at a given time.
- Replayability could be enhanced by tiered difficulty levels.
- While I don't mind it so much, some people will have an issue with the inability to start a new game without overwriting the old one, a new and slightly annoying design trend in games.

The simple Yes/No answer is not really enough when it comes to this type of game review. If there was a "maybe" button, I would choose that for this game. It is not a bad game, but it lacks the same depth and playability as Civ V. It's got some great ideas and fun concepts, but there are too many parts that either don't make sense, or just fail entirely. The upgrading of units is a good concept in its self, however it is also quite restrictive. In early to mid-game you have a very small selection of unit types that are quite weak and by end game a wider range of powerful units become available. By this point however, unless you deactivate the victory conditions, you are not left with a huge amount of time to use them. There is also the big problem of Affinity specific resource. You choose your affinity quite early in the game, however you may find by mid-game you do not have enough of the affinity specific resource and so you cannot build the new units you have spent so long waiting for.
There is also the issue of the tech tree, which is just not user friendly. You really must take time to plan out your discoveries at the start of the game, otherwise you could find yourself missing vital technologies. Also, due to the affinity upgrade system, you end up targeting the affinity technologies to get the better units, and so fall behind in other basic areas.
The intrigue system was quite an exciting concept with some great sounding abilities at the higher levels, however you rarely get to use them (if ever). You can place one agent per city and give them missions that will raise the intrigue level in a city if they succeed (level 0 to 5). The problem is that it takes far too long to raise the level and relies on multiple races targeting the same city. This means you tend to end up only using the level 0 through 2 skills, which are just a bit dull.
In all I was disappointed by this instalment of Civ. I love Civ 5 and just feel they have missed the target with this update - a real shame as Alpha Centuri was a great game. I recommend you save your money, and get Civ 5 instead.

I have not played Blood Money so I cannot compare Absolution to it. I can however give you a review about the game I played.
Absolution features a storyline behind 47's indoctrine into the world of Hitmen. The story starts out with his previous handler gone "rogue" for reasons unknown. 47 ends up shooting her point blank but makes a promise to her that he will keep this girl that she's been trying so hard to protect, safe.
The game play is well rounded in Aboslution, from close combat to ranged. There is a feature where you can mark multiple targets (much like Conviction) and execute them by pressing X (on a 360 controller). 47 is able to take cover by pressing B, and can lean out pressing the L trigger and fire to enemies. Exposure though can cost quite a bit of damage. The main feature I'm assuming in the Hitman series is the ability to disguise the main character as other NPC's from the game.  From a police officer, to janitor, to electrician, to thugs. Just like any stealth game, hiding the bodies becomes key. The player doesn't lift them up, but drags them to the destination. When around dumpsters and closets that exist for the player to dump two bodies into, the player presses Y to enter a scenamatic where 47 hides the body. The fighting in the game is nice as quick time events pop up to counter or combo against foes. When the player presses RB, in game there is a focus meter that high lights surrounding areas of the environment. It will show foes, points of interests, key cards, or even hidden pathways. This button also allows you to sneak by certain groups. In one level you may need it to sneak past thugs while wearing a thug outfit, in another you may need a staff outfit.
Visuals are nice and graphics are up to date. Everything is running smooth and have had no hiccups thus far. Sounds are appropriate and listening to conversations throughout the game, the player can hear some funny stories. I like the way the game sets up and let's the player roam free in an area. Chinatown is a famous example of this where chaos can be created instantly, or, where it can happen quitely or from afar. This part of the game they absolutely nailed.
I would have loved to see a local co-op or even a multiplayer feature, as I may not see replayability here for myself in the future. Hardcore Hitman fans may come back to this and seek a harder difficulty. I did enjoy playing through it none the less as the game play experience was nominal. Reading previous reviews, some reviewers have complained about not having a map. Not playing previous versions of the game I didn't really notice the absense of having a lay out, but it could have been nice to have one. Maybe for future cases keep it, and when you explore certain areas, point of interests become marked out to come back to and use?
Saving scheme may sit well with some, badly with others. The game saves between chapters or new stages, and "checkpoints" are available throughout the level. These checkpoints can not be reloaded once the game is closed, and can only be used currently if you die or want to restart.
Although the game is good, I still feel like they could have done better with what they were given. A lot was done, but something a bit more could have been added to make the game play experience better. The options of how to execute were great, but the process of doing them can be worked on. I also found it kind of weird 47 couldn't hop over a few boxes to get to the other side.

Upon completing Saints Row IV, I said goodbye to my old, violent, purple friends, thinking it the grand finale. I am glad to say I was wrong, because Gat out of Hell is one... well, hell of a postscript. The boss of the Saints (who looks like whatever you made them look like in Saints Row IV) has been kidnapped by the devil himself, and Johnny Gat, the most dangerous man in the world and the last surviving founder of the Saints, must rescue them. You can also play as team genius Kinzie Kensington, since its her birthday. In some ways, it is the most barebones title in the series- not only are there no customization options, there aren't even any story missions save the finale- the gameplay is made up entirely of the series' staple activities, like fraud and survival, with a few new ones, such as an aerial twist on the blazing activity. Speaking of air, Gat out of Hell takes your mobility to the final frontier, adding full-on flight to your already overpowered repetoire of super powers. Your offensive abilities return with elements, such a stomp that vacuums in enemies and pickups and an aura that forces the demons of hell to bow before your Saintly presence. There's also a whole new set of super-guns (and a sword) that correspond to the seven deadly sins, each with nasty side-effects for your enemies. Gat out of Hell is the best elements of Saints Row distilled into a pure form: the mayhem, the power, the guns, the unparalleled sense of catharsis. Not even the legions of hell can stand in the way of your fun. However, it is also the shortest title in the series, though it is priced accordingly. If you've been on a ridealong with the Saints from the very beginning, like me, Gat out of Hell offers some much appriciated continuity nodding, which is remarkably one of the series' strongest points. Much as in IV, you will run into a number of old familiar faces, beginning with none other then Saints Row 2's main villain, Dane Vogel. There's plenty of collectibles and audio logs to find if you'd like to cover every square inch of the city of the damned.  The Saints conquered a street, then a city, a nation, an intellerstellar empire and now hell itself, and STILL there seems to be more for the Saints to do. I hope to don the purple once again sometime in the future. If you have enjoyed ANY of the Saints Row games or crave a sandbox experience that makes you the center of all the fun, Gat out of Hell is a game for you.

Then you are given three tools, 1: A laser cutter that can cut thru anything you encounter, 2: A sticky rocket engine launcher to move everything you encounter, and finally 3: A grappling hook to pull everything you encounter.
"Tiny and Big: Grandpa's Leftovers" is a puzzle game that encourages fast thinking, playfulness and thinking outside the box. For example you can end one of the first boss first faces of in under a minute, by cutting away the ground under the boss to make him fall "to his death", instead of fighting him for around 20 minutes.

Gat out of Hell is essentially a Hell-themed skin of Saint's Row IV. In my opinion it is the worst game in the series. Here's why: They've taken out just about everything I think Saint's Row games are about and didn't put anything worthwile in to make up for that.
There is almost zero customization available, the only thing you can change is your wings color - and that's only if you bought a DLC for that. To me that is ripping the heart out of this particular series, because for most of the franchise you could tailor almost anything to your liking - your gang style, your homies, your character, your cribs, your vehicles, later games even your weapons.
Missions are extremely unimaginative outside of main storyline missions of which there are very little as the game is incredibly short.
You can't even "legally cheat" anymore because you don't have a gang anymore. I'm referring to the "phone menu" through which you could in previous games order a vehicle delivery or zombie uprisings, that is also gone. While the lack of the phone/spawn menu is not as essential part of the game as the customization, the lack of a gang really is a downer and has removed a very essential part of the series. Alright they barely existed in SR: IV either but they were still somewhat there and recruitable.
On an even more personal taste level Gat out of Hell isn't even as funny or entertaining to me as the previous installments, I admit that is perhaps partially because I wasn't a huge fan of either of the protagonists in the game - while I didn't hate those characters, they were not my favourites. Well, not even in the top 7.
Overall if you have any similar preferences to mine, I wouldn't recommend this game at its full price - if you can get it in a sale, by all means, go for it. Like I said it IS essentially a reskinned Saints Row IV, just with a much much shorter storyline and without most of what makes Saints Row, Saints Row, to me at least.

If you put a World War 2 shooter in front of me, I'd usually look up at you and say "Excuse me, this isn't what I ordered! Take it back and try again!". My dislike of them is quite high. So when everyone started singing the praises of Wolfenstein: The New Order, I thought "Looks like I better have a go with at least one of them" and gave Return to Castle Wolfenstein a shot. Turns out I quite liked it.
You probably already know about Return to Castle Wolfenstein. A First-Person Shooter set in an alternate reality where the Nazis usually have access to technology they normally wouldn't do. In this case, it's occult magic! As B.J. Blazkowicz, it is your job to find out what the Nazis are up to, kill them all through fairly linear levels and not say a single word to anyone. Bullets are all the talking this fella needs.
B.J. Blazkowicz will be sent to some very different locations over the course of seven chapters, slowly understanding what Heinrich Himmler and the "SS Paranormal Division" are up to. The locations are nicely constructed and have some nice variation to them.
I have to say, I wasn't expecting as much stealth as there was which was a pleasent surprise. I'd definitely call this a FPS Stealth game. Unfortunately, the game does have a habit of forcing this in some parts of missions. You get seen, its "MISSION FAILED" and back to the beginning for you. That's how real life works right?
These sections tend to be brief though and, outside of these constraints, the overall stealth works really well. You can be rewarded with eavesdropping over funny little conversations the Nazis have if you manage to stealth around. If you screw up majorly with stealthing, not every enemy in the map is alerted about it (unless an alarm goes off). This gaves the player the chance to recover from mistakes and keeps the game interesting.
There are plenty of secrets are to be found around the levels, usually containing Nazi Gold. One thing I really liked about this game is, before you're just about to finish a level, the game will tell you how many secrets and Nazi gold you found, giving you the opportunity to turn around and go back and find it! A feature that needs to be in more games with this sort of stuff inside it. Don't let me finish the level and THEN tell me what I missed, making me reload an earlier save if I have one at all if I want to go find all the goodies.
The secrets aren't too hard to find and don't add anything to the overall outcome of the game, just fun little rewards for exploration.

Battlerite is a very unique and elegantly designed game. There's nothing really out there like it (besides its predecessor, Bloodline Champions). The gameplay is extremely skill based and fast paced, the games are ridiculously short (roughly 5 minutes), and there's a large variety or heroes with different playstyles - which are all huge positives to me. I wasn't a fan of the 3v3 mode personally, but the 2v2 gamemode presented some of the most challenging and intense fights I have ever had in gaming. This game can be hard for new players because of the high skill ceiling, but the overall base design of the game is very simple, making it not a hard game to learn. I'm a huge fan of this art style and the music is nice. I think the biggest problem that some players have with the game is that it feels a little bit shallow at times. There's much more "meatier" (is that a word?) games out there which provide much more heroes, gameplay elements and strategy, but I still think Battlerite is in a really nice spot for many players.

Return to Castle Wolfenstein is a  pretty solid game with some minor issues. Level design is pretty good in this game. It's definitly not a corridor shooter like most modern games. However I felt that a lot of secret rooms should of included health and armor instead of just treasure. Health, armor, and weapons are the reason I look for secret rooms so as to help me progress further into the game not collectables.
The quicksave system is slightly annoying. Whenever I would quicksave and then die shortly afterwards the game would not load the last quicksave but instead whatever was last loaded. So you would die, then the game would load an older save, then you have to  reload the new save. It gets quite irksome after a while and the only way around it is to immediatily quickload after qucksaving.
I felt the gunplay was ok given when this game came out. I do feel that the AI in this game has unreasonable accuracy though. Their were numerous occasions where I was about to snipe someone who doesn't even see me and they would spot me at the last second and immediatly shoot and hit me sometimes before the character model even turned around fully.
I didn't really care about the story that much but I don't think anyone really cares about that.
Overall I would say Return to Castle Wolfenstein is a decent FPS that is really starting to show it's age. It's still by all means playable though and I would recommend it to anyone who wants an FPS that isn't a corridor shooter.

tl;dr: This game is mostly RNG based despite what it tells you, so if you're fine with relying on luck, then you might enjoy it.
If you like to win through clever tactical decisions or being overleveled and steamrolling enemies; this game has nothing to offer you.
I got this game wanting a chill tactical JRPG where I could grind, explore and craft. After about 50 hours in I feel it delivered on the side quest, exploration and crafting side---
HOWEVER:
The combat is insanely RNG heavy.
You don't have control over possitioning of your party and the game punishes you for bad positioning, you also don't have direct control over what attacks/moves your characters perform. Different moves have different modifiers that are strong against different types of monsters but you don't actually get to choose to use these moves, you just have to hope you get them.  There is also a chance you get a roll in combat where your mages only get to choose between Physical attacks and fighters only get to use Magic attacks. The combat can also otherwise completely screw you over when you get a bad roll out eg: you can end up in situations where you need to/want to heal but the game just doesn't let you because you get bad RNG (this has cost my alot of fights). Even if you get the heal option you only really get one of two options: "heal yourself" or "heal someone else" you don't get to choose who that someone else is so you'll just have to cross your fingers and hope.
There is a moral system that supposedly rewards you for making good tactical decisions, increasing your damage and defense when you keep moral high. However most of these "decisions" are actually based on RNG and completely outside your control, and several mobs are immune to it anyway making the combat in general favoured towards enemies, especially vs bosses and Rare Enemies.
There are no random encounters, so that's good, but there's a system where if an enemy sneaks up on you they get a combat advantage, however there is no way for you to get an early combat advantage over you enemy via something like a pre-emtive strike.
If you're the kind of person who likes to spend a lot of time getting good gear for your entire team, this game doesn't allow you to do that either as you only have control of the gear on the main character, while everyone else has their own gear that can only be improved with (say it with me) RNG, as they may ask to have some of the gear you're not using if it's better than what they have. The other way to improve you're allies gear is to gather monster loot where your crew MAY ask to have some of it to improve their gear.
Lastly all the enemies in the game scale with your "levels" so grinding isn't all that useful, pretty much taking all the point out of leveling. Further more you can't watch how much XP you gain to see how much more you need to get new moves or what you need for your stats to increase, which is just another annoyance in my already page long complaint.

Its unfortunate as the game has so much potential, but in reality is nothing but one big grind.
It basicly goes like this, you do a story mission, then you have to grind for hours doing repetitive missions to gain new gear after which you can do another story mission and have to grind for hours again.
When you finaly get the baddest ship in the system the story progresses to the next system and it all starts over again.
The praised music is nice, but it does get repetitve too when you play for a few hours, its like a cd on repeat all the time.
It also bothers me that this game is clearly made to be played with a controller and not with mouse/keyboard.
Aiming is done with the mouse on a 2d plane, but in all modes but broadside the crosshair snaps on targets so there is very little manual aiming to be done.
You simply select a target and click the mouse to fire the weapons group.
Seeing the crosshairs snap your constantly moving you mouse to try and get it to snap on the target you want it.
On a controller this isnt a problem as you just move the analog stick, but a mouse doesnt move infinite.
Ironicly you cant aim up as everything happens in a 2d plane, but small strike craft do fly over you.
Its also not possible to assign weapon groups, the groups are assigned automaticly by the type of weapon used.
They are ordenance, projectile and beams, its not possible to manualy fire a mixed selection, you can only control one at a time with the number keys, they others are ai controlled.
The game does have allot of good pointers though, the graphics are awesome, the mood is good, its casual and laid back.
AI turret control can be set to your preferences, like shooting only selected or target only small craft.
There is a large selection of ships and weapons to be had, which gives allot of variation in tactics.
The ships are clearly a progression over eachother though, they dont give you room to select multiple ships of a same strength, the next ship in line is always more expensive, and somewhat better than the last, yet requiring a different tactic.
Pro's:
Great graphics
Good mood
Very casual
Great controller support
Somewhat intrigueing story
Cons:
Allot of grinding required
Repetitive missions
Poor mous/keyboard support, fixed mouse ballistic
Weapon groups are fixed, no buttons to fire other weapons than the ones selected
Looking back, i may not have bought this.

Fairness be damned, I will compare this to Sid Meyer's Alpha Centauri now and explain why the old, ugly, horribly controlled game is actually better than this entry in Sid Meyer's library.
First things first: I have only recently bought and played SMAC. I have no nostalgic memories off it and I hold it to today's standarts.
Let me start with the gameplay:
Beyond Earth is basically Civ 5 with a few slight differences. The Quest system is nice and cute and instead of barbarians, you have a few different types of alien. Now, you can treat them as such or you can actually just ignore them and they may even come to think of you as allies. (Though that does contradict the Tascendence ending and the whole "Living Planet".)
Overall, the gameplay works. But I can't give it too much credit, since it is basically the Civ5 formula with a different paintjob.
Now, let me go into SMAC: The gameplay is terrible by comparison. The controlls are a nightmare, the unit-making was overly complex and god, you have no idea how much you miss your mouse wheel after a while. Overall, BE is better in this regard because it is more streamlined and much better to control.
And now we come to the crux: Where and why Alpha Centauri was bettter
simply said: AC had everything it needed to make you feel as if you just set foot on a truly alien biosphere. The way that the mind-worms, the fungus and the other critters interacted was a perfect blend. You had conversations with the slowly awakening planet, you learned of their fears of you, how you could soothe or anger them and... well... finally enslave or join.
BE doesn't have a single moment like this. I was honestly surprised that there even WAS an transcendence ending in this game. What also shocked me was the complete lack of flavour text and cinematics in BE. SMAC had a nice little video for every wonder and flavour text for all the technologies. BE has one line at most. Even the victory is a still image.
Now... that does really repulse me in this case. Finding out about the nature of Alpha Centauri was a big draw of the game. And BE completely jettisons the idea.
Another big negative for BE is the complete lack of a "morality" and pollution system.
You see. In SMAC, you could build improvements and buildings that put a harsh environmental strain on the planet and the planet would, since it was intelligent, respond by improved fungus, mindworm and loctus activity.
That was very tense, since you had to either put a lot of funds into the military to keep the constant assault away OR you had to harmonize with the planet.
BE... well... BE tells you that you are doing either thing. Depending on your research choices, you get points for an allignment which represents how you treat the planet. But sadly, that never played into gameplay. I was completely into Harmony and yet there was no punishment for killing off wildlife or building manufactories. The BE plantes seem rather chilled when you build thermal boreholes, but Alpha Centauri would smack you over the head for a single one.
And this is the thing: it is this complete lack of flavour that ruins the game for me. In SMAC, every faction had a unique way of speaking to you, a personality if it came to their goals and code fo conduct and a leader that was memorable at the first sight.
The BE corporations are just kinda... there. Not much memorable about them. No banter between the leadrs and no horrible torture-ending, when you take their leader prisoner. Heck, I hardly noticed that one of them got wiped out during a game.
Final verdict: Don't spend your money of BE. Its lazy and has lower production values than an age-old game by the same company.

A streamlined jRPG that emphasizes plot and stylish combat over the tedium of towns and most of the micro-management. About the only thing left on the latter front is the weapons upgrading, which you can take if you're into it, use a guide to get it out of the way or, so I hear, ignore entirely.
Speaking of plot, it can be a little convoluted and certainly is a lot to take in at first but not to worry, everything will be explained eventually. Often slated for very linear game progression, this game design decision at the very least does its best to help you follow the story instead of having you search for it. Still, there's secrets and the occasional time and place for grinding and side quests if you so choose.
The semi-automatic battle system, aside from being where it's at, takes a little while to get used to. Instead of might-as-well-be-action-game real-time gameplay and the contemplatetiveness of a full-on turn based system, you get an interesting mix of both. First you take your time and plan ahead before battle setting up team formations and then during one, you're fully engaged managing them letting your team play out their assigned roles while reserving the right to more direct control of your party leader.
Audiovisually, the game's got that Squeenix Seal of Quality stamped on it, although some locale and feral creature designs are a bit too gaudy for my liking. Voice acting, for the most part, is alright. Same goes for the characters portrayed but fortunately you can bench the ones you like the least later in the game. Still I wish the entire entourage was visible while travelling, not just the selected battle team.
Technically the game has a some performance issues which can be mostly dealt with guides. With that done, the game plays beautifully with a controller and streams flawlessy to your TV over the Steam Link.

the hitman games is  traditionally not strong for  its story, simply because it evolves around killing a target hence building any scripted events or characters is nearly impossible. the closest we got to a story is in blood money and even by gaming standards its a lacking affair.
the developers saw the need to change this, unfortunately in doing so they had to alter the gameplay and turn it into a hybrid of sorts a mix of the old hitman and other stealth games like splinter cell or MGS.
for the purists or lovers of the old hitman, it would be a disappointment, some levels you only sneak. while others  you  "fail" your mission to allow for a cut scene. it robs the experience somewhat, after a long level where you painstakingly get everything perfect but cant kill the target.
gone too are the large levels where you can plan your way to your kill, the game now is more linear. the first level itself you have only one single entry to the area, which unfortunately is repeated in later missions, room to room, single entry and exit.
the silent assissin rank many loved is changed, the game now has a point system of which the guy with the most points get SA. hence you can kill people and yet given enough points still get that rank.
there are also a few fustrating bugs, once i killed a guard and took his clothes. while hiding it, the guards model appeared behind me naked and floating in the air. then my cover is blown. apparently the game didnt realise i killed the guard.
for an action game with a twist, hitman does tick a number of the boxes. you have a variations of levels both linear or not. but for a purist who wants the same as blood money, it will disappoint and while its rather well polished it doesnt give the same experience as before.

bugs, bugs, bugs, bugs, bugs, bugs and oh...did I mention bugs?  I had a lot of excitement for X Rebirth.  The idea that I could walk on stations, and on the bridge of my own ship, was very enticing.  Unfortunately, the reality was a far cry different than any other "X" game out there.  While you CAN walk around on stations, and inside of your own ship, a lot of the interactions were buggy and time consuming.  Even worse, you are pretty much STUCK on your ship that you begin the game with.  While you can buy additional ships, and hire people to crew them, you cannot pilot them yourself, which is probably one of the main things that ruined the overall experience that has traditionally been a part of "X" games for years.
Also, the control scheme has, if it is even possible, become even more convoluted.  While some things were improved upon, such as the ability to order your traders to buy or sell (A nice little menu, once you get used to it), the overall way you interact with stations has been dumbed down to become "XBox Controller friendly".  I understand WHY they did this, but it didn't quite work.  It just didn't FEEL right.
The voice acting is horrible.  In a game like this, it usually isn't that important, but where EVERYTHING is voice acted, I quickly found myself wishing I could turn off the voiceovers - especially where my so-called co-pilot is concerned.  It went from charming to annoying very quickly.
Over the last year, they've done a lot to patch the game, which is commendable.  The game was simply not playable when it first came out.  In fact, I suspect the game should have been considered early access, not retail release.  It made me wonder if they have a QA department at ALL.  If they did, they should fire their whole department, because they obviously did not do their jobs.  In my opinion, the game could not be considered "retail" until the last couple of patches.
In summation, if you are a fan of the "X" games, I would suggest that you may wish to stay with Albion Prelude and hope that either egosoft scraps this new direction and returns to its roots, or looks at some of the emerging (and perhaps more promising) development efforts under way at various studios, such as Limit Theory.

The follower ships that you're supposed to hire and order around?  Wothless interface for orders, and they mostly just bug out and sit there. I would give Bioshock 2 a 5/10, as it was worse than the original in every way.
Bioshock 2 is a first person shooter with RPG elements, similar to the first game in the series. If you have not played the first game, don't read this review and play the original, as it will be a much more enjoyable experience and set you up for this one in case you wish to play them all. If you have played the original, then know that I thought this game inferior in nearly every way, though not terrible.
Bioshock 2 does add some new enemies, as well as plasmids, to the gameplay, giving a new feel to some of the battles. The loot is still found a plenty, the enemies are still tough, and there are some sequences in the game that you will find yourself really enjoying, just like the first game.
But some of the other aspects that Bioshock did so well, such as interesting villains, moral choices, a sense of new-ness and intrigue, and excellent story progression, this game misses the mark on. I thought the story was lame and that the characters were uninteresting, leaving the only real strenghts as the new additions during fights.
Especially near the end, I found myself becoming bored. I no longer looked forwards to the fights, and I dreaded any plot twists because it meant that the game was going to continue. I simply wanted to finish the game to make sure that I didn't miss anything, instead of the enjoy the experience.
This game wound up being more of a chore to get through by the end than one to enjoy. It does bring some new enemies and plasmids to the game which adds some variety, as well as a couple of new perspectives during some of the levels. Despite that, it just winds up being boring, via both gameplay and story, as i found myself not really caring by the end and just being frustrated. If you are dying to see more of Rapture, or are a big fan of the Bioshock series, you may enjoy it, but just be warned that it is inferior to the first and third installments.

I originally played this on the PS3. I'm not quite as fond of this one as I was of the first Bioshock, but that's kind of along the same lines as saying I don't like peanut butter as much as jelly. They're both solid games, and I would go so far as to say that the plot of Bioshock 2 is better than the plot of the original.
What ended up letting me down in this one is that the environment isn't as nice. It's still interesting, I still wanted to explore it, but it felt so dead that I had troulbe really wanting to spend too much time in it. It wasn't until the last quarter of the game or so that it finally sunk it's hooks into me. The set gets pretty interesting around that point.
Like I said, I think the plot of this one is better than the original. Sure the twist isn't as nice, but this story has more heart to it. It's just a shame that the gameplay and environment aren't as good. It explores the relationships that were some of the most interesting in the first game. The relationship between a big daddy and his little sister. The nice trick for this one is that the story is much more about liberation from social norms. I don't want to give too much away, so I'll just say that it mostly goes around how the big daddy character gets used for most of the game.
If you liked the first one this should be right up your alley. If you're looking for something on the level of Bioshock Infinite you will probably be sorely disappointed. This game is pretty good, and it fits nicely with the original Bioshock.

Intial thoughts and ramblings from a browncoat...
Well played, sir, well played...  While brief, the intro has all the feel of a Firefly episode.  It gets straight to the point in a no frills sort of way.  Definitely hits the nostalgia right between the eyes.  The music genre and selection is a nice touch.  I am enjoying the story line so far.  The credit grind outside the story line can get a little tedious after a while, but if pays to have a 500k credit nest egg when you leave the first sector.  These aren't your Han Solo type of characters that you are working with in the storyline...  More like the type that Jabba feeds to the sarlaac.  Even the good guys are more of a shade of grey.  Outside of you (depending on your game play,) I have yet to encounter one white knight in the story.
The chat option selected does not appear to have any bearing on the storyline.  You still go to all the same story line misisons.  (Even the AAA titles have yet to get this figured out, so I am not going to knock this game for it.)
The controls are a bit different than what I am used to, but seem easy enough to adapt to.  Can't tell you how many times I have absent mindedly fired missiles when I was first starting out.  The militia don't like it when you do that.
For those new to the game like I am, I suggest immediately running off the beaten path and trade between the stations.  Mining isn't all that practical, but the Mk2 Mining laser makes a great anti fighter platform.  You will need the credits for much needed upgrades.  Only buy stuff with red list prices and sell in places where the price turns green.  Taking missions off of the terminal always has a welcoming party near or at the end point waiting to kill you.  You can hire one wingman to bump up your overall firepower.  Freelancer players will take to this game very quickly.
This game rewards caution.  If you charge blindly into a situation you will get smoked.  Sure you can configure your ship to knife fight, but a handful of ships will still mug you if you are not careful.  I found upgrading your engines, booster, shields, armor, and weapons in that order was the best option at increasing your survival rate.
Friendly fire isn't.  The AI ships will go after each other.  If you get between them both sides will shoot you.  If you find yourself looking at a militia destroyer parking itself between you and a pirate, stop firing at the pirate.  You will only end up shooting the militia destroyer, lose massive rep with the militia, and all the militia in the area will start shooting at you.  Your starting corvette is barely able to fight its way out of wet paper sack at the beginning of the game.
Rep plays a part in this game.  Outside the obvious rep for merchants, criminals, and militia, it is hard to tell how rep really plays out in this game.  Join a guild if you want to get your hands on unique ship hulls.  Getting the criminal factions to like you is harder than you think.  Missions from the stations are the easiest to gain rep, but even that is difficult if you are trying to avoid♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥everyone off.  (Yea, you got the criminals to like you.  Now the militia hates your guts...  and they have the strongest ships and in greater numbers in the starting sector.)
Right out of the gate, I see a a couple of obvious areas needing improvement.
1: The multi-function of the 'E' key can be a bit annoying at times.  You are trying to tractor an item and accidently engage the warp drive because you were out of tractor range.  Docking with stations can run into this problem as well.
2: The lack of full 360 degree flight seems a bit odd in this day and age of fully capable space sims.  Those with the expectation of free flight along all axis will by put off by this.  It would be nice if they open up the y axis.  Your enemies and asteroids get to use the y axis, but you don't.  The station placement can cause problems when you leave the area.  Found myself autodocking when I just wanted to leave to the next station.  Probably my biggest gripe of the game so far.
3: If you aren't aware of the tutorial help section, the pop up hints and help tend to come up in a manner of oh now you tell me.
I will add to this as I rack up more playing time.  At any rate, it is a fun game for less than $20.

Short:  Highly recommended, buy it instantly.
Long:  There are many reasons to buy Hatred.
1st - You should always support developers that pushes boundaries of censorship.  Before we know it, we'll be living in a world full of it.
As you know, the game is very similar to Postal 1.  Postal 1 was made in 1997, same year as Carmageddon, another highly controversial title.  These games have done more than you think... and actually, seeing Postal 2 and 3, it's easy to see that this kind of game, such as Postal 1, was not going to be made again.
Yet, Hatred is here, almost 20 years later.
2nd - It's a very good game.  The attention to details is better than most AAA care to afford.  Compare this with Diablo 3, and if you forget the different setting, fantasy vs modern real world, Hatred is even more detailed and better looking than D3.. and for less than 1/3 of the price.  The mechanics are very good, rarely in a top down twin stick shooter you can jump over obstacles, thru windows, crouch...  you can also run, roll to dodge.   even the credits of the game is like a top notch movie intro.
3rd - To support these amazing devs...  yes, they used shock marketing to get themselves on the map, but you definitely want these devs to make another game after Hatred.  And by buying it, you also make sure that Hatred reaches it full potential, cause the devs have further plans for it, based on how well it sells.
4th - They took 1 year to make this awesome looking game with a very unique engine.  Without using Early Access... something rare these days... even more so for an indie studio... imagine what they can do.  They are highly skilled.
5th - It runs great on my 5+ years old computer, consisting of a Phenom II X4 965, GTX 580 1.5gb and 8gb generic ram on a cheap asrock mobo.  Most details to ultra, destruction physics to high, Med AA.. steady 30-40fps with dips in the 20s when there is a grenade blasting an house or something like that, but never it becomes unplayable and a slideshow.
Don't take the game too seriously, this ain't no simulation... the character have a strong Duke Nukem feels to him... he's just not blasting aliens... also, don't worry, there is no background stories on the civilians... you won't feel anything worst killing these than killing anything else in other games... its no worse than killing mushrooms in mario bros really.  When they actually beg and cries, its even more an incentive to hurt them actually.  It's like, come on and put up a damn fight you wussy.
The core gameplay is very nice, it plays well, challenging even on easy, and its worth more than many AAA 60$ games.  The only thing one could argue between this 20$ Hatred and a AAA 60$ is the content itself.  But don't forget that mod support will come in due time, hopefully thru steam workshop, and the devs will likely expand it much further, specially it the sales does well.. so yeah, buy it :)
Did I said that you should buy it?  Not sure... :)  Buy it!
