This review comes from someone whose last Final Fantasy game was FF9, which was the last one made for playstation 1. From there I never bothered to buy another console and stuck to full PC gaming. I was happy to see that they had ported many of the non-MMO final fantasy games to PC a decade later.
I decided to give FF13 a try to see what I've been missing and to get back a piece of the quality gaming that I so dearly recall from my childhood days. However, I was mostly disappointed with the game because with every part of the game that I liked, there was another part that related to it that was a pain in a sense.
For example, the combat system has some complexities and you'll find yourself interacting with different formations regularly and taking active control almost constantly - especially towards the end game. However, you get through nearly 3/4 of the game before this actually happens. I kid you not that you will be wondering if the gameplay mechanics the team worked on will actually be relevant becuase the majority of the game is so *easy* that you can just afk/click and breeze through everything. Once you get to the open world area this completely changes and you'll be getting stomped until you level up but the game is in 'tutorial mode' for farrrr too long. It's one thing to introduce players to new mechanics in the first hour or two of gameplay. It's another to make most of the freaking game so simple that people like myself actually lose interest in playing for days because it's too easy.
The game has 3 phases. Without spoiling too much: there's the introduction phase where you discover the characters and are put on a linear track storyline. There's the 'open world' phase where you level up for the final boss and then there's the final area itself. I don't mind the linear storylines as much as others but the open world area was what I imagine to be a throwback to the old FF open world areas where you explore and fight what's in your path. However, by the time you get that it gets to be extremely mundane very quickly. The battles will last 10 minutes each and are against the same types of enemies up until the ending credits as they occupy the end zone as well...so once you get to a point where you can take on a behemoth you've won the game.
The storyline itself is also so-so. I havn't played FF10+ or many JRPG's but this story feels much more anime/JRPG than what I'm used to. Perhaps it's my age or difference in taste but I felt the older series (FF3/7/8/9) didn't depend on long cinematics to tell the story but were rather driven by the gameplay and battles themselves. It was disappointing that many of the storyline battles that I did get to fight were so bland and easy that they didn't feel epic at all. The exception being the end fight.
Overall I think the game is worth a purchase but I think that anyone that is looking to experience a Final Fantasy similar in quality/style to the ones that they played on their old PS1 will be in for a shock. The game is enjoyable in ways and admittedly I will be buying XIII-2 and Lightning Returns but I'm hoping that many of the complaints I felt were valid here are addressed.

My name is not important... what is important is what I am going to write...
...and so here it is, Hatred. Twin stick shooter where you just shoot civilians. Does it live up to it's hype? Not quite, but that doesn't mean it's bad either.
It's somewhere in between. Certainly a good game when you want to relieve some stress, shoot some people up and then close it, only to come back to it the next day for same short session. Don't expect miracles, don't expect deep story or even name of character, you just shoot people.
You know what? It's not a bad thing at all. Destruction mechanics, shooting mechanics are cool and kinda realistic. It's fun to shoot civilians, but sadly executions get tad repetive. Game is also kinda hard.
I like the game's aesthethic. It's black and white, with some colour from sirens of police cars and few other smaller things. Optimisation is a bit bad but devs will resolve it, I'm sure of it, more after the service they were doing to fans.
It's alright. Strong 7/10, but is it worth the full price asking now? Well for value I got from here so far, I'd say yeah. There are much worse games (Grass simulator) that offer nothing at all, yet they cost $10, and this here? Offers heavy atmostphere, heavy soundtrack that further adds to how intense this game is, destruction physics that allow you to literally destroy entire houses and fun shooting mechanics.
Get it now or wait for price drop. Whatever floats your boat. It's not THAT brutal, it's not bad, it's not excellent, it's alright, and that's more than enough for me to like it.

Lots of people hate this game. I've been enjoying the hell out of it.
To start: I've played about 15 Hrs. My internet connection is spotty sometimes so most of my playtime is offline.
More: I'm old school. I played FFVII on playstation near release. Remember the black-bottom discs(like three of them)? That was my first FF game and since, it has been my favorite. XII is a distant second place for me (in terms of FF games). XIII (so far) has my attention. Granted it has no chance of dethroning VII or XII But the game is enjoyable. Apart form the terrible dialog (which I've actually grown to like form FF games) I have trouble finding much fault. Tunnel simulator? sure. but no more than X. Even VII had the same feeling at points. You may have to search through endless pages of journal logs to find the story but does anybody remember the Kingdom Hearts series? Talk about melodrama, huh?
Now I didn't come on here to bash all of my favorite games. Not at all (and these are some of my favorites (VII and KH topping the list)). The point of all of this is to say that no game is perfect. Every FF game has its quirks. Each game has made different design choices in some form or another. This one is no different. The most outlandish change that this game tries is its paradigm based battle system. Which is its strogest feature. It's not my favorite battle system of the series but it's fast, engaging, and ultimatley enjoyable. For any true FF fan, I say, that there is nothing wrong with this game. You get a pure FF game in XIII. To all the nay sayers, I say, open that small mind of yours and stop being such a genre fanboy. To those of you who skipped this one due to the bad publicity, maybe give it a try (thats why I waited so long).
I bought this on sale but if I would have known the true nature of its reputation I wouldn't have minded paying full price. (Though I am glad I got it on sale, I'm not stupid...or rich). But if it isn't on sale and your in the mood for a FF game and have a few bucks to spare this is a solid buy.
End Review.

An elegant and fresh new take on the genre of sandbox survival. The player controls civillians caught up in a civil war between the government military and rebel forces, trapping the civillians inside the city of Porogen. Your civillians must scavenge throughout the city, reinforce their base, fight off sickness, hunger, and injuries, and keep spirits high. There are many ways to die, and no way to load a previous save if you mess up. You are faced with many choices in the game, such as wether or not to give the helpless children that may come to your doorstep expensive meds for their mother, and to kill or avoid the armed thugs wandering around the medicine cabinet at the location you are scavenging. The game has infinite replayablilty, as there are many different playstyles, and thousands of different choices to be made. Pick up This War Of Mine as soon as you can.

Crysis is an action packed shooter with a vast environment to explore and abilities that allow you to complete objectives in a variety of ways. The story is a bit short, and a bit lacking, but the combat more than makes up for it. Graphics are still quite good, even for todays standards.
Pros:
Graphics.
Destructible environment.
Nanosuit abilities.
Weapon customisation on the move.
Weapons are varied.
Combat is very fun, the nanosuit abilities in conjunction with efficient use of weaponry provide an exciting experience.
Cons:
Dificulty.
Hand gestures are a bit overdone in an attempt to enhance the voice acting.
Short campaign.
Important aspects of progression are not communicated to the player, this makes simple tasks dificult and sometimes forces you to load a previous save because of a missed step at the beginning of the mission (On the last mission you need to find a "Tac cannon" that is seen at the beginning of the mission, the door holding the gun is unresponsive to the "interact" button at this stage. You need to collect it on your way to a different objective. The gun is not even on the path, nor is it mentioned, so you would assume it is useless. I had to restart the mission and get the gun while on the final step of the boss mission) and attemting to destroy helicopters is a EXTREMELY dificult to take out without either a sniper or a rocket launcher, when you first encounter them, you are unlikely to have either, so I recommend picking one of those weapons up as soon as you have the oppurtunity.
Overall I think this game is good because of the combat and mechanics, and not necessarily the story (or much else really). The game is focused on the important factors, and they excel, but the other "insignificant" sub-factors are underwhelming, and this affects gameplay negatively because these small problems represent themselves frequently, despite the larger more vivid picture. I would recommend this game when it is on sale.

I'll be honest, I thought Crysis was more recent.  I didn't realize it was a game from 10 years ago.  It has a high graphic quality, good music, and solid voice acting.  Shame about that story, though.  I feel kind of like they decided what they wanted to show off with their game engine, and then adapted the story and stages to fit.
I also wasn't expecting stages, but something more open world like Blood Dragon et al, however, this isn't Far Cry, but Crysis, and even though there is totally a feel at the beginning of being "open world", that basically ends in the back half of the game.  The gameplay is pretty good, and the mechanics are just interesting enough to keep me playing, though I also admit to slight modification of the energy drain for a more enjoyable experience.  Having the suit to enhance things like stealth or jumping or being human Sonic was fun.  I wish the guns had been as interesting, but as with a fair amount of shooters, all the gun fun is also in the back half.  At least the myriad of attachments allow you to customize the few guns you actually do get into something attuned to your playstyle.
Overall, Crysis is a solid game; it has weird narrative cul-de-sacs it detours into, and it takes a while to get to the inevitable "twist", but it's a fun shooter with enough enhancements and graphical pretty to make me assume it's at least 5 years younger than it actually is.

I wish there was a Neutral option instead of a Good or Bad option, but sadly there isn't.  I loved all the Hitman games, movies, everything about it, and when I heard this was coming out I was REALLY stoked...but after playing the game it feels a little misleading and not like how the older ones were.  I'm just gonna do the Bad first since there is a lot I really didn't like about this game...
BAD:
Stealth System is eck...: Compared to Blood Money and before, instead of being it to where if you did something suspicious with the disguise or you went into a too high leveled area then you'd have a problem with the disguise, but other than that you were free to walk around the whole area (as long as you had clearance) but now apparently EVERY SINGLE PERSON FINDS YOU.  If you are wearing a guard outfit, apparently that guy knew EVERY OTHER GUARD FROM THERE TO AZERBAIJAN, meaning you could basically get caught even if you were blending in with other people, how does that make sense? Compared to the old games where no one else would even care about you, it's just ridiculous.  Not only that but it seems like guards can spot you even if they aren't looking in that general area, I had gotten caught several times while I was to the side of the guard, not even in her peripheral vision, and I still got caught from it.
Point System: This got on my nerves the minute I found out about it, it's basically saying how good you were at the mission area, but in all honesty it's kind of akward.  It feels like the game is judging me, cause EVERYTHING you do that isn't towards the target you instantly get a Negative rate.  Guard caught you and you kill him? -500 points deducted for killing a civi/not the f%$king target.  Got caught? -1,500 points.  Killed a enemy trying to kill you? -350 points.  That's just wrong, at least in Blood Money even if you screwed up it didn't say "Hey, you royally screwed up, nice going.", and it told you at the end how you were and didn't show a ingame counter.  I'm a bit of a perfectionist okay? So after getting caught over and over or killing too many people when I was basically forced to, I just ended up restarting the whole level and just got annoyed from doing everything over and over and F%$KING OVER AGAIN, I Just gave up and didn't even want to keep playing for the rest of the night.
Upgrade system: It's tied to the Point system....and it's not even very good, it's only small little tuneups here and there that you never really pay attention to or even bother with, which means if you sucked on the level, you don't even get the upgrade till you replay it over and over till you get a high enough score to get it, and even then you won't really tell the difference between when you had the upgrade or didn't.
Awful Checkpoint system: I wish they would've just stuck with savestates like before, cause the checkpoints are atrocious, even if you killed/Pacified enemies before the checkpoint (Which you still lose points for I might add) if you reload that checkpoint, every enemy before that checkpoint, will respawn in again, even if they were dead.  And if you get near the end and get caught and don't want to lose points?  Start from the checkpoint and do it ALL over again.
Very linear: The game is extremely linear, compared to other games before or even old games like Thief and Splinter Cell Chaos Theory where they had these quite huge open maps with different pathways to take and use to get around the areas.  Yes they have multiple things to do to neutralize a target but once you get caught and just restart from checkpoint all the time you don't really end up caring and you'll most likely just pick the method you've always used because it seems to be the most effective way.
Instinct is a Hit or Miss: Instinct helps you out in most cases giving you ways to neutralize a target or to see where they are going, which is very nice, but it's also used to blend into a crowd of people if you have the same disguise as they do, but if you run out then you can't blend in meaning you're basically screwed if you have to walk by a whole group of the b%$#ards and you have no instinct left.
The Awful Detection system: There is no way I would skip this, it's really...bad I guess, kind of a hit or miss, like when you wear a disguise that others also have on you can get caught still but it's a lot slower than normal.  But as I said above, even when I wasn't near some guys view I was still getting caught, even if their body was pointed one way and their head a different, one guy I was next to has his body pointing the same way I was and his head was to the side so I figured he wouldn't catch me, then the meter filled almost instantly and he instantly turned around and caught me, then it was back to mashing the f%*king Restart Checkpoint button, if that was a actual button I could hit IRL I would have broken it years ago.
Trying to be More Assault: The game acts like it's trying to be more about Assault since there is taking cover and guns everywhere, taking cover is nice to hide behind crates and such, but once you get caught everyone is on your♥♥♥♥♥instantly and you basically have to just play the game popping your head in and out of cover like a bunch of Oompa Loompas, and since killing or even pacifing the wrong target makes you lose points it's basically trying to force you to hide instead of you know, blend in like how you could in the old games.  How the hell does that make sense? I get into a firefight when I didn't want to and then when I kill the guy I'M suddenly the a%$*ole for shooting him in return?
Challenges: Challenges are there for you to try and do if you feel like it, like collecting guns or outfits or evidence or going through the whole level with just your suit.  It sounds like a nice idea but I always ended up missing half or more of the guns since I tried to go the more sneaky sneaky route and just picked a random gun for backup incase s*%t hit the fan, and even when it did I just restarted to checkpoint cause I didn't want to lose points for getting caught and then killing him.
Distraction items: Instead of having a Coin like before it's now whatever you find in the environment, which isn't a bad thing at times but there are those moments when you kind of WISH you had that bloody coin instead.  One time I had a golf club as a distraction item and I was unsure of whether to keep it or replace it with a bottle, then later when I chose to throw it from behind a wall it got stuck on the wall, made the sound, and every single guard found me, then back to the Restart Checkpoint button it is.
GOOD:
Story: It's pretty interesting I suppose, you meet new characters and people as well as have a different story from just having the whole thing based around shooting a ton of people because you had to, at least now it's about saving a little girl while shooting a ton of people because you had to so at least it's a bit of a step in the right direction.
Hiding: At least now you can hide behind cover and such so you can't get caught AS easily as you could in the game itself which is nice, so that's something at least.
Multiple ways in: There are different ways to get past certain guards or areas but this also goes back to the assassination system thing where you find the one that works and stick with it, I've never felt the need to go and pick a different way into a place because the way I picked last time works just fine so I may as well just stick with it.
CONCLUSION: This game is a hit and miss for people, for the Hardcore fans that love the games and that loved that old stealthy sneaky feel without a atrocious detection system they might be dissapointed, I certainly was, that and the fact it's trying to act like a modern game, which it shouldn't.  It gets a 5/10 It's a half and half for me, with all the new things they've put it and taken out it doesn't feel much like a Hitman game like the ones before, sad.

This is a franchise I have followed for a long time and Civilization V is a game I've spent nearly 500hrs playing. On the one hand it is an extremely enjoyable game and some of the new gameplay systems - the tech web, aliens, enhanced espionage and quests - provide a lot of depth; on the other the game lacks contextual relevance, with technologies, wonders and leaders coming across as rather bland.
This is a game I expect to see develop with the release of content patches and expansions. Obvious areas to overhaul would be the satellite system (which is currently overly gimmicky and tedious), the tech tree (it has variety but it's hard to get a sense of what to research for a balanced game) and sponsors (previously called Civs, they are few in number and extremely shallow). The interface is rather lacking, with buildings and wonders using a monotone colour scheme making it extremely difficult to see at a glance what you're constructing and what you should research.
However, there is a lot that the game gets right. The new expansion system - whereby you must create an outpost and wait for it to expand to become a city - means that you have to be more strategic with your city placement and defence; the quest system allows you to shape the game around your play style; the espionage system allows for capturing cities and requires you to monitor your own cities; wonders are better balanced, as the tech web means players can focus on different areas with less overlap; happiness has been replaced with health and is no longer as punishing, as well as providing rewards for higher amounts.
Those with an open mind and an interest in strategy games will love this. Those extremely attached to previous versions or hoping for a straight remake of Alpha Centauri will be left wanting.

Oh dear.  Nothing new here folks.  Whatsoever.  It's not a bad game, per se.  It refines many of the combat mechanics from the first one, and the voice acting and art direction are stellar.  It lacks all of the originality of the first one though.  So much of what made Bioshock special was the storytelling; that WOW factor.  That great big question of "where are we?" and "what happened here".  All of which are answered before this game even starts.  Also, I found the storyline, as shoddy as it was, difficult to follow.  So many of the story recordings are from, like, 15 years ago, and it's difficult to differentiate which are which.  And once everything does come into perspective, it was difficult for me to care.  Thematically, there are so many things you can do with a setting like this, and this game squandered it's opportunity.  Fun to play though, and very pretty, and runs very well, even on lower end hardware due to the claustrophobic nature of the environments.  It ran me about 27 hours without doing the dlc or multiplayer.
edit:  Huge plus for the recent patch getting rid of GFWL and adding controller support.  This game feels built with controllers in mind.  Bit of a warning though, your save games do not automatically back up with the steam cloud I don't think.

Gray Matter Interactive developed Return to Castle Wolfenstein.  The studio was acquired by Activision in 2002 and later merged into Treyarch of Call of Duty fame.
Return to Castle Wolfenstein; a true classic, a phenomenal FPS that has aged well and plays well on modern systems.

There are very few differences between Bioshock 1 & 2.  They both share the same graphics engine.  However, PC gamers cannot properly enjoy the new particle effects featured by the DirectX10 support without encountering major stability issues.  Therefore, the graphical improvements made from Bioshock 1 are rather incremental.  Both games both share the same audio problems and issues with the mouse sensitivity and controls.  However, as long as you know what files to open and which values to change, the crazy mouse sensitivity and skipping sound should plague you no more than it did in Bioshock 1.  This sequel did not take the franchise in a new direction the way Mass Effect 2 or System Shock 2 did.  However, much like God of War 2, Bioshock 2 had a nearly perfect prequel.  As a result, they took an already winning recipe of extraordinary level design and phenomenal combat, and cleverly refined and modified this formula into another incredible experience in Rapture.  Bioshock 2 delivers a less memorable experience, but certainly not an all-around worse experience.  This sequel takes place 10 years after the events of Bioshock 1 and places the player in the glorified fish tank of Rapture.  Evolution has taken its toll on this underwater utopia, and has become a darker and creeper place with incredibly impressive aesthetics.  Bioshock 2 handles moral choice and its consequences incredibly better than the first game.  It focuses more on personal confrontations and less on the philosophy behind Rapture.  The ending is much more meaningful and emotionally overwhelming as the repercussions of your choices unfold into an incredibly satisfying conclusion.  The secondary goals of finding and defending Adam stuffed corpses offers incredibly rewarding challenges.  In addition, Bioshock 2 features new and overwhelmingly powerful enemies that keep the gameplay fresh.  Exploring the underwater skyscrapers in Rapture has never been this much fun.
Gameplay: 20/20 … PERFECT (While I pine for the prequel’s U-Invent machine, Bioshock 2 enhances the combat in Rapture in too many ways.  Hacking is a much less intrusive feature, researching enemies is much more fun and rewarding, and dueling weapons and plasmids is an impressive gameplay improvement.)
Story: 10/10 … PERFECT (Sofia’s psychobabble and lackluster philosophy is easily forgiven because her personality as a mass manipulator makes me question whether she even cares about her beliefs.  She is a narcissistic woman that thinks her poop doesn’t stink.  Andrew Ryan genuinely values his ideas regarding self-worth and individualism.)
Graphics: 4/5 … AWESOME (Me and countless other Bioshock 2 players experience frequent crashes while playing under fancy DirectX10 settings.  Therefore, I have to make do with launching the game with the DirectX9 command, “-dx9”.  Besides that, the game runs at a solid 60 frames per second.)
Sound/Music: 4/5 … AWESOME (SFX doesn’t appear to cut out as often as it did in Bioshock 1, but enabling EAX requires you to dig around in the ini file.)
Controls: 4/5 … AWESOME (Plasmid hotkeys keep changing as you upgrade them and you’re stuck with all of the predetermined key bindings for your weapons.)
Overall: 93% (42/45) … AWESOME

Grimoire: Manastorm is a very interesting and fresh take on the tried-and-true FPS gameplay. The style is reminiscent of the old school arena action of yore. The days of Quake and Doom echo through the very core of Grimoire: Manastorm, while modern MOBA-styled elements breath new life into it and entangle with Elder Scrolls-esque lore and powerful firey doom.
The central gameplay is entertaining and intense; overpowered wizards struggle in the streets of dingy cities and classic fantasy locales. Unlike the usual first person shooter, you trade in your pistols, shotguns, and rifles for Lightning, Netherworld Magic, and Flames.
Your characters burn, squash, and electrocute eachother to take glowing control points throughout the maps during Conquest, a tense and action-packed team play mode. The team-based combat already feels tight, and the use of tactics can turn the tide of the battle. A single fire wizard moving around the side and flanking the unsuspecting defenders with the use of their Ultimate ability followed by a flurry of fireballs can entirely change the flow of combat.
On the other side of the coin you might find Free-For-All a frustrating mess, or a great source of fun. FFA is chaotic, even by the standards of the Conquest mode. During an FFA match you will often find yourself wandering for a moment before becoming embroiled in the magical hell-storm unfolding in the center of the map. There's little breathing room and most of the time you'll find yourself flailing helplessly in the fray before being cut down by a lucky shot from someone hopping into the fight with full health just after respawning. Speaking of respawning... The spawnpoint system that is implemented in FFA leaves much to be desired. There have been numerous occasions where I literally spawn inside of another player, or someone spawns directly behind me.
Grimoire's initial offering might turn some away. The first match is so absolutely confusing that it feels like you've just been dropped face-first into a malfunctioning nuclear reactor and told to stop it from meltingdown. Okay, that might have been a bit of an exaggeration, but my point still stands that the first match or two might be so off-putting that you'll turn your nose up at it. The controls are a little hard to get used to, but my main suggestion would be to change the controls to FPS in the options menu. This style, I feel, should be the default as it is much easier to use and much more intuitive. Give it a few matches and tool with keybindings before giving up if you find your first match a bit too insane.
The game's graphics also leave something to be desired. The assets used for effects and the magical graphics are certainly fun to watch, featuring a uniquely stylized and fun look, but character models are rather flat. Textures tend to be muddy, and the ground in some areas looks like it was pulled straight from the Playstation 2. However, this is certainly excusable at the moment because you can already see what the developers are going for, and what they hope to one day achieve. However, the graphics aren't so bad that it makes it hard to play, and the gameplay is fun enough to make the visuals often fade into the background.
As it stands, the game is a highly playable and fun romp through chaotic medieval landscapes. While the graphics leave much to be desired, and more gamemodes would be appreciated, the current offerings are enough to provide a good deal of entertainment for the tidy little price of 10 USD (or for free if you got your key from PC Gamer's giveaway). I have only high expectations for the future of this game, and look forward to seeing it improve and to take part in it. For now, I've spent enough time writing out this review, I think it's high time that I put my pointy hat back on and start slinging spells in the courtyard. I hope to see you folks on the field. The tl:dr version: You'll get your money's worth and then some out of this free to play game, just be aware that there are a few areas where you might find yourself slightly disapointed. On a scale of 1-10, I'd give it a 7.
The long version: First, the good. If you decided to hold off on this game because you were worried about bugs and connectivity issues, you can now safely make the leap and commit to this game. I did have some troubles when I first got it, but it has been over a month since I last got disconnected from the game servers. It runs very smoothly, and I have not run into any problems in game with bugs.
I enjot the game itself for the most part, with only a few minor quibbles that I will cover in a bit. The graphics are clean, the animations smooth, and with even a halfway tuned deck you'll be able to grind for gold against AI opponents on hard with a high success rate in your duels. And the card selection isn't just limited to the Origins set; there is a 'base' set of cards that you get to draw on too, and these help make for a wide variety of decks that can be built.
The story mode is something that I highly recommend. It helps get you acquainted with how the game is played in a straighforward manner, although since I have been playing the tabletop version since it first came out, I don't feel that I can give an honest appraisal on how decent of a introduction to Magic the Gathering it would be to someone who has never played the tabletop game before. It also gives you a feel for how the different colors play, and for the players who like the story (like me), it is fun to see how some of the iconic planeswalkers came into their power. And with the in game currency that you get for finishing the story modes, there is absolutely no reason why finishing them all shouldn't be your first priority.
Now, the bad: There is a limit on how many of a card you can have, based on its rarity. 4 of a common, 3 for an uncommon, 2 of a rare, and just one copy of a mythic. While you can build multiple decks with the same cards, and not be forced to decide which one gets your lone copy of Chandra, for example, it does limit your deck building options. Sure, you'll still put those rares any mythics into your decks, but they won't be the cards you'll be seeing every game, so you'll find yourself leaning more towards the uncommons and commons to form the foundation of your decks. So, while it is nice to know you won't have to go up against any decks that are dominating the Pro Tour (or your local card shop for that matter), it is also a bit of a downer that you can't build them either.
Another mark against the game is that there is a limit to how much in game currency you can earn through duels in a 24 hour period. Yes, you can buy in game currency with your own money, and I understand that this is how the game is supposed to actually turn a profit so that the fine folks who did the programming get paid. But if you are like me and might not necessarily have the money to spare, you will find yourself able to earn just a couple of booster pcks a day.
And these booster packs are small: Only 6 cards per pack, 3 commons, 2 uncommons, and 1 rare that might be replaced with a mythic instead. On the bright side, it seems that the game doesn't give you any cards that you already have the max with, and some friends of mine who also play the game have told me the they have experienced the same. So, at least you are guarenteed six useful cards each pack (useful as in for deck construction purposes; whether or not you find the specific cards to be of any use is up to you to decide). These two negatives added together mean that, unless you are willing to fork out a sizable chunk of change, the odds of you getting a particular specific card that you want are really against you (there are even a few commons that I have one and even zero of still, while I have collected both of certain rares and will no longer receive any more of them).
Lastly, a word of warning about the player base, if you want to play against others in ranked matches. In my experience, easily over half of the people I have played against will, once they see the writing on the wall that they won't be getting the win, will quit before the match is over in order to not take a hit to their ratings. The computer will take over, and while the odds are good for you to get the win, it does tend to get old real fast. And with no way to report people who do this, there doesn't see to be much incentive for those who do this to stop. So, if honorable duels are something that you are wanting, I'd suggest checking out your local gaming store instead of here.
Regarding Two Headed Giant mode: It isn't something that interests me, so I haven't played it. I can't give you any feedback on it. Sorry.
In the end though, this is a free to play game. The only investment you have to make is the time needed to download it. And the game is put together well enough that I have frittered away over forty hours in one and two hour chunks. So, if that sounds like something you'd enjoy, Magic the Gathering with current cards on the cheap, take the plunge and at the very least give it a test drive around the block.

After I was done with that and finally got control of my own units, i spent about an hour grinding cause the game kinda didn't tell me how to trigger the next flag. The story is bland as oatmeal, with some voiceovers being really cringeworthy.
But then to the meat of the game, the combat. Much to the credit of the game, they are trying something new, instead of controlling single characters actions you now control a group of characters (called a Union). The combat system is simple enough with a leveling system even simpler, use stuff and it eventually levels up. Although leveling up doesn't help you much since the game heavily relies on numbers and RNG, what those numbers might be I couldn't tell you, since the game in no way explains it. RNG is also a big factor, when against the same mob (as in reloading a save and actually fighting the same mob) the outcome of the first round was wildly different, ranging from killing a enemy union without getting hit to myself being one-shotted, this against exactly the same mob.
The game looks pretty enough (if you can overlook som glitchy graphics) although most of the enviroments seems to be quite boring. The dungeons throws nonsense mechanics at you for no reason at all *door shuts down and you get to fight the same mobs you've been chomping like tic-tacs to get there*. In another dungeon there is a slow-down fog, it does nothing exept slow you down, so instead of wasting 5 seconds running down an empty hallway, you now get to enjoy the same empty hallway for a minute.
All in all, the game reminds me alot of FFX, if you take away intresting scenes, combat and story.

Primal Carnage is a simply excellent online first person shooter / third person biter that embodies the idea of assymetric multiplayer; human soldiers fighting primal dinosaurs. Though there is as of yet no customisation of classes, their individual abilities create an incredibly fun arena that emphasises the importance of teamwork. You won't survive this carnage alone. A lone human can easily be pounced upon by a raptor, carried away by a swooping pteranodon, or blinded by a dilophosaurus' toxic spit. And of course, the quaking of the screen and the cacophonous roar of a T-Rex on your trail is an utterly terrifying experience. On the other side of the game, dinosaurs must fear the paralysing net of the trapper and the blinding flares of the tracker, along with all the other heavy firepower humanity brings to bear, using ambush and co-ordination to get in close and feed their unending hunger. The game remains fairly well balanced, with games won with teamwork rather than lone commandos choosing one particular overpowered class.
In terms of graphics, the game is a stunning product for an indie game. Even if your computer is less than stellar, the game runs well on low graphics, and you can still enjoy the incredible animations of the dinosaur character models, truly bringing the exinct beasts back to life in an amazing fashion.
And whilst you may scoff at the number of different DLC dino skins, when you remember that you control them in the third person, suddenly you may find yourself a little more interested in customising your reptilian killer.
With constant updates coming from the brilliant dev team, I'd say Primal Carnage is only lacking one thing; you!

26 hours in and I'm basically in world 2.
When I play this game, I keep thinking that this is what Freelancer should have been.  When I played Freelancer, I had a "was that it?" feeling.  Contrarily, Rebel Galaxy gives off a "not JUST a space flight adventure simulator" sort of vibe.
Yay:
- Ignore the story, earn money, buy really big ships.
- Ability to join multiple guilds without needing to quit your current one
- Broadside combat in a space sim is surprisingly fun.
- Very responsive devs, check the bug reports part of the forum
- Prices of commodities go up and down in response to world events and planetary type
- Wide variety of missions.  Escort, Pickup, Delivery, Blockade Running, Head hunting...
- No speed lanes, you want to get somewhere fast just point your nose and punch the warp.
- Dynamic system.  In Wing Commander: Privateer, you could watch the news and respond accordingly to major events.  Is there a famine?  Bring food.  War?  Bring weapons.  Market glut, buy low.  This system is rarely found in these space trading games.  I don't think Freelancer had it.
- Good voice acting
- Intuitive game design
- Aliens!
- Varied Nebulas.  Including the classic ones like lightning nebulas that can shatter your shields in a single flash and dark nebulas where danger and mystery lurk within.
- Scanner.  A nifty halo emits from your ship and lets you know of nearby enemies, allies, and items.
Nay:
- Broadside combat is rather easy.  Just manuever until your side is exposed, use precise targetting, and press a button.  The lead is automatically calculated for you.  The only thing you need to decide is how much time to charge the shot.
- Fighters are so annoying since they can go to the 3rd dimension.  Plus the strike craft defense options are a bit lacking due to their extremely limited range.  You're left with relying on general-purpose turrets to pick off the pesky gnats one at a time.
- No speed lanes.  Most of the time, I neglect to plot a proper course before warping so I end up going through like 3 asteroid fields, 2 debris fields, and 1 planet.  That's like hitting 6 red lights when you're trying to get somewhere.
Meh:
- No idle radio chatter
- From what I've played so far, you pass lots of planets but there is no planetary landing.  You always stop at a station in orbit.  I'm guessing the idea is that space ships should stay in space where they're designed to work.

Reading other reviews and watching videos reminded me of Escape Velocity: Nova, a great Ambrosia game from oh so long ago.  I thought that this game could capture the same magica that game possesed but with the updated flare of almost 20 years of gaming advances.
Unfortunatly, I was wrong.
Combat in Rebel Galaxy feels dry, leaving you endlessly flying in circles trying to keep fighters on screen.  Capital ship combat, while entertaining for the first 20 minutes, comes down to trying to land as many broadsides as possible which, once again, leads to flying in circles.
The 2-d movement that was great in a top down space trading game like Escape Velocity is restrictive and unnatural.  At no point could I suspend my disbelief and imagine that I was piloting a space ship.  Any sense of immersion is ruined by this element.
With all that said the game isn't bad looking and the price is pretty low.  That might be enough to make this game an enjoy able experience for some but it didn't make it worth it for me.

So I decided to delete my old review of this game, since it wasnt very good, and give this game a proper review, because I feel like it deserves one.
Sins of a solar empire is quite litterally the best space based RTS game I have ever seen. Granted........I havnt seen a whole lot of them, but the ground work that sins lays down with its mechanics, and its execution of gameplay, and implementation of its features, is a very very good framework that I would eagerly love to see expanded upon and taken further. And there is much strategy behind this game that goes deeper then simply watching your ships blast each other apart.
Story-
So basically, how this game works, is there are 3 factions, and within these 3 main factions, there are 2 subfactions for each, meaning technically there are 6 factions. These all bring unique playstyles to the table, and each one takes full advantage of one aspect of the gameplay to a higher degree then all others can. The 3 factions are the TEC, a group of human traders who simply fell under attack from the other 2 factions at nearly the same time (basically the TEC are screwed). As a result of this, and having fought off both factions, the TEC have become militarized and divided on how to deal with the situation, thus, the issue that causes thier sub factions to emerge. The second faction is also my favorite faction, and the other human faction. They are called the Advent. They are highly religious, and worship some transcendent and omnipotent thing they refer to simply as "The Unity" which I guess is just thier collective conscious as a whole. Their reason for invading against the TEC is revenge, because the TEC kinda gave them the middle finger a really long time prior to this game, so the advent spent all those centuries since then being emo, and formulating a massive revenge war. The advent were weak back then, but they come into this game with WAY more advanced tech then the TEC have, and they seem to be really content with the whole revenge idea, but advent start questioning whether revenge is the right idea since this was not the original purpose of the "Unity" and its from this disagreement that thier subfactions emerge. I do believe its only in the advent, that their 2 subfactions passionately fight each other too because I know the TEC subfactions might disagree, but thier still on the same side. The third faction, the Vassari, are actually the only truly alien race in this game, and I'm gonna say right off the bat, they have the most advanced tech out of the other 2 factions. The advent is barely outclassed in this regard. The Vassari motive for invading against TEC is actually really logical.....Vassari use to have a big empire, but fell under attack by some mysterious force that the game never fully explains to you (HUGE OPPORTUNITY TO MAKE SINS 2 AND ANSWER THIS QUESTION....NOTICE ME DEVS!!!!!!!) anyway the vassari are unable to do jack against whatever this is, so they pick up, and flee, destroying worlds, harvesting resources, and living up life as a nomadic race on the go. -sanic music starts playing- This eventually leads them to TEC space, so of course the vassari just dig right into that nice human pie like right away. The TEC dont know, and certainly dont care what the vassari's problem is, they fight back out of survival, lose several worlds, but do survive. This resistance leads the vassari to kinda stop and think for a minute, and their subfactions form. One side of the Vassari contacts the humans, tells them about whats happening and suggest alliance, while the other side of the vassari is like, F THIS, KILL HUMANS, MINE RESOURCES, RUN RUN RUN -sanic music- both sides of thier faction are kinda right....I mean...whatever killed thier empire IS indeed still closing on them after all.
Gameplay-
SO thats the general story of the game, but the main drawback about this game is actually it is very lacking in story elements........there are no official characters, no official plot, and there is a massive vacuum in this game begging to be filled with stories and lore. That is where this game lacks most, but let me tell ya, the game does not disappoint on gameplay at all. The resource gathering is simple enough to understand, and complex enough to be expanded and taken further. The strategies of implementing certain units into a fleet are effective, encouraging thought out strategies and smart fleet building. Once you get mid game onward into a game, the battles become absolutely epic, and very fun to watch, as well as micro. These battles can consist of several capital ships, frigates, and cruisers tangled up in a big ball of hatred and fighting hard to overpower the opposing side, while hundreds of fighters, and bombers weaving through heavy traffic of ships at war. These battles become more and more climatic as the game progresses too, and you will have fought several of them by the time you gain the momentum to crush the neighboring empires. Also as gameplay goes further and further you are developing your faction's most powerful weapons in order to gain that descisive edge, these include superweapons, and a massive ship of tremendous power called a Titan, and every sub faction has thier own unique one. There is so much strategy involved with this game, and the way that it presents itself offers a groundwork that I would most love to see expanded upon in a future game and taking a step further.
Balancing issues-
This is truly a great strategy game, however, I feel there is some issues with how overpowered certain things are. There are certain things in this game, that pure strategy alone will not overcome. This mostly revolves around:
Capital Ships- These arent so OP enough to where pure strategy wont defeat them, because pure strategy certainly WILL defeat them......but lets be real here. The amount of frigates it would take to take down one capital ship is utterly ridiculous, and cruisers dont stand much of a better chance either. Cap ships are quite a desicive factor in the course of every battle, as losing a capital ship in a pitched battle could instantly start a chain reaction leading to that side losing the battle. Because capital ships are quite litterally the pillar of your fleet. While I do believe thier supposed to be that important, I feel its not really because of anything besides the fact that they obliterate all smaller ships by the dozens.....and dont get me started on capital ships that are leveling past level 6.
TEC starbase- This thing is a big gigantic mine that comes fully equipped with a ship factory, repair docks, various other utilities, and can stock your fleet up and act as a rally point just behind the frontline for you to fall back on and regain your strength. This base actually aint that hard to kill.......but there is great danger in doing so. Kill the wrong base, and it'll blow up right in your face, killing most of your fleet right along with it. This nasty little base is never a pleasant thing to deal with, and it is one of the saving graces for the TEC faction, as TEC is outclassed by other factions on a lot of things.
Advent starbase- The advent base isnt much for utility purposes like the TEC one, but this one is just flatout freaking hard to deal with. Its got massive amounts of firepower, made even greater by the fact that it can rain meteors down on your whole fleet. Killing a fully upgraded one of these is almost always a massively annoying task....and thats only if its just the starbase itself, and not also an accompanying fleet. And good luck trying to bring down its shields when advent faction as a whole, have the best shields in the game.
Vassari starbase- It can move........nuff said
Titans- These things are just OP no matter what you say, especially when past level 6. Nothing stops them besides other titans, they are litterally unstoppable at a high level. Low level titans can be dealt with rather simply, but level 6 onward is unstoppable.

This is a really underrated co-op hack and slash RPG for up to 3 players.
I know not everyone is into Lord of the Rings or that sort of thing, maybe you feel this is only for those who are fans? Well, as a fan I can say they made the world 100% accessable to those who maybe never read the books or saw the films. You can just appreciate it for a fantasy game, but at the same time the game offers options through dialouge trees (a bit like Mass Effect) to ask more if you're interested, and it explains everything, even the most basic plot if you truly know NOTHING about the story.
The gameplay itself is very fun, just basic hack and slash but I was never bored. You get random loot drops that can be sold, traded with party members or equipped.
The storyline takes place during the events of LOTR, and it uses the look and feel of the movies, but they explore places the movies never covered, which for a fan is a real treat, and I think they did a good job. Again, you can just enjoy it for what it is, and enjoy the game just fine.
The enviroments are nicely varied from ancient ruins, to forests, to snowy peaks and inside mountains, and more giving the game a nice feeling of progression and variety without feeling stale.
Being an RPG, you of course gain XP points through combat and questing, and you can level up your character using character trees that fans of Borderlands or Dead Island, and any such games, will understand easily.
You can pick betwee 3 characters - A Dwarf, A Man (Ranger), and an Elven Mage (which doesn't make a lot of sense with the lore, but it's a nitpick). Each character has a special ability that can be tweaked per the player's liking, and you can play your own way.
The game can be enjoyed in single player, as the AI takes over any non player characters, but the game really shines with having 3 players in a game each with their own strengths and abilities.
It's a fun little game, took me about 12 hours to play through, and after you're done, you can do more playthroughs where the enemies and loot are better to go along with your leveled up characters.
So, if you love LOTR or Middle-Earth stories, check it out, and even if you know nothing about those things, but like RPGs, co-op, action packed gameplay, you'll enjoy it, and maybe even become interested in the world.

In brief, I liked this game at first, but the last third of it wore out its welcome and exposed flaws in the combat and game design that kind of ruined it.  Thus, I don't recommend it.
A summary of what effectively turned this from a mild recommendation to a thumbs down.  Think of being juggled by multiple enemies in a brawler.  Now imagine you have 1 life and low health.  Now apply this to a side scrolling shooter with somewhat long stages.  That's sort of it.  You have cover, but you can't simply take cover - you have to roll first, and many enemies instahit you back, and this can cause a multi hit juggle.
Additionally, in the last third of the game there are multiple enemies that are tough and can kill you in 1 hit.  There are also large explosions and other things knocking you about, and enemies that shoot so rapidly you basically have to take hits at times.  Oh, and if you try to shoot an enemy when a stunned enemy is nearby, you will go into an execution animation you can't cancel and leaves you vulnerable.  Also, there are gun upgrades, which are autopickup and can overwrite good ones.  Basically, a whole bunch of things happen that takes control away from you and isn't fun to play with.
To be clear, I beat this game in about 3 hours.  Just the last 90 minutes of that wasn't much fun.  Contrast this to a game like Hotline Miami and Deadbolt, which are harder than this one and took me more tries, but I had a lot more fun with.  I'd recommend them instead.

This is one of my all-time favourites and for me the best game in the Wolfenstein series.
The story is that you play as Bj blazkowicz (you play as him in all of the games), you work for the O.S.A (office of secret actions) and you are to ruin the Nazis plans to bring back an ancient Germanic prince in hopes he will win the war for them, this also delves into the supernatural and horrific science themes, but at the end of the day the story matters least in this game.
Wolfenstein has always been about mixing old with what’ new at the time so the old aspects in this are that: you collect health and armour, you carry all of your weapons at once, you run really quickly, and there are secret areas, other than scopes you fire from the hip. Then there are all of the newer elements such as actual objectives, stealth, a weapon handling system, and stamina. The levels are very diverse and you won’t be in the same looking area in a different section of the game again. The stealth is done  by destroying the alarms, slowly walking or crouching up on enemies and stabbing them with your knife, or you could shoot them with the silenced luger, the silenced sten or the silenced and thermal vision scoped m1 carbine. There are only two missions where stealth is mandatory, the rest you can go all guns blazing. There are a few things that replicate Wolfenstein 3d such as you can eat chicken just like in wolf 3d, there are plenty of secret areas where you’ll collect treasure just like in wolf 3d and you even start out in the same way (in your cell with a dead Nazi soldier only with a pistol and a knife), you have tons of weapons nearly all of them are war time weapons but two of them are: a mini-gun that liquefies people and a tesla gun, all of the machine guns (except for the mini-gun) are best used with controlled bursts to kill the enemies as quickly as possible. There are quite a few types of enemies in this game half of them you’ll find to be really annoying. This game does get increasingly difficult and I half to mention this one boss fight half way through the game is one of the highest difficulty spikes and one of the most annoying boss fights I’ve seen in a game. It’s a super solider (heavily armoured cyborg Nazi) who has a tesla gun (a gun that shoots an electric beam when they use it) so if he can see you he’s going to shoot you and it will drain your health pretty quickly and to make things worse the fight takes place in a very open area.
Now that I mention that when you use the tesla gun it has a really short range, and it isn’t very accurate and it isn’t all that effective whereas when a super solider has one it’s a laser pointer that drains your health really quickly.
Also near the end of the game the regular enemies will sometimes get stuck in this sort of staggering animation where it seems like they take very little damage, and for some reason on the second last mission the paratroopers seem to take much more damage than they can from the rest of the game.
Other than that this remains one of my favourites and you should definitely play this game if you like old school shooters.

Roger Ebert once said that video games cannot be an art form, because they "by their nature require player choices, which is the opposite of the strategy of serious film and literature, which requires authorial control."
This game shows how video games can be an art form not despite of player choice, but BECAUSE of it.
But I'm getting ahead of myself.
The Stanly Parable is, at it's heart, a parody of Video Game (and general) narration tropes. However the point the Stanley Parable tries to make is that narration, as done in most other linear mediums, can't (and furthermore SHOULDN'T) be handled the same way in video games, because the player controls the action and pacing (and sometimes the outcome) of the story in video games. even in completely railroaded and highly linear First-Person Shooters you can still decide to just stand in a corner for 10 hours and not do anything, which would obviously break up the narrative flow of any story.
The Stanley Parable instead delivers a reactive story, one that adapts to any and all choices the player makes. You can decide to follow the narrator's instructions and get a totally boring and clichéd ending, or you can decide to stand in the broom closet for 15 minutes and look at a bucket. Both are narrated.
In Short if you are interested in a game that's NOT just a AAA linear movie-esque railroad, but want to see a game that perfect utilizes it'S medium, this game is for you.

I walked into a storm when I started playing this. I got this game as part of a bundle and got a lot more than what I paid for. This is what happens when Final Fantasy meets Mount and Blades distant cousin. I'll explain that last sentence in better detail below. The Last Remnant uses a battlefield type feature to change the typical dynamic of an RPG.
The Last Remnant is a tale of individuals who accept remnant culture, meaning they accept the magic that comes with remnants. There is an establish figure head for remnants known as "the academy" in which they attempt to regulate the use of remnants (meaning no engineering or manipulating the pieces). An opposition exists that wants all remnants abolished. The story line (if you can sit through the masses of cut-scenes) is quite an interesting one and ties well politically into today's issues.
The player takes control of a man/dude/guy named Rush. Rush is able to freely explore the world as he wishes. More locations will open up the further Rush progresses through his quests. Usually, there is a main quest available and side quests are up to the player to find the right person in town. It was hard at first to find where I needed to go. Upon taking a closer look at the map, "!" mark where quests are available (whether it's in a town or another district). You cannot jump in free roam or any amazing things like that. Free roam is essentially meant for the player to explore or replenish/buy/sell any weapons, armor, stones, dismembered or captured beasts and (not limited to) herbs. Yes, you may capture certain monsters you fight but this is up to the game. The game also decides whether or not "rare" monster will appear. Obviously, these are worth more than your average. Upon leaving the city, the player will engage in a passive attacking free mode. You are only pulled into battle when a monster collides with you, OR when you decide to engage a monster. After a bit of time, a time rift ability appears in which you are able to slow down time and move across any dangers you do not wish to intercept. On the other hand, you may use this ability to sneak up on opponents and get the first strike. Now you have entered a battle scenario. How does this game differ than any other turn based RPG game? Well, you're on a battlefield. You literally have to plan out what your units should do or else you'll get flanked and boom, here comes the "game over" screen.
A union (group of units) may consist of up to 5 units in varying formations (you can choose). You may have a few of these unions. Every character you add, adds extra HP. The issue with unions which makes them sort of mechanical is that you are not able to customize their equipment. Some may find it better this way as micro management isn't such a pain. There are those, however that like to make a connection with their characters. I'm just happy I have such a big party :). When in battle mode, you can choose to do a different variety of things (attack with magic, attack with combat, heal or tell units to use their best judgement). Each unit can be assigned one command. Each unit can also be told which target to attack. This is very vital as positioning of units will change over the course of attacks. If you send a unit to go flank another unit on the other side of the battlefield, that unit may be susceptible to a flank of their own if not properly covered by other units. You cannot physically tell units to move into a specific spot, only which targets they should attack. A neat feature to keep the player involved and on their toes (instead of waiting and watching) is quick time events. Even though it's a small game play dynamic, it still brings me back to the good old Super Mario RPG days where if you timed your attack properly, you could hit your opponent twice. This same idea is here but be careful in choosing turbo mode.
Your chances of hitting the right button becomes quite difficult! Dodging doesn't have this feature but some dodges will give you a QTE to counter an opponent. I'm not a 100% if there is a dodging/blocking feature as seen in Super Mario RPG (where you press A at a certain point of the opponents attack). Beyond the fighting, there are accessories that you can give Rush that boost his HP or certain attributes. Weapons can also be changed or rotated from main arm to side arm. Alternatively, you may give your character a shield for a better defensive chance. The grinding so far into the game hasn't been extremely bad (regarding leveling up) but there are times where you won't be able to beat a boss until you get your level up to a certain point. Some may find this annoying.
The
are actually really well done. When in battle screen and your soldiers and enemies are close together, they will jockey for position and lunge at each other. These are not official attacks but definitely add definitive beauty to the game. I hate seeing steady background when two arch enemies are staring at each other and don't do anything. I'm glad someone paid attention to this.
are suitable to what the games needs are. There is nothing over the top but I think they could have been a bit more creative with the noise. Music on the other hand is quite soothing when not in battle.
Overall, I would recommend this game. Some may find the turn base thing annoying (which I completely agree as I hate turn based games) but I found this game appealing enough to keep at it - and I'm glad I did. The battlefield strategies alongside the QTEs and fluidity of battle cinematics should be enough to make you forgot you're playing a turn based game.

I have loved the space game genre since I was 8 years old. The fact that I am recommending this means that out of the 95% of released space sim titles I have played to death, Rebel Galaxy manages to stand out a cut above many of them. I am not even a quarterway finished with the main storyline, yet 10 hours in, the amount of content is quite impressive, and makes gameplay enjoyable to say the least.
First and foremost, this is a third person spaceship simulator. There is no empire building or 4X gameplay involved.
You primarily fight, trade and explore in Rebel Galaxy, and start off doing the main campaign which you can deviate from at anytime. Of course the campaign has you flying around a little bit to do other things, but fighting is usually involved. Wonderful thing here is though, interactions with NPCs in the campaign and in general allow for non-violent alternatives to do a mission, or, for instance, to handle a pirating attempt or an illegal cargo inspection by system militia.
There are about a dozen solar systems in Rebel Galaxy, so you are given some wiggle room to move around. Content such as missions, NPC spawns, and solar system events are randomly generated. There is enough variety to keep things from going stale, and as you get farther away from your starting solar system, more content (ships, equipment, guild allegiances) is available to you.
Combat is a bit different in Rebel Galaxy. And your ship's motion is limited to 2D movement only (while fightercraft and the environment objects can have 3D motions and positions). I will seperate this into two parts. Offensive capabilities and Defensive capabilities.
Includes 1) A primary weapon 2) A secondary weapon 3) Turret systems 4) Mercenaries 5) Deflectors.
Include 1) Deflectors 2) Shields 3) Armor 4) Hull 5) Engine boosters
Combat aside, the graphics are very nice and well optimized. Also, the soundtrack is wonderful, it reminds me of Firefly.
As with any game, there is a bit of a grind involved to gain credits in order to unlock higher tiered ships and equipment. Best way to go about this is doing a bunch of high paying missions (mission payouts generally increase as your overall strength increases) alongside a storyline mission once in a while. Or however you want. Imo the grind doesn't feel like a grind sometimes. It's pretty fun to blow♥♥♥♥♥♥up.
All in all, I dig it. Combat is different, not shallow. Plenty of content. Good soundtrack. Solid mechanics.  Decent plot. Way to go Double Damage Games. I hope you keep making titles in this genre!

Think a top down space sim like Escape Velocity, Ring Runner, Trancendence or any of those, where you are moving on a 2d plane. But imagine the game has a similar POV as the X series. Its really weird and disorienting to be in front of a station and not be able to dive under it.
Again, let me state that the game is *lightweight*. Not casual, just not as deep as a game like X3. If you love incredibly in-depth games like X3, Eve, or any of those, you will probably find this a bit too shallow.
People just breaking into the space sim genre, or those of you who prefer lighter weight or 2d space sims will probably like this one. For what it is, its done very well.
That lack of a y-axis  is hard to get over though, especially if you've come from a full 3d space sim.

This game represents everything that's right about games.
A couple of guys named Erich Schaefer and Travis Baldree put this thing together. Between the two of them, they've had a hand in Fate, Mythos, Diablo II, and Torchlight. If you liked those games, and have played Freelancer or the little known Escape Velocity, this game should be an instant buy. Even if you haven't played space based ARPGs, you should buy this game.
Why? It feels good to play, and everything in the game is secondary to it feeling good to play. That's how it represents everything that's right about games: it focuses on playing as being the critical element. The controls, sounds, and looks of the game come together to make it feel like you're playing something that's meant, designed, and created to be played, above all else.
What really drives the game is the desire to kill things and become space rich, so you can kill stronger things and become even more space rich. It's the drive to kill, loot, and kill and loot even more that keeps the player going.
If you're into narrative heavy games, then you probably should pass on this. The story is campy, and not something that you'll remember for crazy plot twists or complex drama. But it's just interesting enough to keep you moving forward.
Rebel Galaxy has some sim-lite features, though not especially fleshed out. A player can disrupt a trade convoy, which keeps supplies low and prices high at a station. Or they can break through a blockade, and exploit the need for supplies to work towards becoming space rich.
Looking forward, this game provides a solid foundation for further features to be developed. I think this has a lot of potential to become an even better game, with deeper complexities driving the sim-lite features.
Really though, if you played and loved kill & loot driven games like Diablo II & Torchlight, or especially if you have played Freelancer or Escape Velocity... you need to buy this.

I've been playing Sid Meier's series of turn-based strategy games since Alpha Centauri game out.
Have since played Civ 2, 3, 4, and 5, with a combined total of several thousand hours of game-time.
I have to say I'm disappointed in Beyond Earth for a variety of little reasons.
To begin with, it's not really a "new game", but seems to be a re-vamp of Alpha Centauri (with an alien world, an alien landscape, hostile aliens, alien mist, and a "futuristic" tech tree that is, quiet frankly, terrible).
So, getting right to it, what's wrong with this game:
1) The tech tree.  Terrible for a number of reasons.  If you've played previous CIV games (2, 3, or 4 specifically), you're familiar with the simple, linear progression of the tech trees.  You can look at the starting techs, and easily understand the logic of the progression.  For example: Mining leads to Bronze Working leads to Iron Working leads to Metal Casting.  You knew you needed to discover Gunpowder before you could get a musketman, and then you'd need to learn Rifling before you could get a rifleman.  The trees in 2, 3, and 4 made sense.  They progressed left to right, and you could clearly see the techs you needs to get to the units or buildings you wanted to build.  Unfortunately, Beyond Earth's tech tree isn't so simple.  First off, it's non-linear, and depicted in a circular format, with erratic branches (and sub-branches) arching out from the center.  There's no clear, logical path, and they've gone out of their way to make the tech names sound "futuristic", at the expense of logic and comprehension.  Bottom line, you're going to look at the tech tree and go "What the heck????"  Rather than attempt to figure it out, you're going to simply try to pick the tech with the shortest amount of development time, and you're still going to feel lost and confused.
2) Continuing a poor choice from CIV 5, if you have a unit in the field, and you have that unit "Stay in place until healed", the game does not notify you each turn if the unit takes additional damage.  As an example, your unit is in a fight, and wins, but is at 50%.  So your next unit move is HEAL.  You go off, taking care of unit moves, turn to turn, for your other moves, expecting to pick back up with the injured unit when it's back to 100%.  Unfortunately, while you're off doing other things, that unit gets sniped by an alien or alien landscape feature, each turn, slowly reducing it's health turn to turn until it's gone.  This is a silly coding issue.  They should "activate" any healing unit when it's attacked so that you can see it the next turn and rectify the situation.  It's not a huge issue, but it is annoying.
3) Other leader communications:  PLEASE, for the love of god and all that's holy, give us a switch to shut up ALL the other leaders in the game!  Every time another civilization wants to talk to you, a cut scene of the leader pops up, disrupting the flow of the game.  And if that's not bad enough, the leader TALKS TO YOU IN A FOREIGN LANGUAGE.  Sorry, but that does nothing for me.  It doesn't make me feel "more into" the game.  It makes me feel that the designer really wasn't very sober when they came up with that feature.  Personally, I doubt more than 5% of the people playing this game actually enjoy being spoken to in a half dozen foreign languages, but if you don't wish to deprive them of the game interrupting FUN of hearing "let's make a deal" in a language you don't know (or, heck, even in English),....please, put an option in to SKIP ALL LEADER CUTSCENES.  They're boring.  They're repetitive.  And they completely break the flow of the game.
4) The HELP/INDEX is as useless in this game as it was in CIV 5.  Going to almost any item in the index gives you a general statement about the item.  No stats, no details, no how to use, nothing.  Quite honestly, to whomever designed the HELP/INDEX, you've created the most worthless such section I've ever scene.  Seems to be the same design in Beyond as in CIV 5.  Would have hoped you fired that clown before he ruined another game.  Sad to see you didn't.
Bottom line, if you liked CIV 2, 3, or 4, you're probably going to hate this, same as you hated CIV 5.

I just got this game and its unlike any other survival game I've played before.  And I mean that in a good way.  You start off with three random characters and you struggle to ensure their survival.  During daytime you craft some necessary items like a bed, rain collector, a stove, weapons, lockpicks etc. but at night you scavenge stuff from other houses, some of them might not be abandoned so have a care.   As the days go by, you find it harder and harder to make ethical choices.  Do you steal, or do something worse to ensure the survival of your people?  Its up to you.
Its a game that made me think really hard on what's happening in the middle east, russia and other war torn countries.  We see very small glimpses of the hell they live in in the news, but when you play the game you can't help but realize just how hellish their lives really are.  Kudos to the developers, they've created a game that not only entertains but also reaises social awareness.  It's a haunting, heart-wrenching survival crafting game with rogue elements  Replayability is high as everytime you start a new game you start with different characters and scenarios.

starting off by saying ive never played a 2d platformer, or metroidvania style game. this review is in no particular order, and i havent completely finished the game as of writing this, but i think im qualified as of now to make this review, as ive gotten very far and have seen much of what the game offers. (and yes, i will of course keep playing and finish it!)
8/10 game,  9 or 10 if personal preference of the game type didnt apply. the characters, atmosphere, music, artwork, deep lore (somewhat subtle/obscure at times, similar to dark souls), and gameplay/combat/mechanics are all what attracted me to this game, and i got all of those things plus more. i love the setting, dark and gloomy but with moments of peace and respite, with visions of hope - the artwork and music very much help to amplify this. the story starts out nonexistant, but as it turns out becomes much grander, which fits perfectly with how you upgrade the knight to become much more powerful through the whole game. if you dont care much for music and artwork in games, no worries, the gameplay is very fun! plenty of abilities to use, enemies to face, and charms to mix up for a unique build/fighting style. the mechanics and platforming arent too hard to get used to and learn, but are in-depth still give you feelings of accomplishment when you pull off some neat maneuvering or finally triumph in tense combat.
my only issues with the game are purely personal: theres lots and lots of backtracking. i honestly didnt even know what a metroidvania was until playing this, so its my fault for not expecting it, but its like this: finish a few areas of the game, but theres about ten or more paths that are out of your reach. you have to get different abilities to reach said areas, but once you finally get the abilites you cant for the life of you remember where those places were in the huge map! so yes, its very easy to miss out on a lot of things not considered mandatory. of course i dont want purely linear maps, i love the way the map was handled for this type of game, and this game particularly, but it made me stress out a lot at times trying to remember so many things at once. id highly advise, unless you have photographic memory or dont mind backtracking entire areas again, to write things down, or take a screenshot of the map and edit it in a paint software to make notes. wish i had done that sooner. also, you also tend to enter areas that you are forced to progress through to find a way back to familiar paths, but i do kinda like how it adds to the mysterious and "lost in a new world" feeling, almost like youre a pioneer.
conclusion/tldr: 8/10 - great atmosphere, characters, music, art, gameplay/mechanics, areas, & lore/story. the gameplay, music, and story really makes you feel things, whatever they may be for you, but definitely had lots of love and hard work put into it. my only gripe, being purely personal, is the backtracking made me stress out quite a bit sometimes, but thats just how metroidvanias are, i suppose. definitely a comfy, cute, yet grim game. definitely recommend to 2d platformer players.
