This being one of the formative games of my teenage years, I expected to trip balls on nostalgia when playing this, and delete it and forget it. However, what I found was an incredibly solid and challenging shooter (and the best looking game from its era) that somehow made killing Nazis seem cool and different, despite being from 2001 - the eye of the WW2 shooter storm.
The secret to RTCW's success is solid core gameplay complimented by sound technical design, loads of atmosphere, and a thematically colourful and interactive world. The running and shooting all works very well, and the variety of weapons and enemy types all make for a compelling and exciting FPS. The stealth works, and the number of silenced weapons you are given allow the player the change their play-style from time to time. It's not a central feature, but it works well enough to compliment the game rather than detract from it, which is more than I expected.
But this all would mean little if it weren't for the layers draped over the framework.
The level design, while not always consistent in terms of level length or complexity, is more often than not interesting, and the variety of environments leaves the player feeling like they've experienced a great deal between the beginning and the end of the game. At its best, RTCW has multiple routes that the player can take, and plenty of secrets to uncover for the completionist. However, if one chooses to run and gun, the action is responsive and the enemies well-programmed and well-placed enough to compliment this play style as well.
The game is just dripping with atmosphere, and this is in no small part due to the fantastic sound design. The soundtrack is excellent, and on par with the classic Medal of Honor soundtracks from back when that name actually meant something. Since the narrative covers both battle-oriented military settings and creepy horror, tonally the music shifts frequently and dictates the level of tension in an individual mission, saturating the player with emotion before a single thing has happened - this is especially noticable in the creepier levels. The weapon sounds are similarly powerful and convey a sense of accuracy skewed just enough towards dramatic licence to give each shot a sense of fulfilling drama. A small but powerful feature is the changing sound of the gunfire as the enemies move further away - the crack of a nearby rifle gives way to a dull thud as they are fired in the distance, and enhances the tension of the battles as your brain is left to process the direction and distance of the shot, and you are immersed further into the world.
I found the voice acting to be delightfully tongue-in-cheek as the actors embrace the schlocky nature of the story and deliver their lines entertainingly, allowing the tone of the game to shift from moment to moment and lifting the game beyond a single note played ad infinitum.
I also was pleased with the in-game narrative dealt up to the player. Whilst there are a number of cutscenes that are not always that compelling, from level-to-level one can find a number of papers to read, or pick up on enemy conversations that are shockingly effective at rounding out the otherwise faceless goons that you plow through. One particular example is a conversation between and officer and a subordinate regarding a soldier that has been sent to the wine cellar to find some wine and has failed to return. As you venture around the level you can eventually hear some drunken singing, and you find the soldier in question staggering around one of the cellars. Not only does this give the NPCs some personality, but it also adds to the larger narrative, in which you are infiltrating a city in which there are a number of officers gathering for an event. You know how they're occupying themselves, and how they treat those around them, and it all adds up to make you feel like you're in a real place, which is essential for a game that is trying to sell you a fictional story of such outlandish proportions.
I highly recommend this game to anyone looking for a solid shooter that is a cut above the rest in terms of imagination and personality.
P.S. In 2001, the leather-clad she-Nazis were the hottest things in gaming.

Magic Duels is a complicated review.  I'll start with what works well.  And by that, the entirety of it is the fact that my friend 300 miles away can play Magic with me.  That's great.  Beyond that, there are entirely too many issues to make this game worthwhile.
Firstly, the gameplay is solid on the surface, but suffers when complex combos come into play.  For starters, if I play something that costs one swamp and we'll say one colorless, it will automatically tap two swamps, prohibiting me from using that second swamp for another card.  As well, the instant abilities (and by this I mean activated abilities on creactures or enchantments), only sort of work.  I played a game recently where I attempted to use the Nantuko Husk's acitvated ability to avoid losing it, and it was akin to swinging my arms around and hoping something stuck.  These are just a couple of examples of how the rules have been poorly translated to interactivity.
That being said, if you are hard up for some Magic, this may do the trick.  But I want you to know, going into it, that in addition to the above, the matchmaking is subpar at best, and oftentimes, if you and a friend try to play a match, it will kick one of you and insert an AI opponent.  This game does the trick, only in the sense, that you and someone else can play Magic.  That being said, it's not necessarily, or even often, an enjoyable experience.  I hope that there are significant improvements to matchmaking and simple instant-level gameplay (and by this I include activated abilities) in a very-soon-to-come update.

The Last Remnant's progression makes almost no sense without reading guides making it stupidly difficult to enjoy unless you like alt+tabbing out constantly to look where you can get items and/or strategies.
I like doing side content in most games, but not in this game. You'll get a quest, cheese through the trash creatures and then be faced with an impossible boss that forces you to ditch the quest. Though the 'rare' creatures are optional I like to take them on at the time of encountering them, and there in lies the issue. You encounter ridiculously strong random rare creatures in dungeons which can obliterate a union (a group unit) in 1 attack round. And in many cases that attack is also AoE and takes the majority HP of another union nearby.
Theres a 'flanking' system in the game where if more than one of your 'unions' attacks the same creature you get a damage bonus. Great right? However, every boss and rare can take on multiple of your unions without ever getting flanked because they can do something called 'multi deadlock' which then also allows them to attack multiple times in a single round. And if that creature decides to do it's big attack twice in the same turn kiss your a** goodbye.
Your party members get new abilities along the way, which is nice. But the game picks 4-6 cookie cutter attack patterns based on health, AP, etc. I ended up grouping Rush with Torgal, but because Torgal's combat arts were so strong the game never gave me an option to ever use Rush's combat abilities unless I had built up a ridiculous amount of AP.
There's a morale indicator in each battle. Who knows why. You either handlily destroy your enemies and it's all the way to one side, or you take a bad hit and watch it go completely in the enemies favor at which point it ain't never coming back.
Speaking of useless things there's also a minimap in each battle that shows you the location of every union. But even if you set your unions to attack the closest enemy unions somehow there are still interferences and interceptions. Which makes absolutely no sense how the game judges distances and deadlocks. This part is particularrly annoying because you can send your best union against a larger enemy union, but then the game randomly decides that another enemy union of 1 NPC interceps that union, and then you basically lose 3 of your most powerful attacks for the round.
Overall, if the fights weren't completely one-sided 99% of the time it might be worth continuing. But as is I either destroy the trash NPCs, or get completely blown out by a boss/rare. So overall it's just not a fun game.

First off, be warned: this game is LONG.  I did most of the sidequests and a good number of the guild tasks, and I felt like I was playing forever.  However, that's not necessarily a bad thing (after all, I played Skyrim for the better part of a year...).  Overall, the game is very well-done - interesting plot & characters, decent pacing, beautiful graphics and world design, and an unusual battle system.
There are a few downsides:
- I felt like the main character is super annoying.  He's probably supposed to come off as immature, but at times I think they really overdid it.
- The plot left a lot of unanswered questions, chief among them what the Remnants are and where they came from.
- Some of the maps are HUGE, and the party's movement speed is just a jog.  So some of the sidequests or even just exploring seems like plain old padding at times.
- It's kinda annoying that the game has no vsync, so unless you can fix it with your graphics driver, you'll have to get used to lots of tearing.
- Unless there's something I missed, it looks like you should have 25 slots for active party members, but the most I ever unlocked was 18.  Of course, those 18 were more than enough to make the final battle a curb-stomp.
- I never quite figured out the formations, especially the "more powerful" versions you get as the game goes on.  My squads were just fine mostly sticking with the early-game formations right up until the end.
I mentioned the battle system above, but I think it's worth going into more detail because I thought it was one of the best things about the game.  It's definitely an interesting change from the standard JRPG format.  The biggest difference is that you don't give orders to your party members directly.  You group them into squads, called "unions", and you give general orders to each squad, like "Attack with mystic arts" or "Keep your HP up", and the squad members take whatever actions they can that fit in with your orders.  It adds an interesting bit of tactics and unpredictability to the fights, especially toward the end when each party member has so many different abilities to choose from.  Except for the main character, the party members also manage their own equipment, so there's not a lot of time spent optimizing each and every one like in some other games.
Final verdict: if you like JRPGs but you're looking for something a little different from the usual formula, you'll definitely want to check this one out.

The game isn't as bad as everyone made it out to be. Was the story pretty linear? I suppose so, but if you compare it to the other FF games, they were pretty linear themselves. I think they presented FF13 well enough to make it into the FF series though I didn't really feel an ounce of emotion while playing the game. Sure there were some cliche scenes and dialogue that makes you want to tear your eyes out, but what's an FF game without some cliche scenes and cheezy lines?
The story itself wasn't good or bad. It was pretty much your average save the world story and the ONLY thing I was looking forward to was Serah and Snow getting married. When I finished the game, I was like WHERE WAS THE WEDDING? It was half the reason why I finished the game. The other half was to see whether Fang and Vanille were either in a family-sister relationship or a romantic relationship with each other. I had a feeling that Square Enix was sort of in the middle between the two types of relationships since after all they are a world known company and game developer.
The battle system in my opinion was actually a nice change of pace compared to some of the older FF games. The old turn based battle is okay and all since it gives you all the time in the world to make a strategy or eat a snack! The introduction of the paradigm system made the game refreshing and new, though IMHO it isn't exactly hard to learn or master. You just need to know the weaknesses of your enemies and adapt your paradigm decks to them.
Honestly, the only BIG flaw I cared about in this game was the travelling system, especially if you hadn't completed any missions yet. It's such a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to move through Gran Pulse when you have no way to teleport or travel once you hit chapter 11 in the game. Even post-game, it's still a hassle to move around and that sort of turned me off from actually completing all the achievements in the game.
It took me around 38 hours to beat the game itself. I don't regret wasting 38 hours exploring the breathtaking scenery they created in this game or listening to the beautiful music they implemented for each area. For example, the bgm in Oerba - the home of Fang and Vanille. In my opinion, Oerba had the best bgm out of all the areas because it really made you understand the feeling of losing a home and never able to return to it. The ending song, no not "My Hands" by Leona Lewis (totally ruined the English version of the game), but "Kimi Ga Iru Kara" (Because You Are Here) by Sayuri Sugawara made me feel satisfied with the game.
Are you hesitant to play this game? Just buy it and try it out yourself. You won't regret spending $15 - even though this was gifted to me.

Still hoping for a dinosaur mode in Battlefield? You could keep dreaming, or you can pick this game up instead. I haven't played for very long, but here are my observations.
Here's how a typical deathmatch works out:
1. Everyone starts out seperated. If you're the dinosaurs, you're in for a buffet. If you're the mercinaries, then your best bet is to put away your pride and team up with the nearest person you see. When someone get pounced, you need to save them otherwise you're next. If you come across a T-rex...RUN. Use buildings and use the Rex's turning radius against it.
2. Eventually, all the humans end up grouped together near warehouses where there are meds and ammo. They typically die a lot less, but either the kills become too scarce to stay there or they become overrun.
3. Later in the game, the humans spread out in groups of about five or so and end up camping near ammo and med boxs scattered across the map (normally in 2-3 areas). Don't worry if you're the dinosaurs when the humans begin to camp. There are no invulnerable 'safe' spots for them to hide. If you employ hit-and-run tactics, you'll do fine.
And that's how a typical match works out. If all you play is COD and Battlefield, lemme just say you're in for hurt and there is a steep learning curve (no health regen, fixed classes, no killstreaks). The dinosaurs are also not OP, so don't expect to win because the game is well balanced. If you hate COD and Battlefield and remember better times in gaming, well, your skill wil transfer very well here. However, there is one COD skill that helps-training. If you're a true non-camping pro at zombies, then you know what this is. You can use the turning radius of most of the dinosaurs (raptors, carnosaurs, T-rex) against them. However, do not rely on this solely. This will only work at near point-blank range and you're open to be flanked. While camping is also a valid strategy, again this should not be relied on solely. You can easily be jumped by a raptor if you're alone and picked up by a flying type when roof camping. There are NO invunerable spots that I've seen used successfully. Cheap tactics can only go so far.
Overall, if you're a whinny casual gaming jerk stay away no one wants you. If you're a team-playing core gamer who relys on sound cues and doesn't like information spam or weapon unlock systems, welcome.

After a friend of mine just asked me about this game (since it's on sale atm), I thought it might be time for me to write a review.
If you like strategic FPS(and/or 3rd-person) games like Team Fortress 2 AND if you like Jurrasic Park... This game is just perfect for you.
Primal Carnage is a lot more amusing than I thought it would have been when I tryed it out for the first time.
I thought it would be in some way very serious.
This is not the case at all.
Primal Carnage has this great humor you also see in a game like TF2.
It doesn't take itself too serious and the weird things that can happen in this game makes it so much better to play.
When I play this game I'm mostly laughing all the time... Just as I am when I play TF2.
Things like flying ragdolls and weird death-posisitions brings a lot of humor into this game.
This game is not only about killing everyone you meet who isn't on your team.
Just as with TF2 this game is also a lot about strategy.
Teamwork is key in this game. If you play as 10 humans who aren't staying together as a team - then you're pretty doomed...
There are also different gamemodes - it's not
about killing and slaughtering...
I think some people might say that it is pretty OP that the dinosaurs have a third person view while the humans have a first person view.
I just think that this adds to the feeling of the game.
The feeling of being that lone human who haven't got any overview of the situation while knowing that a dinosaur might be watching you without you even knowing...
Or hearing and feeling the shaking in the ground from the footsteps of a T-rex, well knowing that soon it'll catch up with you.
I have had some very intense moments playing this game - but that is also why I love it.
If you don't like dinosaurs... Then it should be obvious you wouldn't enjoy this game with all it's neck-wrecking, acid-spitting and stamping tiny humans to death...
The only downside to this game is that
the servers don't show up in the server-list... But that's not harder to fix than restarting the game...

This is not a fun game.
It's not fun to watch your scavenger get stabbed as he tries to steal some food to feed his group of four. It's not fun to see your group dwindle down to two after your third survivor gets shot trying to get medical supplies for their sick. It's worse when the second commits suicide because they're so depressed from the death of their friend and only one character is left.
He's joined by one other about a week later, but they can't celebrate for long; they're just barely scraping by as it is.
Stealing and killing, once out of the question, is now routine, and I personally can't tell whether I want the war to be over or my survivors to just die. I'm not having fun; I just want it to be over.
And that's exactly why you should get this game. Because the first time you struggle through, you will feel yourself becoming morally numb and your humanity slipping away. You'll justify it in your head and feel heavy in your heart until you don't.
Fun is not the point. This game is an experience.

Most people talk about money investment, I'm going to talk about time in to fun out, because I can't be the only gamer desperately low on free time, who has to ditch entire genres because he doesn't even have the time to learn how to play a game, let alone sink hundreds of hours into it. I assume most people can afford 20 USD for a game a couple times a month, or at least one -- time is much more than money these days. Games are cheap.
Steam's lying with its 4.3 hours, I got 8, no question. I got 8 hours of flying around, like, Hell -- as Gat and/or Kinsey. I got 8 hours of weird weapons, a fun reskin of the insurance fraud side-activity, legendary weapons, and slightly more content than I even wanted any part of (you grind all the money to max the weapons, I don't have time) -- I got killer cutscenes, and one that was just damned hilarious (think Buffy's "Once More, With Feeling" episode).
If actually prefer this to Saint's Row IV, to be honest. What side-games are there bore me much, much less, and make no appearance at all in the 'main missions'. Just run around causing havok until you feel like crashing a wedding really, that's all there is to it, and I spent most my time flying around, collecting the nearly 1000 (I gave up at the last 100) soul orbs. There's no real need to, but I enjoyed the experience, and that's all I ask.
If you jsut plow thru it, the game really is about 4 hours or so, and it's still worth it even if you don't want to do all the mess around and/or grindy optional stuff. I did some, ignored quite a lot of it, and had a ball. But the main selling point is absolutely just the laughs the story has to offer, and can be gotten in as little as 4 hours.
The 'fun' density is thru the roof, and I'd take 8 hours of this for 20 USD over 20-40 hours of most games for free.
There's plenty of content to get 20 hours or so out of by the way, or just replay it (I might) -- but I won't try to sell it on that. What matters is a compact, enjoyable experience -- extra hours of 'this is all right' are a hindrance, not a help. I don't want fluff that keeps me from the good bits, but I guess it's nice to have fluff that you can totally ignore if you like.

I have mixed feelings about this game as a whole.
The story itself is short, but told decently well through amusing narrative and some funny missions here and there.
The side missions are awesome and fun as always, like hitting frat-demons through goals with a spanking-bat (whatever it is called) or just doing insurance fraud as a condemmed soul trying to decrease the years spent in hell.
The weapons are amazing and fun as always, just from the famous arm-chair, to (my personal fave) the flame-sword Uriel's edge, which casts a blazing inferno of death and destruction.
The powers are also quite good, love being able to summon an large demon to fight my battles for me, or just make demons bow to me with my god-aura.
But where this game really shines for me personally, is the flight and flight controls. I mean GOD DAMN! this is the smoothest, best programmed controls for any flight-system I have ever seen in gaming! this takes the gliding from Saints Row 4 and improves it by 1000 % at minimum.
I can have fun with this game, just flying around for hours, diving and narrowly flying inbetween buildings and through tunnels, getting the thrill of ultimate speed and pure control that reacts to the smallest twitch of the mouse.
I literally can't worship the flight-system in this game enough and I can honestly, and with no regret, recommend this game just for its amazing flight-controls.

Aiming is also fairly difficult, becuase the game camera is not always centered on your character, so your crosshair might not be where you want it when you need to use it.  Crosshair style 2 kind of fixes this, but sets your crosshair at a fixed radius, which might not be welcomed by some (including myself).
The concept behind this game is novel and fun during the easier stages, but when the difficulty ramps up, you begin to realize just how bad the controls are.

If you're reading this, don't keep scrolling down. Don't think about checking out other reviews. This game is worth your time. If you like metroidvania's, this is your favorite game for the next week. Even if you don't like Metroidvania's, you need to play this game.
Now that that is out of the way, let's talk about the actual game.
As I said, you need to buy this game. It's phenomenal. The music is amazing. It can range from a soft piano melody, to a heroic medieval sounding theme, down to a harpsichord violin mix. It's incredible. The range isn't all that's amazing. The sound design in this game is amazing. In some areas, you can feel a sense of dread, just from the sounds. Not even the music. The creature noises can be a cute slight squeaking to a terrifying gurgling/slurping noise, letting you know you are about to dread venturing through this area. Now past music, the art design of this game is extraordinary. It looks beautiful. It's so much different than the generally dark grey of the Souls games (which I will only mention a few times), with it's bright vivid greens and oranges in some areas, and it's darker tones of blue and black in others. The character design is great. Some are cute and adorable, whole others are horrendous freaks of nature and should go back to X-Files. That's just the normal enemies. The bosses are even better, and mixed with the combat, makes them fun to fight.
The combat. This game's fighting system feels good. It makes you satisfied when you kill something, be it a small bug flying around that just won't stop knocking you into the acid I HATE YOU CHARGING BUGS, or a huge boss trying to eat your soul and have your fecal matter as a drink. The combat is tight, fun, fast, and easy to learn. You get a few powers throughout the game that make your combat more interesting, as well as harder to master. These abilities, however, come one at a time, making sure you never feel overwhelmed with ne powerups, and also allowing you to practice and become proficient with one ability before introducing the next. This kind of system makes this game fun without rushing the player to move on already. You have simple moves, side to side attacks that can be preformed both to your right and left, an upward attack, and a downwards slash you can do in the air. All of these moves can be parried, by the way, making your attack deflect off the enemy and, when using the downward attack, makes you fly into the air for some more jump height. These simple moves are utilized so effectively and it makes the game that much more precise.
The bosses. Hollow Knight's bosses are by far my favorite in any game, except maybe *ahem*Cuphe-*cough*. Sorry about that. Anywho, the bosses are a huge part of this game. Usually, each area has two, maybe three bosses. Usually, only one is required to progress, while the other two are optional. Of course, there are exceptions to this, which allow you to completely skip bo csses and get to their guarded areas more "easily". The bosses are all unique, and really make you feel like you're in this dangerous place, filled with unpredictable foes. I know I use the 'huge range of stuff' analogy a lot, but I'm gonna keep using. You can go from fighting a group of three mantis lords to a giant jellyfish which you need help to defeat to a honourable knight just trying to defend his bounty. Each boss has a unique theme and in some cases, an optional powered up version of the same boss, sped up and with new attacks and abilities. I've barely scratched the surface when it comes to the bosses, but I'm running out of characters.
HUGE SPOILERS AHEAD, YOU HAVE BEEN WARNED
The story. You aren't intially aware of what the story of the game is, all you can be sure of is that you're a small, ferocious, yet admittedly adorable knight who ventures into the depths to fight some baddies. As you continue through the game, and encounter more NPCs, the story becomes more apparent. Some plague has taken over the residents of Hallownest, the kingdom the game takes place in. There's still no clue as to how you fit into this, though. But guess what? It all gets covered later on. As you continue, the game gives you story. You can go through the entire game, only ever talk to a few NPCs like shopkeepers, and get barely any snipbit of story, except for the ones forced onto you. You realized that the king tried containing this plague by creating lives, new bugs, to contain it. He failed time after time, all the corpses of his past mistakes falling into an endless abyss. Finally, he found a vessel worthy enough to contain it. the Hollow Knight. You slowly realize that your part in this story is to grow strong enough to become a new Hollow Knight. The king neglected you, too weak to do anything. But now, you are powerful, stronger than the Hollow Knight. And you take his place, living as the new Hollow Knight, containing the plague for more years to come. But that's just one ending. Play the game to figure out the rest, why don'tcha.

SPOILER LAND OVER. THANK YOU FOR VISITING.
So, that's Hollow Knight. I urge you to buy this game, only 15 dollars, and play it. 100% it. You owe yourself to do it. Thank you for reading, my friends. Good night.

I heard a
of bad things about Bioshock 2 when it came out so never bothered to pick it up. Years later when I grabbed the aging title in the steam sales, I got a lot of
remarks.  These comments were taken with a grain of salt, particularly given that some of the naysayers had never played the game. Nevertheless they weren't exactly wrong.
As it turned out, it's not actually a bad game. It's just not as good as Bioshock1, and if I had bought it full price I'd have been far less pleased.
There's no real innovation and frankly being a big slow clumpy metal man is a bit of a drag after having played the original mostly with stealth and traps. Yes, there are clyclone traps, but these were not all that useable in the end.
Throughout the game II found myself constantly having to pop health packs, switch weapons who’s ammo capacity was abysmal, and avoiding enemy fire with line of sight. This rendered the "gimmik" of Project Delta, the main protagonist, rather unusable. What's the point of having a nifty giant drill attack if using it will put you in close quarters out in the open losing a good chunk of your health, and the "ammo" runs out quicker than you can say “this all looks the same.”
There are a shockingly low number of enemy unit types. Sure,  there are a few minor variations on the models, but the actual types? Very few. There's little in the way of environment either, with many assets seemingly plucked straight from the original and no real care having gone into differentiating the new parts of rapture you’re visiting from those you entered in BS1. All in all, the story is decent, and the voice overs very good. What lets the game down is the
Not nearly enough thought was put into "is this actually FUN."
By the end, I was simply glad the whole thing was over (it's quite long if you explore) and I could move on to biosock infinite, so I made no moves towards the DLC, or multiplayer.
If you can get the game for less than 5 euro, it’s worth it if you liked bioshock 1. Turn the difficulty down to easy, and just mindlessly blast your way through while following the story.

I wish I could tell you something meaningful about the gameplay, the quality of the storyline, dialogue, etc, but the truth of the matter is that I've spent more time trying to fix the game to make it playable than I have spent actually playing it. My recommendation? Skip this game.

Quite a nice JRPG from Square that isn't a Final Fantasy.
Pros:
Above average JRPG graphics. Don't expect photorealism however. Some spells and abilities have great visuals though and same goes for invocations.
The combat system and the way strategy is designed make for some nice gameplay.
Unique characters, some of which with backstory to discover in side quests.
The main quest is long enough without being necesseraly tedious.
Unique cities, very varied to visit.
Con:
Character levelling is difficult to grasp since it's dependant entirely on the arts and abilities used in game, which are linked to the chosen weapon, with no real ingame help how to tailor and fine tune it. Player effect on character stats is indirect through equipment solely.
It's a JRPG so it's somewhat on railroads and definitely not an open world like Fallout or Skyrim. A lot more freedom of movement and action in this one than in many other JRPG but it's restrained at times.
If you follow the story, the ending is really expected. So the main story could definitely be improved.
I've overall spent a nice time roaming the various, very unique cities, all of them with a specific style and going through sidequests, not of a few of which are very humorous. The way combat is done may rebuke some, but it's got its advantages although it can be quite frustrating at times. I prefer to have more control on my characters in general, but that was far from an obstacle. Crafting offers some variety though looking for specific components can take some time. Recruiting unique squad leaders and unique/rare bosses make free exploration rewarding.
It's not the game of the century but definitely worth the investment to have a relaxed time in a JRPG by Square Enix. These guys know to make games.

Plotwise, I'd say Bioshock 2 is clearly inferior to the first game. The "twist" was rather weak, and a bit predictable, if you think about it by yourself.
Gameplaywise, it's a damn giant kick in the testicles compared to the first game. First, the weapons. While being more or less the same (pistol, shotgun, machinegun, sniper, grenade launcher), they are different enough to make you feel you're playing a Big Daddy rather than a small weakling, while having a similar behaviour to the first game's weapons. You'll get used to them pretty quickly (here, those are a rivet pistol, a small shotgun, a giant machinegun, a harpoon gun...). So yeah, enough new things to make the weapons interesting. Including a hacking tool. And a camera.
Second, the plasmids. They are also basically the same, while being improved in many ways. To begin with, no more horrifying animation of Jack stabbing a syringue in his arm. Second, upgraded plasmids are now behaving differently from non-upgraded plasmids. While in the first game, an upgraded plasmid just caused more damage, here, an upgraded plasmid can now be charged, or causes other effects.
Third, the Little Sister. Instead of killing the Big Daddy and saving/harvesting them immediately, you know have to escort them while they gather ADAM. Personally, I like those sequences, because they allow me to use weapons I would never usually use (such as the mines), but depending from your taste, you may find it tedious and boring.
Conclusion : a good sequel to an excellent game. Clearly not as impressive as Bioshock was, but it improves many things in the gameplay to makes the game enjoyable. Instead of being a weakling, you are now playing as the hunter, but don't think you'll steamroll everything in sight. The only flaw I could find is that you'll easily hit the ammo limit, so the game is less scary. I would recommend deactivating the Vita-Chamber and the objective arrow to have fun.
Now, let's talk about the flaws :
-10 hours and I finished it in Normal. Let's say 12 hours to finish it in Hard, given that I explored a lot.
-The escort sidequests can be really irritating, depending from you.
-You cannot upgrade all weapons. Depending from your opinion, it's a good thing or a bad thing.
-Compared to Bioshock's, the big bad isn't charismatic at all, and the story isn't really surprising either.
-There is no boss. Just some elite splicers, but no real boss.

I was mid playing the game and minimized and walked away for a good 10 minutes. When I came back my computer was literally unusable because it had reached 100% memory usuage. After more playing around I realized that if you minimize the game your "Non-paged pool" memory climbs at a rate of 10mb per second. After more playing around I also realized in non rendered zones it goes up by 2-3 mb per second, these are things such as the title screen and places like city maps and the world map, however in open areas that you can walk in the non paged pool does not change. All in all I have realized this game is not the most optomized thing seeing these pretty large memory leaks that do not stop until 100% memory usage.
That being said I enjoy the game, it is just issues like these may change how you feel about a game and possibly impact your decision on buying it.

Been waiting for a game like this to scratch my space trading/rpg/combat itch for some time! If you ever loved games like Freelancer or Escape Velocity, this is the game for you!
Pros:
- The 2D plane gameplay environment works great with the captial ship theme. Naval battles in space!
- Said combat is extremely satisfying, and deceptively nuanced. Many types of weapon classes, defence types and equiptment mods provide different ways to go about your battles. Cons:

Kinda con but not really:
- Mouse camera and aim movement has a negative acceleration issue, where faster mouse movement equates to slower in game response, and vise versa. HOWEVER, as stated above, the devs are AWESOME and responded to my concerns on Twitter within minutes, and even asked me to tell them what I think of the patch with an experimental option for it that came out within hours. Especially since I imagine most people use a contoller, and its easy to get used to the mouse issue. I'm gonna move it to a "kinda con" category. There we go, much better.
In short:
The game is awesome. The devs are awesome. The price is awesome. BUY IT!

Gameplay-wise This war of Mine is surprisingly addictive for such a simple game- "one-more-day" syndrome strikes switfly and mercilessly. Some weird designs give visible irk- chiefly the "one guy scavenges"-rule: if there is an empty construction yard with truckloads of stuff and you have 4 able survivors, why couldnt one stay guard and the rest just haul everything at once?
The sneaking is fun, although somewhat overshadowed by the strict time limit- if waiting for a guard to finish his cigarette takes half of the night, you really cant be that subtle. however, especially when skulking around in houses of people you really dont want to harm really makes you try and avoid confrontation at all costs.
Survival aspect of the game is well done, and the changes in the city, season and phases of the war force the player to adjust their plans and priorities.
The story is simplistic but interesting, and although the ending is rather abrupt, reaching it is far more satisfying than in many AAA games.
Given its gameplay values, low price and unique take at war, This War of Mine is highly recommendable both as a game and as an experience. If its on sale, you have no reason not to buy it.

1. Clarien
I hate the term "____ is pay to win." But this is the only instance where this term gets a pass. Clarien is OP. You can't look me straight into the eye and say a energy shield that does damage when going out and that you can summon at any time is not OP. She can also punish anything. Miss jab=combo, miss aerial=combo, miss anything=combo.

The ping in most games is so bad. For some reason this game has great ping when playing with a friend miles and miles away, but can't handle someone who may be like 1 mile away. Just why? Most of the matches are unplayable if your ping is bad.
3. Stereotypes
Now what I mean by this is you'll have this group of people you mostly encounter in online, this includes...
Clarien
Etalus players who make ice platforms and slide across all the time
Books to read
Players who use one combo and only one combo
People who are kinda good with a non-DLC charecter
People who are trying to get better
And finally, people who can't play the game cause of there awful ping... you won't see them often, but I am one so...
Conclusion:
This game is good in play style, creativity, and charecters. But those can't balance out the problems of online play Now you may say to yourself, "Why not just play offline?" Because it is so easy to start up combos and there just no fun. Fix Clarien, fix ping, balance out every charecter, and buff Maypul, he just can't stand his own ground anymore.
If you wanna buy it, go ahead. But don't say I didn't warn ya.

As a long time player of the Civilization series (I have been playing on and off since Civ 2) this game is about what I expected in its current state.  Comparing it to the full Civ V in its current form isnt really fair.  The trend in Civ games as of late has been to release the base product and begin working on DLCs that take at least a year or more to come to fruition and unlike most DLCs you get what you pay for...good old fashioned expansions.
This game is comperable to the base Civ V with many of the same issues it had in its base form.  If you are expecting the COMPLETE Civ experience I would wait.  While fund and certainly different from its predecessors it certainly does feel incomplete (which should come as a surprise to no one...).  If you are a Civ fanatic who has pumped more hours into V than you care to mention (like me) and are expecting a BASE version of Civ its well worth picking up IF you have the cash laying around.  Its definately a fresh look at the series.
I have no doubt that this game will hit the same level of success as its predecessor did.  It simply needs more work...but knowing its future potential I stil highly highly recommend you pick it up at some point.

I'd only recommend this game to FF fans only.
Long story short:
Storyline: Well written. Don't expect anything non-linear it's Final Fantasy we're talking here.
Graphics: Exceptional when you take into account the original release date of the game.
Combat: Combat is challenging. Not only because you need to adjust your tactics depending on the situation but also because the combat system is close to trash. When you switch speed to slow it is acceptable but on normal speed it is not shining at all. Forget about timing and precision because the system is not build with those two words in mind.
Apart from that even routine battles take too much time due to the opponent staggering mechanic where you have to fill a stagger-bar in order to inflict more damage to the enemies. The catch here is that very often it takes forever to build up even when you select the proper roles for each party member making even easy battles last way longer than they are supposed to.
Overall: A good game in overall but since most of the time you will be battling opponents utilizing a combat system which is pretty frustrating most of the time I wouldn't recommend this to anyone but FF fans like myself.

I'm running it on Win 10 x64 , the game doesn't run from Crysis folder , gives an error but works when i launch it from Steam , it looks great and runs fine , didn't used any fix still it worked unlike what i read before buying it and playing on win x64 ....
the game is really fun to play even now , i play it via my wireless controller but noticed there was no option to toggle crouch making it very difficult to walk and crouch simultaneously , i fixed it by this :
Open notepad and type:
con_restricted=0
cl_crouchToggle=1
And save as:
"System.cfg"
Rember to type the ". Otherwise, your file will be saved as a .txt file with the name System.cfg and will not work.
The "System.cfg" file must be placed in C> Program Files or Program Files(x86)>Steam>Steamapps>Crysis>Game>Config,
That's it , have fun :)

If you're a fan of controversy and exploitation films then you need look no further than Hatred, in fact you just might find yourself surprised to find underneath all the layers of controversy the media has placed around the game there's a solid foundation for a great isometric tactical shooter here.
Visually, the art style in the game is very well done and the effects for fire and explosions are very impressive. The environments are destruct-able as well and with a open-level for most levels it gets you the freedom to pick your course. There are linear levels but the themes of them are interesting and will keep you going. It's a pleasing visual and audio experience from beginning to end.
For difficulty it curiously has no normal. It goes straight from 'Easy' to 'Hard' and the masochist in me decided to pick Hard and once the army starts showing up, there was a little regret as I was holed up behind a counter keeping them at bay with a flame thrower seeing dozens of Red within Red circles on the map (the symbol for armed targets). In those times it reminds me fondly of the days I spent playing the earlier Grand Theft games where friends and I would take turns seeing who could hold out the longest against the army. In a surprising twist however, in later stages most civilians will actively seek a means to protect themselves and you'll find yourself not only fending off law enforcement but the populace as well.
As for the elephant in the room? I honestly feel like I've seen worse violence and gore in other games, I really don't understand why the game has people so up in arms for it's content. I guess the difference between Hatred and other games is it's an objective.
So in closing, ignore all the drama, this game is a visually impressive tactical shooting wonderland in a isometric view and I recommend playing it if you're a fan of shooters, or even just a fan of controversy because they're plenty to love here.

First off, I would like to state, this is a fantastic multiplayer game, if you’re a dinosaur vs human fan, or just a fan of one or the other.
But like most games, this one comes with a few issues, I would like to point out, which are:
1) Lack of oceanic servers (One-two)
2) Lack of players (Rarely only 5+ servers at max player cap)
3) Maps with lighting problems
4) Small pool of maps (Only 5)
5) Small pool of class's (5 per team)
6) Little customization (Only has few "Buyable" DLC skins)
Apart from those little complaints/issues, it is a worth wild game to try out, but in saying all of this, do not get your hopes up to high for the gameplay and the game mechanics, that still needs to be addressed, as well with the lack of server diversity.
On the plus side, the following reasons are why you should try this game anyway, which are:
1) Combat (Sound and animations)
2) Stealthing
3) Weather
4) Finishers (e.g., Carnotaurus, with its “head-butting”, making enemies fly like a bird)
5) Rag doll physics
6) Map design
7) Class design
8) First person perspective (Humans)
9) Third person perspective (Dinosaurs)
Besides that, it’s a thumbs up for me, if I had to put a rating on it, it would be a 7/10 for me, but if the issues marked above are dealt with, then it will become a 10/10 for me.

This is not a fun game.
It's not fun to watch your scavenger get stabbed as he tries to steal some food to feed his group of four. It's not fun to see your group dwindle down to two after your third survivor gets shot trying to get medical supplies for their sick. It's worse when the second commits suicide because they're so depressed from the death of their friend and only one character is left.
He's joined by one other about a week later, but they can't celebrate for long; they're just barely scraping by as it is.
Stealing and killing, once out of the question, is now routine, and I personally can't tell whether I want the war to be over or my survivors to just die. I'm not having fun; I just want it to be over.
And that's exactly why you should get this game. Because the first time you struggle through, you will feel yourself becoming morally numb and your humanity slipping away. You'll justify it in your head and feel heavy in your heart until you don't.
Fun is not the point. This game is an experience.

Eidos wrote an open letter to the fans acknowledging the fact that, obviously, the game isn't a real Hitman experience. By talking about the next game, they severly criticised Absolution in their own ways. Just take the time to look at it, you will understand clearly. I could make quotations, like I usually do, but the open letter says it all shortly enough:
Here's my personnal list of the things that have changed that I mostly dislike and "like"...
Negatives:
-Lack of map
-Lack of Sniper Case (Magic Pockets!)
-Can't close the light
-Can't close the doors
-No Keyholes
-The FOV is too low
-Over-the-Shoulder perspective (OTS and TPS are really different and the OTS view sucks. Great TPS : Max Payne, Hitman, GTA... Bad TPS with OTS: RE4, Hitman 5, Warframe...)
-You can't chose between TPS/FPS which you could do before.
-The levels are freaking small
-The level design is awefull (Garbages everywhere is the proof)
-Instinct (Bad because it's been implemented because of the small level design and removed the oh-so-usefull minimap. It's gimmicky and uninspired, they took the idea from DX:HR and Batman Arkham).
-Targeting System (Just like Splinter Cell, DX:HR and Batman. I want to play Hitman, not a bad copy and mashup of other games.)
-Checkpoints replaced the Save System. It's not an improvment. At all.
-The Score system ruins the game
-Lack of old-school scoring (Silent Assassin-Murderer-Psychopathe and many others.)
-QTE... nothing more to say.
-The disguise system just don't work.
-Bad AI. (Disguise system and if you kill someone and they didn't see you, they still know you're the killer for some reasons. Even if disguised...)
-You can't chose your weapons at the beginning of a mission
-Lack of weapon cache/collection
-You can't lean your body which you could do in Blood money. That was an improvement from other games. Absolution regressed.
"Postitives"
+Graphics (Light effects, crowd generator)
+Voice acting (If only the story was good...)
+You can drag people with the fibre wire
+You can hide 2 bodies in garbages (whch can be found everywhere because of the bad level design) and closets.
+Fake arrest
+The contracts mode was a great idea. (But not the scoring system)
The thing to say is that these "Improvements" could have been implemented even within a classic Hitman style of gameplay with better and bigger levels anyway...
"Neutral"
=The cover System (Still, it make the game like all other TPS...)
=Throwing objects (But you could throw coins in Blood Money...)

Gat Out of Hell is a standalone Saints Row adventure taking place right after SR4. The Boss has been dragged to the depths of Hell by a demonic Ouiji board, and it's up to Gat and Kinzie to rescue you. Right away you can tell they're continuing to throw any semblance of realism out the window. I'm down for that.
It's refreshing to see entirely new content. Only problem is it's all in the same hell environment. The perma-apocalyptic evening look with everything adorned in red is really hard on the eyes, and I really would have liked for a way to change the skies. The game world also looks somewhat emptyish, as many of the small details to decorate the city are gone. Understandably it's very time-consuming to craft such environments, but it can't be denied this is a step down. The game world has been drastically reduced to compared to Steelport. I don't mind this change, but since the activity density and decorations haven't been more compacted either, the game is much smaller in scope than before.
The graphics engine looks much the same as SR3 and 4. There's not much music, but it does have an amusing musical number. While I get what they were going for, I feel they needed a better melody for that part in order to make it memorable. Right now I don't remember how the tune or lyrics went at all.
Superpowers make a return, but they are handled differently. You can actually fly this time around, but it's awkward and it takes some getting used to. Sure beats carjacking I guess, which still exists for some reason. They give you your first power within minutes of playing, which, much like SR4, seems like a strange decision. It's difficult to appreciate the city when I am constantly tempted to use my powers to zip all over the place.
The story segments and voice acting, what little there was, were great. I love the writers, the voice actors, and the cut scenes. I could play a whole Saints Row game if it was nothing but these scenes. They just need more of them, and I hope that there's a lot of story for SR5 if and when it comes out.
To advance the story, you must do random activities to cause mayhem in the streets, thus increasing your hellraising bar up top. Once it's full, you get to challenge the boss and beat the game. It's a remarkably simple game in this regard. How you get to that point it entirely up to you. This mirrors SR4's "breaking the simulation" with activities except that in here you pretty much need to do activities to advance the game.
The activities themselves are all right. They range from shooting to flying all over the place. I just wish there was more context to them other than "cause mayhem." I would like this game much more with less activities and more story. Or at least merge some of the activities into one to make them longer, if the story segments need to be spaced out more.
Data clusters make a return in the form of soul clusters, and you use them much in the same way to upgrade your powers. Despite looking cool, I didn't feel as badass with these powers like I did in SR4 (or even SR3's DLC). I guess in a world where everything on fire, you don't stand out as much brandishing your own hellish powers.
The weapons are mostly different this time around. One weapon in particular, the chair, is a hoot to use, though it doesn't aim very high, and has long animation times.
Gat Out of Hell boasts Multiple endings, all of which branch at the very end. Since you can't redo story missions in this game, much like other SR games, I recommend you keep a separate save before beating the game.
I can't deny that they put a lot of work into Gat, but overall it just felt... empty. As a standalone game it's all right, but it's compltely overshadowed by the previous games before it. I can't really recommend it at full price, but if you find a good sale, sure why not. I give this game a 6.5/10.

Many features present in previous Saints Row titles are discarded, like the customization options for both the character and vehicles. That however helps lean it towards a nice polished style and focused features to go through for the game itself.
The main story should not take more than 3 or 4 hours to complete, unless you waim for some completionist levels with the area first - pushing it at most to 7 or 8 hours in length, barring the longer challenges.
The main game mechanic is akin to the Saints Row 4 superpowers, and makes for a rather enjoyable game despite its overpowered and seemingly unbalanced nature. But that's part of the fun.
If I have to fault anything it is the lack of content - it is short. Other than that, it is a good addition to the franchise. If only a bit short and lacking some of the more expansive features in previous titles.
Worth it in my opinion, just not quite at the face-value cost.

Well it was nice of the powers that be to give away the PC remastered version for free (assuming you have the 2007 original). There are still a few glitches despite several patches, but it works and the gameplay is unchanged. As for the remastered visuals: very meh. It now looks like a nine-year old PC game rather than a nine-year-old console game. The low-res shaders that made every surface look like it was smeared with vaseline are updated, as are some of the textures and lighting effects. As usual with Unreal engine games on PC, it still looks like you've forgotten to turn up the settings even when maxed out.
Even the remaster pales in comparison to the first Crysis, released only a month after the original. Still, the console crowd are typically ecstatic about paying £30 for this kind of thing and it's nice to see them happy as a dumb dog with a chew toy: they'll be able to do it again in a few years when they re-re-release it for the updated consoles.
Anyway, the same old Bioshock: not bad but totally overrated. Great start, no new ideas after level 3 (of 10), very repetitive, and made me hate pipemania.

Unfortunately, the crucial multiplayer for which the game was once highly praised has long since died away.
Return to Castle Wolfenstein falls short for most players with only its mediocre single-player.

Firstly, aside from issues with crashing and so on. the game is fantastic. I'm so glad that 2K gave a free copy of the Remastered editions for everyone who owned the original titles. The game is just as fun and immersive as i remember.
So, now the problems...
My absolute biggest issue was the constant crashing, if you play this i strongly urge you to hit the quick save button like every 5 minutes or so. Now there are some fixes out there people have suggested and i will place them below this segment. But please note that i had finished the game before i found these fixes online and never got to try them out so i cannot vouch for them. But if they help then great.
1) Platform Update for Windows 7 (General Crash Fix)
Now if you have a legit version of Windows 7 and keep relatively up to date with windows updates, then more than likely you have this update installed already. (but check by going into Windows update > View update history > See installed updates and type in the search bar at the top right "KB2670838")
if it appears then you have it installed, if not then install it now.
If you do not have the update installed then download it here:
2) Run as... (Small Crash Fix)
ok, this i hate to recommend but people have said that it works.
Locate your Bioshock.exe file in which ever drive you have the game installed.
typically: C:\Program Files (x86)\Steam\steamapps\common\BioshockRemastered\Builds\Final\Bioshock.exe
Once you see the .exe file right click it and go "Properties" then "Compatibility" and tick:
"Run in 640x480 screen resolution" and
"Run this program as an administrator"
This will not set the in-games resolution to 480p but your desktop resolution.
Lastly be sure to launch from the .exe file from now on and NOT from steam.
For quick access to the .exe, hold CTRL + SHIFT and drag the file to the desktop to create a shortcut the file.
So basically that's all i am here to say. Yes these problems should not exsist and should be corrected. but i specifically cannot complain as i recieved the 2 games for free.
, it's a risk but at the discounted price it's not a huge loss. however the choice is still yours.
Ultimately this is your choice, i cannot tell you what to do and i cannot tell you how to spend your money. However i can tell you my experiences and some quick fix info that i found to help you get it running better however i can (should you choose to purcahse the game).

Has everything a Wolfenstein game should have: guns, girls, destructible chairs, zombies, random enemy spawns, creepy tombs, sausage, booby traps, castles, secret rooms, treasure, hard bosses, jump scares, occult horror, cool weapons, Wilhelm screams, spooky skeletons, and great level design.
As the Germans research any and every weapon that might give them an advantage over the allies during WWII, the SS's Paranormal Division stumbles upon the legendary tomb of Heinrich I at Castle Wolfenstein.  Immediately, the Allies send their best agents from the fictional Office of Secret Actions (OSA) to investigate the dig site at Wolfenstein.  Unfortunately, the OSA spies are captured and tortured.  Players take the role of B.J. Blaskowitcz, one of the captured spies.  After escaping Wolfenstein and the Heinrich archaeological dig deemed unimportant for the time being, the OSA send Blaskowicz on various missions to sabotage the Paranormal Divisions's other efforts across Europe.  As he gathers intelligence from his travels, B.J. uncovers the significance of Wolfenstein and the SS's plan for Heinrich I.
RtCW simultaneosly preserves and innovates its lineage.  This is a first person shooter with a great balance between gameplay and story.  Levels appear linear, but further investigation reveals secret levers, buttons, walls that can be destroyed, and other hidden switches that can lead to shortcuts, treasure to increase your score, or secret weapon caches.  Thus while the main goal is to complete the level, RtCW is a fun game just to look around in since you'll never know what you'll find.  In terms of shooting mechanics, their are crouch and lean mechanics giving the game a tactical approach.  Indeed, a stealth approach (silenced weapons, backstabs, minimal offensive fire) is advised and required for some portions of the game.  When the bullet start to fly though, there is a hefty arsenal of tools to employ.  SMG's, pistols, rifles, flamethrowers, rocket launchers, and other weaponry all have their uses.  Every weapons has different stopping power and ammo availibility, so you can choose to save your Thompson for tougher enemies or rely on the weaker but more available German weapons.  I almost consider RtCW to be survival horror at times because many of the supernatural enemies you will fight in the game take a lot of bullets to put down.  The segments with the X-Creatures are particularly tense in this regard.  There is also some puzzle solving and a few logic puzzles.
RtCW is a single player experience with the only game mode being the campaign.  There are mods that can make it co-op (which would be pretty cool) but I did not try them.  That being said, the five or so campaign missions themselves can take quite a while to complete.  Each mission has 4-7 chapters that took me on average a half-hour to complete probably.  The AI can be brutal at times even on normal and some sections are trial and error.  But there are some truly memorable moments here, such as moving through the Saxon tombs in the beginning of the game or later on infiltrating the X-Labs.
Old games do not always translate well but I find RtCW to be one of the best.  The dialogue is great, the music bold and brash but also quite intimidating at times.  The tomb segments are some of my favorites, with dim lighting, armored skeletons, and eery noises.  You certainly do not start this game expecting it to get creepy but it sure does.  Enemies are well animated with only the death animations a little stiff for humans.  The Quake engine may be old, but boy does it hold up here.  Lighting and sound are both excellent and except for the occasional rough looking texture, the game has great atmosphere.
RtCW is a testament to the timelessness of shooters from around the turn of the century.  Despite it's age, it manages to capture the spirit of Wolfenstein and always amps up the action when you least expect it.  Grab your MP40 and return to Wolfenstein in this glorious reboot of the FPS that some consider pioneered the genre.

Compared to previous MTG games that have been released over the years, I'd say Magic Duels is a step in the right direction.
Unfortunately, it's a very clumsy, unbalanced step that ends up dropping the series into a ditch.
Sure, you can now create your very own decks from scratch, but unless you pay up you're going to struggle to find a deck that actually works. Most of the time, your decks wont work. Since you don't have any good cards. And that "Medium" difficulty AI just played his third foil planeswalker. And has two Soulblade Djinn's. And two weird wyvern things that buff other flying monsters that you can't even see in the card collection, so had no way of knowing that your opponent was going to play them.
Yep, a completely fair match to your band of 2/1 tern's and merfolk that have no abilities.
The Deck Wizard doesn't help much either. Sure, it tries to do good by telling you some good strategies, but then it gives you the option of having to choose from only 5 cards at a time, with cards that the Wizard deems 'relevant.' Also, the Wizard limits the number of cards you get to choose in each step. Want a large number of enchantments for this deck about buffing creatures with enchantments? Too bad, you can only have six. Want a lot of spells for your burn deck? Nope, can't have too many of those. Need to save room for more Goblin Pikemen.
It leads to most archetype decks being unbalanced and rife with issues that you can't fix, because the game doesn't let you. Which is bad, since archetype quests are the most common quest type, and are the only way of making more than 15 coins per battle with the AI.
Coming back to the issue of the AI, it likes to stuff the same cards into its decks over and over. This is especially true in Medium difficulty battles, which I've found to be harder than the Hard difficulty. Whereas the Hard AI does actually try to perform complex, unique strategies with its cards (even if that means filling its deck with nothing but legendaries and rares), the Medium AI enjoys nothing more than playing the same cheap cards over and over with the sole intention of making the player miserable.
It plays Foundry of the Consuls multiple times almost without fail, even if it isn't playing an artifact deck, simply to summon those 1/1 Thopters which are almost as annoying to deal with as TF2's mini-sentries. It loves playing Perilous Myr's early in the game to prevent you from doing anything without losing your whole field. It loves playing Languish when you think you're actually winning for once. Every action the player makes, it loves suddenly having just the right card to counter that move.
And yet it still isn't smart enough to play Yeva's Forcemage /before/ attacking, to utilize the buff it gives.
There are a ton of other issues lying around that I haven't covered here, and so the only way I can recommend this game to anyone is if they're looking for a way of learning how to play MTG without having to shell out a lot of money for a deck that they might not even like.
I can't even recommend it as a way of checking out what new cards have been released, what with how few cards are shown in the collection and how you might as well just buy physical boosters, since they give you almost thrice as many cards as the digital packs.

A wonderful sequel to the first BioShock but this time developed by 2K. BioShock 2 does not really offer anything new; it just improves upon the first game. It is an interesting concept to put the player into the shoes of a Big Daddy - it should be mentioned that it is an alpha version, though, so it's not like you are an all powerful being incapable of dying.
Still, it is a nice touch as you can finally use a Big Daddy's drill and while in the prequel you just killed these monstrous creatures to get hold of the little girls now you have to protect the children while they harvest ADAM from the fallen citizens of Rapture. Again, these encounters are optional but well worth the trouble. And once you completed all harvests the Big Sister appears. This is an addition to the boss battles and while the Big Daddies are slow their sisters are much faster so you need to use different tactics.
Other than the harvest part the gameplay remains similar. You keep progressing further and while the game is linear you should look behind every door and open every box to find loot and the good-old audio diaries that further explain the background. Morality choices return but with greater impact and this time you have 3 endings available. Hacking can be done from the distance by shooting darts into the target objects and instead of taking pictures you have a camera that can record your battles with your foes. Again, recording here results in bonuses against the various types of enemies.
Many plasmid types return but there are new additions to an already varied rooster and levelling up them offers better bonuses. We now have multiplayer but personally I found it just average - I guess this was the usual attempt to lengthen the game's replayability but the single player offers at least 3 playthroughs so I believe it was unnecessary. I do not think anybody plays multiplayer anymore, either.
This is the first BioShock that comes with a DLC. On Steam the DLC is part of the game and it should be mentioned that they got rid of GFWL (good riddance!) so we should not bother with this, thank god. Minerva's Den offers us a completely new plot - again, we play as an Alpha Series Big Daddy - and we get a deeper insight into the city's inner workings.
BioShock 2 is an example of what a true sequel should be. It improves upon an already very good BioShock 1, thus, it feels like as if we continued the story where we left off and did not stop playing BioShock.

Now, what I feel the game needs to work on.
-Progression system
-Some sort of personalization(not necessarily a char creator)
-Active blocking. I would like to see a more active blocking system that prevents the use of spells, but allows you to mitigate incoming projectiles(not AOE or skills raining down on you). I am usually quite lazy at writing long articles but after playing this game, I just can't help but to write it a positive review to do the game justice. Seriously, this is a VERY HIGH quality SPRG and the PC ver of the game was made in year 09. Right now it's sold for 13$, but imo, after playing this game and having a pretty throughout exploration of its features myself, i'd price it $40-45+ by today's standard.
A neutral comment from me after playing this game is that; this game is an extremely fine (text book quality) sample on what a good game is like and what 'bad' designs are - The features are just that apparent/distinct.
Before I go into what I like the most, let's start with the fundamentals;
- The plot and chac designs aren't perfect/have flaws but definitely platable, at the very least i'm confident to say it won't make you feel unpleasant/cringe.
- Music is definitely good. Combined with the at times intense combat atmosphere, it really did make me grit my teeth really hard on multiple occasions.
- Content of this game is def more than enough to satisfy you. So many quests awaits that the more casual players might want to cut some slack from it. Dw, the game has great freedom when it comes to difficulty and content length control, by the player/according to how much you've played.
- Feel free to choose between japanese and english yourself. I was using japanese voice + english subtitle no problem, though the choice of words/translation for both languages don't match all the time but well, if you're THAT picky, surely just by listening is fine with you.
Now let's jump to the stuff that I appreciate the most of this game;
First and foremost, its gameplay/combat.
-
. It is really challenging and fun. You will not get tired of it for most of the times, unless you make yourself grind the same type of enemies over and over again then in that case, well, the game isn't a doctor specialized at curing suicidal people with the tendency to bore themselves to death
.
(of course you can still steamroll most enemies once you really outclass them, but the game also has EX bosses for the really hardcores and a hard mode for new game+ for the really really hardcores).
-
. The use of the QTE system here actually keeps the game engaging/interactive at all times, it is not there for fillers but a successful QTE sequence can mean victory/defeat in a disadvantageous fight.
-
. It feels way more awesome than just a few dudes fighting a few monsters. Now you have a dozen of people fighting a few groups of enemies at the same time. Atmosphere aside, game mecahnics wise it also frees up space for customization. Even though you control by the army by 'squad'/'union', each member of your band of heroes is hand picked and developed by you. That includes a certain degree of control over their gear, a certain degree over their class progress and a closer control over their skill progress. Therefore, despite you'll have to buch 3 to 5 of them into a group most of the times, there is still a very distinct sense of character on personal level for each member; you know each of them have different skills and different stats and different uses because you have to participate in growing/crafting each of them (in order to make them as useful as you'd like).
-
But for the good part, it is thanks to the high degree of customization that allows this game to become really strategic than it already is. Sometimes, figuring out the attack patern or capability of bosses just isn't enough, to earch each/every inch of advantage you need for a fight, players must try and min max a bit with its 'formation' and 'union composition' system. Say, some bosses will punish you heavily with AOE attacks so any formation that makes your union members bunching up is bad, spreading too far however will result in lower damage and other stuff which will lead to your defeat in a drag-out fight. How to turn the fight around is totally up to the players; grind more for better gear? Be stubborn and try different compositions out? Or seek help from the vast resources online? Many of us had bled before  you!
This last part is about the 'bad stuff' of the game -_- parts that I am really not happy with. However, thanks to the genuis of this game's community/fan base, most of them can be fixed/circumvent
.
- The game can be extremely and unnecessarily grindy - punish players by having monsters not always spawning and drops with frustrating drop rate. Totally anti fun after a while (that's why after 70% into the game, I decided I want to use the help from TLR planner and have 100% drop rate at all times and telling me if the rare spawn i need to hunt is currently in the map or I need to refresh it).
- The game in its natural state DIDN'T TELL YOU A DAMN. Seriously, there are a few mechanics in this game; Morale, Combat options, Class, friendly leaders' weapon upgrades, Formation upgrade, Skills upgrade, new skills etc. Other than 'Morale' and the basics of 'Combat option',
, and srsly, all of them are pretty damn crucial.
, some more important battle commands only appear when you have say, 'guardian' or 'assassin' class leaders in your union, of coz, the game doesn't tell you they have these classes nor the ways to acquire them... why would they? I have no idea. Even by utilizing the wikia, you still can't get all the infos you need such as the more specific stats (I.E, the game didn't mention what is 'katana 19' at all but guess what? you need that for the assassin class). In this scenario you'll need help from both the wikia and 3rd party softwares like the TLR planner mentioned above or maybe even the TLR trainer, which has far too much convenient cheat options :0)
And srsly, i think at least half of them are just unnecessarily overly detailed/complex. They will affect you when you are starting to really enjoy the game but get frustrated coz you seem to be performing less efficient as the difficulty raises only to find out it is bcoz the game didn't teach/tell you a damn on many of the more important features.
In conclusion; the game is really fun, this price is a killer, get it now if you're a fan of SRPG games. Please read the wikia while you're playing it, it will mean a lot to your actual gameplay experience.

Pretty much the best mix between MtG Online and Duels of the Planeswalker series.  This version has a fairly seamless pace between the turns as it only stops the gameplay when you tell it to or when you have an ability or instant available.  The graphics are a good level without being too strong (interrupting the gameplay) like DotP or none at all like MtGO.  It is freemium like Hearthstone so you can get almost all of the cards if you splurge on boosters but I prefer to unlock them through the daily quests as it gives something to work towards and is similiar to building up your collection slowly like as a kid.  The ranking system is okay but the online matches themselves can create great drama and situations.  The AI matches are a good place to test decks and the campaign was very fun, albeit somewhat short.  The card selection is medium.  Much higher than DotP but much lower than MtG Online.  It has more than Hearthstone, or did until the recent expansion, so there's less of expectation strategies in the meta game.  So far, Duels has been my best experience playing Magic in a non-card format.

Obviously, if you have never played Magic then this game may not be for you.  I wouldn't know how to approach it  unbiased as just an online card game that I've never played as I have been playing Magic for a long time.  I have played a lot of Hearthstone and can tell you that that game may be better to new players as it is more simple on the surface but still very competitive.  However, if you can appreciate the details and art/lore of Magic then I would still try it and at least see how you like it.  It is a free game after all....and a very good one at that.

A mash-up of Rampage by Uwe Boll featuring Nathan Explosion, with bonus content free for everyone to enjoy, tasteless and childish articles by gaming journalism "professionals". If you're a fan of controversy and exploitation films then you need look no further than Hatred, in fact you just might find yourself surprised to find underneath all the layers of controversy the media has placed around the game there's a solid foundation for a great isometric tactical shooter here.
Visually, the art style in the game is very well done and the effects for fire and explosions are very impressive. The environments are destruct-able as well and with a open-level for most levels it gets you the freedom to pick your course. There are linear levels but the themes of them are interesting and will keep you going. It's a pleasing visual and audio experience from beginning to end.
For difficulty it curiously has no normal. It goes straight from 'Easy' to 'Hard' and the masochist in me decided to pick Hard and once the army starts showing up, there was a little regret as I was holed up behind a counter keeping them at bay with a flame thrower seeing dozens of Red within Red circles on the map (the symbol for armed targets). In those times it reminds me fondly of the days I spent playing the earlier Grand Theft games where friends and I would take turns seeing who could hold out the longest against the army. In a surprising twist however, in later stages most civilians will actively seek a means to protect themselves and you'll find yourself not only fending off law enforcement but the populace as well.
As for the elephant in the room? I honestly feel like I've seen worse violence and gore in other games, I really don't understand why the game has people so up in arms for it's content. I guess the difference between Hatred and other games is it's an objective.
So in closing, ignore all the drama, this game is a visually impressive tactical shooting wonderland in a isometric view and I recommend playing it if you're a fan of shooters, or even just a fan of controversy because they're plenty to love here.

Perhaps the FF tropes of characters (I hear that there has been an infestation of broody, aloof, emo protags) has gotten to the point that people are tired but, coming from a new persepctive, I didn't find Lightning grating. While the rest of the cast varied none struck me as awful (by the end, after characters arcs) as people like to rant about.
Worth giving it a go if you like RPGs, especially if you aren't a hardcore FF / JRPG type.
