preface: I play the game in offline mode most of the time; actually been playing for over 10 hours as of writing
It's as awful as people say. I don't feel like I have to give many complex reasons. I'll focus on one: the menus in battles.
Even the MENUS are sluggish. Essentially, there are no actions that execute after selecting commands from the main combat menu; there is always at least one sub menu. For example, the "Attack" command will lead to a sub-menu displaying the "Attack" and "Blitz" commands. After selecting the command, you then choose from a list of enemies in another sub-menu to target, which finalizes the actions of a leader character until the ATB refills. Even Auto-attack requires you to choose a target.
EVERY MENU HAS A LOAD TIME. There is a fancy animation that plays every time a new sub-menu is opened. You can not, say, input a series of commands from the main menu like down-select-select-down-select and know you'll attack with the basic Attack command to the second closest enemy. Instead, you will only get to the first or second sub menu because the game DOES NOT REGISTER INPUTS WHILE NEW SUB-MENUS LOAD. I am explaining this in extreme detail because it is a hard concept to understand; in a menu-based RPG, how can there be periods of dead input between selections? It's because the game wants to play its fancy animations at the detriment to all gameplay. Even the menus need to sparkle and dance for a half-second after each input, making the game's already glacial pace artificially pad in the most inconcievably basic level. Every other FF game I can think of lets you finesse the ATB system by remembering input sequences for oft-used commands. In this game, you have to button mash just to execute an auto attack (when games released before it have a toggle between auto- and manual-battle, this is especially inexcusable; the auto-battle isn't very automatic).
tl;dr THE MENUS ARE LAGGY IN AN RPG WITH MENU BASED COMBAT
I don't wanna write 10 paragraphs about why this game is bad in every detail because it would be an essay. It's just fundamentally, deeply flawed, down to the damn menus.

Definitely one of the best games in my life. Though I finished the game but I still play it. Final Fantasy XIII is a JRPG type game where character development matters more. You need to fight against many enemies to gain a so called Crystarium points. There are 6 characters in the game and you can choose which 3 characters would you take to battle. Beating enemies will give all characters the same Crystarium points. The story is very linear until you reach chapter 11. At chapter 11 you will get to Gran Pulse that is sorrunded with many Cie'th Stones that grant you side mission. There are a total of 60 side missions. Their difficulty is from E-A. Once you defeat Orphan (the final and not the hardest boss) you will grant access to Crystarium level 5 where you can max out all your characters and face Vercigentorix (the toughest boss in the game). The battle system is a paradigm system. There are a total of 6 paradigms: Commando, Ravager, Sentinel, Synergist, Saboteur and Medic roles. You can create 6 different paradigms. During the battle you need to switch between paradigms by using the TAB button on your keyboard. Once you are used to it it can be quite a fun. Mouse is supported in the game for camera control. Game audio is available in English and Japanese. Among the Final Fantasy XIII series I would rate this game as 10/9.

Rivals of Aether’s greatest success was speaking to the young, imaginative child I once was. I recall fondly many instances in my youth when I was brimming with love for and inspiration from wild characters I would see in cartoons or video games. Many afternoons were spent playing pretend, as I embodied a righteous warrior of some kind with spectacular abilities only my youthful and energetic brain could visualize.
This game’s roster feels like an extension of that creativity, as if I, as a young child, were asked to come up with ideas for new and inventive characters. To what source of inspiration would I have defaulted? Clearly I would have put animals and the very elements of nature themselves together into a brawl so epic only I could truly appreciate the awesomeness and majesty of this clash.
Thankfully, Rivals of Aether had more care and work go into making it a good game, rather than smashing two cool ideas together and calling it a day. Of note is how each character finds a successful balance between feeling both fresh and familiar. I can liken certain moves to SSB characters and see their implementation in my mind’s eye, as I’ve seen and performed them myself countless times. But the way these abilities and character designs are remixed give this game a life all its own.
As a fighting game, Rivals of Aether’s endgame is the quest to achieve mastery of the game’s system or a particular character. So while I did not achieve mastery of any character, I did try out all of the game’s available modes. I have played a healthy amount of time as each and every character on the roster, both in the required sections of the story mode and in both local and online multiplayer. When I tried playing online, I got my♥♥♥♥♥kicked, hard. However, I think that goes to show more how technical this game can be, offering pros and newbies alike an experience that can be enjoyable, whether your goal is to play casually or competitively.
As a game trying to use SSB as a jumping off point, I think Rivals of Aether succeeds fairly well. Although I am constantly aware that I am playing what is tantamount to a “smash clone”, the uniqueness of this game’s roster and willingness to cultivate precise and fun systems shows that it has potential as more than just a SSB style game. The inclusion of in-game training tools also shows that the developer is willing to take a good idea and sharpen it to its perfect form.
For anyone with a SSB itch on the PC or console, I highly recommend this game. Rivals of Aether has provided me with a strong replacement for SSB4, allowing me to enjoy the platform fighter genre with a system that is responsive and available anywhere I have a PC.

A bland experience with nothing really interesting to offer made even worse by the absolutely infuriating interface, that seems made by people who only enjoy playing console games and know nothing of how to design for someone using a mouse and keyboard (one basic example: hotkeys are not rebindable).
Trade routes will irritate you into ragequitting and wonders are less wonderful than getting stabbed in the eye. Small outposts will pop up right where you were planning to build your new city (every single time) and are as useful as a bag of dead kittens. Aliens are not really anything but raging barbarians and the terrain isn't alien; it's just a retextured Earth. Factions have no personality at all, and diplomacy might as well be cut out of the game.
The AI (both aliens and other factions) will mindlessly send their units into range of your cities/artillery without ever having a chance of doing damage, and will thereby lose his units one by one. All fighting can be won by letting the AI mess up everything for itself and then mop up the leftovers. Best way of playing is therefore to instantly declare war on every single AI the moment it spawns in the game. Just wait and don't make peace and they will give you their second city as a peaceoffering as long as you have a couple of marines. They will never recover from this.
A better AI would be a bowl of soup, because then I would at least get something warm to eat while not being challenged by this game. And no, the hard settings where the game simply gives the AI gigantic bonuses and free units are not any more fun. I want a challenge on an (almost) level playing field, not just an opponent who cheats.
The game mechanics are broken beyond repair and this seems like it was the design all along. An example of this is city razing. The game mechanic for winning a domination victory is by controlling all the capital cities. So to make sure this can be done, those cities are indestructible. It doesn't matter how badly placed the city is (and every single AI city is placed using a blindfold), you have to keep playing with it. And no, Firaxis does not want you to at least have the option to allow razing.
As the last thing, I would just like to mention the UI again. Oh how it will make even the most tranquil of souls rage. All the info is hidden and at the start of every turn all manner of popups explode onto the screen demanding your immediate attention. Did you just get a peace offer from [bland AI faction 2] wherein they offered you [randomly named city X]? Well then you have to decide right now whether or not you want that city. No, you may not take the time to find out who out of the 8 civs you are figting just offered you a deal, and no, you may not check out the location of the city, you were offered. Choose now.
Were you following an AI unit around the fog of war trying to kill it. Well too bad for you, because while the AI always knows which bit of FoW you moved into, you cannot get this information unless you had the screen centered on the enemy unit when you ended your turn and even then you are out of luck because forced popups will obscure everything. Want to know why an opponent does anything diplomacy-related, well then you have to guess, because the indicators in the game just shows you the "now factors" as in AI 1 likes you now because he likes you now. It does not translate into AI 1 likes you now, so he will be more inclined to liking you in a little while. No matter if he is your soul mate, he will stab you in the eye the moment he decides that eye-stabbing is modern.
Don't buy it. Not even when it is on sale for 1€.

Just played the free weekend leading up to the first expansion and nothing has changed.
To win you just have to declare war on everyone the moment they spawn and build a second city and a few troops, that is it. If you just keep refusing any peace offers you get, all the AI players will give you their second city the moment they have it. This is my first JRPG and I liked it. It was different from any other games I've played. Its combat system is quite different. In western RPGs such as Witcher 3, battle is real time. You can explore and then get into a battle with someone and then fight and win and go back to exploring, or can even run away in the middle of a fight and go back to exploration seamlessly. But in this game, you explore and then when you get into a fight with someone, you enter the battle mode, which is totally different from exploration. You can't run away in the middle of a battle. It will go on until the fight ends.
Exploration in this game is very limited. It has been called a corridor simulator for good reasons, but it's not necessarily a bad thing. Some of the environments are quite beautiful, but it's mostly look-but-don't-touch.
Battle is somewhat turn based, but not exactly. In turned based games or game modes you wait for your turn. But instead of waiting for your turn, in the battles of this game, you wait for something called your ATB meter to fill up. When it fills up, you can fight, which consumes your meter. So again you wait for it to fill up and then fight. That's a very simplistic explanation because the battle system of this game has quite a bit of depth to it and I really enjoyed it. It was refreshing.
When it comes to role-playing, the thing that stands out most from western RPGs is that you can play multiple roles at the same time. And you can change between those roles within an on going battle. For example one offensive role is called Commando and you do mostly physical damage with it. But then if you developed your character as a medic, you can switch to that role mid battle and you can heal yourself and your allies and once done, you can switch back to Commando.
I was enjoying the game till Chapter 11. But Chapter 12 and Chapter 13 were dull and frustrating. There is no story progressoin. They filled the last two chapters of the game with bosses. Even some other enemies were so tough they felt like bosses. It kind of left a bad taste in my mouth. But don't get me wrong, I am still glad I played it because up to Chapter 11 the game is quite fun. The final story progression is after the final boss battle. So they could have removed chapter 12 and chapter 13 completely, and just put the final boss battle at the end of chapter 11. It would have been a much better game. I am glad I finished it and I recommend it. It's a lot of fun.

Games published by Square Enix are often good.
was a masterpiece and although
had a lot of wasted potential, it was still worth the playthrough. This chapter on agent 47's life, however, is both good and bad.
was probably my first experience with a true stealth game and gameplay-wise I was quite impressed by how addictive the genre can be. As agent 47 -- a silent assassin who works for the Agency -- you're tasked with one or more assassination orders every level, the most interesting part being that it's preferred you stay invisible while getting your hands dirty. That aligned to how open the levels can be offers a large variety of approaches, from disguises, to how you'll kill your target, with which weapon (if you use one), then how you'll get rid of the body if that's important and finally, getting out clean. Normally games that promise such variety never live up to it, but
certainly delivers all of its potential. Although some mechanics can be annoying at first, the patient player will find themself repeating checkpoints over and over again until they can get things right. And of course! There's also a competitive online mode simply called "Contracts Mode", where you create assassination contracts from the levels available and play other players' contracts, perhaps even open a competition to see who's actually the best! Unfortunately there aren't that many player contracts, but the idea behind the feature is very interesting and appealing.
Now, for the bad... Although
is very enjoyable, its story is very weak. It relies on cheap resources such as the silent assassin, the dirty-mouth-lunatic villains and objectification of women. Within the first few hours the whole plot is handed to the player on a silver plate. Girl is in danger, hero must protect her. Villains want her for some silly reason, so she's kidnapped and the hero must rescue her. The girl is fragile, kind, cute... Basically the same resource used over and over and over again since ever (this is not exclusive to video games, you see). On top of that, women are usually portrayed as either less than men or extremely sexual, even deserving of a joke such as "you gonna let a
be better than you?" If that's not enough, male characters didn't escape the stereotype hammer. Aside 47 and a few NPCs (most of which you'll kill eventually), all male characters are brutal idiots who think the word "respect" is a nazi code. If you're not as manly as them, then you're no man and should be stoned to death (according to them; this is a joke, if you couldn't get it). The plot twist is revealed just after the prologue and the story drags itself on a confusing run where everything's about the girl, but who are all these people I'm tasked with killing again? Were the gameplay not as entertaining as it is, this would've been a very disappointing title. The voice acting is good, but the plot is weak with a predictable twist and the characters are heavily based on stereotypes.
All in all,
can be an amazing game if you can get over the plot. High replay value, worth the full price!

Defy Gravity is a fairly minimalist 2D platformer. The game’s controls are very simple:
•	You can jump.
•	You can double jump in the air (with a cooldown between aerial jumps – but it is possible to jump more than once if you spend enough time in the air, such as if you’re in a gravity well).
•	You can create a gravity well which sucks you (and gravity-sensitive objects) towards it. You can create one of these at a time, and have two shots before you need to touch the ground again.
•	You can create an anti-gravity well which repels you (and gravity sensitive objects) away from it. You can create one of these at a time, and have two shots before you need to touch the ground again.
•	You have a shield you can activate which prevents you from being affected by gravity (and in some levels, it is always on).
The core gameplay mechanics are decent enough – the game has a very minimalist set of elements (platforms you can jump through (some of which move on their own, some of which fall down a few seconds after landing on them), enemies you can jump on top of to kill them and jump again, enemies you can’t bounce off of, and an enemy that kills you if you touch it which shoots other enemies which kill you if you touch them, and ground that kills you if you touch it). Everything in the game moves in linear, predictable paths. Some enemies can be affected by gravity wells (signified by them being gold-colored), others can’t (signified by them being gray); the same applies to the platforms.
At its core, the game presents about an hour and a half of puzzles with these mechanics, and it is simple enough; it gets progressively more difficult the further you get into the game, and the last few levels are quite difficult. The game is mostly pretty generous with checkpoints, but the second to last level requires you to get through fairly long puzzles without screwing up.
Once you beat the game, the game puts you back at the start in hard mode, in which you no longer have anti-gravity wells and all enemies are affected by gravity, which makes the game significantly more difficult. But the levels are the same as they were before, though I think there might be a few modifications to make it possible to solve some of the puzzles which require too many gravity well shots to solve otherwise.
In any case, this core gameplay is decent enough, and while the game is quite short (about 90 minutes to beat the regular mode), it is probably about as long as it wants to be.
The real weakness of this game is the fact that there is really nothing else here. The game is extremely simplistic, the graphics are clean and clear but pretty lackluster and not particularly pretty to look at, there is no story, and the levels feel clearly designed to be challenges without actually even bothering to feel organic in any way (which, ironically, may actually make sense, as the premise of the game is that you’re in there to… complete challenges…).
Anyway, while this game has a fairly decent score on Metacritic, that is likely because, quite frankly, there’s not much to criticize here. But there’s not much to like, either; this game is extremely forgettable and I feel like I’m going to forget it within a very short period of time. The game never wows you, and that makes it hard to really love it or even care particularly much about it.
All in all, this isn’t bad. But you can probably find a better use for an hour and a half (or three hours, if you really want to beat the hard mode and get 100% achievements) of your life. This game is simply unremarkable.

Did you love Hitman: Codename 47? Hitman 2: Silent Assassin? Hitman: Contracts? Hitman: Blood Money? Any or all of the above?
Then avoid Hitman: Absolution like the plague, because it's really not like any of its predecessors. Admittedly,  it's visually beautiful, with a new game engine and detailed models and textures, and the voice cast alone has some legendary actors featured.
However, the levels are small and linear. The plot is weak beyond belief, as is the dialogue - it feels like a bunch of 14 year old boys tried to write a Tarantino movie. It's truly dreadful, it'll make you angry just watching the cutscenes. NPC speech trying sooo hard to be edgy... constant tiresome unfunny jokes - GTA has a LOT to answer for -  or how someone's a b*tch - you wonder if one of the principal writers had recently gone through a messy divorce, so toxic is the game's treatment of women (they're almost entirely either stupid/hateful/shrewish/strippers/sex toys/victims). The few people who actually cared about Kane & Lynch, IO's other notable game series, will notice a cameo, and it's telling that those seconds with a well-drawn character throw into sharp relief just how utterly cliched and two-dimensional the cast are in H:A. I actually felt embarrassed for David Carradine and Powers Boothe for having to spout the inane bilge that passes for writing.
Even 47 has a contrived and inauthentic-feeling moral epiphany forced on him - this is the man who'll strangle a party clown just to take his clothes as a disguise, suddenly deciding he's going to go against his contract. The story wanders around in a flabby circle, goes nowhere interesting, and ends with an incredibly weak 'twist'
TL:DR - Utter rubbish. Avoid.

Tiny and Big: Grandpa's Leftovers is a wacky, but interesting game. The art style is lovely, the mechanics solid and the two main characters breathe life into a very dusty, though colourful world. One concern I had this this particular title however, is that while the game is reminiscent of games such as Psychonauts or Voodoo Vince, Tiny and Big fails to capture the surreal and humourous nature of its inspiration. Most of its humour comes from the odd world that the game takes place in, and while the world is brightly coloured and fun to romp around in, at times I found this just not enough to carry the comedy. Perhaps this is because the characters don't actually speak, and reading the text that pops up really slows down the pace of the sarcastic wips from the game's protagonist, Tiny.
However, don't assume that I found this game tedious or boring. Quite the opposite. Tiny and Big offers charm and polish, and you'll definitely find in enjoyment in the lasering and placing of platforms, as you carve your own path to freedom. The physics of the puzzles are solid, and while not particularly difficult, I still found myself smiling with glee after I had bodged together a staircase from chunks of the ceiling.
Although the game is short, I found the length perfect; as I was able to enjoy the entirety of this game in one sitting. And while there is not much plot to follow so to speak, there is something very interesting in the small amount of lore that the game provides about its world.
Personally, I found that it probably wouldn't warrant a second play-through, however, since I got it on sale, I'd say I got my money's worth.
Tiny and Big is a very intriguing little puzzler. I recommend it, and I really hope to see more out of Black Pants Studio in the future.

A game ive had my eye on for a good long time, And boy was i far from dissappointed.
Very rarely have i played a game that engrosses me quite so quickly as this. Its fantastic universe, gorgeous art style and absolutely riveting albeit dark storyline is consistent and enjoyable right untill the end.
Pros:
- Incredibly detailed background and lore in a universe were you start with so little, every scrap of information pieces together a incredibly well done puzzle.
- Very original storyline that pushes away from a stereotypical this guys good this guys bad background and produces a very detailed tale of the kingdom of hallownest, from its prosperous beginnings to its bitter end.
- Superb soundtrack from start to finish, with a nice combination of epic combat, relaxing background and even a couple wacky ones.
- Looks absolutely stunning, The drawn art style may not be everyones taste but it produced a fantastic background and universe to play in, with every region having very unique and beautiful areas.
- Suprisingly long, it took me over 50 Hours for complete a 100% run beating the true final boss (I have little experience with platformers so would take still a good 30 for many others).
- Thouroughly enjoyable and adaptive gameplay, The massive variety of charms avalible and vast variety of enemies and bosses means you can take loads of different approaches to fights or exploration.
- Challenging, but not excessive. Every boss fight is often a new challenge and the difficult parkour regions (God damn you White palace) keep you busy trying to adapt to new strategies, But very rarely push you to straight out give up like many other superhard games.
- Get your moneys worth, I spent just over a tenner on a game i got just over 50 hours from, and if you wished to do a true 100% completion you could very likely get even more.
- Free expansions, so far the game has had 2 which add a nice variety of new bosses and flesh out the game even further, and a 3rd free one is on its way.
Cons:
- Not having a controller complicates thing, I played it through using only a keyboard and it did definitly make things more challenging, that said it was far from impossible once you get used to it.
- Couple very wierd bugs, One particular bossfight will outright break when using 2 particular charms (which i unfortunatly used a lot) and i would have to go into keybinds every time before i started playing or i couldnt attack for some reason.
As annoying as these bugs can be they are very few and explained in plenty of detail on the wiki.
Overall a very difficult metroidvania platforming game, all aspects i normally hate but absolutely adored here, combine to make a thrilling and dark game that not only entertains yourself (and those who laugh at your failures when streaming) but also keeps you thinking of what youve seen/read/done and how it changes the kingdom.
This is without a doubt my Solo game of the year for 2017, Absolutely fantastic.

Overall, I would say Magic Duels is at least worth a try.

The Last Remnant is a unique title. It manages to have some of the greatest voices on the face of the planet and still manages to fall short due to its writing. The main character is voiced by Johnny Yong Bosch, so you'd think he'd be able to save the performance, right? Nope, the writing's that dry and cliched...though moreso the former than the latter.
What does make this game worth recommending, however, is the gameplay. When I say that the title is unique, I don't mean because of the writing; games have had great voices and bad writing before. What makes this game unique is that it has a style of gameplay unseen since Chaos World back on the NES. Rather than controlling one character at a time and fighting monsters that way, you take several characters into a fight and control them as squads. This isn't a Turn-Based game, either, though it may look it...or not. This game is the type of thing that is hard to decipher from videos alone, but its more of a Tactical Turn-Based RPG, though I wouldn't go as far as to call it a Strategy RPG.
This game also lends itself to an OK story, but there's enough here to keep one who is having fun interested for a while. The areas are large and open (and this is not a linear game), the customization is one of the more unique things I've seen out of an RPG, and the character recruitment process is slightly unpolished, among other things in the game, but the idea of having so many optional characters with histories and personalities is a nice touch. If the price is low enough (and this game can go pretty low, price-wise) then I'd definitely recommend checking it out, especially if your looking for a unique experience.

When the words Square Enix and RPG go together great things happen, unfortunately The Last Remnant is proof that even the best in the business can get it wrong.  Despite solid potential in the form of an excellent storyline and brilliant characters, the game is let down by an awqward progression system and a difficulty curve that is so inconsistent, a visual representation would look like a bowl of frustrated spaghetti.
The Last Remnant follows an intriguing storyline, vividly brought to life through brilliant character acting and the very best quality voice acting.  The excellent production allows the player to really connect with the characters and experience the feels of story to the fullest.  Unfortunately, the ridiculous jumps in difficulty negate this by forcing the player to spend great lengths of time struggling to progress, ultimately destroying the rhythm of the story.  Impossible chain boss fights are sudden and deny the player any chance for recuperation, so much so that even multiple save files will not save you (hue hue) from hours of punishment.  Add to this the long, arduous random battles which can accumulate into hours of necessary grinding to rectify the tardy and deceptive progression system known as 'battle rank' and any enjoyment quickly fizzles away.
The main point of interest in The Last Remnant is the battle system.  The player controls several parties of characters in the form of a turn based strategy with real time combat elements.  This is not particularly effective as the player is limited to a pre-determined set of attacks depending on the situation, inevitably replacing strategy with luck.  The real time combat elements have been cleverly integrated to sway the tide of battle if executed correctly and play a major role in determining the outcome of each fight.  Outside of battle the gameplay is fairly limited in terms of exploration and despite there being plentiful completionist content and a strangely addictive appeal, the majority is simply empty dialogue followed by a re-run of previously visited dungeons.
Overall, The Last Remnant shows promise but quickly succumbs to its flaws which hinder the game from ever competing on the same level as it's better known stablemates.  If you are an RPG enthusiast with a high tolerance for frustration then you may be able to enjoy The Last Remnant.  If not, you would be better off looking elsewhere.

The ever-expanding Lord of the Rings franchise is one that I constantly find to be treading the treacherous line between gratuitousness and sincere narrative expansion. It remains my fantasy world of choice, and offers an incredibly rich setting in which to stage new adventures and exploits of novel characters. Developer Snowblind (known for RPGs Baldur’s Gate: Dark Alliance and Champions of Norrath: Realms of EverQuest, among others) brought us War in the North, following a previously unseen band of heroes concurrent with the events of the Fellowship, much in the same vein as EA’s The Third Age back in 2004.
Tolkien's vision was of such wide scope that I have absolutely zero problem with this premise, and could happily see it repeated time and time again. In my opinion the source material allows for a massive degree of expansion, which some games have captured extremely well.
War in the North, however, is not one of them.
It’s a hack-and-slash action-RPG wherein you control your choice of an Elf mage, a heavy-handed dwarf with an axe, or the quintessentially rugged Ranger. You are tasked with dealing with Sauron’s forces in the North of Middle Earth, preventing his self-proclaimed right-hand man Agandaur from gaining influence while the Fellowship proceeds south. You’ll bump into familiar faces along the way, gaining experience from fallen enemies to acquire new combat skills and purchasing more powerful gear, which can also be found in chests scattered around levels.
Progression is simple through the segmented areas, and NPCs offer sidequests should you speak to them in each hub area, usually with the promise of a small reward.
As I said, there’s more than enough imagination to go around, but I hate to see the wonder I had instilled in me through reading about Middle Earth abused to shoehorn subpar titles into the marketplace, it really gets to me on a personal level. All the licensed characters are here, Frodo, Gandalf, everyone you’d want to see, but the Lord of the Rings experience feels entirely lacking. The great strength of that mythos is the magnificence of the world; Tolkien's description was so vivid in his attempts to express the beauty and wild danger of the land.
Unfortunately very little of this feeling is captured in War in the North - textures and colours are dull and flat even at maxed settings. Furthermore, the lack of detail was apparent to the point where I was having difficulty distinguishing 1080p from 720p resolution, something that is usually night and day in other titles. There was little variation models and level design is utterly uninspired, even over the range of environments that are present. Getting through the game simply consists of ‘kill a load of things, collect loot, kill a load more things, collect loot’, with little in the way of variety in enemy design or challenge.
Furthermore, there is very little use of licensed music which was always one of the strengths of Peter Jackson’s cinematic imagining. Instead the score is bland and repetitive, not distinctly bad by any means but certainly unremarkable. On the note of sound, many elements of the game’s story are told through cutscenes; while they are rendered in-game using your character’s specific gear sets which is something I actively like to see, the voice acting is just embarrassing on the whole, with the main cast sounding bored and uninterested.
It’s a shame too because the eagle that comes to accompany you on your adventure was cast exceptionally well, being portrayed by the talented John Patrick Lowrie, whom you may have heard as The Sniper in Team Fortress 2, among other roles. Unfortunately the supporting characters generally do not share this fate - Elrond, Bilbo, Gandalf, all of them sound dull, sadly.
All that being said, there are a few features that salvage War in the North from the maw of worthlessness. For all the combat was highly repetitive, it was extremely fluid for the most part, and I enjoyed the fast pacing awarded by ‘Heroic Mode’. Essentially chaining blows without receiving damage increases your capability to deal it, which acts a preventative measure for simply mashing buttons, instead encouraging dodging and well-timed interrupts.
I also liked the item system - drops from enemies and chests are entirely random, meaning that coming across a rare piece of loot gives a feeling of genuine excitement. Themed armour sets can be collected, and suitable gear elements can be adorned with elfstones to provide additional stat bonuses should you need them. Herbs and other flora can be collected around the game world and combined through a limited crafting system to produce potions and items to aid you in battle, often providing powerful abilities such as enhanced strength for a short period of time.
Unfortunately trying to produce an appealing Lord of the Rings game at this point is playing with fire, and I think Snowblind got singed. I do believe War in the North to be arguably adequate as an RPG in its own right, but it falls short of the admittedly very high standard that we have come to expect given the size of the fandom. Pick it up if you want a fast-paced RPG to have fun with, but be aware that no new ground is being broken, and for a Tolkein-esque narrative you’ll definitely want to look elsewhere.

Rivals of Aether is a completely orginal and hand-crafted game with its own completely original cast of diverse fighters with their own respective skills and move sets. Not to mention the variety of stages, with the ability to switch from 'Aether' mode to 'Basic' mode which allows the player to turn off stage hazards and keeps everything on the stage stationary. I don't normally do Early Access anymore, but this is one to make an exception for. If you don't feel like buying it, at least keep it on your list of games to check out again when it's closer to done--there's a lot to be excited for in this.

I loved Civ V. This was a reskin. It really speaks to the industry right now that a company would take an excellent product like Civ V and give it a powerful new setting while doing nothing to improve upon the engine, graphics, ai, or general gameplay. Despite the fact space might offer limitless possibilities this iteration of civ seemed to take no heed of that potential fact and simply generated generally dull, uninspired worlds with new, uninspired resources that essentially do the same thing as the old, civ v resource tiles. I watched a talk with some of the devs where they placed emphasis on the fact that this new civ would feature some more interesting, difficult, and absorbing pVe interactions with ambient species. Same species every world? Weak. Alien AI spends most of its time pacing around the same 4 tiles while the other player ai STILL has to do round for round 'I see that you have become close with x' from civ v? Weak. Economy and battle ai essentially kept the same? So Weak. At least do a tune-up and fix some of the glaring ai errors like workers continually reworking the same tile. If I really could request one thing from this series - if you go into space, think bigger. Think systems with multiple worlds and space matter which could provide resource extraction opportunities or worlds with single settlement, specialized research opportunities. This all would, of course, require a more interesting game environment beyond 'The mind flower has been built therefore you lose' or whatever it is. If you wanted to be lazy and add something to make the game actually replayable, try generating different species. Maybe even a couple different texture rotations on the creatures, anything!
But generally if I had to define this game in one word it would be: weak. Nice job civ franchise with the way this release went and the unrelenting price cuts you have been doing on the game recently I will never be suckered into buying another one of your releases at full price. Sins of a Solar Empire holds a very unique position on the strategy game spectrum. Many people call it a blend of 4X Strategy with Real Time Strategy. Although that is true to some extent, I don't feel the statement is entirely accurate. It's more like a RTS with a bit of 4X management thrown in rather than an equal amount of the two. Rebellion is the standalone expansion for the game, and unlike other standalones, this one includes ALL of the previous content. So not only do you not have to by the original game, you also don't have to buy the two mini expansions, Entrenchment and diplomacy.
Sins of a Solar Empire is already unique as an RTS because it's ENTIRELY space based. You field fleets of frigates and cruisers with your Capital Ships acting as your hero units, meaning they can level up and gain new unique abilites. Rebellion adds a new class of ship to the game. Titans, and they are exactly what they soundlike, they are basically moblie super weapons that can take on a large amount of enemy ships on their own, and they are as fun as they sound. Rebellion also splits the existing factions into two subfactions, Rebels and Loyalists, each with its own benefits and unique titan ships.
On the downside, the game still has NO SINGLE PLAYER CAMPAIGN of any sort, and is basically all just multiplayer or skirmish matches. There's no story development whatsoever outside of what you get in the intro cinematic, which is a shame, because I feel theres some very interesting story development that theyre just ignoring for some reason. The game is also very light on micromanagement if that's something you look for in RTS games, ESPECIALLY in late game and/or in large fleet games. Theres pretty much no point in micromanaging your ships out side of your capital ships, strike craft, and perhaps your flak frigates to make sure they target enemy fighters.
All that being said, the game is still very good at what it does, and is easily one of the best space based RTS games out there (of which they're aren't that many to begin with). If your looking for a game about managing the infrastructure of a Galactic Empire, you may want to look elsewhere. If you are looking for a space based stategy game with a large focus on fleet combat with a bit of Galactic Empire development splashed in, then I highly recommend this game, and as I said before, NONE of the previous games are required. Just get rebellion, and you're good to go.

Very good and feature-complete Smash-like. Great tutorial, great mechanics.
If you are already a big fan of Smash be wary that this game focuses more on the competitive 1v1 asepct than the teams and items. The game also changes a lot of staple Smash mechanics, shields and grabs are gone and are instead replaces with parries. Ledge grabbing is no longer a thing instead recovery is about wall-jumping and works in a different, albiet still fun way.
The biggest difference aside from the above this game has with Smash is the characters and how wierd and unique they are. Wrastor is a character who has air smashes and 3 jumps, Forsburn spreads smoke in the stage that he can hide under and can create clones of himself that he can detonate to confuse opponenets. Absa can control a cloud and manipulate its position to control space, Maypul plants seeds on the ground to set up traps, e.tc. All the characters in this game have some crazy unique mechanics and if you are into that more experimental gameplay you will love the things this game does with the Smash formula.
The game also has many good players online, if you aren't willing to take some time to learn the game you will get smacked up by people online so make sure you go into a discord or something to play with someone who can teach you how to improve.
Overall, if you like 1v1 fighting games, this is a pretty good one and is worth its price.

I found it very hard to decide whether I recommended this game or not.
On the one hand, it's got a lot of the ridiculous fun I wanted and expected from a Saints Row game, the new weapons and powers are a lot of fun, and getting to play as Kinzie was an absolute delight.
On the other hand, the story was exceptionally slight, and the pacing was REALLY frustrating.  I love open world games but I play them for the engaging story that needs to be woven through.  Saints Row The Third and Saints Row IV got this exactly right, with the story parts and the open world distractions finishing up at about the same time.  Sleeping Dogs (another favourite) did a great job of this too.
Gat Out Of Hell frustrated me because at the point where the story endgame began (and was fairly unavoidable), the "city takeover" parts were only about half done.  In fact, it was so early on that I was convinced this must be a false ending with more stuff still to happen.  Once the story was finished, I didn't feel much motivation to go back and finish the other bits because my story-focused brain told me they didn't "matter".
This is mostly irritating because it would be really easily fixed.  Push the arbitrary endgame-trigger back.  Demand more city-conquest before the boss battle.  That way I get a few more hours where my actions "matter" before it turns into a storybook again.
On the other hand, the city takeover stuff WAS fun.  The flight mechanic was well put together and the silly weapons like the armchair gave it a sense of whimsy.  Thumbs up, but only just.  Buy it when it's on sale, or just replay an earlier Saints Row game.

This is probably one of the most pleasantly suprising indie games i've played in a long time. The basic mechanic is this
You can cut anything in the game. With a laser. As many times, and into as many shapes, pieces & bits as you want. I honestly got sidetracked by cutting stuff into pieces and screwing around.

And no, it's not just a special type of block you can cut only a certain amount of times in certain locations. You can cut everything. No, you don't have to have a certain amount of energy to cut something. As long as you can draw a line across it, you can cut it. Even things you'd need to finish the current level. There are as few restrictions as possible.
also you have a rocket tool that can push whatever you can cut and a grappling claw that can pull whatever you can cut.

This is my experience of my first attempted playthrough of This War of Mine with Bruno, Pavle, and Katia *spoilers I think*.
Day 1: The whole gang found plentiful supplies in the house. I build a stove, metal toolbench, and 1 bed.
Night 1: While looting, I find a picture of a strong man and two little girls (I assume they are his daughters). I continue to wander throughout the house until I found a note. It says that this man's two daughters were murdered by raiders. It also says to not look for him. I ponder about the man's fate...
Day 2:  I have my scavenger from the last night sleep all day while my others get to work clearing rubble out and cooking. I build a shovel to clear the rubble. Quite uneventful.
Night 2: While scavenging with Pavle, i find that a couple is living in this house. In particular,I found this out when i get slashed in the chest by the husband. I realized the other use of the shovel, murder. I brutally beat the man to death while the woman hides in the attic. I recieved nearly fatal wounds in the skirmish. It gets near daylight, so i rush for the medicine cabinet to steal a bandage before running away.
Day 3: Pavle uses the bandage, gets a warm bowl of stew and goes to bed for the whole day. Everyone is either sad or depressed due to last night. Katia seems to be the most effected. I build a radio to hopefully cheer them up.
Night 3: Scavenged, good haul, uneventful.
Day 4: I find out that Katia assaulted (the near dead, mind you) Pavle in the night. I don't know how to deal with this, so i give everyone a bowl of stew and build a second bed for katie to sleep in. God, we are already breaking.
Night 4: All the uninhabited places have been raided so i go to an abandoned school (except for the homeless people). While walking around, I hear footsteps once and a while I assume he or she is hostile and try to avoid him/her.Later, I hear someone pacing inside the next room. I take a peek and see a mumblimg to himself about some betrayal. I feel like I have to try to avoid him to not hurt him. I finish up and leave.
Day 5: The first thing i noticed is that I only have enough water for 2 meals. A man knocks on the door to trade. I have Katia answer the door while Bruno makes a meal for himself and Palve. I trade some pills for enough materials to make a water purifier. I wont be able to purify the water on time, but it should help.
NIght 5: Uneventful
Day 6: The house was raided with no one to protect it. I found Pavle's corpse in his bed. Katia is on the floor with blood pouring out of her wounds. Bruno is shocked. I make one meal with the last of our food for Bruno.
Night 6: Bruno is on guard while Katia sleeps
Day 7: Bruno sleeps due to not sleeping for 2 days. Katia also sleeps due to her wounds. I have nothing to make food with.
Night 7: Bruno goes out to scavenge all of the food and materials he can as a last effort. He overhears a man saying that he must protect his parents. Out of desperation, Bruno bashes the poor man's head in and loot's him. He sees an old woman in the other room and kills her too. He peeks through a hole in the door and sees a seemingly unarmed man. Bruno tries to kills the man silently, but the man hears him. When he turns around Bruno sees something he wishes he'd never see in this situation, a shotgun. Bruno rushes the man, but gets knocked down before he can strike. Bruno sees the barrel in the front of his face and... *BAM*
Day 8 (written in Katia's POV): "Oh, Bruno didn't return *cough's up blood*" "I..I..I'm tired, I need to sleep on my decision"
Night 8: Sleep
Day 9: Katia is solid in her decision. She clutches her journal in her final moments. She feels the rope tighten around her neck and... she falls.

A funny, unique game. Bonanza Bros. meets Hotline Miami meets a smear campaign trail led by a purple bunny who speaks as if he just got his hands on a children's thesaurus.
Last time I raided a drug empire in a video game (or rescued a panda from the yakuza, or escorted an old lady to her decrepit apartment), the soundtrack definitely wasn't well-arranged chiptune (think Anamanaguchi circa Scott Pilgrim soundtrack) and "♥♥♥♥ ♥♥♥♥ ♥♥♥♥ money mandem only" definitely wasn't scribbled in pixellated graffiti on the walls. There's a great character about it. I'll say though, that most of the characters being Family Guy-level stereotypes/caricatures got old pretty quickly.
Roll7 keeps everything pretty fresh; the cast of characters give gameplay variety, and the story is just short enough to maintain its charm. The dialogue is just campy enough, the art direction is just detail-oriented enough, and the music rides the line between cheesily-and-daftly-fitting.
Overall, it's put together well, and has a style all its own. Worth trying if you have a sense of humor, political or otherwise.

I hadn’t realized how much I missed really getting into a big Metroidvania until I played Hollow Knight. The game is so densely packed with stuff, I was constantly surprised and delighted every time I realized there was more to see. You keep gaining new abilities that take you to new places, the game constantly expanding in size and scope. Every time I thought I’d seen it all, I’d break down or scale a wall and discover an entirely new zone that I had previously missed. That exploration is difficult, satisfying work too, as you have to explore each area to even find its map, and then fill in most of that map yourself. It also borrows one of my favorite tricks from fellow Metroidvania game Guacamelee: new abilities aren’t just integral to exploration but to combat as well. However, where Guacamelee’s abilities mostly take the form of attacks, Hollow Knight’s are new movement options that become increasingly necessary to dodge the attacks of your foes. By the end of the game, I felt like a master of aerial combat, using double jumps and dashes to dart around through the air as I timed my attacks to bounce off of enemies and strike them from above. Also, the sound design in some of the later areas is fantastically creepy and had me as on edge as any horror game.

How do I describe This War of Mine...
Imagine having the latest COD mixed with DayZ.
That doesn't even come close to what this game is.
In TWOM, you play as a small band of civilians, typically 3-4, trying to survive in a war torn Pogoren, the city you once called home.  Bandits are around every corner, and the homeless population is now HALF of the population.  Military Snipers shoot civilians like fish in a barrel, and armed thugs will kill you just for looking at them, much less attempting to steal from them.  But there is hope.  You can craft and cook things in your home during the day in preparations for the night, where one of your ragtag group of survivors must go and scavenge for anthing and everything of use. After the trials of the night, you come home, afraid that when you get there everything will have been looted, or that one of the survivors has been wounded in a futile attempt to ward off looters.  Fast forward a week, food and fuel are running low, and winter is fast approaching. Hastily you build a heater to protect you from falling ill during the night when suddenly two children appear at your door asking for medicine for their sick mother. They boldly ask for two bottles! You are torn between helping the helpless and looking out for your own. Even if you were to have two or three bottles by some stroke of luck, who knows how badly you will need them in the days to come? But if you neglect to help them, who is to say that the others will feel the same way? Among starvation, exhaustion, infection, and the plethora of ways to be injured, you have to fight off depression! Slowly you begin to wonder how you will survive when it's only Day 10.
All this and more can be seen in this war of ours.

Hollow Knight is my favorite game from 2017, even among other very good titles. Team Cherry has made an absolutely beautiful world that was a pleasure to enjoy and get lost in. It proudly wears its Metroid-Vania influences but takes those concepts and nearly perfects them.
The world and its inhabitants are strange and captivating, If nothing else, I wanted to explore and progress just to see what more it had to offer and I was never let down by what I found.
Due to its structure, the order things can be completed and what upgrades can be found is likely to vary greatly among players. This brings a sense of novelty to the player's own story but it can so lead to some frustration by finding yourself in an area that may be more hostile than you are prepared for. Some of the upgrades can feel few and far between if areas are done in certain orders, and quite a few upgrades seem to be found in the late game. It can take some time before you feel powerful, or even on level ground with your opponents but that feeling of smallness and helplessness permeates the entire world and atmosphere.
Team Cherry has also impressed me with their dedication to the fan base, releasing multiple free DLCs and listening attentively to feedback. It's refreshing to see passionate and genuinely artistic work going on in the video game industry right now. If the art, music, or Metroid-Vania style of the game is intriguing, Hollow Knight cannot be ignored.

People claim this game is like Hotline Miami, but that's not true.
Not A Hero throws you into different levels and asks you to complete a main objective, as well as three optional ones.
There are several characters to pick from and they all have their own weapons and abilities (like a sliding move that can knock down enemies).
You can also take mutliple hits and your health bar regenerates very quickly.
This makes for some very forgiving gameplay (unlike Hotline Miami) and allows for "damage boosting" (taking hits to get through areas faster).
I don't consider this a difficult game at all, but completing it is definitely a challenge.
It also doesn't help that there are elements that are just plain unfair/badly designed.
There are times when the game will push you away from certain structures, or pull you towards them in order to make traversal more forgiving.
Problem is: It makes precision platforming absolutely impossible in certain situations.
After jumping through a window, the game automatically snaps you behind the nearest cover.
If there is an enemy in the way, it will simply punch you in the face before you reach said cover (potentially knocking you out the window again, killing you, or making you lose an objective). I have not found a way to reliably deal with this.
The game is also capable of creating scenarios that make your current run borderline unwinnable by letting enemies stand directly on top of a stairway (doors in the background that let you switch between floors).
Once you enter from your side and pop out at the other side (where the enemy is placed), you'll be knocked about with no way of avoiding it. This is particularly nasty when combined with large, brute-type enemies, which typically do not move by themselves and cannot be knocked down for a quick resolution.
Again, this can kill you, depending on the situation.
What really takes the cake, however, is the hostage level that seemingly changes its own rules mid-stage.
At the beginning of the level, you can kill the guy right next to a room with a hostage in it and nothing happens.
If you do this halfway in at a later part of the level next to a different room, the enemy will be alerted and the hostage will be shot, making you fail an objective and forcing you to restart if you want the 100%.
Even worse, there are no real rules for the player to determine which rooms are safe and which are not. If you kill someone in the room above, it's fine. Kill someone to the right of it and the hostage is killed. This kind of miscommunication is unacceptable in any game and makes this one particular level needlessly frustrating.
Speaking of frustrating: Enemies can shoot and punch you at the same time, making levels that require you NOT to be punched another frustrating affair. Most of the time you'll make it, but there's always this one enemy that will run up to you just to punch you in the face, and those punches come FAST). When to slide and how far to stay away is a science in itself and you're required to master it if you want 100%.
Those (and the lack of a proper options menu for graphics) are my only gripes with Not A Hero.
It's a fun romp with a nice OST and a dumb, but light-hearted "gangster-political" excuse plot.
I don't think it's worth buying at full price, but if you can get it during a sale and the trailer appeals to you, it's probably worth it. Just keep in mind that its lack of polish can make it a frustrating affair at times.

Bioshock (BS1) was probably the best story a video game ever had and really understood the communication medium in storytelling: You just felt sooo angry after all got revealed and the audiotapes next to corpses left a morbid atmosphere of some long faded glory.
[The meta stories connect well between all 3 parts. In BS1 there was the capitalistic or self-inherent threat to an atheist society, wheras BS2 is the religious-collectivistic danger to Rapture's ideals and finally BS Infinite is a Newborn Christian xenophobic "W" Bush type of state.]
But and this was a major "but", the gameplay was more or less in a better beta state.
Subject Delta, in BS2 on the contrary, experiences a still immersive story and a far more balanced gameplay than in BS1. In Detail:
First of all, the Bioshock series ain't RPG but is rather an FPS with strong RPG elements, which includes character building and players' actions which decide the outcome or rather just the cinematic ending, I should say (apart from minor support by characters you kept alive). The level design is in both BS 1 & 2 linear and not open world. BS2 is more tubular than the rather circular maps in BS1, but to the benefit of cutting down on long lonely corridor walks w/o any noteworthy action.
Positive compared to BS1:
The gameplay is a lot better balanced, due to the fact that:
- The one-hit-BigDaddy-killer weapon grenade launcher is given as the last weapon unlike BS1.
- The AI doesn't jump like mad onto you as in BS1, but even Houdinis and Spider Splicers act "normal" and walk around.
- There are no more Nitro (and after half way into the game) no more Thuggish Splicers but all Splicers have a melee and Nitro ability and thus become more versatile in their attack patterns; as well as you got melee abilities with every weapon.
- Double wielding Plasmids and weapons eliminates the need of switching permanently during combat
- The old research cam system, which dragged the game endlessly, used to be the biggest pain in the a... This got now completely revamped, making it much leaner and faster with less categories, less research levels and a video camera system which rolls in the background rather than draining your patience and health during a fight. Just don't forget to turn on, since the best goodies are now at the highest research level!
- There are a lot of good new enemies, like new Big Daddies and one new Splicer type, which add well.
- due to the tubular level design, the gameplay is far more intense.
- The marketing department finally realized that just by making the main character building resource scarce, it doesn't help replayability. Basically Adam was ridiculously scarce in BS1 with an economic system, there you either have to travel back to old levels or having to optimize your character building like a scientific economist in order to gain the maximum outta your Adam.
In BS2, even if you save all sisters, you got almost all the Adam you want and can experiment with Plasmids & Tonics and  still max out Health & Eve and all Plasmid and Tonic slots.
- Elemental Cyclone traps as well as the Insect Swarm3 upgrade are nice features.
- Rocket spear ammo looks really cool beside some other extra ammo.
- Different Plasmid levels have actually more of a difference than just in damage rate.
Another positive point (which is misleading in the screenshot section) is that the game doesn't really recycle too much: The only place in the single player mission is Fontaine's HQ as a sort of connection but besides you got all new areas of Rapture which fit in but are still different to the ones seen in BS1.
Splicer characters are pretty much recycled, a little more mutated though. They seem "fresher" as well as the Spider splicers have now a distinctive design, not to mix them up with the others.
Negative:
The gameplay is still -but a lot less- repetitive. There are no side quests except from gathering Adam as well as the gameplay is very unimaginative: Go here, press button X, research y, harvest or save little sisters (how original!) and collect Adam of course.
As well, it kept some flaws from the old BS1: The boss fights are really dull and the ending or final level is even more boring than in BS1 which wants you stop half way thru the Inner Persephonis. Actually I found myself preparing for a boss fight and collecting all special ammo, once I realized that the game is already over. ;)
There are highs, like the Fontaine and Outer Persephonis level which are exemplary for the great BS cynicism and surreal atmosphere, but there are also extremely dull levels, namely the Siren Alley one: Maybe owed to American prudery, but the Mall area turned red light district would be rated "Parental Guided" w/o age limit because there is nothing except for the names of the places that would make you feel like being in one. Rather a BS Infinite Columbia type of styling with the dullest sub-missions next to the last level.
Again, Ice and Insect Swarm are just killer Plasmids which make most boss fights a piece of cake apart from all the other Plasmids which do the gameplay for the player. Especially Hypnotize and the last Plasmid given.
I played it on an elder system under a 32-Bit XP, but still think graphics are probably only marginally better than in BS1. I had no problems installing like some Win7 users were reporting. Besides 2 medium bugs I encountered, it ran smoothly.
Bugs were the disappareance of Natural Camouflage ability after picking up a certain Tonic in the last level and even more annoying, the fact that scripted events were triggered by opening doors instead of approaching certain points, which led often to action starting and bosses chasing after you, before you even entered the area ("Cathedral" in Siren Alley for example).
Neutral:
- caters a bit to the survival horror community, since it came out at the hype of those games; namely at the end of the Pauper's Drop level (nice though) and by protecting the Little Sisters against waves of enemies. But there is more to the gameplay.
- the old waterpipe  logic & reaction hacking game has been replaced by a pure reaction game which doesn't stop the gameplay (personally, preferred the old one). But I must admit it makes the game more "realistic".
All in all worth it, if you liked BS1 and not that far away from it by quality or even superior if you only count the gameplay. The latter is better but obviously a slightly lamer story. Nonetheless, as well developed characters as in BS1 (I expected more of a twist with Sinclair though).
Update - Minervas Den:
BS in a microcosm: Story with a twist to it. Besides more of the same.
The laser weapon is not worth the addition. And since I hardly chase Houdinis with Winter Blast, the Wintery Houdini doesn't make much of a difference but at least adds. The fiery Brute Splicer is even less noteworthy.
The tributes to famous computer engineers are sort of cheapish; I prefer the cats of BS2 ;). Design is again lovely, but nothing mindblowing new.
And believe it or not: A hint of side quests with the vacuum bots and even the first puzzle since the series started: You have to press a button to remove a hook which blocks your way - wow!!! ;P
Positive is also the way they integrated Plasmids and upgrades into the short game.
Though I got the upgraded Spear Gun before the regular and the new Gravity Plasimd is forgettable: Stage 2 and 3 are just another trap and stage 1 is a "heavier" version of the Telekinesis trap with enhanced optics.

Whats special about this Moba?
-7Abilities (actually 9)
-WASD Movement
-Autoattacks are projectiles you need to Cast and Aim
-2vs2
-3vs3
-1 match needs 3-10 Minutes
-Skillbased (not too casual, not too pro)
-Ability based (no ADCs)
-Choose 1 of 3 Battlerites (Perks) every few Rounds
-Gain Energy (in stages 25-50-75-100%) by attacking or collecting a Globe with HP in the Middle (which both Teams usually fight around so the get their Special (costs 25% Energy) or Ultimate (costs 100% Energy) faster.
Overall:
Battlerites combines fast rounds, with skillbased combat and is kind of the real definition of a Moba (MultiplayerOnlineBattleArena).
Battles are faster than they are in LoL or Dota, Combat is Faster, learning a Champion requieres more time than in other Mobas.
The games has really no objectives exept killing the enemy team. The only objective is the Orb/Globe in the middle of every map that gives the Team that finishes it, a Energy Buff (comparable with baron in Lol, you kill it you get an advantage)
Its faster (and in my Opinion with a better fighting system) than LoL and is perfect when you dont know what to do.

I'm really liking this game! It's a bit complicated to get into if you didn't play anything like this before (just like me) but after the tutorial, which is nice and not boring (or at least for me), and 3 to 4 matches you are alredy trained to actually play "without thinking on where you have to press to activate a certain skill"
Matches are fast (they take like 5 to 6 minutes)
They are played in an arena where 2 teams (made of 2 or 3 people) beats each other up until no one of the other team is alive. Once the round is over, the team who wins gets one point. The first team to get 3 points wins the match.
Battlerite's characters are well done, which means they have a good model (and voice acting) and skills that stay in the context of the character.
Everyone has HP, Energy (which can be obtained by hitting the enemy with the skills or by picking up energy orbs located around the map) and 7 skills. These skills are at least 1 escape and 1 counter, the other ones are for healing, damage or even shields. There are skills called "EX" which change the effect of a skill and make it upgraded, but they require a cost of energy. Everyone has 1 ultimate which depletes the energy bar because it requires 100 of it (the maximum of your energy capacity) but is really powerful.
In Battlerite there is no RNG or such, every character casts his abilities with skillshots and this makes obvious that this is a skill based and also very challeging game.

Ten minutes and I come to realize this is going to a hard game to review. Probably the hardest I've ever done so far.
The Stanley Parable is an interactive (fiction) game where you choose your own path whilst a narrator comments or dictates your actions. Unlike those text-based adventures here you will be required to interact with the environment in any way possible - from pressing buttons to entering doors, from taking detours to staying put. The number of paths is absolutely amazing and endings for every one and each. Good luck finding them all as a challenge.
If you go along the main path you might as well complete the game in 10 minutes. It took me 17 to do so. The real challenge and surprise comes from your subsequent playthroughs as you try to replay the game over and over, perhaps playing the game in the game in the game with an all-knowing narrator. It clearly doesn't take itself too seriously in favor for the player's experience.
You'll jump to familiar places and eerie chambers one moment or the next and there's no reason at all to spoil the experience for you. This is the kind of game to experience blindly as that's where it shines.
The story itself is there but not constricting the player in any way. Themes present are freedom and government control. It is presented in a beautiful and exciting way to lure the player and as such it delivers its morale with delicate hands. That is, if you do not happen to miss the story. With the multitude of endings (counting in double-digits) this can happen. Or be done in 3 minutes.
As of now I would say it's a bit pricey but if you're certain about it or can get it for free, be it in a bundle or as a gift then I encourage you to do. Good saving for a relaxing weekend.

Lord of the Rings: War in the North surprised me. I bought it expecting that it wouldn't be very good, as movie adaptations often suffer from a multitude of issues. This one, though it does have some issues, manages to avoid the worst of them.
It does so by not making the main story or characters have anything to do with the content of the movies, instead focusing on some other folks doing a different quest during the same time span. You get to cross paths with the heroes of the main story, but your story does not really impact the main events of the movies. Some have criticized the game for this, but if you look at it as just another adventure in the lands of MIddle Earth, it's fine.
War in the North takes you through a series of events unfolding, unsurprisingly, in the north part of Tolkien's maps. The villain is a bit contrived, but the rest of the journey is filled with the same kind of delicious aesthetic that the movies used to bring Middle Earth to life. I don't remember everything in the appendices of the novels, so I don't know how much of this stuff they just made up for the game, but it's all believably Tolkienesque enough that you won't think about it much unless you're a Tolkien scholar. In short, they nailed the flavour perfectly.
The gameplay is solid third-person action-RPG fare. Controls and movements are fluid, there are skill trees, and item upgrades galore. Each of the three characters plays differently enough, while still allowing the player to customize the skills and abilities toward their preferences. All characters are capable at both melee and ranged combat, all have damage-boosting abilities, and all have support abilities, so you get to decide what you want to be good at.
There are a couple issues I found with the game, namely the crafting system feels tacked-on and falls short of its potential. Inventory space is limited as well, so you run out of room for all the crafting materials. The two issues are certainly related. Part of that stems from the fact that you occasionally get gems that you can socket in your items, but using them means that you must either destroy them or the item you put them in, which disincentivizes their use. Further, they're rare to find, and have randomly generated stats, like all the rest of the gear. Which is another sore spot.
Gear. The game tries to do the fun loot hunt minigame, but falls short. The items generate very random stats. It incentivizes collecting "set" items that unlock powerful additional bonuses, but there are so many of them and not enough drops happening to make that worthwhile. I found that I was better off just using the best individual pieces of gear, regardless of set.
Sidequests are all pretty bland, fetch-quest type stuff, and kind of feel like filler, or an excuse to involve a given character in the story. Not a high-point, but could be worse.
Each area has enough secrets in it to keep you going back for more if exploration is your thing, and you will have to go through with each of the 3 characters (or play multiplayer coop) in order to find them all. That's not a bad thing necessarily, as I found the world was a joy to explore for the mostpart, and each of the characters was fun to use and level up.
It's priced appropriately, is on for 75% off pretty regularly, and actually a good deal at that price.

TL;DR
If you like economics / 2D naval style combat / challenge, get this game.
It's worth more than you're paying.
Pros:
This game feels highly polished for the ~$20 price tag.
Economics function quite well, are not random, and you can earn Credits fairly quickly once you see the patterns. (i.e. if there's a Militia Embargo on an outpost, bring it military style products for a nice profit)
The ships are interesting and specialized. You feel accomplished when you get the next awesome ship and throw some killer components on it.
Computer requirements are well within reach for most PC gamers.
^>It feels very optimized and lag is infrequent.
The graphics aren't comparable to BF4 but, it's a very pretty game.
The story, though not entirely compelling at first, is well written as are the characters for their minimalistic impact on the game.
There's been ZERO glitching. That's just fantastic.
Cons:
Difficulty may seem overwhelming at first but, you'll quickly understand the importance of picking your battles and what upgrades are needed. Until you learn to broadside properly, high-range turrets will be your best friend.
I can't really think of any others at the moment. I've been having a really good time. :)
Suggestions:
Co-op Play would be EPIC in larger scale confrontations.
When on the Commodity Window make a sortable LIST of the other outposts you've visited and their pricing instead of the slow "here's the price at this location" rotation. I've spent far too much time just sitting in my chair waiting for the outpost i want to see prices for pop up without having to go back into space and look at it on my map.
The distance between the sides of your ship and stellar masses when trying to warp is too great. Front space is wonderful but, if i can turn my Radovich completely sideways and not hit what made my warp stop that's a problem.
Also, a question to the Devs;
Did a few members of your team REALLY enjoy "Armada" for the Dreamcast? Because this feels like what that game should have been. I loved that game when it came out and put far too much time into it and this feels heavily influenced by it.

AMD FX-6300 OC'd to 4.5GHz
Radeon R9 280 OC'd to 280x specs
Ultra setting, Full Screen, 1080p = 140FPS most of the time.

So ff 13 is an upgrade in terms of models and textures but a downgrade in terms of gameplay. Truly one of the worst, if not THE WORST final fantasy game I've ever played.
(Note: my cons could contain possible spoiler alert.)
Pros:
- Graphic details and CGI.
- weapon upgrade system.
- Perfect character model.
Cons:
(Boy oh boy get ready for this one.)
- No more mana system. Now you get to cast infinite magic with no worries of mana management.
- You control only one character in a party. Thats right. JUST ONE. Rest are automatic AI control.
- During battle, 90% of the time you don't play the game, the game plays for you again because you control only one character.
- Hp, Strength and magic. That's it. That's all the attributes you have in this game. No defense, no magic defense, no agility or luck.
- Certain negative status effect are gone like blind, confuse (I can see why since this game has a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ battle mechanic), silence (still there, just that its name is changed to "fog". Like wow.)
- Near impossible Eidolon battle. Had to actually look at walkthrough.
- Eidolons could morph into ♥♥♥♥♥♥ mounts. (e.g Odin transforms into a god damn horse instead of him riding a horse. Shiva sisters transform into a bike!?!?!?!? WTF really!? This is ridiculous.)
- Shiva sisters. Yes, that's right. Suddenly shiva had a twin sister.
- No more limit break system like trance of ff9 or overdrive of ffx.
- Super long tutorial + boring area. The graphic detail of the levels are no doubt high quality BUT I actually don't give a♥♥♥♥♥about exploring and just rush on through as the level design is boring AF. This is something I never do in a final fantasy game. I rather farm for dark matter from dark yojimbo in ffx then doing this.
- Last but not least, the NUMBER ONE bad thing of ff XIII. HOPE. No I'm not talking bout hoping for a miracle, I'm literally talking about the character Hope. A whinny blame everyone for everything little as.
11 cons compare to 3 pros. Take note that I loved to 100% the final fantasy series ff4, ff7-ffx including max everything but for this game I just don't bother. The only thing that keeps me going in playing this game is staring at the chick Vanille.

I've seen a lot more positivity for this game recently, when it first launched on steam a whole lot of people hated it because it wasn't a good port. I'll keep this review short though, as that recent positivity has surely shown you that FF XIII is actually a really great game. Also I do have 56 hours into the game, I played offline ;)
Pros:
+Fun combat especially once the game turns you loose letting you choose your party members.
+Great story. A little confusing at first, but it's still wonderful.
+Good progression system that rewards grinding a little but will halt your progression at certain points. This means each boss fight is still somewhat challenging, even if you grinded for hours. To clarify: grinding isn't required until late in the game. (Side quest show up once you need to grind, making the grind fun.)
+Music. It's Final Fantasy. Duh.
+Some characters are kind of annoying at first, but each character evolves by the end of the game. Love this gang.
Cons:
-Still not the most optimized game you'll ever play. I have an i7 at 2.8 ~ 3.6 ghz, 16gb of ram, GTX 860m. Ran at about 30-40 fps. Sometimes hit 60 fps in smaller battles. 1080p
-Voice acting is hit and miss. Sometimes it's excellent, sometimes it makes you cringe. (I have high standards for voice acting though. The Last Of Us ruined me.)
-VERY linear. Now given, the game is linear because of the story, but a few branching points in earlier chapters would've been nice.
All in all I'd give this game an 8.5/10. If you're a fan of JRPGs or Final Fantasy then go ahead and pick it up. If you're on the fence, I still do recommend it.
Thanks for reading.
