A conversation arose between my coworkers about which is superior: Grand Theft Auto V or Saints Row Gat Out of Hell. The general consensus seemed to be that Saints Row is generally on par with GTAV but "more fun". Now that I have bought and played both games a fair amount (I must admit, I played GTAV more on console) and went insofar as to complete the main quests for SR, I think GTA is overall a better game. However, SR is addictingly fun and totally worth picking up as it plays like a no-holds-barred fantasy take on the GTA game model (except add super sprinting, FLYING, magic powers, near unlimited ammunition).
Saints Row actually surprised me in how enjoyable it was. I never played any game from the franchise but it really didn't matter as the lunacy and implausibility of the story were glossed over in favor of the Grant Theft Auto styled mindless shoot em' up gameplay. Maybe there is something there for fans of the franchise I missed. The game's environment of an urban "Hell" is an endlessly entertaining arena to fly across while raising the ire of Satan (aka Wanted Level). This is achieved by smashing demonic policemen to the pavement, beating up the street-walking proletariat "husks" and shooting every breathing red entity that crosses your path. It's ok though, they are all demons and they probably deserve it. The more havoc and damage you cause, the more goons Satan will send after you. This includes your ordinary demonic cops afoot, some pesky imps and floating devils with energy shields (annoying).  As a last resort, Satan drops a gigantic and menacing ogre-like creature to dispatch of you.
The graphics are actually pretty decent on the highest settings (running a geForce GTX750 2GB DDR5) but are nowhere near as detailed, customizable and clean as GTAV. The game runs flawless for me (3.5GHz 4770K intel i7 Windows 8.1, 16 GB DDR3). Don't read too much into this - it's worth the cash. Highly recommended.

This is actually a really great Civ game. It's just different from Civ V - in fact, it's much more similar to Civ IV:
- More cities
- Larger armies
- Less of a singular focus on ranged combat
- Less of a focus on culture spam.
- Having a strong build order no longer makes or breaks your game. There are many more factors in play. You have to adapt to the terrain more so than any Civ game.
- Affinities separate economic and military strength. Previously, playing economically/culturally (even with a smaller empire) would give you such strong long-term benefits (including military) that rushing the enemy was barely worth it. Now, playing militarily is an extremely viable option, even against the best economic/cultural builds.

Saints Row: Gat Out of Hell is a standalone expansion for Saints Row IV.
Through Kinzie's birthday party the Saints play with an ouija board, which leads to the kidnapping of The Boss by Satan himself. Satan is trying to force him to marry his daughter, Jezebel. Johnny Gat and Kinzie follow them into hell to rescue the President.
In Saints Row: Gat Out of Hell you play as Johnny Gat or you can switch over and play as Kinzie Kensington. While the superpowers from Saints Row 4 are immediately familiar, they are at least in new flavours. There are no shops to change the clothes and no homies to call up and fight alongside. Johnny and Kinzie's entire mission in Saints Row: Gat Out of Hell is to get Satan's attention with murder, mayhem, and chaos.
It takes something around 5 hours to beat the game, to get all achievements it takes 20 hours ( the final achievement is to spend 20 hours in Hell).
The graphics are nearly the same as in Saints Row IV, no real improvement. The city, New Hades, is not Steelport. There are similarities, but it is nonetheless a new place to explore.
Saints Row: Gat Out of Hell has all of the character voices from the previous game. Unfortunately there is no in-game radio stations like it was in the previous games.
Overall I think Saints Row: Gat Out of Hell is still a lot of fun to play if you play with a friend. If the price goes under 10 € you should get it if you are a fan of the previous games.

The Review:
Grimoire: Manastorm is a Capture point style of online multiplayer game where players take on the roles of mages with varying elements of: Ice, Nature, Earth, Lightning, Fire and Nether.
Each element of mage has a different set of 4 abilities with all but Nether also having a trait. For example Nature's trait: On death polymorph into a rabbit, if you survive the duration you will be resurrected on 50% health. The majority of the first spell/ability seem to be essentially be a beam/stream effect, whereas nether's is more of a boomerang and earth's is a shotgun.
You also have a movement ability and a utility ability, As the names suggests depending on the skills you pick these lend you an extra movement or utility ability. By default a short teleport and a spell barrier are active, but you can also pick from others such as timed movement speed increase, A delayed teleport, etc for movements. For utility you can also pick from others such as stoneskin, a trap, etc. There is a bug where unless you manually change them (picking the same as default fixes it) where the icons for the movement/utility abilities will have wrong icons.
As for the game itself it's just a rather generic feeling TDM/Capture Point game (I admit I didn't try TDM but I assume it exists), it's missing 'life' let alone a player base and this review is being written on a friday when it's on free weekend. The combat can feel rather 'empty' with an odd 'ring' as a hit marker sound and bugs on sounds when you take damage; sometimes there are just no hit sounds when you are taking damage.
Overall I cannot recommend the game, It might be fun if you get it rather cheap in a bundle with 7 other friends or so and drink a few beers to just have some stupid fun. The game needs to be ironed out in areas and some more 'life' spruced to it somehow and maybe it would gain a player base but I presume it's already too late, which is rather sad as it's only in Alpha early access.

The ability to alter gravity in a platformer is nothing new, but using gravity wells to do so is a novel concept that I haven't really seen done- at least, not with player controlled wells. At 24 levels, Defy Gravity is pretty short, but...
Despite only having 24 levels, this is one of the most frustrating games I've played in a while. To put it bluntly: the main mechanics don't work right. Sometimes the wells pull you in/push you away as they're supposed to, sometimes nothing happens. Often with the blue wells I found myself looping around the center and dying, simply because the game felt like it. The design of most of the levels, especially near the end demand near perfect control with this utterly broken mechanic.
Oh, and your air jump replenishes weirdly, sometimes triggers on the ground (hello, death!), and cuts all horizontal momentum when you jump.
Hard mode strips you of the anti-wells and the only way to get any reliability from the mechanics is to use both in conjunction.
Literally the only upside to this game is you can buy it, turn around and sell the cards for more money than the game itself. I guess that it's short helps too, but really this is not worth the effort to play through.

I'm torn on this one. First, I'd like to stress how much personality this game has. You won't forget Bunnylord and the overall style of this game. It does remind us of Hotline Miami with its violence and color scheme, but it has its own twist of humor, with lot's of funnny voice acting and characters to enjoy. Maybe kinda cheesy for some, but it will make you chuckle at some points.
But humor and style ain't enough: it's the challenging gameplay that should take the cake in these kind of violent games. It's fast-paced, intense and bloody. You don't need to master to game to play through the campaign, but eventually you want to get all the objectives crossed off the list. This gets good once you get the appropiate characters you unlock. But these objectives get underminded by some mechanics of the game.
For instance, the objective "don't get punched" sounds way easier than it is, in contrast to another objective like "reach the reported in x amount of seconds". However, after finishing the game, I still don't get WHY I can't tackle an enemy but get punched instead. Is it because he is shooting? Or because he is reloading? In either case, I had a 50% chance of successfully tackling him. Another problem is taking cover (which you do with the same button as with tackling). Sometimes my character wouldn't take cover at the column right in front of him, but instead slight right into the fist of an enemy behind that column. This was headache inducing, especially in the last level.
I did get bored with it at times since the game does get repetiive, It helped to take long breaks, and continnue form where I left of, and discover the new characters. (btw: the game has no cloud saves, so dont uninstall of you plan to come back some day.)
Try out the game. Get a refund if it doesn't gell with you, which I would totally understand. Personally, I was suprised that this game was made by only one guy, which I think is atleast worth mentioning.
I'd say its inferior to the main game. You only get 3 more levels, and you can only use 1 character, Bunnylord. The levels are tough, and it sucks that you can't switch characters. One new enemy is introduced, which I don't like at all (a teleporting dog with a gun, which pretty much just stops my killstreak everytime). Get it when it's on sale for a buck, as you won't spent more than two hours with it, thats including repeated attempts to perfect a level.

I really enjoyed this game. At the very basic level it’s just another Sims style game. You get a ruined house with at max four different PC’s to control. They need to eat, sleep, and keep warm. Some minor things like coffee and smokes are added in as well, though not needed they help the mood of the people in the house.
The characters are set and mostly random when you start a new game. The whole point of the game is to survive in a war zone for roughly 45 days. 45 days in game can seem like forever.
The controls are good aside from the combat. Combat in this game can be really annoying at times. Once you understand the hidden numbers for different characters it can help you decide if combat is worth it. But more often then not you are much better off just hiding and ambushing people.
With that being said though, you can get through the whole game without doing any combat. And honestly you are more likely to be better off trying to avoid combat. The game has a lot of feels and messages about how hard it is for people living in a war zone.
However, none of the in game stuff really hit me till I lost my first person. And one ending I got was a major downer and hit me pretty hard. Even though most my people lived through the event, because of the choices I made one killed herself after the war. And the others in my house had almost as bad out comes.
Price wise I think the game is very worth it. I’d really like to see more games like this. In most rogue like games the worst outcome is normally just death. In this death seems like a better outcome when you`re out of food, have no water, and the main savager of your group was killed trying to free sex slaves. And in my case he was a father of two just trying to make it through the world to see his family again.

Yes it has some bugs and glitches, and the UI could be a little better, but I never run into any major issues in almost 50 hours of gameplay, and it is still MTG. This game is "de facto" the best free CCG out there, when it comes to strategic depth and artwork, which are, in my opinion, the definitive features of the genre.
And yes, if you are an experienced player and can't enjoy the game without getting all the rare cards right away, acquiring new cards will seem tedious and/or expensive. But, if you are like me and even a deck consisting mostly of commons, with a pinch of imagination, can be something exciting for you to play, then just keep an eye on your quests and you'll have a steady stream of booster packs, just enough to spice up your decks, and, eventually, even more than you would be able to squeeze in. And you can build as many decks as you want. And all of that for free.
Some people are saying that AI is OP, others - that it is way too stupid. I wish more games had such an entertaining AI.
It seems that the bulk of the negative reviews comes from MTG veterans, who expect this game to give them everything they ever wanted or imagined for free, and that overwhelming negativity drives off the beginners and casual players, who are the actual target audience here. That's just sad -_-. Don't know, maybe it's just not marketed properly.

This game is giving me everything I WANTED from Star Citizen.
Heading into an iceteroid (ice asteroid) field at high speed, drop out, surrounded by Double Jack a-holes, with my Trigun soundtrack blazing (it lets you add your own music to  the already excellent soundtrack).  Take out a few small fry, then scream around a giant iceteroid to sneak up on the big gunship, unleash a swarm of missiles in its face, then a couple broadsides and it explodes, taking out the iceteroid with it. My wingman helps clean up the trash.
It's 'only' 2D, with 3D graphics, but it works really hard to make you feel so f#@$ing epic.
Remember those old Ambrosia games like Escape Velocity (and of course Star Control)? It’s like that except 3d engine and you’re right down behind the ship and that makes things a lot more badass.

It's a really fun, fast-paced game. The matches last roughly ~10 minutes, so it's really easy to play one game or a series of games and gauge your time responsibly. It's also got really low requirements, so it can even be run on computers you buy from a computer shop for $249; does not need a lot of power at all.
It feels really balanced, which is really impressive. If you take a look at the "tier" list of champions, there are some champions that are overall 'really good' but there aren't any champions that are 'really bad'. For example, in the C-tier you have Jumong but I've seen Jumongs out-play many a Varesh, who is in the S-tier.
The community is generally pretty good. Sometimes, if you're playing a champion from a 'higher tier', you'll get BMers saying, "Oh, you're just playing a broken champion," or, "X is just the same as Y from LoL." Sorry? I think this is the caustic mentality that comes from Dota2 and LoL, and I don't think it's bad at all in Battlerite. People tend to be pretty courteous: "GG!" or "Nice job!" or "GR (great round)" are very common.

Okay first off, this game has a lot of potential and the devs say they are going to update this game often so a lot of this could be fixed but until then i do not recommend this game, even though i do enjoy it at times, you can enjoy this game even though it's not in a good state at all, especially with friends even if you can't play all the multiplayer modes together, more on that below.
The campaign isn't great, but it's not bad either but it is really short, like 3 hours short. A short campaign in this game is fine in my opinion but if you want some sort of replayable long campaign, this is not the game. Also after your first run it does not give you anymore coins making it a waste of time, if you could still get some sort of income from it, i would of replayed it a few times. Some of the individual stories are good, and the charactors actions make sense and i can see someone reacting that way to the situation, but some parts seem a little random/forced and it's obvious they didnt put too much thought into them, but i don't think anyone plays magic for the campaign/story so that's not too bad. Also during one of the stages of the elf campaign there are cards that are in the game but you cant see or unlock them any where else meaning they are holding back content from launch, which is something that literally anyone, ANYONE would tell you that is a really bad thing to do that no one likes, but because of the lack of cards this could be due to balance as those cards are OP compared to all the current cards ingame, but seeing as how they were in past games if they just had all the cards from those games they wouldn't be OP beacuse they were balanced in those.
On to the Multiplayer, the removal of lobbies is one of the worst things they have done to the Magic games, it makes 2v2s with a friend almost impossible, either one person gets an error or both do or an endless loading screen. Now when i say they removed lobbies, that's not exactly what they did, they made it so you don't have an option of hosting a game, or joining one and it just instantly starts. If it makes you host one (happens beyond rarely) it works 95% of the time, the other 5% you are on other teams (how does that even happen?) and when it tries to make you join a game the person you invited will have to reselect his deck and somehow that breaks it and he can no longer join, and the person who invited him either gets a loading screen for 20+ seconds that ends with an error or he gets put in a game with a random person on your team that you are either forced to play with or dodge the game and make him play with a AI (which makes me feel bad doing that) talking about playing with a random person in 2v2s, you can't see their deck before the game starts so you have no idea if you guys will be a good match together until the game starts (No chat doesnt help either), and if you aren't it's too late. Also because theres no true lobby, there is no way to rematch someone which is bad in a versus game based on RNG, some people would like to play the same person again because they lost cause of a bad draw, and wants to see if their deck is actually better in a larger sample size. In the older games you could change your deck and fight the same person again which was also great. Another thing is there is no chat box. I can understand not having voice chat, but no chat box? Having no communication in a multiplayer game like this is beyond silly, especially in 2v2s, talking to your teammate is a really good thing this game should have, the multiplayer is so incomplete and bugged. I don't understand why they didn't think to add those features and how those bugs even got pass one day of testing.
So 2v2s are impossible to play over 95% of the time, this is so broken i have no idea how they did that, seriously.
The 1v1s are perfectly fine and work as it should, so atleast thats something.
Now we'll talk about unlocking cards and content ingeneral.
I really, really don't like the lock on how many coins you can get a day, it's a really hard cap too. Instead of having a cap they should have had a lesser percentage for the day based on how many coins you have gotten, i'd rather them have
nothing but they wont do that cause they need to make money somehow (boosters), they are a business so you can't expect them to not have some sort of money grab in a f2p game. Speaking of boosters, i feel like they should have color themed Boosters but i can see how that wouldn't be necessary as of right now due to the lack of cards which is a bad thing, moving onto that...
I don't like how most of the cards in the previous games aren't in this one, i don't get why they would do that, but intime im pretty sure they will all be back, but until then that's a huge, HUGE thing that's horrible, game's should not remove core content from previous games, it's devolving and just not right. Now the gameplay is great, if you like the way magic works, you'll like it, it's simple really, it's a shame the rest of the game isn't good enough to match the perfectly good gameplay, it would make this the best sorce of playing Magic.
Also a little bug that i think is worth mentioning cause i really hate it when games do this, if you have lowered the in-game sound it does not change the opening game sounds and keeps them at full, this is very, very annoying as it is really loud compared to other sound sorces on my PC when im just on it doing my regular stuff. (teamspeak, twitch, background music)
Conclusion, this game can be, and hopefully will be good. But as it is, it's way too buggy and missing a lot of things for me to recommend it to anyone unless they understand what they are getting into. I'm going to rate the game itself and the gameplay differently, cause the gameplay is so much better compared to the rest of the game that it would raise the rating of the whole game overall but i don't think it should because it's so broken, and if i rated it too low it wouldn't be fair to the gameplay.
Magic Duels: Origins - 2/10,  Way too broken, and a pretty bad economy with removed content from previous games, and missing a lot of features that have become standard in most games, i would not play it AT ALL if it was not for the core gameplay.
Gameplay: 8/10, Would be perfect if not for the lack of cards or when you are alt-tabbed the timer bar gets frozen and that no one knows that they should turn off battle effects (Please turn them off, it makes the game smoother and quicker making the gameplay overall a better experience) and that the game has poor controller support, which is weird seeing as how it's on console too.

What is it?
First Person Shooter
It is always difficult to review an older game in modern times. The question becomes does this game pass the test of time? ie. can you still have fun with this game today as you did when it first came out? And for me the answer is no. The first person shooter genre doesn't age as gracefully as other genres because the genre has been developed and refined so much over the years it becomes very easy to see all the flaws in older games.
This game has some serious flaws. First off the level design is big and often times very confusing. I love exploring large levels however when the environments look the same it feels like I'm running through a maze.
In addition the enemies feel like bullet sponges, at the same time enemies can fill you with an entire clip of their weapon in the span of a few seconds making saving and reloading your best weapon.
Then they added stealth in the game. Nothing says fast paced shooting like stealth. I love stealth but in doesn't work in this game. In fact the stealth mission they added to the game is possibly one of the worst implemenations of stealth I have ever seen. You have to do EXACTLY what the developers want you to do or else you will fail the mission leading to some very frustrating moments.
When I played this game when it first came out I really enjoyed it, however the game has aged horribly it terms of its gameplay and design. I actually think the original DOOM games are more fun and aged better than this game.
If you want some nostalgia and want to play this game then you might enjoy it, if you never played this game before your probably not going to like it at all.

Crysis is more than just a game, it represents a time in history where non-gamers started paying attention to gaming graphics, and PC gamers and system builders began asking themselves, "But can it run Crysis?". It's a hallmark of some of the greatest graphics of all time, along with Cryteks expertise with building a solid FPS, means it plays as it should, even exceeding gameplay expectations at times, thanks to the inclusion of nano suit powers. You will run, swim, jump and 'Maximum strength' your way though tropical jungles, sunny beaches, an icy wasteland and even what would become the infamous (Due to its zero gravity controls) alien ship.
All levels are heavily interactive, letting you poke and pick up things, and throw them at enemies with satisfying effect. The sheet metal that makes up most of the houses in the game can be blown apart in an amazing show of particles and physical interactivity with the objects around it. So just when those Koreans think they're safe to bunker down in one of those houses, feel free to show them how wrong they are, dead wrong. I recommend this game to all FPS fans, and people who appreciate Crytek's bold move to release a PC game that only those with the most top of the line hardware could run at the time.

Though erring on the short side (15 hours for the main story, this only shows as 26% completion in the main menu), Hitman: Absolution feels complete. The gameplay is rock-solid and challenges the way you think about stealth games. I played the entire game on "hard" mode, which was very challenging at times but felt appropriate for the style and format of the game.
The game is absolutely stunning even on medium settings and is fairly well optimized overall. All of the environments are engrossing and interesting and there's an infinite amount of ways that you can take advantage of the environments to beat a level. I'd probably say I didn't even see 30% of the game's environments solely due to how hard it is to get into certain areas.
The story and voice acting were generally on-point and I definitely felt like I was invested in the characters enough to care about advancing the plot. At times, I felt like some things weren't explained fully (though again, I wasn't going for completionism so maybe I missed things) but overall the story felt pretty bulletproof as you'd expect from Enix and IO. I'm definitely interested in returning to the Hitman universe in future installments of the franchise.
After not playing stealth-action titles for a few years, Hitman is refreshing and highly entertaining.
Absolutely reccomended.

As a successor to the Civ franchise, this game is great. It takes on some new mechanics while keeping the core Civ experience in mind. The tech web is interesting and allows for two people to play the game completely different, and there isn't really a strong point that I've noticed. The questing system is a great way to provide further customization each time you play, and is great for introducing new players to the game. The setting doesn't exhaust the same old wonders, techs, Civs, and whatnot, but provides an interesting new landscape to explore. The indigenous lifeforms on the planet are much more interesting to interact with than the barbarians of previous games, and the miasma is very reminiscent of Alpha Centauri's xenofungus. Granted, I play quick games with 3-5 other AI, and that usually takes me about an hour and a half to rush victory on the default difficulty. So I'm basing this off of 4 games played across 6 hours, as well as viewing other's gameplay and dev commentary.
One of the recurring themes in the reviews of this game is that it is not as complete as Civ V +DLCs. That's an unfair judgement to make, considering that Civ V has had a lot of time to run the market and put out DLCs that fix player's complaints. The BASE Civ V had plenty of problems, and comparing that to Civ BE makes much more sense. Will Firaxis release DLC for this game to patch out a lot of the mistakes? Certainly.  But as for right now, the game is a playable, refreshing new take on the Civ series. Which leads to another argument: the game is trying to be a blend of Alpha Centauri and Civ V. Perhaps in some ways, this is true. But for the most part, the game is meant to be a new take on the Civ Franchise.
Definitely worth the money. Especially on sale!

I've played through the game twice now, and I can safely say that during my first play-through, I thoroughly enjoyed the game and really appreciate having a few proper FPS Boss sections rather than simply "Press E to beat Boss" nonsense that more mainstream FPSs spit out regularly. Yet, I did have to perservere through some very frustrating sections in order to get to those very enjoyable sections. I had been looking for an FPS that was not your standard COD/Battlefield fare where you just shoot and shoot and shoot with a bunch of set-pieces and an ever more outlandish story. Crysis doesn't follow down that path, though the story is somewhat sci-fi.
Essentially you are part of an insertion team of super-soldiers whose super-suits grant you the use of 1 of 4 abilities at any one time which drain the energy of your suit when in use (energy recharges when not actively using an ability, as does health so long as you are not taking damage).
These abilities are
(on by default this first drains your energy before your health is majorly impacted),
(Can move incredibly fast for repositioning, manouvres and rushing enemy positions),
(used to hurl objects much harder and further, punch through destructible cover, jumping higher and fall further without taking as much damage),
(Enables a cloak that lowers energy all the while that it's in use, moving while cloaked lowers energy faster), you can also change the attachments to your weapons e.g. silencers, scopes and more.
These abilities provide a refreshing gameplay experience as you become more proficient with using and switching between them as you really will start to feel like a super soldier tearing through waves of North Korean military who occupy the island. I only wish the energy bar lasted a little longer, but that might have had the outcome of being a little OP.
It's your pretty standard FPS, nothing too out of the ordinary here really. There are occasionally vehicles that you can drive, but these sections seem put in for the sole purpose of giving an impression of 'scale' to the island rather than actually being necessary in their own right. Afterall, the environments in Crysis are anything but linear corridors, you are usually given wide fields in which to fight, plan and execute your attack strategies on the unsupecting Koreans. Unfortunately, on a second play-through you realise just how similar these environments and 'play-grounds' are to each other, usually involving corrigated iron shacks for temporary cover or ammo dumps, lower metal fences for snap cover and the odd rock or tree. Certinaly on a second play-through this really adds to the gameplay feeling very stale indeed because of the next issue - the story pacing.
The story is your generic action sci-fi with your super-suits, explosions, an archeological find going wrong and aliens suddenly giving the American Military a realisation that they are not the most powerful entity in the universe. Starting in a mode of rescuing the scientists from Korean clutches you explore and realise something more is afoot ultimately leading to the so called "Crysis", the namesake of the game. The problem is that a good 70% of the game is spent in those same environments as detailed above taking on Korean military time and again attacking outpost after outpost and you start to ask yourself - "Why am I still doing this and not doing something new and interesting?" This is precisely the problem with the game's pacing.
This is amplified by the fact that the enemy types have to little to no variation within the Korean military and having to fight cloaked super Koreans comes a little too late and gets old and annoying fast. Equally, sometimes you get to fight a tank or get endlessly harassed by Helicopters. These can only be taken out by rocket launchers, and these only hold 3 rockets... despite 2 being required to take out a single chopper, and you can't stockpile rocket ammo meaning you'll constantly wasting a rocket after kiling a single chopper so you can pick up another full rocketlauncher in case you might need a good 2 rockets for future harassment. Yes, they do harass you, especially if you don't have rockets, these are a sure fire way to frustrate the player.
- fortunately, by the time the aliens do actually get their time in the spotlight, the gameplay changes again as they require an almost entirely different approach, so what worked all game against humans; you might need to adapt and that really was a joy. I must admit that by the aliens show up you are approaching the climax of the game and on a first place you really will feel adrenaline as everything starts happening all at once and you are caught in the middle of devastation and a situation reminiscient of the Dunkirk evacuations as the US military suddenly turns into the French military and, well, runs away.
One thing I did find most infurating however - autosaves. Because these are triggered by your location i.e. cross the pixel and you'll autosave - means that if you're one to go rambo and storm a position first with Super Speed, then you might find that your autosave occurs as you land encircled by Koreans and an attack helicopter. I cannot tell you how many times this happened to me and really ruined my enjoyment at times - the lesson is pace yourself and make sure you have been saving manually.
All in all, there is a great game here, and by and large it shows itself, certainly on a first play-through as you gain proficiency with your new-found abilities. Though you will have to persevere through occasionally bullet-spongy enemies, annoying Helicopters, samey environments and objectives, and infuriating autosaves in order to get to the really good parts of this game which really do give the feeling of a crisis.

Sins of a Solar Empire: Rebellion is the latest iteration of Sins of a Solar Empire, a space themed real time strategy game with a truly fantastic scale. I’ve seen battles with hundreds of ship engaging each other as more reinforcements filter in from distant star systems. Even friendly comp stomp games can last for hours as your forces slowly conquer the cosmos. Whether this is epic or tedious is a matter of taste, but I fall into the epic camp.
Sins plays a little like a 4X game. You’ll explore the universe, colonize and develop planets, research all manner of military and civilian technologies, meet other peoples, and kill them.  Throughout you’ll be struggling with issues like whether asteroid colony Y would benefit more from a refinery, trade port, or capital ship factory. You are Space Stalin, staying up late in your space Kremlin while devising plans to ensure your people are mining enough crystals to build the ships you’ve just researched. This isn’t a game where you’ll dance a little hero unit around the map. Yes, you can do a little micromanagement. However, you’ve got a lot on your plate already. It’s best to just let the Battleship Captain decide when he wants to fire his special Gauss Rail Gun.
If you want to play an RTS during a lunch break then this is definitely not for you. It’s possible that you could order units to help save an ally’s distant home world, step away from the computer, go out and grab some lunch, eat said lunch, and return before the battle finished. That kind of scale and speed will be a turn off for many people. However, I highly recommend Sins of a Solar Empire Rebellion to patient people with an inner Ming the Merciless.

It's absolutely fascinating - and a trademark of the Bioshock series - how Minerva's Den manages to turn a plot about regaining control of a central computer into one of the greatest love stories told in videogames.
Also, one little detail at the end of Minerva's Den gives us - in retrospect - a measure of the savvy with which the world of Bioshock is constructed: in the office of Charles Milton Porter you find a color TV powered up by three brightly colored tubes that stick oddly into it.
Playing through both Bioshocks you see so many grayscale / sepia monitors (most of them with that frozen 'Please Stand By' logo on them) that they actually become a trademark for the series. And at the end of Minerva's Den when you see that color monitor you cannot help but feel that it doesn't belong there, that it cannot be 'in' Rapture, it must be there from somewhere else, from another world, like a seed of a new world that sprouts in dying Rapture, maybe, and you get the feeling that not only the ocean is finding its way into the ruined city, but another - more colorful - world is also leaking through the cracks in Rapture's broken reality and this could be, in retrospect, the moment that Bioshock's universe opens up to the Multiverse that will take the stage in Infinite.

Risky, thrilling and sombre. There are many different emotions to experience throughout this game. You can choose to do many things in here, but you always have to consider the cost. Would you want to go save this stranger that ran over asking for aid, or would you shut the door in his face? Is it the right choice? You get to keep one person in your party, but you don't know what could have happened if you saved him.
Are you going to watch some woman get assaulted in the supermarket and then use the chance to lurk about to get supplies or are you going to save her? Are you going to kill the poor old couple for what they have, or are you going to leave medicine for them?
This is what makes the game beautiful, the things you do when pressed to.

Quirky games are becoming evermore present as new developers come along and fill in niches that we didn't think exist. This 3rd person puzzle platformer has three: the cutter, the puller, the pusher. These mechanics are utilised relative to the camera, so if you want to cut a ramp, there's no need to guess and hope that your action might work. Progression was pretty well paced with them, as they were placed a bit more obviously on the linear path that T&B:GL shows, but it's also handy to poke at when you venture off the path in search for some of the hidden stuff.
Graphically, the assets appear very styled like in illustrations and rough sketches, and it helps warm the atmosphere rather than attempt to attempt replication of reality (hyperrealistic blood, anyone?).
The sounds of your tools are tuned just right so they don't seem intrusive on your ears, and the soundtrack that's scattered throughout the stages are very well fitting for a character in search for his grandfather's pants.
As for the story, it doesn't take much to guess what's going on, and it's executed in a clumsy sort of manner, which is pretty cool. There is little attempt to try and make it fit in place with the game, and it does make it a little bit more the entertaining.
This game is pretty good, but it's also a bit short. You'll enjoy it though, and there's plenty of collectables that you're told about, but you might never see unless you go back and explore the world a little more!

Okay first off, this game has a lot of potential and the devs say they are going to update this game often so a lot of this could be fixed but until then i do not recommend this game, even though i do enjoy it at times, you can enjoy this game even though it's not in a good state at all, especially with friends even if you can't play all the multiplayer modes together, more on that below.
The campaign isn't great, but it's not bad either but it is really short, like 3 hours short. A short campaign in this game is fine in my opinion but if you want some sort of replayable long campaign, this is not the game. Also after your first run it does not give you anymore coins making it a waste of time, if you could still get some sort of income from it, i would of replayed it a few times. Some of the individual stories are good, and the charactors actions make sense and i can see someone reacting that way to the situation, but some parts seem a little random/forced and it's obvious they didnt put too much thought into them, but i don't think anyone plays magic for the campaign/story so that's not too bad. Also during one of the stages of the elf campaign there are cards that are in the game but you cant see or unlock them any where else meaning they are holding back content from launch, which is something that literally anyone, ANYONE would tell you that is a really bad thing to do that no one likes, but because of the lack of cards this could be due to balance as those cards are OP compared to all the current cards ingame, but seeing as how they were in past games if they just had all the cards from those games they wouldn't be OP beacuse they were balanced in those.
On to the Multiplayer, the removal of lobbies is one of the worst things they have done to the Magic games, it makes 2v2s with a friend almost impossible, either one person gets an error or both do or an endless loading screen. Now when i say they removed lobbies, that's not exactly what they did, they made it so you don't have an option of hosting a game, or joining one and it just instantly starts. If it makes you host one (happens beyond rarely) it works 95% of the time, the other 5% you are on other teams (how does that even happen?) and when it tries to make you join a game the person you invited will have to reselect his deck and somehow that breaks it and he can no longer join, and the person who invited him either gets a loading screen for 20+ seconds that ends with an error or he gets put in a game with a random person on your team that you are either forced to play with or dodge the game and make him play with a AI (which makes me feel bad doing that) talking about playing with a random person in 2v2s, you can't see their deck before the game starts so you have no idea if you guys will be a good match together until the game starts (No chat doesnt help either), and if you aren't it's too late. Also because theres no true lobby, there is no way to rematch someone which is bad in a versus game based on RNG, some people would like to play the same person again because they lost cause of a bad draw, and wants to see if their deck is actually better in a larger sample size. In the older games you could change your deck and fight the same person again which was also great. Another thing is there is no chat box. I can understand not having voice chat, but no chat box? Having no communication in a multiplayer game like this is beyond silly, especially in 2v2s, talking to your teammate is a really good thing this game should have, the multiplayer is so incomplete and bugged. I don't understand why they didn't think to add those features and how those bugs even got pass one day of testing.
So 2v2s are impossible to play over 95% of the time, this is so broken i have no idea how they did that, seriously.
The 1v1s are perfectly fine and work as it should, so atleast thats something.
Now we'll talk about unlocking cards and content ingeneral.
I really, really don't like the lock on how many coins you can get a day, it's a really hard cap too. Instead of having a cap they should have had a lesser percentage for the day based on how many coins you have gotten, i'd rather them have
nothing but they wont do that cause they need to make money somehow (boosters), they are a business so you can't expect them to not have some sort of money grab in a f2p game. Speaking of boosters, i feel like they should have color themed Boosters but i can see how that wouldn't be necessary as of right now due to the lack of cards which is a bad thing, moving onto that...
I don't like how most of the cards in the previous games aren't in this one, i don't get why they would do that, but intime im pretty sure they will all be back, but until then that's a huge, HUGE thing that's horrible, game's should not remove core content from previous games, it's devolving and just not right. Now the gameplay is great, if you like the way magic works, you'll like it, it's simple really, it's a shame the rest of the game isn't good enough to match the perfectly good gameplay, it would make this the best sorce of playing Magic.
Also a little bug that i think is worth mentioning cause i really hate it when games do this, if you have lowered the in-game sound it does not change the opening game sounds and keeps them at full, this is very, very annoying as it is really loud compared to other sound sorces on my PC when im just on it doing my regular stuff. (teamspeak, twitch, background music)

I love so much about Hollow Knight, which makes this game such a heartbreaker.
The game is thematically amazing. It does a great job of immersing you in a very creative and interesting world.  It has great exploration, a beautifully designed world, wonderful music and sound, and *mostly* gorgeous art.  It's incredibly stylistic and hits that "exploring all alone in the dark" tone of Super Metroid, which is exactly what I want from a Metroidvania game.
But it has some big problems.  The biggest one being that the combat is utterly dull and boring.  You start the game with one melee attack, and then later you get a sort of super projectile attack that I found myself not using very much.  And... that's it.  You go up to a guy, hit him a few times, and then go up to the next guy, hit him a few times, rinse and repeat.
As you expect in a Metroidvania, the powerups change your mobility so you can access new areas, but none of them really change the way you fight.  Which wouldn't be the biggest deal if fighting wasn't such a HUGE part of the game.  They clearly wanted to make the fighting the focus, as they definitely made the combat more difficult than other games in the genre, but they forgot to make it fun or interesting.
The other big problem is that the truly wonderful art design is undercut by the decision to make everything monochrome.  If you look at the drawings and backgrounds, they are soooooo detailed and wonderful, but everything just looks so flat because it's all the same color.  You walk around in "blue zone" until you get to "green zone", and then after that is "slightly-different-shade-of-blue zone".  It is soooooo drab.  And to take this beautiful, detailed art and make it drab breaks my heart.  While I'm pretty sure it was an intentional design decision, as it does kind of contribute to the atmosphere, I think it was a bad call.
I really, REALLY want to like this game.  But a few hours in, I started to grow tired of it, and I haven't felt the urge to pick it back up since.  Such a heartbreaker.

This is pretty much the space game I always wanted to play.  Not overly complicated with way too many systems to learn, just having fun flying around a beautiful galaxy, trading materials, destroying space pirates, and listening to an awesome Firely-esque soundtrack!
The game takes place on a 2D plane, with an emphasis on broadside combat, but the option for other forms of attack such as turrets, lasers, mines, etc. exists.  Basically, if you've ever played Assassin's Creed IV, the game plays very similarly to the boat sailing and combat, only more responsive and more entertaining.  There are 21 ships available to purchase and fly, as well as many items for customizing them, including weapons, defense, and more!
Pros:
-Runs perfectly with little to no slowdown.
-Beautiful graphics with plenty of options to change.
-Great music, with an easy option to add your own music in a number of areas, such as battle music, ambient music, etc.
-Big universe.  While not nearly as big as other space games out there, it's still plenty big.  I've played six hours so far and haven't even left the first galaxy that you start in, and there seems to be at least 10+ to explore.
-Price: $18 at launch ($20 later) is a steal for this game.  It runs smoother and I haven't encountered any bugs so far, which is more than I can say for many of the AAA games that I've payed $60 for recently.
-Most importantly: FUN!
Cons:
-One of the only cons I would say is that there doesn't seem to be much in the way of a damage model for ships.  If you ship is severely damaged, you may see a few minor explosions and fire going on around it, but you aren't missing any chunks of your ship or anything like that.  Pretty minor in the long run when compared with all the pros.
-Possible con is that many of the side missions are similar, so you could get burned out after a while.  The positive is that you can do the story missions which offer a bit more variety, or take a break and play something else for a while!
-Not really a con, but you can only save when you dock at a space station, which can be a bit annoying if you need to leave suddenly, but there are plenty of space stations, usually less than a minute away, and the game offers an easy option to find the nearest space station.
Overall, if you're looking for a fun game with a cheap price, look no further than Rebel Galaxy.

Plays exactly like Civ 5. Features many great ideas, though perhaps not enough to justify calling it a whole new game.
The biggest problem however is the setting.
Civilization 5 was pure perfection, because it stood upon 6000 years of human history and a great game concept.
Beyond Earth keeps the concept but has nothing else to stand on.
In classic Civilization everything was familiar and needed no introduction, because you already knew about it either from history or from your life. But in far future and on an alien planet, the very same concept suddenly fails because everything becomes nothing but just made up words with no real meaning or relation.
This is where Firaxis failed. I think Beyond Earth would greatly benefit from a proper story campaign, which would ease the player into every part of the setting one step at a time.
All this said I still found myself coming back to the game again and again, just to have another try at beating that strange and hostile planet.

I've played and enjoyed all the Hitman games (except I did not enjoy the very first one, I find it unplayable), so I was looking forward to this. It definitely takes the gameplay a bit into the Deus Ex: HR / Alpha Protocol realm, which I really don't mind since I love those games. The melee is all QTE stuff, but the overall game controls are a huge improvement over Hitman: Blood Money and the earlier games. In Blood Money, for example, pushing the interact button on someone had a completely unpredictable effect; you may punch them, or push them, or maybe knock them out, or maybe just annoy them and alert everyone to your presence. It was really annoying. This game does it infinitely better. The disguise system and blend-into-the-crows system are great, too. The save (checkpoint in Absolution) system is much less versatile, though, which is too bad, but not really too much of a hindrance since levels are generally very small and confined compared to earlier games. Overall, I really like it so far and think it improves upon the series in a lot of ways.
I can see why many Hitman fans didn't like the campaign. Each mission is a series of smallish levels, and only one or two of the mini-levels might have assassination targets. The levels with no assassination targets are more like your standard stealth-action game fare than traditional Hitman style missions. Mostly, it's just sneaking past guys to get to the next area. The actual assassination levels are great, and I like the way challenges give you both goals to play for and hints on various ways to kill a target. Contracts mode is is pretty neat, and can fulfill the desire of series fans for a "murder playground" just fine, I would think.
The controls and the disguise system are really orders of magnitude better than any previous Hitman games, which is great. There are just a few annoying oddities with the disguise system, though. (dressing as a food vendor from one part of Chicago arouses suspicion of food vendors down the street?). I miss having a map, but I think the instinct system is actually more useful (for tracking enemy positions and interactive objects, at least), and is more intuitive (the maps in previous Hitman games for larger levels were needlessly difficult to use, usually not showing you where one floor map connected to others).
I think this game is my favorite in the series. The improved controls far outweigh the decreased sandbox feeling compared to earlier games. The moral of the story (or even the entire franchise) I would say is that "you can solve a lot of problems by killing enough people."
Recommended if you are into video game murder simulators and stealth/action games (e.g. Deus Ex: HR).

Hitman: Absolution's biggest problem is that everything that was gained in Blood Money is simply forgotten about. The instinct system, while clever, creates a mechanic where the entire game is about being literally hidden, instead of the awesome social stealth that Blood Money used instead. The better graphics are in exchange for corridor, box'ish levels, where the goal is to simply get from area to the next.
There is no consequences about open firefights, bar say that Agent 47 will be gunned down by a cluster♥♥♥♥ of enemy guards 90% of the time due to the clunky cover system (or be killed in the most frustrating QTE sequences ever). The disguise system being enhanced by Instinct breaks the entire game on the harder difficulty levels. Since the guards' presence is increased heavily on the Professional difficulties, you WILL be caught and a firefight WILL break out.
Lets say I'm disguised as a vendor clerk for a Chinese food stand. Does every single fast food vendor in a 10 mile radius know my identity and run to the police to say im a dangerously armed assassin?
...They do here.

As you can see by my play stats I have played this game inside out and have come to this conclusion; X Rebirth has loads of potential and scope, but sadly falls way short of what it promises to be.
I have sunk over 500 hours into X3 and X3TC and can say that I enjoy the X games, but this one is simply not what you would expect and to make matters worse it should have come out on Early Access. The game is nowhere complete with functionality lacking and outsight not working in certain situations. Egosoft are patching, but as I have dealt with them before this is nothing new, but still doesn't excuse the mess this game is.
I have had to edit my save file numerous times just to complete the game and was rewarded by a lame end mission which comes and goes without anything happening and you are left wondering 'Ummm did I just finish the game??'. The bottom line is that they sacrificed what the X series was all about in order to attract new customers, which is a viable business strategy but is a very dangerous thing to do with a game such as X.
Because of this decision you get the feeling as if the game was intended for controller use and I think was to be for next gen consoles, but at the last minute I think they pulled the game and Egosoft were left with a game made for consoles which now had to go PC. Now this is speculation, but from the UI layout and functionality it would seem as if this is what the game was geared up for and then had to be quickly ported to PC..... maybe.
My final thoughts;
Space looks lovely at times and flying between floating cities close to a planet looks breathtaking, but on foot in stations and other areas the lo-fi textures are all too evident. Shoddy menu management and design choices (I had to make a whole new set of UI elements as the default set is woeful), buggy/non-working game play elements, annoying travelling mini game, poor ship and NPC AI, clipping and texture issues, sound issues...... in fact let’s just wrap this up into one sentence;
This game in not complete and will not be for at least another 6 months, maybe try back then.

This game woke some pretty horrible memories of mine.
When I was like 7 years old I was in Panama. Panama at that time was invaded by the US. During daytime I cried a lot because the gunshots outside were fricking loud and my mom would constantly comforting me. One night my dad came back in tatters because he was mobbed by some opportunistic robbers. I think he survived because he hid in some trash heaps.
Now consider that the situation in Panama was pretty tame compared to Bosnian war. And This War of Mine was set in such a setting with terrific, even uncomfortable realism. Playing this game will make you feel much less "cool" or "fun" when you play other games about (modern) war, even if you are playing as the righteous, "heroic" side. Playing this game will also make you taste the powerless feeling as a civilian in a war - performing heroism or gung-ho rampage against gangs will make you die in 80% of the cases while in other games it's just 30%. And also, playing this game makes you smell blood and feel horrible when you kill anyone, which is completely unlike the case in games like Skyrim in which you can butcher a whole village gleefully without feeling anything.
This is game that is not labelled as horror. This is a surival game without shambling zombies nor radiated mutants. This is not a game set in a post-apocalyptic Earth nor a city suffering from some virus outbreak. Yet this game is stressful, oppressive, and sad. Because this game is real. All the horrible things you see happened, or is even happening now somewhere (perhaps in Ukraine).
tl;dr
Future history classes should let students play this game when they are teaching the horrors of war.

Bioshock 2 is the full fledged sequel to Bioshock, although at times it feels more like an expansion pack to the original...
Gameplay-
The gameplay of Bioshock 2 is largely an improvement over the original, with the player taking on the role of a Big Daddy prototype instead of Jack. Prototype is the operative word here, however, as with the exception of having a drill and clunky sound effects when moving or jumping, you never really feel like a big daddy. Splicers can often cause you large amounts of damage with small arms or melee weapons in only a few hits, which is very similar to the first game. I understand why this choice was made, for balance purposes, and I actually largely agree with it, but the feeling of being a clunking metal behemoth is never really there.
However, on an overall level, the sequel makes several key improvements. simultaneous usage of plasmids and weapons make combat much more fluid and satisfying, and the introduction of new enemies (alphas, brutes, big sisters) and the revamping of old ones (spider splicers, rumbler daddies) really contribute to this. Also, the game feels a good deal harder than the original without sacrificing the ability to make gameplay choices, and this is partially accomplished by upping the ante of combat. Where before you would only see 2-3 splicers an engagement, in Bioshock 2 it is not uncommon to engage a brute or two and 3-4 leadhead splicers in the same area.
The adopt/save/harvest mechanic with the little sisters works very well, allowing you to kill big daddies as before, and choose whether to a) harvest them right away b) have them gather ADAM for you and then harvest them c) save them right away d) have them gather and then save them. Obviously the best choice either way is to have them harvest ADAM from special corpses in the level first to get more ADAM, but this adds a great deal of moral and gameplay depth to the little sister dynamic. Plus, having the little sister ride on your shoulders and comment on combat as you go along is at times hilarious, or just cute, and a little sad. A very nice touch. Messing with the little sisters angers the big sisters, who often come for you after you've dealt with most of the little sisters in the level. They serve as improvised and random boss-fights, and are most definitely a challenge. They add a new source of tension (and ADAM) to the Bioshock formula.
Another gameplay change is the revamped Plasmid and Gene Tonic system. Plasmids at higher levels (2,3) have differentiated visual and gameplay effects, such as being able to charge up for more powerful attacks and shoot streams of elemental damage. They add a great deal of gameplay variety and re-playability. In addition, gene tonics are now all organized into one large slot, a welcome change, and some new ones have appeared that cover multiple effects, such as the elemental gene tonics. Finally, research remains useful but has been streamlined with a few minor tweaks.
Finally, the much touted ocean underwater sequences remain a pretty but relatively gimmicky and useless area of gameplay, where you are basically placed in a tunnel from one airlock to another. They are incredibly atmospheric, but they serve very little gameplay purpose other than scrounging.
Visuals-
Bioshock 2 is the full fledged sequel to Bioshock, although visually speaking it feels more like an expansion pack to the original. The game runs on the same engine as the original from 2007, and while innovations have been made in art design and level design, the same graphics remain largely untouched. The same low-res textures and effects are intact, and with the exception of new plasmid effects and a few minor tweaks, the technical graphics remain the same as they were in 2007. This is very upsetting, but it is an industry wide trend, and consoles are almost entirely responsible. Therefore, Bioshock 2 will not be penalized too harshly.
Artistically, the game does not disappoint, and the sound effects that accompany these new designs create a great atmosphere for the city of Rapture that feels fresh the second time around. New posters, new music, new character models, new weapons, and new effects.
Story-
In addition, the story, which has received some flak from Gamespot and other websites, is surprisingly good, and the audio diaries continue a wonderful trend from the first game that add a great deal of back story to Rapture and the tale of Andrew Ryan that newcomers and especially fans of the first game will love. Phoebe Lamb is the near antithesis of Andrew Ryan, and just as villainous for it, which is a refreshing change of pace. The ability to kill or spare certain key characters and the fact that such choices actually do have an impact on the story really adds to the replay value here. While the plot lacks the "holy s**t" factor of the original, it is quite well written and acted, and really draws you in, Bioshock fan or not.
Multiplayer/GFWL-
The game also includes a full fledged multiplayer mode, which is pretty much all of the standard fps game modes you would expect, but from a Bioshock perspective. Throw in a Modern Warfare style leveling and unlock system and a surprisingly well integrated multiplayer backstory and you've got a very solid multiplayer mode. A very nice touch is the inclusion of specific characters with unlock able audio diaries, backstories and customizable appearances in lieu of traditional custom skins and models. They also have high quality voice acting for these avatars. A particularly nice touch is the in game player apartment, which serves as a front for a standard multiplayer menu, and gives us an incredibly atmospheric glimpse of life on the eve of Rapture's collapse. Various pieces of furniture and appliances serve as server browser, audio diary storage, loadout customization, avatar customization, and story introduction. In addition, there are a variety of maps, many of them revamped and cleaned up versions of locations from the first game which add a great deal to this atmospheric multiplayer.
However, I have a bone to pick with Bioshock 2, and that is the forced installation of Games for Windows Live, without which you cannot save or load your game. Essentially you are tied to the service, which you are also forced to make an account with. This imposition is reminiscent of Ubisoft's recent DRM debacle and ties PC gamers to what is essentially Xbox Live for PC. I don't want this. Nobody wants this. I already have steam, why should I be forced to install GFWL? A small upset, maybe, but an important one.
Ultimately, Bioshock 2 takes the "if it ain't broke don't fix it" approach as a sequel, with some important and welcome exceptions. It doesn't blow my mind as the first one did, but it does do a great deal right, and with a few exceptions it makes very few unwelcome changes. It's a great game and a must buy for fans of the first.

This was a hard choice. Hatred definitely has some appealing elements to it in its great visuals, working with a reasonable art style and a good base engine at the core. The gameplay is where things start to falter. While you do have several objectives every mission to complete with a little bit of variety, it comes down to shooting dudes, and shooting more dudes. Now while that's what is expected in a top down shooter, the lack of variety in that is what is a huge problem over the long run, as a lack of enemy and weapon variety hurts the games overall execution.
Several game design mechanics work against each other, as in particular the execution system being the only way to gain health does not work with the more high action elements of the game. I love the destruction system however. The final two levels difficulty level is through the roof even on the easiest of difficulties, mostly because of the level design themselves: where the game wants you to play long range when you don't have any good long range options. The controversy of the game is overblown as there is most definitely worse games out there in terms of content, although I will say the audio clips did get to me every so often.
In the end, this game is a tough one. It has strengths, there's no doubt about that, but it's the lack of gameplay variety that ultimately gives the game the game a 5.5/10 for me, which makes it an average game. I'd do a thumbs to the side if I could, but when it comes down to it, I put gameplay as my strongest criteria, and for that I have to not recommend the game: but consider it's strengths and what you're looking from the game in question.

Fresh and simple, this game manages to create the feeling of an enormous, dynamic Freelancer-style sandbox with fantastically simple arcade-style controls.  Easily one of the most intuitive games I've ever played, and one of the prettiest (and in light of that, one of the best optimised too - running far better than games with lower requirements and looking better than some with higher requirements too).
This game feels a lot like Diablo II, perhaps unsurprisingly since those games are amongst the staggering pedigree of the team of TWO core developers.   The two games on Steam that seem closest to it in aesthetics and playstyle would be, I think, Starpoint Gemini 2 and Drifter.  I've got both and after 1 hour on Rebel Galaxy I already know I'm going to spend much more time on this than the other two.  It is far simpler to pick up and have fun with than Starpoint Gemini 2 - a real sense of instant fun and adventure - and it's significantly more polished and deep than Drifter, as well as being much prettier.
My only gripe with the game is that all the action takes place in a plane as opposed to having real 3D movement.  You can't pitch your ship up or down.  Hardly game-breaking, and I suppose it's true that the vast majority of real star systems are organised in a plane, but they are far from 2-dimensional from the point of view of a human space-ship!
Don't expect an X-series experience.  This game is much closer to classics like Freelancer and Tachyon: The Fringe.  It's not shallow, but it's certainly not "spreadsheets in space" either.
I don't know if I'll ever play this game again because my save was overwritten on my Steam Cloud after I let a friend get on his account at my house, but I had fun.

Rebel Galaxy is a fun, arcadey space game that feels like a mix between Sid Meier's Pirates, Freelancer/WC:Privateer, and Assassin Creed: Black Flag naval boardsides combat combined with a cheesy/awesome Western-Rock soundtrack.
There is a main storyline but you don't really have to follow it that much, you can just go around trading/mining/fighting/exploring, but the meat of the game is in the fighting. Thankfully the fighting is pretty fun. Instead of playing as a fighter or small freighter/gunship like many of these types of open-ended/sandbox space games, you start out in a Corvette and eventually work your way up to larger ships, I believe there is roughly 20 playable ships in all. As has been mentioned, the combat plays something like Assassin's Creed Black Flag ship battles, maneuvering on a 2D plane, with a heavy emphasis on broadsides and positioning. Your ship is outfitted with a main battery of broadside cannons as well as some turrets and secondary weapons (like missile launchers). You can customize the weapons of your ship with stuff like long/short range guns, beam lasers, missile turrets, anti-fighter/missile flak guns, etc etc.
The game is surprisingly colorful and ships explode into big bright fireballs when they die. Its fun. The music, as I've mentioned is cheesey western butt-rock and, IMO, quite nice. However if its not your thing, or if you just get bored of it, the game has an option to put your own music into the game (alongside or replacing the soundtrack). I haven't progressed too far into the main plot, but this doesn't seem like the kind of game most would play for a gripping plot, as its pretty basic so far. Basically your aunt, an (in)famous smuggler and overall space Rogue, sends you a package containing a weird alien artifact and the access codes to one of her old ships and tells you to meet up with her and you go off to get into cool space battles and track her down.
The game is only $20 and so far it seems like a lot of fun for that price.

which does NOT limit your number of installations as that version includes NO DRM WHATSOEVER. Also, that version includes the missing 64-bit version of the game.
Why is that 64-bit version of the game so important? This title was one of the first made to support Direct X 10 when Windows Vista was terrorizing the populace. The 32-bit version of the game, especially with mods or maxed out settings, runs terribly due to poor optimization. EDIT: I forgot to mention one thing about this game. For some odd reason Crysis will not run properly at 60fps when playing at 1920x1080. If you play on a TV the game will lock to the cinema mode at 24fps which is game breaking. If you play on a normal computer monitor it will still screw up and lock itself to about 50fps.
There are two ways to get around this...

When you first start the game you are instantly reminded of Far Cry 1 which was also developed by Crytek. I see this game as a reimagining of that game in a lot of ways, from setting, gameplay, colors, graphics, enemies, vehicles, green jungle, clear blue water, sandy beaches and binoculars. The premise is fairly similar as well as its structure. You start out alone on a beautiful island with someone on the radio helping you and you end up fighting science fiction monsters towards the end.

It's a juxtaposition that the shooting, recoil, smoke and line of sight in combat is so realistic yet the plot goes so far off the rails later on. It's like they changed their minds on what the game was supposed to be halfway through development. I would love to see these type of shooting mechanics in something else, like a realistic Vietnam shooter for instance. The first part of the game is superb and anyone who likes tactical shooters will enjoy it. There are no collectibles or audio logs which makes the mission objectives and tactical combat the main puprose instead of exploration. I like this because it doesn't force me to comb the map for stuff, instead enabling me to enjoy the gameplay and tactics purely on its own merits.

The AI isn't the best I've seen, some times enemies will run away from you out in the open like chickens with their heads cut off and this really breaks immersion at times. I was playing on the normal difficulty and maybe this is different in the higher ones but it shouldn't be like this even on normal. There are many little things like that, like when you infiltrate a small village to rescue a hostage and I get in a huge firefight with lots of explosions and shooting but when I get to the building which was right next to where all this action takes place I find a guy interrogating the hostage like nothing's happening outside. Here I am blowing people away with a shotgun right outside the door and he carries on like nothing's happening. At one point I even saw multiple enemies spawn in right in front of me when entering a building.

The graphics are really beautiful, just like Far Cry. At one moment you're in a bloody firefight, the next you're in a tranquil waterfall lagoon just taking it all in. The performance isn't that good though, even with my 780Ti I was struggling to maintain 60 FPS in the most combat heavy sections.

Despite its strong beginning however, when the alien level comes things get boring and frustrating. I don't understand what Crytek was trying to do here exactly. I don't wanna float around in this alien spaceship trying to figure out where to go next, I wanna go back to the jungle and have realistic firefights. I didn't ask for this and I don't want it.

It's got some amazing action sequences that are really fun to play though, involving hand to hand combat, small arms fire and even vehicles. I like the realism of the combat and tactics but it goes a bit off the rails after that and I think Psycho said it best, "I feel like I've jumped into a bloody' comic book here!"

With the huge amount of games available to us through Steam it is very easy to overlook all the smaller games in development. Let's face it, the only reason you know about a lot of the game you are playing right now is because people like us play them and tell you whether they are good or not. The huge flood of Early Access games to hit Steam, and some of the developers bailing on their projects don't help matters at all.

So I guess the question to ask is whether Grimoire: Manastorm is a good game, or do we watch it crash and burn? In its current state I would say that it definitely has potential to be a great multiplayer game. Although the game does barrow from the competitive multiplayer games that came before it, I feel it does a great job of setting itself apart through the combat system. It does follow the standard first person view and arena style map, but it relies on spells instead of guns. This is actually one of the games features that gives it some originality, and makes it a lot of fun. During the course of a match you are attempting to out score the other team via capture points on the map. The guys developing the game didn't invent this style of play but they adapted it to fit their game pretty well.

When it comes to killing the opposing team you definitely have choices. When you start up a match you can choose between Earth, Lightning, Ice, Fire, Nature and Nether for your class. You also have some options for utility and travel spells which help augment our play style. These include spells like Teleport, Repel, Stoneskin, Arcane Barrier, etc. Although each class has the same basic attacks to deal damage they feel very different when you start unleashing the more powerful spells. You can tell when playing each class that later on each one will have a role in a team composition. Since each class has a different set of powerful abilities team composition will become important when playing, like in every other multiplier game.

So is the game worth it? For the huge sum of $13.00, yes, it is worth it. I have spent $50.00 on a game and completely regretted ever loading it up. In the case of Grimoire, it only lacks people to play with. Like every other multiplayer game it requires people to play against each other to be fun. Given some time to polish and balance the game, we could easily see this being a great game that many people will be playing in the future.
