This was an impulse purchase for me, I had never heard of the "X" series before I bought this game. While most negative reviews here consist of betrayed "X" series fans venting, this review will focus on the gamebreaking bugs/problems.
Where to start...
I preordered this game one day before it released, from the little snippets of information I could find it looked like a cross between Descent Freespace, Imperium Galactica II, and Sins of a solar Empire.
1st person combat in space with a living economy that can be exploited for your gain? Why not?
It'd been a few years since I've found a good space sim and was hoping that this one would fill the gap.
Installed it and booted up the game, but I couldn't actually start a game without it locking up at the loading screen. After a quick google search I found a fix, I had to lower the sound quality on my sound card...odd to say the least.
The space combat was amazing! Graphics were spectacular! Textures were pretty low res on the stations.
Now for the bulk of why I recommend you don't buy this game, or at least wait until they fix it. 6+ months from now?
Game breaking bugs! I mean really game breaking, CTD, halting progression, raising your blood pressure bugs.
They have this cinematic whenever you enter the cockpit, your chair turns towards you and you sit down and it turns back. That's great and all until it breaks and the chair doesn't turn to you, but not only is that broken, everything useful you pull up from this panel that comes popping up from the side is. Only it doesn't if the chair breaks, so you get stuck looking 90 degrees to the right with no options to get out of that view because the only way to cancel it is to hit the "x" that is on the panel that never came up! *restart game*
At one point in the game you have to have a cargo carrier of yours deliver power cells. 100 to be exact, out of a 100,000 capactity carrier. Not only does that seem like an absurd waste of time, it has the potential to block you from ever progressing. Once ordered to trade, you cannot cancel the order. Pathing is broken so your carrier might just keep ramming against the station. Or it could fly a few thousand KM away from the station, only to turn around and fly back. Once it actually docks with the station, it might never complete the trade. It will just float there forever. You have to edit your save file to remove the ship from the trade que. *exit game and edit XML files with notepad++*
Corrupted saves! Lost seven hours of gameplay because it crashed after I entered a Space Highway.
The highways are a gimmick that should have never been added, you have to play bumper tag with the other ships that enter to get a speed boost. Only problem is that sometimes ships never enter so you are stuck at slow speed for the next five minutes. That and you might get kicked out of the highway for no reason what-so-ever, so have fun flying a few hundred thousand KM back to civilization since you can't enter the highway again. *Load game that may or may not be recent*
Economy is not what I would call living. Trading is more likely to break your game and takes such an absurdly long time for your ship to go from point A to point B that you can make more money, faster, flying to stations and trading rockets.
The devs boasted that you can blow up/capture a cargo carrier full of *insert item here* and watch the prices spike since the supply is now lower than the demand. Either A. They lied. Or B. The game is so broken that it never registered that I vaporized the cargo after I destroyed the ship that carried it.
You can just capture a battleship and pawn it off for around 120m credits, that really made trading null so I don't know why they bothered. *Just blow it all up!*
Sometimes the game will enable a "noclip" function, you can fly and shoot straight through everything! While amusing for a bit, it becomes less so when you are trying to escort a ship and the mission fails because your projectiles go through the enemy fighters, thus allowing them to blow up the escorted ship at their leisure. Only way to cancel the bug is to reload, which fails the mission anyways, so GG. *try not to cry*
Framrate likes to take a dive in this game, especially at highways. Apparently it was a big problem for most people, some people would get 20 frames regardless. I was lucky to be running at 60+, until they put out a patch and it crawled to 25. I'm not using a potato to play this game either. They seriously broke it.
There are more, but seriously, the list goes on and on and on. I played 50 hours of this mess.
Along with the scores of little bugs that just either break immersion or break whatever else I can't recommend buying this.
After really, really wanting to like this game, I found it to be an exercise in frustration. Joke is on me for getting the CE for a game I didn't know jack about.

Melee remains the best competitive smash game, but its mechanics lack quality-of-life tuning that make it (to some) not feel fun to play.
Smash 4 feels a bit slow with the lack of attack-canceling mechanics and generally longer end-lag on many actions.
For a time, Project M (a competitive brawl mod) was similar to melee but a bit more well-rounded and more fun for your average player. A C&D letter from Nintendo's lawyers shut down development.
So enter Rivals of Aether: an original smash game with a vaguely pokemon/digimon esque cast of characters. RoA strikes a fantastic balance of "fun to play" and "competitive", with the general speed and mechanical demand being high, but not stiff/awkward like melee. It features a smaller cast of characters (8 main+3 DLC so far), but each has extremely unique characteristics which make them feel more distinct from one another than characters in the smash series.
The game is developed by a smash fan for smash fans, and it has been pretty well balanced since even the start of early access. The pixel art has been steadily improving, and if you're the sort of person turned off by pixel art, I think you'll come to appreciate it in time; pixel art makes the readability of frame data, hit boxes, and everything else massively more clear than what you get in 3D fighting games.
The game is totally worth it at full price and a steal if it's on sale.

After the first Bioshock, Bioshock 2 isn't exactly what you may expect it to be. To start things off, many of the familiar gameplay elements have been changed. Combat, physical, and engineering tonics are all lumped collectively under just plain ol' tonics. This gives you a little more customization but also seems to give the player a bit too much power in my opinion. The way you use your plasmids has also changed. Instead of switching from weapon to plasmid, you have both available at the same time. This is one change I did enjoy, but it also hindered my ability to quickly switch to my desired plasmid as the quickselect keys were now F1, F2, etc. instead of the number keys. The main problem I have with Bioshock 2 is the inconsistent difficulty. At first the game is very difficult because you are a slow moving punching bag of a big daddy. As you gain tonics though, the game becomes progressively more easy until you are an unstoppable walking tank. With that all said, this game is an absolute blast to play. Lunging 50 feet and smashing in the face of a punk♥♥♥♥♥little splicer has never felt so empowering. Especially with a big♥♥♥♥♥drill.
TL;DR : This game has inconsistent difficulty, and a few annoying changes, but all in all beating the hell out of splicers with a big♥♥♥♥♥drill can be alot of fun.

RtCW is a brilliantly enjoyable romp through 1943 Germany.
The game generates atmosphere and suspense at an excellent - yet not too fast - rate. With creative weaponry, and carefully hidden secrets, you truly come to try to uncover everything available within a level, as you face increasingly dangerous and monstrous enemies. If I can raise one thing I didn't quite like, it would be some elements of the final Boss fight. Everything builds throughout the game to this, the culmination of Operation Resurrection - Heinrich the first. But, I felt that as he was limited in his attacks and merely a lumbering oaf, that this slightly detracted from my full enjoyment of the battle. I came equipped. I worked HARD to keep my ammunition and health high for this battle. And when he doubled over after my onslaught of lead, I expected a second form to fight, it was too easy. But he exploded and died. Disappointed, yes, but surprised? Not particularly, as this was 2001, and the concept of multiple boss forms was still a new topic, but it was an enjoyable fight while it lasted nonetheless.
I reccomend you definitely spend an afternoon with a thoroughly well executed game such as this, it would be time well spent.

A Fantastic platformer and a much better take on Soulsifying a Metroid Game than Salt and Sanctuary and other titles like it.
Hollow night not only carries over the hard mechanics of the Souls games (Which I shall call Stamina RPGs from now on) while also creating and developing a lore of it's own.
Unlike most Stamina RPGs save for Monster Hunter or maybe LoRule (LInk Between Worlds) Hollow night boasts a wonderful colorful and interestingly depressing world with cute bug characters and a wonderfully depressing story that manages to still stand on it's own and keep an identity away from Dark Souls.
Without getting into the spoiler territory it is well worth going for the 100% ending if you are crazy enough to manage it. You will be rewarded with the only glimmer of bittersweet hope I have seen from a game like this.
Good job Team Cherry, may your efforts bring forth another game of equal value and amazingness.

Ok so reading all of these reviews may build up a bit of hype and while the game is great, its not necessarily the greatest game ever.

Customization is great as far as equipment and such.  I do wish there was the option to paint your ship assuming I'm not an idiot and didn't miss that.
The soundtrack is great with that meaning its along the lines of rock/classic rock which makes keeps your energy up.  My experience comparison is to that of Sins of a Solar Empire... the music alone could make me stop playing the game.
To me its more like, I'm a badass! With a space ship!  Come get some! and lets rock out to that!
not, oh hey... could you pass me that mozart cd so I can sit blowing up stuff with some somber tones running in my head...zzzz
Anyway, this is as close as it gets to feeling like you're really out in your battlestar galactica or star wars destroyer taking on the skum of the universe.
There is some travelling but the space is populated and plenty of things to run into or die from on your own.  I have a knack for running into red threat levels and practicing reloading the game.
The earn money and upgrade your ship works really well, you do need to do some main missions or use your map to find missions.  Flying in a particular direction works too however, you may find you run into near or sudden death encounters with ships you clearly underestimated.
Another way to describe this game is, its like FTL but you dont see through your ship and in order to jump, you best run like hell to reach a safe warp (jump) point!
To summerize:
Pros:
Easy to play and get to the action (and die lol)
Thank god its in 2D because handling a 3rd direction would probably make me sick and be overwhelmed (may be a con for some)
Very good graphics to the point where it looks great and is playable on lower end systems.
It still plays beautifully and perfectly smooth at 4k with a 980 Ti.
Simple but robust upgrade options.
Targeting is pretty easy, the AI can manage some of your guns as well.
The universe is alive, even if you did nothing but fly around you run into stuff and/or cool planets with bases.
Theres a story at the very least.
Awesome sounds and an upbeat sound track.  Your ship makes most of those cool sounds you want to hear when you change directions or power up your warp drives.
Great Value/Price makes this hard to beat!
Cons:
Limited view options (may not be a con but locking the view closer or further would be nice).
Just to add in case a developer reads this, if there was a cockpit view I may have to change my pants every time I play.  That would be amazing and with using the broadsides, having the camera switch to whichever side you're moving your view stick to would be an idea.
Unable to paint or color your ship.
There are a lot of ship choices but I wish there was a variety of each class (not a big deal).
While there is a story its not the most elaborate story or intriguing.  Something more along the lines of a mysterious cosmic disturbance was felt among the universe and a new alien race or super weapon is rumored to be the cause.  Among the warring factions and those at peace, spontaneous attacks from a new enemy emerge and along with your journey between the factions in space, do you suddenly run into unexpected encounters from this new weapon or race.  . . . . just my thoughts, some pulled form mass effect which was great up until they ruined it.  There is just more there to be desired but I'm happy to at least have a story.
No multiplayer...not a big deal but would be fun to do missions or visit solar systems with a buddy.  Doubling the enemies per additional player would seem sufficient.
Final Thoughts:
If the developers are still paying attention (hoping their sales numbers are great or better than expected), this is a great game and starting point that so many others try to achieve and simply fail at.
There is a lot of potential here and simply adding more star systems with harder difficulty and additional story would hopefully not be too much trouble if DLC becomes a future ambition.
I was bored or at least overwhelmed with EVE and it really wasn't enjoyable having to basically learn how complex the game was...especially when you only have a few hours to play periodically.  This game strikes a great balance and at the limit of 2D movement however, I think it was a perfect choice because you can focus on battles! and Blowing stuff up!
I am very pleased with this purchase and with so much room to add on or improve (even when it is already done so well already) I think it is something worth expanding on.
None the less, you will have a blast if you go into this game expecting a space game with simple controls a little travelling here and there (typically no more than 1 minute in the first map), and small battles that grow to epic as the game progresses.
Considering fast indoor go karting costs 20 bucks for 10 minutes.... this gives you a whole lot more with some speakers and a subwoofer .... you will be the next Han Solo in your SS Pea Shooter as I named my ship.
Enjoy!

As I look back fondly at Freelancer and how I could spend nights hunting pirates and trading illegal goods in the edges of the galaxy, I noticed Rebel Galaxy hit steam and thought, wonder if this is going to be one of those “trying to hard” games or actually good.
Well it’s actually good.
Now I’m not going to call it a masterpiece, but I will say it is very entertaining in this day and age where everyone is trying to do something new and innovative. I suppose the kinda new thing is how the combat works, closest example is probably world of warships, but in space and even that comparison is not giving it justice.
--Movement and Combat.--
The ship that you pilot is on a horizontal axis so you can only move back, forwards and sideways, this makes it easier to pilot the ship and aim your guns to your target. Targeting is automatic in a sense that the target you are directly aiming at is your primary target.
The ships you pilot have broadside ports on both sides of the ship and the number of them varies on the ship you pilot, The Broadside is your primary weapon as you can’t set it to automatically fire.
Your ship also has turret spots, however your turrets can be set to automatically fire at set targets and you can choose the primary target for each individual turret.
You also have access to a secondary armament slot that can be outfitted with different armaments ranging from flak fighter/rocket countermeasures to mines and missiles.
--Ships and components.--
As you would imagine, you can buy and outfit a wide array of different ships, each with their own unique specialities. This also means some ships are more heavily armored than others, or boast more potential firepower.
Most things on the ships can be upgraded to a better variant, like more armor plating, better shields, thrusters, engines, bigger cargo hold and so on, you get the general idea.
--Stations and trading.--
Each solar system that you can enter and explore has stations and these stations, mostly, can be used as a hub to repair, refill and outfit your ship to your liking. However, that is not all you can do. You can visit the bar to get the latest news from the news board that gives you an idea what is going on in your solar system, this is an ever changing system, some stations might have a tech boom that bumps up the price of technological trade goods, making it more lucrative for traders to sell their goods to that particular station, this mostly means you.
You can also pick up different missions from the mission board, that all range from, go and kill this dood, defend this dood from being killed by this dood, pick up this thing that this dood lost and so on, you get the general idea.
As you would imagine, one of the easiest ways to earn money is to work the market. Buy a bulk of trade goods for cheap from a back end station and take it to a prime trade port to get the most out of your goods, rinse and repeat.
I remember making convoluted trade routes in Freelancer to earn millions in a few hours simply by working the market, flying from system to system, buy goods that are cheap in that system, fly to the nearest highest bidder and sell the goods and repeat the same thing. I can imagine this tactic would work here and even slightly better because of the ability to steer your ship during warp.
Like I mentioned earlier, stations are not solely for trading however. Some stations are designated as guild bases, like for example the first system you start in houses a merchants guild that offers unique ships and components unique to that faction.
--Interaction.--
What I mean with interaction is just the general interaction with other pilots that you come across while flying around in space. Your choices matter, not much, but they matter. The same goes for your story missions, like for example, one mission in the beginning you have the chance to bribe a pirate to make themselves disappear or just kill him like you’re asked to.
These sorta decisions keep popping up all along your adventures and even in random encounters while exploring, like for example, you just saved a trader from pirates and scanned his cargo hold to find some very expensive materials, do you kill the guy or let him go?
--Verdict.--
I would imagine that Rebel Galaxy is very good for what it is trying to do, it’s deep enough to keep people of different moralities happy. Sure it’s not the most beautiful looking game out there, but it’s not a game you want to put a paper bag over either. Combat is nice and simple and offers variety of what weapons you can and want to use, same goes for ships and other components. For people looking for a slightly more casual space sim, Rebel Galaxy is your game.
And let’s not forget the bloody music, oh my gawd the music. So Firefly, So Firefly.

I bought The Last Remnant for $3.74 in 2011, and it took me four years to finally get around to playing it.  It took me 99 hours to get to the end because I went out of my way to do all of the important sidequests, so if you're not interested there, you can be done much faster.  There's also a demo if you want to try a bit of the game out for yourself.  I played the game entirely with the Xbox360 controller and did not try keyboard and mouse.
The Last Remnant is a type of strategic RPG that masquerades as a standard JRPG.  There's a lot that it does differently than compared to a JRPG, but then it's also pretty different from your standard SRPG too.  Or tactical.  Whatever.  I've seen it compared to Ogre Battle and I've heard that TLR was originally a SaGa game, but I haven't played anything in either series so this game stands as quite unique for me.  The story is kinda all right, I liked being able to go back to the city sector screen from anywhere in town, and there are a few catchy battle themes.
Combat is a fairly different affair compared to the typical "everyone stands in a line and makes hitting motions at the enemy" kinda game.  Instead of having between three and five people out at once to save the world, you field a max of 18 in the second half of the game, though it's not entirely as though everyone's running around doing their own thing.  You put your characters into small parties of up to five members each, or unions, where everyone pools HP and AP for special moves--but the enemy does it too.  This is a game where positioning and attacking the enemy's side is important, but unlike grid-based strategy RPGs, you can't directly order your your unions into a position to trap enemies.
The game works on a Deadlock mechanic.  Basically, two opposing unions meet on the battlefield and fight it out until one of them is dead.  At least you can break Deadlock to attack another group or heal, and the enemy can't.  But the idea is that both groups are focused on only the other, so you can have another group attack that preoccupied enemy group to flank them, and continue to gang up on them to get further damage and morale bonuses.  Of course you're vulnerable to being flanked, so it's generally a good idea to assign everyone their own target, and to target the flunkies in boss battles first since those focusing on the boss first leave their backs open.
There's also the morale feature to keep in mind.  Unions have their own Limit Break-styled morale meter, but there's one at the top of the screen that affects both sides of the battlefield.  Most battles start with it in the middle where neither side benefits, but one side getting an advantage will result in better combat performance.  Enemies appear in the field and you're given an opportunity to initiate combat (on top of trying to draw as many into one fight for a higher challenge and more rewards), but if they catch you, they'll start with a free turn and the bar in their favor.  A stat buff for the majority and a stat debuff for the minority sounds insignificant, but it's very noticeable in practice.  Some tougher enemies will use devastating attacks when they control the morale bar, so shutting them down is a top priority.
There are QTEs during battles.  I know some of you are rolling your eyes already, but I like to think of it closer to a timed-hits mechanic versus "press this button to not die" like in some games, since the prompt comes up during the same part of the animation.  The chance for the prompt is tied to the battlefield morale, and during an attack, you're given one of five buttons (default A, B, X, Y, and right trigger for X360 controls).  Successfully press the right button in time and the next person on your side in that Deadlock will leapfrog to the top of the action queue and do their move, getting another prompt.  Hit all of the prompts to finish the combo and the last person on your team will attack with a guaranteed critical hit.  There's a prompt when being attacked too--parrying results in a stun, blocking with a shield results in a damaging shield bash, and evading results in a heavily-damaging counter attack.  Given battles are largely an affair of picking orders and then watching everything play out, this does keep things kinda engaging, though you can also set the game to handle the prompts for you at a lower success rate.
When it comes to control, there's not a lot that's in your hands.  You're given a choice of up to five orders per union, ranging from "attack with your weapon!" to "use Combat Arts!", but you may not get the prompt to heal or revive somebody when you really need it.  And even if you do pick "use Combat Arts!", that doesn't mean everyone in the union actually will, even if they have enough AP.  Some of it is down to union composition, though there's also union morale to consider.  You can at least turn off individual arts if you don't want people using them.  You can't directly give any equipment to anybody except the protagonist, Rush.  There's an .ini edit to circumvent this, though that has its own hangups.  There's a pretty robust item creation/upgrade system, but your characters can only request things you have in your inventory already and they may not ask for or even use things that logic states they should.  You can assign unions their own formations, but you can't exactly move people away to avoid the big boss' area-of-effect attack, so you have to hope that everyone is standing in the right place to not get torn apart.
The only real problems I had with the game were texture pop-in and laggy gameplay, even on a solid-state drive.  Cutscenes weren't immune to this either, but at least you could pause to let everything load, or pause and then skip them if you wanted.  The game was also more difficult than I'd consider other JRPGs or the like, though I wouldn't put it up there with the hardest games in the genre.  A lot of it can be avoided by setting your teams up well, though there's still a luck element involved.  This is also one of the few games I've played where trying to do all of the major sidequests makes the final boss significantly harder.  Given you have to beat a very difficult boss for that 100% completion before a certain part of the story, it's not really suggested to attempt this on your first time through--there's a New Game Plus feature so try it on your second loop.  I kinda hurt my enjoyment of the game by having to grind out because of my unknowing mistake.
But despite all that, I really did enjoy my time with The Last Remnant.  I've never quite played anything like it, and while there isn't as big a drought for JRPGs on PC now as there was in 2011, this game is certainly unique enough to be a keeper in my book.  If you have any interest in the game at all, you really should try the demo out.  It manages to be a fun experience without falling back on established Final Fantasy references or the like.

Worst JRPG I've ever played.
I really wanted to give this game a chance. 16+Hrs of playtime speak for themselves.
The graphics are good, can't say anything against that. But the rest of this game makes me run away as soon as I try to play it.
Didn't see that much of the story, or at least i hope so. So maybe the story is decent but the gameplay kept me from it.
Now i start with what really makes this game the worst JRPG i've ever seen.
1. The characters : The main Character Rush is a dumb, hotheaded but far to talented kid who just doesn't think about any consequence his actions could have. Too often I was sitting there watching him rush(no pun intended) into dangerous situation and i was left with one big question : WHY?!
The cast of other characters makes even less sense. Rush meets them and after less than two lines of dialog : "I'm gonna help you." Again same question... WHY?! These characters never met before and just exchanged less words, than Hodor from Game of Thrones has in his entire repertoire, and they are acting like BFFs?!
2.The character growth system: The game punishes you for ending your fights as fast and efficient as possible. As your character's hp don't grow if the they don't get damaged. This learning by doing stuff was allready bad in one of the older Final Fantasys back on the SNES. And that's not wine, it doesn't get better with age.
3.The battle system/battle rank system/enemy scaling : The Battle system itself seems interesting at first glance.Especially the Unit-Formation-Leader stuff really has a lot of interesting and strong points. But then the atrocities begin. The Battle system itself is a lot of random, luck reliant stuff. Which is never good in a turnbased game.
You get no indication which Unit moves when, you have no Idea of the enemy's speed. And you get no information on the enemy's movents at all. How is any human beeing supposed to formulate a strategy without even the most basic of information provided? How am I supposed to keep my morale up if the enemy Interferes with any of my moves?
Your party strength plays no part in the enemy scaling to your party at all. As you fight more enemys, what you sometimes have to do, your battle rank rises. The higher your battle rank, the stronger the monsters. That system is supposed to balance itself out. But I tell you one thing: It doesn't because at some point enemys will start using Area of Effect Attacks which damage your Unitmembers Individually this is going to oneshot whole Units, at some occasions even the whole Army, as happened to me several times. making fighting impossible because there is no flee option. Then there are these Special Arts that some characters have. They can use them if a gauge on the Status screen of the Unit is filled. These gauges fill as you attack, and drop as you take damage. So these Special Arts are supposed to give you an even greater edge when you are allready dominating the fight. But anything like a strong "last resort" type of attack would maybe make many fights less frustrating.
So I would not recommend this game, even if I would get paid for that.

A fun arcadey space trucking game. Starts slow, but really opens up after you leave the first system, with lots of equipment and ship classes to grind for. Though I'm not sure $18 is a fair price for the amount of content you get, I'd recommend waiting for sales.
I do have some problems with its game design, though.
1. Escort missions simply don't work. Warp pairing just boosts the chances to break warp from proximity to objects tenfold, and since escortees can't navigate space for♥♥♥♥♥♥and just fly in straight line, if you're lunky enough to get some asteroid field or nebula in a way, have fun waiting 5 minutes for NPC ship to slowly fly through it. Not only that, paired warp speed is also extremely slow compared to how you normally travel by yourself.
2. Warp mechanics in general are hit and miss. For example, there should've been different ranges that trigger warp break for different types of objects. There's absolutely no reason why some asteroid or piece of junk should stop the warp unless you're REALLY close to it, it's not an enemy dreadnought that pose any threat. Jumpgates on the other hand are extremely easy to miss.
3. Not only the UI is pretty ugly thanks to huge prompt icons, it also suffers from many problems. Why do loot and small ships have the same color on radar? When I use gamepad, I sit a bit further away from the monitor and it's impossible to tell what's a small square and what's a small circle on the radar. Why doesn't mission board show location of the objective on the map? Why can't you wave traders goodbye right after trading with them and instead have to go through all dialogue screens again? Why can't you just use B to go back in dialogue? Why can't you use starmap to check available equipment/ships on stations you visited? Why can't you see where jumpgates lead if there's a mission marker on them?
4. Its's another game that treats you like a r-e-t-a-r-d and constantly gives you tips how to return to broadside mode, use scanner, etc. I don't need to see these tutorials a hundred times, nor am I dumb enough to forget which button does what. These things just clutter UI and get on my nerves, there always must be an option to turn those off.
5. Systems lack hand-crafted environments and originality. Every nebula and asteroid belt is just a copy-paste of another one, all of the same size, there are no really unique formations and places to visit. Every system is the same, just with differently colored star and background. It's true even for the blocked-off alien world you get to visit in the end of the game. When you have only a dozen systems to offer, you could at least try to make them feel original and interesting in some way.
6. Holding A activates tractor beam, docking, warp and opens dialogue if you're receiving a call. Want to quickly warp out but some pirate is calling you? Need to enter the station with full cargo but there's a bunch of illegal materials floating about? Tough luck.
I mean, it's good fun, but these amateurish and obvious problems really keep the game from being as enjoyable as it should be.

Many other people have reported technical issues with the game. I did not encounter any, use at own risk.
An adrenaline-fueled first-person-shooter, introducing the, by now, legendary Nano-Suit to the gamer population. Despite being
by now, it still holds up graphically absolutely beautiful. The levels are so large the game might as well be open-world and allow for absolutely any approach the player comes up with.
Stealthy approach with silencer and observation and marking of the area and enemies in it? You bet you can do it.
Charge in guns blazing? Sure thing. If you manage that on harder difficulties without dying I salute you.
Drive through the enemies with a car, ignoring them entirely, just to get to the objective? Also possible.
Another plus-point, which will not age with time is the superb AI. The enemies will talk with each other (English on easy, normal and hard, Korean on Delta), plan on how to attack you, flank you, patrol the level and inform each other with light signals if you have been spotted somewhere else. If you miss out the opportunity to kill a patrol while you're sneaking around, they might stab you in the back later when they are called in as reinforcements if you get spotted. Also, the differing languages they speak is a fascinating concept, difficulty wise.
I will say that the driving in the game isn't very good, but you don't do it that much, and if it bothers you too much, you don't have to do it all. I don't mind that much and use the cars quite often.
Story wise I also find the game interesting, although it obviously isn't a 10/10, it manages to keep the game's focus and is tightly and cohesively written. It makes you interested in what is going on, even if the characters are a bit forgettable, having said that, I haven't finished the game yet, so maybe my opinion of the characters will change. I like the guy I'm playing, and I love the fact that for once, I'm playing as a
, in an FPS none the less!
If you like shooters, a definite recommend. Considering you can play the game any way you want (something companies claim is possible with newer titles but often isn't), I'd recommend it to someone who exclusively plays Splinter Cell just as I'd do the same to someone who plays Call of Duty only.
Despite the constant crashes, lossing Save files, & urge to delete the game many times, i enjoyed the story very much & would definitly recommend the game for hardcore gamers.

Ratings:
Overal Rating: ★★★
Plot Overview:
This game continues right where Saints Row IV left off, so if you haven't played it, you will be confused. Instead of playing the Saints leader, you can either play Johnny Gat or Kinzie Kensington. During Kinzie's birthday party, Matt convinces the gang to play with an ouiji board. They continue to play around with it until they ask if the boss will ever get married. The board then continues to move and spells out the name "Jezebel" and the boss is sucked into a portal to Hell. Determined to get him back, Johnny makes the ouiji board open up another portal for him, and Kinzie joins him. While there, Johnny and Kinzie team up with Dane Vogel (Saints Row 2), Blackbeard, Shakespeare, and Vlad in order to take down Satan. In order to save the boss, you have to obtain an invitation to the wedding between the boss and Jezebel (Satan's daughter).
Pros:

Cons:

Endings:
Censored out to avoid spoilers. (mouse over them to view)
Commentary:
I've been a fan of the Saints Row series for a while now, and I loved the fourth installment to the series. When they announced that the Saints would be going to Hell, and that you would be playing someone other than the boss, I was excited. I was even more excited about the Fallen Angel wings that you get. Unfortunately, the wings turned out to be a major let down. The wings give you the ability to fly, just as you could in the fourth game, but it came with a price. You have to keep up at a certain speed or you will "stall" and Johnny/Kinzie (whoever you're playing) will start to fall. The wings cause you glide very slowly, and to increase the speed, you must flap your wings. This wouldn't have been a problem if you didn't have a limit. When flying, you have a limit as to how many times you can flap your wings to pick up your speed. At first you start off with just one, and as you level up, you can purchase upgrades to increase this number. I found the wings to be extremely annoying. Whenever you jumped, just even a little bit, the wings would spring out. I don't think it will be a problem for you, if little things like that don't bother you.
Moving onto the story plot. I felt that the story plot was kind of basic, and that not a lot of thought was put into it. All you do is run around doing things to fill up a bar (located in your Hub) which is Satan's rage bar, until it's full and it triggers a cutscene. Until that bar is full, you're not doing anything important. Most of the missions you do aren't substancial to the story plot, but are rather filler missions in order to make this game longer. I enjoyed the game in parts, but for the most part, I felt that it was slightly rushed. You spend hours doing nothing, until the rage bar is full at which then, you're back to actually completing the main story line. I enjoyed the cutscenes where it shows a story book, it felt as if you were reading a story or watching a movie, rather than playing a game. I still enjoyed Johnny's typical behavior of saying that he wanted to shoot Satan in the face.
A new feature that I liked was that the game offers multiple endings. Instead of having to complete certain tasks to unlock them, once you defeat the final boss, you're taken back to the story book, and you select the ending that you want to choose. I would have enjoyed this more if the endings were longer than 30 seconds - 1 minute. A few of the endings seem like they could be future expansions to the franchise, but the endings gave very few details for you to be able to tell.

In conclusion, Saints Row: Gat Out of Hell was an entertaining game in certain places. It still has the same humor from the previous games, and has new weapons and demon super powers for you to play with. If you are a dedicated gamer, this game is rather short, and you can complete it in about 1-2 days. But I would recommend this game to someone who needs something to pass the time for a day or two. In my opinion, the game isn't worth $19.99, but if you're serious about purchasing it, I would wait until steam puts it on sale for at least 50% off.

This level (or lack therof) of quality and innovation of this game is unacceptable for this day and age, and for carrying on a series this far. Firaxis was plain lazy. I find none of the bad elements of Civ are ever remedied in the next sequel.   I have played it twice through and have no desire to play again.
Why?  Because:
-Just like other civs, game becomes slow, boring grinding turn passing after a certain time, re-confirming a bunch of trade routes every few turns (unless you are doing a global conquest)
-Technologies are new but a completely unintuative in their organization and have no real sense of direction, other than to pick the ones needed to fullfil the type of victory aiming for.
-AI is idiotic, and as unrealistically backstabbing as usual
-Diplomacy has nothing new at all compared to CIV 5, just different leaders and voices (leader 'catch phrases' are lame too) .. 'favours' are new, but almost useless, there is almost no point to communicating with the other nations.
-Far less resources to trade compared to other civs
-"Happiness" from civ5 has been replaced with "Health" and decreases for the exact same reasons (number of cities, number of specialists, population) which doesn't really make sense and is annoying to try to constantly keep above zero for most of the game.
-Landscape is new and pretty is some ways, but I find it overly busy colour wise.
- End of game is BORING - STOP making uncreative end-game sequences with absolutely no substance - a screen and a voice saying you won with a small blurb. No score, cinematic, nothing. No one likes an anti-climactic game ending.
-"Quests" (which aren't quests by definition, just a 2 option decision) add little to the game.
-Units are fairly dull, no weapons of mass destruction like nukes in other Civ games
-miasma is annoying
-games are relatively short and small maps compared to other civs
Positives
-espionage is a little more interesting
-option to kill or adopt local alien creatures in different, as is the path and objectives to reach your victory goal
-satellites and space layer good idea but not developed enough
-pre-game bonus choices a good addition

Too many bugs. The idea of the game seems fun and I'm really trying, but I have to fight the interface (worse than prior X games) every time I want to do a task. Submenus upon submenus upon submenus, under the menu, only to find that's not the right place to send a fleet command for your non-combat ships to stop following, even though you were looking for fleet commands. Missions are fairly broken as well, you will need to do save game editing to fix/get past some of them. In fact, I'm stuck on selling 300 Food to some station in Fervid something as they won't seem to accept any of the 5,000 Food I've picked up in my Construction Vessel nor a Lepton that has precisely 300 Food on it. Neither of those ships will complete the trade with the mission station. I've heard that I have to buy the 300 Food from a specific station, but the mission never mentions it and the mission "briefs" are just that, brief and uninformative.
The walking around in stations is a huge waste of time and is often laggier than being out in space. Trying to do trades in the game is a joke, especially if it's a trade for a mission, your ships will often get "stuck" traveling between systems or even wandering aimlessly around a station and never dock, like its supposed to, to start the trade. I've watched one of my ships (Construction Vessel) dock twice at the correct port, only to never unload its cargo and instead immediately undock. This game is an endless series of frustrations with a few glimmers of joy.
I almost forgot to mention your singular ship that you fly, which can only have one gun of a certain type (plasma, mining, etc.) "active" at a-a-time, you cannot have, say, four plasma cannons all blasting away. The only way to upgrade your weapon is to upgrade that one weapon to a strong version. Also, any time you open a menu while your ship is flying, your ship will STOP. So don't even think about multi-tasking while flying to some distant object, even for a brief moment. All forward momentum will immediately cease.
Oh, and yes you can capture ships, but only to sell them. In theory you can fly the ships, but as part of your boarding process you destroy the jump engines and drives, which makes the ship incapable of moving and there's no way to repair the ship if it doesn't already have Construction URV drones on it. Some ships don't even have drone bays and it's only a random chance (I have yet to see any included Construction URV drones after capturing 9 vessels) that they would pre-exist. You then put an Engineer on the ship which randomly (or you edited your save game) has Construction URV drones who then may, or may not, repair the ship. I have three Balor class ships sitting around with engineers and Construction URV drones, but the engineers refuse to do anything. One says he's repairing, but it's been 15 hours of in-game time of nothing. The other two engineers aren't even pretending to do their repair work on the engines.
Did I mention selling the ships you captured? Well, that's only if you didn't tell one of the first ships to dock at the Ship Trader (you can only modify/sell ships to specific traders that know/want that type of ship) and repair itself, only to find out that the ship cannot move to the repair dock because the engines are destroyed and the engineer won't repair it. Now that Ship Trader is "stuck" on that order and will refuse to do any business with you, including selling any of your other ships. The only way to fix this is, again, to edit your save game and remove the repair order or just delete the offending ship. Also, you need Pilots to capture small ships (e.g. Fighters) and Captains to command the larger capital ships, plus an engineer to (maybe) repair the capital ship, but you may only carry a few (seven I think?) crew on your ship. You need a Marine Officer to even do the boarding, so that's one down already, so don't even bother with Pilots and trying to capture smaller ships. Best bet is to capture the ship, destroy anything Yisha asks you to in order to help the boarding process, and then immediately sell the ship. Don't try to fix anything. If you want a ship, go buy one from a Ship Trader.

Very fun and underrated game. By far the best attempt at a competitive platform fighter outside of Melee and Project M that's out there.
I'm a competitive smash player and this game is an amazing stress reliever for me. Even if you're not into competitive smash, this game is a lot easier on the hands and more intuitive to pick up and play than those games since a lot of the tech skill from smash isn't there, the only thing you need to learn is wavedashing which is very easy to do in this game since you can just input sideways + airdash at the same time for a shortcut.
Despite being a much easier game to get into the game still maintains that fast, chaotic, destructive feeling that Melee and PM have and doesn't go to being a slower game like the newer smash bros games are. The skill ceiling is still huge, the combo system is still deep, you can still do a ton with movement.
This is also the only Platform Fighter game (other than Brawlout) that doesn't just rip off smash characters. The characters might take some inspirations here and there, but they all feel like individuals and not just bootleg melee characters. In an aspect I love, all the characters have a mechanic (or even several mechanics) completely unique to them that changes up the gameplay in a big way. I'm going to list a few of them just to show the MMO-like variety available here.
Zetterburn - Specific moves give a burn status that does extra damage over time, burned characters take more knockback from smash attacks
Wrastor - All of his smashes are in the air rather than the ground, one of his moves summons a wind aura that buffs his movement
Etalus - has several moves that coat the ground with ice, this ice coating greatly enhances his wavedash and dash attack length. Several of his specials also have different properties if used on ice, including freezing the opponent and giving Etalus ice armor.
Each of the 9 (soon to be 11 as of tomorrow) characters has something of that variety. The music, aesthetics, and presentation are all also very solid. This game has the potential to create an entire genre, and I wish more titles would follow its passionate example and give us a greater variety of Melee-like games.

Rivals of Aether is a platform-fighting game similar to the Super Smash Bros. Melee. Don't make the mistake of calling it a smash clone, because that's where you are wrong. It is in the same genre as Smash, as a fighting game based around knocking you opponent off the screen, using percentages, however there are many differences, big and small.
Key Differences:
No shielding or grabbing.
Airdodging acts like Melee, however you act after doing it (it makes wavedashing possible)
You can wall jump out of everything (including special fall)
There are no ledges.
All stage hazards can be removed by entering 'Basic' mode.
Jumpsquat is universially 5 frames.
Practically no landing lag on any aerials.
A lot of these are good changes that help the game feel more agressive.
There are many more changes and features.
The only con is that there are a couple of balancing issues.
If you have a couple of friends and controllers, expect a great time, as long as no one picks Zetterburn.

Rivals of Aether is an indie brawler the takes its gameplay mechanics from Nintendo's Super Smash Bros. series, as such this game will feel
familiar to veterans of the series. Being a long time fan of the Smash series, I was able to pick up and play this game without going through any of the tutorial/practice stages. For newcomers, the controls, mechanics and characters are very easy to learn, but very hard to master which is a very big plus in my book.
The mechanics, as mentioned earlier, are almost directly ripped from the Smash series but with a few changes that have a drastic on how the game is played. For example, Smash fans will notice that there are no shields with them being replaced by the parry system (time the button press before an attack hits you to stun the enemy and counterattack). These are one of the few major changes that make this game familiar to Smash fans as well as help the game stand on its own two feet. Rivals of Aether also takes a few techniques from Melee, such as wavedashing which is an intended mechanic this time around, teching and many more techniques that I won't bother to list.
All of this culminates in a very fresh and enjoyable experience that is fun for both hardcore Smash fans, and newcomers alike, both casual and competitive (though the game caters more so the competitive scene).
However the only very,
minor gripe I had with the game is the controls which may confuse long time fans as the default controls have three face buttons set to attacks (one for jabs/tilts, one for smash attacks and one for specials), but the controls are configurable and I rebinded my gamepad's face button to the stock standard Smash control setup (two buttons for jump and B and A for jabs/tilts and special moves respectively), so this was only an annoyance for the first few minutes of play.
Overall, I strongly reccomend this game if you're a Smash fan, or a newcomer and are willing to drop 14 bucks on a very well made tribute to the franchise instead of settling for a subpar f2p knockoff (sorry Brawlhalla, but that's how it is ;) ).

This is a game meant for Smash Bros. Melee players. Not for Smash Bros enthusiats like myself. The gameplay is fluid and feels solid, followed by some of the glitches in Melee remaded into proper game mechanics. Overall, everything controls tight, solid, and feels good in your hands.
...If you're playing Locally.
One thing I've seen a lot of complaints about is that the netplay is trash, and I can attest to that. If you're ping is above average, you will have a couple frames delay. Now this isn't bad in most games, since framedata isn't that important... but in a fighting game, especially one like RoA, it's the most crippling detriminte to any game, and reduces what should be a fluid, even match into who gets the first attack. If you're the aggressor, fantastic, you look like a combo-legend and feel ready to go to tournaments. If you're the recipient, well.. enjoy watching yourself plummet off the stage.
This wouldn't all be so bad if this game wasn't so harsh to new players. Ranked matches are obviously competitive but Exhibision matches are just as serious. While the tutorial does do a decent job at teaching players the game mechanics, the only way players learn those mechanics is by playing against others. So either you have a friend who wants to jump into this game too, or you find one.
Another problem I have with this game is the Roster, now at base you get the main cast of 8: Forsburn, Zetterburn, Orcane, Maypul, Kragg, Wrastor, Absa and Etalus. Right now at the time of me posting this, Ori and Sein have been released as DLC, and two additional characters are planned to be released in the future. Judging by video I've seen of those two characters in the menu screen, they seem to plan to add an additional two characters beyond that given the two additional slots in the character select screen. The DLC is already rising to a point where it's going to be as expensive as the game itself, with each character costing about 5$. If anyone's played fighters competitively, which is unfortunatly the only real way to enjoy this game, you will know that it's rather important to get a feel for all the characters you're potentially fighting for match ups, movesets, and maybe even finding a new main.
In summary, this is a game you'll only get millage out of if you enjoyed the competitive scene of Smash Bros Melee, but didn't want to play Melee, do not care about fighting people online and have a friend or two who you can play with IRL, and don't mind spending about 20$ or so to keep up with the DLC characters. What an amazing game.
The player conducts a small group of civilians in a war, and the objective is to survive and to remain human. Of course, surviving sometimes is at odds with retaining one's humanity, and that is precisely where this game comes alive. From looking into abandoned places to getting into direct confrontation with other people in the war-torn city we live in, the player is faced not with the adrenaline that is usual in war games, kill baby kill style, but with those emotions which actually can be associated to what war-survivors tell when they write their memoirs: fear, compassion, uncertainty, so much uncertainty, hope, and above all, despite for war and those who pursue it.
Everyone who ever played a war videogame from the pov of the soldier should play this game. Hell, this game could very well be the basis for a whole new industry that does not only require students to read die welle (germany) or lord of the flies (USA), but indeed requires them to play games in order to look at things in new ways, and truly without much effort. This is an amazing piece of art. The only way in which the word "entertaining" is applicable is if taken in the same sense clockwork orange, or the pianist, are "entertaining movies". Most of all, they are captivating experiences.
Perhaps the best game of the year, despite (or perhaps precisely because of) coming from such a small studio, and capable of making a lot of people take videogames more seriously.

Bioshock 2 is one of those cases where a beautiful iteration of a game is overshadowed by its predecessor. Despite looking similar to the first Bioshock; Bioshock makes a huge jump both in terms of the depth of the story, and gameplay.
This time around, we're playing as a big daddy porotype and are sent on a quest of finding our little sister. While the first game focused more on the city itself, and why it failed, Bishock 2 gives a much more deal of attention to the people of rapture and further develops its ecosystem.
The locations are richer and more detailed allowing for perfect exploration environment that often encourages you to go off the path.
Despite being put into a suit of a big daddy, the game play got faster and feels like an improvement over the first game. The combat is more fluid thanks to the ability of being able to use both your weapon and plasmids at the same time. The change to hacking system (while hated by some) feels like a welcome change in favor of faster gameplay. There are still upgrades to be found and, despite most of the being flat stat upgrades, they still feel impactful enough to change the way you'd handle a certain weapon.
All in all, Bioshock 2 is an improvement over the original game and is one of those adventures that are hard to forget. With its improved story, gameplay, and an assortment of new plasmids, weapons and tonics it does not fail to keep you engaged for the entirety of the main campaign. For those hungry for more of the story content or smart gameplay, there is also Minerva's Den (a single player story DLC) and a Trials DLC (a number of Challenges that unlock concept art, trivia about Bioshock, and more).

If you're a fan of Super Smash Bros... then this game is NOT for you.
This game lacks ledge grabbing and smash directional influence, and it really shows.
Edit: The game does have normal DI, but SDI as it is In Brawl/Smash4 lets you move all over the place when hit by a smartbomb, but while fighting this game's boss and getting hit by its similar multi-hit black hole attack, I was only able to very slightly inch a pixel at a time. Overall it felt like I had no control.
If you're not sure what I mean by SDI, skip to 2:41
The existence of this kind of quirky movement helps you feel like you have more control over what's happening, even if it's not doing much, this is part of the game feel in being able to wiggle around even while in hitstun.
In any case, weak SDI isn't the worst problem here - there's no ledge grabbing and many of the up-specials (the ones that general are your main recovery tool in SSB games) are rather bad for recovery.
I'm constantly frustrated by scenarios I keep expecting to survive,
In other words, you'll die to a lot of situations where it feels you've lost complete control of your character.
Don't think it's important? Going for a more "competitive" or "pro" fighting design?
Skip to 1:57
In this case, the game has double jump, but the lack of ledge grab just has you dying in lots of stupid ways you could be recovering from if you were playing Smash 4 instead.
On top of that, a lot of the recovery abilities (equivalents of up-specials in SSB) are rather difficult to use in a pinch when you need them most. Aside from not being able to ledge grab, some of them require a bit of "pre-planning". This would be the dolphin's puddle that needs to be placed before you fall (and can disappear/be destroyed), or the maypul's leaf on the enemy that is needed for him to lasso onto the enemy who needs to be close by or unobstructed for you to be able to recover.
Not all of the up-specials give you upwards movement. In Brawl, almost every character at least had an upwards movement with their up-special, even if it was meant to be a "heavy" character or one that doesn't exactly have much "verticality". In SSB, the only characters who didn't inherent upwards movement were Ness and Lucas, but their up-specials could still be used in a pinch without any prior setup, so they're still better than what Orcane and Maypul have.
Even Ivysaur and Omar, whose up-specials are ledge grabbing lassos, still actually give them a little bit of satisfying upwards momentum, which helps the player feel in control, rather than helpless, even while falling off the map.
In its place, the game does have a walljump up-special system which technically does let you do more, as walljumps refresh your up-special, but this is far less intuitive and requires dipping into the tutorial or hearing about it beforehand to know about. This kind of thing will give you a bad first impression if you jump in after playing Smash and expect familiarity in the games mechanics.
I think the game would be vastly improved by improving these three things, because otherwise, it's unplayable to me.
Don't get me wrong, this game does many things right.
- Excellent sprite art.
- Excellent music.
- Excellent game feel. This one is actually the very reason I bought the game after seeing some footage of Clairen - I could tell that this game had very well polished and solid game feel.
- You can emulate SSBB's controls.
- No tripping.
- Second versions of stages without the gimmicks.
I don't plan to refund this game, and do plan to keep up with it in hopes that maybe these things will change.
Well, I'm not particularly hopeful, because I would imagine they've already had criticism about this kind of thing in the past, and that it's been out long enough that anyone playing would probably be used to how it is, but eh. I wouldn't want to keep this unrecommended if things do change.
----
There are good ways and bad ways to make spiritual successors to old games.
Here are examples of good things games have done:
SSBBrawl -> Smash 4
1. They removed tripping
2. They made competitive versions of every map
(Both things Aether has also done)
Team Fortress 2 -> Overwatch
1. Removed weapon switching from most classes, which makes it easier and makes players less likely to fumble.
2. Overwatch improves many systems TF2 has in order to make players knowledgeable of exactly what enemy is going after them, to give them every chance to succeed and have a fair fight.
2. Increased footstep volume, especially of enemy heroes you're weak to. Gives purpose to the normal footsteps TF2 has.
3. Every weapon/hero has unique sounds you can pick out from a distance. This feedback lets you identify enemies easily and know what's coming for you. Overwatch's sound design is said to be good enough that blind players can successfully play overwatch.
Again, an improvement of something that TF2 somewhat does, though it's not as easy to pick out different rocket launchers from each other based on the firing or explosion sounds, some things can be picked out, like shotguns vs rockets vs pipes vs miniguns.
4. Every projectile particle effect and hitscan tracer is unique looking, also allowing you to instantly identify your enemy.
This is something people never think about with the trails on rockets, pipes, and arrows in TF2, and Overwatch applies this concept to its entire set of heroes. It definitely is something that helps people succeed.
5. Auto-callout of enemy sentries/teleporters/stealth characters.
This is simply an improvement of TF2's manual voice chat, turning it into something that ensures these callouts actually get used and get used properly, helping your entire team identify what threats it should be dealing with (like sentries).
Super Mario 64 / Collectathons -> A Hat In Time
1. Improved movement with more recovery options.
2. A camera that's coded not to get stuck with bad camera angles.
----
The point is, these games add things to help the player succeed, be more in control of what's happening to them, and technically, "make things easier for the sake of more widespread accessibility".
Now, I know "dumbing things down" can be seen as a bad thing for players who want a less hand-holdy challenge, but I would say that all of these games are examples of making these improvements without hurting the main challenge.
The thing is, if you take A Hat In Time for example, if you decide that its movement controls are doing too much stuff for you automatically, that just means A Hat In Time could create more challenging platforming scenarios without frustrating the player, whereas it may have to avoid doing so if the controls themselves were a challenge to use.
Smash 4 and Overwatch are multiplayer games, so fighting humans with the same abilities will always be its own kind of challenge and making the controls easier only means more people will play and the good players will sit that much higher than the skill floor.
And since the skill floor will be lower, you'll have a bigger playerbase that can grow more over time.
More importantly, a lot of these top seller games all have this trait in common, and if you're going for a more punishing type of game, then your game will always just be
.

Great music! Good concept. Good graphics. Crucially flawed gameplay. The key problem is the mouse interface. Whenever you touch the mouse (I tried several), to do things like aim in a firefight, it automatically zooms in to a top down view of the ship, so you can get a closeup of your ship taking damage and do nothing useful to change things. To get the view up, you must scoot the mouse about four feet with max sensitivity to see who is attacking you and keep scooting the mouse to aim or get a glimpse of the object you're about to run into. It's basically a FPS where it defaults to looking down at your feet and you have to scoot like mad to glance at the enemies.  I can't believe they actually released a game where the mechanics of gameplay fundamentally don't work.
Addendum: I'm on a Mac. The fix to the mouse control largely fixed the issue. Broadside aiming is still quite difficult because the camera still pans down automatically, although it is much, much easier to compensate for and the ship still often obscures the view of the target. I find I'm still guessing where the enemy is and firing blind, although often accurately. While clunky, it is now playable.

The Last Remnant: The Salt Bringer
Seriously this game has made me so happy yet so mad, the sheer fact my old 360 and this PC have remained intact over the fruitless years of trying to conquer this game (With the physical strategy guide, mind you) is proof enough this game is worth playing.
Synopsis:
You start the game as Rush Sykes, who's sister, Irina, has been kidnapped. You venture off to lands unknown to find her, meet up with some people who think your parents (famous scientists btw) are amazing people. These new allies not only help you find your sister but eventually place you both on a gigiantic pedestal of world changing proportions, facing down enemies beyond that of a teenage boy who has yet to say a single curse above the occasional "damn." Also, character development, plot, twists of plot, and other RPG centric stuff occurs.
Review:
Yeah yeah, we get it. "The combat system is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t." Well, Square saw you wanted a "Final Fantasy"-Esque game without the convoluted self-serving plot, and a new combat system, and you very well F!^&#!%! got it. Yes, it's randomized based on your weapons, party members, remnants, etc. But it adds a new difficulty to the game that all you weeaboos and achievement whoores have yet to appreciate. As an RPG fan, and even as a FF fan, this combat system makes me rage, quite a bit honestly. But, when you finally beat that one spot, the one you've been stuck at for ages, it's like a long awaited ♥♥♥♥♥♥. It is just fulfilling and makes you dizzy with delight... then you find another boss immediately after who wrecks your♥♥♥♥♥♥and sets you back to square one.
Now you may ask; "well if that's how you feel, why reccommend it you masochistic prick?" Because it's difficult, because it's a mixture of chaos and control that's amazingly frustrating and we all hate ourselves that much to force ourselves to commit to something that might give us a goddamn heart attack when you finally get to the end of the game, just to get your♥♥♥♥♥♥stomped in because your remnant never f!^@%#^! showed on the f!&#*@^ action wheels... <Insert Pant-Like breathing>..
Honestly, the story is actually quite phenominal if you're willing to murder yourself over it, the characters are well developed by the end and it's a difficult task to beat, but we all need relentless challenging. So go kick some "A." enjoy some of the frame drops (that can be quite hilarious at times) and most of all, find a way to kill Mr. Dig and his nightmare eyes.

Wow
This game has blown me away. Everything from the theme down to the actual gameplay. I love the music and the look and feel of the game. Really captures that same theme that things like Firefly managed to capture.
My main concern when going into this game was knowing that it didnt have full free range 3d movement. You are basically a boat, on a 2d ocean that spans in all directions. (ie: you cant go up or down like in most space sims). Shortly after playing though I realized something. You arent a space pilot in some action game. You are more like a bridge commander. Piloting and combat are more akin to something from the startrek films than being seating in the pilot seat of an X-wing.  Does this work? Yes, it does. Quite well in fact. I quickly stopped caring that I didnt have full 3d range of movement, and found myself just enjoying the "flow" of the game.
The music is great btw, really helps bring the game to life.
Combat is quick, and very "Edge of your seat" once you get past the first couple of tutorial battles. Sometimes you have to run. The game doesnt scale stuff to your level, and you often find yourself in over your head. Escape is a viable tactic and meant to be part of the gameplay. Dont worry though, you wont find yourself running often unless you go charging head first into some space pirate zone.
The game actually has a LOT more depth to it than I expected it to. The further I played, the more features I discovered. Its so much more than just a funky space combat simulation game. I personally cant wait to play more, and really start diving in to what the game has to offer. Its got me hooked.
My only real gripe is how there isnt an option to pull the camera back some during broadside combat. I feel a bit "boxed in", which really hinders my combat awareness of things around me. You can find youself crashing head first into things during broadside combat because your field of view is so limited due to how close you are zoomed in to your ship. They really need to add an option to configure the distance you want the camera to be at, or add a toggle that works similar to the camera view distance in a car racing game.
The other nice feature that easily goes over looked, is how well this game performs. No performance issues, no GPU or CPU load issues. Overall its a well optomized game. (it could use a few higher quality textures here and there though)
So... overall...
Do you like space games?
Do you like star trek style combat between big ships?
Do you enjoy the backwater, wasteland themed style of Firefly?
If so, I highly recommend this game.

While I'm not a diehard fan of civ games, I played civ 5 quite a bit. When I heard about this game, I thought, cool, maybe it'll start you on a fully developed, but overpolluted homeworld and you'll have to send colonist vessels out to other planets. Then maybe you take over a planet and send invaders to a planet settled by another civ. I also imagined multiple intelligent alien races that you would either meet as inhabitants of these new worlds or as colonists from another species, or maybe as invaders. I didnt really look too much into it in an effort to keep from getting too excited. Well, I got the game for christmas. There are many things I like about the game. But, it is nothing like what I imagined.
The good stuff
-Im probably one of the few that actually ejoys the clean looking UI in a sci fi setting. I felt like it fit pretty well
-I kind of like how it feels a lot like civ 5 from a mechaincs perspective
-I really liked the addition of the orbital layer of the map. Gives more options to the player which is a good thing.
-I liked the alien resources
-I liked the tech web for my first couple playthroughs.
-I liked the customizability of the military units, but this needed work.
The bad stuff
-Military. Yeah in civ 5, military was somewhat based on how deep into the tech tree you could get to unlock better troops than your opponent. But you also had to have the resources to upgrade all those troops and there was a good variety of troop types. In this game, research is literally all that matters. The upgrades for each tier is insane. One time, I was invading someone and my troops just couldn't seem to hurt the cities very much. Plus the ai's military was about the same level as mine, so I was fighting a losing battle. Then my explorer finished an expedition and gave me an affinity point. this upgraded the majority of my troops (rangers) and I was now blasting through the ai's military without much effort because of a random bonus. There should have been twice as many upgrade teirs with more gradual upgrades.
-Each playthrough feels the same. Same 8 civs, same personalities and affinity choices unless they hit really weird map conditions. Same race to the endgame wonders. I had hoped different virtues would be good in different situations, but I still pick growth every time because of the health bonuses.
-Same useless aliens every time. Not going to go into detail because, with my high hopes, it would just turn into a rant. Other reviews have done a great job talking about why they suck though.
-As others have said, this would be amazing if it were just a mod for civ 5. But it just feels boring and empty as a standalone game.  I was hoping for so much more. I think it could've been more if they'd continued development for as long as it took to make it as awesome as it sounded. I would've been happy to wait for an amazing game vs getting a mediocre game sooner.

Imagine James Bond or Jason Bourne.  Imagine being the man that kills both of them before lunch.
You are Agent 47, the worlds deadliest contract killer.  In Absolution, find a rich story, deeply developed characters, solid weaponry, noir cinematics, an inspired musical score, and the stimulating freedom to kill the target your way.
Here's what I think people will like:
- Several levels of difficulty suitable to all levels of gamers
- Full freedom to satisfy the objectives in your own way and be rated and rewarded for how well you do
- The story is solid, fluid, and stimulating
- Great levels / maps
- Good AI
- It's not just about a powerful gun, it's having a powerful gun but getting the deed down without it
- Puts you in the mindset of a hitman
- Good graphics that aren't too hard on midrange PC's (I played this on an Acer laptop)
The things I didn't like about this game:
- At one point it kept crashing when encountering a Directx error that I had to read the Steam forums about, but I was able to solve because a lot of people had the same problem (not that bad because the community does have the answers)
That's honestly my assessment.  There is a lot to like and keep you playing for hours.
Should you buy this game for your kid?
I am going to go ahead and warn parents that it's very mature with lots of swearing and mature themes.  There might be a way to turn that off, but I'd just say, let your kid play GoldenEye on an old N64 and then play this game when they are a bit older.  It really isn't any worse than anything you'd find on HBO, so you can use that as a benchmark.
Is this game replayable?
I would say yes.  I beat the single player campaign fairly quickly.  The nice thing is that as you satisfy the objectives you are awarded points for how you get the job the done.  This means that you can go back and replay for a better score and try out different styles of being a contract killer.  This game also has a multiplayer feature that sounds intriguing but I have not yet tried.
Do you have to be a Hitman officiando to enjoy and beat this game?
No.  I have played other Hitman games that felt very closed off and extremely difficult.  I felt that this game deviated from the constraints of past games in the franchise.  This is a real winner and I hope they continue the franchise in this way.  If you only play one Hitman game -- this should be it.  Chances are that you'll enjoy your experience so much that you'll check out the other games too -- and all are very very affordable since they've been out for many years.

Defy Gravity is a fantastic platformer with great gameplay elements. This platformer utilizes gravity as the main mechanic. The player can create gravity and anti-gravity pockets to proceed through the levels. I would say that it has a similar difficulty curve as found within Portal, but it lacks story elements. Being a platfomer, however, it doesn’t require story elements, just quality controls. Graphically, it’s lacking, but having solid controls is what makes this game fantastic. This game also has a “Hard Mode”, which requires you to only use gravity pockets, and the enemies are affected by the gravity. This “Hard Mode” extends the gameplay you will find within Defy Gravity, but it doesn’t come off as too forceful. The only real reason to play through “Hard Mode” is to get all of the achievements. I will recommend this game to anyone looking for a new affordable experience.

Absolution is both good and bad.
If you're a purist with the franchise, you may not like it.  If you've never played another one before, it'll probably feel awesome playing it.
It has a decent story and the graphics are nice, but coming from having spent years playing all the other games as they were released, I can't say I'm necessarily pleased with where Square Enix is taking the franchise.
Personal peeves:
The ease with which people wearing the same type of outfit as you can see through your disguise.  This makes even less sense when you're wearing a disguise that covers your entire body and about half of your head and face.  "Instinct" drains very, VERY quickly when being used to blend in, which made me feel like the game was promoting more of a stealth-based Splinter Cell or Metal Gear type of gameplay.  In all of the other Hitman titles, guards could see through your disguise--provided you were acting like a lunatic, or carrying weapons not befitting your outfit.  That said, they didn't have some preturnatural sixth sense to just say "Hey, that guy's not one of us!".  When you're dealing with massive areas and dozens upon dozens of employees in a specific outfit, there's no real way that every single person could pinpoint you as being out of place that quickly.  Wasn't a fan of the pretty much forced stealth based, take cover behind every object you can gameplay when that has traditionally not been how the games play out.

A simple but brutal game that does exactly what it sets out to do: makes the player think very, very hard about the choices they make to stay alive.
"This War of Mine" isn't exactly what I'd call "fun," but it's important, and it delivers its message well through mechanics, story, and visuals, which is my holy gaming trifecta. That said, I did appreciate the challenge of properly allocating resources and skills, and like all good sims the desire to make my environment "better" got addictive pretty quickly.
What's impressed me most about "This War of Mine" so far is how relentless it is. There's little in the way of combat, and the fighting you do encounter is more likely to make you feel powerless and angry rather than victorious, even if you win. Death carries significant weight in this game, whether it's the loss of a companion or the execution of a stranger over a cache of resources. Awful things happen randomly, and often enough they occur just when you can least afford them. You're constantly aware of the fact that you're barely scraping by, teetering on the edge of disaster. The goal of this game was to make you consider what it'd be like to live in a war zone, and it delivers admirably.
