But I will have to learn to life with all my guilt for the rest of my days...
"This War of Mine" kicked the living daylight of of me.
Unforgiving like FTL and with an art-style close to LIMBO, this game is compelling and intense without any of the overused tropes like a zombies-apocalypse or any form of goofyness to soften the blow. The setting is frightfully close to reality.
This game depicts life in a warzone where every action can have fatal consequences and you have to survive somehow. You grow fond of your little group and if you lose somebody this is more gutwenching than in any AAA FPS-extravaganze. There, a predetermined plot decides who dies, no matter what you do. Here it´s all in your hands and that really gets to you.
Somebody died because you made a mistake and he will never come back...
Moral choices don´t feel "tacked on" but an essential of the game. Sometimes you have to do the immoral things. Not to play as the "anti-hero" or to get a different reward or see the "bad" ending, but to survive. The message of this game comes across without ever being in the way of the game.
Give it a try if you want to experience war beyond the modern military shooter genre.

This is one of the best games I have played in 2017. You could kinda compare it to Ori and the Blind Forest and to be honest... I think I like Hollow Knight a littlebit more although Ori still has the edge when it comes to viuals.
Also, 10 bucks (sale) is criminally underpriced.
I just love this game.

You don't exactly get what you pay for, the game starts with 8 characters which isn't much and for some reason you have to buy the rest. I could understand Ori a little bit as that is a crossover character but for the original characters that is not ok. It seems like Zetterburn and Etalus are just out right better than the rest of the cast, Zetterburn having a spammable projectile and can easily kill you at 40% while Etalus just having amazing frame data and high knockback on his attacks. The singleplayer content is kind of lacking, the story mode is barely what I call a story or even arcade and theres the abyss mode which is nothing but tedious grinding, if it were online that I could see purpose in the mode. Speaking of which the online is very unstable and you likely wont have a good time unless if you can somehow put up with inconsistent lag, im talking like 1.5 seconds of input delay for a good match, online is terrible. You cant do 4 player online however you can still do 4 player local. I tried to do team battle online with a friend but it seemed to have put him on the opposite team everytime and didn't function like you think it would.
For the gameplay its often fun but a lot of moves just seem to have way too much hitstun making it too easy to do combos, characters like Zetterburn can dash attack into dash attack. This means that you can Fireball>dash attackX>Side Smash, simple combos like that will kill you instantly with little effort. Now while you make think you can DI in this game it is actually very insignificant when it comes to combos and only seems to affect long distance knockback, this basically means that if anything can do enough hitstun then it can be made into a true combo. Each character generally has different gimmicks, this also includes recovery gimmicks so with that being said some characters rely on stage control as they have little to no recovery with it. You can wave dash but it feels very artificial unlike Melee, same goes for teching. There are no grabs like Smash bros but additionally to that instead of a shield or spot dodge you have a parry, I was excited to hear about the parry until I realized how dumb it actually is. If you successful parry a projectile it reflects it, thats fine but if you successfully parry an attack it freezes the opponnent for around a second or so which is absolutely not fine, it reminds of a witch time and I wish it didn't, parries feel more like counters. Stages aren't all that interesting so there really isn't much to say about them, the game does offer stage data in the stage select so you can see blast zones and stuff like that which is nice. The color editor is pretty nice too but in order to unlock a new color slot you need to complete some ridiculous achievment, if I could buy it with the in-game currency then that would have been fine. Speaking of which the in-game currency isn't really that useful, you can use it to buy 2 of the 8 characters that come with the base game, you can use it to buy stages which seems pointless because if you flip that sucker on tourney mode then you get all the stages unlocked, you can also use the currency to buy upgrades for abyss mode, its not all that useful.
As for the DLC
$5 - Shine Zetterburn
$5 - Arcade Maypul
$5 - CEO Ring
$5 - Burrito Kragg
$5 - Ori and stage
$3 - Summit Orcane
$2 - Summit Kragg
$2 - Spangled Wrastor
$2 - Panda Maypul
Totals up to $34, more than twice the price of the actual game
Plus however much the two new characters will cost.
Overall the game shows great potential with problems that can be easily fixed and pointlessly large amounts of DLC.
If these issues were fixed then I'd be able to fully recommend the game, otherwise I suggest buying it on sale like I did.

First of all before i go into the review for this game i just want to put a couple of things out there. When this game was announced i was actually super hyped because i loved Saints Row 2, 3 & 4 and i had been excited to play it ever since. I ended up buying this game recently during the Steam Summer Sale 2015 at 50% off (£7.49) and because i had not looked into this game very much except seeing it announced plus a trailer, i wasn't aware that this was actually a Standalone DLC for Saints Row 4.
So the review, unaware that this is Standalone DLC i jump into the game and start the story and it has all the usual Saints Row characters and humor etc etc. I found that incredibly early into the game you were able to fly assuming you have the stamina (which is upgradable in the exact same manner as Saints Row 4) so i was free to do whatever i wanted in this openworld City inside Hell and im able to fly.
The first thing i see to do is collect Soul Clusters which are also the same collectables found in Saints Row 4 (possibly with different name, i can't remember) and i decide to collect all of the visible ones of these while flying around exploring Hell.  After collecting in the region of 300 of these Soul Clusters (out of 940) i had also found a couple of Audio Tomes which are humorous audio logs from some of the characters within the game including Satan.
I was then pulled unwillingly into a story mission due to having♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off Satan enough for the story to progress. I won't spoil all the details for this game but to give you an idea as to where this is going, i had around 920 Soul Clusters just from flying around right off the bat when i was able to finally shoot Satan in the face thus ending the story for this game. At this point i thought to myself 'is that it for the story?', so in total i think there were around 5 story missions.
This for me was mildly disappointing but there is so much else still to do within the game such as collecting all the Audio Tomes, Soul Clusters and also Commentaries (similar to Audio Tomes but for the TWO playable characters - Gat & Kinzie). Plus there are challenges, activities and achievements to complete, which for me has taken 28 hours of taking my time while playing. Having read various comments and reviews both during and after this time, it seemed some people were able to achieve around 97% in about 6 hours, but im assuming this is mostly 100% takeover of the city by completing activities and the main story missions since the collectables and challenges were only a couple of percentage.
A couple of things i should also note is that the highest level you can achieve in this is 20 and considering i put 28 hours into this first playthrough i could have achieved level 50+ since i hit level 20 so early into the game. Also one of the challenges in the game is to upgrade ALL of your weapons to maximum capabilities, which is fine but the only way you seem to be able to make enough money late game is to kill enemies over and over again because either there arn't enough paying story missions or activities or the upgrades cost too much. So i spent alot of time after completing the story and activities killing enemies for all the challenges and to make enough wages to spend on upgrades.
Saints Row: Gat Out of Hell is also the first game in the series that allows you to play as more than one character. You can switch between either Johnny Gat & Kinzie Kensington as often as you like, both of these characters also have their own commentaries which are quite funny to hear.
The upgrade system for both Health, Stamina etc and Arcane Powers are exactly the same as the previous game which for me is a bonus because it works really well and the prices for each of the upgrades is very well balanced for the length of the game. The powers themselves from what i can remember of playing Saints Row 4 are fairly similar but i feel like i had alot more fun playing through this game with these powers and even game myself a mighty shock at one point using summoning powers, which made me literally laugh at myself not realising what i had done. The powers do seem more powerful than the previous game too but having used all of them for completing all the challenges i think they work really well for the game.
All in all, for the price i paid and unaware until pretty much after completing the story, that this was Standalone DLC, if you are a fan of the previous Saints Row games i think this is a fantastic game despite how short it might be and i would definitely recommend it.

This is a game worth playing if you've both played the original and find it cheap via. a sale; I think it's worth playing the original before this one for many reasons.
In any case the main reason to play it is the improved gameplay, as a Big Daddy no less - more plasmids, finally plasmids plus weapons at once, better melee (your Drill!), some more varied enemies and better tonic upgrades. Combat in this is great fun with some upgraded abilities!
The plot is so-so. I enjoyed some characters and situations (one at the end was very fun), but the overarching antagonist and story just fell flat; it was very impersonal, and frankly, just a bit boring. You explore different places then the first, but essentially is the same look, so nothing that different (by which I mean areas are still small, no big expanses here). Underwater parts don't add anything either.
The main downsides are the escort quests - little sister defending is just a chore - and linearity of most of the levels. Enemies do respawn but since there are limited reasons to re-explore this doesn't matter as much, while there is pretty much in every setpiece the "wave of enemies" syndrome.

a 20 euro expandalone, get it on sale for half the price, and you should have the 1 euro = 1 hour policy working. IF you go for a full city takeover and do all sidequests, the main "campaign" (story?) can be completed in about 1-2 hours if you dont mess around. the whole customisation element of the game has been removed and you can only play as either Kinzie or Gat which is kinda cool in theory yet not as good as you would expect.
For a saints row game this one has it's moments, but it is far from as quirky as the predecessors and that takes away from the overall feel.
however 10/10 would punch satan in the face again

Brief:               -------Very decent sandbox space shooter, full of charm and visually beautiful.-------
Pros:
The soundtrack is spot on, fits the bill to a T for all fans of Cowboy Beebop and the like. Fight the bad guys or skirt the law, it suits both perfectly.
Graphics are wonderful, the backgrounds are easy on the eye, the laser and engine effects are beautiful, and the asthetics of the ships, stations and other objects are up to par.
The atmosphere you get from jetting from one point to the next gives you the sense that its a lonesome place out there, and even though you meet npcs frequently, there's no way to shrug off the lone wolf vibe. Both good and bad, but certainly most of the time feels great.
Combat is tight. The whole game works on a 2D axis, which at first I thought would be missing a huge opportunity to give the space combat its full potential, but in truth it simplifies it enough that you never really get the feeling of being overwhelmed; it is straight forward, easy to master, and never really gets dull when you're fighting at your level or something tougher.
Cons:
The NPCS feel bland. In over 8 hours of gameplay so far I've yet to meet any characters that I can say stuck in the memory or that I really liked. You could replace any of them very easily and wouldn't feel a loss of any sort.
The story hasn't got me hooked thus far, I don't particularly care about the objectives being laid out before me, nor the people who are integral to it. This could be because everything early game plotwise has been done many times before, the characters, dialogue and scenario all feel as though they've been lifted out of several other titles/stories the writers or developers have experienced and put together for their own project.
Occassionally travelling can be frustrating. Sometimes the large distances can be boring, though in truth adds hugely to the atmosphere of the vastness, so a double edged sword. However getting interupted from your warp because of misc objects is irritating, making me think warp lanes or shipping lanes might have been a nice addition.
I also feel the developers missed a trick not including simple add ons like being able to hire your own crew, making a diverse mix of aliens or humans to operate your ship, needing more the larger the vessel you acquire. It would have been a great opportunity aswell to put in some excellent personalities and vary up the dialogue during fights. That said, it would serve to remove the lone wolf feeling.
You can hire your own merc to help out in the fighting, but can't really interact with them at all; no dialogue to get to know them or character development, just one liners from them saying if they're taking fire or going on the attack.
Overall:
All in all, it is a brilliant and fun game. The lack of a killer story (at least early on) or solid characters doesn't detract from the fact that it is visually stunning and just flat out fun to play. I bought it the night of its release day and haven't really been able to put it down for wanting to get a better ship, better guns and take them into combat.
For those who love a space setting, bounties, smuggling and everything that goes with the territory, this is well worth the pricetag to kill some time. Better ships to buy, choose your own armaments and enhancements, join factions and improve your standing with them. Its a well put-together space sim.

Pros:
+ Deep and thought provoking narritive into the victories and how you advance as a civilization. Augmenting yourself with technology or becoming more alien, or rejecting the two.
+ Huge UI improvements, everything is much neater than Civilization V, no more right-clicking through 200 Citystate messages and quests.
+ Non-Linear technology web, allows players to plan and use more strategy in their game.
+ Steam Workshop Support
+ Builds off the Civilization V engine, allowing newcomers to feel welcome and experts to jump right into the game and expierence the new features themselves.
+ Revamped policy system,  lots of bonuses and extra goodies allowing for a much better time for those who don't rake in loads of culture, while rewarding those who do.
Cons:
- Lack of content is HUGE in this game, especially coming off the wealth of content Civilization V with all the DLC had. Games take nowhere near as long as in Civ V. You will find yourself out of things to build reletively quickly, not many buildings and units.
- Maps are reletively small and barren, there aren't any landmarks to discover and there aren't enough Civilizations to have a large map akin to Earth like in Civilization V, there's no real thrill to exploring, just getting slaughtered by aliens.
- Diplomacy is non-existent. It's just like how it was in Civilization V, but doesn't take intol account the futuristic setting very well. Trading resources means nothing because you don't need any (besides oil), the ones you need are granted to you by developing affinities, and they do not do anything for your people (no happiness increase, no city-state quests to fufill, no we love the king day)
- AI is brain dead. Every game I've played the AI doesn't go for a victory other than Domination. They end up warring with each other eternally, attacking aliens (attacking aliens make every alien on the map more hostile to any civilization) and just having so many units that they lose hundreds of energy (currency) per turn.
- Barely any buildings to make, no units either.
- No Great People, even Generals and Admirals.
- Games take a short amount of time, even on Normal and Epic times due to the ease to achieve victory and lack of other content.
I'd give it about an average score, 6/10. What's there works well and blends nicely into the game, it runs very well and everything looks gorgeous. But it's not enough to keep your attention for more than a little bit at a time (you can obviously tell from my playtime. I have ten times this on Civ 5.) Wait until more expansions come out and the price drops. This game is NOT worth $50. It's worth $20.

I think this game deserves more credit than it is given.  Criticism is being thrown around saying it is just a reskin of civ 5, which I believe is a bit unfair.  New things in this game include virtues, affinities, permanents unit upgrades, and a multitude of new buildings and units.  Virtues are basically policies, except I found them to make a larger difference on stats like health, science, and energy.  Granted, policies did some of these but virtues change things to a further extent.  Affinities are a really great new addition to a game.  They succeed where ideologies failed in civ 5;  they determine what type of victory you can aim for (other than the general ones).  They also allow for permanent upgrades to troops and, by extension, special units.  This changes the look of your troops and really bolsters their effectiveness.  New buildings in this game make the city management aspect fresh, rather than just renewing the same buildings from the last game.  All of these things contribute to a great game.  Don't get me wrong, there are flaws.  The tech web is messy and confusing, health can be unmanageable, and depending on your starting area your civilization can get overwhelmed by aliens relatively early.  Also, the different civilizations are pretty much without personality which can make inter-civ interactions boring.  These things can easily be fixed in updates and dlc though.  So if you are a true civ fan, or at least enjoyed civ 5:  Give it a try, you wont be disappointed.

If you go in expecting sci-fi Civ 5, you'll be getting exactly that. Beyond Earth uses a lot of the same mechanics and world generation style of Civ 5, similar to the relationship between Civ 4 and Colonization. What makes BE unique is its emphasis on pre-game and the new Affinity system. The pre-game setup adds a layer of customization to a player's faction, by allowing them to choose their civilization, a preliminary stat bonus, a gameplay bonus, and a free unit or building to be given at the start of the game. The Affinity system is a unique and original way to further customize one's faction. There are three tracks to follow: Harmony (adapting to and with nature to survive), Purity (remaining solely human), and Supremacy (using technology and integrating it into humanity). Each track offers unique bonuses, units, and special unit upgrades to make a player's faction feel their own.
Unfortunately, what results from all this customization is a lack of personality for each of the factions. In Civ 5, each leader had a unique personality, and experienced players had a sense of what to expect going against that leader. In Beyond Earth, the factions are simply one step in the game setup, and offer little more than an empire-wide bonus. The AI's personalities will be dictated more by which victory they attempt to go for, and which Affinity they've chosen that game. Despite this flaw, Civilization Beyond Earth is a great and original entry to the franchise, and definitely recommended for fans of the 4X strategy genre.

Starts off nice and hack and slash, doesn't give you much variation in attack styles. Whichever character you pick you're still left either at the mercy of your cohorts to revive you or trying to revive them which during battle soon gets old. You don't exactly get what you pay for, the game starts with 8 characters which isn't much and for some reason you have to buy the rest. I could understand Ori a little bit as that is a crossover character but for the original characters that is not ok. It seems like Zetterburn and Etalus are just out right better than the rest of the cast, Zetterburn having a spammable projectile and can easily kill you at 40% while Etalus just having amazing frame data and high knockback on his attacks. The singleplayer content is kind of lacking, the story mode is barely what I call a story or even arcade and theres the abyss mode which is nothing but tedious grinding, if it were online that I could see purpose in the mode. Speaking of which the online is very unstable and you likely wont have a good time unless if you can somehow put up with inconsistent lag, im talking like 1.5 seconds of input delay for a good match, online is terrible. You cant do 4 player online however you can still do 4 player local. I tried to do team battle online with a friend but it seemed to have put him on the opposite team everytime and didn't function like you think it would.
For the gameplay its often fun but a lot of moves just seem to have way too much hitstun making it too easy to do combos, characters like Zetterburn can dash attack into dash attack. This means that you can Fireball>dash attackX>Side Smash, simple combos like that will kill you instantly with little effort. Now while you make think you can DI in this game it is actually very insignificant when it comes to combos and only seems to affect long distance knockback, this basically means that if anything can do enough hitstun then it can be made into a true combo. Each character generally has different gimmicks, this also includes recovery gimmicks so with that being said some characters rely on stage control as they have little to no recovery with it. You can wave dash but it feels very artificial unlike Melee, same goes for teching. There are no grabs like Smash bros but additionally to that instead of a shield or spot dodge you have a parry, I was excited to hear about the parry until I realized how dumb it actually is. If you successful parry a projectile it reflects it, thats fine but if you successfully parry an attack it freezes the opponnent for around a second or so which is absolutely not fine, it reminds of a witch time and I wish it didn't, parries feel more like counters. Stages aren't all that interesting so there really isn't much to say about them, the game does offer stage data in the stage select so you can see blast zones and stuff like that which is nice. The color editor is pretty nice too but in order to unlock a new color slot you need to complete some ridiculous achievment, if I could buy it with the in-game currency then that would have been fine. Speaking of which the in-game currency isn't really that useful, you can use it to buy 2 of the 8 characters that come with the base game, you can use it to buy stages which seems pointless because if you flip that sucker on tourney mode then you get all the stages unlocked, you can also use the currency to buy upgrades for abyss mode, its not all that useful.
As for the DLC
$5 - Shine Zetterburn
$5 - Arcade Maypul
$5 - CEO Ring
$5 - Burrito Kragg
$5 - Ori and stage
$3 - Summit Orcane
$2 - Summit Kragg
$2 - Spangled Wrastor
$2 - Panda Maypul
Totals up to $34, more than twice the price of the actual game
Plus however much the two new characters will cost.
Overall the game shows great potential with problems that can be easily fixed and pointlessly large amounts of DLC.
If these issues were fixed then I'd be able to fully recommend the game, otherwise I suggest buying it on sale like I did.

A suprisingly un-enjoyable expandalone to Saints Row 4. The superpowers are both more overpowered and less enjoyable to use than the SR4 counterparts. Flight being introduced very earlier in the game as a major transport mechanic relying on your stamina. However the missions are very unvaried and quite linear, short and really shouldn't be counted as a storyline, more so a forced interaction with the various side missions (also less interesting variants of their SR4 counterparts, save one where you fly around saving souls from being damned or rising to the heavens [makes little sense, but it is SR so that is a minor part].) Cutscenes are void of existance with replacements being offered in the form of a story board with narration. If this is what we are to expect from Deep Silver with the Saints Row franchise, expect to be dissappointed with no real progression, consistant repetition, little explanation and near zero of the classic SR humor found so commonly in SR2 and SR:TT. Overall Saints Row: Gat out of Hell was a money grabbing release, offering no real improvement to the base game. Save your money and spend it on a promising Early Access or Indie game.

If you enjoyed the competitive aspects of any of the Super Smash Bros. series, you've got a high chance to enjoy this. It may take some getting used to, but the gameplay becomes very rewarding and satisfying as you learn to utilize many of the game's techniques. Especially once you get used to each character's unique mechanics, but, as with every fighting game, some tend to be more powerful than others. However, due to the relatively small roster size and the active team, you'll find that no character is particularly unfair to fight against (Except
Ori and Sein, but they're supposedly being changed soon). Some things to note before you purchase, though:
And as far as the gameplay itself compared to other Smash-esque games goes...
Also, something else worth noting is that the game's music and artwork are beautiful and refreshing, despite following the infamous and in some cases boring pixel art style. In turn, due to the graphical style, you'll find that this game can run on just about anything at a smooth 60 fps. Your old computer, your laptop, your gameboy, your refrigerator, your couch, your soul, you name it. ...Okay, maybe not ALL of those things...
Overall, I recommend that any competitive Smash Brothers player try this game. Heck, maybe you'll enjoy if you like competitive games in general. It takes inspiration from the Smash Bros. series while providing many new and unique mechanics to keep it from being a clone. While the game is missing some things that will be added in the future, what it does currently have will keep you occupied for quite a while. If you have 15 dollars to spare, this game might be worth picking up if it's many high points intrigue you.

This game... It's OK, it's different, but I'm certainly not sure whether I can recommend it as such. Pity there's a "Not Sure" button" to choose from in regards to this. I'm choosing "no" mainly because at best, I can only recommend to try it out for an hour or so before deciding.
What it basically tries to achieve is to combine the personal turn-based fighting of the  Final Fantasy games with turnbased unit fighting. To achieve this without making the game bogged down in commands, each unit gets a few overall choices, instead of each person in the unit getting their own command. Magic is a shared resource in the unit that replenish a few points every turn.
How well does it achieve this? Well, the main problem is, things tend to turn out rather random. Battles soon turn intensely chaotic, and trying to keep track of everything that is relevant can be quite a task at certain points. Often the same enemy that made short work of your party will easily fall the next time because the game chose some different commands for you to try out. And this makes it hard to feel that
are accomplishing something in terms of smarter fighting.
The randomness continues when it comes to leveling up. Oh, to be sure, you can semi-control the leveling of skills, but sometimes it takes ten battles for something to happen with a particular character, and then the next three battles in a row, the same character will gain several stat and skill incrases. There's really no way to know exactly what and how much is needed to get that character to whatever you want it to be.
Apart from that, what is there to this game? Well, a fairly typical Square-Enix storyline (which is sort of in its own place, inbetween the JRPG and the CRPG style of story and characters), and... not much else. Sadly, in this modern day and age, these games tend to be rather void of anything to do but plot and combat, and I think that's a shame.

Going into this game I was hoping to find a classic JRPG made by sqeenix, with the acceptable grind, lovely characters and an enjoyable time. Well I got anything but that last part.
The maing gripe I have with the game is the difficult combat system paired with the penalizing Battle Rank (BR) system. The combat is nice once you get the hang of it, though I find it very confusing that the only way to learn the combat normally; trying to get into as many fights as you can, is penalized heavily by the BR system.
The BR system is not your level, but it's a rank that goes up according to the amount of fights you've had, the higher it gets the more difficult the enemies get. Not so bad right? Well if you manage to somehow get your BR high before a section of the game played in Nest of Eagles you may very well get stuck here, this only being the first half of the game leads you to redo the entire game up to that point, mostlikely following a guide telling you to keep your BR low. (Not what happened in my case, but I was close to doing this)
Not only does the BR system make the fights harder it also makes powering up the later characters you get in part 2 harder to make useful. Now this happened to me. The workaround being farming a unique monster called Bai Ze or in this releases case you could also opt to farm insects at the cost of two unique units. This allows you to farm your characters up to an acceptable stat range or to help you in cheesing the game.
The combat is done in unions; groups of characters in formations, different formations give different stat bonuses. The unions then have "random" actions that they can do. Herein lies the problem, the actions I want to do are the actions that, most of the time, are not readily available while I feel this takes away from the strategic point of view, it enforces defensive play and working with what you have; it does however make the difficulty of the strategy feel articficial since instead of giving a difinitive way to take on a fight, you have to hope you get those actions to pop-up.
The problem comes from the combat and penalizing BR system, you try to learn the game and do all the sidequests once they're all available, raising your BR to a level the game didn't expect you to have and making the rest of the fights too difficult to progress. The sidequests may be optional but some of them become too much to handle, the solutions being to farm a unique monster, to spam hard to trigger arcana spells, and to change your formation into one that simply bumrushes the boss and hope that they die before you get killed. If you still think the game is a fair challenge after this go ahead and buy it, I know it's old but for a game to be unforgiving to a point where you cannot progress the story is just wrong.

Well, this is a Square Enix game, turn based basic combat.
I thought that the squad-based thing might remove some of the parts I find boring in the normal turn based systems, but overall, it makes for a fairly dull system.
I only had the patience to go through the first two areas, so it might get a bit better later on, but so far, here is what I found wrong with it:
- The movements on the map scenes are slow.
- The environments are empty, adding to the slow movements.
- Everything dies in a few hits, both you and the enemies (even in the first area), but the HP is restored to full after each fight.
- Random chances to get critical hits in or to get hit by one.
- No real control over the fights, making it seem like a merry mess of randomness.
- Gain of "stats" after a few fights, seemingly unrelated to what action you chose (levelling up?).
- No way to skip animations, and somewhat poor quality animations anyway, making the "watch what happens" phase boring to watch. Added to the fact that the camera switches all over the place instantly, and you get a messy presentation instead of a cinematic one that seems to be intended.
All in all, I don't know what I was expecting, it's a Square Enix game, and I really am bored of those menu based combats with occasional QTE.
I can get over it whan the games try to do things I find interesting, like the moe system in Mugen souls, or when your choices are a bit more varied, with actually reasons to defend and other similar actions.
I guess this game can please some people, because it doesn't seem broken or bad per say, but it definitely is not my thing at all.

As most other reviews will tell you, This War of Mine (TWOM) offers a gaming experience from a perspective rarely seen in urban warfare environments - that of the civilians. This game charts the progress of a group of mismatched individuals who find themselves trapped within a wartorn city that is under siege by the military trying to wrest control of it back from rebel forces. There is no infrastructure, no power or running water. The city is crumbling, withering on the vine, and the group you control are right in the middle of the rotting heart.
Your survivors begin the game in a relatively large abode they have chosen as their base camp. To call it a home or even a house is laughable - the walls are falling down, there is debris everywhere and the fridge is empty. The primary method of control is point and click - you click on one of your civilians to select them, then click on the action you wish them to take. Actions are context-sensitive - if there is a locked door and you have a lockpick, an appropriate icon can be found next to the door. If there is salvageable debris on the floor, clicking on the hand icon above will direct your civilian to search it. The simplicity of this system helps negate the confusion that can arise from playing the game for the first time and being suddenly presented with dozens of different icons around the abode.
Your survivors spend their days inside their abode, as it is too dangerous to venture outside due to snipers. This is the resource management/crafting section of the game. During this time you can build additional facilities such as stoves, workbenches and rain collectors (assuming you have the resources to build them), you can let your civilians rest/eat, and possibly barter with a passing trader. There are a comprehensive number of different structures that can be built around the place, and many of them can then be upgraded further to either access new items, or make it easier to create existing ones. It is also the part of the game where you will maintain your group's wellbeing, including feeding them, tending to their wounds, and sending them to bed to help them get over their misery.
When night draws in, choices must be made. At this point in the game you can send a single soul out to different locations around the city to scavenge for goodies, be they food, medical supplies, weapons or something else desperately needed by your camp. Once a location is selected, the game becomes a point and click stealth sim, akin to Mark of the Ninja or Deadlight. You have a cone of vision, and other NPCs in the location, if you can't see them, may make themselves known to you by their sound, which will appear as a pulsating red circle.
Night scavenging is a diabolically tense affair. When approaching the door to an unknown property, you will have a vague idea what to expect based on the brief synopsis of the area the game gives beforehand. You look through the keyhole and, seeing nothing of note, you open the door and stalk your way into the lounge. Searching a cupboard you find a few blocks of wood and some vegetables. Suddenly, you see it (or rather, hear it). A pulsing red circle, on the ceiling above you. Someone (or something) is here in the house with you. Do they live here? Are they friendly?
Are they alone?
And so the decisions of TWOM assault you, not through binary text choices or sterile morality wheels, but through pure choice.
Do you leave immediately, unwilling to incur the wrath of the inhabitant but knowing you will return empty handed?
Do you try to sneak around the ground floor, searching for what little you can, knowing there may be more upstairs?
Do you charge upstairs before whatever it is can prepare itself, and ready your crowbar for a fight?
Do you draw your pistol, carefully counting the three bullets you have left?
TWOM is not a game you win. It is a game where you try to stay alive as long as you can, doing whatever is necessary to survive. And as the days drag by and the food supplies dwindle and the cold laps at your fingers and Pavle starts getting sicker and the looters get bolder, you will be called upon to answer the question - are you willing to diminish?
Are you willing to steal medicine from a desperate hospital, or let Pavle die from infection?
Are you willing to rob a man and his sick father at gunpoint for the food you traded them two days ago, or let Katia starve for another day?
Are you willing to murder a vicar in case he has something you can use?
The presentation of TWOM is well considered, using a pencil-sketch art style with 2.5D environments. The game brilliantly conveys a sense of devastation and disrepair within the locales you investigate with little effort. The macabre atmosphere is enhanced by a haunting, albeit not very varied soundtrack containing reverb-drenched guitars, sombre strings and oscillating, industrial percussion. The gameplay, despite using essentially the same mechanics throughout. manages to achieve two very different, almost schizophrenic styles in the contrast between night and day. Days are quiet, slow, reflective encounters, while nights out scavenging are stressful, deadly and panic driven.
The game is not perfect. Combat can be clunky and confusing affair, although this is possibly part of the game intent, demonstrating that violence should be an absolute last resort. However, this does not prevent the immense frustration that I felt when (for the second time) I sneaked up on an armed guard with my shotgun, only to get TOO close at which point my civilian decided that rather than fire a round of buckshot through the guard's back, he would instead try to melee him to death with the butt of the gun. Needless to say, my game ended there. The roguelike element of TWOM means that you will never become "good" at combat, although that's probably the point. As mentioned before, the music could do with a few more tracks, and does get repetitive (though this does help contribute to the relentless, monochrome tone of the game overall).
I recommend TWOM on the basis that it has the potential to invoke the same ambivalence of mind that can come from, say, the decisions you make in the Walking Dead series, or Dragon Age, but through gameplay rather than specific story choices.
One last thing to mention. After you have started your first game, two options appear on the title screen - Continue, and Another Try. Not "New Game". Another Try.
And who knows? Maybe this time you won't die like a dog for no good reason.

This game requires good forward thinking, great hand-to-eye coordination and an unearthly amount of patience to beat, especially if you want to get all the achievements.
The use of gravity wells to adjust your jumps is the gimmick in this game, it is implemented to the core style of play and you’ll find yourself using it pretty much for all kinds of situations. Thankfully, the mechanics are very easy to learn, though it will take more than a few tries for the trial and errors to take hold in experience.
There are 24 levels in total, you can expect to die countless times on laser traps, football-like projectiles, collapsible platforms, shuriken shooting bots, moving walls of doom and the classic never-ending pits of doom. It won’t be unfair to call this game brutal, but you’ll have unlimited continues in your disposal, along with a save point practically after every trap.
The length of this game will vary depending on how good you are at it, a speed runner can do this in 20 minutes, a good player may get away with 2 hours, it took me around 12 hours to complete it entirely along with the hard mode.
If you are someone who likes a real challenge, get this. If you’re a casual gamer who can’t take setbacks very well, please avoid it like the plague.

Having completed the campaign, made a decent deck and battled a few people online, I felt like it was time to review.
When you start the game you will be faced with unskipable (at least, not to my knowledge) tutorials which can be VERY annoying for experienced players but VERY useful for begginers.
Then the game points you towards the campaign. It consists of roleplaying a plethora of planeswalkers to complete a series of challenges for each. I found it equally frustrating as it was fun; I was not going to stop playing until I beat the enemy. Your decks in the campaigns are built around the person you are playing but essentially, it works like any game of magic: the luck of draw (you cannot modify those decks throughout your play).
Completing the campaign will earn you rougly 900 coins, 300 coins gives you two packs to open in the store (the minimum amount of packs available). You can buy more coins with real money. Once you have a bunch of cards, you can make a deck. The deck builder interface is nice, friendly and organized. It has filters, stats and even an autocomplete deck button based on your choices.
Battle mode includes Solo, Vs Player, and Two-headed giants. You can earn a bit of coins by doing Solo which is against AIs (^difficulty=^coins). Playing against players will earn you 20 coins per match won as well as a +1 rank (I think the game tries to match you with similar ranks but that wasn't always the case). I haven't tested 2HG, sorry.
Aesthetic wise: the "battleground" has a slick and simplified look. Your icon consists of the associated face+background you chose for your deck box (this is what your opponent will see). The game moves the cards where they need to be for you. It also reminds you of any playable cards (including activated abilities who are playable this turn) by surrounding them red (useful for people who forget to put their lands down).
TL;DR
Pros:
-very good way to introduce your friends to Magic the gathering since it's a good learning tool.
-good way to play against other people if you can't play IRL.
-fun challenging campaign.
-the interface during battles is quite likeable, I mean, I like simple things and that's exactly what this is.
Cons:
-you will either need to invest money or spend an excruciating amount of time battling AIs/players for coins to expand your library.
-the game has several bugs regarding the mechanics of some cards / gameplay (see the Bugs report discussion board).
-bland repetitive music. I played mostly on mute or with my own music due to annoyment (but Nissa's song was nice).
-short campaign life. I honestly wish there was more planeswalkers (or at least my favs) because I loved the campaign, but this is easily fixed with a DLC.

What if I told you there was a game, in this world, that possibly gave you the choice to go through either the left door or the right door? How would you react? How would you go on living?
The Stanley Parable is possibly a parody. I'm not sure of anything anymore after playing it all the way through. What I do know is it's short. Like, really short. Like, dangerously not worth full price short.
Am I missing the point here? Did I waste my time? Do I always waste my time? Did I have a choice to waste my time? Did I have any real choice at all? Is the game making fun of me? Am I supposed to be laughing at the game or with the game? Is the game laughing at me? Should I ignore the game lauging at me and just enjoy the five or more possible endings of the game? Is this even a game or just a deconstruction of everything I've ever known, or is the game just laughing at me? All these questions flew through my head while playing it.
Its a type of game for a very specific type of person. If I'm being honest, there was a certain amount of amusement I had gained by listening to the narrator and then doing stuff. Or not doing stuff.
Here's what this all comes down to: did I have fun? I felt that a couple of the story trees were worth some fun, yes. Another one was a brutal deconstruction of the modern lifestyle; and it's not the obvious one, at least from my perspective. Everything else was just kinda... meh.
That's what really sums it up. I like the idea, its just... two hours for meh..? I want to give this more credit, but for $15, I've had more interesting experiences.

If you like metroidvanias and hard games that require perserverence, Hollow Knight is perfect. I've played many metroidvanias over the years but this game is the only the metroidvanias I would consider better than Symphony of the Night or Super Metroid.
Gameplay - 10/10
Intense combat, a strategic healing system, customization options, difficult-but-not-impossible platforming. I've yet to play another metroidvania that delivers better gameplay than this one. If you want to master this game, you will need to do things that few other platformers will ever ask of you.
Story - 8/10
If you 100% the game and still don't feel the plight of your soulless horned bug, I don't know what to say. This game has a powerful story that told through few words. It's only shortcoming here is that it would be very easy to miss the amazing parts of the story by speeding through the game and not 100%'ing it.
Music - 10/10
I judge a game soundtrack by how many songs it has that I will be listening to months to years after I finish it. Hollow Knight has several tracks that fit this category and they are all used to great effect in game when they are needed.

Replayability / Difficulty to 100% - 8/10
Hollow Knight asks a lot of you. The hardest acheivement in the game is to 100% the game without dying. For most people, this is going to take several runs of extreme stress along with full mastery of the combat (boss rush would help here). While the game is excellent for a normal playthrough, I wouldn't recommend 100%'ing it unless you consider yourself an extremely skilled gamer.

Pros
+ Story - The story isn't actually all that bad. While it definitely has its ups and downs, as a whole it changes some of the same old broing troupes of JRPS, while keeping others. The dialogue and voice actors sometimes help make the story predictable, but there are some neat twists and some great characters.
+Gameplay - The game is remanisent of an MMO and traditional JRPG in that there is an overworld map, which you can choose a location to go to. You are then entered into a 3D enviroment where you can move and see enemies running around, like an MMO or Chrono Trigger. You enter combat by engaging with the enemies on these fields and to help do that you have a special ability that allows you to slow time and link enemies together to fight at once, or manipulate in other ways (like avioding them). The combat system is great for seasoned JRPG fans. Its great fun and sometimes great strategy. You can enter towns and go shopping, grab new quests, do guild tasks, and talk to randoms.
+Graphics - For a game thats getting older, the URE3 hold up decently, not ground breaking by any means. Environments are beautiful and fairly detailed, and there are a lot of them.
+Completion - It takes over 60 hours to 100% this game. Took me double that. The list I went by is:
1. All Quests
2. All Guild Tasks
3. All Weapon Upgrades Maxed
4. Rank 8 Conqueror
5. All Arcana Abilities (because they are awesome)
For completing the game you get a new game +. For doing all of those individual things, you should get a lot of items to carry over and a gold bonus, as well as proving you can take down the badest of the bad in the normal game.
Cons
- Story - Short imo. But I guess thats not so bad see as how this game took days of my live away.
-Graphics - Even after years the game still suffers from texture pop ins and Rush's skirt....wtf
-Gameplay - Battles can feel tedious many times over. Sometimes you will get frustrated with certain enemies, most in the story mode. White Conqueror took me 5 attempts. No minigames :(.
-Completion Bonus - All the purple shiny items you get are just Trophies for when you play the new game + mode. That sucks. Also no achievements.

This game should be on any short list of the best games that exist so far.
Coming quite late on in the heyday of PC FPS games, its glory is somewhat tarnished by two terrible sequels (something it shares with FEAR) although Crysis Warhead is what DLC was before it became called DLC - a Mission pack - more of the same, and just as good (with slightly better performance although that shouldn't matter nowadays).
Mission Brief:
Make your way from Point A to Point B.
Here's a gun.
Here's a supersuit that can:
armour you;
make you invisible;
give you super speed;
make you absurdly strong.
But only one at a time, and there *are* limitations.
During your journey you will encounter people with issues around your continuing to breathe.
Deal with them as you wish.
"As you wish" was the point.
Here's an otherwise deserted village full of enemy troops who won't even get to know me before they open fire, which is just rude.
Should I:
Crawl prone (yes it has a prone key) around the edges, taking a real-time hour to recce the place and tag everyone there with my magic binoculars before choosing my positions and sniping every mf in town;
Steal a truck, race manically at the barricade and rely on wits and armour from there. And guns, obviously;
Walk slowly towards town carrying an indestructible dumpster to protect me, throwing it hard at the first cluster of dopes with guns to get in the way, and continuing the physics object murder until all is calm and all ragdolls have stopped spasming;
Sneak invisibly in, biding my time between super-strength silent strangling of hapless lone troops by hiding prone on rooftops?
The presence of a prone key might evoke slightly-too-realistic-to-be-just-fun games such as Arma but the supersuit ensures that this doesn't take hours and hours of repeated deaths and frustration to play, although there is a very high difficulty level for those people and a variety of options for bedroom/study/gamingroom SEALS.
MOST importantly there is quicksave and you can save at any point except in cutscenes. Lack of this killed Crysis 2.
Yes, there is an escort mission. It's annoying (also in story context) but the freedom the game gives you means it can be done without too much frustration; your protectee isn't suicidal and will stay put somewhere safe if you ask until you've cleared the area.
Yes, the aliens change the gameplay sometimes a bit much and remove many options.
Yes, the final level is completely different and you lose choice again. And MASSIVE SPECTACULAR STUFF HAPPENS. I couldn't have played a game like that all the way through but as a finale it works.
Also it's beautiful, the locations are wonderful despite what's going on even if nowadays there are better-looking games but not as many as you might expect. Also mods.

GET THIS GAME!!!  Even if you didn't grow up with RTCW (I didn't), you will thoroughly enjoy this game. The graphics themselves are nicely detailed.  Some textures on the terrain are what you'd expect from early 2000's, but the characters themselves are actually very nice looking.
Most of your guns are from the appropriate WW2 era, but you get some interesting ones like the flamethrower, tesla gun, and venom machine gun; you'll probably stick to the mp40 and sten 80% of the game though.
Only complaint with the game is that it might break it when adjusting the screen resolution higher than 1024 width, so be sure to visit pcgamingwiki to figure how to adjust the resolution and you'll have NO problem at all!
All in all I'm impressed with how well this game has held up and entertained me after over a decade of not even knowing about it.

I was sceptical at first, but this really is an exceedingly well thought out, well crafted and well executed game.
It's dark, it's dreary, it's brutally unforgiving, and as a result, is the best game representation that I've ever seen of the struggles of those unwillingly caught in the middle of a war.
Excellent base facility building, punishing material needs with limited time to gather them in (And limited space to carry them home), the ever present threat of non-friendly humans each time you go out, and genuine worry when you've consumed your last bit of food... It's been a while since I last played anything that did all of these things well.
Do you want to build that workbench upgrade or fireplace to keep your people warm? If so, you'll need to bring all these components back, but that means not bringing something else back tonight, something that you might end up needing more tomorrow! I've even ended up writing shopping lists and inventory numbers for when I go out scavenging, so I know what I need to look out for most.
TL;DR: If you like small group survival games that challenge you, make you think and doubt your own decisions, and that don't hold your hand, I highly recommend this. Go and watch some Let's Plays on YouTube to get a feel of how the game plays (And to get a better idea of whether or not it's your cup of tea), then jump straight in. It's a fantastic little time sink with a surprising amount of replayability due to the random start conditions and random locations each time.
It's also one of the VERY few titles that I would quite happily offer to pay extra for more content in DLC form. Take that as you will.

This game is like the Sims for adults. The mechanics are quite simple: you have a house with a couple of survivors and you need to keep them alive. Easier said than done. Food is scarce in wartime and sometimes they have to do horrible things to get food.. So horrible it gives them a trauma and breaks them mentally. I had a couple of survivors who were so devastated they refused to get up, they didn't even sleep anymore. The atmosphere of the game is very dark and grim, like a war game is supposed to be, and I felt guilty even when my characters were doing well, because you'll encounter lots of other characters you cannot help. They can also get sick, wounded or even die during attacks or raids. Every single character has their own bio about their past and diary entries which help to gauge how your survivors are doing and how they can be made to feel slightly better. Some survivors also have special skills like being supportive of others, they are better at bartering or they are even trained at combat. These things can come in very handy at times. I really enjoyed playing this game and it will entertain you for many hours, since a lot is randomly generated and the 'simsy' aspect keeps it engaging to play. You start sympathizing with some of your survivors, feeling sad when they get ill, or, so utterly annoyed by the attitude of others, that you start to try making them have an 'accident'.

Everyone is raving about This War of Mine.  Let me tell you about the positives for the game.
The game has a very unique plot where a group of people come together to survive, each bringing their own skills and talents.  This concept has exploded in gaming.  I really like this a lot and it would be cool if the game could be multiplayer which would be difficult.
Another aspect of the game is crafting, though limited.  This is interesting because it determines how you will play the game depending on which main items you create.  The main items you create determines the subset of items you craft.  The game goes through a hot season (summer) and a cold season (winter).  I prefer to start out in the winter.
I feel the concept is a good concept.  The thing that really trips me up which I don't see many people talk about is the controls especially when you're at home base.  You only have a limited amount of time at home base and at times you have a lot to get done.  I can assign the people task pretty quickly.   While at home base, if I am clicked on someone and maybe trying to direct them to another part of homebase or to task and I have another person doing a task, the game will occasionally (not all the time) when a player finishes a task the game will send you to that player which has caused me to click on the players location.  This will cause the player that I was trying to get to do something to go to the player's location that had just finished a task.  This may happen when a player wakes up when sleeping.   If you've played the game this will make sense.  Also, if someone finishes a task at home base, they'll start to wonder from the task location.  This can be annoying especially when you're rushing to get multiple tasks done.
At homebase, the game essentially switches you to the character if they say anything, which can cause you to send someone to some erroneous point due to this.  The control are in my opinion subpar when you are at homebase ESPECIALLY when you have a dozen tasks to be done.  You have to essentially babysit your characters because I've had characters that I've told to do a task and either have had them only do some of the task or not even start the task.  In the mssion setting of the game, the controls are tolerable but still not that good.
What I would do to improve the controls?  I strongly feel when I say this a lot of players will agree with me:  At homebase, if I can assign the people a list of task to do. Example:  Gather snow, then go to sleep. or make filter, make alcohol, grow plants, cook food, then go to sleep.  If they can't complete a task, you don't need to send me to that player, just send me a stupid message saying that the task couldn't be completed and have them go to the next task.  Because when you're at homebase, there have been times that I'm rushing around trying to get a bunch of task done and an accidential click sends a person to another location within the homebase because the computer brought them up because they said "I'm freezing my bones in here" by bringing the person back to whereever they were at I lose like ~30 minutes.
The concept of the game is good (I don't see why people are saying it is great) but the controls are really subpar.  In my opinion really affect the game play. If I could trade this game I would.  If you want to try and trade I will.  I feel like I got ripped off because the controls of this game highly aggravate me!

Having completed the campaign, made a decent deck and battled a few people online, I felt like it was time to review.
When you start the game you will be faced with unskipable (at least, not to my knowledge) tutorials which can be VERY annoying for experienced players but VERY useful for begginers.
Then the game points you towards the campaign. It consists of roleplaying a plethora of planeswalkers to complete a series of challenges for each. I found it equally frustrating as it was fun; I was not going to stop playing until I beat the enemy. Your decks in the campaigns are built around the person you are playing but essentially, it works like any game of magic: the luck of draw (you cannot modify those decks throughout your play).
Completing the campaign will earn you rougly 900 coins, 300 coins gives you two packs to open in the store (the minimum amount of packs available). You can buy more coins with real money. Once you have a bunch of cards, you can make a deck. The deck builder interface is nice, friendly and organized. It has filters, stats and even an autocomplete deck button based on your choices.
Battle mode includes Solo, Vs Player, and Two-headed giants. You can earn a bit of coins by doing Solo which is against AIs (^difficulty=^coins). Playing against players will earn you 20 coins per match won as well as a +1 rank (I think the game tries to match you with similar ranks but that wasn't always the case). I haven't tested 2HG, sorry.
Aesthetic wise: the "battleground" has a slick and simplified look. Your icon consists of the associated face+background you chose for your deck box (this is what your opponent will see). The game moves the cards where they need to be for you. It also reminds you of any playable cards (including activated abilities who are playable this turn) by surrounding them red (useful for people who forget to put their lands down).
TL;DR
Pros:
-very good way to introduce your friends to Magic the gathering since it's a good learning tool.
-good way to play against other people if you can't play IRL.
-fun challenging campaign.
-the interface during battles is quite likeable, I mean, I like simple things and that's exactly what this is.
Cons:
-you will either need to invest money or spend an excruciating amount of time battling AIs/players for coins to expand your library.
-the game has several bugs regarding the mechanics of some cards / gameplay (see the Bugs report discussion board).
-bland repetitive music. I played mostly on mute or with my own music due to annoyment (but Nissa's song was nice).
-short campaign life. I honestly wish there was more planeswalkers (or at least my favs) because I loved the campaign, but this is easily fixed with a DLC.

Excellent game that's a hack-and-slash and platformer combined.
10/10 Art style. Absolutely gorgeous, hand-drawn environment and characters.
10/10 Music. Beautiful, haunting soundtrack that fits the bleak world of Hollow Knight.
10/10 Story and Lore. Haunting lore that honestly surprised me from this cute little game. There were some legit shocking, frightening, and saddening moments. There were also things that made me laugh. Probably the best part of Hollow Knight, in my opinion.
10/10 Replayability. Definitely can replay and masochists can try to get the speedrunning or permadeath achievements.
10/10 Difficulty. This is a difficult game that will make you tear your hair out. However, with all the upgrades, it's not impossible for the casual player to beat. It really is like a cute Dark Souls. Be advised if you hate hard games, this might not be the one for you.
8/10 Platforming. Some parts required a bit too much finesse, and a controller is absolutely required. However, you do get upgrades in the game that can make you forego some hazards.
Overall one of the best games you can get for under $15, or $10 if it's on sale. And the developer added DLC for free? This is a no brainer if you like story rich, gorgeous, and challenging games.

What if I told you there was a game, in this world, that possibly gave you the choice to go through either the left door or the right door? How would you react? How would you go on living?
The Stanley Parable is possibly a parody. I'm not sure of anything anymore after playing it all the way through. What I do know is it's short. Like, really short. Like, dangerously not worth full price short.
Am I missing the point here? Did I waste my time? Do I always waste my time? Did I have a choice to waste my time? Did I have any real choice at all? Is the game making fun of me? Am I supposed to be laughing at the game or with the game? Is the game laughing at me? Should I ignore the game lauging at me and just enjoy the five or more possible endings of the game? Is this even a game or just a deconstruction of everything I've ever known, or is the game just laughing at me? All these questions flew through my head while playing it.
Its a type of game for a very specific type of person. If I'm being honest, there was a certain amount of amusement I had gained by listening to the narrator and then doing stuff. Or not doing stuff.
Here's what this all comes down to: did I have fun? I felt that a couple of the story trees were worth some fun, yes. Another one was a brutal deconstruction of the modern lifestyle; and it's not the obvious one, at least from my perspective. Everything else was just kinda... meh.
That's what really sums it up. I like the idea, its just... two hours for meh..? I want to give this more credit, but for $15, I've had more interesting experiences.

First off, let me give credit to where credits due.  The game is cute, its adorable in a dark slapstick, nonsense kind of way, with colorful characters and a very fun story.  The gameplay?  Frustrating... tedious.  It reminds me of Hotline Miami, but instead of having floors and checkpoints, your expected to do the whole level with one life.  It makes the game fun... until you die the first time, then you repeat what you did, die again often from frustration and carelessness, then repeat what you did again, over and over again, until you finally complete the mission with all of the challenges thrown in.  Its nerve wracking, its frustrating, I never have fun playing this game.  The first few levels were a blast, because they werent to difficult and I was allowed to complete them in my own way, having fun with the levels.  Towards the end you will be memorizing every single enemy encounter, every single time you shoot you will count your shots to reload so you dont make a turn only to find you have no bullets in your gun and instantly die from a katana.
In short, the game is a grind, a completionist grind where you have to behave in a scripted, overly cautious manor to complete any of the end game levels, thus making all the color and humor pointless.

The short: if you like strategy games, this one does some things well, but I found it a bit lacking in areas I enjoy. Recommended with reservations. Worth catching on Steam sale for $5
The long: Though I've only put around 40 hours into the game thus far, it's demonstrated a number of pros and cons. In many respects, the UI is a bit cumbersome, as is the case with many "space strategy" games though it does have a few nuanced touches that are easy to overlook at first (such as the spread of culture being shown as a colored line slowly creeping between jump-points).
There are a number of research trees to advance your civilization, allowing for some degree of play-style accomidations... but the game has an obvious slant towards military combat as the primary win condition.
The game, though sporting 3d graphics is, dissapointingly NOT in a 3d world. All the planets and points of interest exist on a plane. Ships move (more or less) in a planar fashion.
Considering how older games like Homeworld did combat in a 3d space so well, it was dissappointing to see a title like this opt out of allowing players that degree of control. It's all the more dissapointing that the combat system is fairly shallow since it's what the game is clearly geared towards. You can set your units to automatically attack anything around the gravity well (or planet or object units can hang out by), locally (not sure HOW local that is), or to be passive. You can manually or automatically use special abilities (manual isn't very practical though) of your units. You can specify single targets as well, if you really want. Otherwise, your units will just attack threats with what looks like a preset unit and proximity priority. The combat AI isn't terrible, but it's definately not great either.
I get the impression the developers were doing more of a rock, paper, scissor approach (find the best combo of units / upgrades to beat the opponent's units / upgrades) to combat while trying to keep a fairly strong emphasis on resource management. I also liked how there's an NPC "pirate" faction that will attack a player if other players place the highest "bounty" on them through bidding resouces.
There's pretty much NO story or interesting stuff about the cultures you play / interact with other than unit variance / some special abilities or structures that are unique to each faction. The is no story mode.
The game's pacing is also fairly slow (which can be either a pro or con, depending on what you're looking for), though it can be accelerated a bit in single player mode.
6.5 out of 10. Recommended with some reservations. If you like slower games that are more about resource and upgrade management and less about complicated combat manuevering, you may really like this game.

+ Solid gameplay mechanics and progression that'll keep you busy for hours, having fun being your own space captain. Solid combat (deflector shield = timed block, broadside ship combat), calming (if flashy) mining, and cutthroat trading are all here. Be a Han Solo, or a Boba Fett, or more.
+ Quirky singleplayer storyline, but as with an open-space game like this, you can easily ignore it and go your own way. Think Skyrim + Space Cowboy and you're not far off.
+ Colorful and unique art direction for environments, ships, and characters that you meet. Ships and weapons have clear design lines they follow. Enemies are color-coded for easy identification. Space is colorful and interesting to look at. Damage on ships is well-rendered, complete with breaches in the hull, burning, and metal skeletal remains in impact holes. Weapons are visually impactful, and can be clearly discerned in the heat of combat.
+ Characters you meet have a lot to say, voice-acted too, complete wtih unique alien languages to boot!
+ Excellent "cowboy" music that sets the mood perfectly, firing at the perfect time. Crescendos with the right track for high-intensity combat. Drops it down to a mellow tule when in station. A forlorn tune for when travelling. Its perfect, and when you dont like it, there's support for inserting your own!
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
- Camera is too zoomed in. Its difficult to keep situational awareness when the camera zooms so far in you cant see your entire ship anymore, let alone whats immediately around it.
- Game's graphical fidelity with texture quality is a bit lackluster in places. Character fidelity is serviceable, whilst lip syncing is a bit off.
- Space travel and combat is exclusively 2D in nature.
- Minor problems here and there (the odd V/O line thats not volume-balanced, odd UI design choices, etc) detract from the game little by little. Take for example the UI display for shields and hull plating. They fade as they take more damage, when it would make more sense for them to work like bars taht decrease in size the more damaged they are to make the information more clear to the player. The default E key is used for far too many things. Default bindings may be a bit off-putting for some folk, like mistaking Secondary Fire (Shift) for Deflectors (Space) in the heat of battle. Very distinct (if not difficulty-spiking) power gaps between upgrades on equipment and ships and enemies in general. Things of that nature.
- Default music may not be to the taste of some.
- No multiplayer support.

Im playing on the Free Week. So my review will be of the game on a free model scenario.
Combat: 10/10
Fights feel fluid, intense and balanced. There is a lot of skillcap, but nothing that requires being an asian starcraft god player. A little bit of practice and knowledge about the characters and you are good to go. Remember this is a twinstick isometric MOBA, so there is no such thing as "right click to autoattack" as in DOTA. Here you have to aim every single attack or skill, and every character has 9 skills (Q,E,R,F, space, L&R Click and 2 alternate skills used with l.shift).
Menu, Friend list, in-game shop, etc. 5/10
This is were the game needs some polish. By playing you earn lots of stuff for free by completing missions or achievements, including crates or cosmetic currency. The game lacks of an in-game shop were you can easly browse and see all skins, bundles, special offers, etc. As it is now, you have  to browse what skins are "unlockable" with currency on the character select menu.
If you are using steam, invites from your steam-friendlist will come as in other games like DOTA 2 or PUBG (a steam message basically). In order to get in-game invite notifications you will have to add friends to the game friendlist.
Price. ?/10
The game will be F2P and will have a similar model as Paladins or LOL. The character rotation pool feels a bit limited, but you can unlock "cheap" characters with just a few games.
If you BUY the game, you will get ALL characters, so you will only use your in-game currency you earn by playing for cosmetics (crates/chests). In its current price (50% discount) of 9.99$ I would say its a real good deal, since you will get all characters and access to the early access of the game. If it was at full price I would wait until the game leaves EA and goes F2P.

Add this one to the list of games that I disliked that everyone else seemed to enjoy. There wasn't anything particularly redeeming about this game. The whole demolishing-things-by-splitting-up-geometry was a good idea and all that, but the execution was pretty terrible. The voice acting was meh, the humor was childish, and the gameplay was negligible at best. It's a physics toy, really. I couldn't get past the first area because either the game glitched or there was nowhere to go. But after running around for half an hour, trying to figure out where I was supposed to go next, destroying everything, I just got bored. I want games that give me the power to do anything I want in an environment that's cool and interesting, rather than cut up the same rocks over and over in some random desert. Don't get me wrong; I love physics-based games, but there's a fine line between fighting a "realistic" physics simulation and having objects interact realistically. This game and Vessel often fall into the former, while amazing games like World of Goo and Little Inferno fall into the latter. So go play a good physics game with actual worldbuilding and good gameplay, not this one.

The short version: Extremely exciting PvP action game that I highly recommend.
This game gets me hype as ♥♥♥♥. No other competitive PvP game can hook me like this. I've played my fair share of them: SC2, LoL, Dota2, CS:GO, Overwatch. IMO none of them can compare to the sheer energy and excitement of this game, not even close. I loved Bloodline Champions (the game that this is basically a remake of) back in the day and was sad to see it die out. Hopefully this game can maintain a decent player base, or even get huge!
So, what is this game exacty? First of all, it's not like DOTA or LoL, except in the top-down persective. I think their own description is pretty accurate:  "[...] the unique combination of a top-down shooter with a fast-paced fighting game." You move with WASD, aim with the mouse, and shoot your various abilities off with the mouse buttons and keyboard keys. I am a huge fan of twin stick shooters (Nuclear Throne, Assault Android Cactus) and find the control scheme to be incredibly satisfying and intuitive to use. Matches are structured as 2v2 or 3v3 deathmatches played to the best of 5 rounds, and last a blistering 3-10 minutes.
One of Battlerite's highest marks is its character roster. Each character is hugely unique to play, and all quite rewarding and fun. The characters are divided generally into melee, ranged, and support, but within each category there's a big variety. The characters range in complexity, and the more straight-forward are nicely marked as beginner friendly.
There's a tutorial campaign which does a decent job of teaching the basic controls, but frankly leaves out a lot of essential info and does a poor job prepearing you for actual matches.
My biggest gripe with the game is its tone and aesthetics. It's technically sound, but lacks any real inspiration. It's basically just generic video game fantasy art. Ultimately it gets the job done, and most importantly the game is legible during play, but I wish the characters had more creativity to their designs. The female characters are especially same-y, which is a shame. The voice acting/dialogue is similarly hit-or-miss, ranging from decent to nearly unbearable. These issues, while unfortunate, all wash away while playing because the game is just so damn fun.

Anyone that played Bloodline Champions will feel right at home since it's basically 2.0 of the concept from the same studio. They've cleaned it up quite a bit and it plays smoother, has more mechanics and overall feels less restricted. The UI is atrocious though and the game sure *smells* like a F2P beta but for anyone that was around when LoL or any F2P really started will know that it's really only a sign that the studio focuses on the really important parts.
I admire Stunlock studios for realizing that they had game designed themselves into a corner with Bloodline Champions and starting over from scratch is no easy feat. I think this game can be a sleeper hit with its easily consumed arena gameplay and "just one more match" feeling. The only concern I have is if Stunlock truly learned their lesson, there are signs they have, how health works and the fact that you can't just heal up from 0 to full is one massive improvement, that no champion kit completely dwarfs another is another improvement.
The only sign they might not have is the fact that we still see very loaded kits on a few champions, such as Jade who has (without battlerites): A stun, A conditional silence, A knockback, A aoe shield, Stealth, A jump, A root and some pretty darn high damage. Sure she lacks the very powerful counter mechanic and has no reliable self heal and I wouldn't go so far as to call her unbalanced but once you start overloading kits you get into a situation where if everyone can do everything then the only difference between champions will be numbers and reliablity and while that is certainly good from a balance stand point it reduces identity and makes the meta stale, predictable and boring which is the bane of a game centered around competitive fun like this.
Overall though I have faith that Stunlock has taken the lesson to heart when they had to kill their previous game and Battlerite sure is a fun game so give it a try!
