As most other reviews will tell you, This War of Mine (TWOM) offers a gaming experience from a perspective rarely seen in urban warfare environments - that of the civilians. This game charts the progress of a group of mismatched individuals who find themselves trapped within a wartorn city that is under siege by the military trying to wrest control of it back from rebel forces. There is no infrastructure, no power or running water. The city is crumbling, withering on the vine, and the group you control are right in the middle of the rotting heart.
Your survivors begin the game in a relatively large abode they have chosen as their base camp. To call it a home or even a house is laughable - the walls are falling down, there is debris everywhere and the fridge is empty. The primary method of control is point and click - you click on one of your civilians to select them, then click on the action you wish them to take. Actions are context-sensitive - if there is a locked door and you have a lockpick, an appropriate icon can be found next to the door. If there is salvageable debris on the floor, clicking on the hand icon above will direct your civilian to search it. The simplicity of this system helps negate the confusion that can arise from playing the game for the first time and being suddenly presented with dozens of different icons around the abode.
Your survivors spend their days inside their abode, as it is too dangerous to venture outside due to snipers. This is the resource management/crafting section of the game. During this time you can build additional facilities such as stoves, workbenches and rain collectors (assuming you have the resources to build them), you can let your civilians rest/eat, and possibly barter with a passing trader. There are a comprehensive number of different structures that can be built around the place, and many of them can then be upgraded further to either access new items, or make it easier to create existing ones. It is also the part of the game where you will maintain your group's wellbeing, including feeding them, tending to their wounds, and sending them to bed to help them get over their misery.
When night draws in, choices must be made. At this point in the game you can send a single soul out to different locations around the city to scavenge for goodies, be they food, medical supplies, weapons or something else desperately needed by your camp. Once a location is selected, the game becomes a point and click stealth sim, akin to Mark of the Ninja or Deadlight. You have a cone of vision, and other NPCs in the location, if you can't see them, may make themselves known to you by their sound, which will appear as a pulsating red circle.
Night scavenging is a diabolically tense affair. When approaching the door to an unknown property, you will have a vague idea what to expect based on the brief synopsis of the area the game gives beforehand. You look through the keyhole and, seeing nothing of note, you open the door and stalk your way into the lounge. Searching a cupboard you find a few blocks of wood and some vegetables. Suddenly, you see it (or rather, hear it). A pulsing red circle, on the ceiling above you. Someone (or something) is here in the house with you. Do they live here? Are they friendly?
Are they alone?
And so the decisions of TWOM assault you, not through binary text choices or sterile morality wheels, but through pure choice.
Do you leave immediately, unwilling to incur the wrath of the inhabitant but knowing you will return empty handed?
Do you try to sneak around the ground floor, searching for what little you can, knowing there may be more upstairs?
Do you charge upstairs before whatever it is can prepare itself, and ready your crowbar for a fight?
Do you draw your pistol, carefully counting the three bullets you have left?
TWOM is not a game you win. It is a game where you try to stay alive as long as you can, doing whatever is necessary to survive. And as the days drag by and the food supplies dwindle and the cold laps at your fingers and Pavle starts getting sicker and the looters get bolder, you will be called upon to answer the question - are you willing to diminish?
Are you willing to steal medicine from a desperate hospital, or let Pavle die from infection?
Are you willing to rob a man and his sick father at gunpoint for the food you traded them two days ago, or let Katia starve for another day?
Are you willing to murder a vicar in case he has something you can use?
The presentation of TWOM is well considered, using a pencil-sketch art style with 2.5D environments. The game brilliantly conveys a sense of devastation and disrepair within the locales you investigate with little effort. The macabre atmosphere is enhanced by a haunting, albeit not very varied soundtrack containing reverb-drenched guitars, sombre strings and oscillating, industrial percussion. The gameplay, despite using essentially the same mechanics throughout. manages to achieve two very different, almost schizophrenic styles in the contrast between night and day. Days are quiet, slow, reflective encounters, while nights out scavenging are stressful, deadly and panic driven.
The game is not perfect. Combat can be clunky and confusing affair, although this is possibly part of the game intent, demonstrating that violence should be an absolute last resort. However, this does not prevent the immense frustration that I felt when (for the second time) I sneaked up on an armed guard with my shotgun, only to get TOO close at which point my civilian decided that rather than fire a round of buckshot through the guard's back, he would instead try to melee him to death with the butt of the gun. Needless to say, my game ended there. The roguelike element of TWOM means that you will never become "good" at combat, although that's probably the point. As mentioned before, the music could do with a few more tracks, and does get repetitive (though this does help contribute to the relentless, monochrome tone of the game overall).
I recommend TWOM on the basis that it has the potential to invoke the same ambivalence of mind that can come from, say, the decisions you make in the Walking Dead series, or Dragon Age, but through gameplay rather than specific story choices.
One last thing to mention. After you have started your first game, two options appear on the title screen - Continue, and Another Try. Not "New Game". Another Try.
And who knows? Maybe this time you won't die like a dog for no good reason.

TLDR: Coming from Hearthstone, I highly enjoy it. The game shows a
of promise, but instability, silent devs and slow patches are testing people's patience. Also may be too altruistic with its business model, because there's next to no reason to spend real money.
The fairest business model I've seen for an online CCG. And it's MTG no less, which in paper form is the most p2w card game since Yu-Gi-Oh! Who saw that coming?
2v2 mode, i.e. Two-headed Giant!
The AI is moderately competent, so you can play even when the servers are down - though only rewarded if online.
Unlimited deckslots! Tinker all you want!
Turns feel faster and smoother than my previous experience with Duels of the Planeswalkers.
It's fun!
Unstable servers - vastly improved since launch, but expect having to click "reconnect" twice after each game to record your progress and get rewards.
Some people have reported crashes and bugs of varying severity.
The UI is clunky at times, seems optimized for consoles. Deck building features preset filters but no text search, and if you have a lot of decks, scrolling to the right one before each match can get pretty old. "Deck wizard" decks can be pretty bad and can't be customized when they're assembled.
Fairly limited card pool (only part of the Origins set) even with a few of ye olde MTG filler cards that are simply unusably bad. There are enough exciting cards to sometimes make excluding cards from your deck hard but other times you have to default to the least bad.
Comparatively little mana fixing, making it hard to create good multi-color decks. Due to the limited card pool monocolor is also hard to pull off, so most decks use two colors.
No lobby or chat, which is primarily a problem if you want to play Two-headed Giant with people you don't know outside the game.
It's MTG, so you'll unavoidably lose some percentage of your games at the whims of land draw, which can be just as frustrating as Hearthstone's RNG mechanics.
It's digital MTG, so there are a lot of timers that have to run whenever your opponent hypothetically
respond, simply to not give away any information if they can't. That said, it's in a weird middle-state where main phases are skipped if you can't do anything, but you still have to wait for other timers when both players are tapped out without activatable abilities.
The business model is almost
fair. It's very easy to grind the gold to buy the entire card pool, and after that you can only spend your gold on foiling your cards. Even f2p players are swimming in excess gold, making spending real money somewhat pointless. This may doom the continued development of the game - though it's done everything right in the business department to attract new players, it desperately needs gold sinks like Sealed or new card sets to retain them and sustain a profit. One card expansion is on the horizon, but existing players are likely to hoard too much gold to need to spend real money on that.
Also, the vocal part of the community is reaching MOBA-level toxicity, which might actually make the lack of chat be a positive thing.

War has never been so much fun... Or is it? First you try to keep those ungrateful ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s of your team alive through war. You'll do everything. Rob robbers by sneaking or killing, rob innocents and hospitals. You collect trash from derelict places for supplies. Eat anything. Anything.
If you don't starve to death, die by illness, freeze to death, die by wounds inflicted by continuous assaults to your house, sniper fire, too risky salvaging trip or your team fighting eachother then... Well... Then they probably will be sad, depressed or broken. Or they abandon your team and steal it's possessions on their way. Or lay in hangover, weeping and crying. From day to day.
Places vary from game to game : loot you find, characters you meet, dangers you are pitted against. You never know what to take with you when going to raid after supplies. Weapon - knife, axe or gun. Or makeshift tool like shovel or crowbar to go past obstacles - be them concrete, wood or flesh and bones. Or saw and lockpick for grates and locks. Or items to barter with some not-so-hostile NPC's. Ofcourse you can kill them or steal from them. If your character can live with his actions. Whatever you take with you takes space from loot you're able to carry back so it's better to choose well.
It's all about suffering and pain from the hopeless start to the very unhappy ending. Because you know, there's no happy endings in war, only choices to make, survival or death. Little meaningless people trying to struggle through hell. Alone. Suffering. Depressing? Oh yeah! Fun? Not really. Interesting? Definitely. Enjoyable? In it's own masochistic way.
It is possible to achieve different kind of endings to the story. Not to just survive but achieve characters own personal goals. It is possible to do few single heroic acts. Odds are always against you. So be ready to enjoy your victories with grain of salt.
If your character dies it is permanent for that playthrough. This makes both wins and failures feel like personal wins or losses. You will be genuinely happy if you do well. And it will really♥♥♥♥♥♥you off when you fail. Ragequit is not a remote possibility.
This game makes you think about what you value most. In the end, if you manage to do one or two unselfish "humane" decisions and still survive... Even that feels good. Characters do have personality  : some of them you like, others you tolerate. Or not. Even NPC's are well scripted. Most of them feel like believable characters. To hear them talking about atrocities, crimes they are going to do, about their miserable lives, their kills... Oh boy. Best and worst of mankind. You will hate those heartless murderers even when you see some of their point of view. And the price you pay for your little piece of heaven. Or bread. It will cost you. LOT.
Most important thing about this game though : it really makes you value your own life, everything you have. From food and water to warmth of home and friends. And it makes you value peace.

The human reverses to give way, but alas the overlord now provoked, moves forwords again blocking the human. The human reverses some more, now completely entangled within his own equipment and vehicle. The overlord with his beady, waxy eyes stares at the human, and ruthlessly moves forewords that two precocious feet, again blocking him. They are at an impass. Captor and slave, demigod and mortal, coiled in a steel embace.

What if I told you there was a game, in this world, that possibly gave you the choice to go through either the left door or the right door? How would you react? How would you go on living?
The Stanley Parable is possibly a parody. I'm not sure of anything anymore after playing it all the way through. What I do know is it's short. Like, really short. Like, dangerously not worth full price short.
Am I missing the point here? Did I waste my time? Do I always waste my time? Did I have a choice to waste my time? Did I have any real choice at all? Is the game making fun of me? Am I supposed to be laughing at the game or with the game? Is the game laughing at me? Should I ignore the game lauging at me and just enjoy the five or more possible endings of the game? Is this even a game or just a deconstruction of everything I've ever known, or is the game just laughing at me? All these questions flew through my head while playing it.
Its a type of game for a very specific type of person. If I'm being honest, there was a certain amount of amusement I had gained by listening to the narrator and then doing stuff. Or not doing stuff.
Here's what this all comes down to: did I have fun? I felt that a couple of the story trees were worth some fun, yes. Another one was a brutal deconstruction of the modern lifestyle; and it's not the obvious one, at least from my perspective. Everything else was just kinda... meh.
That's what really sums it up. I like the idea, its just... two hours for meh..? I want to give this more credit, but for $15, I've had more interesting experiences.

Have you ever wanted to get into politics but hate the thought of talking to people and NOT shooting them and running from explosions? No? How about helping a purple bunny in his quests to be mayor? Still No? FINE. Would you like to run through a 2D environment shooting racially generic villains with a variety of foul mouthed characters? Probably? Then why not join BUNNYLORD in his quest for world domina… er, I mean, public office.

In this latest offering from publisher Devolver Digital (Hotline Miami) and developer Roll 7(OlliOlli) we take the role of a “political aide” for the central character BUNNYLORD who sends a varied cast of quirky, violent assassins on increasingly dangerous missions to shoot bad guys (sometimes police), acquire necessary objects (sometimes parrots, sometimes coffee) and get out before getting shot to death. At the end of each level you are rated based on tasks completed, with playable characters being unlocked as you complete tasks on offer.

The style and delivery of the game is reminiscent of other games that came before such as Hotline Miami and Broforce, from the 2D perspective, to the “die and try again”approach to game play, to the pixelated art style that goes well with the humorously violent themes. You start off with a cut scene in which you are told by BUNNYLORD that if he isn’t elected mayor then bad things will happen,illustrated by a picture of an explosion with the word “BAD” written across it.Next you pick the character named Steve, who’s equiped with a pistol and wears a balaclava (which looks like a beard thanks to the 8-bit art style) and speaks in a British accent. Then you are dropped into the first level which acts as the tutorial, complete with large signs explaining the various mechanics such as shooting, sliding, cover, execution and special weaponry. After you finish the level, you receive a ranking and watch BUNNYLORD and your character talk about your performance in a dinner called “Aunt Ruby’s”, during which you have the options to continue with the story, select a new character (if unlocked),select a different level or return to the main menu.

Much like its contemporaries, NOT A HERO mixes the fast, tense game play of games like Hotline Miami and Bro force with a refreshing sense of humour akin to Jazzpunk and Mcpixel. Much like Hotline Miami, the game has a vibrant art style and a reliance on skill, but make no mistake, you will get shot! However, unlike Hotline, one shot isn’t enough to kill you, it’s running out of shots in the open and having to reload that will most likely get you killed, at which point you just start over again until you finish.

The character designs and function do a good job at encouraging different play styles. Steve, for instance, does a good job at acclimatising the player to the mechanics of the game, with his basic pistol and fast reload, whereas Cletus (first unlockable character) encourages players to get up close with his shotgun and either blow enemies back or straight up murder them. It is the quirks and dialogue attached to each character, however, that makes them so hilariously fun to play with, from their little quips when picking them, to the things they say during missions.

Overall, I had a generous amount of fun playing NOT A HERO. Its story is funny and engaging while its level design and game play are great for encouraging trial and error. My only criticism is that the level design can be rather generic with limited variation, but as I said, I still had fun playing this game and I consider it a worthy release by Devolver Digitaland Roll 7. I recommend anyone who enjoys a good 2D run and gun to pick up this title off Steam or GOG. Vote BUNNYLORD.

Tiny and Big is a rock cutting simulation first a 3D platformer second, both in focus and quality. There are some really cool ideas here to be sure, but the inconsistencies between the various elements makes it a rather uneven experience, and one that is over just as quick as it begins.
Diverging from genre tradition, Black Pants Studios doesn't give you many conveniently placed platforms and instead asks you to make your own using a high powered laser to cut a path through the environment. Physics naturally play a role and make finding the perfect point to slice a rock or beam a largely freeform affair. Unfortunately this also works against the game in many ways do to how easy it is to make a small mistake and have to restart the area (which also resets any collectibles you recently picked up, or cutscenes that played out). On the whole there is simply too little direction, and I found myself getting lost or stuck on numerous occasions.
Tiny's unimpressive jump and fickle controls present yet another problem and make navigating the world largely unenjoyable. Movement is jerky and the camera far too slow to compensate, while attempting to cut a rock as it flies through the air (something that happens quite often) typically resulted in me being crushed beneath it as I wrestled to place the cutting line where it needed to be.
Artistically T&B is what I expect the illegitimate offspring of Adventure Time and a Graphic Novel would look like. It's a display of deliberate strangeness and creativity, but unfortunately the muddy textures and poor animations don't do it justice. If the developers got anything right though it is the sound effects, which makes you feel like a boulder lumberjack as the booming crashes threaten to blow out your sub. This was easily the highlight and has me wishing there was simply a mode that allowed me to do nothing but tumble giant rocks, and I daresay would almost make it a game worth playing in and of itself.
With only six levels which take 15-30 minutes to complete, Tiny and Big falls halfway between an extended demo and a full game. A handful of great moments stand out, but given how short the experience is they hardly justify the price. If not for the poor controls I could see myself recommending it anyway, but for now it's a very hard sell.

I remember a news feature on a guy who has been playing a game of Civilization 2 for the past ten years. The world had been reduced to three factions, each in perpetual war and every single turn over a hundred nuclear devices would be produced and detonated. The game was a total stalemate and the planet had been reduced to an uninahibtable ball of dirt.
Beyond Earth proposes the outcome of the end of the world. Beyond Earth picks up right where the science victory (or the nuclear holocaust) has left the planet. The world has suffered a horrible man-made calamity and now the people flee to the stars in order to find a new home. You take control of a sponsored faction. Make planetfall on a planet with an above average sustainability and you begin to colonise.
Beyond Earth essentially is just Civ 5 with a very elaborate reskin, but there is more to it than that. The standard Civ games retell the journey of mankind through the ages. Beyond earth explored the unknown; the final frontier, and with it come some new considerations. For instance, your faction will need to make decisions regarding the local wildlife, refugees from less fotunate factions and most importantly: the local wildlife. Unlike earth, where the occasional barbarian would kidnap your workers, the planet pays host to a remarable menagerie of extra terrestial horrors. From the small wolf beetle to the awe inspiring siege worms; your military's first task will be to control the monsters, before you seek to undo your fellow humans.
Because you're in the future now you'll no longer be inventing things like the wheel or dynamite. We're taking gene splicing and nano technology here. The tech tree has been refurbished into the tech web. Your choice for military R&D might eventually lead you away from sustainability or prosperity or vice versa. You can choose your own technological agenda.
Eventually, you'll have to decide how the human race will proceed. The game introduces an affinity system. You can pursue Purity, Supremacy or Harmony. Each affinity brings its own boons. As purist, you'll maintain humanity the Warhammer way; by shunning any and all foreign and alien influences to your technology or biology. It paves the way for incredible weapons and amazingly polarised world views. Supremacists fuse their bodies and minds with machines. The result is an efficient human race that seeks to remove any and all inefficiencies. Even if that means getting rid of biological components all together. Harmonists seek to use the new world and its bounties to their adavantage and eventually evolve to be at home in the hostile world. Each affinity comes with its own special victory. The purists claim the new world as their own, while the supremasists travel to earth to upgrade the people there. The harmonists transcend humanity as collective hivemind with the planet itself. Each victory requires a vastly different approach to resource and tech management, as well the application of your forces. The supremacists need to sacrifice their troops to subjugate the population on earth, while harmonists will want to keep their assets close to defend their cities before transcendence is achieved.
Naturally, you can still just destroy all your enemies like back in the olden days with military might. Or you can go for a more peaceful solution and attempt to make first contact. The new world is open to any and all options.
The whole newness is what makes this game so different then. It still works the same; turn based, resources, explore, dumb AI who can't value a deal. However, everything is new and looks differently. It is really hard to come to terms with unknown and in the first few games you play you'll be wondering if you're doing it right. In fact, even after a few turns you're wondering why the AI has such a great health record and why your cities are dying from disease and malnourishment. The game also lost a tick in its pace. Somehow it feels slower. Between the many new technologies, you won't notice much of a change until you reach a certain level of affinity. It makes your actions seem useless and it kind of ruins the game as it slips into its fourth quarter. The late game units are a blast to use when you can, simply because of their insane proportions, but it takes too long to get them, and you won't have much time to use them.
All in all, Beyond Earth is very familliar, but at the same time so outlandish and new that you'll feel like you're exploring new worlds. It's a nice change of pace when you're fed up with racing to build pyramids and stonehenge. The aliens allow for a more active use of your military than in regular Civ and that is a nice step up. However, the crash in pace might turn some people away. If you like Civ and sci fi, then this is certainly for you.

The Game’s Actual Name: Ah Final Hallway Thirteen. This isn’t a joke, most of the game is on rails, just hallway after hallway, but that’s what makes it a Final Fantasy Game. Grinding out game experience is something RPG and MMO Fans hold dear to their heart in joy or in anguish.  My first time grinding out EXP in a bunch of hallways was Final Fantasy 5 on the SNES.
The Grind: This FF Game is an Item Grind. Less Character EXP, and more emphasis on improving your Weapon and Accessory Slots. You can totally complete the game without a huge investment in grinding, it’s just much harder to complete. Like and grinding game (and achievement wise) it’s going to take upwards of +100 hours to nab all of these if you’re going for 100% completion. Many guides exist to show you grinding locations. Pro Tip: Search FFXIII Adamantoise Farming in Google for starters and get ready for spamming Death with Vanille. (is this considered a Spoiler?)
Game Mechanics: For those of you who have played all the previous FF Titles, it is a more chaotic, fast paced, and refined version of FFX-2. Now hear me out before you curse me for mentioning that game… Eventually each character can spec into each role, Commando, Ravager, Medic, Synergist, Sentinel, and Saboteur. Each character is better at one role than another and bring their personal flair into it. In battle you set up Paradigms which are a combination of your role across your 2 or 3 active characters.  You can preset a stock of up to 6 different Paradigms. These can be switched freely in battle at any given time, even mid attack animation.  Each Role has a function it carries out.
Character Stats this time around a much more simplified than other Final Fantasy games. You have Strength, Magic, and HP. Strength determines your Physical Damage (Com) and Magic, your Magical Damage (Rav).
Weapons & Accessories: Your Weapon then adds some baseline stats to your overall Strength and Magic Values. Weapons also are part of an Item set that confer bonuses to specific actions or other game mechanics. Accessories augment your character by either raising stats, conferring resistance to elemental attacks, increase HP, and a different variety of things. Guides exist to show the item set each piece belongs to, but that is outside the scope of this Review.
Stagger Bar: Each enemy has a Stagger bar which ones it hits a certain threshold, the enemy is “broken” and damage to it increases at an accelerated rate. In this state some enemies don’t even attack.
Roles:
Commandos are direct damage dealers who cause the stagger bar to deplete at a much slower rate.
Ravagers are magic and weapon imbued magic damage dealers whose main purpose is increasing the progress of the Stagger Bar.
Medics heal and dispel negative effects.
Synergists pass out party buff spells like Protect which reduces incoming physical damage.
Saboteurs dish out magical debuffs to the enemy like Slow and Poison and act as the magic version of the Commando.
Sentinels absorb damage and taunt enemies with Provoke. They are the Tanks and can even Counterattack while Defending.
My 6 Stock of Paradigms are Relentless Assault (Com,Rav,Rav) // Diversity (Com,Rav,Med) // Evened Odds (Sab,Syn,Med) // Smart Bomb (Rav,Rav,Sab) // Solidarity (Com,Sen,Med) // Combat Clinic (Sen,Med,Med) Of course some fights do require to you change up a bit when time is of the essence. Try Tri-Disaster (Rav,Rav,Rav) at 50% stagger bar for Quick Kills.  At the end of the day though, slot in the 6 that fit you best.
Final Thoughts: It has a great story in my opinion with over the top cliché voice acting. For its current price of $16.00 USD I’d say it’s a good buy.
As Always watch gameplay videos before buying!

Crysis is definitely a game that everyone should play at least once, if for no other reason than just how technically amazing it is. This game was such a huge step up from everything that had come before it. For the first time the graphics were pretty much indistinguishable from the real world, at least when it came to the environments. The gameplay is also damn exhilirating at times, with heaps of great setups to get the blood pumping. Despite all of this awesomeness, the plot is totally cliche, and there's just something about it's James-Cameron-crossed-with-Independence-Day-ness that rubs me up the wrong way. Enemy AI is decent from afar, but terrible at close range too, and I found myself just hiding and waiting for the enemy to line up and waltz out into the firing line. All up I'd say that Crysis is an epic first experience, but it's not a game that would really reward repeat playthroughs.

While it's not my favorite FF game, I'd still recommend it to both fans and people that were previously not fans of the series.
Real-time combat with a lot of customization.  Each character can be assigned multiple roles (tank, dps, magic, heal, buff, debuff) and you can really come up with some interesting combinations for any situation.  It's nothing like the old turn based combat the series is known for which is a big positive to some gamers.  I could care less as long as it's fun which it is.
It's extremely linear for most of the game but it does open up for exploration later on.  I personally prefer the old world map exploration but they made up for it with some impressive dungeons and challenging combat.
The characters are memorable and I'd argue that each one is less annoying than Tidus from FFX so that's a huge plus.
I wish there was an option to adjust sound settings (music, voice, sound effects, etc) because I don't like being forced to hear one thing over another if I just want to zone out to the BGM.  That's my biggest complaint.
I'm a Squeenix fanboy but Square Enix has♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off plenty of times so I'm not afraid to call them out when they do something silly.  This is not one of those things in my opinion.  It's a great entry in the series, a great RPG for non-FF fans to play, and it's worth at least a single playthrough (I'm on my 3rd playthrough which will likely be my last).

This game is not happy. It doesn't pretend to be create a shroud of invincibility that your immortal characters stroll through leisurely; perhaps through infinite respawns or just god-like powers and abilities. It's a tale about people living in a bombshelled city during civil war. Most likely, you'll lose characters along the way. You will be faced by times where you need to choose between food, medicine and weapons to defend what little stockpile of resources you have. Do you use your last bit of scavenged fuel on feeding your hungry people, or staving off sub-zero temperatures that will inevitably result in illness. The decisions in this game feel real and they're not arbitrary. There are some moral decisions - mostly about whether or not to help neigbours with various (random?) problems which may or may not come back to help you and carry their own consequences.
That being said, this is one of the most personal games I've ever played. If you're thinking about it or are on the fence about getting this game - get it.

Im leaving my original review in place because its exactly how i felt at that point in time, up until chapter 10 nothing really notable happens. chapters 10-13 are the only interesting ones and even then they are lackluster. also you cannot finsh the story unless you have been following a walkthrough from the first minute or get very lucky as you will be grinding the same mob as there really are only two or three particular different mobs in the end of the game. This is even worse when a player like me really just wants to see the rest of the story and bypasses many enemies on the way through and ends up underleveled in the last chapter of the game. the enemies here spike up in difficulty incredibly, in fact i would say that the trash mobs on the way to the final boss are far harder than the final boss actually is. This is a major problem as it was deliberately made that way so you would have to grind in order to complete the game reguardless of your skill level or the fact that you just want to finish the game and move on.
Speaking of difficulty spikes, this is a major problem throughout the game. Immediately after beating bathandulus the second time (which was a particuarlly annoying fight) the mobs afterwards are easy and then suddenly begin to 1 shot you about 20 minutes in to the next stage. Cheap deaths that require you to turtle hard, buff up and kill trash mobs is not fun and would make sense if they were to give much better rewards, but they dont. as a heads up to anybody looking to finish this game, make sure you level up evenly. I had fun with this title and would recommend it to action rpg fans in general and anyone interested in Lord of the Rings. I got it for a decent price around $8 and it provided me with around 12 hours of gameplay so I think I got my monies worth :)
You pick one of three characters and journey to stop one of Sauron's generals who plans to start war in the northern realms. You can pick a ranger who can dual wield, a lore master (healer mage) or a tanky dwarf. They generally all play the same with a few unique skills attached to each class. Combat consists of mashing the normal attack and hitting the strong attack once enemies are weak to cause critical damage or finish them off. Levels consist of areas where you have to defeat waves of enemies before the next area is unlocked and you pick up gear for your characters and level up.
I played this game solo but I can see the real fun is with playing with friends which I haven't tried, not even sure if it works or not considering this is an older game. Your AI companions can be pretty dumb often getting preoccupied fighting one weak goon while you get swarmed by enemies. You can only switch between the characters at checkpoints which is a shame and only your main characters look will be affected by what they are wearing.
The music and the voice acting are great although some of the dialogue is cliche. You do have some dialogue choices during the story but it doesn't really matter what you pick. The story itself is weak and predictable and when you finally defeat the last boss you instantly find out that the original Fellowship completed their epic journey making your efforts seem kind of pointless.
Overall great game and still playable in 2016. I only wish you can freely swap between characters in battle and setup all your characters with loot and equipment that you find in the game.

This is a sad attempt from Wizards of the Coast to compete against Hearthstone. This is especially sad because I am not a big fan of Hearthstone.

After few hours of playing, I experienced the horror stories myself. The game crashes even though my computer CLEARLY surpasses the minimum requirment. Wizards need to realize that people are willing to pay money for solid, technically competent, fun, digital Magic product. Why won't Wizards take my money? I simply don't know.

Rivals takes the foundation of Super Smash Bros. but makes it better. Don't get me wrong, Smash is amazing, but I feel like it sometimes finds it hard to find a good balance between casual and competitive play. Rivals was built to be a competitive fighting game for tournaments, while still having some fun stuff for casuals.
Here are some major perks about this game:
-All of the stages have a "basic" and "Aether" form. The basic forms have no stage hazards and all of them are tournament legal. Aether stages have hazards and are meant for casual matches. This option is amazing. It is what Smash 4 did with Omega stages but so much better.
-All of the characters are super unique. No two characters feel the same, and all of them feel fresh and new. None feel like they were ripped from Smash or don't feel unique. All of them feel so different from one another and you can't play any two the same way. The cast is also a LOT of fun, no matter who you pick. There is nobody who is boring to play as.
-All of the characters are balanced. All of the characters in this game are extremely well balanced. No character is definitely the best. All of them have their strengths and weaknesses. Plus patches are still being added to balance the cast further.
-It was made for tournament play. There is even a "tournament mode"  setting in the menu for local play for running tournaments. This mode gives you access to how big the sets will be, such as best of 3 and best of 5. It even shows the player's win count at the top in matches.
-The basic techniques from Super Smash Bros. Melee(Wavedashing and dash dancing) are made a lot more accessible, meaning that you spend more time focusing on learning combos and everything else and not having to spend lots of time learning movement options. It also makes you feel a lot more free and fluid in your movements, which feels amazing.
-The online mode is good. Unlike Smash 4, the online mode in Rivals is good. They are even played in sets instead of individual matches, further giving to the competitive vibe of the game. There are ranked matches, where you will fight players depending on your rank, which goes up or down depending on if you win or lose. Exhibition mode is basically unranked matches which pool all of the players together, no matter your rank or skill. There is also friendly matches, where you can play people on your Steam friend list.
-Great training mode. There are tons of options available to you in the training mode that are not available in Smash. For example, you can turn hitboxes and hurtboxes which are really useful for learning more about your character and testing combos out. You can also turn on frame advancing, which freezes time and lets you do movements on certain frames. There are a bunch of other options too, like changing the computer's DI, teching, action, etc, allowing you to practice all types of stuff.
-Fun single player mode. Unlike Smash 4, I found myself coming back to single player mode of Rivals. There are story modes for each of the six original characters, and I found myself coming back to it to try to beat them in the fastest time possible.
-At the time of this review, they are still adding content! This is what I used to love about Smash 4. Rivals is still getting new characters, stages, skins, patch updates, and features! It definitely keeps you invested in the game and excited for what they will announce next!
So, to conclude my review, you should definitely buy this game, especially if you like Smash or other platform fighters. It is a great fighting game and even surpasses Smash in many areas, in my opinion. It's fun to play both competitively and casually, and you will definitely get a lot of fun out of it, no matter what kind of player you are.

I played this game on the 360 when it came out back in 2010. I blazed through it in one night, and revisited the multiplayer once or twice. As a result, I didn't remember much about it. I got into PC gaming a few months ago when I built my first rig, and have really enjoyed it. In the spirit of nostalgia, I bought the Bioshock double pack during an Amazon sale, curious how the games would look on my new machine. So, I embarked on a back-to-back Bioshock playthrough, and I wasn't disappointed. Though the first game is spectacular, and one of my favorites, I found that I enjoyed the sequel far more. I realize this is an unpopular opinion, but bear with me.
The mechanics are far more refined and enjoyable compared to the original game. Allowing the player to wield weapons and plasmids simultaneously in particular really spices up the gameplay. All of the weapons are fun to use, notably the trap ammunition. I also felt that the story was much more engaging, and had me more invested than that of the first game. Though the "WYK" twist is certainly one of the best moments in gaming, it is both the high point, and most memorable story element from the first game. In Bioshock 2, the narrative is woven in a much more consistent manner. Everything you do has purpose, driving you towards your end goal. I didn't get this same feeling in the first game - areas seemed strung together, giving it a more level-based feel.
I could extoll the virtues of this game for many more paragraphs, but the only way to truly appreciate it is with first-hand experience. Don't be deterred by those who paint this game as the cash-in middle child of the franchise. Sure, it didn't inject the series with a bunch of new mechanics, but that's not what the development team set out to do. They did, however, deliver a solid game that is worthy to sit on the shelf (or desktop) beside its more well-received siblings.

I initially gave this game a negative because of the save system (I left the original text below, if you want the details about it), but everything else about the game has made me change my recommendation to a positive because, well, everything else is wonderful.
The developers were trying to create the feeling of the TV series Firefly, or of being Han Solo, and they capture that feeling beautifully. It's hard to put into words, but it all just works. I've constantly found myself making tough decisions, mainly along the lines of "Should I help this merchant/militia out, or leave them to their fates?" or "Is this fight really worth it?" or "Do I really want to investigate this unidentified signal and risk getting into trouble?" I've found myself facing battles with enemies tougher than me that I've escaped from by the skin of my teeth. I've found myself desperately speeding through a blockade, hoping my boosters last long enought to get me into dock before the siegers blow me to bits. That's the Han Solos experience right there.
Surprisingly, the game also has a bit of that Euro Truck Simulator zen travel vibe as well. There are times when my trips are quiet, and I'm just zooming along, enjoying the experience. This doesn't happen often (there's always trouble out there, it seems), but when it does, it's awesome.
I still dislike the save system but, once I adapted my playstyle to account for that, I'm loving it. So, yeah, I recommend this game, even at full price, for people who like the space combat/trading genre.

All planets orbit solar systems, and depending of the type of them you landed into you are going to get different things out of it, with some producing more of an specific resource, other being better for military bases, other being great for civilian and/or echonomic propuses or other just being uncolonizable at all and having a nexus role. Your ships travel between worlds by phase jumping from one to another, and with proper research you can even travel to other solar systems! Or just build superweapons in your planets and bombard the hell out of other solar systems in the other side of the galaxy.
The game gives you a gigantic research tree for you to investigate and invest in which you think is going to be more useful for you at the moment. There is also a real-time market for resources constantly changing shared between all players in a match (which, BTW, can totally boom or crash if someone buys or sells a little bit too much, creating opportunities or fatalities to the rest of the people). This game introduces as well the concept of "culture", that is something like propaganda extending across your Empire having a lot of positive effects to you and negative to your enemies (but be careful, they can do the same to you and culture clashes are terrifying!). Finnaly, creating alliances is incredibly hard because it's not what you think about another player, is what YOUR PEOPLE in the Empire thinks about other player's people, making for a lot of degrees of allieances and a branch of the research tree specially dedicated to that topic; and if everything else fails, you can always make a deal with the Pirates and place a bounty on your enemy's head.
+ Three factions to play with vastly different playstyles (actually six factions, since each one has two variants).
+ Randomly generated maps and preset ones. You are the one choosing!
+ Management of complex real-time military, echonomic, civic, cultural and diplomatic issues ALL AT ONCE. At GALACTIC scale!
+ Gorgeous graphics with very detailed textures. The ships, buildings and planets designs are awesome.
+ Multiple ships for you to choose from, including skycraft, frigates, crusiers, capital ships and titans, each with their own ability set.
- The game's complexity and focus requirement on the player can very well seem overwealming to newcommers, and some very brief tutorials leave you to learn most things the hard way. Don't worry, it's all about playing it once or twice before gitting used to it.
- REALLY LONG matches. The shortest will take you a couple of hours of gameplay, but the longest may have stick to your screen for more than ten hours! It's not as bad when playing singleplayer, since you can always save and continue later, but can be terrible at LAN matches or across the Internet. It's not a problem for me, but I know that for some people it is.
- Lacks a campaing mode. The intro tells you briefly the story and you can always check the instruction manual for the full version, but being all about "skimirshes" certainly does look like something's missing. The variety of maps and victory conditions are big enough for you not to care about it, but it feels weird nontheless.
This game gets a 9.5 out of 10.

This doesn't feel like a full game. Not yet anyway. With DLC or something, like, ya know, free patches and additions, this might become a much more enjoyable game. Till then? This is:
Civ5 Lite, in space.
Don't get me wrong, there is tons to like in this game. The aliens are so much more fun than the barbarians. The orbital units are fun and functional, and there are truly hundreds of ways to PLAY the game! Plus, the affinities add a nice turn away from religion and idiology, if only by combining the two in a new way.
The tech web is mixed... IF it was more linear to certain affinities, it might feel more important. Though, the 'leaf techs' to each main tech IS fun to think about ("Do I get this, or further expand on this? CHOICES!"), it still feels a bit too scattered around.
There need to be more Civs and there is a HUGE desire to have different starting bonuses than the few they have. My biggest issue though? As a Civ fan for a while now, I can not understand WHY you can not turn off time/turn limit victories! ESPECIALLY when playing against the AI and trying to experiment with it... Yeah, why does there have to be a limit to that?! Jeeze Firaxis...
Would I recommend this game? Yes, but only to those who love Sci-fi and/or Civ5. To people who just want to start playing Civ? I'd still tell them to go play Civ5. (though to be fair, Civ5 only feels 'complete' when you have all the DLC so...)

So generally the first couple hours can be filled with fluff and character building which is expected with most RPG's. However, it just seems like this process never stops. After a few days playing maybe 1 hour or so a night, it felt like a chore to turn it on. I'm only roughly 6 hours into it but haven't picked it back up in months.
I can't say the game is bad because it's very different from the traditional FF games. The combat is super fast paced but really not difficult. I find myself just hitting Auto Battle more than anything else and just Switching to Healing Paradigm when my health is low.
Overall, I would still recommend playing this game if your a fan of the series but for me, personally, I just couldn't get through it out of boredom.

Grabbed this game during special discount for around 5 bucks. After all these years, it still packs quite a punch even to high-end rigs (if you record gameplay at high settings that is). Suit-based combat and on the go weapon customization offer unique gameplay value. There are not many weapons, but you can always pick and customize them for your needs, whether it's close or long-range combat alongside heavy weaponry (missile launcher, minigun). Storyline is fairly simple, but fits well into the free-roaming environment and it's not really what your experience should base on the most. The real purpose of the game (at least for me) is finding new and exciting ways to crush enemy defenses. Put your suit to cloak mode and sneak behind enemy lines and steadily pick them one by one using silencer attachments (like myself). Maybe you're up for some action and would rather go full berserk and tear everything apart using speed-armor-strength suit mode combo while throwing grenades and shooting missiles. You have all the time and space on this KPA occupied island to choose your style of combat and get a few hours of enjoyment.
Just make sure you have a missile or two ready for the most annoying chasing choppers in the history of FPS gaming.
Other than that, I don't feel there's really much challenge, but then again, the game is all about improvisation so suit yourself.

I wanted to wait until I had truly completed (all acheivements) the game before posting a review. This was to maximize my exposure to any bugs that might remain in the game.
Texture-wise I would say this game barely distinguishes itself from the original Bioshock, so I can understand those that call it a cash grab considering the minor changes that seem to have been done to it.
It does seem to be more resistant to alt-tabbing than the original. Even with this improvement, the majority of my crashes were because of this (it could tolerate around 10-20 alt-tabbing incidents before crashing). There were only 2 times in both of my runs (first time on normal difficulty, second on survival) that my game truly crashed separately from alt-tabbing. Both of them happened in the same room on the Point Prometheus map (second floor, behind ice covered door). This would only happen if I did not entirely remove the icicles.
An annoying piece of this game is if you try to change the keybindings in the settings (for me it was the weapon aim button). Once you do this the mouse is basically useless in all menus and all button prompts revert to console controller (don't even have one of those so it's not something connected to my computer). You have to restart the game before it goes back to normal.
These downsides, though, are easy to work around as you only need to adjust these settings once (before the patch any crash would reset all settings to default, so thank god for that patch!) or just melt all the ice.
As many have said, if you don't have any version of bioshock you might as well purchase this one when it goes on sale, as it is a bit more robust. I do recommend the game, as I think everyone should experience the story somehow, whether through playing themselves or watching someone play it.

In short, I am recommending this game because it is worth buying when it goes on sale.  I paid $5.  At $15 it is not worth it.  Here is why...
The Good:
Great foundation for a fun sim game.  The variation in difficulty levels allows you to make money faster or slower depending on how involved you want to be in the game.  Downloading and using mods is pretty easy, but not the best system (more on that later).  Mod tools from the dev are in the game files and can be installed so you can mod the game.  It does get a little repetitive, but you can "hire" people to do the mundane tasks for you.
The Bad:
Needs more different kinds of equipment/fruits.  Needs to be in the steam workshop.  Needs better optimization.  Multiplayer needs a little refinement.  Graphics aren't the best.  A bunch of things should be in this game by default instead of relying on mods.  Should have more maps than 3.  This game should be $10 by now.  The game feels like an early access game.
I read a review before I bought the game that said the devs rely to much on modders to finish their half done game.  I thought it was a bit harsh until I played it.  You get 3 maps and a handful of equipment to purchase.  Thankfully, you can download mods and expand your library, but you never know if a mod is going to get wonky and either not work or break your game save.  Installing mods is easy, once you figure it out.  It would be nice if this game had a steam workshop, that would make mods easier to find and install.  There are many things which should be in the game, but you will have to search for a mod get it.  Renting equipment is a perfect example.  When playing online there are frequent stutters and lag issues which are mostly due to poor optimization.  When I look at FS17 and read reviews about it, I am disappointed that they haven't added more stuff or fixed more problems.  This is such a great start to a game, but it is lacking too much stuff.  Especially at the price! The whole time I have been playing this game I cannot stop thinking about all of the things I wish were in the game.  That is the main thing that makes it feel like Early Access.
In case this ends up being read by the devs, here are some things that I would love to be added that would make this good game franchise a great one and also make it worth the price they ask at release (At least in my opinion):
-Cotton
-Cotton strippers, trailers, compactors, stripper/balers, etc...
-Peanuts (and the neccessary equipment)
-Sesame (and the neccessary equipment)
-Fruit trees (apples, oranges, etc) and neccessary equiptment
-Hitch drawn batwing mowers
-Fencing that can be purchased and placed around fields
-More animals and ability to put them in multiple fenced locations
-Ability to interact with animals (feed them cubes/sweet feed, take them to the vet, take them to auction, etc)
-Possibly a game mode with seasons and a more realistic harvest timeline
-RENTAL Function (For the love! How about the ability to rent equipment and land?)
-Rain, snow, drought that affects harvest.
-Insurance to protect against a late freeze or hail storm that will wipe out your crop on the rare occasion.
-Ability to hire the local Farmers Co-Op (I am not sure what it is called everywhere else in the world) to spray/fertilize your field
-Multiplayer mode where you can manage separate farms and have separate bank accounts
I think most of these things, if not all of them, would be a great addition to the game and fairly simple to add to the game.  Some of this stuff is already being done by modders.  If FS19 had this stuff I would pay $40-50 for it when it releases.  If it is like FS17 and adds silly stuff like the ability to strap down your loads and pretty much nothing else of consequence, I will wait 2 years for a christmas sale like I did for this game.
Thanks for reading!  If you are thinking of buying, I hope this helps you know what to expect.  If you are making the game I hope this helps you know what I expect.  Haha.

Oh my, where to begin?
This War of Mine places your small group of survivors in a run down building for the duration of a war that's taking place as a setting in the background. You and your companions are victims of circumstance and don't actually affect the outcome of the war or take part in it, you're merely trying to survive. The game frequently asks you to make difficult decisions in order to survive. To what lengths will you go to keep yourself and your friends alive?
This War of Mine is a bleak game and very moody. If I had to boil the game down to a gameplay description, I'd say that This War of Mine is a resource and risk management game with survival and stealth elements, base building, worker placement, and heavy theme; but it's so much more than that. Every decision you make comes at a cost. Everything you build costs resources and your nightly scavenging excursions can only bring back so much. Do you build a bed for everyone, or do you hot rack and sleep in shifts? Should you trade your medicine since it's worth a LOT, or do you give it to Katia, who is developing a cold that may get worse?
I knew this game had a hold on me the very first time I played it. Winter had set in by about day 30 or so and food had become even more scarce. We had resorted to trapping rats in our patched up house for a meager amount of meat every few days if we were lucky. Pavel, our best and agile scavenger, had been nearly killed while looking for supplies and it made the rest of us sad and scared. We had come to rely on him for bringing back what we needed every night.
This War of Mine starts with a random group of 3-4 survivors (randomized each time you start the game anew) each with different skills and potentially different vices as well. Some of the skills I have seen so far include 'good cook,' 'trained in combat,' and 'runs faster.' Some skills seem more useful than others and some I haven't found a use for yet (if there is one). The vices I have seen so far include 'coffee drinker' and 'smoker.' The vices affect a survivor's mood. This makes each playthrough different and challenging because you might end up with a very difficult spread of skills and vices to manage. The game also starts in a random season (hopefully not winter, good luck with that).
There is no handholding in This War of Mine, nor is there a tutorial. That said, I never felt like I needed one. The UI in TWoM is simple and effective, elegant even. You always know what you can interact with and how. There is a great deal of trial and error here, in a good way.
The game is separated into two phases, the day and the night cycle. During the day, you basically assign tasks to your survivors in real time (and the clock is running during this phase, but I wouldn't say you feel rushed by it; I've always had enough time to complete the goals I set). Maybe you want to build a still to produce liquor for trading (or consuming), or build a bed so you don't have to sleep on the floor. You'll do this in the day phase. Also during the day phase, a traveling trader might stop by to barter with you or a neighbor might come asking for help. You can choose to help or ignore these people. Sometimes people will show up asking to join your group. These are decisions you must weigh carefully, as they will be one more mouth to feed, one more person getting sick that needs medicine, etc. But they might also bring something valuable to the table, that is up to you to determine.
You can build a lot of different things in your shelter and everything you can build can also be upgraded with very few exceptions. Some of the things you can build include rainwater collectors, a radio (that works), a still, an herbal workshop for rolling cigarettes (to feed vices and also to trade), a metalworking table for making weapons and tools, and lots of other things.
When night falls, you are tasked with deciding who gets to sleep (and where), who should stand guard (if anyone), and who will go out to scavenge for supplies (and where). Other survivors can raid your shelter, so if no one stands guard, there's a good chance they will steal some of your things and this should be avoided at all costs as they can run off with a LOT of stuff if given the chance. Even if you have guards, there's always the chance they can be wounded in these raids. When you decide where to scavenge, you're given a set of locations to choose from, each with a description of what you might encounter there so you can come prepared. A bombed out school may indicate you should probably bring a shovel to dig through rubble piles more effectively. A military outpost may have goods for trade, or they may shoot on sight. There's always a risk everywhere you go. Available locations change over time, as well, with new locations opening up, and some closing due to the war or inclement weather. As far as I can tell, these are heavily randomized for the most part as well.
There is combat in the game, including stealth kills and a cover system that I have not experimented with too much yet as I try to avoid combat as much as possible (it's super deadly). Most tools can be used as weapons (crowbars, shovels, axes) and you can also find and repair firearms or trade for them occasionally, but ammunition is rare (but can also be crafted with the right facilities and components). Again though, what are you going to give up to be able to craft your own guns? Heat in the winter? A safe place to sleep?

Introduction:
=========
This War of Mine definitely delivers!
A game where rather than playing as someone on either side of the war (the military or the rebels), you play as a simple group of survivors trying to survive.
A fun, difficult at times, new experience on life during the war. Each character has a unique story, which fits well within the game, and if you survive long enough to make it to the end of the war, you get to find out what happens to each character... But is it positive?
Brief Review:
==========
I have made two runs of the game, and made it through both.
Pros:
-------
-Difficulty Increases; Survivor group dependent.
-Originality; Each playthrough is slightly different. (Locations change, Scenarios change, Seasons change)
-Melee Combat; Number generated, more likely to win if your character is well fed and content
-Graphics; Simple, gritty, and beautiful
-Resonably priced
Cons:
-------
-Easy base raids; You will rarely lose a raid with guns for each of your survivors and 10+ ammo
-Scavenge Combat; If your scavenger is fully equipped, you are pretty much unstoppable
-Sneaking; Sometimes you will be found even though you're making no noise whatsoever.
Thoroughly enjoyed This War of Mine, there is so much potential to replay! Change character group, try different locations for scavenging, and survive many, many a war.
Rating: 8/10
In Depth Review:
=============
After playing the game through a second time, I can safely say I have grown more in love with the game.
My first playthrough the war last a very long time. My base become fully secure, I had 5 survivors, and 10 days before the war ended, I had enough medicine, bandages, food, weapons, and armour that my survivors were well fed and content. We never lost raids, and no one could oppose me while scavenging.
My second playthrough the war was very short, lasting half the time of my first playthrough. However, this playthrough had me getting very angry every night. The war started in winter, for almost half of the war, everyone was sick and wounded, and there was very little I could do about it. I could never gather enough resources. The raids started very early, and got very aggressive even earlier, that is what frustrated me the most. Just as I was finally getting a nice stockpile of resources, they would disappear.
However, the difficulty increase was refreshing and unexpected and made me strive to beat the game!
Both playthroughs had me in different bases, different seasons and some different starting locations. This was perfect, as it created originality in a sense. First I had to replan my base, as this one was completely new to me.
The starting locations were different but familiar. However, even though they were familiar, they had changed ever so slightly. Instead of starting on the left side of a location, I started on the right side of some of them.
Scenarios changed, I went to the supermarket and my first playthrough was the 'drunken military officer' scenario, the second was a 'band of thugs'. This through me off, as I only expected one scenario, so I set up for that particular scenario, however I had to retreat and be left with a very unproductive night of scavenging.
On my first play through I didn't really need the alcohol distiller, so I didn't bother seeing what it did and learning what I needed for it. However, on my second play through, making pure alcohol to make bandages and herbal meds, really was a must.
I will update this section with each playthrough, rewriting things that need rewriting and updating new things.

This game should be called Splinter Cell Absolution.
You spend most of your time sneaking behind cover, subduing enemies, and crawling in vents through linear, segmented levels. The very essence of what makes a Hitman game is lost here. The Instinct system favors improvisation over careful planning, all the more since the maps have been replaced by a useless radar. That and the new disguise system makes blending in incredibly frustrating, so you have to make sure nobody sees you instead of hiding in plain sight like in previous iterations.
Gameplay-wise, this is clearly a waste of potential. If you are a Hitman fan, avoid this game. If you're not, then you'll probably be better off playing Hitman Blood Money anyway.

As somebody who aggressively loved Hitman: Blood Money, hearing that this game was less Hitman and more of a cover-based stealth game, I wasn't too horrified. I mean, Deus Ex Human Revolution was good. And hey, they talk about an end to hive-mind system that bugged me from every stealth game ever made!
What followed is the least enjoyable experience I have ever had playing a video game. This is not the worst game ever made, it's just the most disgustingly large turd on a franchise I so eagerly follow. Anybody who has played a Hitman game and enjoyed it, stay away, and for anybody else who was looking to pick up this game I'd still be wary. Now, let me go on a far-too-long rant on why that is.
For starters, the story is trash. The only reason the story exists is because Agent 47 equips and unequips his emotions as frequently as most people equip and unequip a watch when bathing in 94 different bubble-baths getting dressed between each. Blake Dexter is a complete♥♥♥♥♥♥who sets up a framing job before lighting an entire building on fire. His girlfried/wife/whatever stays with him even though she remains the "voice of reason" throughout the game up until the third-to-last level. Victoria is a character who only exists to be a macguffin whose biggest accomplishment is killing about ten guys with guns before refusing to kill the villain because OH GOD I'M A MONSTER LET ME STARE IN ANGUISH AT MY HANDS. I could write a thesis on how this game's plot is awful, but I digress because Hitman was never about the story anyway and is just filler and justification for the levels.
...and the story is only used to vaguely justify killing some people that the game explicitly states as evil. Multiple times. Even by the mooks that litter the levels. The only exception to the rule that everybody is shown as a monster before you kill them because morals are the horrible fetish nuns. Why are there horrible fetish nuns? And why can't they tell if there's rat poison in their coffee even after looking at the inside and smelling it? Why don't people see the difference between the wrestler they were just training and a bald white guy who looks like he guts domestic animals in his free time? Nitpicky, but stupid how a judge that they refer to on a first name basis is a better disguise than some nameless police officer that nobody cares about unless they see him holding a gun?
And yes, the hive-mind system works in theory. It's just that if somebody is firing a gun at where they think your cover is, regardless of if it's a ♥♥♥♥ing bookshelf against a wall, they get alerted, plug themselves into the ♥♥♥♥ing paramilitary archives, find out what your disguise is and start firing where they think you are. And everybody who sees the two people who saw the first guy go hostile. And everybody who sees the five people who saw the first three go hostile. And soon you have a generic cover-shooter fight with an absurd amount of people that's only exceptional in how bad its aiming is, unless of course you have a sharp object for the game to aim into their neck or if you use Red Dead magical i-just-murdered-everybody-in-three-seconds-o-vision.
The amazing talents behind this game decided to focus their efforts into filling the game with a ridiculous amount of dialogue that, in the long run, is a less charming version of "GET LOST CHUM-LY" whenever you run or get too close to somebody. Or, of course, the game wants to show you how funny it is with such award-winning lines such as "didn't you use to date my sister?" or "heard of breath mints before?" And you'd better believe that you'll get maymay'd on so many times over the course of this game akin to water torture, just with your eardrums and people who cannot believe their eyes every time they see somebody at a light jog.
Praise for this game starts and ends with potentially good levels and easter eggs. Except for the strip club, the multiple levels in Chinatown, the subway of much spinning in place and the fact that they wanted to shoehorn in Kane and Lynch not once, but twice.
Increases in difficulty just put more guards around the place that block different ways to kill your target. Additionally, you lose points with every pacification/kill/walking two inches too far down a hallway/fun. It's like the game developers decided that they wanted to make a game with a lot of ways to kill your targets before poking the player in the ribs every time they don't do an accident kill. This is assuming that you actually have a target in your level. The lack of killing in this game for a game about a contract killer is mindblowing, and when you are killing people it's silhouttes that the game call "evil masterminds" and "story-relevant". The last people you actually kill as a player in the game are three ♥♥♥♥faces that haven't been mentioned in the slightest up until that point, before you take out the main villain in a cutscene in a sequel hook that only made me wonder where Hitman Absolution stopped taking itself seriously and finally downed the bottle of♥♥♥♥♥♥it didn't realise had been sloshing down its throat the whole time.
Playing through this game using only a suit actually introduced challenge and interesting things into this game up until one level that had an un-detectable disguise sitting in the middle of an empty room that was all-but essential for clearing this level with good points. And so, rather than taking out the last target in an interesting and challenging manner, I exploited the person I had to knock unconscious and then lobbed a screwdriver into the other target's skull with unparalleled accuracy from a second-storey window. I then proceeded to get Silent Assassin.
Other greatest hits from the "Silent Assassin's Golden Memories" folder includes grabbing a knife in the middle of a crowd and putting it into my pocket before anybody noticed, weaving my way into one of the billion ♥♥♥♥ing bins in Chinatown and waiting until the target went to sample some sushi before throwing it into HIS skull. Skip forward a few missions to the next mission in Chinatown and I went with the very exhausted option of gunning down all three of my faceless targets, hiding in cover a few metres away from the exit and waiting for two minutes for the police force to drain approximately $6,000,000,000 worth of bullets into a box. When they decided that they'd done a good enough job, they walked forward a few steps, loudly proclaimed "HE'S VANISHED" and walked away from the only exit to Chinatown.
And the cheat meter. Revolutionary to Hitman games is the ability to brainwash people into forgetting about you, detect people/weapons/ways to kill people/secret god damn doors from miles away and take away the only form of challenge with accident kills by telling you where to use a wrench as well as babying you to the point of telling you that a lever right beside electrical equipment emits electricity.
I could go on even longer about how much hellfire and brimstone this game makes me want to explode out into HTML, but I'll just stick to ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ out salt for the next couple of weeks from the discomfort of my own home. If you have standards low enough to ignore 90% of this stuff, or have enough cynical tolerance to happily crap all over the game, then go for your life. To anybody who wants a good stealth experience, Blood Money is always a far, far, far more desireable experience past the tutorial. And to anybody who loves Hitman and is nitpicky, you'd probably also vomit in your mouth when you see the crow suit easter egg.

Great game. This is the first Hitman I have ever played, so I really cannot compare this one with the previous games, but I was expecting a conventional shooter and what I found was a fun, intelligent and slow-paced game. The plot is more or less something we have all seen about a thousand times in action movies, but it works nicely in the game.
As my first time playing a Hitman game, the amount of options available amazed me. It really does make you want to play some of the missions again. I played the game on the professional difficulty, and it was, indeed, very challenging, yet also rewarding.
I wish there was an option to turn the score marker off. I think that is one of the biggest complaints I have. It's just annoying to be reminded that you are making mistakes, and it just makes you want to restart the level... and after restarting about 10 times, you probably get bored and just stop playing for a while. It really can make the game tiresome at some points.  It'd be better if the game didn't encourage you to start all over again all the time.
The style of the interface is beautiful and the game itself is indeed a piece of art, at least as far as its visual aspects and sound are concerned. The gameplay was nice and the controls were intuitive and easy to learn. I didn't quite like the costume system, however... C'mon, it is impossible for every policeman of Chicago to know the whole police department of the city! That really annoyed me a lot. They could have done it in some other way... With the current system, you can simply move in circles around a circular object and no one will 'sound the alarm' (basically because they don't have enough time to stare at you and 'detect' you) but yeah, I don't think that would quite work in real life, haha.
Overall, this is an amazing game. It could've been perfect with just a few small tweaks, but it is still a great game. I enjoyed both the gameplay and the story, as well as the astounding art of the game. 47, you've managed to kill my prejudices towards the Hitman games. Great job!

It's a decent game, there are just some flaws which bring it down. I originally played through basically the entire game on PS3 until a glitch occurred that made it so I was unable to progress past the spider boss regardless of how many times I beat it.
The game is quite a bit of fun on co-op and the combat is simple and satisfying. However, quite possibly the biggest problem with this is that the game forces voice chat upon you. There is no options in-game to disable the voice, make it push-to-talk, or to even mute other players. There is no way to disable the voice in this game without disabling the audio entirely. This wouldn't be a problem if the game chat was half decent, but from my experience it's delayed, echoey, and just overall unpleasant. Apparently there are work arounds for this, but I couldn't manage to figure them out, and really, I shouldn't have to go through that just to do something that should be so simple. Eventually I found the voice chat as part of the game's charm, but I don't really mean that in a good way.
The skill trees offer a basic variation to each of the characters' playstyles without getting unnecessarily complex. Treasure chests and hidden caches give a reason to off the path in search of better gear. There isn't much exploration to do otherwise, though. If you enjoy always getting new gear and improving stats (like me) then you will enjoy the equipment aspect of this game.
Combat can get a bit tedious and there doesn't seem to really be variation in objectives. It's always going to be go here, defend here, open this all whilst holding off waves of orcs and the like. This is kind of to be expected, though. It's not like there was much else that could have been done with this style of game, but in long sessions you may find the game becoming repetitive.
If you have friends to play this with I would recommend it. Maybe not for $20 though. If you don't have friends, well, the AI isn't all that sturdy from my experience, so you'll be doing a lot of reviving.

A truly wonderful space based RTS. The 3 races play very differently from one another and the sub-factions are distinct enough to make you change your style depending on whether you're the Loyalists or Rebels.
The game's pace can be easily adjusted in the pregame options to suit your skill and the AI does a good job of building counters to your units (e.g. you build long range, AI builds corvettes). Having said that, the AI has a greater emphasis on the Artifical as opposed to Intelligence as it essentially attempts to win through attrition.
But such AI strategies are to be expected and, in my opinion, lead to some pretty epic battles. Build a starbase on a key chokepoint and station a fleet there to try and hold the line, if you're playing Hard or higher the AI will be charging your line in no time with capital ships, frigates, corvettes, cruisers and even titans.
The game is also extremely moddable. If you can read this review you can mod a good portion of Sins of a Solar Empire: Rebellion. There are also tonnes of mods already created (Halo, Star Wars, Star Trek, etc.).
Finally, while the game does not have a campaign I personally feel this is no loss. Honestly ask yourself, "Would I play the campaign more than three times?" Probably not unless there was some meaningful reward (which would be difficult to work into the game). As a result, the omission of a four to eight hour campaign is no big loss.
I could go on and on but I'm worried you'll keep reading when you should just go get the game already!
